note: Both speak in the woman's voice after a promise not to part is broken by his leaving: the Kural asks if the believer is at fault; Akananuru 1 asks whether he has forgotten (மறந்தனர் கொல்லோ).
teaches: The Kural turns the broken promise into a question of blame, while the Sangam heroine keeps it a question of memory; the poem shows a woman who will not yet say he broke his word, which the couplet's moral question has already assumed.

note: The couplet says a ruler who does not attend and judge perishes by himself; Saccandan, who gave up rule for pleasure, perishes, but by a minister's treachery, and is mourned as just.
teaches: The epic splits the couplet's single cause: neglect opens the door and another's crime walks through, so the ruin is self-made in the Kural's sense yet not self-inflicted.

gains.a: the lament gains a standard that names the king's own share in his fall, which 290 leaves unsaid
gains.b: the couplet's bare தானே கெடும் gains a mechanism, the trusted minister through whom a neglectful king's ruin actually comes

note: The patikam says the two women vowed not to bathe in the festival water if they lost; here the wager is spelt out: the loser forfeits the water-play and pays crores of gold.
teaches: The patikam's single vow turns out to be one half of a two-part stake, honour and gold, and only the honour half is followed through the story, which shows which loss the poem thinks matters.

note: The god foretold that the king who guards the earth would give Civakan his flawless daughter; the onlookers now say the king will give him the maiden today.
teaches: The prophecy reaches the crowd as gossip: what the god told Civakan privately is now guessed aloud by strangers who do not even know who he is, so the story's foreknowledge passes from the divine to the public before the king has spoken.

note: The Kural's woman says her eyes do not sleep whether he is away or near; Padumai told her eyes not to sleep so she could keep sight of him, and they slept, and he went.
teaches: The couplet's sleepless eyes are the lover's watch against loss; the epic shows the watch failing once, so the eyes are blamed not for their suffering but for the one night they rested.

gains.a: a reason, from the Kural's chapter on the eyes, why the night's sleep is a fault and not a mercy
gains.b: a case where the eyes' vigilance actually lapses and the feared parting happens, which the couplet only fears

note: Kural 916 scorns women who spread a base goodness (புன்னலம் பாரிப்பார்) to all; in 1200 the river, sharing its own goodness to feed the world (தன்னுடைய நலம் பகிர்ந்து உலகம் ஊட்டலின்), is called a courtesan with approval.
teaches: The same act, a நலம் given to everyone, is a mark of baseness in the Kural and of bounty in the epic's simile, which shows that the Kural's contempt lies in the sale of a person and not in the sharing itself.

gains.a: a reminder that the courtesan figure carried moral weight, so the epic's praise of the river is a deliberate reversal and not a neutral image
gains.b: a case where the courtesan's openness is turned to praise once nothing personal is sold, sharpening what exactly the couplet condemns

note: The verse measures a breast's shrinking against a king who will not hear justice; Kural 553 says such a king loses his land day by day.
teaches: The poet treats the sceptre's decline as a stock yardstick to measure the shape of a body, so the epic's court ethic works as common knowledge rather than argument.

gains.a: A known doctrine of the king's loss that makes the simile of shrinking legible without explanation.
gains.b: A sign the couplet's rule was assumed outside moral discourse, used even in description of a woman's body.

note: The Jain epic says the fruit of deed cannot be overcome; Tirumular says a teacher's fire makes deed-seeds that do not sprout into births.
teaches: Set together they show the epic's karma as a debt that must be lived through, against the Tirumanthiram's karma that grace can scorch before it grows.

gains.a: the epic's rule that deed's fruit cannot be beaten meets a rival school that says it can be burned
gains.b: Tirumular's seeds that will not sprout gain the stubborn picture of a fruit that must be eaten, which his claim opposes

note: 2015 sorts meditation into four kinds by their fruit, two bad and two leading to heaven and release; Tirumanthiram 598 gives three objects of meditation, Shakti, the Supreme and Siva as guru.
teaches: The two works sort meditation differently, by moral fruit in the epic and by the divine object in the Saiva text.

gains.a: The fourfold sorting gains named objects, since it never says what is to be fixed upon.
gains.b: The Saiva list gains a test of fruit, that some meditation leads astray as well as upward.

note: 2099 has a king give army and earth to his sons and put off his crown by choice; Naladiyar 21 says even kings under umbrellas have been carried off as dead.
teaches: The same fall of a king from rank that Naladiyar reads as death's work is here done by the king's own hand while alive.

gains.a: The king's laying aside of the crown gets the contrast of what happens to kings who wait to be taken by death.
gains.b: The quatrain gains a king who is not carried off but leaves before he must.

note: Kattiyangaran sinks in grief when the herd is lost; when he hears Civakan has recovered it he is enraged as if a spear were thrust into a sword wound.
teaches: The usurper grieves the loss of his herd and rages at its return, showing that what wounds him is a rival's glory, not the people's loss.

note: Naladiyar 384 praises a wife who knows when to sulk and relents sweetly; Ilakkanai relents only when the birds' scene makes her laugh, and gives the smile as her reward.
teaches: The quatrain's wife relents of her own judgment, while the epic's wife is brought round by a joke at her own expense, so the ideal is softened by what the story shows of how quarrels actually end.

gains.a: Ilakkanai's smile is read as the sweet relenting the quatrain prizes in a wife
gains.b: the quatrain's ideal is given a scene that shows what makes a sulk melt

note: 1666 has the king soothe the frightened woman; 1667 shows him driving off the elephant and adorning her.
teaches: The rescuer is the one who sent the danger, and the comfort completes his ruse.

note: 1649 has the women's girdles and anklets answered by the hill; 1650 has the hill take their lisping and answer it as mockery.
teaches: The echo of metal in 1649 grows into an echo of speech in 1650, which turns the sound from answer into jest.

note: Yugi swore in verse 66 to destroy Ujjain, and in this verse its king gives him two brides.
teaches: The vow of vengeance ends in a marriage gift from the enemy, so the plan to destroy is replaced by a bond of kin.

note: Verse 786 has the moon-hued prince say 'these are yours, see them'; verse 800 repeats the 'see this' as he points to the marutham water.
teaches: The pointing opened at the start of the tour is carried through the whole series up to the farm country.

note: In 899 Suramanjari vowed to hold out until Civakan came beaten and worshipped her anklet-feet; here he is inside her house as a begging old brahmin, singing to bring on the wedding.
teaches: Her condition is met in mockery: he does come to her low and dependent, a supplicant fed at her hands, yet the humbling is a mask he wears to win her, so the vow is kept in form and defeated in substance.

note: The Kural's lover cannot tell whether the woman is a goddess, a peahen or a woman; the Cintamani's kings ask how she is not Rambha and then notice that her eyes blink (இமைக்குங்கண் இவையோ).
teaches: The pair shows the lover's doubt can be settled by a sign: where the couplet leaves the heart reeling among three guesses, the epic supplies the blink that separates a mortal from the unblinking gods and ends the doubt.

gains.a: the kings' remark is seen as the closing move of a set doubt-scene whose first move the Kural states
gains.b: the couplet's unresolved question gains a test of the kind its own three guesses never apply

note: The astrologer sets aside courtesies, waits for the king's sign and speaks; Kural 696 tells a speaker to know the mood, weigh the time and say what is wanted and not disliked.
teaches: The astrologer keeps the Kural's rule of reading the king and timing his speech, but the poet names his aim as showing his learning, a motive the couplet never allows for.

gains.a: The wait for the king's sign is given a stated rule behind it, so it reads as court craft and not mere delay.
gains.b: The couplet's advice is shown in a scene where the speaker has something the king will welcome, and where the speaker's vanity can still sit under a correct manner.

note: The brahmins here claim a fresh-killed buffalo for the rite and eat it as holy; Tirumular names flesh-eaters as vile ones seized by Yama's messengers.
teaches: The two texts judge the same act in opposite voices, one by merit and the other by hell, so the reader sees that the epic leaves the verdict to the story and not to a threat.

gains.a: The brahmins' claim of merit meets a Saiva text that calls the same eating base and punishable.
gains.b: The Tirumanthiram's threat of hell meets a case where the eaters think they earn heaven for the dead.

note: Yugi's deceit is for keeping a sworn vow; the couplet says wealth gained by deceit does not hold.
teaches: Deceit that serves a promise and not wealth is not judged by the couplet, which shows how far its warning reaches.

gains.a: the ruse gets a rule against which to see that its aim is a vow, not gain
gains.b: the couplet gets a case where deceit serves loyalty, which tests whether its warning covers it

note: Naladiyar 16 sets a kid nibbling the leaf garland before it in the fierce ritual ground; verse 59 sets two youths at the place of killing, smiling.
teaches: The kid is glad because it does not know where it stands, while the youths' smile at the same kind of place rests on knowing, so the doomed creature's calm turns from ignorance to composure.

gains.a: the youths' smile is read against a stock image of unknowing gladness and shown to be its opposite
gains.b: the kid's gladness gains a counter-case, one who sees the killing ground and is not shaken

note: Tirumular threatens unending hell to a king who fails to guard cows, women, the virtuous and the holy; Civakan, not a king, binds himself to the same guard on pain of a eunuch's shame.
teaches: Read together, the duty to guard cows, women and the holy passes from the failed king to a private man, and its sanction moves from hell after death to dishonour in this life.

gains.a: the oath gains a measure of what the king himself owed and failed to give, which Civakan supplies
gains.b: Tirumular's rule, framed for the king's office, gains a case where the office fails and the duty is taken up by one who holds no office

note: The king takes the nature of women as a reason to leave; the quatrain says no guard will keep them from fault.
teaches: The quatrain says guards cannot hold women's conduct; the king's answer is not a stronger guard but his own departure.

gains.a: The king's remark on women's nature is given as a general rule that others also hold.
gains.b: The quatrain's counsel of guarding gets a different answer from a husband who has seen guarding fail.

note: Kural 388 gives the title of lord to the king who guards by justice; verse 561 claims the title by a line of kings who never drew reproach.
teaches: A clan's boast of blamelessness is a debt to be repaid in each reign, which the couplet makes clear and the priest's speech blurs.

gains.a: The priest's descent claim gets a test: the line holds only while each king keeps the guarding that the couplet names.
gains.b: The couplet gets a case where the title is claimed through ancestors, and its test then falls on the heir.

note: In 620 the poet says the king destroys in anger without weighing a matter; in 1149 he says he will gather his people and then decide.
teaches: The king who was drawn as acting without thought now says he will consult, but only after his anger has already taken form.

note: Naladiyar 23 sees wedding drums that may be funeral drums by evening; Soolamani 1107 ends the rites with some who leave for the forest and some who go home amazed at the wealth.
teaches: The same festival shows the transience of the day for some and wonder for others, so the Soolamani lets the Naladiyar's lesson be heard only by those who leave.

gains.a: The wedding verse gains a rule of why some depart to the forest, which the verse leaves unsaid.
gains.b: The quatrain gains a scene where its lesson is taken by some and missed by others, which it states only as a rule for the wise.

note: With Asanivegam Civakan only dodged between the tusks and drove the beast away; here he mounts, harnesses and pats the must elephant until it obeys gladly.
teaches: Set side by side, the two elephant scenes show the hero's mastery grown from escaping a beast to commanding and calming one, the step from youthful daring to the skill a king's court rewards.

note: Garuda comes as Tivittan's mount in 1443 and as his weapon in the same shape in 1452.
teaches: The bird changes from a helper that arrives to a weapon that is released, showing it as a power he can both ride and shoot.

note: Verse 249 says what comes like fate takes shape in the counsellors' deliberation; Naladiyar 101 says an old deed seeks out its doer as a calf finds its mother among many cows.
teaches: The epic lets fate arrive through chosen acts of counsel, while the quatrain says the old deed finds its doer whatever he does, so the two differ on how far deliberation shapes what comes.

gains.a: The unavoidable pursuit by an old deed, which the verse softens by placing fate in counsel.
gains.b: A route by which an old deed arrives: through the choices of counsellors.

note: The son kills a buffalo as an offering to the goddess; the father refused to take one life to save his own.
teaches: Setting the son's offering against the father's refusal shows that the king's act in 191 undoes the very standard his father kept at 139.

note: Verse 107 reads the dream as a Vidyadhara king who will come and give a daughter; the letter in 515 gives her as the younger prince's through an envoy, not in person.
teaches: The dream's promise returns as a formal proposal sent by letter, so the prophecy opens a scene of answering and choosing rather than ending in a bare fact.

note: Naladiyar 38 says a small gift grows vast when it reaches worthy hands; the verse says it grows like a hill when the giver's heart melts.
teaches: Both say a small gift grows huge but place the cause differently: the Naladiyar in the worth of the receiver, Sirupanchamoolam in the melted heart of the giver.

note: The minister's hidden guest of 137 is the one he asks a boon of in 138.
teaches: The reader sees that the queen is brought to the minister not by chance but to be asked for her consent to the parting.

note: Civakan swore to join her tomorrow on pain of becoming a king who lets dharma go; her father gives her to him in marriage.
teaches: The oath sworn in secret is kept through the father's public gift, so the secret union is made lawful by the kin rather than by the lovers alone.

note: Tirumanthiram 2030 gives fate's great strength as the sea-girt earth; verse 668 pictures that strength as fate upsetting a city and handing its wealth to others.
teaches: A one-line claim that fate's power is the earth is shown as a scene of one city's wealth passing to another.

gains.a: The verse lacks a general statement that fate's power reaches the whole earth, which would make the loss of one city an instance of that law.
gains.b: The verse of the Tirumanthiram lacks an enactment, which the epic gives in a king reasoning that his own city may be taken and given.

note: Tirumular says the three cities Siva destroyed are the work of the three malas; the Jain hymn gives the destroyer of three guarded forts to the Jina, who rose to the world's summit.
teaches: Both a Saiva and a Jain poet read the three-city myth as the destruction of inner bonds, but they give it to different destroyers, so the pair shows the myth as ground the schools contested and allegorised in rival directions.

gains.a: the hymn's bare epithet gains its source: it is Siva's deed, taken over for the Jina, and the allegorical reading of it was already current
gains.b: Tirumular's correction of 'fools' gains a rival who also refuses the literal myth yet keeps no Siva in it, a sharper opponent than literalism

note: Bhadragiriyar asks when he will cut the sunken root of desire at its base; the epic says Accanandi cut the root of desire (ஆர்வ வேர் அரிந்து) and went on to austerity and release.
teaches: The same image of desire as a root to be cut is a lament of 'when?' in the Siddhar and a finished first step in the Jain epic, where it is only the start of a path that still needs austerity before release.

gains.a: the epic's one-phrase report gains the inner struggle the Siddhar voices, so the reader sees how hard that cutting was meant to be
gains.b: the Siddhar's longing gains a sequel in another tradition: what is said to follow once the root is cut

note: Verse 1024 narrates the youth's heart burning for a woman's body as the natural course of love; Tirumanthiram 204 tells the heart to turn away from such burning.
teaches: What the epic narrates as an unfolding desire, the Siddhar-side verse treats as a trap, so the two disagree about what the heart should do with beauty.

gains.a: The verse lacks any judgment on the burning, which the Tirumanthiram supplies as a warning.
gains.b: The Tirumanthiram lacks the felt scene of a young man wasting with desire, which shows why the warning is needed.

note: Verse 247 makes a king one who acts calmly on what the learned choose and tell him; Kural 638 says the man at the king's side must tell him what is good even if the king knows nothing and spoils wise counsel.
teaches: The epic sets the king's duty to act on counsel beside the minister's duty to give it, where the couplet shows only the minister's duty when the king will not hear.

gains.a: A case where the king refuses counsel and the minister must still speak.
gains.b: A test of kingship: the king's standing comes from acting calmly on the counsel he is given.

note: Both have the wife's side refuse the husband who has been with other women: the Kural's woman will not touch the chest other women's eyes have fed on, the friend of 46 refuses him the door and says 'go, who stops you'.
teaches: The Kural compresses into one refusal what the Sangam poem makes a situation with a hidden buffalo image, a report of a new marriage and a mocking release, so the couplet is the end point of a whole marutham scene.

note: Tirumular's Siva-yoga ends in the Lord's abode, given by Nandi; Somaprabha guards his yoga so that his own deeds end, with no god named.
teaches: The two texts use the word yoga for a discipline of release but one gives the release to the Lord's grace and the other to the ascetic's own guarding, so grace and effort part on the same practice.

gains.a: the epic's yoga is set beside a text where the same practice is a gift of grace, showing what the Jain ascetic does not invoke
gains.b: the Tirumanthiram's grace claim meets a case where the same discipline of release is held up without a god

note: Both use a damaged great building that keeps its function: Naladiyar 147's decayed house still has a dry corner, Pazhamozhi 60's assembly hall stays a hall when cut into. The reading of 60's proverb is uncertain.
teaches: The same image works from two sides: the Naladiyar uses it for what the well-born still do in hardship, Pazhamozhi for how others must still regard the great when their standing is damaged.

note: The younger king's promise that Dhumaketu's match will come is kept in 1325 when Dhumaketu rolls from the field.
teaches: The prediction made in the taunt is fulfilled in a few verses.

claims.gist: a bride's family does not ordinarily offer its daughter unasked
the word of true sages foretells a ruler's future and does not fail
a man dies when the days of his life are used up
austerity and clear knowledge, with the body's passing, lead the mind to the divine seat
the god of gods reached the highest unfailing bliss by his own effort and abides in unceasing qualities
union with a worthy husband is the fruit of rare penance done in a former life
the embrace of a seductive woman who is not what she seems drains a man's life
the blame that lust brings cannot be hidden and spreads through the world
a king's good lies in standing impartial and guarding the world
animal births are graded by number of senses, from one to five
a battle, once joined, becomes a flood of blood, so it must be weighed before it is begun
a woman owes lifelong service to the man who risked himself to save her, as the wage of his labour
the body is foul beneath its perfumes and ornaments
release is taught in the scripture of the Jina under the pindi tree
those who never give what they have gathered leave no fame behind
the gods honour the Tirthankaras at their festivals while remaining in their own forms and world
a king's learned retainers, bound to him by love, give their lives when need comes
deeds that cannot be turned aside drive beings through births, including animal births
the soul is formless and stainless, endowed with knowledge and perception, and is other than the body
karma, though bound fast, is not the soul's own nature

note: Naladiyar 48 mocks those who praise sandal paste and garlands without knowing what the body is; the crowd of 680 calls the sandalled, garlanded dancer a goddess or a daughter of the immortals.
teaches: The epic stages exactly the admiration the Naladiyar scorns and gives it to the whole city without rebuke, so the two works disagree on whether adorned beauty is a fit object of wonder.

gains.a: a Jain didactic verdict against which the crowd's rapture can be weighed, which the narrative itself withholds here
gains.b: a full scene of the praise it condemns, showing how adornment, music and dance build the illusion the quatrain attacks

note: The verse praises the land by festival and wealth only; Kural 738 lists freedom from disease, protection and yield as a land's ornaments.
teaches: The epic shows a land's greatness by its splendour alone, so the reader sees what the Kural's list adds that this praise leaves out.

gains.a: A test of what a land's wealth should rest on, which a bare picture of splendour lacks.
gains.b: A concrete land to which the five ornaments can be held up, where the couplet only names them.

note: The Kural defines தவம் as enduring pain and not harming; 101 gives a king who loses his land and then takes up yoga to end old deeds.
teaches: The verse shows tavam taken up after loss and aimed at ending vinai, which the Kural's definition of endurance and non-harm does not say.

gains.a: the Kural fixes what the sage's austerity must mean, an endurance of pain without harming
gains.b: the couplet gets a worked case in which a man chooses austerity after losing a throne

note: The captor confines her and then tries to break her steadfastness; the Kural says only her own firmness guards a woman.
teaches: Here the confinement works as the couplet says it must: the captor holds her body, yet only her silence and thought of her husband stand in the way, so the guard is inside her.

gains.a: The abducted girl's silence and memory show what the guard inside a woman is made of in practice, which the epic otherwise leaves unnamed.
gains.b: The couplet's claim that confinement guards nothing gets a hard test: she is truly confined, in the house of a king who wants her.

note: Civakan adorns the dancer by the stage rules, tying the band, crowning, setting sandal and jewels; the bride's dresser, who knows every treatise, dresses the bride's hair by the hand-books.
teaches: Both scenes make dressing a learned craft with its manuals, so Lakkanai's toilet is told as an art practised by a master and not as vanity.

note: 1569 has the jester say his belly is full of many modakas; 1570 has him deny eating any.
teaches: His pain is only greed for a feast to come, so the first claim is turned into a joke by the second.

note: 2124 throws away the sword of meditation once the karmic kings are dead; Kural 350 says to cling to the clinging of the one who has none, so as to let clinging go.
teaches: A useful hold, whether the sword or the clinging to the unclinging one, is to be dropped at the end of its work.

gains.a: The throwing away of the sword gives the Kural's paradox of a last clinging a scene in which the tool is dropped and an entry follows.
gains.b: The couplet's holding that lets go gains a picture of the very moment the tool is dropped, and of what comes after, an embrace and a city.

note: Both warn that women and liquor ruin a man; the verse follows the ruin past this life.
teaches: The couplet counts the loss in fortune; the story counts the loss in the next birth, so the harm reaches beyond this life.

gains.a: the brahmin's fall gets a rule that names his company as the mark of a man whom fortune has left
gains.b: the couplet's ruin gets a case in which the cost is a birth as an elephant

note: The sage tells the king that his sons will serve one man; in 81 Vyala meets Naga Kumara and calls himself the small one.
teaches: The prophecy names no master, so Vyala's self-lowering at first sight shows the foretold service beginning as a choice of bearing and not a forced bond.

note: Purananuru 290 tells a king to give toddy to the warrior whose forefathers died for his, because he will shield the king from the spear; the epic's warrior says it is for a day like this that lords keep their men.
teaches: The two show the same exchange of sustenance for service from both ends: the Sangam poet urges the lord to pay in advance, and the epic's warrior, arming, counts himself as that payment falling due.

gains.a: the warrior's brief remark is seen as part of an old covenant between lord and fighter rather than a passing thought
gains.b: the bard's plea to the king is answered by the warrior's own voice accepting the debt

note: Verse 408 has the astrologer say that the marriage will bring the king both rows of the ridge; verse 548 tells that the silver mountain was first given to Nami, a man of Kasi.
teaches: The ridge the astrologer promises is shown to have begun as a gift to a man, which supports Marusi's claim that the Vidyadharas are men.

note: 1998 refuses merit to giving harmful things to evil-doers; 1999 compares such a giver to one who feeds the cruel and asks their service.
teaches: The comparison turns a moral rule about giving into a plain foolishness, so a listener sees harm to the giver and not only a fault.

note: Thazhumban's Unur stands as the measure of wealth in both, here as the region beyond which the lover's noisy departure is likened to Marungur's market, there as the town a girl's beauty is compared to.
teaches: A chieftain's town famous in puram praise was reused by akam poets as a ready scale of plenty, so a patron's fame circulated as a stock of comparison across the two kinds of poem.

note: Saying 8 ranks serving the learned above learning; saying 46 denies the name of learning to what is learnt without submission.
teaches: Across two tens, the book first puts reverence for teachers above learning and then makes it the condition of learning, so reverence moves from the greater good to the thing without which learning does not exist.

note: 445 defines the Lord by the burning of the eightfold seeds; 458 uses the burnt seed that never sprouts to explain why the released soul is never reborn yet remains.
teaches: The same image does two jobs: first it defines what made the Jina Lord, then it answers whether release is extinction, so the seed shows that what is destroyed is karma while the soul persists.

note: 1842 has the king ask for more seed to sow for austerity; 2005 calls the harvest of austerity a wealth that grows in kinds.
teaches: The sage turns the king's idea of sowing into a promise that the austerity crop multiplies, so the vow rests on growth and not only loss.

note: 2000 says gifts made by one who has grasped the true principles raise the giver among the best of the gods; 2047 names who these are: householders who give, avoid wine and flesh and stay true to the beloved.
teaches: 2047 widens the ground of 2000 from giving alone to abstinence and faithfulness, so the householder's whole conduct is what raises him.

note: 2065 says the highest gods have no lord over them and none greater; Tirumanthiram 266 says the ripened see the Lord's feet and the resolute rule his heaven.
teaches: The epic's top heaven stands under no ruling god, while Tirumular's heaven is the Lord's own; the conflict depends on reading கோனிலா as 'with no king above' and on taking 'his heaven' as lordship, not only as place.

gains.a: The claim of no lord over the highest gods meets a rival picture of a heaven that belongs to a Lord and is entered by grace.
gains.b: The Lord's heaven meets a counter-picture where beings of the highest rank answer to no one.

note: 1448 sets brave speech among one's own against facing the foe; Kural 664 says speaking is easy and doing as one has said is hard.
teaches: The epic gives the Kural's remark a speaker and a test: the hilltop boaster must now act, which the next verses show.

gains.a: The rebuke gains a general rule that talk is cheap, so it reads as a measure of action and not only a sneer.
gains.b: The couplet gains a scene where the bragger is made to act within a few verses and his weapons fail.

note: Verse 402 says the lord will take the discus and life of Ashvagriva because of a girl; verse 632 has the astrologer call the youngest Podanam prince a foe of old.
teaches: The same prince is named as the threat from the rival's court that the earlier verse named as the taker of his life.

note: The cause of the queen's longing is given and the means of flight supplied.
teaches: The longing for the sky is explained as the doing of the being in her womb, so the flight is both a cure and a sign of the child's nature.

note: The Neelakesi excuses its flaws with the moon's spot and this poem with the lamp's smoke, both asking the learned to keep the work.
teaches: The lamp is smoky yet bright and the moon spotted yet loved: the two images make the same plea for a work of mixed quality, which shows it was a stock gesture of the Jain poets.

note: The simile of 1557 sets Civakan's leaving beside men who renounce dancer and wife; 27 tells his final renunciation at the feet of the Knower.
teaches: Read together, the narrator's simile for a lover's journey is an early rehearsal of the end the patikam promises, so the hero already leaves his marriages in the manner of a renouncer long before he renounces.

note: Tirumular says one who comes to seize the world for others or himself has the nature of a pouncing tiger; 262 shows Kattiyangaran's seizure: kin chained, wealth given to those who submit, one umbrella over the land.
teaches: The Tirumanthiram names the usurper's nature, and the Cintamani shows his method, buying loyalty and chaining kin, and calls the result a lamp of infamy.

gains.a: the narrator's verdict of blame is seen to match a doctrine of kingship outside the epic
gains.b: the verse's tentative line about seizing the world gains a worked case of usurpation by a minister

note: Kural 1086 says her eyes would not cause him trembling pain if her curved brows would straighten and screen them; in 1482 her brow is a strong bow bent at the middle that beats him.
teaches: In the Kural the brows could be the eyes' restraint if only they were straight; in the epic the bent brow is itself a weapon in league with eye, hair and breast, so the hope of a screen is gone.

gains.a: the idea that the brows might have held the eyes back, which shows what the epic's brow-as-bow has abandoned
gains.b: an extended scene of capture in which the brow joins the eyes as attacker

note: In both works a king's own greying body is held up as the plain proof that youth does not last.
teaches: In the Silappathikaram a sage says the king need not be told since he sees his grey frame, whereas Asokan draws the conclusion himself and acts on it.

note: The Kural says the weak who harm the strong beckon Death with their hand; the city women say the king who seizes Civakan has clapped his hands at Death and will perish with his line.
teaches: The women apply the couplet against the one who holds power, so the 'weak' party is the reigning king and the 'strong' is the bound merchant's son, which makes strength a matter of worth rather than of office.

gains.a: the women's curse is seen to rest on a received rule about provoking the stronger, not on mere anger
gains.b: the couplet is shown to be usable against a king, with the strong one being the person he has in chains

note: 2127 has Death and Desire flee the hero who wins by full knowledge; Tirumanthiram 345 tells of burning Death in the fire of yoga at Kadavur.
teaches: Both texts have Death beaten, but one by a man's own knowledge and the other by a god's fire.

gains.a: Death's defeat, which the Soolamani gives to an ascetic's knowledge, is set against a defeat worked by the Lord.
gains.b: The yoga-fire gains a human counterpart who beats Death without any god, so the Kadavur tale is no longer the only way to beat Death.

note: Kural 216 likens the wealth of a kindly man to a fruit tree ripening in the middle of a town; 119 likens Pari to a lone tree on a long road without shade.
teaches: The Kural puts its tree where everyone can reach it, while 119 puts it where nothing else gives shelter, so the poem adds that a giver's worth is measured by how few others give.

note: 2099 has the king leave wealth, army and earth to his sons; Tirumanthiram 168 says join the true wealth before the elephants, chariots and wealth pass to others.
teaches: Both tell a king to leave his wealth while he lives, but the epic hands it to sons and takes no god, while Tirumular names the one to join.

gains.a: The king's giving of the realm to his sons gets a rival reading, in which the wealth should be exchanged for the lord, not left to heirs.
gains.b: The Tirumanthiram verse gains a case where the same urging is met without a god, by a vow and a handing over to the next generation.

note: Kural 28 says the greatness of those whose word is full shows in their hidden words; 269 says what such ascetics will comes about, even the cloud, and puts this under fate.
teaches: The epic places the ascetic's power in his will and under fate, where the couplet puts it in the word.

gains.a: 269 gains the Kural's claim that greatness is known through the word.
gains.b: Kural 28 gains a kind of proof, rain and destruction at the ascetic's will.

note: Kural 81 says all of a household's keeping of goods is for caring for guests; the epic lists eating with guests as one item among the city's perfumes, gold and beds.
teaches: Where the Kural makes hospitality the purpose that justifies household wealth, the epic sets it inside a catalogue of pleasure, so the duty becomes one ornament of a city that will soon fall.

gains.a: The verse's single mention of guests is shown to carry the one moral justification of wealth in a run otherwise given to luxury.
gains.b: The couplet's rule is seen in a setting where wealth has outgrown the purpose the couplet gives it.

note: The king has the power to strike and the cause, and holds his anger.
teaches: The couplet separates guarding anger where it can take effect from guarding it where it cannot; the king's stand is the first kind, with a sword drawn.

gains.a: The story shows anger held when the means to act are in hand, which is the couplet's hard case.
gains.b: The couplet gets a king for whom guarding anger is a stayed sword, not a mood.

note: Civakan raises a golden image and a dance to the friend who wiped away his trouble, and that friend was once a dog who changed birth; the couplet says the friendship of those who wiped away sorrow is remembered for seven births.
teaches: The Kural's memory across births becomes a literal chain from dog to god, and the epic makes the memory public and material in image and dance where the couplet leaves it in the heart.

gains.a: the couplet's measure that a rescue is owed memory beyond one life, which explains why a gold image is not too much
gains.b: a case where the friendship does cross births and is kept up in public ritual, which the couplet has only as a promise

note: The astrologer read that the princess's destined husband lives in Rajamapuram; Padumukan declares her the chaste bride of Civakan whom no one can take.
teaches: What the horoscope fixed as her allotted portion becomes, once she has chosen, her own karpu, so the fated union is defended in the hall as a matter of the woman's chastity rather than of the stars.

note: Kural 55 makes the chaste wife command the rain; the benediction of 604 asks for rain and for women's unswerving chastity side by side as goods of the realm.
teaches: The pair shows two ways of joining chastity and rain: the couplet gives one wife's karpu power over the sky, while the city's blessing wishes for both as gifts and gives women's chastity no power at all.

gains.a: a sense of how strong a link between chastity and rain the tradition could make, which the benediction leaves unclaimed
gains.b: a civic setting where the couplet's single wife becomes all the women of a city, wished steadfast rather than credited with power

note: The quarrelling pair of swans: in 96 the drake leaves the flock after a quarrel and sits alone like an ascetic; here the drake ends the quarrel and unites with his mate.
teaches: The epic uses the swan's quarrel for opposite ends, the drake's withdrawal as a picture of the yogi's solitude in 96 and the drake's reconciliation as the sight that draws Civakan back into longing here, so the one image holds both the renunciant's and the lover's path.

note: The Kural's lover says all five senses find their objects in one woman; verse 194 gathers sound, scent, sight and touch in Vijayai and calls the joy inexhaustible.
teaches: What the Kural states as the joy of union, with no cost named, the epic puts in a king, and four verses later shows the cost: a man whose senses are all fed from one source slips from guarding the land (198).

gains.a: the sense catalogue is read as a deliberate totality, not ornament, setting up the king's neglect
gains.b: the couplet's praise of complete delight is given a setting, kingship, where that completeness becomes a danger

note: 1485 shows the queens barring desire with the fence of chastity and the lock on the senses; Kural 57 calls a woman's own restraint the best guard.
teaches: The epic's widows guard themselves by their own restraint, which is the kind the Kural prefers to confinement.

gains.a: The widows' act gains a test: it is the self-made guard the couplet praises.
gains.b: The couplet gains a case at the point of greatest loss, after the husband's death, where outside guard has gone.

note: 1581 has the jester say the grove has no guard at all; 1582 has the king answer that many warriors keep the wall, so the two contradict each other on the same grove.
teaches: The dispute is settled only in 1583-1584, where the guards turn out to be the monkeys the jester then calls thieves, so the question of who guards is itself the joke.

note: Naga Kumara's king crowns the young prince and rises to austerity; Udayanan crowns Gomukhan, not the son he has just called.
teaches: In the Naga Kumara story the crown goes down the family line, and here it goes outside it, so Udayanan's renunciation is not a settling of an heir but a handing of the realm to whoever can rule it.

note: The epic says every being from Indra to a monkey eats the fruit of its own deeds, with release by understanding; the Saiva verse says the Lord stands beyond the two deeds and is the seed of the world.
teaches: The two give opposite places to the divine in karma: for the Jain verse no one, however high, stands outside deeds, for the Saiva verse the Lord alone does.

gains.a: The epic verse gains the Saiva claim of a Lord beyond the two deeds, a figure its own teaching of universal karma has no place for
gains.b: The Tirumanthiram gains a direct rival: that the highest being is also bound to eat his deeds, and that knowledge, not the Lord's stance, ends them

note: Tirumanthiram 518 says that if pujas in the First One's temple stop, kings suffer, the rains' bounty falls and theft spreads; the epic says the Jina's shrines everywhere keep the city's wealth from failing.
teaches: A Saiva manual and a Jain epic share the belief that shrines keep a land prosperous, but the Saiva verse ties it to rites that must not lapse while the Jain verse credits only the shrines' presence.

gains.a: The epic's brief claim is set in a wider Tamil belief tying a city's welfare to worship, so it reads as doctrine rather than mere praise.
gains.b: The Saiva warning is shown to be not only sectarian: a Jain text makes the same causal link without the threat of lapse.

note: The mounting arrows of 180 end in the ruin of 181.
teaches: The sky-darkening arrow exchange is the cause of the field's ruin, so 181 reads as the cost of the fight in 180.

claims.gist: those who have done evil suffer endless bodily torture in hell each day
a warrior's name is made to stand by victory over those who hate it
renouncing those who love is not a thing of worth
a ruler may spend freely on an ally who equals him in birth and virtue, and no blame attaches
a servant's fortune rises and falls with his lord's, so loyal service brings fame
dreams are not true and need not be feared
to be born in a good, settled land is hard to gain
the women's renunciation is a great effort like holding up a mountain
the wealth of sweet-smiling sons is sweet to everyone
anger, pride, deceit and greed are the four passions to be destroyed, the last by dispassion
a kindness done in distress can never be fully repaid
the gods are pleased by the blood of a slaughtered animal
Vidyadharas are not a different kind from men, and differ only in their lore
the counsel of the learned flowers through the merit of kings who rule with a straight sceptre
the first lord ordained the five royal lineages together with their conduct and occupations
a king guards the world by the book of justice
wealth that stays with a man hides his virtues and produces anger and pride
the lower hells have forty-nine layers and eighty-four lakh dwellings
deeds compel new action, and the fruit of one deed breeds further deeds
beings keep suffering through births until they reach a refuge that stops the fall
human life is suffering: wants unfulfilled, parting from the loved, loss of youth, old age, contempt
the torments of hell are the ripening of the sufferers' own deeds
deeds ripen in their own way and not as one wishes, so a loss is to be borne as the nature of karma
a learned sage with direct sight can show the fate of the dead
those who kill living beings for food from the sea fall into hell
the Jina's light is the world and the world is contained in his light
the real can be known only by understanding the Lord's feet
embracing this king's chest is the fruit of merit won earlier
worship of the lord's feet clears the sin gathered through earlier births
a service that wins one earth and heaven has no repayment that can match it
those who have gained a great one's friendship do not abandon it

note: Naladiyar 51 uses lamp and darkness to state that sin cannot stand before austerity and returns when good deeds are spent; 343 makes the departure of darkness at sunrise a figure for evil deeds' suffering leaving when old merit comes forward, on the road to a hermitage.
teaches: The quatrain's doctrine becomes the epic's narrative weather: the dawn that ends Vijayai's flight is the merit-and-darkness image itself, placed just before she enters the very austerity the quatrain says sin cannot face.

gains.a: the dawn simile gains a doctrinal warrant, so the reader takes it as a forecast that her turn to tapas will hold off misfortune
gains.b: the quatrain's abstract lamp gains a dated moment in a life, a widow at sunrise on the way to the ascetics, where its rule is seen applied

note: 2052 lists the gods' play, Indra's company and jewelled terraces as heaven's whole stock; Naladiyar 137 asks whether heaven's city is sweeter than the gathering of learned men.
teaches: Naladiyar weighs heaven against the company of the learned and finds it no sweeter; the epic describes the gods' pleasures as only entertainment and ranks them below the teaching of 2067.

gains.a: The gods' amusements get a human measure by which they look modest.
gains.b: The comparison gains a full picture of what heaven's pleasures consist of, so the contrast is not left abstract.

note: In 514 the shipwrecked merchant is reproached for taking wealth as the one thing of worth; in 533 he enters a city where jewels lie in the street because no one wants them.
teaches: The man who lost everything for wealth is led into a place where wealth has no pull, so the description quietly answers the reproach of the wreck.

note: 1965 lists animals killed as offerings to deities among their torments; Kural 259 weighs a thousand oblations against not killing one creature and eating.
teaches: The Kural ranks abstention above sacrifice, and the Soolamani shows from the victim's side what the offering costs.

gains.a: The sacrificed animal gains a ranking: the Kural says the rite is worth less than leaving the animal alone.
gains.b: The Kural gains the victim's side: the epic puts the offered animal among the beasts' sufferings, a cost the couplet leaves unsaid.

note: 1169 says a lowly jackal rising against lions would only be laughed at; Kural 500 says a jackal can kill an unflinching elephant in mud where its feet sink.
teaches: The speaker assumes the lowly cannot beat the great, while the Kural says the ground can let a jackal beat an elephant.

gains.a: The speaker's scorn for the jackal ignores the place of battle, which the Kural makes the deciding thing.
gains.b: The Kural's jackal and elephant have no council that dismisses the jackal, which the epic supplies.

note: 1181 asks which kind of war to fight; 1200 has the prince take the war upon himself.
teaches: The council's question about the kind of war is answered when the prince claims the fight as his own, after the lords' boasts.

note: The Kural says a king with no one to rebuke him perishes though he has no enemy; Saccandan had counsel (சொல்லாறு) and would not hear it.
teaches: The Cintamani's king shows that having rebuking counsellors is not enough, since desire can make a king deaf to them, so the Kural's safeguard fails at the point of hearing rather than of supply.

gains.a: the king's fall is given a named failure of rule, not only a lover's weakness
gains.b: the couplet's guard is shown to need a king who listens, which the couplet takes for granted

note: Dharmadattan names the king's own fault, his woman and his grace among what kills him; the king, consoling his queen, says death and birth come from the fruit of one's deeds.
teaches: The councillor places the cause in faults of this life that the king could have avoided, while the king refers it to deeds in general, so his doctrine of karma softens a blame the earlier verse fixes on him.

note: In 241 Kattiyangaran claims a great deity hostile to the king possesses him and urges the killing; 250 calls that a deity of his own mouth, after 247 has made the king himself the great deity.
teaches: The usurper's appeal to divine compulsion is answered by moving divinity to the king, so the regicide is recast from obedience to a god into an attack on one.

note: In 2094 the princes ask what fault they have done; in 2106 they call their quarrelsome prattle foolish and bow to the lord's grace.
teaches: The sons' first grief as a charge against themselves turns, after the sages' consolation, into acceptance of the king's act as grace.

note: Kural 545 says rain and harvest gather in the land of the king who wields the sceptre by its nature; 2583 says that under Civakan killing and miserliness are banished and the land becomes like Uttarakuru, with fish leaping into the fishers' yards.
teaches: The couplet's rule is carried to its extreme here, where just rule ends killing and scarcity as well as drought, but the epic offers it only as praise, so the couplet's causal claim remains unproved.

gains.a: the Kural's measure by which the praise is read, rain and harvest as the sign of a just sceptre
gains.b: a case where the sign is raised from rain to a golden age, which shows the couplet's limit: it names the sign but not how far a king's rule can reach

note: Kural 1225 asks what good she did to morning and what harm to evening; Ainkurunuru 116 has evening come while they weep, having driven before it a morning like itself.
teaches: The Kural keeps a kind morning against a hostile evening, while the older poem, on one reading, lets the evening swallow the morning too, so the couplet's neat split of the day is a later tidying of a grief that had no safe hour.

note: The epic likens death and birth to putting off a cloth and leaving a house for another; the couplet likens death to sleep and birth to waking.
teaches: The epic's cloth and house are things a person does and leaves, while the Kural's sleep is something that happens to one, so the two images differ on whether the change is in the soul's hands.

gains.a: a figure of death as a daily act with no break in the one who lives on, to calm a frightened girl
gains.b: a purpose beyond mere statement, a comfort spoken at the moment of arrest, where the couplet only describes

note: Yugi falls as if speared (65) and then rises and sets his plan; the couplet's strong in mind who do not give way where things fall apart.
teaches: The couplet's firm elephant is a person who stays upright; Yugi shows the other half, a man who is struck down and then gets up to act.

gains.a: The epic verse gains a measure for Yugi's rising: not stoicism but the strong mind that recovers and acts.
gains.b: The couplet gains a case in which firmness does not mean never falling, since its elephant stands under arrows and Yugi first collapses.

note: In 684 the dancer rejoiced that his hand had touched her hip and that the toil of bearing young breasts was over; in 2598 the ripened love is enjoyed as a harvest.
teaches: The joy in 684 was only a promise made on being touched; 2598 shows what became of it, which is the epic's picture of love as a field worked for a harvest.

note: Verse 944 gives the host's standing by its look: elephants like hills, banners like streams, warriors like tigers; Kural 768 says an army without striking power still gains standing from its martial bearing.
teaches: A host at a wedding is shown by its bearing alone, which is the standing the Kural says an army can have even before it fights.

gains.a: The verse lacks any statement of what such bearing is worth.
gains.b: The couplet lacks a picture of the bearing it names.

note: Kural 292 lets a falsehood stand as truth when it yields good free of fault; Dharan's wreck and his 'no deceit' promise are falsehoods serving his king's purpose of bringing a guardian for the princess.
teaches: The pair tests the couplet's limit: the epic's lie does produce good, but at the cost of a man's real grief for friends he believed drowned, so whether its good is 'free of fault' becomes the question.

gains.a: a measure by which to judge Dharan's staged disaster, which the story itself excuses with laughter in 582
gains.b: a concrete case where the beneficial lie causes real suffering before the benefit arrives, which the couplet's bare rule does not weigh

note: The treasure the king searched for in verse 162 is shown to him in verse 163.
teaches: The king's loss is turned into Urumannuvan's service, so the search sets up the trust that follows.

note: In Puram 19 Death itself runs away ashamed from the field where mothers of old houses weep over their sons; in 2233 the Earth goddess, unable to look at the cruelty, veils herself in a red blanket of blood.
teaches: Both poems make a cosmic power recoil from the field, but the Sangam poem turns the recoil into praise of the king's valour, while the epic gives it to the Earth the hero fights to win, so the prize cannot bear the war waged for her.

gains.a: the conceit gains an older pattern in which a cosmic witness flinching from the slaughter measures its scale
gains.b: the Puram's recoil, used there to praise the victor, is shown able to judge the war instead, when the one who flinches is the land being won

note: Kural 322 makes sharing food the chief of all precepts; Thirikadugam counts living beside those who do not share their food as something that yields no good.
teaches: The couplet praises the sharer; the verse shows the cost of the non-sharer falling on his neighbours, so sharing is a public good of a settlement, not only a private virtue.

note: The epic compares gifts to seed in good and poor soil; the quatrain compares even a small virtuous deed that reaches worthy hands to a banyan seed whose shade makes the sky seem small.
teaches: Both make the recipient decide the harvest, but the epic adds the poor-soil case, where the gift is lost, which the quatrain's banyan does not show.

gains.a: The epic verse gains the quatrain's picture of a tiny gift that grows greatly, which gives the good-soil half its scale
gains.b: The quatrain gains the opposite case, seed in barren soil that yields little, which shows what a gift to the unworthy costs

note: In 1062 the astrologers fix the day and the party sets out for a bride; here the astrologer lays out the days for the elephant-lord and the wedding is carried out on the day named.
teaches: The astrologer's fixing of the day is the Cintamani's regular first step in a royal marriage, and here it gains a royal scale: a hundred and eight dressed elephants and a seven-day city festival.

note: Both poets answer the fear of fault with the moon's spot: the Neelakesi's poet says even the moon is not spotless and he will own a fault, the Soolamani's says the moon's spot does not stop some from worshipping it.
teaches: The Neelakesi's poet takes the blemish on himself, while the Soolamani's poet asks the good to look past it, so one image gives a confession in one work and a plea in the other.

note: 1418 leaves one man burning at the news of defeat; 1419 has Ratna Greevan lift the mountain.
teaches: The news of the defeat is turned into an act, which shows what anger does with grief in the epic's warriors.

note: The city women see Civakan's arrest as the fruit of deeds; the dog beaten at the festival was said to have fallen into the net of strong karma, and Civakan freed it with the five mantras.
teaches: The same karmic explanation covers the beaten dog and the bound hero, but the story has already shown Civakan's own good deed to that dog, so the crowd's 'fruit of deeds' is about to ripen as the god's rescue of him.

note: The king says life would fall apart if harming stopped; the sage answers that even a killing in intent alone sends the killers to hell.
teaches: The pair puts the king's claim that rule needs killing beside the sage's reply that killing costs the killer more than it gives, which neither verse shows alone.

note: In both, the flesh the eater took from another is answered in the eater's own body: the crab-eater's fingers rot, the queen's limbs are cut off for her to eat.
teaches: Together they show the deed answering in kind, once in a diseased human body and once in a hell where the body will not die.

gains.a: The epic shows the same retribution in a hell with a tormentor's speech, where the quatrain gives only a result on earth.
gains.b: The quatrain gains a longer, harsher case in which the eater is made to eat herself, not merely lose a limb.

note: 1946 gives the hell-beings' body size in a measure of bows and cubits; Neelakesi 92 gives the dark hells' beings as five hundred bows.
teaches: Two Jain epics share a table of hell body-sizes, so 1946's hard measures may be read against the Neelakesi's figure.

note: The god foretold the friends would come to him drooping like stars that have lost the moon; they waste at home and set out.
teaches: The friends' wasting like a burnt summer hill is the drooping the god foresaw, so their grief is part of the plan that brings them to him, not a delay in it.

note: Kural 1154 asks whether those who trusted the assuring words of one who was gracious can be at fault if he leaves; Padumai calls Civakan one who walks by grace and speaks dharma, and asks why he shows her no grace.
teaches: The couplet sets the fault on the gap between the lover's word and deed; the epic sharpens it by making the deserter a man praised for grace and dharma, so his own virtue becomes the charge against him.

gains.a: a moral frame in which her reproach is not mere grief but an accusation of broken assurance
gains.b: a deserter whose public virtue is named, so the gap between word and deed is measured against a whole character, not one promise

note: Verse 108 foretells a man who can speak well coming down with a letter; here the Podanam king defines such a man as the voice of the king's body.
teaches: The foretold messenger is received as a part of the other king's body, which the astrologer's foretelling alone does not say.

note: Yugi removes the king's kin to safety, appoints rulers and plans to answer force with guile, which are three of the minister's skills in the couplet: dividing, holding his own side close, bringing back those who left.
teaches: Kural 633 lists a minister's skills as bare terms; this verse shows one minister doing them in order at a moment of loss.

gains.a: The epic verse gains the Kural's name for what Yugi is doing, a set of skills and not one clever act.
gains.b: The couplet gains a minister at work in a defeat, which its three terms give no scene for.

note: The king is set above the love-god among women; Tirumantiram 203 says even those who hold knowledge are infatuated with women who bewilder and cannot change a mind once bewildered.
teaches: The epic's compliment to the king and the Saiva verse's warning describe one hold, and the reader learns the praise is also a statement of how firm that hold is.

gains.a: The praise of the king as the love-god's love-god gains a hint that those who hold such knowledge are no safer than the ignorant.
gains.b: The verse's general warning gains a named king, a court and a chapter just before his own turning away.

note: In 356 the deity hid her land and lineage when commending her to the ascetics; here she herself refuses to tell her clan.
teaches: The concealment first done for her by the deity has become her own habit, so that she withholds her identity even from her son's companions and the recognition must wait on their story.

note: The woman of 2624 would give anything for boiled milk in a golden bowl; in 354 the good women offer milk-nectar in a gold vessel to Vijayai in the ascetic's hermitage, and she will not even look at it.
teaches: The milk in the gold vessel is the same thing wanted by one and refused by the other, so the epic puts the beggar's lack and the nun's refusal on one object to show what renunciation means as a choice.

note: Kovalan frees a Brahmin from a rogue elephant and tames it, and Naga Kumaran subdues a maddened elephant that has been wrecking the city: the same feat of a hero.
teaches: In the Silappathikaram the feat is an act of compassion for one man; in this epic it is a sign of a foretold destiny and a cause of royal suspicion.

note: In 2148 the king laughs at the letter that the wretch is calling Death with his own hand; in 2174 the usurper does not know that Death has come and camped outside.
teaches: The king's jest becomes the narrator's description: the Death the usurper summoned by letter now sits at his gate, and the gifts he sends out are his welcome to it.

note: The rutting elephant is stilled by the vina's song; Tirumular's five elephants are held by the goad of five letters.
teaches: The same picture of a raging elephant brought to rest differs in who tames it, music held by a captive or a mantra held by the self.

gains.a: the elephant's bow reads as a taming of the passions in the bystander's eye, not only a feat of music
gains.b: the inward elephants of the verse get an outward counterpart, a beast whose rage is visible to a city

note: Kural 619 grants that the deity may deny the end but says effort still pays the wage of bodily strain; Pazhamozhi 227 asks what effort can do at all once the deity has settled the end.
teaches: Both start from the same concession, that தெய்வம் can deny the goal, and part over what is left: the Kural keeps a wage for effort, while Pazhamozhi leaves it nothing, so the pair locates the precise point where the two works divide on effort and fate.

note: Kural 230 says death is sweet when giving is out of reach; in Kalittokai 61 the friend says the girl, who would find it better to die than live unable to give to suppliants (ஈதல் இரந்தார்க்கு ஒன்று ஆற்றாது வாழ்தலின் சாதலும் கூடுமாம்), would give him whatever he lacks.
teaches: The friend's offer turns the Kural's maxim into a trap for the household: once the lover presents himself as a suppliant for grace rather than wealth, the giving ethic obliges the girl to yield.

note: The Kural's man laments that his might, feared by enemies in battle, broke before her bright forehead; 161 shows a king whose spear killed kings at the height of his fame just before he meets Vijayai.
teaches: Read with the story that follows, the couplet's lover's hyperbole becomes literal history: the warrior whose strength breaks before a woman is a king, and what breaks is his kingdom.

gains.a: the praise of Saccandan's martial peak gains a known pattern that foretells its undoing by beauty
gains.b: the couplet's complaint gains a case where the broken might is public and political, not only the lover's pride

note: 183 likens Vijayai in her father's palace to Tirumakal on the lotus; 232 has Tirumakal leave Sachchandan without a word, the king left alone.
teaches: The king wins a woman praised as the goddess of fortune and, through his absorption in her, loses the goddess of fortune herself: the epic turns its own epithet into the measure of the cost.

note: Mananigai's eight thousand strikes answer the despondency of Dattai's party in 228.
teaches: The gloom with which Dattai sits defeated in 228 is not lifted by Dattai herself but by a stranger's play, which shows the poem making skill the cause of reversal.

note: Verse 95 sets a fanged beast on the throne gripping an elephant calf as the king's emblem; in 723 the real lion is seized and torn by the prince.
teaches: The royal lion of the throne is an image of power, and this verse puts the prince above the beast the throne imitates.

claims.gist: the Arhat is untouched by praise, yet merits love for the joy he brought the world
sensual pleasure, like a fruit taken and lost, does not last
the one who has shed his deeds has a form like this, radiant as the sun and the opened lotus
the hero's power over rivals is the fruit of his merit
hoarding wealth without householder's giving leads to hell
reviling poets and doing wrong through ignorance leads to hell
sila blunts the intoxication of the senses and thins one's deeds
deeds without number make sharp suffering
hell's suffering falls on those whose own anger and deeds earned it
every being, from Indra to a monkey, eats the fruit of its own deeds
one who knows this is neither elated by the great nor scornful of the humble
youth's beauty fades and the body is not what it seems
wise kings put away anger with mercy and do not show what they desire
a wife who seeks another man while her husband lives comes to suffering
one who deserts a faultless lord, or fails to honour elders, comes to suffering
one trained in the exact science knows what happens far away by thought
the Arhat takes no joy in worship, yet his unreturning state earns love
a warrior's prowess, not his flesh body, is what stands in praise
one who has absorbed the Jina's subtle scripture should not grieve like one without understanding
giving to cruel men is self-destruction, not a gift
everyone born dies, and austerity is the best answer
the sage's teaching of dharma washes away the stain of great sorrow
a destiny formed in the past sprouts and drives a man past every warning
the Arhat has conquered strife and carries no weapon, but even so he is hard to know

note: The Kural says those who reach the Lord's feet swim the sea of births; Civakan's hymn worships the Jina's lotus feet from within that sea and asks that attachment's bonds be untied.
teaches: Set beside the couplet, the hymn names what reaching the feet is supposed to do in a Jain frame: not a crossing given from outside but the loosening of attachment (பசை), so the same image of feet and sea carries a doctrine of release by unbinding.

gains.a: the hymn's sea and feet are placed in the oldest Tamil statement of the image, which shows that the Jain poet is answering a known formula
gains.b: the couplet's unnamed Lord and unexplained swimming gain one school's account of both: the Lord is the Jina and the swimming is the ending of attachment

note: Verse 188 says the god takes no joy in praise yet is loved; Kural 4 says the god without liking or aversion frees those who reach his feet.
teaches: The epic turns the Kural's rule of the one without liking into a devotional posture: love offered without any hope of being pleased.

gains.a: A reason why the worshippers do not need his pleasure, which the verse does not state.
gains.b: A scene of worship that tests the claim that the one without liking cannot be moved by praise.

note: In 1245 the hymn asks who rose to the summit of the worlds and answers that it is the Lord; in 2739 the question is turned on the worshippers, who are those that wear his feet, and the answer is the honour they receive.
teaches: The question-and-answer form that named the Lord in the young Civakan's hymn is now used to name the reward of devotion, so the hymn teaches why one worships and not only whom.

note: Kural 1081: the man seeing her first cannot tell whether she is a goddess, a peahen or a woman; the crowd at the dance names her peacock, swan, golden creeper, lotus goddess or daughter of the gods.
teaches: The couplet's one man's bewilderment becomes a whole audience's at a staged dance, so the doubt about her nature is produced by art and costume, not by a chance meeting.

gains.a: the Kural's frame of first sight, which shows the crowd's guesses as the confusion of love rather than mere compliment
gains.b: a case where the woman's seeming divinity is made by adornment and performance, which the couplet's private encounter does not consider

note: A warrior advancing laughs that men bold among women but trembling in battle have no manliness; Arichandan shames fleeing warriors whose heads women's feet have kicked.
teaches: The same taunt, the lover who yields to women must not yield in war, is spoken by an attacker scorning cowards and by a captain stopping a rout, which shows the epic's measure of martial shame is drawn from love and serves either army.

note: In the Kuruntokai poem the woman prays that even when this life turns into the next he may be her husband; the epic's narrator calls the couple's love one joined through seven births.
teaches: What the akam speaker can only pray for, the epic narrator states as fact, yet ten verses later the hero leaves this bride in the night, so the seven-birth bond in the epic marks the depth of love without securing its continuance.

gains.a: the phrase எழுமையும் இயைந்து is seen as the old wish for a husband across births, which the plot then strains
gains.b: the poem's prayer is set beside a story where love across births is granted and still does not stop separation, which shows why the woman must pray rather than assume

note: Both give the thirsty a false drink: poison pools here, water that turns to pus in the Cintamani.
teaches: Relief that destroys the sufferer is a standing device of the Jain hell, shown with different liquids in each epic.

note: In 1153 the kings wonder whether the king rages at Death or at those who rule through the ages; Naladiyar 21 says even kings under umbrellas on elephants are carried off as dead.
teaches: The courtiers imagine his anger reaching Death himself, the very pride the quatrain says Death gathers in.

gains.a: the epic's courtiers show how far a king's pride can be imagined to extend, to Death himself
gains.b: the quatrain's anonymous fallen kings get a living counterpart whose court takes him to be above their end

note: In 190 king and queen drink each other as nectar and wine; in 199 they drink the flood of love without pause while fortune slips from the king of the moon-white parasol.
teaches: The drinking image moves from mutual delight to unceasing consumption: what was a figure of shared love becomes the measure of the time in which the king's fortune leaks away.

note: 1493 has the father say he reached fatherhood through penance; Kural 70 says the son's help to the father is the question of what penance he did.
teaches: The father in the epic asks the question the couplet puts in others' mouths, so the son's worth is credited back to the father's penance.

gains.a: The father's remark gains a rule that a worthy son is the world's proof of his father's penance.
gains.b: The couplet gains a father who answers it himself, making the saying his own humble claim.

note: The king says no one can turn the ripening of deeds from him; the queen uses the same words to excuse her own deed.
teaches: The same doctrine from a victim and from the poisoner shows karma can be spoken as comfort or as an excuse.

note: In the Vettuva Vari the herds the hunters' brothers brought back from the raid fill the yards of the smith, the drummer and the yazh bards; in the Cintamani the hunters are routed and the herd turns back to the shouting cowherds.
teaches: Held together, the two epics show the one cattle raid from both ends: the Silappathikaram's hunters' seizure feeds a whole village of dependents, while the Cintamani's recovery returns the same kind of herd to its keepers and leaves the raiders faceless.

note: Vijayai dreamt in 223 that the ashoka (பிண்டி) fell and a shoot rose from its foot; in 384 the teacher sits in the shade of an ashoka to tell that shoot of the felled tree.
teaches: The heir learns of his father's fall under the very tree that figured the fall in his mother's dream, so the revelation scene closes the dream's image on its fulfilment.

note: The epic uses the same compound அறவாழி for the lord of dharma ('wheel of dharma' with வேந்தன், king, set against the Kural's reading of the Lord as a sea of virtue).
teaches: The epic's use of ஆழி with a king points to the wheel of dharma rather than the sea as the compound's meaning, which the couplet's other seas set against it leaves open.

gains.a: The epic verse gains the couplet's claim that nothing else can carry one across, which makes devotion the necessary way
gains.b: The couplet gains an early reading of அறவாழி as the king's wheel of dharma, tied to a doctrine of five, six and nine, not left abstract

note: 2907 says a king who takes revenue in measure keeps the treasure flowing; Kural 552 says a sceptred king's asking is like a robber's demand at spear-point.
teaches: The Kural condemns heavy taking as robbery, and the epic gives a prudent reason for lightness: the field that is grazed bare yields nothing.

gains.a: the verse's advice to take in measure gains a moral name for the opposite, robbery under a sceptre
gains.b: the Kural's charge of robbery gains a worldly argument that the grabbing king ruins his own treasury

note: 2846 names knowledge, faith and conduct together as the fire that burns the tree of deeds; 3064 has Civakan cut the eight karmas himself by the firmness of his mind.
teaches: The sermon gives the means of release as three jewels and a fire; the life shows the one quality of mind that does the cutting, so release is both taught and done.

note: Kural 10 says that those who reach the Lord's feet swim the sea of births; 2741 praises the Lord who crossed the sea of karma and makes his praisers lords of the wheel under the three umbrellas.
teaches: The couplet promises crossing the sea of births, while the verse promises kingship to the worshippers of a crosser, so the two disagree about what a follower gains.

gains.a: the verse's reward of sovereignty is set against the couplet's promise of escape from birth, which shows that the hymn's worldly reward is short of the end that the sermon later takes up
gains.b: the couplet's Lord, whom the Kural leaves unnamed, gets a form here, a crosser of karma under three parasols, and a stated fruit for those who praise him

note: Kural 81 says the whole of living at home and guarding one's goods is for feeding guests; Kalittokai 8 ends that living in one's own house, protected by the king and tending guests, is itself wealth.
teaches: The friend turns the Kural's account of what wealth is for into an argument against the wealth journey: if a household already feeds its guests, it already has what wealth exists to buy.

note: The ministers list Udayana's merits to temper the king; the king answers by raging and ordering him seized.
teaches: Telling an angry king a rival's merits does not calm him, it sends the ministers toward a plot.

note: Kural 414 says listening to the learned is a support in one's faltering (ஒற்கத்தின் ஊற்றாந் துணை); 1595 says learning is a companion to the heart in its weakness (மெலிவிற்கோர் துணை) and asks the learned Pavadattan why he grieves.
teaches: The epic applies the Kural's promise to a man of many treatises and shows it failing: his learning does not console him, and he is comforted only when a mantra returns his wife.

gains.a: the authority of a Kural teaching, which makes Civakan's rebuke to the grieving scholar a reasoned one
gains.b: a test case in which the support learning offers is tried against the loss of a wife and found insufficient

note: In 556 the Vidyadhara king asks the merchant to be father and mother to the princess; in 607 the proclamation calls the merchant her father outright.
teaches: The private charge to stand in a parent's place becomes, in the public decree, plain fatherhood, so the trust hides the princess's Vidyadhara birth from the city that will compete for her.

note: The Kural calls it the lowest folly to take what does not last for what lasts; Mokkalan and Neelakesi dispute whether a thing can both last and not last.
teaches: The couplet assumes things fall cleanly into the lasting and the passing, and the debate shows that division itself was contested, the Jain holding one thing lasting in substance and passing in its modes.

note: 1792 has young women's eyes fall on a handsome prince; Naladiyar 102 says beauty, youth, wealth and awe do not last.
teaches: The pull of the prince's looks is shown at full strength by the very verse that the quatrain would call short-lived.

gains.a: The moment of beauty's pull gains the quatrain's reminder that what draws the eye is passing.
gains.b: The quatrain gains a case in which beauty actually moves a whole assembly, so its claim is set against real force.

note: In 106 the friend urges the queen to shut up her restraint and drop the keeper; in 110 she resolves to go to him.
teaches: The friend's refusal gives way within a few verses, so the poem shows restraint offered by an attendant as only as strong as her pity.

note: The patikam's summary joins the shooting of the boar to the killing of the enemy in one line; Govindan's proclamation starts the scene that keeps that pairing.
teaches: Read against the patikam, the bride-contest was never chiefly about a bride: the work announced from its opening that the boar and the death of Civakan's enemy come together.

note: Ainkurunuru 154's woman can only call the town a liar and ask what she can do; in Kuruntokai 34 the friend says the town would not believe their denials (மறுப்பத் தேறலர்) and is silenced only by the sweet news that the lord will marry her.
teaches: Read together they show that in the neythal love story gossip cannot be ended by calling it false, since the town does not believe denials, and the only cure the poets allow is marriage, which turns the lying town into one that rejoices.

note: Kural 221 says giving to the destitute is true giving and the rest a loan with return; 2995 has the king give to those who ask in great want on the eve of leaving.
teaches: The king giving just before he leaves the world where any return could come is the case the couplet's test points to, so the epic shows the rule in its purest form.

gains.a: the farewell gift is shown to be of the kind the Kural calls true giving, with no return possible
gains.b: the Kural's test of no return gets a case where the giver leaves the world in which returns could come

note: Verse 249 says even what comes like fate shows itself within the counsel of counsellors; Kural 620 says those who strive without flagging see even fate's back.
teaches: The epic puts fate and effort together in the council hall and finds that deliberation is where fate takes shape, while the couplet says effort can turn fate back.

gains.a: A place where fate and effort meet: counsel, not only labour, is the effort.
gains.b: A limit on its boast: effort works through counsel, and counsel is the stage on which fate shows.

note: 1594 has the king strike the jester and the jester threaten to tell the queen; 1595 has the king take his hand and promise never to do it again.
teaches: The jester's threat of the queen's knowledge is enough to make the king, lord of the world, give way, which shows who rules in the household.

note: Kural 46 asks what one gains by going outside if the household is led in virtue; the king takes his queens and ministers with him.
teaches: The Kural weighs the household against leaving it, while the king's whole household leaves together, which tests whether renunciation is abandoning dependants.

gains.a: the king's exit gets a standard, that a virtuous household needs no leaving, against which it must justify itself
gains.b: the couplet gets a case in which the household itself, and not one man, chooses the outside way

note: 1088 bathes the groom with water poured from pots; 1091 bathes the bride with mountain water and flowers.
teaches: Both are bathed before the fire but she is bathed by the Vidyadharas from above and he by kings, so the two sides bring different guests.

note: The city women bless the unknown youth with பூமியும் புணர்க, 'may he wed the earth too'; the patikam's verse 26 puts his marriage to his uncle's daughter and the spread of his umbrella and sceptre over the land in one verse.
teaches: The epic pairs bride and kingdom twice, once as a crowd's wedding blessing on a merchant's son who does not know his birth and once as the outcome, so the blessing works as an unwitting prophecy of his recovery of the throne.
