note: Civakan's teacher says those great in knowledge reach the path where hard deeds wear away; after the battle Civakan removes the battlefield's sin by an image of the Jina, a festival and gifts.
teaches: The epic gives the householder prince a route to clearing sin by rite and giving, beside the teacher's route of knowledge that wears deeds away, so the work holds two Jain answers to bad deeds at once and assigns them by station.

note: Both say lust breeds the evil that ends in hell; Manimekalai puts it in an ascetic's sermon on the five things to shun, the Cintamani in the hero's thought about his own wife.
teaches: The Buddhist epic uses the rule to say lust must be renounced and only ascetics manage it, while the Jain epic lets a married hero apply it mid-romance and simply turn his mind, so the same doctrine works there as a householder's brake, not a call to the robe.

note: Verse 23 makes guarding the gate of a wall-less old town painful; 24 makes living in an old town without protection painful.
teaches: The second verse moves the pain from the guard's futile labour to the townsman's daily exposure, so one weakness is felt by both its defenders and its dwellers.

note: The sage's dream-reading promised a son who would bear great austerity and cut off karma; verse 59 shows him grown in learning by the sage's teaching, the first step toward that end.
teaches: The prophecy of renunciation is paired here with a worldly rise, so the story shows the prince's skill as a stage on the way to release and not a rival to it.

note: Dharmadattan warned Kattiyankaran that a king is a fire that burns whoever touches him; Padumukan warns the kings that fire burns when touched.
teaches: The fire that was said to guard the true king now guards his unknown son against the same usurper's tools, so the proverb points at Civakan's royal birth before anyone in the hall knows it.

note: Tirumular has grace come as the guru and end the soul's own doing; in the Cintamani the guru is himself a karma-bound ascetic who goes off to wear down his old deeds by his own penance.
teaches: The two texts set the guru on opposite sides of karma: for Tirumular the guru is the descent of grace that ends one's deeds, while the Cintamani's teacher, having formed his pupil, must still work off his own past by effort.

gains.a: the teacher's departure is seen as a doctrinal statement, release by one's own penance with no grace to end it
gains.b: the Saiva verse's guru as grace gains a clear contrast, a guru who needs release himself, which sharpens what 'guru as grace' claims

note: 1113 lets the pair dissolve in a daze of union; Tirumanthiram 1960 teaches union in which the bindu is kept and infatuation dies.
teaches: The epic gives the surrender that Tirumular's discipline of union is set against, and the Saiva verse asks what the daze costs.

gains.a: The epic verse gets a question it never asks, whether the daze of union is a loss, and a measure by which a yogi would judge it.
gains.b: The Tirumanthiram verse gets the householder's full surrender as the ordinary case its restraint is defined against.

note: The king ends his queen's sulk by praise and an embrace, which is what the couplet urges for a sulker.
teaches: The couplet says not to leave the sulker unembraced, while the scene adds that he first praises her beauty and wins her mind.

gains.a: the verse gains a rule that makes the embrace more than lust, an answer owed to someone already hurt
gains.b: the couplet gains a concrete order of acts: praise first, then the embrace, with a king as the one who must yield

note: The maiden-city built in 899 is where the maiden lands in 900.
teaches: The city is built before she arrives, so her descent into it is a planned reception and not a stray landing.

note: Kural 445 calls counsellors a ruler's eyes; verse 234 pictures a king opening like a lotus by the sun only through the learned who consider.
teaches: The epic gives a picture of how counsel acts, a bloom that opens only at the sun's touch, where the Kural gives a rule that counsel should be taken.

gains.a: A plain rule that counsel is to be taken, behind its picture of the lotus.
gains.b: A figure that shows kingship as a bloom needing the light of the learned.

note: 1251 reports the broken army to the proud king; 1255 gives the king's answer, a laugh.
teaches: The king's laugh meets news of ruin with a boast, making defeat into proof of the foe's single-handed skill.

note: The couplet ranks the strength of those who relieve hunger above that of those who endure it; the ascetic's endurance fails and a child's feeding saves him.
teaches: The epic stages the couplet's ranking as one scene: the ascetic's strength to bear hunger breaks, and the boy's strength to relieve it restores him and gives Civakan his teacher.

gains.a: the meal gains a moral rank: the boy's act stands above the ascetic's vow, not merely beside it
gains.b: the couplet gains a case in which the endurer is himself rescued by the reliever, so the ranking is shown to be needed, not only stated

claims.gist: those in hell entered it through their own earlier deeds and cannot be rescued
austerity ends the birth of woman and brings a man's state in heaven
full knowledge (kevala) sees the true thing and conquers Death and Desire
a king's lost rule is recovered only if he is drawn out of his pleasure by stratagem
the intent to kill, even where no life is taken, bears the fruit of killing
those who kill without pity for life go to hell
one who lets go of attachment and the fear of death and takes the Lord's five padas reaches a good state after death
Vidyadharas are greater than men of the earth
a woman's love, once openly given, should not be left unanswered by the king
the stench of hell kills other living beings within a yojana around it
a gift to the unrestrained is rewarded by birth with a strange body on a sea-island
even Indra-like lords of the gods lose their forms and die
right knowledge is knowing what is real
right faith is clear seeing of it
right conduct is holding both firmly within, free of the two bonds
whatever rises falls and whoever is joined parts
those born die and the dead are born again through countless kinds of birth
one should think of austerity and not rely on riches
lust for another man's wife brings heavy suffering, so desire must be put down
when good deeds of the past come to fruit, the suffering due to evil deeds departs
life lived on pleasure alone has no worth once death comes

note: Verse 9 calls lust for women not one's own what fools love; verse 19 says the man at another's door by night hangs by a thread.
teaches: Within the book the same act is first a fool's desire and then a mortal danger, so the book judges it both by the wanting and by the result.

note: Verse 10 has the sword-eyed mother keep a vow that her son may live; in verse 23 the grown son, with brother and friends, comes to bow before her.
teaches: The mother's austerity, kept apart from her son, is answered when he returns alive to bow to her, and the patikam places that homecoming just before he turns to win back the kingdom she lost.

note: Verse 845 shows Arkakirti standing proudly on his elephant at the head of a host; verse 962 shows him folding his hands to the Podanam king.
teaches: The warlord of one scene is shown as a bowing guest in the next, so his pride is placed beneath his courtesy.

note: 53 says the only weapon abroad in his reign was Kama's arrows; 66 shows the same flower-arrowed god working inside the palace to join the king and the two queens.
teaches: The praise of a bloodless reign leads to the place where Kama's arrows land, showing the opening claim as the first note of the palace's own story.

note: Kural 263 asks whether others, wanting to provide for renouncers, have forgotten their own penance; the proclamation in 605 bids people give to ascetics and also strive at hard penance themselves.
teaches: The epic's decree answers the couplet's chiding question by refusing the division of labour it criticises: giving to ascetics and doing penance are both laid on every listener.

gains.a: a sharp statement of the danger its double command guards against, that support for ascetics could stand in for one's own penance
gains.b: a public, Jain-framed instance where the couplet's implied rule, that penance is not only for renouncers, is proclaimed to a whole city

note: Verse 49 puts the பத்தினி among the old courtesan's models; verse 57 explains that model as serving in every way those who give matching wealth.
teaches: Only the gloss in 57 shows why a chaste wife stands in a list of rivers, lutes and beasts: her devotion is taken over as a technique that lasts exactly as long as the payment.

note: Kural 904 says the man who fears his wife gains no distinction from his deeds; Kattiyangaran's self-curse is that if he loses in valour he may become a base man who fears his wife (இல்லாளை அஞ்சி) and slights a guest.
teaches: The vow ranks fear of one's wife as a disgrace equal to defeat in battle, which shows the couplet's household fault serving as a warrior's measure of shame, the worst a king can wish on himself.

gains.a: the oath's odd household content is explained: it names a vice the moral tradition already marks as ruin of a man's action
gains.b: the couplet's fault is seen weighed against cowardice in war, which places it among the gravest failures of manhood

note: Siddhar 301 also strips the body to wind, bile and phlegm and foul matter, but the poet confesses he still runs after women and begs the Lord's grace to free him; Civakan recites the catalogue and simply refuses.
teaches: The same catalogue that the Saiva poet finds powerless without grace is, in the Jain epic, enough by itself to master desire, which shows the two traditions disagreeing about whether self-knowledge alone can free a man from lust.

gains.a: a contrast that brings out how self-reliant Civakan's restraint is: no god is asked for help
gains.b: a case where the catalogue works without grace, which makes the Siddhar's plea a claim about his tradition and not a fact about the body

note: Naladiyar 370 makes the fresh flood (புதுப்புனல்) a type of what does not last: it ends when the rain ends; Paripadal 7.84-86 prays to the Vaiyai's flood that the bathing in it may never be left (நின் படிந்து நீங்காமை).
teaches: The same new flood that the ethical quatrain uses to prove that pleasures and loves dry up is, in the festival hymn, the object of a prayer for permanence, so the pair shows the didactic poet reversing the devotional value of the river by fixing on its ending rather than its yearly return.

note: Kural 448 says a king without rebukers perishes even with no enemy; the king hears Rudradattan's rebuke, rejects it, and the counsellor withdraws.
teaches: The epic shows the middle case the couplet skips, a king who has a rebuker and sends him away, and its ruin comes through the trusted man, so the danger lies in refusing rebuke as much as in lacking it.

gains.a: the counsellor's failure is given the weight of a known rule of kingship
gains.b: the couplet's 'having no rebuker' is shown to include a king who drives rebuke off

note: Kural 586 sends the spy into closed places in the guise of renunciants, undiscovered whatever is done to him; Civakan enters a house closed to men in the guise of an old Brahmin and holds his part under the women's threats (2014-2015).
teaches: The statecraft couplet's method, borrowing a status no one guards against, is shown working in love, and its clause 'whatever is done to him' is tested when armed women surround the disguised man and he keeps silent.

gains.a: the trickster scene gains a named technique, the spy's guise of the harmless, which explains why the Brahmin disguise works where force could not
gains.b: the couplet gains a demonstration of the guise's real lever, the protector's scruple, since the women spare him because harming a Brahmin is sin (2016)

note: The friend says she once foretold a cruel trouble from a fanged snake; 1271 tells how a snake living in the grove bit the princess.
teaches: Her old warning, proved by the snakebite that brought Civakan to Padumai, is what gives her new omen of his return its weight.

note: Both warn men against women's smiles.
teaches: Tirumular's etti fruit says only that the smile is poison under a fair surface; the Jain sermon says what the poison does, endless rebirth in states of sorrow, and in 1555 offers heaven to those who refuse it.

gains.a: the epic gains Tirumular's image of fair leaves over a poisoned fruit, which explains why a smile should be distrusted
gains.b: Tirumanthiram 204 gains the karmic consequence it does not state, in the Jain terms of the gatis

note: 2124 has the liberated one embrace the maiden called முடிவு; Cintamani 3117 has the king embrace the maiden Kevala with unblinking eyes.
teaches: Both Jain epics speak of release as a bride, but the Soolamani's bride is the end of birth and the Cintamani's is knowledge.

note: 1153 asks what is the root of the king's anger; 1156 has the people stop guessing and fall silent.
teaches: The frightened crowd moves from asking the cause to waiting without words, so the dread grows as the cause stays unknown.

note: At 216 Saccandan drinks unwearied the nectar of Vijayai and his fall begins; at 491-492 Padumukan drinks Govindai's nectar and loses all awareness in unguarded pleasure.
teaches: The poet gives the bridegroom the very image of the king whose drinking cost him his kingdom, so the epic's warning about pleasure lies under even its happiest wedding, though the narrator blames no one here.

note: The Naladiyar calls those who prattle of astrology the greatest fools; in the epic the astrologer's verdict of death fails while a bird omen of rescue comes true.
teaches: The Jain epic does not dismiss divination wholesale as the quatrain does: it splits it, letting the star-reader's verdict be overturned while an omen pointing to a rescuer is fulfilled, so the scorn of the quatrain falls on fatalistic forecasting rather than on every sign.

gains.a: the omen and the astrologer gain a measure: the epic's tradition holds such readings in suspicion, which makes the success of the one and the failure of the other a pointed choice
gains.b: the quatrain's blanket scorn gains a narrative in which signs are tested against outcome, showing which kind of foretelling the scorn fits

note: 1824 says the herald's showing was needless because her lot of enjoyment had already ripened; Kural 380 asks what is stronger than fate, which reaches first even when one tries another way.
teaches: A choice that looks free and quick is shown to have been set before the guide's words, which a bare general rule about fate does not show.

gains.a: The verse gains a general rule that fate comes before any human device, which would otherwise be only an aside about her lot.
gains.b: The couplet gains a scene in which a formal, careful introduction is overtaken by fate in a glance.

note: The king's question in verse 342 about his love for the elephant is answered by a past birth in verse 346.
teaches: The king's love for the elephant is answered by a birth he cannot recall, not by anything in the elephant.

note: The Siddhar asks when darkness will leave births as grass, beast and worm; the verse shows one man made a beast.
teaches: The Siddhar names the beast-births without saying why; the verse supplies a cause in a life of drink and lust.

gains.a: the elephant's rebirth gets the Siddhar's longing to escape every such birth
gains.b: the Siddhar's list of births gets a case with a stated cause

note: 1721 has Tivittan show jewels and gold to his guests and invite them to take them; 1737 has him give a share of his treasure to the Vidyadhara messenger.
teaches: The giving at the son's birth and at the nephew's news both follow the same open-handedness, so Tivittan is drawn as a king whose joy is shown by giving.

note: In 1132 Gunamalai, near death with grief, clung to the sage's words as a raft; in 2099 Civakan says he survived by her penance.
teaches: The grief that the narrator showed Gunamalai surviving by holding to a prophecy is renamed by the hero as தவம், so her endurance becomes the cause of his rescue rather than only her consolation.

note: 2125 has the freed soul swallow the world and non-world together once the coverings are gone; Cintamani 3082 has the hero swallow the three worlds and the world of non-world after the four enemy kings fall.
teaches: The same formula for omniscience appears in both Jain epics, and only the Soolamani names the removal of coverings as its cause.

note: Kural 539 bids one swollen with joy think of those ruined by negligence; verse 619 shows Acuvakanthan so swollen.
teaches: The couplet's advice is the thing Acuvakanthan does not heed, so the story reads as its example.

gains.a: The verse lacks the explicit warning that joy breeds negligence, which the couplet states.
gains.b: The couplet lacks a named man to stand for the ruined, which the verse supplies.

note: Kural 1274 says something lies within the bud of the girl's smile like scent within a bud; in 1004 the friend reads the bride's silent smile and gives it words.
teaches: The couplet's hidden meaning in a smile is shown here as read and spoken for her by a friend, which makes private signal into public courtesy.

gains.a: The verse lacks the couplet's picture of a smile whose meaning is real but unseen, as scent is in a closed bud.
gains.b: The couplet lacks the case where the smile is read aloud by a third person who then acts on what it says.

note: Kural 773 calls help to a foe in trouble the cutting edge of valour; 783 has the companions cripple a chariot and then bid its charioteer yoke fresh horses.
teaches: The epic turns the couplet's ஊராண்மை into a battlefield move: the generosity is not mercy that ends the fight but an invitation to go on fighting on equal terms.

gains.a: a concept that makes the companions' strange order a recognised height of valour rather than a jest
gains.b: a concrete act that shows what the help to a stricken foe looks like in a chariot fight

note: Kural 1067 begs the beggars not to beg of those who conceal; verse 784 likens a deer's thirst to a high-born man who begged from a low man's eyes and earned blame.
teaches: The verse makes the cost of begging of the wrong person a stain on rank, where the couplet gives only a warning.

gains.a: The simile lacks the Kural's rule that the fault lies in begging of those who conceal, which names why the noble is blamed.
gains.b: The couplet lacks the sense that the shame falls harder on the high-born, which the verse's noble adds.

note: Both make a recited formula the agent of a change of state: Tirumular's சிவாயநம is an alchemist's pill that turns the body's cage to gold; the Cintamani's five padas are water that washes off black karma and bring a new god's body after death.
teaches: Set side by side, the two mantras do different work: the Saiva syllables transmute the body the devotee already has through the Lord's act, while the Jain padas clear karma so that a better body follows in the next birth, with no Lord who acts.

gains.a: a Saiva counterpart in which the mantra changes this body rather than the next, which shows that 951's change comes only with death and a new birth
gains.b: a case in which the mantra works on one who cannot melt or contemplate, a dying animal, so that devotion of the mind is not what gives the formula its force

note: Kural 269 says that those who attain the power of austerity can even leap past death; here the ascetic's words, remembered, keep the stricken merchant alive.
teaches: The Kural places the power of tapas in the ascetic's own victory over death, while the epic shows it working on householders, through a foretelling whose remembered word revives a father who stood as if dead.

gains.a: a name for the force that holds up the merchant: the power of penance, here exercised through speech
gains.b: a story in which that power reaches beyond the ascetic to the lay people who fed him

note: The Naladiyar says the noble cannot bear one stain as the moon bears its spot; the poet asks that one smoky flaw not make the lamp be thrown away.
teaches: The ethics book sets the noble above forgiveness of their stain, while the poet, claiming no such standard, pleads that a stained thing still be kept.

gains.a: the poet's plea is seen to relax the Naladiyar's strict standard of stainlessness
gains.b: the quatrain's rule is shown to be a standard for character, which a poem may leave aside

note: Kural 381 counts an army first among a king's six limbs, while verse 838 raises the host as a marriage escort, in the likeness of a sea swallowing the world.
teaches: The pair shows an army used for display and escort, a use the couplet's list of royal strengths does not name.

gains.a: The verse lacks the couplet's view that an army is a standing limb of rule, not raised for a single occasion.
gains.b: The couplet lacks the case of a host raised for a wedding, where numbers show a king's worth to his allies.

note: 2079 has the king's own ministers urge him to give up the crown for the austerity that ends the disease of birth; Naladiyar 53 says the best people, seeing that home, youth, wealth and strength do not last, renounce them without delay.
teaches: Naladiyar 53 describes a person giving up a house and wealth, but 2079 shows the same renunciation asked of a king, where the crown and a kingdom's charge must be laid down.

gains.a: The ministers' plea gets a general rule, that the wise renounce on seeing that things do not last, to rest on.
gains.b: The quatrain gets a case in which what is given up is a kingdom and its cost to others, which a householder's renunciation does not show.

note: 2796 says taking and guarding the earth is pain for kings; 27 says Civakan, fearing kingship like a snake struck by thunder, renounces after hearing dharma.
teaches: The hero's renunciation is the answer to this teaching, so the reader sees what the teacher's argument was meant to do to him.

note: 1752 likens the returning balls to lovers who will not be held off; Thiruppugazh 586 asks Murugan not to let the poet waste away over women whose palms ache from ball-play.
teaches: One text enjoys ball-play as courtship, and the other treats the same game as the snare from which a devotee asks to be freed.

gains.a: The epic's lively ball-play gains the devotee's view that this very beauty is what he must be saved from.
gains.b: The Thiruppugazh's brief mention of ball-playing women gains a full scene of what the game is, with its clinging balls and flying powder.

note: Maruci's report in 901 draws the king's reply to him in 906.
teaches: The envoy's report wins a lodging and a reply, so the envoy's word is what sets the king's preparations moving.

note: 1663 names the rutting elephant with a spread face-cloth; Kural 1087 likens the cloth on a woman's breast to the face-cloth over a rutting elephant's eyes.
teaches: The same elephant's face-cloth marks erotic danger in a couplet and is used as a stage prop to scare women into a man's arms in the epic.

gains.a: 1663 gets the face-cloth read as the sign of a threat that is also desire, so the elephant's fright is a love-device.
gains.b: Kural 1087 gets a scene where such an elephant is actually set before women, showing the image as a danger they flee, not only as a metaphor.

note: In 409 the speaker says within a month Tivittan will split a lion's mouth; in 707 he swears to split the lion's mouth, on the minister's bait.
teaches: The enemy's trap supplies the occasion on which the earlier sign is to be met.

note: 326 likens the young woman's unerring eyes to the spear raised by Pazhaiyan, lord of Por and the Cholas' champion; 44 recalls the battle in which Pazhaiyan fell (பழையன் பட்டென) and Chenni avenged him.
teaches: Akam poets drew on both halves of one champion's story, his unfailing aim for a woman's dangerous eyes and his death for the scale of a war that keeps a husband from home, so the hero's fame served love poetry whole.

note: 1482 has the women's tears put out the victor's wrath like water on fire; Kural 555 says the tears of the afflicted wear away a king's wealth.
teaches: Tears are a force against a king in both, but the epic turns them to a mercy that ends the fire while the Kural makes them a loss that grows.

gains.a: The scene gains a rule: the victor is shown ruled by the weeping, as the couplet says a king should dread.
gains.b: The couplet gains a case where the tears act at once and quench, not only wear away over time.

note: The couplet defines penance as bearing the pain that comes; the ascetic's penance gives way under the hunger-fire and he goes to the city to eat.
teaches: The epic marks a limit to the couplet's definition: there are pains, sent by past deeds, that a penitent cannot bear, and his penance has to be suspended and later resumed.

gains.a: the ascetic's lapse is measured against a standard, so his leaving the vow reads as failure under pain rather than mere misfortune
gains.b: the definition gains a case where the pain that comes is beyond bearing, raising what penance does then

note: The Kural calls craving the seed that yields unceasing birth; the friend's tree has ignorance as its seed and desire as its root.
teaches: Put beside the couplet, the verse shows a different order of causes: craving is not the first cause but what anchors the tree once ignorance has sown it, so cutting desire alone would not uproot it.

gains.a: a known single-cause maxim against which its own order of seed and root stands out
gains.b: an account of what lies behind craving, which the couplet leaves unasked

note: Pattinathar asks how many mothers, wives, children and births he has had and has yet to have, and cries to the lord of Ekambam; Saccandan reckons births past the sands of the shore and tells his wife kinship lasts two days.
teaches: The same reckoning of countless births and passing kin brings the Siddhar to despair and a cry for Siva's help, and brings the Jain king to composure with no god, so the argument's outcome turns on where release is placed.

gains.a: the king's consolation is shown to be the renouncer's argument, turned to comfort a wife at a parting rather than to leave the world
gains.b: the Siddhar's anguished count gains a reader who draws calm from it through scripture, the answer his song looks for only in the Lord

note: 1989 shows household love bringing sufferings with its ties; 1990 offers vows as the one lasting course for those born in this state.
teaches: The sage sets vows as the answer to the pain that household desire cannot remove, which 1989 only states.

note: In 996 Gunamalai says her heart burns like the sacrificial fire; in 1059 Civakan's mother's unfailing chastity is like the flame of the mantra-fed Vedic sacrifice.
teaches: The same ritual fire stands first for a girl's consuming desire and then for a matron's chastity, so the epic uses one Vedic image for passion and for the discipline that marriage is meant to make of it.

claims.gist: a lord must wipe out the name of one who insults him
counsel is a better power than strength of arm for a king who would win the world
great penance brings whatever one desires
a gift made with thought for later births returns merit multiplied
souls whirl through four destinies as a wheel, a ring and dust turn
no stratagem overcomes death
each order of gods has a fixed span measured in palya and sagara and then a destiny of its own
learning can turn against the one who has it, bringing him to harm
a son repays the one who raised him in rank and land
the Lord is the opponent of deluding deeds and taught the way that avoids rebirth in the dark world
beholding the festival of the Lord brings the sight of the world of merit
worldly pleasure is as short-lived as a rain-bubble and is to be given up with desire
renunciation, restraint, kindness to others and care of kin are named as duties, with giving one among them
meditation on the soul destroys both kinds of deed and ends birth and death
an enemy must be uprooted while he is young, since once grown he cannot be cut down
play undertaken for pleasure can become the cause of grief and separation
a king who errs is destroyed by his own fault, his passion, his wealth and his misplaced grace
daily devotion to the Jina leads to kingship under a white umbrella
bearing sorrow as if it were joy is harder than weeping or dying

note: Civakan pledges to wed her with his word not falling short (சொற்குன்றா); Gunamalai, having read his letter, offers worship so that he may not fail his word (சொற்குன்றான் ஆக).
teaches: The hero's own phrase comes back as the heroine's prayer, so the pledge he treats as settled she treats as needing divine witnesses, which marks the unequal risk the two carry in a promise of marriage.

note: The Kural's lover asks whether the lotus-eyed one's world can be sweeter than sleep in the beloved's soft arms; Civakan, having tasted a nectar-like bliss, no longer wants the pleasure of women whose beauty makes the heavens bow.
teaches: The lover ranks the beloved's arms above heaven, while the epic's hero, having tasted a higher bliss, finds women's embrace unwanted, so the two verses make opposite rankings of the same two goods.

gains.a: the patikam's closing simile gains an opponent: it reads as a rebuttal of the lover's ranking rather than a bare statement
gains.b: the couplet's open question gets an answer from a renouncer, showing what the lover's ranking denies

note: In 407 the astrologer says the girl is fit to rest on the lord's breast; in 603 the envoy asks what austerity earned that seat.
teaches: The woman on the lord's breast first comes as a forecast, then as something already earned, so the prophecy turns into a reward.

note: 1261 has the eldest brother vow vengeance; 1265 has the lord, cooled by the brothers' words, send them to fight.
teaches: The brothers' vow of vengeance is turned into their lord's permission and a goal of making their names stand.

note: Kural 376 says what is not one's own will not stay though guarded, nor what is one's own leave though thrown away; Pazhamozhi 231 shows a palmyra guarded all night whose fruit still falls to the one it is due to.
teaches: The pairing turns the couplet's abstract 'guard' into a watchman shouting through the night under a tree, and adds a second person the couplet lacks, the passer-by who gets the fruit, so the loss of the guarder is someone else's unearned gain.

note: Tirumanthiram has Yama's messengers seize the flesh-eaters and break them in fire-mouthed hell; here the dwellers of hell burn and split her with no god's order named.
teaches: Both fill hell with fire and breaking, but only the epic leaves the tormentors without a lord, which shows how little each needs a judge.

gains.a: The epic's hell has no named judge or messenger, only its own dwellers.
gains.b: The Saiva verse's Yama's servants stand out as one way of staffing hell, not a necessity.

note: In the Purananuru poem a king's demand for a girl her father will not give brings war on the town, and the mother who reared her beauty is blamed; here kings rise to seize a bride already won in an open contest.
teaches: The epic removes the father's refusal that drives the Sangam bride-war, since the bride's father set a fair contest and she has chosen, so the suitors' war stands as bare lust and the blame moves from the girl's rearing to the kings and their instigator.

gains.a: the scene is placed in the old category of the bride-war (மகட்பால்), which shows what it changes
gains.b: the poem's blame of the mother is shown to be one choice of cause, which a later poet assigns instead to the suitors' desire and to a schemer

note: 3030 has Civakan pluck his hair like a lion shedding its mane; Naladiyar 53 says the best renounce home, youth, wealth and strength at once because none lasts.
teaches: The epic does what the quatrain counsels with the same word for leaving, but shows a king with all of them to give up.

gains.a: the verse's act of tonsure gets the reason the Naladiyar gives, that none of these things lasts
gains.b: the quatrain's advice to renounce without delay gets a worked case at the height of a king's power

note: The astrologer's reading of her பான்மை is taken up by the king in 554, who refuses every suitor because none can stop a portion when its time comes.
teaches: A horoscope cast at birth becomes, years later, the king's reason for refusing all suitors, so the prophecy governs a political decision rather than merely forecasting a marriage.

note: At 427 the ministers choose Maruci as one who can carry what he has learned and say what is fit; at 495 his first act on reaching the princes is to rise and bow.
teaches: The envoy named for his speech opens with a bow and not with the message, so his fitness shows first in manner.

note: Vipulan offers the enemy heaven in exchange for leaving fame on earth; the challenger who answers him is killed and received into heaven by the celestial women.
teaches: The taunt turns out to be a literal promise kept: the one man who takes up Vipulan's offer gets exactly the heaven it named, so the challenge is courtesy as well as threat.

note: 986 says whoever wins the bride must have great earlier austerity; 1117 has the groom claim he did austerity to touch her.
teaches: The groom's claim fulfils the father's prediction and turns the language of penance from release to desire.

note: 394: Kuttuvan gives a killer elephant, and when the frightened bard returns it gives a bigger one, ashamed the first seemed small; Kural 221: true giving is giving to those who have nothing.
teaches: The Kural defines a gift by the receiver's want, but Kuttuvan's elephants are sized to the giver's honour and are useless to a hungry bard, so the poem shows a royal giving that the Kural's definition would hardly count as ஈகை at all.

note: The thousand and eight and the feet on the head recur: Kavunthi will speak only the ஆயிரத்து எட்டு நாமம் and bear only the flower feet on her head; the Cintamani's god bears ஆயிரத்து எட்டு marks and the poet sets his lotus feet on his head.
teaches: The number 1008 is a fixed token of Arhat worship that one epic attaches to names spoken and the other to marks on the body, while the feet-on-the-head gesture stays the same in a nun's vow and a poet's invocation.

note: The epic gods, with fifteen days left, blink and see their garlands fade and grieve like those who ate poisoned nectar; the Saiva verse says countless gods have died while the one with the forehead eye stays.
teaches: The two texts share the mortality of gods but part on the cure: the Jain verse leaves no god to rest on and moves the hearer to release, the Saiva verse moves him to the one undying Lord.

gains.a: The epic gains a rival answer to the fall of the gods: an unchanging Lord to rest on, which a Jain account of gods without such a Lord lacks
gains.b: The Tirumanthiram gains a concrete picture of how a dying god feels, the signs, the regret at wasted pleasure, that it only states in a line

note: Verse 182 says even calling the Arhat all-knowing does not let one know him; Tirumanthiram 32 says no one knows the lord's nature, and the all-pervading lord is praised only in part.
teaches: Both say naming does not reach the god, but the Jain verse accepts omniscience as a true name while the Saiva verse denies any measure of the lord.

gains.a: The verse's refusal is made sharper: it concedes the epithet and still holds the god beyond it, where the Saiva line denies all naming.
gains.b: A rival that praises by listing epithets, so the lord beyond naming can be seen as a stand against it.

note: Both name the star Arundhati as the measure of a woman's chastity: Mrigalochana is like her, and in the Cintamani a woman is said to put her aside.
teaches: Two Jain epics use the same star as the yardstick of wifely chastity, one saying a queen is equal to it and the other that a woman surpasses it.

note: 1608 has the queen burn with anger at the king's praise of a stranger's footprint; Kural 1313 has a woman angry at a wreath she says was worn for another woman.
teaches: The epic gives the wife a real occasion where the couplet's wife sulks on a pretext, and shows the husband pleading as the couplet's man does.

gains.a: The queen's anger gains a measure: the Kural treats the jealousy of love as sulking even when nothing was done, and here something was.
gains.b: The couplet gains a case where the husband did give cause by speaking of another woman, so its jest has a dark side.

note: 1111 has the groom's ardour carry her shame off; Kural 1134 has the flood of love carry off the raft of shame and manliness.
teaches: The same flood that costs the secret lover his standing in the Kural is blessed here, because the epic's shame falls away inside a wedding.

gains.a: The epic verse gets the Kural's naming of shame as something love sweeps away, and so as a loss, which its cage image hides.
gains.b: The couplet gets a case where losing shame costs nothing, showing the loss it names depends on love outside marriage.

note: Purananuru 185, by Thondaiman Ilanthiraiyan himself, says the realm is a cart that runs well only if its driver is skilled and otherwise sinks in the mire of enmity; the idyll shows the same king's court running smoothly, justice and gifts granted to all.
teaches: Read beside the patron's own conditional maxim, the bard's portrait answers the king's worry with a finished picture: what Ilanthiraiyan states as a risk depending on the driver, the guide poem states as already achieved, which shows the work praise did for a king who wrote about failure.

note: Naladiyar 221 says the faults of those taken as good are kept within, as rice has its husk; Soolamani 5 asks that the poet's fault count for nothing before the good.
teaches: The Naladiyar's rule keeping faults hidden between friends becomes a poet's plea that readers apply it to his own work, which turns a rule of friendship into a rule of reading.

gains.a: the plea to overlook a fault is given a rule behind it, a standing habit of the good to keep faults within
gains.b: the rule of keeping faults hidden is seen applied from a poet to his readers, outside the friendship it was written for

note: 1859 shortens the term to a blink before Death; Kural 334 calls the day a blade that saws the life.
teaches: The epic shortens the quantity: the couplet measures life as days, the verse measures it by the blink the minister names.

gains.a: The blink gains the blade as an image for time's cutting.
gains.b: The couplet gains a minister who counts the cut in a blink.

note: 3118 has the king live with a woman who has no old age or death; Naladiyar 14 has the once-desired woman bent over a staff and a torment.
teaches: One text shows what the loved woman will become, and the other the woman who never becomes it.

gains.a: the verse's ageless bride is shown as the answer to the old woman the quatrain describes
gains.b: the Naladiyar's bent old woman gets the Jain promise of a partner who does not age, offered to those who give up the first kind

note: The Siddhar wishes to see the lives he might kill as his own life; the kid in 197 is, literally, the king's own father.
teaches: The Siddhar's stance of 'thinking of them as my own life' is a wish; the epic gives it a literal case, where the creature eaten is the eater's kin.

gains.a: The recognition in 197 gets a Siddhar's name for the habit of mind that would have stopped the rite.
gains.b: The Siddhar's 'as my own life' gets a story where it is literally true of the victim.

note: Purananuru 192 says good and ill do not come from others, and the speakers neither rejoice that life is sweet nor curse it as bitter; Civakan is freed by a god yet calls the freeing his own former deed and feels neither joy nor grief.
teaches: The pair shows the Sangam sage's 'not from others' being kept even when the rescue plainly does come from another: the epic folds the rescuer into the hero's own deed, the dog he once helped.

gains.a: the hero's two-line equanimity is set against a fuller statement of the same stance, with its image of life carried like a raft by the river
gains.b: the poem's abstract claim gets a narrative in which an outside helper exists and the claim must explain him, which it does by tracing the help back to the self

note: In the storm Sridattan urged laughter in trouble; after the rescue his companions laugh that the wreck was a play.
teaches: The laughter urged as courage before the outcome returns as relief after it, which shows how differently the same laugh weighs once the danger is known to be staged.

note: The chief queen loses her life in 1470; the other wives fall in 1471.
teaches: The queen's collapse leads the rest of the household, so the grief runs outward from her to all the women.

note: At Gandharvadattai's song the trees bud and the birds fall entranced; at the song of the suitors, called faultless and like Ananga in music, the birds fly off as if laughing.
teaches: The poet lets the birds give the verdict the narration withholds: the suitors' music is praised in words and condemned by nature, so the contest is judged before any human judge speaks.

note: The Kural says the tears of those who cannot bear oppression wear away the oppressor's wealth; when the usurper falls, the tears in the story are those of his own women.
teaches: The ruin that the tears of the oppressed bring on a bent sceptre falls in the story on the oppressor's women, who now weep in their turn.

gains.a: the women's tears get a cause beyond the scene: the wealth they lose was worn away by the tears of the city in Saccandan's fall
gains.b: the couplet's abstract 'wealth' is shown to include people, and its justice is shown to land on those who did not themselves oppress

note: In 1003 Civakan paints Gunamalai on cloth as she stood trembling before the elephant; in 1047 the nurse says the cousin worships a likeness of her painted on cloth every day.
teaches: The nurse's test gives the rival suitor the very gesture Civakan made, so Gunamalai's refusal shows that what binds her is the man she chose, not the devotion paid to her image.

note: 2984 sets wealth against the funeral rice and the wife's tears at the burning ground; Tirumanthiram 149 gives the man's public mansion, palanquin and three crores and then his silent going.
teaches: The Tirumanthiram shows a life of building and giving with no look back; the epic shows what the household is left with, so together they give the whole before and after.

gains.a: the funeral picture is set after a life like the man's, in which a mansion and palanquin were all in public view
gains.b: the Tirumanthiram's man who did not turn back gets a household to leave, with a widow's tears and a funeral rice

note: The minister lists Asvagriva's army, its order and the food supply among the reasons none equals him; Kural 381 counts army, people, resources, ministers, friends and fort as a king's six limbs.
teaches: The minister's praise follows the Kural's list for army and food but adds the discus, the lineage and learning, so the poet counts as kingly worth what the Kural's checklist leaves out.

gains.a: The speaker's list of army, food and ministers gets a stated standard of what a complete king must have.
gains.b: The couplet's six limbs meet a king whose praise adds lineage, learning and a magic discus, so its checklist is tested against what a court poet values.

note: 2871 puts another's wife as a sword over the neck and heavy suffering; Kural 146 says enmity, sin, fear and blame never leave one who crosses another's threshold.
teaches: The Kural lists four worldly costs and the verse gives one inward one, so the verse adds fear and the Kural adds blame.

gains.a: The verse's suffering gets named costs, enmity and blame, and not only pain
gains.b: The Kural's costs get the Jain view that adultery is also a deed that sends one downward

note: Kural 85 asks whether the field of a man who feeds guests and eats the leftovers even needs sowing; in 333 the wife has fed guests until she must pound the seed millet itself.
teaches: The Kural's rhetorical promise that the hospitable house needs no seed is played out literally in the poem, where hospitality has eaten the seed, so the pair shows the real cost that the maxim's confidence passes over.

note: Kattiyangaran fears that the escaped 'tiger' will crush him; in 2206 a voice from the sky proclaims that the lion Civakan will swallow the life of the elephant Kattiyangaran.
teaches: The usurper's private dread in 2197 is answered by a public sky-voice in 2206 with the same beast imagery, so his fear turns out to be accurate foresight rather than panic.

note: The king takes up the sword to follow her and, at the climax of his anger, his hand is stopped.
teaches: Carrying the sword in verse 118 makes the check in 123 a choice taken with the means to kill in hand, not a failure of means.

note: Verse 161 likens the wealth of the worthless to kongu trees that bloom without scent; Kural 1008 likens the wealth of the unwanted to a poison tree fruiting in the town.
teaches: Both name a tree whose outer splendour fails its purpose, one for giving no scent and one for giving poison, so wealth without worth is shown useless in one case and harmful in the other.

gains.a: A harsher side of the image: wealth without worth does not merely fail to please, it can poison those who come near.
gains.b: A softer case: wealth may leave the others unharmed but unattended, like blossom that no one stops for.

note: 2093 has the king say his own days are few and he has resolved today; Kural 342 says renounce while there is time.
teaches: The Kural's urgency to renounce in time becomes, in the epic, a king's own reckoning of his remaining days against those of his people.

gains.a: The king's haste gets a rule from outside the story: the time to renounce is limited and it is wiser to act before it runs out.
gains.b: The couplet gains a person who is at once a ruler and a father, whose leaving has to be explained to those he leaves.

note: The Naladiyar says kings who rode in state fall when their deeds give out and their foes take the wives they married; the Cintamani's victors break into the fallen king's palace and drive his women out.
teaches: The epic stages the quatrain's fall of a king but changes its last turn: the victors expel the dead king's wives rather than take them.

gains.a: the expulsion, which the verse narrates without comment, gets the quatrain's frame of a fall that comes when one's deeds run out
gains.b: the quatrain's 'foes take the wives' is shown not as the only end: a victor of the Jain epic sends them away instead

note: 1381 says the mountain Vidyadharas fled from men whom fate has marked; Kural 380 asks what is stronger than fate.
teaches: The epic gives fate as the one reason a strong flying army can be turned by men with no such powers.

gains.a: The Vidyadhara retreat gains a cause beyond skill or number: the opponents are fated to win.
gains.b: The couplet gains a battlefield instance in which fate beats a stronger force without any scheme being named.

note: The question who she is, goddess or woman, is answered in the next verse by the fading garland, blinking eyes and feet on the ground.
teaches: Read together the two verses make the doubt and its clearing a single step of the kalavu sequence, in which the man must establish she is human before he may approach her.

note: Kural 341 holds that from whatever one has let go one suffers no pain; Vijayai lets go her ornaments one by one (349 to 353) but ends with a vow for her son, whom she does not let go and for whom she grieves in 355 and 359.
teaches: The piecemeal renunciation the couplet describes is acted out jewel by jewel, and the pain the couplet promises to remove returns exactly at the one tie the queen keeps, which shows the couplet's claim from its other side.

gains.a: the stripping scene gains a rule by which to measure it, so the son's survival in her vow reads as the unrenounced attachment
gains.b: the couplet's 'whatever, whatever' gains an ordered sequence of things given up and one thing held, with the pain located where letting go stops

note: Vijayai fell lamenting that she had seen her son once and failed to see him again; hearing of her, Civakan weeps.
teaches: Read together, the mother's and the son's tears are the two halves of one grief, each learning of the other only through the companions who carried the story between them.

note: Naladiyar 46 breaks the woman into entrails, fat, blood and bone to cure desire; verse 71 calls the body a hut of filth and the dharma what ends desire for sense-pleasure and the cruelty of killing.
teaches: The quatrain cures desire by looking at the parts; the epic ties the same look to a dharma that also ends killing, so the contemplation of foulness shares a root with the mercy that stays the king's sword.

gains.a: the body-as-filth gains a concrete inventory of parts, which the epic names only as filth
gains.b: the quatrain's disgust is set in a system joining it to non-killing and release, not only restraint of lust

claims.gist: hearing the true teaching lets the light of knowledge split the darkness of evil deeds
the fierce karmas fall to meditation's attack in a fixed order of forts
counsel is the highest of a king's three powers, and a king guided by able ministers finds nothing too hard
the weight of breath is not seen in the empty conch, so absence of a weight does not show that nothing left
clinging draws the soul into the four states of rebirth, and giving it up at the Jina's feet leads to release
the teacher takes in the lord's word and sends down dharma on living beings like rain
complete austerity in a past life brings a ruler the obedience of all kings
a man wins a rare bride by penance done earlier
the wives' place is with the husband, in austerity as in the household
suffering inflicted by another is the sufferer's own deed come back, and the ascetic sees no 'ours' or 'others'
even the greatest ruler should be led by the counsel of the wise
desire for the body is the seed from which the disease of birth grows
the body kept for pleasure is only a bundle of disease and hatred
a mind that wants something is less steady than lightning, and company and counsel cannot hold it
right knowledge is to know things as they are, and right faith is inner clarity and joy in the Jina's dharma
the lord knows the three times and burned all old deeds
he taught the five categories and said the supreme state is one
the earth has no family or virtue she keeps to and follows those skilled in stratagem
a wife's penance can preserve her husband's life
this too is a portion allotted by fate
affection felt in one birth comes from a bond of an earlier birth
attachment, hatred and anger lead to animal birth
brave talk to one's own men from a safe height is worth nothing in front of the foe
the god split the fierce karma and stands as a light of the world above
those who master the scriptures and teach them wash away the hearers' karma
the vow of fasting is kept on a fixed fifth day of a bright fortnight over five years and five months
the middle world is a continent ringed by oceans and further rings, each twice the width of the one before
when love's pleasure is not to be had, restraint gained through penance is what becomes a man

note: At the princes' birth the clinging moisture of evil deeds is said to dry up for many; Kural 5 says deeds of darkness do not cling to those who delight in the Lord's praise.
teaches: The Kural lifts the hold of deeds through the devotee's own praise, but the epic lifts it for many through the birth of a great being, so each work places the loosening of karma somewhere different.

gains.a: The epic verse gets a stated condition for karma's loosening, the devotee's praise, which it does not state.
gains.b: Kural 5 gets a case where the hold is loosened by someone else's birth and not by the sufferer's devotion, a test of how exclusive its condition is.

note: 2088 says the earth has enjoyed countless men and left them, and has not stayed with the next; Siddhar 286 says crowned kings are burnt to a fistful of ash and become earth.
teaches: The two reverse the same image: the king thinks he holds the earth, but 2088 says she leaves him and the Siddhar says he is returned into her.

gains.a: The earth that deserts kings gets an ending, that the kings she leaves are laid in her as ash, which the verse does not state.
gains.b: The Siddhar's ash gets a living figure for earth, the woman who goes from king to king, so the fact of burning is given a reason.

note: 271 says the ascetic thinks of pain inflicted as his own deed; Naladiyar 58 says the worthy grieve for those who scorn them, fearing the hell that will follow.
teaches: Together they show that holding hurt as one's own deed does not leave the ascetic cold: Naladiyar adds the pity for the offender that 271 omits.

gains.a: 271 gains a feeling for the offender that its karma explanation leaves out.
gains.b: Naladiyar 58 gains a king with dogs as its case: the scorner is shown at the moment before the fall it fears for him.

note: Naladiyar 23 says the wedding drums of one hall can be the funeral drums for the bridegroom the same day; verse 1052 reports a drum sounding tomorrow's wedding.
teaches: Read beside the quatrain, the drum of joy carries the warning of the same drum's other use, which the epic's happy scene does not say itself.

gains.a: The verse lacks any thought that the festive drum could mean loss, which the quatrain supplies.
gains.b: The quatrain lacks a drum that is only the announcement of a coming wedding, with no loss in the story.

note: Dharmadattan warned Kattiyangaran that a king is a fire that turns nectar or poison as it will; at his end Kattiyangaran says it is good or bad deeds that turn poison to nectar and nectar to poison.
teaches: The same nectar-and-poison figure moves from the wronged king's power to impersonal karma, and the shift lets the usurper blame his fall on deeds in general rather than on the king he wronged, as he was warned.

note: 2017 says those with the lamp of vision reach heaven or the bliss without return even without vows; Kural 356 says those who learn and see the true thing reach the path of no return.
teaches: The epic loosens the couplet's chain, holding that sight alone, even without vows, opens heaven or release.

gains.a: The vowless seer gains a precedent, since the couplet already gives seeing the true thing the path of no return.
gains.b: The couplet gains the claim that vows are not required, which it never says, and the lesser reward of heaven.

note: Verse 105 shows Vasavadatta with the arts that verse 103 had her taught.
teaches: The lute lessons planned in one verse come out as proof of mastery in the next, so the teaching is shown as having worked.

note: The Kural pictures the life leaving the body as a bird flying from a nest left empty; the epic pictures ascetics leaving the body as an exchange for an imperishable golden one, and uses it for the merchant leaving his dead son for a living child.
teaches: Leaving the body is loss in the Kural's figure and gain in the epic's, and the difference is the penance done beforehand.

gains.a: the simile gains a contrast that shows what penance adds: without it the body is only an abandoned nest
gains.b: the couplet gains a limit: the epic admits a departure from the body that is not mere desertion but a passage to a better frame

note: 2018 names the lamp of vision as seeing the true thing and says that, once lit, the darkness of deeds cannot stay; 2072 shows the path in which vision and knowledge, with meditation, lead on to the world of release.
teaches: The lamp of vision in 2018 is a first step; 2072 sets out what must follow it before the deeds are gone and release is reached.

note: Kural 380 says that nothing is stronger than fate, which arrives first even when one devises another way; verse 358 says that when they plan, fate gives the result and a strong plan may end otherwise, and Sumantiri still goes on to counsel.
teaches: The couplet gives fate as a rule; the minister uses it as a caution that does not stop deliberation, so the rule is shown as bounding counsel and not replacing it.

gains.a: A use of the fate rule as a counsellor's caution, which the couplet's flat statement does not show.
gains.b: A scene of deliberation where the rule is applied, so its strength is tested against a council that goes on planning.

note: Soolamani 202 describes release as a shining form and limitless, unfailing bliss; Tirumanthiram 136 says the soul subsides into Sivam as salt returns to water.
teaches: The two release verses differ on whether the freed self keeps its own form and bliss or subsides into another, if the salt image is read as loss of separate being and the Jain 'shining form' as a kept one.

gains.a: release is shown as a state the freed self keeps as its own, since no one else is named for it to join
gains.b: the salt image meets a Tamil account in which the freed soul keeps form and bliss, so merging is not the only picture of release

note: The Kural says birth is alike for all living beings and distinction comes from the work they do; Civakan's lore sorts even snakes into four varnas known by the smell of their bite.
teaches: Read with பிறப்பொக்கும் as denying rank by birth, the couplet stands against a lore that fixes varna in nature down to snakes; the pairing shows that the Cintamani's hero carries birth-rank as plain knowledge even where the Kural, speaking of all living beings, had set it aside.

gains.a: the snake lore gains its weight as a claim about birth, which in the story passes as neutral technique
gains.b: the couplet's 'all living beings' gains a test case among animals, where the opposing view assigns rank by birth alone

note: 2070 traces how birth turns to desire and hatred toward sense objects, heaps up deeds and brings the same nature back after death; Kural 349 says that the very moment attachment ends, births are cut.
teaches: The couplet's moment of cutting is shown in 2070 to be the point where the chain from senses to desire to deed to return is broken.

gains.a: The chain of sense, craving, deed and rebirth gets a plain statement of where it ends, which 2070 leaves unsaid.
gains.b: The couplet gets the working of the births it cuts: attachment makes deeds, and the deeds are what bring the return.

note: Verse 4 states in the abstract that a deed binds and ripens; verse 326 gives a case, killing and its fruit.
teaches: The opening claim about deeds that ripen is given a concrete case here: a named deed, its sorrow and its hell.

note: Both name bathing at Kumari to be rid of a bodily affliction; the Thiruppugazh poet asks not to go there and be laughed at by many as a diseased wretch, and the epic's old brahmin goes there and is laughed at (பெரிது நக்கு, 2021).
teaches: Holding the two together shows that the afflicted pilgrim to Kumari was a stock figure of ridicule, and that Civakan chooses that figure as a disguise precisely because a man so laughable is trusted inside a guarded house.

gains.a: the epic's pretext is shown to be a recognisable, mocked practice rather than an invented whim, which explains why Suramanjari laughs instead of suspecting him
gains.b: the shame the Thiruppugazh poet fears is seen acted out, the laugh given by the very person asked for help, and turned to the trickster's profit

note: Vijayai urged her son, before bright youth lapses and black hair greys, to do hard penance and give; the teacher now lists the lapse of youth and the coming of old age as one of the standing sufferings of men.
teaches: The mother's household warning about youth is shown here as one item in a Jain account of suffering, so her urging reads as the doctrine put plainly for a son who might delay.

note: The couplet says to renounce while there is time; the king crowns his son first and then renounces.
teaches: The couplet gives only the timing, and the story adds that a king's renouncing in time includes installing his heir first.

gains.a: the king's exit is read as renunciation in time, with the succession first
gains.b: the couplet's time gets a king's duty: the throne is handed on before it is left

note: Kural 1268 says let the king fight and win, and let us feast at home in the evening; Akananuru 44 opens with the king's work done and the tribute paid, and bids the chariot race home to sleep on her breast.
teaches: The Kural's couplet is the akam homecoming formula of the returning warrior reduced to its two clauses, the king's victory first and the household's evening second.

note: Kural 586 counsels the king to use spies who go in the guise of renunciants and wanderers; 47 insists that the bard's wandering life, crossing many wastes from patron to patron, harms no one. On the reading that 47 answers a suspicion of the wandering bard, the two disagree about whether such travellers should be trusted.
teaches: The Kural's advice to disguise spies as wanderers is the very reason a real wanderer could fall under suspicion, and 47 gives the wanderer's side, a life of gifts and honour that 'knows no harm to others', so the pair shows the cost the state's craft laid on the travelling poet.

note: The Naladiyar says kings who rode under the umbrella at the head of armies fall when their deeds turn, and enemies take their wives; 161 shows Saccandan at the full of his fame, the starting point of such a fall.
teaches: The quatrain gives the general fall of the umbrella king; the epic fills in one fall step by step, with the king's own infatuation as the turn and his queen driven out, so impermanence works through character and not only fortune.

gains.a: the epic's high point of praise gains the moral frame within which its listeners would hear it as the top of a wheel
gains.b: the quatrain's abstract turn of deeds gains a narrated mechanism, desire and a trusted minister

note: Both poets defend flaws in speech by an image, the Cintamani's unwashed gem and this poem's lamp with smoke.
teaches: The apology for a flawed poem is a set piece of the Jain epics, but this poem argues from the lamp's worth and the Cintamani from the washing that cures the flaw.

note: Both poets ask the learned to deal with the flaws of the work, but the Cintamani asks that they wash the flaw out with their wit, while the Soolamani expects the wise to guard the lapses of people like himself.
teaches: One poet asks the reader to correct the flaw and the other to shield it, so the two Jain epics set different tasks for the learned in front of a faulty work.

note: Arkakirti's bowstring is named for shame (நாண்) and he prizes the bow above life; the couplet says the honourable give up life when honour is lost.
teaches: The epic gives the hero's honour a physical thing, the string, that the couplet only states as a rule.

gains.a: The verse gains a statement of the stake: shame at disgrace outweighs life, with the bowstring as its image.
gains.b: The couplet gains an image of honour as something one wears and draws, the warrior's bowstring, instead of the yak's hair.

note: Both have a mother figure following an eloped girl and asking those on the road whether they saw her: in Akananuru 7 the foster mother asks a doe and a hill girl; in Kalittokai 9 the mother asks brahmin ascetics, who answer.
teaches: The Akananuru leaves the question unanswered on the empty road, while the Kalittokai brings in renouncers to answer it with a doctrine, so the later anthology turns the mother's lament into a debate the elopement wins.

note: 261 makes the king's surrender of his army in pleasure the opening for the treachery; 290 mourns him as the sun of the just sceptre swallowed by the minister alone.
teaches: In death the narrator moves the blame wholly onto the usurper, so the epic holds both a negligent king and a righteous one and lets the lament forget the first.

note: Kural 267 says austerity burns pain as fire burns gold so that it shines; 3070 has the sun's own fire ring burn on Civakan for four months while he stands on the elephant of knowledge.
teaches: The couplet gives the gold-and-fire image of austerity in general; the verse sets it in a particular season of heat and ties the shining to knowledge, not to appearance.

gains.a: the verse's four months of burning sun are given the principle that the heat is what makes the ascetic shine
gains.b: the Kural's gold in fire becomes a named ordeal, a season of heat with an ascetic standing in it

note: Kural 55 praises the wife who rises worshipping her husband and not a god; Vijayai rises, worships the god's feet, and then goes to her lord's feet.
teaches: A Jain epic keeps the wife's devotion to her husband but sets worship of the god first, so the couplet's exclusive ranking is answered with an order of two duties rather than a choice between them.

gains.a: the queen's morning is seen as a deliberate ordering of devotions against a known ideal
gains.b: the couplet's 'not a god' is shown to be a position a later work could decline while still honouring the husband

note: Kural 367 says that if craving is cut off thoroughly, unfailing deeds (தவாவினை) come as one wishes; 913 pictures giving to suppliants as damming the sea called அவா, with தவாவினை at its shore.
teaches: The epic takes the Kural's pair of craving and unfailing deed and makes festival giving the practical means of checking craving, where the couplet names only the cutting itself.

gains.a: the doctrinal source of its compressed image: the words அவா and தவாவினை are the couplet's own pairing, which explains why deed and craving share one metaphor
gains.b: a concrete social act, gold poured out to suppliants on a festival day, as the way craving is held back short of renunciation

note: Verse 46 asks whether there is fear in leaving this life of fearful births; verse 62 shows the youths without trembling at the killing ground.
teaches: The earlier fearlessness was a resolve made in a garden of talk; here it is tested at the place of death.

note: 1903 asks whether the Lord's red feet are reddened by lotus petals or by their own rays; 181 has the king praising the red lotus feet of him who conquered the dust of deeds.
teaches: The red feet appear in both shrine hymns, first as a fact and then as a riddle of cause, so the later hymn plays on the earlier plain praise.

note: The soldiers hold that only bound fate may take a life; Kural 380 asks what is stronger than fate.
teaches: A warrior class that claims only fate may kill makes its own arms the servants of fate, which the couplet's praise of fate's strength never says.

gains.a: The verse lacks a rule that fate outruns every other plan, which would explain why soldiers can speak of fate as the only killer.
gains.b: The couplet lacks a picture of armed men who put its claim into their own battle-cry and so make Death tremble.

note: Desire breaks through the restraint of the one who was to be the tempter.
teaches: Vegavati was sent as the instrument of a plan, and she meets desire the Kural says does not stop to ask whether one is firm in restraint, which makes the plan itself the thing that fails.

gains.a: The verse shows desire overcoming the person of the plan, a case the couplet's general remark does not name.
gains.b: The couplet's general claim that love ignores restraint gets a case where it defeats an agent with an assigned task, not only a lover who is open to it.

note: Vijayai's dream in 223 of the ashoka tree falling, its garland crowning a shoot, is what the king says in 267 has now come true.
teaches: The fallen tree of the dream is the king himself, which the earlier verse could only hint at, while the shoot points ahead to the son not yet born.

note: Verse 108 says a man able to speak well will come with a letter into the garden Pushpakarandam; verses 429 and 430 bring Marusi to a grove with that name.
teaches: The astrologer's date is kept by the story's own messenger, so the plot is built on a promised arrival rather than chance.

note: 2563 hymns the lord as the one who understood without fault, the wheel that removes stain, and who set bounds to the senses; 3023 hymns the same lord as the sea of virtues and the wheel of dharma that clears hunger, hatred and disease.
teaches: The same epithets, wheel and a sea of virtues, recur at the king's last bow, so the earlier hymn's titles are seen to be the book's one settled form of praise.

note: Verse 243 puts truth after not killing and gives each its fruit, as the couplet puts not lying second to not killing.
teaches: The couplet only names the order of the two virtues, and the verse adds what each is said to yield.

gains.a: A ranking that puts not killing before truth, which the verse's list of five leaves unspoken.
gains.b: A fruit in this life for each of the two virtues, which the couplet leaves out.

note: Rudradattan argues that lust's blame cannot be hidden and is drummed through the world; Naladiyar 89 says lust burns the mind itself, worse than fire or sun.
teaches: The counsellor argues from public disgrace and the quatrain from inward burning, so a reader sees that the ethics of desire had two separate arguments and that the epic, speaking to a king, chose reputation.

gains.a: the counsellor's choice of argument by reputation stands out against an argument he did not use
gains.b: the quatrain's inward harm is set beside the outward cost it leaves out

note: The Kural makes not killing the whole of virtuous action; the verse makes a lord of that vow the one whose worship cuts the evil birth.
teaches: The Kural sets non-killing as the rule, and the verse makes it the lord's own vow, so worship of him is worship of the rule kept to its end.

gains.a: the vow is set in the Tamil rule that killing brings all other deeds, so what the god is praised for has a reason
gains.b: the rule is made a person: the lord who kept it all the way and is the end of its path

note: In 14 the woman says his past praise of her shoulders, eyes, teeth, brow, hair and breasts has turned to estrangement; in 22 she asks whether he has praised the same teeth, hair and breasts as they will be when old.
teaches: The two poems run the same catalogue of praise through time: 14 looks back at praise already withdrawn, 22 looks ahead to the aged body, so together they make the lover's blazon a promise that covers the whole life of the body, which leaving for wealth would break.

note: Naladiyar 13 condemns the old who lean on a staff, toothless and tottering, yet keep their eyes on desire; Civakan, young, puts on that very figure with staff and white hair for love of a woman's beauty.
teaches: The quatrain's figure of shame, the old man still ruled by desire, becomes in the epic a costume a young lover wears to reach a woman, so the image meant to turn men from desire is used as an instrument of it.

gains.a: the comic disguise gains a moral shadow: the narrator's 'became even a ghost' reads as the quatrain's verdict on desire that will not let go
gains.b: the quatrain's staff and failing body are shown to be imitable signs, so its warning rests on a look that a lover can counterfeit and that guards pity rather than scorn

note: Vijayai dreamed that the asoka tree fell and was utterly gone; in 289 the king falls to the earth and goes out like the setting sun.
teaches: The half of the dream the king refused to read at 225 is fulfilled in his fall, so the battle is the dream's first image enacted and Civakan, the shoot, is still to come.

note: Paripadal 12 has Madurai dress, perfume itself and mount she-elephants, horses and chariots in a rush to meet the Vaiyai flood; the Cintamani's city sets out with litters, elephants and carts for its spring water-play by the river.
teaches: The epic keeps the Sangam river festival's order of dressing, mounting and rushing to the bank, but its festival honours no river or god, and is likened instead to the Jina's assembly, so the old civic rite is re-made as pure pleasure under a renouncer's image.

gains.a: a precedent showing that its procession is a set piece of the Tamil river festival rather than an invention
gains.b: evidence that its catalogue of the crowd's preparations survived as a convention into the later Jain epic, cut loose from the river's worship

note: In 907 her father buys a royal order with a priceless necklace that ends men's coming and going and even makes the carved figures female; in 2013 the guards let a man in out of pity for an old Brahmin's hunger.
teaches: A ban bought with the three worlds' worth of jewels fails not by force but through the guards' compassion for hunger and age, showing that the exclusion was drawn against young men's bodies and could not see past a guise of decay.

note: 1466 says the discus he threw became his own enemy; Purananuru 227 calls Death a fool that cooked and ate its own seed by taking Valavan.
teaches: The epic shows the king as the agent of his death while the Sangam poet blames Death as an outside foe, so the two poems disagree on who ends a king.

gains.a: 1466 gives the fall as the king's own deed and lacks the Sangam poet's view that Death is to blame.
gains.b: The Sangam poem blames Death and gains the epic's case where the weapon of the dead man killed him.

claims.gist: old age cannot be undone, as a dead tree cannot be revived by rain
a warrior king's pride (maanam) holds him to battle though he knows it brings his ruin
gathered merit comes back as sovereignty and pleasure in a later stage of life
it is false that a dancer's chastity breaks for gold
the god conquered the whole sum of karma by a knowledge that spread through all things
those who bow at his feet are freed of their karma
those bent on hell cannot be brought to take the vows even when the truth is proclaimed to them
evil deeds cling to the soul through every change of body and burn it with suffering
those who repeat the Jina's word are freed of suffering for ages
the liberated lord has eight qualities
one who never leaves home, like a fish in a well, knows nothing of other lands
the merit of a gift is exactly as great as the gift, and it carries the soul to its next birth
even Mal worships the Jina's feet with flowers and folded hands
a king may hand his rule to his son and leave for austerity
eating the flesh of living beings is repaid in hell by being made to swallow what burns
a conquering king should grant mercy and let the defeated kin live
a deed of a former birth drives the king into prison
the sin of killing a life ripens in many sorrows
right vision once perfected is easily gained by the great and rarely by others
the opposite of the merit-bearing practice ripens into torment
the king's conquest and protection of the world bring great sorrow
the Jina, turner of the wheel of dharma full of compassion, conquered Kama
conduct is giving up killing, lying, stealing, desire for another's wife and clinging to wealth
a follower also gives up flesh, honey and toddy
a lesser king owes an overlord, on demand, tribute of treasure, women and the marks of a king
praise and flowers at the Jina's feet remove one's fault
a small kindness joined to abstaining from liquor brings kingship in a later birth

note: In 2008 Civakan judges the gate easy to pass if he goes as a Brahmin; in 2016 the women hold back their weapons because touching an old Brahmin is sin.
teaches: The plan's premise is confirmed by the guards' own ethics: the protection owed a Brahmin is what admits the intruder, so a religious scruple becomes the hero's key.

note: 1930 says sufferers entered the pit by their own earlier striving and no one comes when they cry; Tirumanthiram 165 sends those who do not worship Siva to the seventh hell where they cry out.
teaches: The cry in hell is answered by neither text, but the Jain verse locates the cause in deeds and the Saiva verse in worship withheld.

gains.a: The cry of 1930 gains a Saiva counterpart in which a withheld act of worship, not a deed's weight, is the cause of the same crying.
gains.b: The Saiva hell gains a Jain rival in which no rescuer is named because no god sits above the deeds.

note: The king's vow follows earlier merit, as the couplet says austerity comes only to those who already have it.
teaches: The couplet's circular rule is shown working in a life, with the vow following earlier merit.

gains.a: the king's turn to a vow gets a ground in earlier merit rather than seeming sudden
gains.b: the couplet's circular rule gets a story in which it works

note: 1906 says there is no other god to count, and the Lord is easy for those who worship his feet; Kural 7 says only those who reach the feet of the one without a peer can remove the mind's anxiety.
teaches: The hymn names its peerless one by what he does to living things, while the couplet leaves the feet unnamed and so open to any tradition.

gains.a: The hymn gains the couplet's claim that the anxieties of the mind are removed only by those feet.
gains.b: The couplet gains a candidate for the one without a peer, whose peerlessness is given as harmlessness and ease of access.

note: 80 likens the women's sidelong glances to Kaman's arrows; Naladiyar 17 warns against desiring a woman of spear-like eyes, for she too will lean on a staff.
teaches: The epic shows the glance as a weapon at the moment of its force, and Naladiyar names the later fall of the same weapon, so the pair sets the glance's power against its short life.

gains.a: The epic's glances get a limit it does not state, that the spear-eyed will stoop and walk with a staff.
gains.b: Naladiyar 17 gets a scene of the spear-like glance at work, so its warning is aimed at what the reader has just watched.

note: The quatrain says an old deed seeks out its doer as a calf seeks its mother; the kid in 199 is a king found by his own deeds.
teaches: The quatrain gives the mechanism and the epic gives the case: the doer is found even across births and in a lower body, and still hears the deed named as its own.

gains.a: The kid's line 'the fruit of the deed I produced' gets an image for how the fruit finds the doer.
gains.b: The calf-and-mother image gets a doer who is a king reborn as a kid under his own son.

note: 280 has the king resolve to offer his own head; 281 says that to destroy one's own life is not grace.
teaches: The rule against killing is used here to forbid an act of reverence by the doer on himself, and so it does not give way to atonement.

note: Akananuru 355: in spring bees hum on the budding branches like the strings of a paalai lute touched by a master, the season in which the heroine fears her man's going. Thinaimozhi 16: bees hum the paalai melody as the man leads the girl away.
teaches: The same sound of bees playing the paalai mode marks the spring of a parting in the Akananuru and the spring of an elopement in the venba, so the image does not carry a fixed mood but takes its grief or its promise from the uri it serves.

note: 1512 shows the hero lifting a gem mountain with both arms; 303 shows him as a youth rolling a rock heap that two hundred elephants might raise.
teaches: The boyhood feat of 303 is the first form of the strength that lifts Kotisilai, so the mountain is the proof of something already known.
