note: In 1996 Civakan praises Vimalai's breasts as enough to make the released fall; in 2671 the king, with women skilled in writing, song and dance, is called the love-god of the love-god.
teaches: The poem moves from a lover's praise of one woman to the poet's claim for the man among many, the height of pleasure just before the hero's renunciation.

note: Kural 5 says the two deeds do not cling to those devoted to the Lord's praise; the verse says they are burned in meditation.
teaches: The couplet makes freedom from the two deeds a gift of praise, and the verse makes it the fruit of effort, so the cause of release differs while the word for the two deeds is shared.

gains.a: the verse gets an older line that the two deeds can be shed, so its claim is not a private doctrine
gains.b: the couplet gets a story of how the deeds actually end, by burning in meditation and not by devotion

note: Verse 426 resolves to send a messenger to Tivittan's father to settle the match; verse 590 recalls that father speaking kindly, becoming kin and giving gifts.
teaches: The embassy's aim is reached only after a silence and an objection in 588 and 589, so the match is won and not simply given.

note: Kural 1228: the herdsman's sweet flute is evening's envoy and a killing weapon to the woman whose lover is away; 2050 is a sweet vina-song whose evening enters like a spear into a wound.
teaches: In the Kural sweet music wounds a woman because her lover is absent, while in the epic the lover himself plays the music to a woman who has no lover yet, so the evening-song creates the sickness it laments.

gains.a: the epic's song gains the Kural's figure of music as evening's weapon, which explains why a lament can work as a seduction
gains.b: the couplet gains a case where the weapon has a wielder with a purpose, turning the woman's complaint into a strategy someone else can use

note: Naladiyar 84 asks the adulterer what pleasure he had, since the act brings disgrace, a cut leg and long hell; 2769 sets the adulterer in hell with a glowing copper woman in his arms.
teaches: The quatrain names the price of the act and the epic shows the price paid, so the pleasure is seen turning into the pain it earned.

gains.a: the verse's embrace gains the quatrain's question about what pleasure was gained, which turns the scene into an argument
gains.b: the quatrain's phrase 'long hell' gains a specific image, the copper woman

note: 2789 sends those who revile ascetics and the sinful to animal birth; 943 tells a dog that, leaving its dog's body, it will gain a god's body through the mantra.
teaches: The same Cintamani shows rebirth moving down by sin and up by holy words, so an animal body is not final.

note: Kural 557 likens the king's lack of grace to the world's lack of rain; Kalittokai 10 likens the drought-dried waste to a world under a crooked-sceptred king whose men rob and kill.
teaches: The comparison runs both ways: the ethics book explains tyranny by drought and the love poet explains drought by tyranny, so the bond between bad rule and failed rain was common enough to be used as vehicle or as tenor.

note: 1706 has the moon enter the queen's mouth as the sign of Tivittan's son; 1730 has a gem come to the Vidyadhara wife in a dream and swell her breasts.
teaches: The poem uses the same dream of a bright thing entering the mother for two houses, so the Vidyadhara child's birth is told as a parallel of Tivittan's own.

note: The sage's rubbed-wood fire answers the executioner's claim that a cut body shows no life.
teaches: The story gives the materialist test and the Jain reply side by side, so the reader sees the argument as one of method: whether failing to see a thing on cutting shows that it is absent.

note: Vasavadatta's dream foretells a taking-away by a man, read by experts as a marriage; Kannaki's dream foretells the carrying off of her husband and a false charge.
teaches: A dream in these epics gives the story's course in advance, but the same image foretells a bridegroom in one poem and a ruin in the other.

gains.a: The Udayana verse gains a contrast in which a dream's reading is joyful and its reader is an expert, as against Kannaki's dread.
gains.b: The Silappathikaram passage gains a second story where the dream is read by others and comes true, so its dread is one case of a convention.

note: In 351 the widowed Vijayai strips her pearls, bangles and rings; here Nandattan reasons from Gandharvadattai's unremoved ornaments that Civakan lives.
teaches: The stripping of ornaments that the epic first showed as a widow's grief becomes, read backwards, a sign a kinsman can read, so jewels on a wife are public evidence of a living husband.

note: 1970 sends those who deny soul and rebirth to the nigoda state; Tirumanthiram 2558 sends those who say there is no higher state to hell.
teaches: Both texts answer denial with a bad end and not with argument, but one end is a lower birth and the other is hell.

gains.a: The Jain threat gains a Saiva twin, showing that sending the denier to a bad end is a shared habit of polemic.
gains.b: The Tirumanthiram's denial gains a content: the Soolamani says what is denied, the soul, rebirth and the difference of good and bad.

note: 1839 bids all remember the fruit of deeds; 1842 shows Payapati reasoning that the pleasure of his grandchildren is the fruit of swollen merit with more seed to sow.
teaches: The poet's general advice becomes a king's own reasoning, which turns the closing moral of one sarukkam into the opening act of the next.

note: Two prophecies by sages, one for the youth's Vidyadhara rule, one for his marriage and earthly rule.
teaches: The youth's promised rule is told from his side by one sage and from the bride's side by another, so the two prophecies fit together into a single destiny.

note: Verse 354 foretells that a youth who gives up rule will reach Indra's world for seventeen oceans of time; verse 560 has an ancestor who gives up rule take kevala and become rare even to the gods.
teaches: The renunciations in the story do not end alike: one ancestor goes past the gods, while the foretold youth first holds a god's seat.

note: The Naladiyar calls the meat-eater's belly a burning ground for beasts and birds; the Neelakesi places its flesh-eating demon hosts and a goddess's shrine inside a real burning ground.
teaches: The quatrain's metaphor joining flesh-eating and the cremation ground becomes the Neelakesi's literal scene, so the epic's first quarrel over flesh is staged where eating bodies and burning them meet.

note: Both call the Jain god a lamp: the Soolamani's சுடர் that stands as the world's light after the deeds are split, the Neelakesi's ancient lamp of dharma who knows all things.
teaches: The lamp is the Soolamani's god in the world above, the Neelakesi's god as the source of dharma, so the image moves from where he stands to what he teaches.

note: The king's right eye throbs as a good sign and his drums roar as he sets out; in the usurper's palace the women's right eyes throb, owls cry by day and the victory drum falls silent.
teaches: The poet gives the two camps the same signs with opposite values, the throbbing right eye good for the marching king and bad for the palace women, the drum loud in one and dumb in the other, so the omen code is read by sex and by side.

note: Both are men arguing with hearts set on wealth, and both make the desert's killers the argument: in 327 the archers pity no victim and grieve only when they miss; in 337 the Mazhavar kill a starving messenger in case he has gold and leave scorning his rags.
teaches: Side by side they show the road weighing a man's life only by what he might carry, which is the very reckoning the heart is making when it trades her company for wealth.

note: 1571 has the king test a gift-seeker by Vedic learning; Kural 134 says a Brahmin can relearn the Veda but loses his birth if conduct fails.
teaches: The king's test is of learning, and the couplet's is of conduct, so the jester's comic case falls under both and passes neither.

gains.a: The king's rule gains a rival test, so the gift is shown to rest on a narrow ground.
gains.b: The couplet gains a brahmin who has neither Veda nor conduct and appears at the king's court.

note: Kural 509 bids a ruler trust no one unexamined; the king vouches for Kattiyankaran by love and past victories and forbids further words.
teaches: Loyalty and battle service, the very grounds the king gives, are not the examination the couplet asks for, so the scene shows how trust can feel tested while skipping the test of fitness for power.

gains.a: the king's grounds for trust are measured against a stated rule and found to fall short of it
gains.b: the couplet's bare 'examine' is shown failing in a case where the examiner thinks he already knows the man

note: The Kural warns one who is about to oppress the weak to think how he stands before the stronger; Civakan sees that the strong seize the weak's wealth and draws not a rule for the strong but a reason to leave.
teaches: The warning that assumes a ruler who will listen is answered by a ruler who, having seen the same fact, withdraws from rule altogether.

gains.a: the verse's remark on the strong and weak gets a moral measure it lacks, a rule against oppressing the weak, so Civakan's renunciation reads as a response to a recognised wrong
gains.b: the couplet's appeal to a fear of the stronger is tested against a hero who owns power and finds that no fear or fairness but only leaving settles the matter

note: Verse 458 has men grant that the women's long dark eyes kill and bow to them; Naladiyar 44 refuses to call eyes spears or carp, since he has seen the eye is a scooped-out palm fruit.
teaches: The Soolamani gives the lover's image of the lethal eye a scene of surrender, and the Naladiyar answers with a renunciant who would not give way, so a reader sees the image only works on one who agrees to be struck.

gains.a: A refusal of the image of the killing eye, which the verse alone only enjoys.
gains.b: A scene in which men yield to the very image the renunciant's resolve is set against.

note: Both Jain epics describe a Vidyadhara city by its splendour, this one as a golden city on the southern ridge, the other as a casket of gems opened.
teaches: Both epics fix the Vidyadhara realm in the reader's mind as a city of gems and gold above the plain, so the genre's convention is clear from the pair.

note: Dharan vows to restore all without any deceit (வஞ்சமொன்று இன்றி); in 574 the Vidyadhara lord himself declares the storm was a deceit (வஞ்சம்).
teaches: The word that guarantees the promise is the word later used to explain the whole wreck, so the rescuer's honesty consists in undoing a lie he told.

note: 1962 gives the animals' pain at the killers' hands; Siddhar 269 gives the killers' own end, when Death seizes them for the sake of the body's pot.
teaches: The Siddhar says the killer will answer to Death, while the Soolamani implies what answering means: birth as the beast he hunted.

gains.a: The animals' sufferings gain a reckoning: the Siddhar shows who comes to answer for them, at death.
gains.b: The Siddhar's threat of Death gains a content: the Soolamani says what follows death, rebirth among the beasts.

note: The Kural has the son's merit read back as the father's tapas; the verse has the sage promise a virtuous son when the queen asks for tapas.
teaches: The Kural reads a son as the proof of a parent's penance and the verse reverses it, making the promised son the answer to a request for penance.

gains.a: the sage's answer gets an ordinary Tamil frame in which a son is a fruit of tapas, which clears the odd turn from tapas to son
gains.b: the couplet's 'what penance did his father do' is given a scene in which the penance is asked for and a son promised

note: 2841 says the middle sort of gift is paid by whatever one wishes in the land of enjoyment; Kural 222 says giving is good even if there were no higher world.
teaches: The Cintamani ties each gift to its reward, while the Kural cuts giving loose from reward by a hypothetical.

gains.a: the verse's rewards (wishing trees for the middle gift) are shown as one of the things the Kural's hypothetical sets aside
gains.b: the Kural's hypothetical gets a full account of the other-worldly rewards it asks us to imagine away

note: 1383 asks whether the flesh body must break for honour's sake; Kural 969 says the honourable give up life when honour is lost.
teaches: The epic's taunt tests the Kural's rule on men who run, showing it as a shaming speech to the living where the couplet states a private resolve.

gains.a: gains a measure for its taunt: honour is set above life as a standard
gains.b: gains a spoken use in battle, where the rule becomes a challenge hurled at cowards

note: The teaching the ascetics arrive to give in 318 is heard in 323.
teaches: Verse 318 only names the ascetics' skills and arrival; verse 323 shows what their teaching says, that life is a fearful bondage.

note: In Rajamapuram the king saw that the dancer's longing had gone to Civakan and went in with resentment; in Chandirapam the prince follows the dancer's gaze to Civakan and is glad.
teaches: The poem stages the same scene twice, a ruler reading a dancer's eyes fixed on Civakan, and makes the ruler's response the measure of him: jealous enmity in the usurper's city, affection and alliance in the Pallava court.

note: Kattiyankaran bowed and vowed to bear the yoke of rule blamelessly for Saccandan; now he offers his life and owns Govindan as lord.
teaches: The minister's vow of loyal service, already broken once, is reused word for word in spirit as bait, so the story teaches the reader to weigh his pledges by what followed the first one.

note: Wealth does not come across seas and mountains without fortune, and may come home to those who go not a cubit; the couplet says what is not one's own will not stay and what is will not leave.
teaches: The epic draws the practical conclusion the couplet leaves unsaid: if wealth is the share fortune gives, the effort spent seeking it is better spent on tapas.

gains.a: the couplet's flat rule about fate that grounds why effort for wealth is not the safe course
gains.b: a seafaring merchant's world of crossings and sickness, which the couplet gives no instance of, and a use for the rule in recommending tapas

note: In the Silappathikaram the Pandya, inquiring into nothing, orders the guards to kill the thief and bring the anklet (கொன்றச் சிலம்பு கொணர்க); in 1080 the angry king's men run to kill and bring Civakan's life (கொன்றுயிர் கொணர) on a mahout's word.
teaches: The same unexamined order to kill and bring yields Kovalan's death and the bent sceptre in one epic but only a binding in the other, because Civakan chooses submission and a god he once helped intervenes; the Cintamani turns the scene of ripened evil into one where restraint and past kindness turn it aside.

note: The king reasoned that desire wastes the body and fame; the queen's body is wasted.
teaches: His reasoning from the night of the tryst is borne out on her body, which turns a private resolve into a visible fact.

claims.gist: birds crossing the path and ill signs are warnings of coming harm
kin are parted by the working of deeds and no companionship is lasting
attachment to kin brings pain, so it should be given up
giving safety to all lives and abstaining from killing, theft, lust, lying and possession keeps dark karma from joining
the fruit of keeping the Lord's dharma is the joy of the gods' world
a king sees through ministers, hears through spies and speaks through envoys
to blame former deeds and sulk when fortune turns is not wisdom
men of low station rise to greatness by accumulating small gains
a teacher who forms one is a father, and his penance a mother
the worth of things is not fixed but turns good or bad with their condition
the king is the life of the world, as rice and water are the life of men
a woman is great who is born to see such a man, and loses her bloom for desire
what is by nature fleeting is not to be cherished as one's own wealth
the liberated soul has endless knowledge, perception, energy and bliss and goes up to the upper world
the union of loving partners is worth more than the state of release from death and birth
those who die in attachment go on to many births
the loss of her husband came from the ripening of her own deeds
joy in this life is the fruit of austerity done before, and such fruit does not fail
when both kinds of deeds are gone nothing further arises, and release is the one road of the great ascetics
true seeing, knowledge and conduct faithful to the scripture are the means the Lord taught
those who have done no penance have no way to reach what they long for
a king who sets his sovereignty upon a single man drives prosperity from his land
hearing and holding the five sacred padas washes away dark karma and wins a god's birth
a god born in heaven knows his past state by clairvoyant knowledge (avadhi)
a cruel sceptre spreads darkness over the land
every heaven lies at the Jina's feet and the wheel of grace goes before the rest
the Jina is the father of the sages who hold the rare scripture
a king who takes revenue in measure keeps the treasure flowing, while one who grabs ruins the field
those who honour ascetics become lords of the gods and those who scorn them fall to the lowest hell
the holy ones are without favour or anger, like shade that shelters whoever comes
women lack inner restraint and yield to persistent pressing

note: Naladiyar 137 doubts that the city of those in the wide heaven is sweeter than learned men gathering and laughing together; verse 279 praises a heaven-like realm that only the meritorious can enter.
teaches: The quatrain tests the heaven the epic praises against the pleasure of a company of the learned, and the epic's heaven is praised for its senses while the quatrain finds its sweetness no better than conversation.

gains.a: A measure to doubt its own claim: a pleasure the Naladiyar sets against heaven's.
gains.b: A full picture of the heaven it weighs, which is the one this verse and its neighbours describe.

note: Konganar's Vaalaik Kummi counts going to foreign lands (தேசாந்திரங்களும் செல்லாதே) among things to avoid, with facing a tiger in the forest and courtesans' ways; Civakan calls those who never leave home fish in a well and sets out, and the god's road then holds elephant forests and ghoul-women.
teaches: On the same question, whether to go to other lands, the Siddhar's caution and the hero's resolve give opposite advice, and the epic's road is made of exactly the dangers the Siddhar lists, so the epic treats them as the hero's schooling rather than a reason to stay; the conflict holds only if the kummi's line is read as general advice and not as a rule for the adept alone.

gains.a: the hero's departure is seen as a choice against a known prudential rule, not a mere plot device
gains.b: the kummi's terse prohibition gets its strongest counter-case, a traveller whom the dangers it names do not ruin

note: Udayanan stands under a rain of arrows and answers with his bow; the couplet gives the bull elephant under a sheaf of arrows.
teaches: The couplet's elephant only stands firm; Udayanan stands firm and also shoots back, so endurance in the story includes acting.

gains.a: the defence gets a name for the quality shown, steadiness when things fall apart
gains.b: the couplet's image gets a man who stands and answers where the elephant only stands

note: In 1148 Acuvakandan boasts of turning mountains and rolling the world; Tirumanthiram 1686 lists burning with anger and boasting of greatness among what is not the nature of one near the Lord.
teaches: The Saiva list names as marks of the unripe what the epic's rival king shows as his great-hearted rage.

gains.a: the epic's boast is classed by a Saiva text among the faults that mark a man far from the Lord, a reading the Jain narrator never states
gains.b: the list of faults gets a king in whom anger, scheming and boasting of greatness all appear together

note: The Kural commands making wealth as the sharpest weapon; the hero leaving for wealth that is hard to earn counts what the going costs the girl he leaves.
teaches: The Kural's bare imperative to make wealth is weighed here against a girl's quoted plea not to stay long, showing that the duty the maxim states without condition was, in akam, always paid for by someone left behind.

note: 1445 is a boast of what the speaker is; 1448 answers that this is talk among his own band.
teaches: Boast and reply are a pair: the boast is judged by where it is spoken, not what it says.

note: The couplet says nothing that can be gained equals wise children; Civakan counts children among the gainable and sets a brother beyond gain.
teaches: Civakan's list puts children with wealth and wives among the things a man can acquire, and names the brother as the one bond that cannot be got at all, a value the Kural's ranking of gains has no place for.

gains.a: the epic verse gains the Kural's frame of 'things that can be gained', which shows how far his praise goes in placing the brother outside it
gains.b: the couplet gains a rival answer, from kinship by birth rather than by begetting, to its question of the greatest gain

note: The Puram queen refuses to be one of the widows who go unanointed, eat cooked leaves and sleep on gravel, and chooses the pyre; Vijayai lives that very widow's life, unanointed, on greens (354), as a Jain ascetic.
teaches: The life the Sangam queen scorns as the wretched alternative to the pyre is the one the Jain epic gives its queen as a penance lived for a son, so the two show the widow's choice valued in opposite ways.

gains.a: the epic's unanointed ascetic gains the older measure by which her survival was the lesser choice, sharpening why she lives on: for her son
gains.b: the Puram poem gains a widow who takes the 'leaf-food' life deliberately and turns it into austerity, a reply its speaker does not imagine

note: 2776 sends those bent on killing into hell on the cars of their sins; Kural 321 says killing brings all other evil deeds with it.
teaches: The couplet states killing as the root of other wrongs, and the epic adds the journey to hell as its end.

gains.a: the verse gains a rule naming killing as the first of all sins, which it presupposes
gains.b: the couplet gains a picture of where such deeds lead, which it leaves unsaid

note: Vegavati's trick in 261 is carried out as a disguise in 262.
teaches: The guile that was only named in 261 is shown as taking the very form of the woman Naravahanan is looking for, which turns his search into the means of her plan.

note: The patikam's 28 says that his brother, companions and wives renounced and the master of the vina went to the unequalled state; here the same hero laughs with delight at a ghoul dressing in the slain.
teaches: The Jain epic lets its hero relish slaughter fully before it turns him to renunciation, so the release it promises in 28 is a turning from a violence he once enjoyed, not from one he never knew.

note: 2951 has the wives ask whether he will cast them off, while 1097 has him say he will not melt in grief and that even a sesame-seed of attachment is a fault.
teaches: His own earlier teaching to weeping women is now turned on him by wives who ask for what he then refused to grant.

note: The Kural trusts the concurring word of three spies who do not know one another; the friends' three spies come back together (ஒன்றி) with one report.
teaches: The epic keeps the Kural's number three but drops its safeguard of mutual ignorance, showing a band of friends using the statecraft rule loosely, with trust in place of cross-checking.

gains.a: the friends' three spies are seen to follow a recognised rule of intelligence rather than a chance number
gains.b: the couplet's condition that spies not know one another stands out once a story shows three who arrive together

note: 1967 says that those who take austerity and then practise deceit are born as beasts; Kural 274 pictures the false ascetic as a hunter hidden in a bush, snaring birds.
teaches: In the Kural the hypocrite hunts the innocent, and the Soolamani turns him into the hunted: the same fault, paid back in the animal's birth.

gains.a: The hypocrite's rebirth gains an image of what he did: the hunter in hiding whom the Kural names.
gains.b: The Kural's hunter gains a sequel: the epic says what becomes of him, since it is the beast's form.

note: Purananuru 55.1-2 (மலைப் பெருவில் பாம்புஞாண் ... ஒரு கணை ... மூவெயில்) and Paripadal 5.24-25 (நாகம் நாணா, மலை வில்லாக, மூவகை ஆர் எயில் ஓர் அழல்-அம்பின்) give the three-forts deed in the same parts: mountain bow, serpent string, one arrow; both also turn on Siva's forehead eye.
teaches: The same tripura formula serves a puram poet as the vehicle of counsel to a Pandya king and a devotional poet as the prelude to Murugan's birth, showing that Siva's deed was common stock usable for statecraft and worship alike in the Sangam period.

note: Civakan's acceptance in 484 turns on an obscure kinship word; at 489 he receives the gift water on behalf of Padumukan.
teaches: Read from 489, Civakan's quick acceptance was always an acceptance for his friend, which lets him keep both Nandagon's honour and his own rule of rank.

note: Tirumular's dead man has his nine gates shut while the loving ones weep and leave; the Cintamani's dying lover has his eyes closed by the beloved and goes.
teaches: The epic turns Tirumular's unnamed mourners into the very women of the man's pleasures, so the lovers who melt in his arms are those who close his eyes, which joins the critique of desire to the meditation on death.

gains.a: the epic's refrain gains the Saiva verse's frame of the body's impermanence, showing the lover's death as one case of a general account of the body's end
gains.b: Tirumular's 'loving ones' (அன்புடையார்) are given a particular identity, the beloved of the bed, which makes his mourning scene a rebuke to desire as well as to attachment

note: The king introduced with a gracious sceptre and a single command is, some sixty verses later, the king who slips from guarding the land to cling to his queen.
teaches: The poet sets out the full catalogue of a just king's marks so that the reader can measure how far this king falls from them.

note: The prince wins at dice from the kings, as the Kural warns that what a gambler wins is like the hook's metal in the fish.
teaches: The Kural treats winning as the lure; the epic gives a winner who is not caught by it because he gives the winnings back, which shows the rule is about the winner's grip on the goods.

gains.a: The prince's win gains a measure: it is the keeping of the winnings, not the playing, that the couplet condemns.
gains.b: The couplet's warning gains a hard case, a winner who takes nothing, which tests whether the warning is about the game or the hunger.

note: Verse 1 praises the god of gods who reached by himself (தன்னின் எய்தி) the supreme bliss that does not fail; verse 29 ends the patikam with Civakan in a flood of bliss (இன்ப வெள்ளம்).
teaches: The patikam opens on a god who won unfailing bliss by his own effort and closes on a man who reaches a flood of bliss, so the hero's whole story is framed as walking the road the worshipped one walked, not as receiving a gift from him.

note: Purananuru 369 sings the Chera's battle as a season of tillage, arrows for rain, heads for crop, ghouls threshing; 757 uses the same sowing-and-harvest field, with ghosts fed on flesh and blood, as a warning to rivals before the fight.
teaches: The bard's after-battle praise image, sung to earn a gift, becomes in the epic a combatant's threat spoken before a blow is struck, so the convention moves from rewarding a victory to predicting one.

gains.a: the full Sangam convention of the battlefield as a farm, which the verse compresses into four lines without naming it
gains.b: a use of the convention outside the bard's request for gifts, as an argument about who deserves a bride

note: Kural 559 says that when a ruler bends justice the sky bends the rain; verse 263 says that a cruel king is to the world as a sea-scorching sun is to its creatures.
teaches: The Kural names rain as the lost gift, but the epic names the people's suffering as the creatures' in a burning sea, so the ruler's fault is one of heat, not drought.

gains.a: The measure of the loss: not a missed crop but life in a sea turned hostile, which the Kural's line does not give.
gains.b: A different figure for the same fault, in which the injured are creatures with nowhere to go, not a land that goes dry.

note: Kural 385 names a king as one able to create, gather, guard and apportion wealth; verse 626 gives the same four acts and says it is the learned man who becomes the protector of others.
teaches: The couplet's four tasks are tied to learning, so the verse makes the king's wealth-work depend on what he has studied.

gains.a: The verse lacks a compact statement that these four acts define rule, which the couplet gives.
gains.b: The couplet lacks the condition that only the learned can do it, which the verse adds.

note: 2127 calls the lord who has conquered his enemies the crest-jewel of the world; Soolamani 1 opens by praising the one who conquered the whole sum of his deeds and now stands as a shining form.
teaches: The close of the poem answers its opening, so the praise promised at the start is now earned by the war just fought.

note: Two hymns to the Jina in neighbouring episodes: the woman's song in 1467 warns that those who do not praise will not reach release; Civakan's hymn argues that praise follows from what the Lord is.
teaches: Held together, the two hymns show the epic grounding worship two ways, as a condition of release in the singer's warning and as the only fitting answer to the Lord's nature in Civakan's reasoning, so praise is both means and response.

note: The patikam's line வஞ்சம் மறவர் நிரை வள்ளல் விடுத்த வாறும் announces that the liberal one freed the herd from deceitful hunters; 451 to 455 tell it, ending with the herd turned by the bow's sound and no man lost.
teaches: The patikam's word வள்ளல் for the rescuer of a herd only makes sense once the telling shows a recovery that is given back to its owners without loss, so the summary's epithet anticipates the bloodless manner of the deed.

note: The epic arms the wall with self-acting engines and names no defender; the Kural says every excellence of a fort is nothing without men excellent in action.
teaches: The epic's picture of a wall that fights by its own machinery is exactly the kind of fort the couplet calls empty, so the Kural supplies the missing term by which this lavish security can fail.

gains.a: the catalogue of engines gains a standard that shows what it leaves out: the people who must work them
gains.b: the couplet's unnamed excellences of a fort gain a concrete inventory of what a later poet thought those excellences were

note: Neduncheliyan swears that if he fails to take the kings who scorned him, the poets led by Mangudi Marutan may cease to sing of his land; Civakan swears that if he fails to bring the raiders to bow before the king, his name may not go out in the world of song.
teaches: The epic keeps the Purananuru's vanjinam form, a war vow whose penalty is the loss of poets' praise, but its hero swears it for another man's king and against raiders who prove to be his friends, so the oath of fame becomes a set piece the plot quietly empties.

gains.a: Civakan's vow gains its form: the vanjinam kanchi self-curse, which shows his oath stakes the same thing a Sangam king staked, fame in song
gains.b: the Purananuru vow gains a later life in which the curse is softened into a love simile and sworn by a hero in exile on a host's behalf

note: Kural 1130: he lives joyfully in her heart, while the town says he is unloving and lives apart; Kuruntokai 289: she grieves for him out in the rain, and the clamouring town grieves for her more.
teaches: In both the woman's thought goes out to the absent man while the town's goes to her plight, but the town's verdict differs, blame in the Kural and pity in the poem, so the town's talk in akam is not fixed as hostile gossip and can be her chorus.

note: 2130 shows the dark and white princes worshipping under the lotus feet of the liberated lord; Soolamani 2 says the story is of the one who in an earlier day went to him for refuge.
teaches: The refuge sought at the beginning becomes the festival of worship at the end, which gives the story a completed arc.

note: 2018 has the lamp of vision end the darkness of deeds; Naladiyar 51 has the lamp of austerity end sin as darkness dies, and darkness return when the oil runs out.
teaches: The lamp's light is credited to vision in the epic and to austerity in the quatrain, with only the quatrain saying the light can fail.

gains.a: The lamp of vision gains the warning of the oil, that light can go out unless fed.
gains.b: The quatrain's lamp gains a source in the knowing of the true thing, where it names only austerity.

note: Padumai asks for the lute lessons that verse 103 gave Vasavadatta.
teaches: The lute lessons that began Vasavadatta's tie to Udayanan are now claimed by a second wife, so the same craft becomes a place where two wives are measured.

note: In both the sulking woman's charge turns on eyes: in the Kural all women feast on the man with theirs, in the Cintamani the women say his loves are in his eyes, and refuse him.
teaches: The Kural keeps the eye-charge inside the couple's quarrel, while the epic lets the same charge end in snapped girdles and spilled gold, so the sulk becomes a sign of the city's wealth rather than a turn in a love.

gains.a: the epic's brief quoted words are recognised as a set move of the sulking wife
gains.b: the couplet's private reproach is shown being absorbed into public description of a prosperous land

note: The brothers destroy both deeds by meditating on the soul, where Tirumular says the worshipped fire burns up deeds.
teaches: The two accounts reach the same freedom from deeds by different agents, the practitioner's own meditation against a fire that burns them, so the dispute is over who does the burning.

gains.a: the brothers' liberation is set against a view that gives the work to a worshipped fire
gains.b: Tirumular's fire is shown to have a rival account in which no fire is needed

note: Kural 3 places the god on a flower and says those who reach his feet live long on the earth; the hymn has the lord seated on a lotus and promises Indra's rank to those who worship his feet.
teaches: Both couplet and hymn set the god on a flower and promise a reward for reaching the feet, but the hymn's reward is rank in heaven while the couplet's is long life on earth.

gains.a: the hymn's lotus-seated lord is seen as a Jain case of the flower-borne god of the Kural's opening
gains.b: the couplet's reward of long life on earth is set beside a hymn that pays in heaven's rank

note: Neelakesi argues in debate that trees live, as their change with the seasons shows; the Cintamani's narrator says the same from their flowering at a woman's glance.
teaches: The Jain thesis that plants live appears both as a debater's proof and as a narrator's aside in a love scene, showing the doctrine was common enough to be argued from a poetic convention.

note: Kural 1224: with the lover absent, evening comes like enemies to a killing ground. Ezhupathu 17: as kodal buds and thunder greet the rains, the little evening comes like killers so that those with no one to embrace them tremble.
teaches: The Kural's image of evening as executioner, spoken by one woman of one absent man, appears in the Ezhupathu tied to the rainy season and widened to a class (those with no one to hold them), which shows the image was a mullai convention of the promised-return season before or beside its use as a private complaint.

note: Verse 934 shows the king's white umbrella raised in the ride that cools the world; Kural 389 says the world lives under the umbrella of a king who can bear bitter words.
teaches: The umbrella cools only for a king who has the character the Kural names, which the display of the ride cannot show.

gains.a: The verse lacks the condition of character that makes the umbrella a shelter.
gains.b: The couplet lacks any picture of the umbrella in its pomp as the world sees it.

note: Vijayai once wept alone in the burning-ground forest for her lord; in her brother's palace she is the one who ends the household's weeping.
teaches: The widow whose solitary grief the poem dwelt on now stands among her own kin and stops their lament, so her restraint marks the turn from mourning to the counsel of revenge.

note: In 1963 Vimalai holds that restraint and desire cannot coexist; in 1964 she stands steadying herself with restraint while desire seizes her.
teaches: Her rule that restraint and desire exclude each other is contradicted at once by the story, which shows a woman holding restraint and burning with desire at the same moment.

note: The father bought a king's order to keep men from his daughter; now that a suitor asks for her he can neither accept nor refuse.
teaches: His wealth could shut out a whole city's men but cannot settle a single proposal, and he falls back on the lack of past penance to explain a bind his money made.

note: Verse 237 says that without counsel a king's life does not flourish and that even Indra's lordship rests on a thousand counsellors; verse 250 has the king himself rank counsel above his other powers.
teaches: The poet's maxim about counsel becomes the king's own weighing of counsel against his other powers, so the section turns a reflection into a decision.

note: Naladiyar 110 says what was fixed at the start neither shrinks nor grows, so why grieve in ruin; 269 says birth and death come from one's own deeds and grief is want of understanding.
teaches: Both forbid grief by appeal to a fixed outcome, but the king speaks while his own fault caused the ruin, so in his mouth deed-fruit is also a confession, which the Naladiyar's impersonal fixed mark is not.

gains.a: the king's consolation is placed within the ethical books' argument against grieving
gains.b: the quatrain's fixed fate is set beside a version in which the fixing is one's own past action

note: The Jain hymn calls the Jina the one who scorched Kama; Tirumular makes the destruction of Kama's work Siva's yoga at Korukkai.
teaches: The pair shows two traditions claiming the same feat for their own lord and reading it the same inward way, as desire overcome in austerity, so the rivalry is over who did it, not over what it means; the tension holds only if the epithet is read as a title one lord alone may bear.

gains.a: the epic hymn gains the Saiva background against which giving the Kama-burning to the Jina is a pointed claim, not a stock epithet
gains.b: Tirumular's verse gains a rival who claims the same conquest of Kama without a god's grace, by the Jina's own discipline and compassion

claims.gist: good penance outweighs all the wealth of the world
Fortune stays with the one who lets go and never clings to the one who holds on
the soul has taken countless bodies in the realm of animals under the fire of its deeds
one who destroys the two kinds of deed reaches the world of bliss
youth and life wither as a leaf does, yet the unwise ignore it
lords who bear the lapses of the lowly are followed and honoured by the whole earth
houses equal in lineage and wealth should be joined in marriage
the Vidyadhara king descends from Nami, son of the king of Kasi
a girl's desire is known only by love, not by an outsider's reckoning
in a woman's marriage one should follow the way of those versed in the treatise
giving food to the hungry bears fruit in a later birth as a king
adultery is punished by the burning embrace of a red-hot image
Right vision (darsana) shakes off the stain of heavy deeds
the goddess of wealth leaves those she has joined and longs for new men
the faults of a poet's work do not count before the good, as the moon's spot does not stop its worship
women's hearts, like enemies' hearts, do not run straight
beggary now is the fruit of never having given
outcomes arise from deeds, and one who understands this gains true companions and joy
only the noble share what they have with others
deeds produce further deeds and a fruit that is to be shunned
a warrior who dies helping the master who sustained him wins heaven's women, poets' praise and a hero-stone
nothing offered should be accepted until its purity has been examined
great kings make themselves ridiculous by raging against lowly foes
merit done in earlier days helps in the present and brings plans to success
a soldier who carries arms must win on the field or die as a feast for the gods
the soul is a being of great undivided knowledge, grasped by the mind
wealth and pleasure sought without mercy, at the cost of lives, bring ruin

note: 1356 spends the perishing body for fame that stands for ever; Kural 233 holds that nothing in the world stands undying except renown.
teaches: The epic's call to a warrior to give up his body for fame puts into action the couplet's claim, and shows who is asked to pay for it.

gains.a: The verse gains the couplet's flat claim that only renown does not die, which it uses as its reason.
gains.b: The couplet gains a scene where the price of that renown is a warrior's body in the heat of a rout.

note: The king refuses all suitors, citing a seer's word and the destined time; the patikam names among the episodes how the Vidyadhara king's daughter was defeated at the vina.
teaches: The patikam already tells the outcome the king says no one can prevent, so the father's appeal to destiny is answered by the epic's own plan: the destined man is the hero.

note: The king sends Chandakarma into the city to seek the twin children, and the youth and maiden in ascetic dress enter that city.
teaches: The search for victims and the entry of the pair meet in the city, so the dress of renunciation, put on in verse 27, is what brings them into the king's hands.

note: 1697 has the envoy take the letter, wait for the king's order and then bow and speak; Kural 687 says the best envoy knows the protocol, the moment and the place.
teaches: The epic shows an envoy in the sequence of bows, seating, gifts and leave to speak that the couplet names but does not show.

gains.a: The scene gains a standard by which the envoy's waiting and bowing read as skill and not only as courtesy.
gains.b: The couplet gains a concrete order of events in which an envoy shows he knows protocol and time.

note: Kural 1103 asks whether the world of the lotus-eyed one can be sweeter than sleeping on the beloved's soft arms; verse 1049 sets the lovers' union above the state without birth and death.
teaches: The Soolamani friend raises the Kural's comparison from a god's heaven to release itself, the goal her own Jain work teaches.

gains.a: The verse lacks a model for weighing love against the highest good, which the Kural's open question gives.
gains.b: The couplet lacks the case where the thing weighed against love is release from birth, not a heaven.

note: In 261 the usurper planned to kill the king who was sunk in pleasure with his queen; in 2610 Vijayai tells her son that the king was swallowed by pleasure as the moon by the serpent and would not take counsel.
teaches: The ruin that the poet told as a plot is retold by the survivor as the king's own failing, so the reader sees that the epic gives both the plotter's cunning and the king's desire as the cause.

note: In 1574 Civakan, tempted, asks his heart whether a world of women's pleasure ending in death is good; in 27 he hears the dharma and renounces.
teaches: The pair shows that the hero's renunciation has a rehearsal mid-story, but here the reflection serves only to keep his restraint against one woman, and he goes on to marry again, so the epic separates thinking renunciation from doing it.

note: The king's vow in 171 to remove the foes is carried out in 172 by Udayanan's army.
teaches: The vow is kept by the guest and not by the host, so the alliance in this chapter runs on Udayanan's arms.

note: Kural 1060 says the asker must not be angry; 196, after naming the king's fault, blesses his sons and leaves.
teaches: The poet shows how the Kural's demand for an asker without anger can be met without silence: he names the fault plainly and still blesses, so rebuke and the absence of anger are shown to go together.

note: The fire set in verse 136 has its effect in the king's collapse in 139.
teaches: The tunnel and fire are not an end: their purpose is the king's belief, and verse 139 shows him believing it.

note: Kural 745 praises a fort that is hard to take, holds stored food and is easy for those inside to hold; 44 tells a besieged king that sitting secure behind shut gates and a long wall is shameful while his elephants starve and his people cry for milk and water. On the reading that both judge the king who holds out in a fort, they disagree.
teaches: The Kural values the fort as a means of holding out, while Kovur Kizhar sees the same holding out from inside, through starving beasts and infants, and calls it neither aram nor maram, so the pair shows the fort's strength and its moral cost as two views of one siege.

note: The Naladiyar says the same wedding drums that sound in the hall may be funeral drums that very day; here a wedding drum thunders for seven days and the city is told to live.
teaches: The Cintamani's wedding drum is heard here only as joy, while the Naladiyar hears in the same sound the fragility of the groom's life, so the two give opposing readings of the same instrument.

gains.a: the epic's drum gets a shadow of impermanence which the Jain poet leaves unspoken here but may mean the reader to carry from the epic's end
gains.b: the Naladiyar's warning is given a concrete scene of seven days of festival to be undone, not only the bare image of a drum

note: 2884 asks whether the kin he cannot be rid of are kin or enemies; 2885 answers that they are neither, being strangers in past births and in those to come.
teaches: The answer is a rebirth argument and not a complaint, so the question of kin turns on how many lives one counts.

note: Verse 902 orders gate-arches, gold pots and a decorated city; verse 923 carries the order on to saffron and sandal mud, aloe smoke and gold powder.
teaches: The wedding is prepared in stages, from the frame of the city to its scent, and the second order goes beyond what the first asked.

note: Kural 215 likens the wise man's wealth to a full village tank everyone draws from; verse 106 has the inner city's families bring wealth from overseas islands and feed many (பலர்க்கு ஆர்த்தி).
teaches: The couplet says shared wealth is like a common tank but not where it comes from; the epic supplies the source in perilous sea trade and makes feeding many the mark that justifies calling the city heavenly.

gains.a: the epic's praise of wealth is given an ethical test, that the wealth is used to fill many
gains.b: the couplet's image of a public tank gains a whole merchant class acting it out

note: The Cintamani's wall is armed by Yavana engines that throw molten metal, arrows and stones outward; Kural 747 names three ways a fort is taken, the third (அறைப்படுத்தல்) by working on those inside.
teaches: Read together, the two show that the epic's elaborate machinery answers only the outward assaults of the couplet's list, leaving the inside danger by which this city is in fact lost to its own minister.

gains.a: the engine catalogue acquires an ironic edge, since the couplet names the threat no machine can meet
gains.b: the couplet's abstract third danger gets a concrete case of a fully armed city whose defences all face outward

note: In Akananuru 151 the woman reports the man's reason that the poor cannot support dependents or laugh among kin, and says his heart has set grace aside; verse 44 gives the same reason, feeding kin's hunger, as one no one could fault.
teaches: The argument for leaving to earn wealth is the same in both, but the akam poem lets the one left behind weigh it against grace, while the fragment's voice treats it as needing no answer.

note: The narrator says her adorned beauty would bewilder even the steady; the Tirumanthiram tells the heart to turn from women who smile and show their breasts, as the etti tree's fruit is good to look at and not to eat.
teaches: The narrator and the Saiva teacher agree that adorned beauty overcomes the heart, but the narrator offers it as wonder and the teacher as a poison to resist.

gains.a: a remedy, the turning away of the heart, which the narrator names as a sickness but does not prescribe for
gains.b: an instance of beauty so dressed and so praised that the warning is tested against the strongest case, not left as a general rule

note: Kural 978 opposes greatness that bows to smallness that admires itself; the paddy simile sets the base man's erect wealth and the learned man's bow in one stalk at two ages.
teaches: The pair shows that the bow and the raised head can be stages of one thing rather than two kinds of people: what stands erect is empty, and the same stalk bows once it is full.

gains.a: a general maxim that its farm image is illustrating, which lifts the last verse of the chapter into a lesson
gains.b: a picture of how the change from pride to humility happens, by ripening, which the couplet's fixed opposition does not show

note: The Kural says one who tends his guests becomes a good guest of those in the sky; Vipulan calls his challenger a guest and gives him the first blow, and it is the guest, killed, who goes to heaven.
teaches: Read with the couplet, the duel inverts its exchange: in the Kural the host earns heaven by feeding the guest, while on the battlefield the host's hospitality is the first stroke, and heaven goes to the guest he kills.

gains.a: the word விருந்து in a duel is shown to carry the full weight of the guest-ethic, so the courtesy is not a figure of speech
gains.b: the couplet's tie between hosting and heaven is seen working in a setting it never imagines, where the guest is an enemy and the welcome is death

note: 1465 says that the man who came yesterday under the umbrella is felled today; Kural 336 says the world's greatness is that one who was here yesterday is not here today.
teaches: The verse gives a king's fall as the proof of the couplet and adds that the end comes by his own weapon, so impermanence is shown with a cause the couplet leaves out.

gains.a: 1465 shows the fall but lacks the couplet's plain statement that loss between yesterday and today is the world's greatness.
gains.b: The couplet is an abstract rule and gains a king felled by his own discus as a case.

note: 1816 places a king at Urandai among swans, drums and banners; Akananuru 385 uses Uranthai as the standard of a house rich in festival.
teaches: Urandai is the name of wealth in both books, so the herald's list of its splendours carries a meaning already known from the Sangam poem.

gains.a: The epic city gains an earlier use of its name as a measure of richness.
gains.b: The Akam poem gains a king's side of the city, whose wealth it uses only as a comparison.

note: Consoling the queen, the king asks whether a dream's nature is truth; at 267 he tells her the dreams have all come true.
teaches: The king's dismissal of dreams was comfort he did not believe, since the same man had read the dream by the treatise and later concedes its truth.

note: Naladiyar 51 says that sin cannot stand before austerity as darkness dies when a lamp comes, and returns when the oil runs out; 2745 asks for grace as a flame that will clear the darkness of the evil deed.
teaches: The quatrain gives the lamp's work a limit, since the dark returns, which raises the question whether the grace Civakan asks is a lasting cure.

gains.a: the verse's flame of grace gains the quatrain's warning that a lamp clears darkness only while it burns, which makes the plea more urgent
gains.b: the quatrain's lamp of austerity is put into the mouth of a king asking for it, and is thus a gift sought from another and not only a thing one earns

note: 1387 shows an unnamed youth in ornaments; 1390 gives his name and sets his kin's host moving.
teaches: The description of the youth and the report of his name together show that one hero is both the sight and the cause of the army's rising.

note: In 1488 Civakan says one woman's beauty made her an enemy to Murugan, Kama, himself and the matted-haired god; here he praises the Jina who scorched Kama.
teaches: The same hero who, newly in love, ranked Kama among those a woman's beauty conquers, now, having left that woman, praises the one who conquered Kama, so the hymn marks the swing in Civakan between desire and its mastery that the ilampakams keep repeating.

note: Kural 342 says renounce while there is something to renounce, and many things come after; 3016 has the Jina tell a king, who has the most to give up, that renunciation is the excellent course.
teaches: The Kural counsels renunciation in general and never says who it is hardest for, and the verse sets it before a crowned king as the hardest case.

gains.a: the Jina's counsel to the king gets a general rule that one can renounce only what one still holds, which is why the king's case is the gravest
gains.b: the Kural's bare 'renounce while it is yours' gets a concrete test, a ruler with a whole kingdom to give up

note: Both prize what brackish ground or brine produces: the Naladiyar's salt above rice from good fields, the Cintamani's coral, conch and pearl though they taste of the sea.
teaches: The Naladiyar argues that a person's low origin does not lower his learning, and the Cintamani applies the same reasoning to a poem's faulty diction, so the brine image carries one argument about worth and origin from persons to texts.

gains.a: the apology is seen resting on an argument the ethics books had already made about rank
gains.b: the quatrain's claim about birth is shown extending to the standing of a work and its words

note: 2614 tells in Vijayai's words how Kattiyangaran conquered the kings and sent her off by the peacock machine; in 2726 Civakan sets him beside the monkey who seized the fruit and himself beside the one who lost it.
teaches: The old usurpation, told as injury in the mother's tale, becomes in the monkey scene an instance of seizing and losing that teaches the hero how little taking or holding is worth.

note: In 2052 she resolves to worship Anangan and win a boon; in 2058 the boon is granted aloud, by a man's voice she takes for the god's.
teaches: The boon she set out to win is granted, but by Civakan's companions, so the plot turns the god's grace into a human contrivance the narrator names as deceit.

note: In 314 a deity took the form of the hunchback Chanbakamalai, the maid who never left Vijayai's side; in 358 the deity leaves under the errand she gave it, calling its own guise a deceit.
teaches: The disguise that gave the queen comfort in her worst hour is the same means by which she is left alone, and the deity's own word for it, வஞ்சித்தேன், admits the cost of a kindness worked by pretence.

note: 3098 gives the bad deed a child nursed by anger and desire; 3099 gives the good deed a child nursed by compassion.
teaches: The two verses pair the same upbringing image so that the difference between kinds of deed lies in what feeds them.

note: The patikam sums up the Takka episode as living with the merchant's daughter as one life and then leaving her; here the leaving is told.
teaches: The patikam's bare 'he left her' becomes a stealthy departure from a sleeping bride, so the summary's single verb hides the secrecy the story stresses.

note: The king consents to the flour-cock offering his mother proposes.
teaches: His doubt in 144 shows the loophole of 142 does not satisfy even the one who takes it, which prepares the cry at 146.

note: The Naladiyar gives it as a rule that kings who rode in state are carried off and spoken of as dead; here a king's sword snaps and he is seized, but he is afterwards to be rescued.
teaches: The Naladiyar's rule of the ruined proud king is true of the captive here, but the epic makes the ruin a seizure to be undone by a minister, not a final end.

gains.a: The epic scene gains a general statement that kings in elephant-borne state are carried off, so the seizure reads as one case of the rule.
gains.b: The quatrain gains a named king whose fall is not final, which the quatrain's claim that none are left over does not show.

note: The sage's reading of the dream in 282 answers the dream the girl tells in 279 and 280.
teaches: The dream's lion, fish and curse stay riddles until the sage names a bridegroom and an empire as their meaning, so the reading is the dream's fulfilment.

note: Akananuru 45 has the lover cross a summer forest with rattling dry pods and a tiger on the waterless track; verse 781 shows the same dry forest, with trees keening like a mourning house.
teaches: The same summer forest is a woman's dread in the Sangam poem and a mourning house in the epic.

gains.a: The verse lacks the human reason for the forest's dread, the parted woman, which the Akananuru poem supplies.
gains.b: The Akananuru poem lacks the image of the forest as a house of mourners, which the epic adds.

note: The Acharakkovai sets out the mouth-rinsing the great have seen as the way: three sips, wiping, and touching the face's parts with the fingers; Civakan sips three times, wipes three times and touches his face with his fingers.
teaches: The rule book's after-meal rinse appears in the epic, step for step, as a mark of the hero's breeding, performed under the eyes of a king who will next examine him, so the code of conduct works in the story as a credential.

gains.a: the source of its unusually exact sequence, which shows the poet is narrating a known rite and not inventing detail
gains.b: a scene showing the rite performed by a prince as a sign of refinement, beyond the bare prescription

note: At 310 Vijayai, alone in the burning ground by a hostile city, says she does not know how the child could be raised; at 1913 she names herself the base woman (கயத்தியேன்) who left him there.
teaches: The mother who was shown as helpless now judges the same act as her own baseness, so the reunion is weighed down by a guilt the narrator never laid on her.

note: Purananuru 359 gives the burning ground of owls, corpse-eating jackals and ghoul-women dancing by pyre lamps that has received even conquerors; 309 has jackals as drums, pyres as lamps, ghosts dancing and owls praising at a prince's birth.
teaches: The same creatures and lights that in the Sangam poem greet the end of kings serve in the epic as the band and lamps of a future king's birth, turning a warning about death into a grim birth-festival.

gains.a: Vijayai's bitter question gains its weight from the old image of this ground as where kingdoms end.
gains.b: The Sangam image gains a reversal it never shows: the ground receiving a beginning rather than an end.

note: In 213 the king says that pleasures and days of life are measured out for those who guarded penance; in 2728 Civakan names wives and children as the fruit of that merit and says the wind of sin will bring the tree down.
teaches: The earlier remark that pleasure is a measured ration of merit becomes here a reason to give it up before it runs out.

note: 1632 builds the women's beauty out of gold, leaves and sprouts to delight the king's eyes; Naladiyar 46 asks which part of the fresh-garlanded woman is she, among entrails, fat, blood and bone.
teaches: The poem makes the body a thing of ornament and the quatrain takes it apart into its parts, so the two disagree on whether the adorned body is a person to be praised.

gains.a: The adorned women gain a test of what is being praised once the leaves, gold and sprouts are taken off.
gains.b: The quatrain gains a body shown at its most dressed and admired, so its question has an object that actually looks like a woman.

note: Both poets ask the learned to take a flawed work for its worth, using a gem as the image.
teaches: A gem image serves the Jain poets as a standing apology, one for flaws washed off and the other for plain wrapping carrying value.

note: In Akananuru 167 the man tells his heart, which is pressing him to leave for wealth, that after a sweet night with his wife in the tall house he would lie sleepless in a ruined village hall, and gives up the journey; in Natrinai 366 he tells his heart that whoever leaves her washed, flower-tied hair and soft bed in the north wind that shakes the sparrow's nest is a fool.
teaches: The two give the same refusal two arguments: Akananuru 167 sets the home against the terror of the road, while Natrinai 366 never reaches the road and argues from the season alone, a cold wind that even a bird's home must withstand, so the stay-at-home decision could rest either on fear or on a general law of the world (உலகியல்).

claims.gist: eating flesh and starting deeds that the noble avoid mark a low kind of human
a woman's chastity and self-restraint fence off desire, and the senses are doors that can be locked
a demand for tribute is a fair test of a rival, and his refusal clears the demander of fault
even what arrives like fate takes shape in deliberation, and those skilled in counsel rise as kings
what is given to ascetics bears the fruit of painless pleasure in the next birth
the soul is other than the body it is joined to
taking refuge at the victors' feet and leaving the body is the right act for one who sees this
those who dwell on desire and wealth lose their lives through small understanding
those who have done no penance do not get to keep what they love
one who provokes the stronger calls Death down on himself and his line
a father who hands over his son to harm commits a cruelty
captivity and release alike come from former deeds, so neither calls for grief or joy
those who do not praise the Jina with flowers and the tongue do not reach the world of release
those without merit cannot enter such a world
a woman's allure depends on her adornments, as a snake's danger is met only with charm and medicine
austerity kept by rule and ended in the fast leads to birth among the gods
one who walks by grace and speaks dharma should not withhold grace from the one who suffers for him
kings who lose a contest held by the agreed rule disgrace themselves if they seek the prize by force
kings do not slay ministers
the householder's wealth and duty are a yoke of suffering
a son who eats the flesh given in the rite raises the dead father to prosper in heaven

note: 1470 shows the chief queen failing at her husband's body; Cintamani 293 shows women beating their breasts as the king lies dead.
teaches: In both epics the king's death is felt first by his women, so a fall in battle becomes a household loss and not only a political one.

note: Gunamalai wasted like a garland in a ghee-fed flame; Gandharvadattai's sulk blazes like fire with ghee poured on it.
teaches: One simile serves both women: the fire that consumed the girl's longing now feeds the wife's jealousy, so the poem sets the two women's passions, love and anger, burning from the same man.

note: 2060 hints at a state above heaven's ending joy; 2068 shows the sage, once the heavens are told, setting out how to reach endless bliss.
teaches: The hint of a state beyond heaven's end becomes, in the sage's closing, the thing the teaching moves toward: bliss that has no end.

note: The soothsayer warns that setting power on one man will drive prosperity from the land; in 241 Kattiyankaran, now holding that power, says a deity urges him night and day to kill the king.
teaches: The prophecy names no traitor, only the structure of power, so its fulfilment shows the epic locating the danger in the king's act of delegation before it locates it in the minister's character.

note: In 962 the practiser yokes the plough, tills his own body and guards it with the senses' fence until release ripens; in Tirumular 1875 the first Lord has taken the poet's soul as his field to plough, and praise and blame fall away.
teaches: The two pictures of the tilled self disagree on who holds the plough: in the Jain allegory release is the crop of one's own labour, in Tirumular the Lord does the tilling, so the shared farm figure carries the dispute between release by effort and release by grace.

gains.a: a Saiva counter-picture that brings out how wholly 962 leaves the work to the practiser, with no god in the field
gains.b: the Jain alternative it implicitly answers, which makes its passive 'he has taken my soul to plough' a claim about grace and not only an image

note: The brother bids his sister think of the soul as other than the body and leave it in the victors' refuge; the couplet likens the tie of body and life to a bird flying off from its nest.
teaches: The couplet calls the tie light and the epic makes it a choice to be carried out, so the same lightness is turned into an act of leaving.

gains.a: the idea that the tie to the body is a loose one, which makes its giving up no loss
gains.b: a pair who act on the image, two who choose the departure and say where they go

note: 2780 attacks the sacrifice of a lamb for the gods' pleasure with the recompense in Yama's world; Kural 259 weighs a thousand oblations against not killing and eating one creature.
teaches: The epic condemns the sacrificer by his punishment while the Kural condemns by comparison of worth, so the reader sees two ways to refuse sacrifice.

gains.a: the verse gains a measure of worth for sacrifice set against not killing
gains.b: the couplet gains a consequence after death and a scene of blood, which it lacks

note: Verse 427 chooses Marusi because he can put the kin and the matter in words; here he opens his report by promising the descent, the entry and the host's words, in that order.
teaches: The ministers' reason for choosing him is tested by his first act on return, which is to set out his account in the order it happened.

note: 1483 lays a king on a bed of silk and gives him to the fire; Naladiyar 21 says kings under moon-like umbrellas have been carried off and called dead.
teaches: The fire takes the proud king as the quatrain says it takes all, and the honour of his funeral does not alter that.

gains.a: The funeral gains the quatrain's lesson that rank is no shelter from death.
gains.b: The quatrain gains a named king whose cotton and silk bed does not save him.

note: Both give knowledge, faith and conduct as the triple discipline; Neelakesi makes it a medicine against rebirth.
teaches: Neelakesi's frame of birth as a disease for which the three are the cure is not in the Yasodhara, which rather lists their by-fruits of heaven and rule beside release.

note: 1572 has the jester boast of winning debates; 1573 gives his method, a stick for those who recite.
teaches: The boast gets its method, which shows that his debate is a comic beating, not an argument.

note: Right faith as clarity and joy in the Jina's dharma here, against right faith as eight limbs and longing for the one with eight excellent things in Neelakesi.
teaches: The two Jain epics define the same faith differently, one by an inward state and one by a list of acts and freedoms, so the reader sees how a school could teach one term more than one way.

note: 78 lists conch and discus on the younger prince's palm; in 109 the court names him one who will guard the whole world under one umbrella.
teaches: The body marks listed as ornament in 78 are read, in 109, as a sign of universal rule, which changes how the earlier portrait should be heard.

note: The Kural says a jackal can kill a war elephant when its feet sink in mud, so ground decides; the epic says a single lion kills a herd of elephants, so the nature of the fighter decides.
teaches: Both answer how the few beat the many, but the couplet credits the place of battle and the epic the strength of the one who fights, two incompatible accounts of the same reversal if each is taken as the cause.

gains.a: the epic's boast gains a rival explanation it does not consider, that its small band might have won by terrain or timing rather than by nature
gains.b: the couplet gains a counter-image in which the elephant is the victim of a stronger beast, not of bad ground, which shows its claim is a choice of cause

note: Arunagirinathar calls the nine-gated body a house Brahma built; the Cintamani's hut of flesh is built by a carpenter that 1578 names as the deed (வினை).
teaches: Holding the two together shows that the same anatomy of the body serves opposite accounts of its maker, a god in the Thiruppugazh and one's own deeds in the Jain epic, and that the disgust can be shared while the theology differs; the contrast rests on reading 1577's builder through 1578.

gains.a: the epic verse's unnamed builder is shown to be a doctrinal choice, since a devotional text with the same inventory names a creator god instead
gains.b: the Thiruppugazh's attribution to Brahma is shown not to follow from the inventory itself, since a text with the same list of body parts gives the work to karma

note: Verse 427 chooses Marusi as one who can say what is fit; in 529 his first words are called unfit and he is ashamed.
teaches: The minister's praise of Marusi's speech is tested at once by a slip, so his later success in 531 is recovery from a fault and not ease.

note: The Cintamani's god is worshipped as the one who cut away his own ghati karmas; Tirumular's grace-power comes as guru and removes the soul's bonds.
teaches: On the reading that the Jina is honoured for destroying his own karmas, the two texts disagree about what a god does with karma: the Jain god is the one who freed himself and is a model to circle, whereas Tirumular's Lord is the agent who frees the bound soul, so the worshipper's release comes from his own effort in one and from descending grace in the other.

gains.a: the epic's brief epithet காதி கண் அரிந்த is shown to carry a whole doctrine of self-won release that it states without argument
gains.b: Tirumular's grace gains a rival account in which no god acts on the soul, which sharpens why his verse insists that one's own agency must end

note: Both speak of eight qualities, here a freed soul's own, there the Lord's.
teaches: The Jain verse makes the eight the property of any soul that is freed, and the Saiva verse makes them the Lord's, so the reader sees where the two schools put the one list.

gains.a: A rival owner of the eight qualities, a god, against which its claim that the freed soul has them unaided can be seen.
gains.b: A school that gives the eight to a freed soul with no god, which tests the Saiva claim that they are the Lord's.

note: 1931 has tormentors tell sufferers to take the fruit of their own deeds; Tirumanthiram 198 has Death's servants bind killers and drive them with the very commands they gave.
teaches: Both hells have punishers who echo the victim's own deed, but only the Saiva servants act for Death, while the Soolamani's act for no one.

gains.a: The tormentors of 1931, named only by their trade, gain a Saiva figure to compare with: a servant who acts for Yama.
gains.b: The Saiva hell gains a Jain counterpart in which the punishers speak only of the deed the sufferer sowed.

note: The poet announced early that the hero hears the dharma and, afraid of kingship like a snake struck by thunder, renounces; the sermon's lesson that all embodied life, even a god's, is suffering is the content of that dharma.
teaches: This unit is the first body of the doctrine whose effect on the hero the early verse reports in a line, so it shows what the renunciation was a reply to.

note: Both kings, told of a cattle raid, order the army to go swiftly and turn back the herd (விரைந்து தொறுமீட்க, 432; வல்லே படுநிரை பெயர்க்க, 1858).
teaches: The repeated order scene makes Tadamittan stand where the usurper Kattiyangaran stood, but where the usurper's army was routed by real hunters, this king's whole army rides out against a raid staged by friends, so his rage meets no enemy.

note: The Kural's man asks whether Vishnu's world is sweeter than sleep in the beloved's arms; the epic answers by likening the lovers to those beyond birth and death.
teaches: Set beside the Kural's open question, the Jain epic lends sexual bliss the very vocabulary of release, then ends that bliss within the chapter by the hero's leaving.

gains.a: the epic's simile is shown to answer a known question about whether love can rival the gods' world
gains.b: the couplet's question receives a narrative test, in which the answer 'yes' holds only for two months

note: Kar Narpathu 9: the flowers speak many sweet words announcing his return. Akananuru 74: the heroine tells the friend she could hold firm on her many sweet words of reassurance (வன்புறை இன்சொல் நன்பல) were it not for the herders' flute at evening.
teaches: Akananuru 74 gives the heroine's answer that the Kar Narpathu never records: sweet words of comfort hold her only until the evening flute, so the reassurance the venbas repeat is shown elsewhere to fail at its own hour.

note: Fire of 1453 is put out by the Varuna arrow of 1454.
teaches: Again the answer is the opposed element, which makes the fight a sequence of matched counters.

note: In 1459 the king's discus hides the hero; in 1461 the same discus, hurled back, kills the king.
teaches: The weapon that seemed the king's whole safety passes to his enemy, so the first strike is shown to be only half the story.

note: The jackals and ghouls feeding on the slain in 181 are the carrion eaters the Siddhar names when each claims the body as its own.
teaches: A battle's bodies are the same flesh the Siddhar tells us is only meat for jackals and kites, so the glory of the field is also the end of the body.

gains.a: The field's feast of jackals is read as the fate of every body, not only of the slain king's soldiers.
gains.b: The Siddhar's abstract claim that the body is prey gets a scene in which the body is the price of a king's glory.

note: Tirumanthiram 219 says the fire worshipped and risen burns the deeds of ages; the verse says meditation burns them.
teaches: Both texts burn the deeds with fire, but in one the fire is the Lord's, worshipped, and in the other it is the sage's own meditation, which shows where Jain and Saiva release part ways.

gains.a: the verse gets a Saiva statement that deeds can be burned by fire, which shows its own fire is the sage's meditation and no god's gift
gains.b: the Tirumanthiram verse gets a case where the same burning is done by the sage alone and no deity helps

note: Akananuru 168 compares the roar of the waterfalls to the kitchen of Udhiyan, bound to the duty of giving; Purananuru 2 praises the Chera king who gave great food without limit to the armies of the war.
teaches: The akam poet can borrow the noise of Udhiyan's kitchen as a simile because his feeding was proverbial in puram praise, so a king's fame for food had become a stock measure of uproar.

note: Soolamani 200 makes the feet of the beginningless Lord the refuge from great suffering; Tirumanthiram 138 says the holy feet are Sivam, Sivaloka and the path, and a refuge for those clear within.
teaches: Both name the feet a refuge, but the Saiva feet are the goal and the way at once, while the Jain verse sets the refuge apart from the state it leads to, described in 202.

gains.a: the refuge is shown as a means only, as the goal is another thing, by contrast with feet that are also the goal
gains.b: the feet as goal and refuge together are shown as one answer among others, since a Jain verse names them only as a refuge

note: The lute's wood is born of the earth-maiden and reared by the sky as foster mother; Civakan, born in the burning ground, was handed by Kantukkatan to a foster mother.
teaches: The instrument Civakan chooses has his own hidden history, a mother who bore it and another who reared it, while the ones he rejects are faulted for their origin, so his judgement of pedigree reflects on the birth no one at the contest knows.

note: The Tirumanthiram says only the vows kept and the knowledge gained go with the dead; the verse lists what the vow buys after death.
teaches: The Tirumanthiram names the vow as what travels past death, and the epic adds a ledger of what it buys: Indra's rank, kingship, then the end of deeds.

gains.a: the vow's journey after death gets a stated ladder of rewards
gains.b: the Tirumanthiram's bare claim is given a worked sequence that the Jain epic fills in

note: Verse 514 reads the Vidyadhara king's letter to the lord of Podanam, which sends gifts and good wishes; verse 662 reads the discus-king's letter to the same lord, which demands them.
teaches: A letter sealed and read at the same palace first carries a gift and a request and then a demand, so the same act of reading shows two different powers dealing with Podanam.

note: The king orders a pair of human children brought for sacrifice to avert the goddess's anger; the Kural says not to do a deed that takes another's life even if one's own life be lost.
teaches: The king takes lives to avert harm to his city, whereas the Kural allows no exception even for the life of the one who decides, so the scene tests the rule against the case of a ruler who thinks he acts for his people.

gains.a: the order is seen as the act the Kural forbids even to save oneself, and here is done to save a city
gains.b: the couplet's absolute rule is tested against a ruler's duty to protect, which it does not mention

note: 1101 shows the priest's fire fed while the groom's desire is kindled; Siddhar 147 asks when he will kindle the homa fire inside to cross the sea of desire.
teaches: One fire serves desire on one side and ends desire on the other, so the rite is the same fire put to opposite uses.

gains.a: The wedding fire gains a rival use, as a fire inside the body that ends the desire it kindles in the groom.
gains.b: The Siddhar's inner homa gains the outward rite it turns inward, with a priest's actual oblation set beside the longing.

note: In 947 Civakan gives the dying dog the five padas and it leaves its body; here the dog, now a god among goddesses, comes down to save the one who gave it the mantra.
teaches: Read together, the two scenes make the mantra given out of pity into the cause of the hero's deliverance, the Jain epic's way of showing a good deed returning within the same story.

note: Verse 109 has kings linger in the courtesans' quarter out of desire; at 206 a counsellor warns the king that many who gorged on women's pleasure fell into sin and blame.
teaches: The pleasure that the city praise lets kings enjoy without comment is the same pleasure that the story will turn into a warning to its own king, so the description quietly prepares the charge.

note: Kural 872: take on the enmity of ploughmen whose plough is the bow rather than of those whose plough is the word. Thinaimozhi 17: the woman fears for her man passing the hamlets of those who live by ploughing with the bow, while her shoulders slacken because he left without grace.
