teaches: The Kural ranks the bow-ploughmen as the lesser enemy, and the venba agrees in its own way: the bowmen are only a feared danger on his road, while the wound she actually bears, slackened shoulders, comes from his word, the promise and grace he withheld.

note: Kural 389 says the world rests under the umbrella of a king who can bear words bitter to the ear; verse 620 names a king by the opposite temper, striking in anger and unable to bear a word against him.
teaches: The couplet's virtue is given its negative portrait in a ruler whose pride goes with his intolerance.

gains.a: The verse lacks a measure by which this temper counts as a failing, which the couplet supplies.
gains.b: The couplet lacks a figure who embodies the opposite, which the verse supplies.

note: The dresser nips flowers with her curved nail to print the bride's forehead mark, the opening of a householder's life; Vijayai, turning ascetic, takes the mark off with her finger, with the ear-rings and pearls, to close it.
teaches: The same mark and the same ornaments are put on to begin a marriage and taken off to end a life in the world, so the epic shows adornment as the sign of entry and renunciation as its undoing.

note: Verse 395 has the world take refuge in the grace of the first lord who bears the wheel; Tirumanthiram 349 says the bright-flamed First gave the discus to Achyuta.
teaches: Both texts make the wheel the sign of a first lord, but one makes it his own dharma-wheel and the other a gift he hands to a lesser god, so the wheel's source is claimed for two rival firsts.

gains.a: A rival claim, in which the discus is given and not borne, against which its own claim that the first lord holds the wheel stands out.
gains.b: A Jain account in which the wheel belongs to the first lord and is not passed to any god, against which its gift of the discus reads as a Saiva claim.

note: Naladiyar 200 says the base fill themselves on rice and fried dishes a great patron gives, while to the self-reliant water won by effort is nectar; the verse says all the low delight in rice from paddy.
teaches: Both books define the base by being satisfied with rice, but the quatrain sets against them those who live by their own effort and the verse those who delight in their due standing, so the opposite of the base is labour in one and honour in the other.

note: Kural 1251 says the axe of desire breaks the door of restraint bolted with shame; in 1472 Kemasari's inner restraint and modesty (உண்ணிறை நாணும்) break together at the first sight of Civakan.
teaches: The Kural's woman says this in separation as a confession of defeat; the epic makes the same breaking happen at first sight and treats it as the sign that the destined man has come, turning a lament into an omen.

gains.a: the frame of நிறை as a door with நாண் as its bolt, which explains why the two words break together
gains.b: a scene that moves the breaking of restraint from the end of a love to its first instant

note: Kural 377 says that even those who amass millions enjoy them only as the apportioner has apportioned; verse 527 has the king say that only former deeds strive and later effort does not win what is not due.
teaches: The epic gives the couplet's unnamed apportioner a face, the person's own earlier deeds, and uses it to settle who may marry whom, where the couplet only consoles about wealth.

gains.a: A statement that a lot is fixed by something other than present effort, which the king asserts without a general rule.
gains.b: A case where the rule is used as an argument across a divide of rank, not as comfort about wealth.

note: Kural 1125 has the man say he would recall her only if he forgot, but he does not know how to forget; 990 has the girl say that if she tried to forget, fate itself would drive her back to remember.
teaches: Both deny forgetting, but the Soolamani lays the compulsion on fate, which the Kural leaves to the lover's nature.

gains.a: The verse lacks the compact logic that remembering needs a prior forgetting.
gains.b: The couplet lacks a cause for the failure to forget; the verse supplies fate, and the girl's inward cry that the world does not know it.

claims.gist: a bad deed is like a child nursed by anger and fed on desire that then wanders among painful births
the body weighs the same after death, so nothing has left it
a man shut in a pit shows no exit for a soul at death
against a weak foe a strong man needs neither strategy nor allies
right view, knowledge and conduct together make the path of the ascetic
the splendour of a king's body is like an illusion
a woman's rank and kind can be read from the beauty of her footprint
the Jina's presence under the tree ends the disease of birth, and his dharma is a nectar to be eaten
a worthy husband comes as the fruit of penance done in former births with a faultless mind
a warrior who flees in fear and lets others take his valour loses his manliness
it is not courage for one to stand aside while another comes forward to fight
a king's sole sovereignty arises by the grace of the first lord
kindness to living souls makes the old deed yield what one desires
meditation in the fast carries the soul to a heaven after death
a wife who shares the husband's vow shares his heavenly birth
austerity ends all evil and brings one to liberation
kings' wealth is not a real thing to rely on
the Lord has conquered and reached the limit of all things
those who bow at the Jina's feet bloom in light and joy, beyond reason
those who shun women's beauty are reborn as gods and rule heaven
a king's white umbrella is the shade of dharma that shelters the world
birth is a disease from which a person asks to be freed
a woman is not to be put to death, whatever her fault
a king's sword is too high for a small and base person

note: Padumai, left behind, called him a deceiver; Civakan himself says he left her by deceit.
teaches: The epic lets the hero confirm the abandoned woman's charge in his own word வஞ்சித்து, so her bitterness is not a lover's exaggeration but a judgment he accepts without excuse.

note: The poet says the soul is stainless and other than the body and that its karma is not its own nature; Tirumular says the stains go only when the sun of grace stands over them.
teaches: The epic leaves the stain's end to the soul's own knowledge of itself, while Tirumular needs a light from outside, so the two give opposite sources for the freeing.

gains.a: a rival account in which the stain leaves only when an outside light appears, which shows how much the epic leaves to the soul's own knowing
gains.b: a case of a stainless soul known apart from the body with no god's presence in the account

note: She now says she did not grasp the words about the bee that Civakan spoke before he left.
teaches: Read together, the bee speech that sounds like idle love-play in 1502 proves to be his only farewell, and her failure to decode it becomes part of her grief.

note: Naladiyar 48 asks whether those who praise sandal paste and garlands have not seen vultures tear the stinking cart of the body; Kundalakesi 12 asks what delight is left in shoulders praised as Mandara when vultures and dogs pluck at them.
teaches: The Naladiyar turns the contemplation of carrion on a body adorned for love, usually the woman's; the fragment turns the same contemplation on a man's heroic shoulders, so the discipline is shown to apply to desire for either sex.

note: Saccandan, before his death, tells Vijayai that dying and being born come from one's deeds and that grief comes from want of understanding; his son, now seized by the same usurper, tells the women of his house that one who knows births and release will not grieve.
teaches: Father and son meet the usurper's violence with the same doctrinal consolation to the women who love them, but the father dies after speaking it and the son walks on alive, so the teaching recurs as the epic's own answer to tyranny rather than one man's farewell.

note: Tirumular has grace-power come as guru and end the malas when one's own agency ceases; the Jain hymn praises the Jina who ended karma that cannot be ended and taught the path of no return.
teaches: On the reading that the Jina ended his own karma and teaches others to end theirs, the two verses give opposite answers to who removes karma: in the Saiva verse one's own doing must stop and grace acts, in the Jain verse the liberated one is the one whose own effort ended it.

gains.a: the hymn's 'karma that cannot be ended' gains its contrast: the Saiva text agrees it cannot be ended by the soul alone but supplies a divine agent the Jain hymn does without
gains.b: Tirumular's demand that one's own agency end gains a named rival doctrine in which the agent of release is a man who acted, which shows what the demand is arguing against

note: The king's wish to give up the kingdom was real; the queen offers the same renunciation as bait.
teaches: The poem sets sincere and false renunciation in the same words, so the reader sees renunciation can be counterfeited by one who means murder.

note: 139 urges the lord of Nanjil to give now, since he does not fear death for his king and a battle may come any day; Naladiyar 5 says not to hold back a gift thinking it can be given later, since Death drags all away.
teaches: The Naladiyar's general reason for giving now, the certainty of death, appears in 139 as a bard's practical argument tied to the warrior patron's own courage, which shows how the moralist's maxim was already a working plea in the bard's trade.

note: A mother asks for one killing as an offering to a goddess; the couplet says not killing beats a thousand offerings.
teaches: The couplet compares not killing with great offerings, while the story puts the offering on a mother's lips as a cure for her son's fear.

gains.a: The story shows the offering asked at a moment of personal fear, which the couplet's comparison lacks.
gains.b: The couplet gives the king's refusal a ground in a rule above the king's own reasoning.

note: In both a father gives his daughter to the man who has done a deed for him: Nandagon to whoever recovers the herd, Padumai's father to the man who saved her life.
teaches: Nandagon offers his daughter in advance as a public prize for any warrior, but Padumai's father reasons afterwards from the hero's bodily marks and makes the gift wait on his consent, so the epic's brides-for-deeds are not all of one kind.

note: Akananuru 296 says the man's bathing in the great Vaiyai with the dark girl has become gossip in Koodal (அலர்ஆ கின்று, அது பலர்வாய்ப் பட்டே); thirattu 2.51-56 shows a woman wearing a garland from the flood openly, for the land to know (நாடு அறியப் பூ மாலை அப்பி), and the town's gossip following (ஊர்த்து அலர்).
teaches: The fragment shows how the gossip the Akananuru friend throws at the man was made: a love token worn in plain sight at the river festival, chosen by the woman as display, so the akam reproach of public shame rests on a festival custom in which the other woman wanted to be seen.

note: Kural 473 says many who did not know their strength rose on zeal and were broken midway; Pazhamozhi 317 says that even capable men who rush on an unequal foe come to harm, like a hand struck on stone.
teaches: The couplet blames ignorance of one's own strength; Pazhamozhi adds that being able (ஆற்றுவாரேனும்) is not enough, since what counts is the match (நிகர்) with the enemy, so the weighing is relative, not absolute.

note: The Kural ranks highest the woman who suffers a sea of desire and does not ride the palmyra horse; the parrot says maidens hide their love-sickness from even their nearest, out of shame.
teaches: The silence the couplet praises has a working cost the couplet does not show: because the girl will not speak even to her confidante, the knowledge of her illness has to travel by a go-between who asks the man to diagnose it.

gains.a: a rule stating why Gunamalai must use a messenger rather than speak, which the scene assumes but does not argue
gains.b: a scene showing who carries the woman's unspoken desire once shame forbids her to declare it

note: In both a woman takes the lute after the man's songs and begins her own; the Cintamani's நிலத்தோர் and gods wondering (729) echo the Silappathikaram's நிலத்தெய்வம் வியப்பு எய்த, and both close on பாடத் தொடங்கு-.
teaches: The same turn at the lute, his songs then hers, ends in a garland in the Cintamani and in Kovalan's leaving in the Silappathikaram, which shows that the outcome lies in how the man hears her reply, as yielding or as a hidden intent.

note: In verse 49 the brother bids his sister give up the body in the refuge of the victors; verse 325 shows them doing it.
teaches: The plan made under threat of the sword is kept after the threat ends, which shows it was a choice and not only a reaction to danger.

note: 2781 asks whose eyes would look on the creature cut apart and wailing; Kural 257 says flesh would not be eaten by those who saw it as another's wound.
teaches: The epic stages the very seeing that the couplet only wishes for, and shows it fails when appetite rules.

gains.a: the verse gains a name for what is being asked, seeing flesh as a wound
gains.b: the couplet gains a scene of the wounded animal, where it states only a condition

note: 1904 says those who do not grasp the Lord's greatness quarrel and are bound by a quarrel of deeds; 182 says that even when called the knower of all the Lord is hard to truly know.
teaches: The earlier verse says why the Lord is hard to know and the later says what follows from not knowing him, which is the quarrel that binds.

note: Kural 1033 says the ploughman alone lives on his own, while all others bow (தொழுது) to eat; in the Cintamani the sower himself bows (தொழுது) to the seed as he sows.
teaches: The ploughman whom the Kural sets above all bowing still bows, to the crop on which his independence rests, so his self-sufficiency is itself a dependence.

gains.a: a sense of why its farmers' gesture matters: they are the ones the Kural says need bow to no one
gains.b: a limit: the independence it praises rests on a seed the ploughman must greet with folded hands

note: Saccandan's women stripped off their necklaces, garlands and ear-rings and cried that the king's cruelty was cruel; now the usurper's women put off ear-rings, bangles and garlands as a burden.
teaches: The stripping of ornaments that opened the epic as the price of the usurper's deed closes his reign on his own women, showing that the widowhood he caused is the widowhood his household inherits.

note: 2910 says learned kings put away anger with mercy and keep what they desire hidden; Kural 590 says a king who honours a spy openly lets out his own secret.
teaches: The Kural treats concealment as a rule of spycraft, and the epic treats it as a trained temper in which anger is put away and wishes are kept back.

gains.a: the verse's hiding of desire gains a working case in which showing favour betrays a secret
gains.b: the Kural's rule gains a temperament behind it, mercy that has put anger aside

note: The narrator reports that the pleasure of Vimalai's breasts is worth the three worlds; the Naladiyar, a Jain didactic work, lists entrails, blood and bone and asks where among them the garlanded woman is.
teaches: The epic gives full voice to the valuation that the Jain didactic tradition exists to unmask, and hedges it as hearsay, so the praise stands as the worldly view that Civakan's later renunciation will have to undo.

gains.a: The hyperbole is placed as the very error a Jain reader is taught to dissolve, which gives it weight in the epic's arc toward renunciation.
gains.b: The quatrain's dissection gains a live instance of the praise it attacks, made within a work of the same religion.

note: 1561 has the chief queen resolve to see the parijata wed to the Kama creeper; 1628 has the queens dress the bride and join her to the tree.
teaches: The queen's wish ends in a ritual the women perform themselves, so the festival is theirs and the king only attends.

note: The king's plunge into a sea of pleasure is set beside the quatrain's lamb eating the garland before its slaying.
teaches: The epic scene only lists pleasure's delights and the quatrain adds the shadow of the slaughter ground over them.

gains.a: The scene of delight gets the foreboding the verse itself does not state.
gains.b: The lamb image gets a concrete king, wealthy and at ease, who is as unaware as the lamb.

note: In the Kalittokai the herd girl is cried as the prize of whoever takes the fighting bull, and the taker himself has her; here the herd chief's daughter is the prize for recovering the herd, and the winner passes her to a friend.
teaches: The epic keeps the mullai custom of a herd girl won by a public feat, but moves the feat from the herders' bull-pen to a prince's war and lets the prize be transferred, which the bull-catch, where the girl goes to the man who wrestled, does not allow.

gains.a: the herders' wedding is seen to rest on an old custom of the herd girl as prize of a feat, which explains the father's proclamation in 440
gains.b: the bull-catch's bond between feat and husband is shown to be what a later courtly telling could loosen, the girl becoming a gift between men

note: The youth said harm once done to bodies brought sufferings in birth after birth; here the flour cock killing is the instance.
teaches: The general claim of verse 63 is given its measured example, in which even an effigy's killing is followed for lives.

note: Naladiyar 60 says fools long for pleasure though suffering mounts, and the higher look to the pain in it; 619 shows a king past all noticing.
teaches: A verse of ethics gets a king's case, where the cost is a realm and not one man's comfort.

gains.a: The verse lacks the judgment that pleasure holds its own pain, which it only implies.
gains.b: The quatrain lacks an example from the seat of power, where the fool's pleasure ruins others.

note: Poison, hiding and the elephant's tusks are the dangers the strong in tapas escape; the couplet says austerity's power lets one even leap past Death.
teaches: The Kural states the power of tapas at its limit and the epic lists the particular harms it turns aside, and adds that when tapas is spent no flight saves.

gains.a: the couplet's claim that tapas power reaches even to Death, beyond poison and tusks
gains.b: named perils (poison, the tusker) and the warning that spent tapas leaves no hiding place, which the couplet's bare 'even leaping past death' lacks

note: 1155 asks who would anger a king no demon can match; 1158 gives the cause, a rumoured pledge of a daughter to a human.
teaches: The court's puzzle in 1155 is answered by a rumour the king repeats as fact.

note: Naladiyar 33 says the fool grieves when the fruit of past deeds comes, while the wise take it as an old desert crossed; verse 670 accepts the fruit of deeds without grief and answers by paying.
teaches: The same calm acceptance of deeds' fruit that the quatrain offers as freedom is here the mood in which a king submits.

gains.a: The verse lacks a way to meet the fruit of deeds without fretting, which the quatrain gives as passing the desert.
gains.b: The quatrain lacks a case where such acceptance becomes political submission, which the king's use of it supplies.

note: In 232 Fortune leaves the clinging king without a word; in 2983 Civakan says she never leaves the one who lets go.
teaches: The goddess of fortune who abandoned the grasping king in the first ilampakam is shown in the last to stay with the king who gives up, so the story's arc on wealth reverses.

note: Both use iron turned to gold for a change of being: Tirumular says gold once made never turns back to iron, so one who has the guru's grace is not born again; the Cintamani's iron-to-gold is a dog reborn as a god.
teaches: The same alchemy marks a final release in Tirumular and only a rise within the round of births in the Cintamani, so the image's 'no return' belongs to the Saiva claim, not to the figure itself.

gains.a: a reading of its own image as a step and not an end, since the god of 951 is still embodied
gains.b: an instance where the gold is a higher birth, which shows that the couplet's finality is a doctrinal addition to the metallurgy

note: Kural 6 praises the one who quenched the five gates of sense (பொறிவாயில் ஐந்தவித்தான்) and promises long life to those who keep his path; 1468 calls the Jina lord of those who slew the five senses (ஐம்பொறியும் அட்டு) and promises heaven to those who sing his feet.
teaches: The Kural's sense-quencher is a teacher whose path is followed; in the hymn he is the head of a class of victors, and the reward moves from long life on earth to the world of the gods.

gains.a: a named model for the Jina's epithet, which shows the hymn speaking the Kural's language of sense-conquest
gains.b: evidence that the couplet's sense-quencher was read in Jain circles as the Jina and his followers

note: In 1451 the astrologer foretells that the man at whose sight Kemasari instantly feels shy (கதுமென நாணப் படுவான்) will be her husband; in 1475 she looks at Civakan and turns her eyes away.
teaches: The averted glance is the very sign the astrologer named, so a lover's ordinary modesty becomes the proof of fate, and the reader knows the marriage is sealed before anyone speaks of it.

note: 497 ends பொய்யில் பொருளே பொருள்; 514 has the shipwrecked merchant tell himself பொருளைப் பொருள் என்று கொண்டாய், as a reproach.
teaches: The wordplay on பொருள் as wealth and as the thing of worth is turned against its speaker, so the wreck reads as a verdict on his creed and not only as bad luck.

note: Kural 10 says those who reach the Lord's feet swim the sea of births; 3091 prays 'let our birth end' to the Lord who destroyed Desire and Death.
teaches: The Kural says the feet carry across, and the verse names who the Lord has beaten (Desire and Death) and why they should be prayed to.

gains.a: the prayer for the end of birth is given a wider rule that reaching his feet is the way to cross
gains.b: the Kural's Lord, who is left unnamed, is shown as one who has killed Desire and Death

note: The Kural's எண்குணத்தான் (one of eight qualities) and the verse's இருநான்கு குணமுடைய இறைவன் (the lord with twice four qualities) are the same number.
teaches: The Kural's unlisted eight is matched by a Jain count of eight qualities, so a Jain poet can read the couplet as meaning his own liberated lord.

gains.a: the Jain poem is shown to use the eight-quality formula the Kural already uses
gains.b: the couplet's unlisted eight is given a Jain reading by a poet who also leaves the eight unlisted

note: The hymn's three verses promise rule on earth and in heaven (118), Indra's rank (119), and release (120).
teaches: The hymn arranges worship's rewards as a ladder, so release comes as the last step above the worldly kingship the prince himself holds.

note: Kural 751 says nothing but wealth makes people of no account into people of account; 1922 says wealth makes the diminished into mountains, and 1924 names the speaker and her son as those diminished in lineage and treasure.
teaches: The epic turns the couplet, often read as a dry observation about upstarts, onto a fallen royal house, for whom wealth is the way back to the standing birth once gave.

gains.a: the mother's maxim gains a sharper edge, since the Kural's rule about the lowly is applied to princes who have become lowly
gains.b: the couplet gains a case where wealth restores rather than creates standing, which tests whether its rule is only about the low-born

note: The man who is her chosen lover beats her to the ground; the husband she betrayed holds the sword and refuses to strike.
teaches: The two scenes set the lover's blows beside the husband's restraint, so the reader sees whose hand the woman was safer in.

note: Both turn on eating flesh to swell one's own flesh.
teaches: The couplet asks how the flesh-eater can have compassion; the epic adds the end of the fattened body, carried only to feed vultures, so the cruelty is shown to profit no one but the birds.

gains.a: the epic verse gains the couplet's moral charge that flesh-eating defeats arul, beyond its picture of waste
gains.b: the couplet gains an ending for the body it fattens, which it leaves unstated

note: 2727 has Civakan reflect that to subdue oneself in time, do penance and reach a world without affliction is better; in 2988 he speaks it to his wives and calls them to come.
teaches: The reflection made alone in the earlier chapter becomes an invitation, so the resolve is seen first as thought and then as something shared.

note: The courtesan who ruins whoever falls into her net, refused by the citizens in 78, returns in 98 as the moat that ruins whoever falls into it.
teaches: The vice the poet praises the city for shunning becomes, twenty verses later, the figure of its defence, so the same destroying woman is a danger to citizens and a weapon against enemies.

note: Kural 698 warns against belittling a ruler as young; in 703 Acuvakanthan waves off the prince as a child and the story then lets the prince take up his challenge.
teaches: The verse shows the belittling the couplet warns against and what it provokes, a prince who vows rather than withdraws.

gains.a: The verse lacks a measure that names Acuvakanthan's dismissal of youth as the fault it is.
gains.b: The couplet lacks a case where the belittled youth answers with a vow, not submission.

note: The Kural praises womanhood that suffers a sea of desire and does not ride the palmyra horse; Gunamalai, with longing like the sea, considers riding it.
teaches: The epic shows the couplet's praised restraint from inside, as a near thing: the heroine reaches the very thought of the madal before turning to a go-between, so the Kural's 'does not ride' names a line held under pressure, not an absence of the wish.

gains.a: Gunamalai's thought of the madal gains its measure: it is the one act the ethical tradition says a woman forgoes
gains.b: the couplet's abstract womanhood gains a woman who voices its praise of herself (998) and then wavers, which a gnomic line cannot show

claims.gist: those who wear the Jina's feet on their heads are themselves praised and honoured by the world
the ascetic keeps the three restraints, overcomes the four instincts and holds the five senses
the Jina's endless knowledge holds all existing things and the three times
the layman's four virtues lead through rebirth as Indra and as an earthly king to release from birth
renunciation shuts the road by which desire comes
those who live for pleasure will suffer grave pain
every life is equal to one's own life
bowing at the feet of the ascetics who guard lives carries one beyond one's deeds
deeds ripen in hells of seven kinds, each named for its ground and its pain
a woman whose body a man has touched belongs to that man
what is apportioned by fate ripens and comes to the one it is due to
the feet of the austere sage are the only refuge against death
a life may be taken only by the fate that is bound to it, and by nothing else
only the ascetics of the true path are a refuge for the world
worship at the Jina's feet is bowing that cuts the deeds
a king who gives up rule for austerity gains the lordship of the gods
the pain of the hells grows twofold in each lower layer
the Lord rose to the summit of the worlds by destroying three fortified bonds

note: 159 says the whole world rests in the cool shade of Saccandan's umbrella as under a father's feet; 290 says that when the minister swallows him the darkness of the bent sceptre spreads and the people grieve.
teaches: The shade praised as the world's settled condition proves to depend on one man's life, since one betrayal turns the straight sceptre's shade into the bent sceptre's darkness.

note: In 350 Vijayai takes off the tilaka, earrings, neck ornaments and the pearls on her breasts when she is received into the hermitage; 2635 has the women scatter garlands and ornaments in a prepared hall.
teaches: What one forlorn queen did alone in a forest is done here as an ordered rite for many, so the epic shows renunciation first as a refuge and last as an institution.

note: 2876 says the deed clings to the soul like a thread in a lotus stalk and follows it into each body; Naladiyar 120 says nothing goes with a person but the deeds done.
teaches: One gives the thread image of how a deed follows, the other the fact that only deeds follow, so each answers what the other leaves open.

gains.a: the verse's following deed gains the plain statement that it is the only thing that goes with the person, body and wealth being left
gains.b: the quatrain's 'what goes with a person' gains a picture of how it goes: an unbroken thread that burns as it follows

note: 1499 crowns the hero because the discus won the war; Kural 546 says victory comes from the sceptre that does not bend, not from the spear.
teaches: The epic gives the title to the winner of the weapon, which the Kural would call a lesser ground than justice.

gains.a: The crowning gains a stricter standard: is the discus a better ground than a straight sceptre?
gains.b: The couplet gains a king whose title rests on the weapon, which tests its claim that the spear gives no victory.

note: Kural 9 calls the one to be worshipped எண்குணத்தான், the one of eight qualities, and calls a head that does not bow useless; in 1469 those who do not praise the Jina have the eight qualities taken from their souls by their deeds.
teaches: The eight qualities that the Kural gives to the one worshipped are, in the Jain hymn, the soul's own, lost to karma by those who will not praise, so the failure to worship costs the self what the god possesses.

gains.a: a source for the term, which shows the hymn reworking a couplet every Tamil hearer knew
gains.b: a Jain reading in which the eight qualities are the soul's nature, so the couplet's god is what the freed soul becomes

note: Kural 830 counsels that when a foe must be treated as a friend, one should befriend with the face and drop friendship within; the Videha king makes himself one with the usurper so as to kill him by the sword of love.
teaches: The couplet's face-friendship is a defensive mask with an exit, while the epic turns it into the method of a killing and calls it வஞ்சம் even on the hero's side, so the pair shows how far the Kural's permission can be stretched once the foe is a usurper.

gains.a: the epic's ruse gains a rule of statecraft that makes a just king's deceit look like prudence rather than treachery
gains.b: the couplet gains a case where the outward friendship is not a passing shelter but the weapon itself, which its own wording does not reach

note: The deity names the ascetics' hermitage as their refuge; in 347 Vijayai reaches it, and the narrator says she suffered through a deed from a former birth.
teaches: The road to the hermitage is laid by a deity's counsel, but on arrival the narrator explains the exile as karma, so divine help and former deeds are given together as causes.

note: The Kural prefers a spear that missed an elephant to an arrow that hit a hare; Vipulan will not strike even a rutting elephant, since a beast brings no distinction.
teaches: The Kural ranks quarry by size and danger and puts the elephant at the top; the epic's warrior ranks by kind and puts every beast below a man, so the two measures of a worthy target diverge exactly at the elephant.

gains.a: the oddity of refusing an elephant in war is sharpened against the proverb that makes the elephant the noblest mark
gains.b: the couplet's scale of targets is shown to be one of several: a code of honour among men can rank the elephant as no target at all

note: Kural 30 says those called அந்தணர் are so because they bear cool kindness to every living being; in 934-936 the men skilled in the four Vedas, with minds of fire, beat a dog to death over a heap of rice.
teaches: The epic stages the Kural's definition as a test the Brahmins fail, and gives the cool kindness the Kural requires to the hero instead, so the name and the conduct come apart exactly as the couplet's reasoning allows.

gains.a: a standard, from outside the Jain frame, by which the Brahmins' violence is condemned without the epic having to state it
gains.b: a scene showing what follows when the title is kept and the conduct lost: the couplet's 'because' becomes a charge

note: 1453 tells how the merchant fed 1008 people daily for twelve years for the sake of the திருமகன் who would be his daughter's husband; in 1465 he reads the stranger's body and names him திருமகள் கணவன்.
teaches: The twelve years of feeding were a long wait for a sign, and the sign comes as a body to be read, so the epic turns the merchant's charity into the means by which the fated groom is found.

note: The Silappathikaram opens its Puhar with the earth as a woman, sea for garment, hills for breasts, rivers for hair; the Cintamani makes the city wall a maiden with the moat for garment and bastions for breasts.
teaches: The same body-map moves from the whole earth to a single wall, and the Cintamani's word கன்னி turns it into a figure of a fortress never entered, which the Silappathikaram's earth-woman does not carry.

note: 1118 makes the girl both his life and his rare medicine and him her servant; Kural 1102 says she is the cure for the sickness she brings.
teaches: The cure is a bondage in the epic, since the groom who is healed is enslaved by what heals him.

gains.a: The epic verse gets the argument behind its list of titles, that a cure ordinarily differs from its cause but here is the same person.
gains.b: The couplet gets a sequel in which the cure becomes servitude, which its single line leaves open.

note: 2885 says kin were strangers in past births and will be strangers in births to come; Naladiyar 30 says kin come unasked and go wordlessly, leaving the body like a bird its nesting tree.
teaches: The quatrain holds within one life and the verse extends the same estrangement across births, which turns a sad fact into a ground for cutting the bond.

gains.a: the verse's no-kin argument gains the plain picture of kin arriving and leaving unasked in a single life
gains.b: the quatrain's passing kin gain a reach into past and future births, and with it a reason to cut the tie

note: The poem opens by saying it will show how deeds ripen, and the teller here draws that lesson for Maridattan.
teaches: The closing lesson at 160 answers the promise at 4, so the reader is told that the whole tale was an argument about deeds.

note: Verse 14 has Civakan give nectar to a dog dying in the bathing pool; verse 16 has a god free him, arm him with spells and ask to be remembered.
teaches: Set beside each other, the dying dog's gift and the god's rescue show the patikam placing a kindness and its return two verses apart, leaving the reader to see the debt repaid before the story names the god.

note: The youth said fear of what is due gains nothing; here the disciples fear the ripening of deeds and that fear drives them to austerity.
teaches: Fear of karma is useless as dread but useful as a reason to act, so the earlier advice is limited by what the fear is turned toward.

note: 1553 shows great treasure arriving and the king drowning in it; Kural 332 compares wealth's coming to a crowd gathering and its going to the crowd's scattering.
teaches: Read together, the epic shows only the gathering of the crowd, and the couplet supplies the scattering that the festival hides.

gains.a: The scene of arrival gains the knowledge that the sea of wealth is a crowd at a show that will break up.
gains.b: The couplet gains a king at the height of his fortune, not an anonymous owner, so the image is tested at its peak.

note: 959: the god promises to stay like Civakan's shadow and come if he thinks of him in trouble; patikam verse 15 tells how, when the king throws Civakan into prison, a god comes down the sky like lightning and carries him away.
teaches: The patikam's rescue is the promise of 959 kept, so the god's later appearance is not a chance intervention but the return of a debt owed for the mantra.

note: Kuruntokai 174 says that if he leaves her for wealth across the waste, then wealth alone is wealth and grace exists nowhere; Civakan's saying makes leaving for deeds and wealth a man's duty and staying a woman's.
teaches: The Sangam woman's voice hears the man's going for wealth as the end of grace, while the epic puts the same convention in the hero's mouth as a duty, and uses it, untruly, to cover a departure that is neither for work nor for wealth.

gains.a: the akam convention it quotes, with the woman's protest that the hero's maxim leaves out
gains.b: the man's own statement of the rule as duty, which the woman's lament answers

note: Kural 55 promises that the wife who rises worshipping her husband commands the rain; 1598 describes chaste wives who live worshipping their husband's hands (கணவற்கை தொழுது வாழ்வார்) as a few against the many of 1597.
teaches: The epic keeps the Kural's figure of the husband-worshipping wife but makes her a rare exception within women's general frailty, and drops the rain, so her power shrinks to ending her husband's distress.

gains.a: a known ideal against which the hero's two-part teaching on women can be measured
gains.b: a reading in which the husband-worshipping wife is defined by her renunciations in his absence, not by power over nature

note: Kuruntokai 40's lover marvels that strangers' hearts mingled like rain and red earth; Civakan asks whether the woman who took his heart with one look knew him in a former birth.
teaches: Facing the same mystery of a stranger's sudden hold, the Sangam lover lets the merging stand without cause, while the Jain epic's hero reaches for a past birth, so the pair shows rebirth entering the love lyric as an explanation.

gains.a: Civakan's question is seen as a choice: the old poetry had answered the same wonder without any former life
gains.b: the Kuruntokai's uncaused union is set against a later frame in which love itself has a karmic past

note: The Kural says neither shaving nor long hair is needed if one gives up what the world condemns; Civakan says matted hair, robes and the skull bowl are seeds of a mean birth.
teaches: Where the couplet sets the marks aside as unnecessary, the epic counts them as harmful, sowing rebirth, so the pair shows two degrees of the same critique of outward signs.

gains.a: a neutral maxim that makes plain how much further its own judgment goes
gains.b: a case where the marks are not merely superfluous but are taken for the path itself and so mislead

note: In 200 the narrator introduces Kattiyankaran as a man of flawless learning (வெளிறு இலாக் கேள்வியான்); in 385 the teacher, telling the story to the son, calls him the unlearned minister (கல்லா மந்திரி).
teaches: The same minister's learning is affirmed by the narrator at his rise and denied by the teacher after his crime, so the epic counts learning by its fruit in conduct, not by what a man has heard.

note: 1463 ties the death to the rebound of a weapon sent against the blameless; 1466 says the discus he threw became his own enemy.
teaches: The rebound is first a simile and then a plain statement, so the onlookers read the king's death as his own act turning back.

note: 1520 has the kings bow their crowns in fear as the hero holds the mountain; 1530 has kings hail him from their war-elephants as he enters the city.
teaches: The fear before the mountain becomes open praise in the city, so the feat is turned into public kingship.

note: 2870 teaches the giving up of theft and gambling to the prince; Naladiyar 157 says those of faultless vision do not steal, drink, scorn others or lie.
teaches: Both put the vows in a list for a lay hearer, so the list of vows seems a common teaching form.

gains.a: The verse's vows get a more general frame, the sort of man who keeps them, 'of faultless vision'
gains.b: The Naladiyar list gets a speaker, a king who gives it to a son with the cost of each breaking

note: In 2607 Vijayai begs the eight wives, who came in her dream as eight garlands on the king's crown, never to part; in 2987 they decide to renounce.
teaches: The dream's garlands that were never to part are parted by the story's end, showing the epic setting a mother's wish against the wives' own turn from the household.

note: Verse 396 gives the lord who has no taste of the senses the work of opening doors that end hunger; Kural 225 ranks the strength of those who endure hunger behind that of those who remove it.
teaches: The epic's lord is at once the senses' renouncer and the hunger-remover, so he fills both places the couplet sets in rank order.

gains.a: A test of its claim, since the couplet ranks the ascetic's strength below the giver's, which the epic's lord meets by being both.
gains.b: A figure in whom the ranking does not split, a renouncer who is also the giver the couplet places higher.

note: Verse 402 has the lord foretell that the Kesava will take Ashvagriva's discus; verse 114 has the ministers say the young lord will hold the discus weapon in his hand.
teaches: The ministers' reading of the palm marks is borne out by the lord's own foretelling, which names the discus's source as a rival's own.

note: The couplet says giving and sweet speech gather kin around a man; Civakan says friends and wives can be gained but a brother cannot be made.
teaches: Set beside the Kural's way of winning kin by gifts and kind words, Civakan's saying separates the circle that can be won from the brother who can only be born, so not all kin answer to the Kural's means.

gains.a: the epic verse gains a contrast with the Kural's claim that kin can be drawn by giving, which sharpens what 'cannot be made' means
gains.b: the couplet gains a limit: the kin it gathers are the acquired circle, not the brother of one's birth

note: The teacher tells Civakan that his enemy still stands and not to lament; the next verse shows the rage this rouses, which the teacher must then restrain.
teaches: The consolation that turns grief into thoughts of the enemy produces the very anger the teacher at once has to check, so his own counsel makes the year of restraint necessary.

note: Both use the simile of a poor man's youth (பொருள் இல்லான் இளமை, 38 line 15; the waste's trees in 10): poem 10 measures a withered landscape by it, poem 38 the girl's face drooping after a night of fear.
teaches: The paalai poet and Kapilar draw on one stock of moral similes, but Kapilar moves it from the land to the woman's body and pairs it with its opposite (the gracious man's wealth), so the girl's face becomes a landscape that his coming can drought or rain on, which is the kali form's way of turning a moral maxim into a lover's argument for marriage.

note: Purananuru 66 praises Karikal Valavan's victory at Venni but says the defeated king who fasted to death for shame at his back wound is better than he; the epic's Valavan is checked by no rival, only by the Himalaya.
teaches: The Purananuru sets a moral limit on the victor through the vanquished man's honour, while the epic removes every human limit and lets only a mountain halt him, so the later memory of the Chola has lost the Sangam poet's check on royal glory.

note: The disguise as merchants carries out the stratagem Urumannuvan promises in verse 165.
teaches: The stratagem is a trade, not a battle, which tells the reader how Urumannuvan means to win.

note: 2051 itemises the gods' mansions, couches and cars as the whole of heaven; Kural 50 says the one who lives life as it ought to be lived will be counted among the gods.
teaches: What the couplet offers as the reward of right householding is shown by the epic as a list of comforts and then, in 2060, as a reward that has an end.

gains.a: The gods' world gets a stated goal in a householder's right life, which its inventory alone does not give.
gains.b: The couplet gains content for 'among the gods' and a limit on how far the reward goes.

note: 2115 has samadhi give the sword that cuts the foe; Tirumanthiram 121 has the Siva-yogi cut bonds and remain with the body as if dead.
teaches: Samadhi is a weapon of conquest in the Jain epic and a quiet stillness in the Tirumanthiram, so the same state is used for opposite pictures.

gains.a: Samadhi gains an aggressive purpose, in which it is the sword, where the Tirumanthiram uses it for rest.
gains.b: The still, deathlike state gains a battle in which it is the weapon that ends the enemy.

note: At 215 the narrator says the king ignored counsel because a destiny formed before sprouted in him; Nandagon, telling the same fall, blames only the king's own desire and choice.
teaches: The epic keeps two causes for Saccandan's fall in two voices, so a former deed in the narrator's account never excuses the choice his subject remembers.

note: In the Kural the slipping bangles spread the news (தூற்றா) that the lord of the shore has left; in Ainkurunuru 199 the woman names him by the bangles he loosened and asks to climb the high dune to gaze at his land.
teaches: The couplet's woman fears her bangles will publish the loss to the town, while the Ainkurunuru woman makes the loss her name for him and climbs where all can see her looking, so the same token can be suffered as exposure or claimed in the open.

note: Kannaki, her husband killed by the king's error, asks whether she must waste away in grief like the women who keep hard observances when their husbands go to the pyre; Vijayai, her husband killed by a usurper, is led by the ascetic women into exactly such observances.
teaches: Two wronged wives face the same choice and the epics give opposite answers: Kannaki refuses the widow's penance and turns her grief on the city, while Vijayai accepts it and keeps her grief for a son still living, which shows the son as the difference.

note: The king is lord of a rutting war elephant and in rage; the Siddhar song kills anger as a mad elephant's rut with the goad of reasoning.
teaches: Anger as a rutting elephant is a royal fact in the epic and a figure in the Siddhar, which shows what the goad of reason would have to stop.

gains.a: The epic's king has a real elephant and a real rage but nothing that checks the rage, which the Siddhar's goad of reason supplies.
gains.b: The Siddhar's elephant of anger lacks a king who actually rides one, which the epic gives.

note: The verse says the people honour only the rich and the poor have no kin, using it as a simile; Kural 752 states that everyone scorns the poor and honours the rich.
teaches: The Kural states the world's partiality as a fact and the epic applies it as a simile, showing the poet treats it as shared knowledge and as a cost on the neglected waist.

gains.a: A flat statement of the rule that the simile of the neglected waist depends on.
gains.b: A case of the rule seen in an unexpected place, the jewelling of a body, not in money.

note: Paripadal 6 sets the river play out as a battle array, with bathers drilling rivalry 'as in war' and carrying syringes (சிவிறியர்); in 966 the bathers spray with syringes (சிவிறி) and the play goes through a campaign's whole course, the enemy's back seen, the offender fined with garlands, tribute taken.
teaches: The Sangam festival's figure of water-play as battle is carried by the epic from the array to the victory and its exactions, and set just before a real terror breaks out (973), so the mock war of desire gives way to a true danger.

gains.a: the Sangam convention of the festival as a war of pleasure, which explains why the verse reaches for rout and tribute
gains.b: a later use of the convention that completes the war figure with conquest and penalty, which the Paripadal's arrays only begin

note: 1510 has the hero without swelling pride at the moment feats are listed; Kural 979 calls greatness the absence of pride.
teaches: The epic shows modesty arising from counting those who came before, a source the couplet does not name.

gains.a: the epic verse lacks a name for the hero's lack of pride, and gains the couplet's term for it as greatness
gains.b: the couplet lacks an occasion in which pride is tempted by lists of earlier deeds, and gains one

note: Natrinai 23's friend says the girl's thinness is hidden by her bangles and her loose hair excused by play, but her eyes cannot hide love; Kural 1271 has the man tell her that though she hides it, her kohl-lined eyes go beyond her control and have something to say.
teaches: The Natrinai supplies the test behind Valluvar's claim by sorting the signs of love into those an excuse can cover and the eyes, which none can, so the couplet's 'though you hide' turns out to name a practice of concealment the older poem lays out part by part.

claims.gist: gods and men who conquer their deeds include the king and his ancestor Bharata
a purpose is fulfilled only when it ripens with difficulty; none completes what he intends by wishing
a messenger with a letter will descend into the Pushpakarandam garden after seven have passed
a deed of a former birth rises into fruit and shows that it was real
a sage's sign tells what will befall a king's sons
the earth is a disc hung in the air with Mandara at its centre and the jambu tree on it
the body falls soon like ripe fruit, so one must not linger in pleasure
austerity done in the Jina's form leads to the joys of heaven
a lord appears to remove the sorrows of living beings and is praised by all worlds
a king guards the whole world evenly so that all of it is cooled
the pleasures one enjoys are the fruit of one's good deeds, given by fate
the world accepts what accords with the treatise of policy
karma that cannot otherwise be ended was ended by the Jina, who taught the path of no return
those who do not come to the Jina fall under their deeds and whirl in a sea of sorrow
the life span of hell-beings rises in each lower layer, each layer's minimum equalling the layer above's maximum
the great state of insight that cuts birth cannot be won by those without a mind of dharma
the highest gods are free of desire for women and enjoy unbroken pleasure
only austerity frees one from the net Death has laid, yet those who know it still turn to pleasure
desire is the one sickness in the world for which there is no remedy
the king fallen in battle has gone to heaven, where celestial women are his company
the wealth of those without virtue spreads no good, as the kongu tree in bloom spreads no scent
a king should keep to truth and let no falsehood pass his lips
by good deeds poison becomes nectar, and without them nectar becomes poison
the wise do not think of killing or being killed, since the outcome lies with deeds
the Lord surpasses the dark-blue discus-bearing god, who bows to him
a king who only destroys leaves his people no refuge
the tormentors tell the sufferers they are receiving the fruit of earlier deeds
a king is one who acts calmly on what the learned advise
a minister is one who both advises and carries out what the learned choose

note: In 349 Vijayai takes off the gold garland and necklace while her musk-dressed hair grieves; in 2637 the matrons themselves pluck their dark hair without a flinch.
teaches: The grief of the hair in the forest is replaced by an act done without bowing, so the epic shows the same hair going first with sorrow and then with composure.

note: 3105 pictures desire as grass that lures souls into the four-state pen and says reaching the pure one's feet lets one go to release; Kural 10 says those who reach the Lord's feet swim the sea of births.
teaches: The verse supplies the trap that the Kural's sea leaves unnamed, and the Kural supplies the crossing the verse only names as going.

gains.a: the verse's pen of four states gets the picture of a sea crossed, which turns the escape into a swim
gains.b: the Kural's sea of births gets a reason people are in it, the grass of desire, and a price for crossing, love sold

note: The onlookers name the fruit of a woman's cruelty as leprosy, coming to her body; the couplet says only that harm returns of itself.
teaches: The epic shows the return of harm as a long delay in which the doer is first shown eating and then rotting, which the couplet's afternoon-for-forenoon image cannot show.

gains.a: the unit gains a plain rule that harm to others comes back to the doer, without needing a past birth
gains.b: the couplet gains a case in which the return takes years, passes through a body and is read by onlookers as karma

note: Kural 1228 has the herdsman's flute as a weapon that kills the lonely woman at evening; verse 34 has the herdsmen's konrai flute so sweet that the asunam beast sleeps.
teaches: The same herdsman's flute soothes the beast and wounds the parted woman, so its effect lies in the listener's state and not in the music, a point neither verse shows alone.

gains.a: The verse gets a hearer for whom the flute hurts, which shows that its sweet peace holds only for listeners at ease and sets a limit on the land's contentment.
gains.b: The couplet gets a flute that is gentle to those at ease, which shows that the woman's pain is her own separation and not the sound.

note: Both are Kayamanar's poems of the foster mother after the girl's elopement: in 17 she sits at home picturing the girl's small feet on the waste; in 7 she has followed into the forest and is asking a doe and a hill girl for news.
teaches: Together they give the foster mother's grief two stages, imagination at home and pursuit on the road, and show that the poet built the udanpokku mother as a figure who moves through the story.

note: Tirumanthiram 307 calls life and body a close support and the mind on Siva's feet the firm support that ends birth; 2748 lists the body hard to gain and its destruction among the sermon's topics, with release.
teaches: Both begin from the body, which the Saiva verse treats as a support to be used, while the Jain sage announces it as a thing that is rare and must end.

gains.a: the announced sermon gains a Saiva view in which the body is a means that is used on the way and not merely lost
gains.b: the Tirumanthiram verse's body-as-support is set against a view that treats it as hard to get and bound to end, which adds the Jain sense of its loss to the claim

note: 28 says only that Civakan goes to the ever-new state; 3073 gives the ending of the austerity by which he gets there, with his family waiting.
teaches: The opening summary states the destination in a half-line; the closing shows the cost, the family watching and the hand held back from food.

note: In 347 Vijayai's distress comes because a deed of a former birth stood waiting; in 2763 the same ripening is told of all who do evil, with fruits dropping from the palm.
teaches: The single case of the queen's fate and the general teaching that deeds come to fruit are placed side by side, so the reader sees the sermon as the rule behind a plot he already saw.

note: In 1040 the maiden prays that the sickness of birth leave her; in 1049 a friend says the love of a united pair outweighs even the state without birth and death.
teaches: The same eve holds two valuations of release, a bride's prayer and a friend's boast, and the poet leaves them standing side by side.

note: Verse 866 has learned men fix the hour for the bride to board; verse 958 has the kings meet at the hour the astrologers named.
teaches: The same trust in the astrologers' hour governs the leaving and the meeting.

note: The Kural's lover says anicham and swan's down are like nerunji to her feet; the epic has a whole city's women whose feet shiver on flowering cotton while they wear anicham.
teaches: A lover's private hyperbole about one woman's feet becomes in the epic a stock trait of a whole class of wealthy women, showing how the Kural's love conceits turned into description.

gains.a: The verse's strange shiver of feet on cotton is legible as a known conceit, so its point is degree of wealth, not novelty of image.
gains.b: The couplet's image is shown to have become public property, attached to a city's luxury rather than one lover's gaze.

note: 1165 calls anger a fire that gives birth to pride and a sword thirsty for blood; Kural 306 calls anger a fire that burns even one's own safe raft of kin.
teaches: The warrior prizes anger as the fuel of his sword, while the Kural counts the same anger as what burns one's own people.

gains.a: The warrior's praise of anger names no cost, which the Kural states as the burning of one's own kin.
gains.b: The Kural's rule has no one who values anger as martial fuel, which the epic supplies by letting a warrior praise it.

note: Tirumanthiram 905 promises that chanting சிவாயநம ends birth, by grace; in 946 the Lord's five padas, taken at death, bring the dog a good state (நற்கதி), a better birth.
teaches: Both are five-part formulas given at the decisive moment, but the Saiva five letters promise an end to birth through grace, while the Jain five padas here promise a better birth by the dog's own letting go of attachment and fear.

gains.a: the measure of how modest its promise is: a good birth, not release, and won by the hearer's renunciation rather than by a god's grace
gains.b: a rival five-fold formula against which its claim that the five letters end birth stands out as a stronger claim

note: 195 has the king linger with his wife as a monsoon cloud lingers; 198 says the king slipped from guarding the earth (மண் அகம் காவலின் வழுக்கி) while joined to her.
teaches: The lingering that the wedding verses present as pure delight is the same act that 198 names as a lapse in the king's guard, so the romantic sequence is already the first step of the political fall.

note: Kural 742 counts a shady forest as one of a fort's four parts; verse 785 shows who holds the forest, men who live by violence and serve the king.
teaches: A forest that guards the realm is held by violent servants, a cost the couplet's list of fort parts does not show.

gains.a: The verse lacks the idea that the forest is itself a defence, which the couplet names.
gains.b: The couplet lacks the picture of who actually keeps the forest, which the verse adds.

note: The king lists what desire destroys; the couplet says pain ends when desire, anger and confusion lose even their names.
teaches: The couplet states the cure; the king's list shows what it costs when desire is not removed, and he begins the cure by leaving the court.

gains.a: The king's list of damage remains a mood until a doctrine says desire can be removed.
gains.b: The couplet gets a concrete account of what the removed desire costs a man who was ruled by it.

note: The epic teacher says all who have a body suffer, even gods bowing to higher gods; the quatrain says parting, grievous illness and ruin come together to all who take a body and bids the heart cling to the wise.
teaches: The quatrain's advice to cling to the wise is shown to need the epic's wider claim, that no heaven escapes the suffering it names, before it becomes more than comfort.

gains.a: The epic verse gains from the quatrain a remedy, to cling to the wise who see through birth, where the epic only states the diagnosis
gains.b: The quatrain gains the extension to the gods: if even heaven is under suffering, no birth, however high, is a place to rest

note: The companion appeals to the deity that dwells in the house; Kemasari then installs the bees as the gods of her house.
teaches: The house god that the household turns to for her survival is answered by her own choice of new household gods, the bees of his parting words, so worship shifts from the family's deity to the creature his parting words named.

note: Both say a deed finds its doer; the epic adds that it outlasts her death.
teaches: Putting 217 beside the calf-and-mother image shows that the Jain epic makes the deed's claim reach past the doer's body, a step the quatrain does not take.

gains.a: the unit gains an image of how the old deed finds her, as a calf picks out its mother
gains.b: the quatrain gains a limit case, where the deed still stands after the body has failed

note: Neelakesi asks what cause brings the elements together, since they cannot join themselves; Tirumular sets unknowing maya beside the knowing soul and calls the making of elements and senses the fivefold work of grace.
teaches: Both texts deny that unknowing matter assembles itself into a knower, but where the Jain debater leaves the cause in the soul and its deeds, the Saiva verse gives it to grace.

note: 1111 shows her shame breaking like a cage; 1122 shows her still shy and stranger-like in his lap.
teaches: The bride's shame is not undone in one embrace, and the groom still feels the distance it leaves after the cage is said to be broken.

note: Sathanikan crowns the heir first and then turns ascetic, in the order the Cintamani's chariot-king lays down: guard the kingdom, give it to a worthy son, and only then renounce.
teaches: The Cintamani states as advice the order that this king follows in the story, and the epic adds that he passes over his two named sons for Udayanan.

note: 2929 shows a man who never gave now begging in cold rags; 2624 shows a woman who drank boiled milk from a gold bowl now worn by hunger and cut off from her fortune.
teaches: The first pictures the beggar's state and names his past failure to give, the second pictures a fall from wealth, so together they show beggary as both the fruit of not giving and a turn of fortune.

note: Natrinai 8 places in Poraiyan's Thondi neythal flowers that look like eyes; in Akananuru 290 the heroine says her eyes, once like the cool neythal of Kuttuvan's Thondi harbour, have lost that beauty.
teaches: The Thondi neythal and a woman's eyes were a fixed pair that ran both ways, the flower measured by eyes in a man's first praise and the eyes by the flower in a woman's grief at separation, so one token marked beauty found and beauty lost at two stages of love.

note: 986 says the winner of the bride will surely rule the wheel; 1127 calls her the great queen of the wheel-ruler.
teaches: The singers speak as if the father's prophecy were already true, so the wedding is also the first coronation of her place.

note: Kural 376 says what is not one's portion will not stay however guarded and what is one's portion will not leave; the king, told his daughter's portion lies in Rajamapuram, neither gives her to the gift-bearing kings nor tells them so, but keeps them waiting with his intent hidden.
teaches: The pair shows that knowing one's portion in advance does not end action: the king turns the couplet's resignation into policy, managing powerful suitors while waiting for fate to arrive.

gains.a: a general rule of allotted portion behind the king's refusal to accept the suitors' riches
gains.b: a case where the rule is applied to a daughter rather than to wealth, and where the one who knows the portion must still act with craft to protect it

note: In 473 his foster father Kantukkatan receives him lovingly as if Indra's son had come; here the women call him a lion fed by Kandukkan.
teaches: The merchant's rearing, hidden in the early books, is now the credential in the city's praise, showing his birth in a merchant house is part of how he is seen as a king.

note: In 455 one who hears of Civakan's recovery of the herd rages like a man whose last day has come; in 670 the king, burning like gold in fire, stands ready to kill him.
teaches: The ruler's anger first stirred by the hero's fame now becomes a plan to murder him, so Civakan's public successes are the very things that endanger him.

note: 1735 names the boy Amitatejas for his boundless might; 1791 has the prince Amitatejas enter the swayamvara hall so bright that other kings are dimmed.
teaches: The name given at birth is made good at the swayamvara, so the boy's later outshining of kings is shown as the sign promised at his birth.

note: The poet said he would teach release through leaving cruel deeds; the king's refusal is the first such act in this story.
teaches: The opening promise of the poem is enacted in the first refusal of killing, long before any release.

note: Kural 500 has the jackal kill the fearless elephant once its feet sink in the mire; 1928 has the roaring lion caught in the hunters' net in the forest.
teaches: Both reverse the strong beast by its setting, but the epic puts the reversal in a mother's answer to a son who has just called himself the lion, so the maxim is aimed at a person and not at kings in general.

gains.a: the epic's lion gains the couplet's structure, in which ground and not courage decides, so the net is read as the place chosen by weaker men
gains.b: the couplet gains a living addressee, a young claimant who must hear that his own strength is what the trap relies on

note: The Kural says all pain falls on those who caused pain; the king reads his own life as a ripening of the pain he gave his father and mother in their births.
teaches: The couplet's rule becomes a confession in which the doer sees the pain return across several births.

gains.a: The king applies the rule to himself and to kin in earlier births.
gains.b: The couplet gets a speaker who feels the rule falling on him.

note: 1305 brings Kamukan, learned in all arts, with bow and arrow; 1306 shows him ward off the volley and shoot his foe.
teaches: The note that he had learned all the arts is made good in the next verse, so the learning is shown as a fighter's skill.

note: 908's condition, joining Civakan's chest or no one breaking her nirai, is met when Suramanjari's heart rises to sink into his chest in her own ilampakam.
teaches: The exception she sets in anger becomes the desire that ends the vow, so the epic keeps her nirai intact by letting the one permitted man be the one she longs for.

note: Civakan swears to bring the raiders to the city with their crowns at the king's feet; three verses later the raiders fall at his own feet as his companions and ride into the city honoured on elephants.
teaches: The vow is kept to the letter and reversed in substance: the raiders do come to the city bowing, but as friends at the hero's feet rather than captives at the king's, so the epic turns a war oath into a reunion.

note: The townspeople tie sickness to the goddess's anger and ask for worship to prevent it; the Siddhar says the offering of goat and cock at the shrine does not stop the sickness and the family deity is not its cause.
teaches: The two disagree on whether a deity's anger causes disease, so the epic's chain from the goddess's anger to the king's sacrifice rests on a belief the Siddhar rejects.

gains.a: the people's fear is seen as a belief another voice in Tamil rejected, so it is not simply the setting
gains.b: the Siddhar's mockery of the goat and cock offering gets a case where the same belief ends in a human sacrifice

note: The பிண்டி whose fall in the dream meant the king's death is in 271 the tree of the Jina whose scripture the king offers his wife as consolation.
teaches: One tree carries both the loss and the remedy: the royal asoka falls, and the Jina's asoka stands as the ground for not grieving that fall.

note: The hunter boasts that one man in a chariot can do nothing even if he is Death; in 450 the hunters say a chariot-flood has surrounded them, victory is hard, and a hunter lied to them.
teaches: The raiders' contempt for a single foe is reversed by their own words, and 450's charge that a hunter lied shows them blaming a speaker rather than their dismissal of the omen.

note: 2125 places the liberated soul in the state called சிவகதி and wins it by its own meditation; Tirumanthiram 6 says apart from the Lord there is no hard penance that can achieve and no way into his city.
teaches: The two texts both speak of an unreturning state but disagree on whether penance alone reaches it or only the Lord opens the way.

gains.a: The state of release, which the Soolamani reaches by effort alone, is set against a view in which that effort is useless without the Lord.
gains.b: The claim that no penance achieves without him gains a rival case in which a hero wins release by his own meditation with no god acting.

note: Naladiyar 347 says a gem-set golden sandal is still for the foot, so the base are known by their deeds though rich; Pazhamozhi 72 says a gem rolled in mud is still a gem to those who know.
teaches: Together they make one rule from both directions: wealth does not lift the base and mire does not lower the noble, so neither fortune changes what a person is.

note: Patikam verse 14 tells that on the same day the hero gave nectar to the dying dog at the bathing festival, he overcame the victorious elephant that had terrified Gunamalai; 973 is the elephant breaking loose as the festival crowd returns.
teaches: The patikam binds the mercy to the dog and the mastery of the elephant as one day's deeds, so the chapter's turn from the god's farewell through the water-play to the rampaging tusker is a single day planned as a pair of the hero's virtues.

note: Verse 107 has the astrologer say a Vidyadhara king will come and give a daughter to the young lord; verse 530 raises the doubt that Vidyadharas and men do not marry.
teaches: The prophecy skips the custom against such a match, and Marusi's reply is the story's way of making what was foretold pass through argument before it can happen.

note: Tirumanthiram 724 nurtures the body because without it true knowledge cannot be gained; 605 bids all strive at hard penance while still in the body.
teaches: Both make the living body the only place where release can be worked for, but the proclamation spends the body in austerity while Tirumular guards it as the means of knowledge, so the same premise yields discipline in one and care in the other.

gains.a: a statement of why 'while in the body' matters, which the proclamation's compressed phrase leaves unsaid
gains.b: a contrasting use of the body as the seat of penance, in a Jain frame, against which Tirumular's nurture of it stands out as a choice

note: Verse 53 shows Payapati's land troubled only by Kama's arrows; 599 holds up a king who cannot sleep for fear of failing his people.
teaches: The envoy's praise of the king's sleepless care sits beside the poet's own earlier description of him, whose days were spent among queens.

claims.gist: the Jina conquered the three worlds without strife and gave the world a threefold teaching
love directed to the worthy brings wealth
keeping a grown daughter long unmarried brings sin and fault on her guardians
awareness is the goad that drives knowledge along the right path toward the enemy
making the likeness of a living creature is felt to be like killing
hearing the dharma checks the influx of karma, brings its shedding and ripens the hearer for release
a bond with Vidyadharas, who are god-like, is hard for men of the earth to gain
the Jina has completely conquered the two kinds of deed
the teaching that ends birth is rarely won and must be used before death, since nothing can be done once the pyre takes the body
difference of lineage should not bar a marriage, since gods wed a hill girl and a herd girl
a king ruling with a faultless sceptre rules in ease and wins the praise of other kings
a missile loosed in hatred must kill and no one can turn it back
beasts and birds born in the enjoyment land also rise to heaven
a counsellor must speak for his king's good even at the risk of the king's anger, as the books of dharma direct
the three ranks of beings, best, middle and lowest, are the fruit of the good done before
a life of austerity ends in birth among the gods
one who spends the stock of good deeds without renewing it falls to hell
the good deed is the one benefactor that accompanies the life
rage in a warrior's heart gives force to the arrow-rain that wins

note: 2819 makes virtue (sila) the armour of warring kings; in 3074 mercy is the armour and sila the sword.
teaches: The same virtue moves from a guard to a weapon, showing that in this ascetic war sila both protects and wins.

note: 1561 has the chief queen resolve to see the plants wed; in 1564 the king smiles and accepts, and the grove outing follows.
teaches: The queen's wish becomes the king's plan only through the maid's message and his answer, so the outing is shared.

note: The Pandya's war proclamation in Puram 9 tells cows, brahmins, women, the sick and the sonless to get clear before battle; Civakan names cows, renunciants, women, children and brahmins as those he must protect.
teaches: The same list of the protected is in the Sangam poem those a king spares from his own arrows, and in the epic those a warrior must defend from another's raid, so the duty widens from restraint to rescue.

gains.a: Civakan's oath gains a Sangam pedigree: his list is the old code of who stands outside war
gains.b: the Puram poem's code of sparing gains its active counterpart, an obligation to defend the same people when someone else attacks them

note: The goad in line 4 is the tool of the elephant keeper; Tirumular's goad is the five letters that rein the five elephants.
teaches: The goad that in one poem governs a real elephant becomes the word that governs the senses in the other.

gains.a: the taking of the goad gets an inner reading as discipline over a creature of great force
gains.b: the image of the goad gets a scene in which it is used on a real elephant that has bowed already

note: Kural 9 says a head that does not bow at the feet of the one of eight qualities is as useless as a dead sense; 3022 has the king bow with his gem crown, ear-rings and bands shining on the ground.
teaches: The Kural gives the cost of a head that does not bow, and the epic shows the most ornamented head in the book putting its crown to use by bowing.

gains.a: the king's crown, ear-rings and garlands are given their one use, the bow, which the couplet makes the measure of a head
gains.b: the Kural's useless head gets its opposite, a head heavy with ornaments that is not useless because it bows

note: The teacher asks Civakan to bear no anger for a year; his own penance had been undertaken so that fierce anger would wane.
teaches: The request for restraint is the teacher's own discipline passed to his pupil, asked by one who knows how hard anger is to wear down.

note: The Kural's spy goes in the guise of renunciants (துறந்தார் படிவத்தர்) and gives nothing away; Padumukan's spies (படிவ ஒற்றாளர்) have found Civakan in disguise and are rewarded on their report.
teaches: The Kural writes spying as a king's instrument against enemies, while the epic turns the same disguised spy to a band of friends searching for their lost lord, which shows the technique is a means that serves loyalty as well as statecraft.

gains.a: the epic's spies gain from the couplet the sense of படிவம், a borrowed and often ascetic guise, which the verse names but does not explain
gains.b: the couplet gains a case where the spy's master is not a king and his search is for a friend, not for hidden enemies

note: Kural 901 says men who fix their desire on the wife miss life's fine fruit; 196 measures the king's wedded intimacy as greater than the sea, and the story goes on to make that desire lose him his realm.
teaches: The Kural's chapter on following the wife assumes a fault in the yielding; the epic gives a blameless, chaste queen (verse 7, வீடாத கற்பின்) and lawful marriage, and still the husband's boundless absorption alone ruins him, so the rule holds without any fault in the woman.

gains.a: the celebration of the wedding season acquires its moral edge from a stated rule
gains.b: the couplet's claim is tested on a case where the wife is beyond reproach, showing the danger lies in the man's desire, not in her

note: Kural 550 allows a king to put the cruel to death as weeding the crop; 54 has this king subdue even opponents by bowing them, and not slay in anger.
teaches: The couplet's weeding is the harsher rule, and the verse shows a king who treats killing as what grace avoids, so the two differ on whether death is part of a king's work.

gains.a: The verse gains a rival standard in which a king's killing counts as justified, against which his restraint reads as a choice, not a rule.
gains.b: The couplet gains a king who will not weed even his foes, showing how far a ruler can go without using death.

note: 1932 stages lust's punishment as a forced embrace of fire; Siddhar 450 has the pit of hell say it will eat the lustful and the loins say they will ruin him.
teaches: A Siddhar's warning in the speaker's own body becomes in the epic a scene of wardens and figures, so the same fear is placed inside and outside the sinner.

gains.a: The embrace of fire gains an inner meaning, that desire itself is what the pit feeds on.
gains.b: The Siddhar's threat gains a literal staging, in which the loins' ruin is acted out as an embrace.

note: 2887 shows a clinging that holds like the monitor's grip broken by a single word; Kural 350 says to cling to the clinging of the one without clinging in order to let clinging go.
teaches: The Kural names the means as a right object of clinging and the verse names a single word, so the means can be a sentence from a teacher.

gains.a: the single word that broke the prince's clinging gains the Kural's account of why a word can work: it points to the unclinging one
gains.b: the Kural's command to cling in order to let go gains a case where one saying did it

note: Tirumanthiram 1527: when the two deeds stand balanced, grace comes as the guru, and when one's own agency ends the impurities go; Cintamani 380: a past good deed drives Civakan and his own understanding reaches out, and he takes refuge in the Arhat.
teaches: Both put a teacher at the turn toward release, but for Tirumular the teacher is grace descending once deeds cancel and one's agency ends, while for the Jain epic it is the push of a good deed and the youth's own understanding that bring him to the teacher's Lord.

gains.a: Civakan's conversion is shown to need no descent of grace: karma and his own understanding suffice
gains.b: the Saiva claim that one's own agency must end is set against a release story in which agency is one of its two causes

note: The king refuses to kill even to save his own life, and gives the cost in the next world and the shortness of this one.
teaches: The couplet gives the rule alone; the king adds the reason that makes it bear on a man whose own life is threatened.

gains.a: The king's refusal is shown to rest on a known maxim, not only on his temper.
gains.b: The couplet gets a man whose own life is truly threatened and who must pay for obeying it.

note: In 409 the astrologer reads from the horoscope that within a month Tivittan will split a lion's mouth; in 769 the lion's blood is seen running down the hill.
teaches: The prophecy's fulfilment is shown only through its aftermath, the blood stream, so the reader sees the foretold deed by its trace.

note: In 228 the king soothed Vijayai by calling belief in dreams a woman's credulity; in 267 he tells her that all she dreamt has come to pass.
teaches: The king's dismissal of his wife's dream is reversed by his own admission, which turns his later lecture on detachment in 269 into a man correcting his own earlier error.

note: Kar Narpathu 4's friend points to the bloomed konrai as the season and the cure of pallor; Kuruntokai 66's friend calls the bloomed konrai foolish, fooled by stray rain, and denies that the season has come.
