teaches: The friend's comfort can use the konrai either way, as proof the promised season is here or as a false sign to be dismissed, which shows that the consolation lies in the friend's argument and not in the flower itself.

note: Kural 539 bids a man remember the ruined when swollen with joy; the king of verse 124 forgets even his own ruin.
teaches: The couplet's remedy needs a remembering mind, and the poem shows the king in whom nothing remains to be reminded.

gains.a: The verse gains the couplet's name for the fault: joy that swells past remembering.
gains.b: The couplet gains a king whose own loss, not another's, is the ruin he forgets.

note: In 467 the city women say only those whose penance has earned it may drink Civakan's beauty; in 640 the suitor kings say that if they cannot win Gandharvadattai they will do penance.
teaches: The epic gives the same belief to both sexes, that tavam is the price of a beloved, but turns it round: the women look to past penance as the cause of a lucky union, the kings to future penance as the comfort for a lost one.

note: In the Kaanal Vari the man sings that a cruel Death with spear-like eyes lives in the shore grove in a girl's form, and that had he known he would not have come; in the Cintamani onlookers tell the suitors that she is Death and bid them run while they can.
teaches: The two epics use the woman-as-Death figure at opposite moments: the Silappathikaram's singer learns it too late and says he would not have come, while the Cintamani's crowd says it beforehand to men who stay anyway, so the warning that comes too late in one comes in time and fails in the other.

note: Both are the man's first sight of the woman and both reach for அணங்கு; the Kural's lover wavers among goddess, peahen and woman, while Sachchandan, on the likelier reading, takes her for an அணங்கு without doubt (ஐயுறான்).
teaches: The Kural's perplexity at first sight is a lover's healthy doubt; the epic gives a king who does not doubt, and his certainty that she is more than human is the first step of the absorption that later costs him his kingdom.

gains.a: the king's untroubled certainty is seen as a departure from the expected first-sight wavering, marking his surrender as complete
gains.b: the couplet's three-way doubt is shown to hold a check that a man without it, a king, loses

note: Civakan imagines his wife wasting and burning on her bed; in 1509 Kemasari, left by him, cries that her life is leaving her body.
teaches: Read together, the lament the epic gave Kemasari in her own voice returns here as the hero's guess about another wife, so the poem lets the reader measure his pity for the absent Tattai against his silence toward the wife he has just left.

note: Kural 335 bids good deeds be rushed before the hiccup stops the tongue; Cintamani 377 asks whether anything intended can be done when the fire takes the body, after the teaching that ends birth has been rarely won.
teaches: The couplet's urgency rests on how near death may be; the epic adds that the means of release is already in hand and wasted by pampering the senses, so delay is the squandering of a rare gain and not only a race with death.

gains.a: the teacher's rhetorical question is grounded in a rule, act before the end
gains.b: the couplet's general 'good deed' is specified as using a teaching already obtained, and its limit moved from the death rattle to the pyre

note: Verse 561 presents the king's greatness as coming from a high clan; Naladiyar 195 says good and bad caste are words and that austerity, learning and effort make a lineage, which holds if 'clan' is taken to mean birth alone.
teaches: The priest's boast of birth is checked by the poem's own ancestor, who gained his rank by renouncing, which is the test the Naladiyar sets.

gains.a: The epic's clan pride gets a standard it passes only because its founder earned his place by austerity.
gains.b: The quatrain gets an example where a king's lineage is named as the cause of greatness, so its claim is against a living boast.

note: Naladiyar 72 says to bear in silence the unfit words of those who are not one's equals; verse 529 has Marusi ashamed because the king bore his unfit words.
teaches: The quatrain shows forbearance as the superior's duty, and the epic shows what it does to the one borne with: shame and a calmed anger rather than a grudge.

gains.a: A rule that explains why the king's patience is praised and why Marusi feels small.
gains.b: An effect of silent forbearance on the speaker who was borne with, which the quatrain does not show.

note: 1630 has the king hidden among the women; 1631 has the chief queen guess it and send more women out to play like children.
teaches: The queen answers the hiding by staging the game she thinks he wants to watch, so the women's play is her reply and not only their sport.

note: 255 says the girl's grace resembles the mountain goddesses (வரையர மகளிர்ப் புரையும்); 256 says she herself is a great அணங்கு.
teaches: Two consecutive poems on the same opening line move from likeness to identity, so the decade itself shows a comparison with the hill goddesses hardening into the claim that the girl is one.

note: In 803, at his first battle, Civakan watches a ghoul dress herself in the slain and laughs with delight; in 2235 the same ghoul's feast is made from bridegrooms whose wedding garlands their brides had strung.
teaches: Where the first battle offers the ghoul's feast as spectacle for the hero's laughter, the final war sets it against the brides' garlands, so the same image now carries the cost of war to the women left behind.

note: Both measure a small but fatal thing as a split sesame seed: the Kural an inner enmity that holds ruin, Civakan the least attachment, which he calls a fault.
teaches: The sesame measure moves from a king's household enemy to the attachment inside the self, so the danger the Kural locates in a court the Jain hero locates in the heart that clings.

gains.a: Civakan's rule is given a familiar measure of how little it takes to ruin, transferred from politics to the soul
gains.b: the couplet's warning that a tiny hidden thing contains ruin is extended to attachment, a second enemy within

note: In Kural 1320 she is angry even at his gaze, asking whom he thinks of; here she is angry at his gaze on a painted figure, and he claims he took the picture for her.
teaches: The epic supplies the object the couplet leaves imagined, a painted woman on the wall, and turns the lover's defence round: his gaze was faithful because he mistook the picture for her.

gains.a: the epic scene inherits a precise oodal type, the jealousy of the gaze
gains.b: the couplet's suspicion gets a concrete rival and an answer the man can give, which it never offers

note: Kural 687 ranks highest the envoy who knows the protocol, weighs the moment and place, and speaks after thought; at 500 Maruci opens with a bow and a courtesy that honours the princes before any message.
teaches: The epic shows an envoy meeting the Kural's test of protocol, and shows that what he first says is praise and not the matter of his errand.

gains.a: A standard that names the opening courtesy as part of the envoy's art and not a mere ornament.
gains.b: A scene in which the protocol it asks for is carried out, with praise placed ahead of the message.

note: 1953 puts those who hoard without householder's dharma and die hard-fisted in hell; Naladiyar 273 says the hoarder is laughed at by his own wealth.
teaches: The miser is mocked in life by the wealth he stored and punished after death for it, two sanctions for one fault.

gains.a: The hell verse gains the earthly shame of the miser, which it omits.
gains.b: The quatrain gains the afterlife penalty it does not mention.

note: 396 praises Ezhiniyathan of Vattaru, whose land has the toddy-drinking Kosar; Akananuru 216 names Athan Ezhini, lord of Selli, among whose people the young Kosar make garlands, and compares the parathai's pain to the elephant his spear pierced.
teaches: If the two Ezhinis are one chief (both are named with the Kosar), akam remembers him by a war wound inflicted on an elephant, used as a courtesan's image of suffering, while puram remembers him as feeder of the kinless, showing how a patron's two reputations were divided between the genres.

note: 76 opens: killing and being killed is not new (புதுவது அன்று), it is the way of the world; 192 says dying is not new (சாதலும் புதுவது அன்றே).
teaches: The same commonplace serves opposite ends: in 192 the oldness of death leads to calm toward great and small alike, while in 76 it is granted only so that one king's feat can stand out as the thing never heard of before.

note: The couplet names quarrel, reconciliation and union as love's rewards; the epic stages that sequence in the swans and has the hero watch it.
teaches: The couplet lists oodal, understanding and union as what lovers gain, and the epic shows that sequence complete in birds before a man who is parted, so the reward the couplet promises becomes, for the onlooker who lacks it, the cause of pain.

gains.a: the epic verse gains the couplet's order of quarrel, reconciliation and union, which explains why the swans' episode ends in union and not in the sulk
gains.b: the couplet gains a watcher outside the pair, for whom the rewards of love seen in others turn into longing

note: 1427 has a spell command Death to finish his work at a king's wish; Tirumanthiram 176 says no one can fight when life leaves and only the thought of the Lord turns Death's messengers.
teaches: The epic's Death takes orders from a spell while the Saiva verse holds Death answerable to the Lord alone, so the two disagree over who commands Death.

gains.a: the unit gains a view in which Death does not serve a king's spell
gains.b: the verse gains a scene where Death is commanded by a human wish, which the verse denies

note: In the Nedunalvadai the king walks the camp at midnight to look at the sword wounds of the warriors; in the epic the wounded are laid in ghee, have spearheads cut out, and are given purses and ornaments.
teaches: The Sangam poem shows care for the wounded as the king's sleepless looking, and the epic turns that care into a practice of treatment and payment, so the reader sees the duty to the wounded grow from presence into provision.

gains.a: the epic's list of treatments gains a source in the old ideal of the leader who goes himself to the wounded, which it leaves to friends and women
gains.b: the Sangam king's visit gains a picture of what was done for the wounded after he looked, which the poem does not tell

note: Vijayai said that, like clouds struck by wind, we are scattered by the force of deeds; the teacher says that Indra himself and a small monkey alike eat what their deeds have made.
teaches: The mother's saying of parting by deeds becomes a rule with no exemption, since it covers heaven's king, so no rank of birth can be claimed as a refuge.

note: Kural 731 names unfailing yield, worthy people and wealthy people as the marks of a land; verse 29 gives only the yield, in stored grain that does not shrink as it is eaten.
teaches: Read against the Kural's three-part definition, the epic's country is first described by what it yields, and the people and the rich come only later, so the poet is building the land from its harvest outward.

gains.a: The verse gets a criterion that shows why grain heaps count as describing a land and not only as a list of crops.
gains.b: The couplet's abstract 'unfailing yield' gets concrete grains stored in houses and not diminishing when eaten.

note: Verse 266 says that nothing is better for the world than the shade at the feet of a king who stands in aram and guards the people like his own life; verse 140 faults a king who has every virtue but lacks grace to the lowly.
teaches: The counsellor's ideal king guards all like his life, and the poet's own Vidyadhara king, perfect but lacking grace, shows the ideal cannot be taken as met by any one virtue.

note: 1646 sets the artificial hill with gem waterfalls as the place the women reach; 1650 makes the same hill answer them and mock them.
teaches: The hill that was scenery becomes a speaker, so the grove ends the run by playing back at the women.

note: Arkakirti's wrath rains arrows and blood; the couplet says to guard against anger, which kills the one who does not.
teaches: A speech that glories in wrath as war's fuel meets a rule that says it destroys its own bearer.

gains.a: The boast gains a warning it does not hear: the wrath that drives the arrows can also destroy the archer.
gains.b: The couplet gains a counter-case where anger is praised as a duty, so its advice is tested against the warrior's ethic.

note: 1827 has kings with every means to win her calm themselves because deeds ripen as they will; Kural 377 says even those who have gathered millions enjoy only what the apportioner has apportioned.
teaches: Fate's apportioning is shown over a bride and not over wealth, among men whose rank and army were equal, so the rule is tested where effort was all in place.

gains.a: The kings' calm gains a stated general law behind it, which the verse leaves as their passing thought.
gains.b: The couplet gains a contest in which every competitor had equal means, the case where apportioning alone must decide.

note: The patikam tells that at the festival bath two young women quarrelled over their powders and swore not to bathe if they lost; here the two, Suramanjari and Gunamalai, sit together in the grove free of grief.
teaches: The patikam's quarrel is set against this calm first sight of the rivals side by side, so the story's discord grows out of an easy companionship and the festival's own luxury.

note: 1128 warns the kurava tree not to grow as fragrant as the bride, lest it be plucked; Kural 1111 greets the anicham flower and says the beloved is more delicate.
teaches: Praising a girl by comparing her to a flower carries a threat in the epic, where equalling her gets the flower plucked, and only flattery in the couplet.

gains.a: The epic verse gets the Kural's form of speaking to a flower, so that its warning can be heard as a courtly praise.
gains.b: The couplet gets a darker side to the comparison, since a flower that equals her is in danger.

claims.gist: the last state of the eight qualities is reached only by those who have cut craving and attachment, and others cannot know it
heaped deeds ripen at death and send the dying into animal births
plucking out the hair is borne with patience as an austerity
the shrine of the Arhat removes ills, ends births and gives boons
those who die in the land of enjoyment are reborn as gods
to take wealth for the thing of real worth is an error
food given to the destitute is a well of reward in heaven
one who protects all lives and abstains from honey and flesh owns earth and sky
a chest scarred by an elephant's tusk is a warrior's beauty
the Jina marked by the threefold signs is the lord to follow
knowledge, right vision and right conduct together, each made full, end both good and evil deeds
right conduct is restraint of the five senses and not harming any living being
a marriage comes about when the couple's apportioned portion is for joining
the ascetic's earlier penance brings rebirth in a divine world
to go under the king's protection is the virtuous course
present helplessness is the fruit of deeds undertaken earlier
earlier kings ruled by pleasing the overlord, and that is the precedent
those who kill beasts and fish for sport or trade are tormented in hell daily
the adorned body is only humours and foul matter beneath its scents and flowers
the five great vows ward off the karma that is coming in
deeds that ripen bind the self, and they can be shed in due order
the one before whom the whole world bows will become lord of the discus, a universal ruler
those who bully the weak with force should give it up, live rightly and guard their lives
with the coverings removed the soul knows world and non-world at once and remains in release
those who lose their sweetness lose their followers, even the rich
the doer of the deed receives its fruit, without doubt
the one who has come to the Jina's feet has risen out of the sea of birth
a king cannot bear the world alone and bears it with the learned beside him
from ignorance come deeds, from deeds pain and desire, and from these love, sorrow, affliction and at last death

note: Purananuru 109 is Kapilar's boast during the siege of Paari's Parambu that the three kings cannot take it by force; Akananuru 78 recalls Paari with Kapilar beside him, holding out for years and driving away the kings with elephants.
teaches: The akam poem treats as settled fame what the puram poem speaks in the middle of the siege, so Paari's resistance with Kapilar had become a reference point another poet could use to praise a girl's fragrance.

note: 1517 praises a mountain-lifter whom kings and gods hail; Tirumanthiram 350 tells of a lifter of the great mountain who was crushed by the Lord and then given grace.
teaches: The epic stops at homage to the lifter, while the Saiva verse asks what becomes of that strength before God.

gains.a: the epic scene lacks any verdict on mountain-lifting strength beyond the kings' homage, and gains a measure from the lifter who is crushed
gains.b: the Tirumanthiram verse lacks a lifter honoured and unpunished, and gains one whose feat is a king's proof, not an offence against a god

note: The Kural's lover says he once had modesty and manliness and now has only the palmyra horse; the epic's maxim says restraint is the beauty of manliness when love fails.
teaches: Against the Kural's man who says love has taken his manliness, the epic defines manliness as the restraint that remains when love is denied, so the same word marks opposite outcomes of desire.

gains.a: the epic's maxim is seen as a reply to the Kural's account of love overcoming manliness
gains.b: the couplet's despair is set against a path the lover does not consider, restraint through penance

note: Both open by praising the Jain god, but the Cintamani defines him by the bliss he reached by himself and his unceasing qualities, while the Soolamani defines him by the sum of deeds he conquered and by the freeing of those who bow.
teaches: One invocation names what the god is, the other what the god did to deeds, so the Jain epics share a god but each praises a different side of him.

note: 2824 names what the ascetics do to quench the five senses (wither them, keep from four sins); Kural 25 says only that the strength of one who has quenched them is witnessed by Indra.
teaches: The Kural gives the strength of one who has quenched the senses without the practice, and the verse gives the practice without the strength, so the two together show both sides.

gains.a: the verse's practice of withering the senses gets a measure of what it wins, a strength that heaven's king himself would witness
gains.b: the Kural's quenching of the five gets a concrete discipline (withering the body, keeping from lying, killing, theft and lust) that its praise leaves open

note: Verse 936 gives the roar of pipes, drums and horns at the wedding ride; Naladiyar 23 says the drums that sound for a wedding may sound the same day for the bridegroom's funeral.
teaches: The wedding's noise is the same instrument as the funeral's, so the Naladiyar turns the verse's joy into a warning without changing the sounds.

gains.a: The verse lacks any thought that its music could change meaning.
gains.b: The quatrain lacks the wedding's full noise that makes its reversal strong.

note: In 901 Maruci goes to the lord of Suramai to announce the Vidyadhara's arrival; in 943 he goes the other way to tell the Vidyadhara king that the lord of Suramai is coming.
teaches: The messenger crosses between the two courts in both directions, so each side is first hosted and then hosting, and the welcome is mutual.

note: 453 calls the women's sword-like eyes the mark of every killing art of love; Kural 1083 learns what Death is from a woman's large war-making eyes.
teaches: Both name the glance as a killer, but the couplet is one man's astonished cry and the epic makes it a settled doctrine of the women's whole equipment.

gains.a: A first-person confession that the eyes kill, which the epic's catalogue states only as a fact of their bodies.
gains.b: A general rule about what such eyes carry, given as the sum of breasts, brows and arts rather than the eyes alone.

note: The ochre-dyed fine cloth (கல் தோய் நுண் கலிங்கம், 353; நுண்டுகில் கல்லரத்தம், 1783) that Vijayai put on 'that the strong one's son may rise'.
teaches: The robe she took as a vow for her son's rise is still on her years later and is now listed beside the son as a burden, so the renunciation proves to have been made for him rather than from him.

note: The wedding spends its verses on adorning the body and delights of marriage; the patikam says that Civakan, afraid of kingship, hears dharma and renounces at the Knower's feet.
teaches: The lavish bodily pleasure of this marriage is the very life that the patikam says Civakan will at the end put down, so each wedding adds weight to the later renunciation.

note: Padumukan guesses that only Civakan's parents could have bound him; the spy reports that the father embraced him by a stratagem and the weeping mother bound his arms.
teaches: The friend's reasoning from the hero's invincibility is confirmed by the report, so the one force the story allows to bind Civakan is filial obedience, not the usurper's army.

note: 1207 shows the hero's anger at petty words in his body; Purananuru 72 turns Neduncheliyan's rage at kings who mocked him as young into a vow with named forfeits.
teaches: The Sangam king binds himself in public speech to avenge a taunt, while the epic hero is let burn first and be confirmed by gods afterwards, so anger at a taunt is lawful in both but sanctioned differently.

gains.a: The epic hero's anger gains a Sangam precedent of a king answering mockery of his youth, which marks it as a king's duty and not temper.
gains.b: The Sangam vow gains a view of the same rage seen from the body and the heavens, and of a hero left to stand on others' pledge, which the vow has not.

note: The Kural's lover says love's flood carries off the raft of modesty and manliness; Kanakamalai says she sold her modesty to buy a garland.
teaches: The epic turns the couplet's loss into a trade: modesty is not swept away but given in exchange, and what it bought, the garland, becomes the new raft of 1663 and 1674.

gains.a: her bargain is read as the woman's version of the loss the Kural gives to a man
gains.b: the couplet's image gains a sequel in which the lost raft of modesty is replaced by one of love

note: The king ends the day in song and pleasure; Naladiyar 60 says the higher ones look to the pain in pleasure and do not cling.
teaches: The chapter shows a whole day of enjoyment with no word of its pain, so the quatrain's test of pleasure is left unanswered by the story here.

gains.a: A measure the narrator does not apply, so the night's pleasure goes unjudged in the verse.
gains.b: A king who is shown enjoying, not a fool, which tests whether the quatrain's contrast of wise and foolish fits a ruler.

note: 1597 has the jester claim that a man-eating spirit lives in the stone; 1600 has him see that his own shadow imitates his acts, and he is calmed.
teaches: The claim in 1597 is made through the scene itself, not by argument, and the later verse answers it by showing the fear to have no source outside him.

note: The couplet says the sweet words of women who seek a man's wealth and not his love bring him harm; here a courtesan writes to a man who has lost his wealth, asking only what her fault was, and he judges her blameless and himself at fault.
teaches: The pair sets the Kural's rule that a courtesan's sweet words are for wealth against a courtesan's letter written after the wealth is gone, so the epic tests the rule on the one case it cannot explain and has the man himself withdraw the charge.

note: The Kural says austerity is practised because it brings what is wanted as it is wanted; the narrator explains the kings' six days of failure by their ignorance of the greatness of ripened austerity.
teaches: The pair shows the couplet's promise worked out as a plot: what the kings want, they cannot get by wanting, and the one who wins does so by merit of austerity, so tapas becomes the hidden cause of a marriage.

gains.a: the narrator's aside gains a known maxim behind it, making the failures a lesson rather than a joke
gains.b: the couplet's general 'whatever is wanted' gains a concrete case where desire and skill fail and only earlier merit succeeds

note: 1797 sets her procession to the sounds of praise and music from all quarters; Naladiyar 23 shows wedding drums in a hall turning to funeral drums for the groom.
teaches: The poem fills the bridal march with music and hope, and the quatrain says the same drums can announce the end of the groom.

gains.a: The procession gains the shadow that its music may not last, which the poem leaves out here.
gains.b: The quatrain gains a wedding at its brightest, before any reversal, which is the moment it warns against trusting.

note: 1992 grades gifts into best, middle and lowest by receiver, giver and gift; 2000 says gifts of one who knows the principles are not placed within three grades.
teaches: The gift of the knowing giver is said to go beyond the three-grade scheme, so the grading does not describe the highest case.

note: The couplet says all pains rest on those who caused pain; the sage says the pain of killing returns to the killers birth after birth.
teaches: The couplet states the return of pain as a rule; the verse shows it falling across births on two named kin who thought their killing was only a rite.

gains.a: The verse gets a general rule that makes the long suffering of the king and his mother a law and not a freak.
gains.b: The couplet gets the cases of kin reborn as birds, which show how far its rule is meant to reach.

note: Civakan vows to see the kings' backs and then embrace the lady; in 817, having seen the field where the enemies fell, he enters his house with her, surrounded by his friends.
teaches: The vow's two conditions are kept in its own order, the routed field first and the bride brought home after, so the marriage is presented as the vow's discharge.

note: The mother warns that dying of separation loses both worlds; the narrator says Kemasari lives only by his words to the bee.
teaches: Holding the two together shows the doctrinal consolation failing: what keeps the bride alive is not the threat of losing both worlds but one covert sentence of love.

note: 1707 leaves the queen trembling and whispering, and 1708 has the king answer by reading her vision as the coming of a son.
teaches: The poem passes the fright of the omen to the king's reading of it, so the vision becomes a promise before the child is born.

note: Kural 1100: once eyes agree with eyes, spoken words are useless; Anangamaalai sends her love to Civakan by a 'letter' of her eyes carried by her smile, in the middle of a public dance.
teaches: The epic keeps the couplet's wordless eye-language but makes it one-sided and public, a message sent across a crowd, and shows its cost when the king's enmity follows from it.

gains.a: the Kural's rule that the look can replace speech, which makes the eye-letter a full declaration rather than a flirtation
gains.b: a case where the silent message is unreturned and dangerous, a consequence the couplet's mutual glance does not weigh

note: In both verses the king sees the dead queen in something else, first flowers and then Padmavati.
teaches: A habit of seeing her likeness in things turns from a poet's sorrow into a real mistake that begins the new marriage.

note: 2035 has the human pair rise to heaven after their span; 2038 says the beasts and birds of the same land rise to the kalpa world as well.
teaches: The rise of the pair is not a human privilege: the land's own merit carries even its animals up, so the climb belongs to the place.

note: Both use Anni's cutting of Thithiyan's punnai at Kurukkai: 45 measures the gossip by the bards' clamour that day, 145 wishes on the foster mother's hand the fate of that felled tree.
teaches: One puram event served akam poets in two opposite ways, as a measure of noise and as a curse of destruction, which shows these battles were a shared stock of reference the audience was expected to know.

note: Kural 215 likens the wise man's wealth to a village tank full of water; the verse makes the gift of water itself the first of five charities.
teaches: The Kural's tank is a figure for wealth all may draw on; the verse makes it literal and the lowest step of a scale that ends in founding temples and halls.

note: 757 calls the slaughter a harvest that wins the victory; in 820 the victor makes a golden image of the Jina, holds a festival and gives gifts to put away the sin (பாவம்) of the battlefield.
teaches: The same killing is first boasted as a crop and then expiated as a sin, so the Jain epic lets the heroic idiom stand in the speeches and corrects it only after the battle is won.

note: 1463 says a harm aimed at a blameless man returns on its sender; Kural 319 says hurt done in the forenoon returns in the afternoon of itself.
teaches: The couplet makes the return a rule of time, while the epic makes it happen through the victim's own hand turning the weapon back, so the return has an agent.

gains.a: 1463 lacks the couplet's plain rule that wrong done is wrong received; it only has a simile.
gains.b: The couplet gives the return without a means; the verse shows the thrown weapon as that means.

note: In 1037 Gunamalai draws circles in the sand, asking whether she will unite with Civakan if his errand prospers; in 1063 the wedding drums sound.
teaches: The sand-circle divination she made in doubt is answered by the wedding within the same ilampakam, so the epic lets a folk rite of the anxious lover come true.

note: The patikam says the lion-like royals of the middle country kept Civakan and gave him a girl in marriage; 1215 has the god foretell that the king will give him his daughter while he stays there.
teaches: Read with the patikam, the marriage that looks like the royals' choice to bind a strong stranger was promised in advance by the god, so the hero's marriages come to him as foretold gifts rather than conquests.

note: The Kural asks what a sword is to those without courage and what learning is to those who fear the assembly; Padumukan mocks kings who lost at the art and turn to the sword.
teaches: The Kural tests the sword and learning separately, each by its own courage, but Padumukan adds that one who has failed the test of art cannot seek the same prize by the sword, so the second arena only confirms the first defeat.

gains.a: the sarcasm வாழ்க நுங் கலை gains a standard: the kings fail both of the Kural's tests at once
gains.b: the couplet's paired measures gain a rule of contest about moving from one to the other, which the couplet does not state

note: In 554 the king refused all suitors until the time fate set for his daughter; in 848 he tells the son-in-law that what is to come will come unsought.
teaches: The king who once used fate to wait for the destined husband now uses it to promise that husband his kingdom, so his trust in destiny moves from patience to assurance.

note: Tirumanthiram 499 has karma bring the soul to wombs and then knowledge reach Siva; verse 329 says the dharma holds karma off and leads on to release.
teaches: Both give heaven or birth as a stage, but one reaches release through the Lord and the other through the dharma's own power.

gains.a: the verse lacks a Lord who brings the soul to release
gains.b: the quatrain lacks a way of holding back karma by conduct

note: The king asks who can turn aside the ripening of deeds.
teaches: The couplet says fate outruns any other device; the king acts that out, trying the mother's device and finding the fruit still comes.

gains.a: The king's question gets an authority that answers it before the story does.
gains.b: The couplet gets a scene where a device is tried and fate comes first.

note: 272 grounds 'all lives are like my own' in an ascetic's grace and a result beyond karma; Kural 315 tests understanding by guarding another's pain as one's own.
teaches: The epic puts the rule into a speech to a hunting king, so that guarding other lives has a named cost to him: his hounds and spear.

gains.a: 272 gains the Kural's plain test: understanding that does not guard another's pain is empty.
gains.b: Kural 315 gains a person who does the opposite, a king hunting with a pack.

note: In 205 the king refuses the astrologer's warning, saying he has done his part for Kattiyangaran and let him do as he will; 260 lists the king's own grace among the things that will kill him.
teaches: அருள் கொல்லும் names the king's trust in 205 as a fatal fault, so his generosity is counted with lust and wealth among the causes of his fall.

note: The Kural says tapas is striven for here because one gets what one wants as one wants it; the bride's falling garland is read as a call to all the world to do tapas.
teaches: The Cintamani takes the Kural's frankly worldly motive for tapas and fixes it on a bridal union, showing how far that motive reaches in a work whose hero will at last renounce such joys.

gains.a: the poet's fancy gains a rule that makes it more than a compliment: the joy is the earned fruit of former tapas
gains.b: the couplet's unnamed 'what is wanted' is given a concrete object, sensual and married, which the next couplet's condemnation of desire leaves out

note: Verse 409 reports the sign that within a month Tivittan will split a lion's mouth; verse 828 brings word that the lion has in fact been destroyed.
teaches: The prophecy is shown fulfilled by a spy's report, so it reaches the Vidyadhara king as news, not as a vision.

note: 1356 asks warriors to stay and die for fame; Kural 780 calls such a death worth asking for if those who sustained one weep for it.
teaches: The couplet makes the dead man's supporters the judge of the death, which the epic speaker, urging flight not to be done, leaves out.

gains.a: The verse gains the test that the death should be one whose supporters mourn it, not one spent for its own show.
gains.b: The couplet gains a speaker who uses the worth of such a death as a reason to stop a rout.

note: The mantra and smoke that free the elephant at the post become its killing run through the keepers.
teaches: What looked like a rescuer's stratagem shows its cost at once, on men who were only keepers.

note: The Kural calls those lands whose riches need no seeking; the Cintamani's pools are strewn with gold beads from broken girdles that no one troubles to gather.
teaches: Set beside the reapers and threshers of 55 to 59, the gold no one picks up shows the epic taking unsought wealth to mean surplus beyond need after labour, not riches without work.

gains.a: the image of the gold-starred pools is read as a mark of the ideal land rather than as mere ornament
gains.b: the couplet's riches that need no seeking are given a scene where the absence of seeking is visible

note: In 885 the maid disputes Civakan's powder verdict to his face; in 2043 she repeats the grievance to him in his disguise, and he condemns the young man who gave it.
teaches: The judge of the powder contest now hears his verdict judged by the loser's household and joins in cursing himself, which is how the disguise wins their trust.

claims.gist: great earlier austerity wins the bride and with her sovereignty
evil deeds sown in the soul are eaten later as suffering
hell's suffering is great beyond telling
ascetics of great tapas travel the sky
a dream of an elephant garlanding a youth foretells a bride given by a king of the Vidyadharas
a faithful wife keeps her husband in her heart through his absence and spends her days worshipping his feet
the pomp of kings does not last
giving, right conduct, austerity and worship of the Omniscient beget the merit that carries one to a higher state
only that merit is truly one's child; children of the body belong to others
the fruit of a former evil deed follows through births
subjects should not even think or speak against the king
no one can undo the fortune that is someone's lot, though it may reverse the natural order
a warrior who flees to save his life throws away his honour
in hell the sufferer cannot die, however the body melts
deeds whirl the soul through births in the four states of existence, past counting
clear mind, non-clinging and abstaining from flesh, honey and toddy bring beauty, victory and good birth
fate takes what a man has gathered and gives it to others, and nothing can hold it back
men who were guarded by a king owe him the protection of his fame
separating creatures from their kin and caging them causes suffering
a chaste woman who belongs to one man is beyond the reach of any other
a man learned in the books can see all three times, past, present and to come
unbroken meditation soaked in samadhi is the sword that cuts karma
those who take up austerity and later practise deceit are reborn as animals

note: 2977 compares the vanished smoke of incense and garlands to the fame of misers who gave nothing; Naladiyar 9 says the miser who guards his wealth is already counted as one who has lost it.
teaches: Together they show the miser losing twice, his goods in the Naladiyar and his name in the epic, so hoarding gets a fate in memory as well as in wealth.

gains.a: the simile of vanishing smoke gets its ground, that the miser is already counted as a loss
gains.b: the Naladiyar's loss of the hoarder gets a trace in memory, his fame disappearing like the smoke

note: 1951 names those who leave their wives for others' as falling into deep sorrow; Naladiyar 84 lists disgrace, a cut leg and long suffering in hell for the adulterer.
teaches: Naladiyar counts the worldly penalties before hell; the epic puts only hell and gives the torment in detail.

gains.a: The adulterer's fate gains the earthly costs of disgrace and mutilation that the sage's hell leaves out.
gains.b: The quatrain gains the long torment that it names only as hell, shown in the verses before.

note: The Kural says penance is striven for because it gains what one wants as one wants it; Gunamalai says that if Civakan refuses she will win him even by penance.
teaches: The girl takes the couplet's motive for தவம் at its word and aims it at a husband, which exposes how far the Kural's argument for penance rests on desire rather than release.

gains.a: a doctrinal ground for her resolve, which the verse states without explaining why penance should work
gains.b: a concrete wish, love for a man, that tests the couplet's open promise of getting whatever is wanted

note: Tirumular calls flesh-eaters புலையர and sends them to hell; Civakan says the hunters were born low because of former killing and eating.
teaches: Tirumular makes baseness a name earned by what one eats now, whatever one's birth, while the epic makes the low birth itself the fruit of past eating, so the two texts tie the same stigma to flesh-eating from opposite ends of the karmic chain.

gains.a: Civakan's account of low birth is shown to keep birth-rank as real and deserved, which the comparison with Tirumular's moral use of புலையர் exposes
gains.b: Tirumular's after-death punishment gains an earlier stage in the chain, a birth already lowered by flesh-eating, which his verse does not consider

note: Kantukkatan reasoned that opposing a king is the work of the doomed and that sending his son bound would cool the king's anger; now he adds twelve crores of gold to quench it.
teaches: The father's policy of submission is completed by payment, so between these two verses his defiant words to the crowd (1114-1115) stand as consolation only, and his actual answer to the king is obedience bought with gold.

note: Both use death, old age and disease as the spur: Naladiyar 92 to share wealth while it is in hand, Pazhamozhi 365 to do aram while one can.
teaches: The same triad backs sharing wealth in the Naladiyar and the use of a rare human birth in Pazhamozhi, which ends the triad with death as a stupor that puts one to sleep, so the urgency rests on the rare chance as well as on the threat.

note: Kural 1011 says true shame is shame at wrongdoing and anything else is only the shame of women; 1103 gives the bride's trembling shyness at the first clasp.
teaches: The bride's shyness is the kind the Kural calls a woman's own and not yet the shame of deeds, so the verse shows what the couplet sets aside.

gains.a: The bride's trembling gains a name for what it is, the shame of the bright-browed that the Kural separates from moral shame.
gains.b: The couplet gains a living case of the shame it sets aside, which it names without showing.

note: The Kural asks how one who eats another's flesh to swell his own can have grace; the hunter says he needs meat merely to keep his body alive.
teaches: The couplet's eater fattens himself by choice, while the hunter claims he must eat flesh to survive at all; the epic thus raises the case the couplet passes over and answers it not with grace but with the threat of hell and the promise of heaven.

gains.a: Civakan's demand gains a measure from the classic statement that flesh-eating swells one's own flesh at another's cost, which is what 1235 line 1 restates
gains.b: the couplet gains a hearer who objects from need, not appetite, which tests whether its rule holds for people who live by hunting

note: The cocks say that the teacher's dharma has freed them from the fever of rebirth; Tirumular's guru makes the deeds into burnt seeds that will not sprout into seven births.
teaches: Both free through a teacher, but in the epic the cocks' own vow and memory do the work while in Tirumular it is the guru's act that burns the seed, and no god is named in the epic's verse.

gains.a: The verse gets a Saiva picture of how a teacher's act ends rebirth, which it only reports as a result.
gains.b: Tirumular gets a case of a being freed by teaching and its own vow, without a god's act.

note: Marusi calls the king hard for kings to reach yet easy for his own servants; Kural 386 praises a king who is easy to see.
teaches: The epic limits the couplet's easy access: it is a favour kept for a king's own men and withheld from rival kings.

gains.a: The verse lacks the named virtue behind its claim, easy access, which the couplet makes a ground of a land's praise.
gains.b: The couplet lacks the limit that a king may be easy to some and closed to others, which the verse shows.

note: Verse 305 reckons the girl's birth as the moment Asvagriva softened; verse 310 gives the birth as the moment the astrologers set down her horoscope.
teaches: One birth is read twice, by a minister as the cause of a change in the suitor and by an astrologer as the moment her fate was fixed, so the story weighs politics against the stars.

note: 2906 tells the heir to keep dharma with learned poets; 2916 sets the learned, blameless sons of his father's comrades beside him.
teaches: The advice to rule with the learned is carried out by the old king before he leaves.

note: Both set knowledge and trust before conduct in the sage's teaching.
teaches: Both Jain sages put conduct after discernment of true things, though the Soolamani gives it as three steps and this verse buries it in a long list.

note: The opening verse promises the tale of the red-eyed one who tore open the lion with the gaping mouth; verse 723 shows the tearing.
teaches: The poet's first promise is kept here as a deed in a scene, and the lion in the invocation is now seen as an actual foe.

note: Naladiyar makes the sun Death's daily measure of one's days; the epic tells one day's sun as a whole life from infant to desireless old man, and the lovers go to bed.
teaches: The epic uses the Naladiyar's moral image of the sun as a life measured out, but withholds its moral, letting the lovers' indifference to the dying sun foreshadow the night that ends their union.

gains.a: the sunset's life-stages carry the ethical charge of the day as a portion of life eaten by Death
gains.b: the quatrain's abstract measure gains a concrete picture of a day as infancy, youth and old age

note: The poet bows to a named tirthankara; the couplet praises the feet of one free of liking and aversion without naming him.
teaches: The Jain epic gives a name and a seat under the pindi tree to the one the Kural leaves unnamed, so the same freedom from liking and aversion can be read as a particular lord.

gains.a: the invocation gets a stated quality of the one worshipped, freedom from liking and aversion, which the verse leaves unsaid
gains.b: the couplet gets a named, seated figure that it never gives

note: 1437 compares the bow's arrival to a friend won in a former life; Naladiyar 101 says an old deed seeks out its doer like a calf its mother.
teaches: The simile gives the old deed a good side: what returns can be a helper in need, not only a penalty.

gains.a: The bow gains a possible source in former good deeds, which the narrator only hints.
gains.b: The quatrain gains a case where the old deed returns as a weapon in a fight, not as suffering.

note: Kural 760 says that for those who have made bright wealth the other two aims, virtue and pleasure, come together; 1923 makes gold yield army, army land, land wealth, and wealth everything.
teaches: Where the couplet makes wealth the way to virtue and pleasure, the mother's chain loops wealth back into power and more wealth, and only her own first condition in 1920, wealth got by justice, ties it to அறம்.

gains.a: the chain gains a measure: set against the couplet, it shows how far political counsel has narrowed wealth's ends to power
gains.b: the couplet's ஒண்பொருள் gains a contrast case, a cycle of wealth for power whose brightness depends wholly on how it was got

note: The hero asked the sage about his pleasure and heard dharma; here he follows that teaching to its end, by conquering karma and reaching siddhi.
teaches: What the hero hears in the earlier grove scene is the cause of the choices he makes here, which shows the poem's plan: hearing dharma comes before renouncing.

note: 2086 tells the sons not to trust the goddess and to love the learned, whom she scorns; Tirumanthiram 169 calls bewildering wealth a waning moon and bids the reader seek the king of the gods, who becomes great wealth like a rain cloud.
teaches: Both give up trusting wealth but name different things to trust in its place: the Jain king names the learned, Tirumular names a god who is himself wealth.

gains.a: The advice to attach to the learned gets a rival answer, a lord who stays, so a reader sees that the choice of refuge is itself a doctrine.
gains.b: The rain-cloud wealth of the Lord gets a worldly alternative in which the refuge is people, not a god, and it is held without worship.

note: Verse 14 says begging rises quickly in the pit of poverty; verse 15 says one who wants pain should rise to beg.
teaches: Read together, the book gives begging both a cause and a fruit: it grows from poverty and it yields pain.

note: The soldiers eager to carry arms and win; the Siddhar says horses, elephants and infantry shine under the parasol and are nothing without the ash.
teaches: The soldiers' pride in their strong shoulders is set beside a verse that says armies are worth nothing without the right mark, so the epic's boasts are weighed against a Siddhar's measure.

gains.a: The soldiers' boasts lack any measure of what an army is worth beyond winning, which the Siddhar sets in grace.
gains.b: The Siddhar's list of horses, elephants and chariots lacks men who speak, which the epic gives by letting soldiers boast.

note: Kural 830 counsels befriending a feigned friend with the face while letting go in the heart; Govindan proclaims through the city that he has become one with Kattiyankaran while mustering his army.
teaches: The couplet speaks of an individual's face and heart; the epic turns the face into a public proclamation and the hidden heart into a state secret guarded by threat, so the mask needs the silence of a whole city.

gains.a: the epic proclamation gains the Kural's licence for a face of friendship toward a false friend, which makes the king's feint a known policy and not mere cunning
gains.b: the couplet gains its political scale: when a king wears the friendly face, his people must wear it too, and the cost is a gag on every tongue

note: Kural 974 says greatness exists only for one who holds himself as single-minded women (ஒருமை மகளிர்) do; 1208 likens a straight unforking road to the minds of chaste women (கற்புடை மாதரார் மனம்).
teaches: Both texts use the chaste woman's mind as the model of an undivided line, for a man's greatness in one and for a road in the other, showing that karpu was read as singleness of direction rather than as purity alone.

gains.a: a precedent that the chaste mind is a figure of oneness, which explains why the epic chooses it for a road without forks
gains.b: a concrete picture, a straight road strewn with flowers, of what the couplet's single-mindedness looks like in space

note: Sin overtook the ascetic in his first penance; at the end he goes to resume penance to wear down old deeds.
teaches: The teacher's life runs in a circle through Civakan's house: a penance broken by the fruit of past deeds is taken up again, with the wearing away of those deeds now named as its aim.

note: 3105 says that giving up clinging at the pure one's feet lets one reach the state of release; 3121 shows the women, free of desire and love, reaching heaven.
teaches: The promise to the women's sermon is kept, though what they reach is heaven rather than the release the verse named.

note: The Acharakkovai lists what one does not do in a great man's house: spit, climb a high seat, chew areca, speak out of turn, lie down; in the king's house Civakan sits on a high flower seat, chews areca and lies on a couch.
teaches: Civakan does three of the five things forbidden in a great man's house, and does them at the king's command, so the pair shows that the rule binds the dependent and the visitor and is suspended for an honoured guest whom the host himself seats, serves and beds.

gains.a: the rule against which its hospitality reads as a deliberate honour and not a mere list of comforts
gains.b: a limit to the rule: the prohibitions assume a lower visitor, and the host's own gift lifts them

note: Naladiyar 53 lists beauty among the things that fail to last, which the best renounce; 999 praises the bride's beauty as so bright she cannot be looked at, and says nothing of its end.
teaches: The poet gives full praise to beauty that his school's moral verse calls perishable, so the reader sees the praise and the warning side by side without either answering the other.

gains.a: The verse lacks any limit on the beauty it praises, which the Naladiyar supplies by naming it as one of the things that go.
gains.b: The quatrain lacks a concrete case of the beauty it says does not last, set in the full pride of its glow.

note: Verse 244 makes the ministers the king's mind, eye, living, strength and sceptre; Kural 445 calls counsellors the king's eyes and says he must take them after testing them.
teaches: The epic widens the Kural's single image of eyes to the king's whole body of rule, while the couplet adds a duty of choosing that the epic leaves unsaid.

gains.a: A rule for choosing: the king must test his counsellors before taking them.
gains.b: A fuller count of what rests on counsellors, from sight to the sceptre itself.

note: Akananuru 38 has the ashoka as the lovers' old swing-tree now empty; verse 757 has the ashoka in red pollen and humming bees, likened to adorned youths.
teaches: The ashoka stands for young lovers in both, one time in their absence and one time as their likeness.

gains.a: The verse lacks the ashoka's use as a trysting place, which the poem gives.
gains.b: The poem lacks the ashoka's red pollen and the likeness to adorned youths, which the verse gives.

note: 2117 kills anger and its fellows one after another in a fixed sequence; Siddhar 87 asks when anger, speech and action, the 'I' and the mind will die so that release can be reached.
teaches: The Jain epic gives a battle order for the passions where the Siddhar only longs for them to die all at once.

gains.a: The passions, which 2117 names but leaves as figures in a rout, are made into an ordered list the seeker must wait out, with the mind and the 'I' added at the end.
gains.b: The Siddhar's longing gains a plan, in which anger falls first and the others follow in turn, in place of a single wish for the end of all.

note: Udayanan, a captive, rides in triumph on the elephant; the quatrain says kings who rode elephants fall when their deeds turn.
teaches: The story reverses the quatrain's fall, showing a captive king raised through skill and not through deeds, which limits how far the quatrain's warning is the whole account.

gains.a: the captive's triumph gets a reminder that a king's elephant-riding rank can be lost
gains.b: the quatrain gets a case in which a fallen man rises on an elephant by skill

note: The mother dreamed that a flower pond ran dry and reads it as the girl's maidenhood gone; the secret union of 2063 is the event.
teaches: The dream is read after the event it pictures, so it serves the mother as confirmation of what the foster mother reported rather than as a warning.

note: The god promised to come if Civakan thought of him in trouble; in his account Civakan thought of him and he came.
teaches: The retelling shows that the god's promise worked as a pact of thought: Civakan's only act in the crisis is to think and praise, and the friendship made with the dog he once helped is what saves him.

note: The elephant that bows at his lute in verse 19 pledges itself to him in a dream in verse 20.
teaches: The taming ends in a bond of loyalty, so the music wins a companion and not only a mount.

note: Kopperunchozhan, the poet of Kuruntokai 53, is the king of Purananuru 216, who tells the doubters that his unseen friend Pisirandhaiyar wants no lie that would spoil his fame and will come to share his death. In Kuruntokai 53 his friend-speaker holds a lover to an oath sworn before the hill-goddesses, which he has broken.
teaches: Read together, the king's two voices weigh faith two ways: in puram a friend never met keeps faith with no oath at all, while in his akam poem a lover breaks faith despite an oath sworn before goddesses, so the poet who staked his death on unsworn friendship knew how little a sworn word could hold in love.

note: 3106 tells the women to hate the body kept for desire; 3120 shows them doing it, seeing their adorned bodies as stained.
teaches: The sermon's advice to hate the body and the women's act of seeing it as dirt are the same turn, the teaching and then its keeping.

note: Kural 249 likens virtue done without அருள் to a confused man seeing the truth; Valayapathi 66 lists அருள்இல் அறன் among four goods it calls darkness put inside darkness.
teaches: The Kural makes graceless virtue a single paradox, while the fragment sets it in a series with a vow without forbearance, a lineage without wealth and a kingdom without ministers, so grace appears as one of several enabling conditions without which a good is void.

note: 1426 orders the spell to destroy mankind; 1427 has the spell pass the work on to Death.
teaches: The command goes from king to spell to Death, so the epic shows destruction as a chain of obedience with no one pausing.

note: Tirumular puts the flesh-eaters' pain in hell, after death; the epic spends its verses on the animal's pain first.
teaches: The epic puts the pain first on the animal and sets the eater's suffering later in this same life, where Tirumular's punishment lies only after death.

gains.a: the unit gains a Saiva voice that also holds flesh-eating to be punished
gains.b: the verse gains the animal's side of the pain, which it does not describe

note: Kural 10 says those who reach the Lord's feet swim the sea of births and others cannot; 3019 says those who do not reach the lord are kicked by their deeds into the sea of sorrow and whirl like thread on a shuttle.
teaches: The Kural states the crossing and the failure to cross but gives no cause or picture for the failure, and the verse supplies deeds that beat the swimmer down and a turning that never ends.

gains.a: the verse's sea of sorrow is given the Kural's single condition for crossing it, reaching the lord's feet
gains.b: the Kural's 'cannot swim' is given a cause (deeds that strike) and a picture (thread wound without end on a shuttle)

note: The Siddhar's woman is a pit of sores by nature; here the sores come on one woman as the result of what she did.
teaches: The epic places the body's foulness in a deed and its time, where the Siddhar places it in woman's nature, so the two verses disagree on its cause.

gains.a: the unit gains a rival account of the foul body in which the foulness is a lure, not a punishment
gains.b: the song gains a case that says the sores follow a deed, which unsettles blaming woman as such

note: The Kural uses the spot on the moon to say a fault in the well-born is seen from far; the Cintamani uses it for a fault in a moon-full work and asks readers to wash it, not to see it.
teaches: The Kural's moon makes height expose a fault, but the Cintamani turns the same image into a reader's duty of charity, so the exposure the Kural warns of becomes something the audience may decline.

gains.a: the poet's request is seen to answer the expectation, stated in the Kural, that a high thing's fault draws every eye
gains.b: the couplet's warning is shown to depend on the onlooker, who can be asked to clean rather than point

note: Suramanjari vows to wait until Civakan comes defeated and worships her anklet-feet; in her ilampakam Civakan sets his head on the anklet of her feet, says the great forgive the wrongs of the small, and ends her sulk.
teaches: The vow is kept to the letter, his head on her anklet, yet the hero turns it by calling his own slight the wrong of a lesser one forgiven by the greater, so her condition is met and her pride still yielded.

claims.gist: those who worship the lord on the lion throne become gods and then reach release with the soul shining
what was foretold at birth has come to pass as destiny, so the marriage must follow
the supreme one has conquered fate, the sum of deeds
the discus won in battle is the sign of the title Vasudeva
worship of the goddess dissolves the evil that a bad dream foretells
the presence of the Jina's shrines throughout a city keeps its prosperity from failing
the body perishes but fame stands for ever
a warrior should give up the body for lasting fame rather than flee
a lord called master of deeds orders that men hear one another's word, act on it and so live
release is a state without disease, age or pain, with a shining form and unfailing bliss
those who fulfil the three means attain it
austerity taken at the white hair ripens into a long life among the gods
the First One, the summit of sagehood, alone holds solitary supremacy
one should make dharma, give up anger, look to knowledge and guard the vow
a proud king prefers shame at his own weakness to returning to his mountain refuge
a prudent trader gives up a small thing rather than lose his capital
those who have come to know their births turn away from the talk of kin and desire nothing
a dream seen by a woman foretells her marriage and her husband's rule
an old deed stays and burns in hell until it is spent
merit is the provision one must take for the road of death, which one walks alone
worldly life is a fearful bondage of suffering
renunciation requires giving up fine food and begging alms
the way of Kama's father that we follow is the safe and pure path
a giver must have seven qualities, among them non-attachment and absence of regret
desire is an intoxicant that clouds the mind of one who drinks it

note: 188 likens the wedded pair to the three-eyed god and his goddess joined; in 208 a counsellor cites the god's taking the mountain king's daughter into half his body as a great blame (பெரும் பழி).
teaches: The same divine union serves the narrator as the highest praise of the couple and the counsellor as a warning of shame from desire, so the epic lets its own simile be turned against the king within twenty verses.

note: Verse 873 has the host's drums and bells roar like the sea as it leaves; verse 950 turns the sea into the milk-sea of the sky.
teaches: The sea simile follows the host from departure to meeting, changing from noise to something heavenly and calm.

note: 1174 has the king thunder that he is faultless and then go to the council hall; Kural 568 says a king who lashes out in anger without thinking with his circle loses fortune.
teaches: The king rages first and consults after, so the epic shows the order that the Kural warns against, though it ends in council.

gains.a: The thundering king in 1174 shows no sign that the council will check him, which the Kural gives as the test of a king's anger.
gains.b: The Kural's circle that must be consulted is only a principle, and the epic shows a king who enters the hall after his rage has begun.

note: In 299 the queen, riding the peacock machine, faints like a struck doe as the usurper's drum sounds; in 2614 the same machine is called the deed's peacock (வினைமயில்) that sent her away while he went to the sky.
teaches: The carpenter's flying peacock of 235-239 is named here as fate's instrument, so what was a clever device comes to be read as the working of deeds.

note: Akananuru 242 calls the velan who holds the veri rite ignorant (அறியா வேலன்): he blames the god for what is love; Paripadal 5.15-17 says the velan's praise and veri are neither true nor false, since the world lies within the god's bound.
teaches: Read together, the pair shows that the akam mockery of the velan was not a rejection of Murugan: the devotional poet keeps the rite valid at the level of the god while conceding that its particular verdicts may miss, which is exactly the room the akam friend exploits.

note: The couplet calls a king who torments his people crueller than a killer; here the king seizes merchants' goods over a horse.
teaches: The epic's king acts from a sudden anger, not from habit, so it shows how the couplet's cruelty can come from one incident and an unexamined report.

gains.a: the unit gains a rule by which the seizure can be called cruelty
gains.b: the couplet gains a case of tyranny arising from one angry order, not a settled vice

note: The couplet says the fruit of hospitality is as great as the guest's worth; the merchant's house that fed a hungry stranger gained a Vidyadhara king as the teacher of its son.
teaches: The epic shows the couplet's measure working through time: the guest's worth was hidden when he came hungry to the door, and the fruit appeared only as the education of the boy who fed him.

gains.a: the long stay of the cured ascetic is read as the return on a gift, which the verse itself leaves implicit
gains.b: the couplet's measure by the guest's worth gains a case where that worth was unknown to the host, so hospitality cannot be rationed by it

note: 2846 says the three jewels burn the tree of deeds and release is freedom from deeds; 2985 applies this to Civakan's wives, saying even the fruit of good deeds is poison.
teaches: The sermon's doctrine of freedom from deeds is turned into advice to the wives, and it is made to include good deeds that the sermon does not single out.

note: Naladiyar 77 says the great bear faults hard to bear, which is why their friendship is sought; Civakan uses the same maxim to plead with a sulking wife after denying any fault.
teaches: A maxim about the forbearance of the great in friendship turns, in a lover's mouth, into flattery that makes the angry woman the great one and so obliges her to forgive.

gains.a: the hero's maxim is seen to be a borrowed rule of friendship pressed into love's service
gains.b: the quatrain's rule is shown working as rhetoric: naming someone great lays on them the duty to forbear

note: 1128 closes the songs' warnings about being plucked; 1129 shows the bride's smile after hearing them.
teaches: The songs tease the groom as the one who plucks, and the smile is the only answer given.

note: Both open with the shedding of former deeds; this verse adds the order and ripening.
teaches: The Jain account of karma shedding that the Naga poem states in a line is here set out as an ordered ripening.

note: Salankayan, who showed the false elephant in verse 41, now speaks of dharma texts with Yugi.
teaches: The minister who ran the trap is now Yugi's friend in learning, so the quarrel is shown to end between ministers before it ends between kings.

note: Verse 242 has the king say he can grasp subtle things only through the learned treatises; Kural 637 says that even one who knows the method must act by knowing how the world goes.
teaches: The council's first claim makes the treatise the king's only guide, where the couplet warns that a treatise's method must still be tested against the world, so the two disagree on where good judgment is found.

gains.a: A corrective: the books the king defers to still leave him to read the world's own way.
gains.b: A case for deference: why a ruler should hold a treatise above his own sense.

note: In 2619 Vijayai tells the people to do hard penance and give before youth lapses; in 2848 the king bathes in the sage's dharma-water and loses the stain of sorrow.
teaches: The mother's exhortation and the sage's sermon reach the same hearer in the same ilampakam, and the sermon is what makes the king act on them.

note: 1763 beats a drum to announce a wedding; Naladiyar 23 says the drums that sounded for a wedding may sound the same day as funeral drums.
teaches: The same drum that proclaims joy is, for the Naladiyar, the sign of how quickly joy passes into death.

gains.a: The epic's wedding drum gains a shadow: the sound that calls the kings is the sound a worldly man should fear.
gains.b: The quatrain gains a case where the wedding drum is proclaimed with royal pomp for a bride not yet chosen.

note: Kural 218 says the discerning do not falter in ஒப்புரவு even without means; the Innaa line counts a man without wealth desiring to be liberal as painful. Not a tension on our reading: the Innaa line names a cost, not a fault.
teaches: The pair shows the pain hidden inside the Kural's praise: giving steadily in want is admirable, and the wish to give without means is also an ache.

note: The people of Govindai's ilampakam said that the good mother who bore the lord must have done great penance and asked on which hill she did it; here the women of the city again set a mother's penance behind the son's glory, and name Sunandai as the great vower.
teaches: The street's guess that a hero's greatness is a mother's earned penance is first a wonder at his youth and is now a verdict on his rule, and the woman named for it changes from the one who bore him to the one who raised him.

note: Senguttuvan has the image of the pathini goddess carved from the Himalayan stone and installed in her shrine; the Manimekalai's shrine holds an image of both Kannaki and Kovalan, and the goddess in it speaks.
teaches: Where the Silappathikaram's royal shrine sets up Kannaki alone as a goddess of the realm, the Manimekalai makes the image a family one with the father beside her, fit for a daughter's prayer, which reshapes the cult toward the household the later epic cares about.

note: 2115 has the lord draw the sword of unbroken meditation soaked in samadhi; Neelakesi 86 says that humans of the land of deeds see their dark karma leave by penance.
teaches: Both Jain epics say karma is removed by the ascetic's own effort, and one gives that effort a face as a sword.

note: Verse 70 says hearing the dharma checks karma's influx and sheds it; Tirumanthiram 1527 says grace comes as the guru and, when one's own doing ends through the knowledge it gives, the three impurities end.
teaches: Both make a teacher's word the means of release, but in one the hearer's own checking and shedding does the work, and in the other his own doing must cease and grace does it.

gains.a: the Jain account of release by the hearer's own stopping and shedding is set against a rival where grace comes as a guru
gains.b: Tirumular's 'when one's own doing ends' meets a doctrine where one's own effort is the whole means, sharpening what it denies

note: The Kural says understanding is seeing the true thing in whatever thing, of whatever nature; Neelakesi says no thing has ever been made clear except through its qualities.
teaches: The Jain makes the couplet's 'whatever its nature' into a method: the true thing is reached through its qualities, not by stripping them away, which is why she can claim the soul is known by knowing and seeing.

note: 55 puts kings and sages in the shade of the king's umbrella and feet; 69 puts the whole earth asleep under the one white umbrella while the king bathes in the queens' breasts.
teaches: The shade that began as the world's refuge ends as the setting for the king's pleasure, so the umbrella changes from protection to the sign of a wealth enjoyed.

note: 2794 says the householders' wealth is a yoke of toil and pain; Kural 46 asks what one gains by going outside the household life if it is lived by dharma.
teaches: Whether household life is a yoke or the best path depends on the claim of 2794, and the two works cannot both hold it.

gains.a: the verse gains the Kural's own defence of the householder, which it argues against
gains.b: the couplet gains a counter-view that names the householder's wealth as the pain

note: Vijayai says she has done no good deeds (நல் வினை செய்து இலாதேன்); in 343 the narrator likens the passing night to evil deeds that leave when old good deeds come forward.
teaches: The mother's self-condemnation is overruled by the narrator a few verses later, who credits her with a store of former merit that now begins to ripen.

note: Kural 388 makes the ruler who does justice and protects an இறை for the people; verse 773 sets the king's sons under the same duty and says it outweighs their own lives.
teaches: The duty to protect reaches the king's sons and is stated as a willingness to lose their lives, which the couplet leaves unsaid.

gains.a: The verse lacks a status that rewards protection, which the couplet states as being counted an இறை.
gains.b: The couplet lacks the cost of protection, the prince's risk to his life, which the verse names.

note: Naladiyar 14 says a once-desired woman, bent and shaking on a staff, torments men who still desire her; verse 286 describes lovers whose desire sprouts without end in a heaven-like city.
teaches: The epic's desire without end belongs to a realm without death (278), so the quatrain's old age has no place there, which shows that the quatrain's argument depends on this world.

gains.a: A world where the quatrain's decline does not happen, and so a limit on the quatrain's lesson.
gains.b: A picture of the endless desire against which the quatrain's old woman is the corrective.

note: In 899 she vows to keep her vow until Civakan comes defeated and worships her anklet-feet; in 2056 she sets her own head on the temple floor and joins her hands to pray for him.
teaches: The prostration she demanded of the man who shamed her is performed by her, in his hidden presence, so the vow is undone in its own terms of who bows to whom.

note: A deed that seeks out the one who did it, like a calf finding its mother in a herd.
teaches: The quatrain's image says deeds find their doer; 153 shows how: they come in at the hour of the poison and ripen into animal births.

gains.a: The deeds that 'came in' are given an image of seeking the doer out.
gains.b: The quatrain gets a death in which the deed ripens by an unrelated hand.

note: The queen puts away pleasure for austerity; Naladiyar 53 says the best of people consider slowly and give up home, youth and beauty without delay.
teaches: The epic shows the quatrain's counsel taken by a woman at the court while her husband is still held by pleasure, which makes giving up one's own household look like a path that is left open and not forced.

gains.a: The queen's austerity, narrated in one verse, gets a stated reason: the things she gives up are the short-lived goods of the quatrain.
gains.b: The quatrain's counsel of quick renunciation meets a case from a royal house, where the one who gives up is a wife and not the head of the family.

note: 2869 says the true word lifts to the towers of the upper world and the lie to hell; Kural 293 says that after lying your own heart burns you.
teaches: The Kural puts the punishment of a lie within and the verse sets it in the next world, so the two give two places for the same cost.

gains.a: The verse's heaven and hell for speech get an inward witness, the liar's own heart
gains.b: The Kural's burning heart gets a cosmos, in which what the heart knows is carried to a birth

note: Verse 427 chooses Marusi to put kin and the matter in words; verse 549 is where he does so, naming the line the two houses share.
teaches: The envoy's task of setting out kin is carried out in this closing, where the shared descent from Nami is the reason offered for the marriage.

note: Verse 83 says the fire of desire burns women within and none bears it more heavily than the shame-bound; in verse 465 the men voice it aloud to the women.
teaches: The epic first shows desire borne in silence by women and then spoken freely by men, so the burden is set unequally by who may say it.

note: Both are a deserted woman weighing the assurance of the man who left.
teaches: The couplet asks whether those who trusted an assurance are at fault, and the epic heroine answers both ways at once, calling his word a lie and naming herself the one of evil deeds.

gains.a: the epic verse gains the couplet's moral question, so her cry that he lied reads as a judgment on who answers for a broken assurance
gains.b: the couplet gains the promise in its exact words and a speaker who does not acquit herself, which it never shows

note: Naladiyar 27 sets the body as a bubble in pelting rain; 520 calls the human body a frothy hollow. The first uses it to urge ending the cycle of births, the second to bar men from a Vidyadhara's wealth.
teaches: One image of the body as foam serves a teacher of release and an envoy's claim of rank, so the image shows weakness only and takes its direction from who uses it.

gains.a: 520 gains the sense that its froth-body is a commonplace of teaching on impermanence, so using it as an insult turns a lesson into a boast
gains.b: 27 gains a use of the bubble-body to exclude rather than free, showing that the image alone does not call for renunciation

note: Naladiyar 103 says each one's enjoyments are measured by their own course, as no one rounded the vilam fruit; 848 says the sea need not fetch water nor the river beg rain.
teaches: Both argue from unmade nature, but the quatrain's fruit shows a lot fixed in advance while the letter's sea and river show a lot that flows in, so the same proof from nature can counsel content or confidence.

gains.a: the letter's images are placed in the didactic argument that nature's givens prove fate
gains.b: the quatrain's measured lot gains a picture of fate as abundance flowing toward the fortunate

note: The couplet says all five senses find their objects in one bright-bangled woman; the epic names the same five, smell, taste, music, the sight of dance and her touch, as the round of the hero's pleasure.
teaches: Where the couplet gathers all five senses into one woman, the epic spreads them over perfumes, food, string music and dance with only touch left to her, showing a prince's pleasure as a court of arts rather than the single person the couplet praises.

gains.a: the verse's list of senses is recognised as the Kural's fivefold scheme of the lover's delight, not a random catalogue
gains.b: the couplet's claim of concentration is set against a scene where the senses are served by many things, which shows how strong its claim that one woman suffices really is

note: 1523 shows the pearl parasol bringing joy to the people and the sea-ringed world; Kural 389 says the world rests under the parasol of a king who bears bitter words.
teaches: The epic's parasol is the sign of conquest, while the couplet makes shelter depend on a king's patience with harsh speech.

gains.a: the epic verse lacks any condition on the parasol's shelter, and gains the couplet's test of hearing bitter words
gains.b: the couplet lacks a visible sign of sovereignty, and gains the pearl parasol of a triumphant king

note: 1449 shows anger rising at insult and arrows poured out; Kural 305 says to guard against anger or it kills the one who has it.
teaches: The arrows are beaten away in 1450, so the epic shows the Kural's warning working out in the battle rather than as a rule.

gains.a: The rage gains a cost: the arrows turn back on the shooter's hopes, as the next verse shows.
gains.b: The couplet gains a king with an army whose anger leads him to weapon after weapon that fails.

note: At Krishna's flute in the Thiruppugazh dry trees in the forest sprout and birds come down to the ground; at Gandharvadattai's yazh the trees of the grove put out shoots and the birds forget themselves and fall.
teaches: The same marvel of music that moves trees and birds is a god's sign in the hymn and a contest's evidence in the epic, where 659 adds the reverse, birds fleeing bad music, so the image becomes a measure as well as a wonder.

gains.a: the epic's marvel is shown to use a stock image of divine music, so that the girl is raised to the level of Krishna's flute
gains.b: the hymn's image gains a version in which nature can also refuse, which the hymn's all-conquering flute never shows

note: Kural 1183 says love has taken the woman's grace and modesty and left sickness and pallor; verse 1045 shows a maiden who tries to hide her sickness and is betrayed by her pallor.
teaches: The epic shows the moment when modesty tries to hold and pallor breaks it, a step the couplet only reports after the fact.

gains.a: The verse lacks a statement that pallor is the price paid for modesty, which the couplet states.
gains.b: The couplet lacks a maiden before marriage who still has her modesty and is losing it.

note: The patikam says he delighted in her for two months and then took the road again; this verse gives the two months, the night departure, and his destiny as the chariot that carries him.
teaches: The patikam reports only the length of the stay, while the narrative adds that the leaving is driven both by the hero's own rising heart and by fortune, which the summary line never says.

note: In 829 the bride's father judges the girl fit only for the lion-killer and begins the wedding rites; in 1012 the groom's mother, seeing only the portrait, welcomes the match as ripened merit.
teaches: The match made by the fathers is accepted by the groom's mother through a painted likeness, so the women make the bride a member of the family before she is seen by the groom.
