note: In 495 Sitattan calls it a failure of understanding to blame former deeds when fortune turns; in 510, in the storm, he makes the fruit of former deeds the only ground on which the good survive.
teaches: The merchant's creed of effort over fate lasts only until the sea rises; under the storm the same man falls back on karma, so the epic stages the Kural's own pull between effort and fate as one character's change of mind.

note: Vimalai calls desire the one sickness with no medicine; Kural 1102 says the woman who causes the sickness is herself its cure.
teaches: Read together they show the two sides of one sickness: to the sufferer who cannot speak of it, it has no cure, while the couplet, spoken from the side of union, finds the cure in the beloved, which the story will supply by marriage.

gains.a: Vimalai's despair is shown to be a stage, not a verdict, since the couplet names the cure her story reaches
gains.b: the couplet's paradox gains a woman's voice, where the Kural gives the man's, and the cure turns out to be needed on both sides

claims.gist: no people on earth are greater than kings
the Lord gives unfailing bliss to those who serve his feet
a maiden's inclination follows the youth who wins her, as the poets' treatises lay down
the Lord's feet are to be praised, and those who understand the story gain an undying light
island-dwelling Milechchar humans are classed with animals
gods take their food by mere wish of the mind
in the long round of births one has already shed more tears for parted kin than the sea holds
true austerity belongs to those who have left this life for the next with zeal
one who takes refuge at the feet of the Jina gains the true path to release
a man grimed with dust is not worth the king's bowing
a king who guards the earth with an unbent sceptre and keeps dharma with the learned has no higher joy
wealth that does not lead to heaven or release is not worth the name
the Dark One (Krishna or Vishnu) bowed his crown at the feet of the Great One whose word the mountain's dwellers keep
what is due to come will come, and fearing it avails nothing
fear is itself suffering and feeds the deeds that afflict a person daily
the lot of enjoyment ripens by itself and the herald's introduction adds nothing to it
an unmarried girl will not name her love-sickness even to those closest to her, from shame
desire and the senses are outposts of the karmic enemy that must be cleared before its stronghold falls
the strength of earth-dwelling men looks mountain-large only to the fearful and is nothing to the strong
a husband's going, even in the sweet hour of a sulk, takes his wife's life from her
death in samadhi after the vow brings a heaven in proportion to what was done
a chaste wife dies with her husband, renounces adornment in his absence and lives worshipping him
virtue (sila) brings rebirth as a god in a heaven
another sort of merit brings a world-ruler's umbrella and delights
household pleasures end in death by sickness as suddenly as a wreck at sea

note: The couplet puts the lotus goddess in the effort of the unslothful; the verse says she will not embrace those who slip.
teaches: Where the Kural earns fortune by effort, the epic loses it by a lapse, so prosperity is shown as something kept by conduct and not only won by work.

gains.a: the blessing gains the couplet's account of what Lakshmi rewards, so the warning becomes a condition
gains.b: the couplet gains its negative side: fortune can be lost by one slip as well as missed by sloth

note: The epic says deeds whirl the soul like a wheel through the four states; the couplet names craving as the seed of unceasing birth.
teaches: The epic gives the wheel's driver as deeds and the Kural gives craving, so the two books hold different roots of the same round of birth.

gains.a: a named seed of the wheel in craving, which the verse leaves unsaid
gains.b: a picture of the wheel itself, four states and births past counting, which the couplet states only as 'birth'

note: Verse 126 has women playing with youths on the Vidyadhara hill until their powder stains the rocks; verse 747 has bangled women at play and petals falling in the lion's mountain.
teaches: The poet reuses one pleasure-on-the-hill picture for two different mountains, so the lion's range is painted as a pleasure ground as much as a hunting ground.

note: The counsellors tell the king to go in at once and not let counsel drag; Kural 638 says a minister must tell even a king who has ruined wise counsel what is good for him.
teaches: Here the counsellors' advice is a plain urging of haste that the king accepts, so the Kural's hard case of an unheeding king meets its easy one.

gains.a: A test of what it looks like when counsel is taken without a quarrel, which the verse alone does not discuss.
gains.b: A scene of a minister doing his duty before any failing of the king, which the couplet only imagines after the failing.

note: In 455 an unnamed hearer rages at the news that Civakan recovered the herd with no man lost; in 693 Kattiyankaran, hearing the same deed retold by his men, decides Civakan is the way his kingdom will be taken.
teaches: The anger left nameless at the cattle raid is given its owner and its reason here: the deed that saved the city's herds is what tells the usurper he has a rival.

note: Kural 1067 begs all beggars not to beg of those who conceal; Pazhamozhi 224 says those who beg of hard-minded men get nothing, like seeking alms in a monastery.
teaches: The Kural gives the warning; Pazhamozhi gives the reason in an image, that the hard rich man yields no more than renouncers who own nothing.

note: Kural 8 says other seas are hard to swim except for those who reach the feet of the one called அறவாழி; 3023 uses அறவாழி for the wheel of dharma and also calls him a sea of virtues.
teaches: The Kural's single word அறவாழி can be a sea or a wheel, and the epic shows the lord named as both in one verse.

gains.a: the verse's wheel of dharma and sea of virtues are read as the two sides of one name, so its praise echoes the couplet's term in both senses
gains.b: the Kural's compound அறவாழி gets a use in which it is a wheel and the sea is named separately, so its single word is seen to carry two images

note: Kural 543 makes the king's sceptre the origin of the books of the learned and of virtue; 2746 gives the ascetic the duty of telling the king dharma and leaves the king with the sceptre.
teaches: Where the couplet makes dharma depend on the king, the verse has the king come to the ascetic to hear it, so the two disagree about which gives the other its authority.

gains.a: the verse's two duties, scripture and sceptre, are put against a couplet that derives the first from the second, which exposes the ranking that the verse leaves open
gains.b: the couplet's claim that the sceptre is the source of dharma gains a story in which the sceptre's holder goes to be taught and leaves the sceptre

note: Verse 324 shows the feast of birds that the killings of 314 leave.
teaches: The elephant's violence in 314 is followed by its leaving a feast, so its cost is seen in what scavengers gain.

note: The Kural names the army that does not collapse; 1250 shows drums split, crowns sunk and chariots overturned in a collapsing army.
teaches: A rule that an army must not collapse is tested against the detail of what a collapse looks like in a field.

gains.a: A standard to measure the broken host against, so its rout reads as failure of what an army must be.
gains.b: A worked case of collapse, which the definition names but never pictures.

note: Kural 894 says a weak man who harms the strong beckons Death with his hand; verse 686 makes the demander, who counts himself strong, the fool who beckons.
teaches: Strength is not settled by who sends the demand, and the couplet's rule can be turned against the one who thinks himself the strong party.

gains.a: The verse lacks a rule that harming the stronger is a gesture that summons death, which gives the cobra image its warning.
gains.b: The couplet lacks a case where the apparent strong man is the one deceived about strength, which the epic supplies.

note: The Kural's one who walked on the flower and his noble feet and the epic's wheel-king who walked on the open lotus and his feet which the virtuous praise; both give the lotus walker as the object of devotion.
teaches: The epic names what is learned at those feet, five, six and nine, where the couplet names only the reward of long life on earth.

gains.a: The epic verse gains from the couplet the promise attached to reaching the feet, long life on the earth, where it states only knowledge
gains.b: The couplet gains a lotus-walker with a doctrine, who teaches what is to be known, in place of an unnamed figure

note: 2960 asks whether renouncing wives can be worthy, while Naladiyar 53 says the best renounce home, youth and beauty without delay.
teaches: The Naladiyar's praise of the best renouncers leaves out the people left behind, whom the wives put forward as the cost.

gains.a: the wives' question is given the opposing view that the best of men renounce what they love without delay
gains.b: the Naladiyar's praise of renouncing gains the weeping wives that its list of things given up does not name

note: Verse 549 judges the match fit because both houses have high lineage and wealth; Naladiyar 195 says high and low caste are only words and that austerity, learning and effort, not famous wealth, make a lineage.
teaches: The two disagree about what equality of houses rests on: the epic points to descent and riches, the quatrain to conduct and learning, and the clash holds only if lineage in 549 means inherited standing.

gains.a: A test of the match by learning and conduct, which Marusi does not apply.
gains.b: A case of a match argued from descent and riches, the very ground the quatrain calls empty.

note: The freed elephant kills the keepers who try to enclose it, as the quatrain says an elephant may kill even its keeper.
teaches: The epic shows the quatrain's keeper-killer elephant as a weapon someone else has deliberately loosed.

gains.a: the keepers' deaths read as a known risk of the beast, not as an accident of the rescue
gains.b: the quatrain's general warning is given a scene where the elephant is not merely ungrateful but sent

note: 1647 has the guards search the caves and thickets and then watch every side; 1630 has the king already hidden among the women by art.
teaches: The guard stands around a king who is already inside the place it guards, so the watch protects the game and not the king.

note: Tirumanthiram 200 has those who give up killing, theft, lust and lying reach Siva's feet; the verse has worshippers of a lord who has kept non-killing reach release.
teaches: Both name feet and release for those who keep the vow, but the Saiva verse makes the worshipper the keeper of the vow and the Jain verse makes the lord the keeper.

gains.a: the worshipper's gain is set against a Saiva account where one's own giving up of killing is what earns the feet
gains.b: the Saiva list is shown to have a Jain counterpart in which the god, not the worshipper, is the one who has kept the vow

note: The Kural calls an eye that blinks at a flung spear flight; 1247 has whole ranks blind with arrows, puzzled, hiding and falling.
teaches: The Kural counts flinching as flight, but 1247 shows troops struck blind by a dark of arrows, where fear and confusion are not the same.

gains.a: A name for the fear it shows, making the rout a failing of courage and not only of fortune.
gains.b: A case where the eye cannot see, which tests whether blinking is always cowardice.

note: The astrologer in 539 places the princess's destined husband in Rajamapuram; 610-612 bring kings from Hastinapuram, Kampili and Varanavasi to win her.
teaches: Read against the horoscope, the far kings' arrival is a journey already in vain, and the open contest is the means by which the prophecy picks its man from the city it named.

note: 1279 has warriors who do not fear Death send the fearful away; Kural 765 calls an army one that stands against raging Death.
teaches: The epic turns the couplet's test of an army into a selection, since warriors themselves dismiss those who fear.

gains.a: The warriors' call gets a standard for whom to keep, since the couplet names fearlessness before Death as what makes an army.
gains.b: The couplet's standing together is given a speaking crowd who sort themselves, which the couplet itself does not show.

note: The couplet says sin, fear and blame never leave one who crosses into another's home; here a wife crosses, and the fruit falls on her.
teaches: The couplet is spoken to a man; the epic carries the same four ills onto a wife and adds the one the couplet lacks, the disease of her own body.

gains.a: the unit gains a stated rule that the crossing carries its own ruin
gains.b: the couplet gains a woman as the one who crosses, and a bodily fruit beyond blame

note: In 640 rival kings vow to plunge into war if another wins the vina contest; 844 reports that a wicked one, burning, said she belonged to the strongest spear and made war.
teaches: The suitors' threat comes true not as their own act but through a single instigator who turns their wounded pride into a war, so the contest's law is broken by one man's design.

note: In 157 the king is fierce as a poisonous serpent's fire; in 290 he is the sun of the Kuru line swallowed by the great serpent of his minister.
teaches: The serpent's wrath that made Saccandan terrible to enemies is turned back on him from inside his own court, so the image of his strength becomes the image of his end.

note: Naladiyar 11 says that the wise renounce in childhood because they know grey hair will come; verse 351 shows a youth who turns from music, dance and heaven-like pleasure while still young.
teaches: The Naladiyar gives the reason for early renunciation and the epic gives a young man living it, so the reader sees how the reason looks as a character.

gains.a: A reason for the youth's distaste, the argument from coming old age, which the verse never gives.
gains.b: A named young man who has already done what the quatrain says the wise do.

note: The sleep arrow of 1455 is undone by the awakening arrow of 1456.
teaches: The last pair completes the pattern: each of Asvagriva's divine weapons has its answer, so none is decisive.

note: A queen leaves her son for the nun's life and is rewarded in heaven, while the couplet asks what a householder gains by going to the outside way.
teaches: The story answers the Kural's question by showing a woman rewarded for leaving, so the couplet's praise of the householder is met by a Jain ideal that holds the opposite.

gains.a: the queen's leaving is set against a rule that makes the home the greater path
gains.b: the couplet's challenge is met by a case where leaving is rewarded, not wasted

note: Tirumanthiram 724 keeps the body alive because true knowledge needs a living frame; verse 775 holds that a man should give even himself to end the world's pain.
teaches: A Jain epic's praise of the body given away for others and a Saiva text's care for the body to win knowledge set out two uses of the same frame.

gains.a: The verse lacks any limit on self-giving, the claim that the body must be kept for the sake of knowledge.
gains.b: The mantra lacks a counter-ethic, the claim that the body may be spent for another's pain, which tests its practical argument.

note: 3101 has the Lord's feet cut through the hard-gathered karma like a blade; Kural 5 says the two deeds do not cling to those devoted to the Lord's true praise.
teaches: The verse gives the means by which the deeds are removed and the Kural gives the assurance that they will not cling.

gains.a: the verse's cutting spear is given an outcome, that the deeds do not attach to the one who praises
gains.b: the Kural's promise that deeds do not cling is given a picture of how, a cutting of the root

note: Both set hell's dogs on the victims; 1933 adds that the wardens raised them in cages and that the victims flee up a tree of thorns.
teaches: The dog and the thorn tree recur as fixed parts of the Jain hell, while 1933 shows the dogs as reared for the work.

note: Naladiyar 51 says austerity drives sin out like a lamp but that sin returns when the oil of merit runs out; 3064 has the eight karmas cut to pieces by one firm mind.
teaches: The quatrain's lamp-and-oil picture makes the effect of austerity last as long as its merit; the epic claims a final cutting, so the two differ on whether it can return.

gains.a: the verse's total destruction of karma is tested by the rule that austerity only keeps sin away while the merit lasts
gains.b: the quatrain's returning darkness meets a claim that the cut is final

note: Naladiyar 322 says those not disposed to virtue cannot take it in, as a tanner's dog that chews leather cannot take the taste of milk rice; in 944 a dog pricks its ears, weeps and takes in the teaching.
teaches: The quatrain uses the dog as the type of the creature who cannot receive dharma; the epic answers with a dog that hears and consents, so receptivity is made a matter of the moment of hearing, not of the hearer's kind.

gains.a: the force of the inversion: the dog is the proverbial non-hearer, which makes its listening the point
gains.b: a limit on its image: the dog's inability is a habit, which the epic shows can be broken at death

note: The vow of 1336 to take the earth or the world of the gods is met when the arrow fells Suvarnaketu in 1350.
teaches: The vow of earth or heaven is ended not by either prize but by an arrow, so the warrior's two-sided promise leaves out the third outcome of defeat.

note: Kuruntokai 320: on the dune of drying fish and prawns she has not even one day's laughter with the shore lord to be blamed for, yet the town gossips. Kainnilai 54: on the same drying-ground he lied to her and enjoyed her beauty. On a plain reading one heroine denies what the other confesses.
teaches: The prawn-drying ground serves one heroine as the scene of an innocence the town will not credit and another as the scene of her seduction, so the stock place of neythal kalavu could carry either a defence before the town or an accusation of the lover.

note: The Naladiyar likens a miser's hoard, enjoyed by a stranger, to a lovely daughter of the house who goes to an outsider in due season; the king says daughters are like the conch's pearls, which profit others and never the conch.
teaches: The same commonplace, that a daughter is raised to go to another, serves the quatrain as an image of loss through folly and serves the epic as a father's consolation, so the pair shows the saying could carry blame or comfort.

gains.a: the king's saying gains the quatrain's point that the daughter's going is as certain as a season, which is why it can console
gains.b: the quatrain's simile gains a scene in which the daughter's leaving is felt by the father, not only used as an image

note: 292 defends a warrior who stopped the king's toddy being mixed and will not wait his turn; 298 has a warrior angry that the king does not tell him 'you go first'.
teaches: Both turn a quarrel over drink into a claim to the front line, which shows the feast's order was read as a promise about the battle, and a warrior who seized one was claiming the other.

note: Kural 504 says to examine qualities and faults and take what predominates; the roll of princes names only qualities, and verse 334 ends on a danger.
teaches: The council's list of suitors names only merits and the last verse adds a warning, which shows the Kural's rule to weigh faults was missing from the roll.

gains.a: A named rule by which the one-sided praise of the roll is judged and found short.
gains.b: A court scene in which the praise-only roll of candidates is the failure it warns of.

note: In 686 the usurper closes on the garlanded dancer and strips her; in 2587 she recounts that, once she had bowed to Civakan, the cruel spearman threw her off the stage and jailed her.
teaches: The letter gives the dancer's own account of what 686 told from outside, which shows the violence as something she carries as an injury against Civakan, not only as the usurper's crime.

note: 1988 pictures pleasure as honey tasted by a man hanging above a pit with an elephant and a snake; Naladiyar 60 says the higher ones see the pain in any pleasure and do not cling.
teaches: The parable explains why fools do not renounce: the honey is real, and the danger is out of sight while one tastes it.

gains.a: The parable gains a statement of what the wise do while the honey drops, which the image does not give.
gains.b: The quatrain gains an image for the fool's blindness, so that his not renouncing is shown as enjoyment of a real sweetness.

note: Verse 262 says lords who bear the lowly's lapses, like sandal under the rutting elephant, are bowed to by the earth; Naladiyar 66 says the well-born bear the base's stone-like words and let them pass, held back by their lineage.
teaches: The epic names the reward of forbearance in the king's public standing, where the quatrain names its reason in birth.

gains.a: The reward of forbearance in public honour, which the image alone does not name.
gains.b: A political result for the restraint that the quatrain justifies only by lineage.

note: Tirumanthiram 198 has Death's servants bind and drive the killers into fire-mouthed hell; in 2764 the hell-beings rise and fall on the blades with no jailer named.
teaches: The Saiva verse puts Yama's servants in charge, while the Jain verse leaves the pain to the deeds and the place, so the two show different views of who runs hell.

gains.a: the verse's hell gains the contrast of a judge's servants at work, which brings out its own lack of any
gains.b: the Tirumanthiram verse gains a hell without servants as a rival picture, in which the ground itself does the work

note: 1419 lifts the mountain; 1420 shows the Suramai army scattering as he advances.
teaches: The scattering shows that the mountain wins by fear before it falls, so the plough-bearer's earlier victory is reversed here.

note: In 302 Vijayai grieves alone in the burning ground and has no fear; in 2603 she turns the place of her fall and rescue into a painted memorial on her mansion, with a town granted to her rescuer.
teaches: The burning ground that was her lowest place is made at the end into a thing gratefully remembered, so the reader sees grief turned into a debt honoured.

note: Kural 507 says trusting the ignorant out of fondness brings every folly; Sirupanchamoolam 39 says giving treasury, accounts and stores to men without understanding is setting a crow to guard rice.
teaches: The couplet locates the fault in the master's fondness; the verse measures the appointee (understanding that does not match his size) and shows the result as the guard eating what he guards.

note: 1722 gives the newborn the name Vijayan, and 71 earlier tells of the birth of the elder Vijayan at the start of the story.
teaches: The name Vijayan returns in the next generation, so a reader must keep the uncle and the son apart while seeing the name tied to fortune and victory.

claims.gist: the learned books name the unequalled giver and the unequalled warrior as the highest of men
release is won by right vision, knowledge, a conquered mind and long meditation, and there is no return from it
the sorrows of hell double in each lower layer
gifts of food given house after house turn into a mountain of wealth
pleasure enjoyed there is the fruit of old merit and also a bond
union with such a man is gained as the reward of penance
the one who has no taste of the senses is the giver who ends the hunger of the afflicted
the lord set up the orders of people and their qualities
fate, as a deed's working, carried the king away from her
a deed ripens and brings its fruit to the doer
the usurper who seized the land will meet his death through the rightful heir
right vision of the Lord's teaching, the conduct of not killing and the renouncing of meat lead to a higher state and bliss at the end
one resolved on the austerity that ends the disease of birth looks for no ties
a king should give up his crown for release
a mastered mantra commands the gods who answer to it
a counsellor must voice a fault he has seen, even against a colleague's agreed praise
such a union is the fruit of austerity, so all should hasten to perform it
a king is made great by forbearance
bearing children is rarer for women than wealth
the wealth gained by austerity grows in kinds and multiplies
a householder who gives, keeps from drink and flesh and is true to the spouse is born among the gods
the highest gods have no lord over them and none greater
some souls who rise to a better state do not remain in it, and those in hell do not grasp the dharma
renunciation is entered through reflection on the settled meaning of the scripture the Lord taught
the will of one-minded ascetics is fulfilled, even to bringing the rain-cloud

note: Kural 549 counts guarding the people and removing wrongdoing as the king's work and no fault; verse 140 faults a king on the ground of grace toward the lowest lives, which the Kural's list does not ask of him.
teaches: The epic widens the king's duty to grace toward all lowly lives, where the Kural's duty stops at the people and the removal of wrongdoers, so the two hold different measures of a good ruler.

gains.a: A rival standard, the Kural's, by which the king is judged only on what he does to his people.
gains.b: A test of its limit: a king who punishes wrongdoers by the Kural's rule may still lack grace toward lower creatures.

note: Purananuru 35 tells the Chola his tall umbrella is not for shade but to shelter suffering subjects, and warns him the world blames kings when things go wrong; 159 says Saccandan's umbrella already shades the world like a father.
teaches: The Sangam poet gives the umbrella as a duty the king must be urged to keep, the epic as a state already achieved; set together, the epic's praise lacks the warning that the story will soon need.

gains.a: the epic's settled praise is seen to omit the counsel that in the Sangam poem accompanies the umbrella
gains.b: the poem's admonition gains a later narrative in which a praised umbrella king does lose the world's shade

note: Both make the god the one to whom deeds do not cling; the king praises a lord who himself defeated hard deeds.
teaches: The Kural says worshippers are freed from deeds by praise, while the Jain king hymns a lord who won against deeds by his own conquest, so the same praise stands on different grounds.

gains.a: the king's hymn is seen to give a conquering lord, not a pure being to be reached, as the one praised
gains.b: the couplet's lord is shown to be read in a Jain way as one who defeated karma

note: 1438 calls Civakan the man whose body bears the true marks; from 1460 the marks are listed one by one.
teaches: An epithet that seems mere praise on the road becomes the evidence by which a stranger is recognised as a destined husband, so the body itself carries the plot.

note: Verse 243 says the learned keep blame and fierce deeds from a king whose sceptre is unbent; Kural 547 says justice guards the king if he does not falter in it.
teaches: The epic names who keeps a king from faltering, the learned counsellors, where the couplet names only the law that guards him if he does not.

gains.a: A reason why the sceptre stays unbent: it is kept by the learned.
gains.b: Persons who do the guarding the couplet gives to justice itself.

note: 1476 asks whether a king who lay on a golden couch with wives rubbing his feet should now lie on an elephant's brow; Siddhar 642 says the throne of pure gold does not go with the body when Yama takes it.
teaches: The epic shows the couch lost by a battle and the Siddhar shows it lost by Yama, so one losing of luxury is told as a war and as the common end.

gains.a: 1476 gives a king's lost luxury but does not say that no luxury could follow him in death.
gains.b: The Siddhar verse speaks to anyone and gains a particular king's fall as a case.

note: Kattiyangaran had told the suitors that only Kama himself could beat Gandharvadattai at the vina and that no such man was present; the women now call the king's slayer the vina-master.
teaches: The usurper's own boast that no rival existed names the man who would kill him, so the vina contest becomes the first sign of his fall.

note: The Akananuru man remembers a wedding of sand spread under a pandal, lamps and garlands at an auspicious dawn; the Cintamani's order has plantain and areca, aloe pots, lute and dance and golden flags across the city.
teaches: The same wedding adornments grow from a household's sand pandal to a king's command that the whole city be decked, and so show how rank changes the scale and not the parts.

gains.a: the epic's royal decking is seen to rest on the household's pandal, sand and lamps, which it enlarges and does not replace
gains.b: the Akananuru wedding, remembered only in the bride and groom's house, is set beside a city-wide wedding and shows how small and private it is

note: In 1420 Civakan praises the Jina who teaches that the eight karmas (எண்வினையும்) pass through love and yet do not pass because of love; 1469 shows the eight qualities of the soul seized by those karmas.
teaches: The two hymns of this ilampakam make a pair: the eight deeds of 1420 are the robbers of 1469, so the reader sees what the soul loses before the paradox of love and release in 1420 can be weighed.

note: The patikam sums up Suramanjari as resolving to look on no male form; 908 has her vow already reserve one exception, Civakan.
teaches: The vow the outline reports as a refusal of all men is in the story a vow with Civakan written into it, so her seclusion is a waiting as much as a withdrawal.

note: 3082 has Civakan win omniscience by his own war on the karmas; Tirumanthiram 113 has the Lord come down in a body, set his feet on the devotee's head and cut away the stain.
teaches: One text has the soul win release by its own battle, the other has it given from above, so the two disagree on whose act cuts the deeds.

gains.a: the war of the passions is set against a release that is given and not fought for, so its self-reliance becomes a choice
gains.b: the grace that cuts the stain is set beside a release won by effort, so its giver is seen to be what the Jain refuses

note: Kural 636 says no over-subtle scheme stands before keen native wit joined with learning; verse 695 rests the scheme on the target's lacking the sense to tell good from bad.
teaches: A scheme's success is shown to depend on how the target is judged, which the couplet alone does not say.

gains.a: The verse lacks a standard by which the minister's contempt for the prince's judgement can later be tested.
gains.b: The couplet lacks a schemer who bets openly on his target's inexperience.

note: Both women swim love's flood alone in the night watches (யாமம்).
teaches: Where the couplet's woman sees no shore and is simply alone, the epic adds the watchers who laugh at her, so the solitude of the night becomes public shame by day.

gains.a: Kanakamalai's 'sea of the night' is placed in the Kural's convention of the midnight flood of love
gains.b: the couplet's bare 'I alone' gains a social side, the women who mock the lovesick girl

note: Civakan let himself be bound because his parents asked it and told him his manhood would not be lessened; here he goes bound like a lion held by a spider's thread.
teaches: The thread that binds the lion is the parents' word of 1091, so the spider's thread is the image of consent, and the arrest becomes a test of filial obedience rather than of strength.

note: Verse 29 says Civakan will no longer want the pleasure of women; 2477 shows the pleasure he had in marriage in its fullest.
teaches: The full wedding night shows what the hero gave up at the end, so his later renunciation of pleasure counts for more than a hero who never knew it.

note: In Puram 385 the lord of Ambar, hearing a bard's drum at another man's door, strips off his earth-eaten rags, dresses him in white and ends his hunger; the guide promises that Karikalan will strip off the bard's stitched rags and give him silk before he asks.
teaches: Puram 385 tells the removal of rags and the gift of cloth as one patron's spontaneous kindness, while the guide poem can predict it as the first step of a known sequence, which suggests the re-dressing of the bard was a recognised rite of reception rather than a single generous act.

note: In Akananuru 369 the foster mother laments that her girl refused the rich wedding her kin had prepared and went off across the waste with a youth; Gunamalai, told by her nurse of a match with a rich cousin, names death or penance as her only alternatives.
teaches: Beside the Akam girl who answers an unwanted family wedding by elopement, Gunamalai answers by a vow spoken to her nurse, keeping the refusal inside the house where it can move her parents instead of leaving them.

gains.a: the akam convention of the refused kin wedding, which marks the nurse's report as the familiar trigger for a heroine's flight that this heroine declines
gains.b: an outcome in which the same refusal, voiced rather than acted on, ends in a sanctioned wedding, a path the elopement poem never shows

note: 1860 asks for a refuge beyond Death; 1862 answers that none exists but the austere sage's feet.
teaches: The question and the answer divide the council's work: the king asks, the minister names the sage's feet.

note: This verse praises the lord who burned all old deeds by his own renunciation; Tirumular's sunstone burns the malas only when the Lord's sun appears.
teaches: Jain deliverance burns karma by the liberated one's own effort without a god, while the Saiva text burns it by presence and grace, so the two disagree on whether anything outside the soul does the burning.

gains.a: the Jain hymn is shown to stand against the Saiva view that grace is needed to burn deeds
gains.b: the Saiva image of grace burning bond is shown to be one answer to a question the Jain poet answers by effort

note: Both set grey hair and the loss of women's regard against the pleasure of Kama.
teaches: The Siddhar's youth who spends everything on women ends with a staff in his hand, while Asokan reads his first white hair in time to leave, so the two verses show the same fall averted and unaverted.

gains.a: The king's fear that women will turn away gets the full course of a man who ignored it, which the verse only hints at.
gains.b: The Siddhar's ruined youth gets a counter-case, a man who is warned by the first sign and leaves.

note: The Kural asks what a virtuous householder would gain by going the outside way; the Neelakesi's ideal land has virtuous householders and also those who leave home's troubles to wear away their deeds.
teaches: The Jain poet answers the couplet's question by naming a gain the household cannot give, the wearing away of deeds already done, while still praising the household's gifts and conduct.

note: 1243 has the Vidyadharas' arrows darken the sky; 1246 has the hero's arrows rise, strike their eyes and darken it again.
teaches: The darkness changes sides inside four verses, so the same arrow-shadow that shields the attackers blinds them.

note: 2024 ranks beings best, middle and lowest by the fruit of earlier good deeds; Kural 37 points to the bearer and the rider of a palanquin as the visible proof of virtue's fruit.
teaches: Rank that Kural 37 reads from one palanquin is stretched in 2024 into a ladder of births, so one visible difference becomes a whole order of worlds.

gains.a: The ranking of beings gets a plain proof from daily sight, the palanquin, in place of a bare claim about the fruit of deeds.
gains.b: The couplet gains a longer horizon: the difference it sees between rider and bearer is only the near end of a graded series of births.

note: Verse 106 tells a night dream that the court takes as a true sign of this match; in 526 the king says that he can take the offer only as a dream. This holds if 526's dream means a thing not to be trusted.
teaches: The same word, dream, stands for a sure sign in the court's mouth and for something too good to be believed in the king's, and the plot rides on that gap.

note: 1925 makes Civakan a thunder-voiced lion who needs no stratagem against a jackal; 1928 has a cave lion, roaring and leaping, fall into the hunters' net.
teaches: The counsel defeats the hero with his own image: the lion stays a lion, but the reply shows that strength without judgment is just what a net is made to catch.

note: 2941's speaker, who ate rich ghee-scented food, fears the begging that renunciation brings; Naladiyar 1 says those who once ate six-flavoured food served by a willing wife may end up begging for gruel, so wealth is no support.
teaches: The quatrain uses the fall to beggary as the argument for renouncing, while the epic's speaker uses the same fall as the reason to fear renouncing.

gains.a: the speaker's fear of alms is answered, since the quatrain says such beggary comes anyway to the rich
gains.b: the quatrain's warning about lost wealth meets a person who feels it and still hesitates

note: The verse sheds heavy deeds by right vision; Tirumular burns the many ills of deeds by worship of the fire.
teaches: The deed is shed by sight and understanding in one and burnt away by worship in the other, so the means of release is what they dispute.

gains.a: the shedding of deeds by sight gets a rival that burns them by rite
gains.b: Tirumular's fire gets a rival in which no worship is needed and sight alone is enough

note: 1844 says those who cut the root of good deeds will be kings in the hells; 1923 counts the layers and dwellings of those hells.
teaches: The hells of the earlier threat are shown to be a ranked place with room for every kind of fallen king.

note: Peacocks dance to the clouds' roar here, and in Akananuru 82 the hill is a stage where the peacock is the dancer.
teaches: Both make the hill a stage on which weather and creatures perform together, but the Akananuru names the full orchestra while the epic gives only clouds and peacocks.

gains.a: A fuller account of how the hill's sounds become music, which it only hints at.
gains.b: The same scene shown as ordinary prosperity, free of a lover's longing.

note: Kural 1151: if you are not leaving, tell me; tell your quick return to those who will still be alive. Kalittokai 5 ends: whatever day you go, on that day her life will go.
teaches: Both refuse the comfort of a promised return by tying her death to the moment of departure, and the Kalittokai shows the couplet's sharp line as the close of a full argument, after images of the emptied festival ground and the lotus out of water have prepared it.

note: Thirikadugam 50 names three separate 'planets' that cut off rain: a greedy king, deceitful men and a woman who crosses her bounds; 255 makes the bent sceptre the one cause from which failed rain and broken chastity both follow.
teaches: Where the Thirikadugam gives the king, the liar and the unchaste woman equal blame for drought, the Cintamani makes women's lapse a symptom of the king's fault.

gains.a: the epic's causal order stands out against a list that treats the three as parallel
gains.b: the verse's planet image, கோள், is shown read in the epic as literal disorder of the planets

note: Both set the cowherds' flute in the evening pastures: a sign of plenty here, a torment to the waiting wife there.
teaches: The same flute is joy in the public landscape and pain in a private heart, so the reader sees how the sound takes its meaning from who hears it.

gains.a: A listener inside the scene, which the epic's description does not give.
gains.b: A public, cheerful reading of the flute against which her pain stands out.

note: 3072 has Civakan spend four cold months in the open field, using the body up for release; Tirumanthiram 724 says if the body perishes the life perishes, so the body is nurtured to win knowledge.
teaches: One text treats the body as the means to be spent, the other as the means that must be kept alive, so they disagree on what a body is for.

gains.a: the verse's exposure of the body is set against a school that says release needs a body kept alive
gains.b: the Tirumanthiram's nurturing of the body meets an ascetic who spends his on release

note: Love said to cling like a shadow in 1511; her actual reflection taken for a companion in 1524.
teaches: The love she said should cling like a shadow has gone, and what stays is her literal image, which she then comforts as a friend, so the simile becomes her situation.

note: When Kantukkatan sneezed over the child in 323, a voice hidden in the branches said சீவ, 'live'; in 361 the child is named Civakan.
teaches: The hero's name is the fulfilment of an omen at his finding, so the name itself carries the blessing 'live' given over a child left in a burning ground.

note: 3022 has the king bow to the feet that walked over the lotus with its bees; Kural 3 praises those who reach the feet of the one who walked on the flower.
teaches: Both place the object of worship on the lotus, the Kural without a name and the epic with a figure the king can bow to, so the stock image is shown being used as a scene.

gains.a: the verse's lotus-treading feet are shown as the stock image of the Kural's opening praise, so the king's bow is the act the couplet commends
gains.b: the Kural's 'one who walked on the flower' gets a staged scene, a lotus in an assembly with a king bowing before it

note: Kural 497 says no ally is needed but fearlessness, provided one thinks everything through and acts by the place; at 1925 Civakan claims no strategy or allies are needed because he is strong.
teaches: Civakan keeps the couplet's conclusion and drops its condition, and the mother's next verses restore exactly the weighing of place that the couplet made the price of going alone.

gains.a: Civakan's boast is shown to be a half-quoted rule, which explains why the mother answers with place and time rather than with doubts about his courage
gains.b: the couplet's proviso (எஞ்சாமை எண்ணி இடத்தால் செயின்) is shown to be the part a brave young man leaves out, so it reads as a warning and not a licence

note: The Kural's wife calls her husband a philanderer because all women feast on him with their eyes; Dattai's anger at his second marriage is the same grievance.
teaches: The epic shows what the Kural's grievance leads to when the husband is a king who really does take another wife, so the complaint is tested rather than only voiced.

gains.a: Dattai's anger is given a name and a ground that the verse itself leaves unspoken.
gains.b: The wife's complaint, which in the Kural stays a lovers' quarrel, is carried to a real second marriage and a quarrel that is settled by her bowing.

note: The narration says the minister, a great snake, swallowed Saccandan; the letter says an elephant threw and killed him and the sceptre merely slackened.
teaches: Setting the narrator's account against the usurper's shows the epic staging propaganda: the same death is a cruel sceptre spreading darkness in one telling and a stable accident in the other.

note: Kattiyankaran promises the kings fortune if they kill Civakan; Padumukan says his plan is to let them destroy one another and rule alone.
teaches: Padumukan's reading turns the promise of sovereignty into its opposite, showing the reader that the usurper's incitement of the suitors repeats the method by which he took Saccandan's throne.

note: The Kural praises the manhood that does not look at another's wife; Nandattan, who must meet and speak to his brother's wife, keeps his eyes on her anklet.
teaches: The couplet forbids the look outright, and the scene shows how the rule is kept when a man must face and address the woman: the gaze goes to her feet, where looking becomes reverence.

gains.a: Nandattan's lowered eyes gain a named virtue, so the verse reads as conduct and not only courtesy
gains.b: the couplet gains the case it does not cover, a kinsman's obliged meeting, and the bodily form its restraint then takes

note: Kanaiyan appears in 44 as the chief captured by the Chola after Pazhaiyan fell, and in 386 as the patron shamed when Paanan broke his Aariya wrestler.
teaches: The akam poets used Kanaiyan only in defeat, once in capture and once in public shame, so his name had become a byword for humiliation before an onlooking crowd, which is exactly what the wife of 386 feels.

note: Verse 409 has the Vidyadhara astrologer give the month's limit for the lion; 607 has a counsellor give it again to the Podanam king.
teaches: Two courts, with the same date in each, act on one word, so the lion-killing is a shared fate rather than one court's hope.

claims.gist: a king of renown does not go to his end until he has sent his household ahead
for a man, death is far better than a life saved from danger by a woman
a low birth is the fruit of the sin of killing and of eating meat, honey and toddy
those who live in the forest cannot keep their bodies alive without meat, honey and toddy
good deeds of a former birth sprout as present wealth
greater merit now wins the world of Indra
the slaughter of a creature for the table is a long torment to it
a king who will not hear justice shrinks and loses what he has, while a just ruler's wealth fills all space
royal honour is given by one's own good deeds as by a deity
a house is made whole by wives, children and elders together
fate presses the mind to remember the beloved
a lord whom gods hide from and foes bow to is not to be faced by one who wants to live
love's sickness has no cure
pity makes a fighter's hands fail in battle, so force and not talk must settle the matter
turning away from sensual pleasure marks one fit for release
every good state carries its opposite within it: youth age, wealth affliction, union parting, health disease
the freed soul has eight qualities, among them endless knowledge, vision, strength and bliss, and is eternal
the freed soul stands for ever at the top of the three worlds, free of anger and the like
the wicked are born in pits of mire in the hells
one who plots to kill by deceit may rightly be killed by deceit
a warrior should not strike a beast, since there is no distinction in it
a man already wounded by another is not to be struck, being another's leavings
a warrior should not strike the young or the old, who are no match for him
right seeing, knowledge and conduct together close the evil states of birth and open the way to boundless bliss
a king's worth shows in a learning that takes in and surpasses the learning of others
a man of understanding withdraws his heart when it goes out toward another man's wife

note: 1395 shows the flood of blood and broken tusks as a spectacle; Purananuru 62 asks what victory there can be when both armies have died.
teaches: Set side by side, the epic dwells on the field's carnage without cost where the Sangam poem measures it by the widows and the empty claim to victory.

gains.a: gains the question it never asks: what is won when the field is full of the dead
gains.b: gains the epic's long image of the carnage, which the poem only sketches

note: 2868 teaches against killing as a cause of suffering ripening from deeds; Tirumanthiram 200 names killing, theft, lust and lying as sins great as mountains whose giving up reaches Siva's feet.
teaches: The same sins are shunned in both, but one pays out as karma and the other as arrival at a god's feet.

gains.a: The Jain king's rule, which has no god to reach, shows the Saiva reward as a different end for the same practice
gains.b: Tirumular's giving-up of the four sins, which says what is gained, shows the Jain view that the fruit is only the working of deeds

note: Both argue that the days before age are few and that austerity should be taken up before it arrives.
teaches: The Saiva verse points to the mountain of great austerity as the use of youth, while Asokan turns to the forest mountain and has no god to appeal to, only the fleeting of youth and kin.

gains.a: Asokan's leaving gets a Saiva statement of the same urgency, with a named goal of austerity beside the forest mountain.
gains.b: Tirumular's advice to hurry gets a case of a king who actually hands over the throne and goes.

note: The couplet asks what one gains by leaving a household life lived in dharma; the epic holds that once a man resolves to leave home for penance, the wise speak of no other dharma.
teaches: The two meet on a condition the couplet leaves out: the Kural weighs the householder's path before the choice, while the epic speaks of one who has already resolved, for whom the household dharma is no longer an option.

gains.a: the epic's claim is placed against the strongest defence of the household, so its scope (one who has resolved) becomes visible
gains.b: the couplet's rhetorical question gains an answer from a man who has lived both lives, an ascetic who spent years in a merchant's house and returns to penance

note: The prologue's summary joins two acts in one line, that Civakan shot the boar and killed the enemy; 2204 performs the first.
teaches: The prologue binds the contest shot to the killing of the usurper, so the reader knows the winning arrow here is the opening blow of the war, not a feat for a bride alone.

note: The couplet calls children a man's wealth; the riddle says children of the body are others' and only merit is one's own son.
teaches: On the reading that line 4 denies ordinary children are one's own, the Jain riddle answers the Kural's householder by taking the very word மக்கள் and giving it to merit.

gains.a: the riddle gains the Kural's claim as the view it overturns, so its paradox reads as a reply
gains.b: the couplet's crux over whose deeds and whose wealth is sharpened by a text that assigns the only lasting gain to one's own deeds

note: Purananuru 182 says the world stands because there are those who strive not for themselves but for others (தமக்கென முயலா ... பிறர்க்கென முயலுநர்); Akananuru 54 calls Pannan தனக்கென வாழாப் பிறர்க்கு உரியாளன்.
teaches: The kaanchi poem's general ideal and the akam poem's praise of one patron use the same contrast of self and others, so the maxim was already a phrase of praise for real patrons.

note: Naladiyar 3 says that kings who rode under the royal umbrella fall when their deeds turn against them; 69 shows a king at the height of his umbrella-wealth, with no word of what deeds will bring.
teaches: The quatrain says the umbrella's glory lasts only while deeds hold it up, and the verse stops at the glory without the fall, so the reader supplies the warning from the quatrain.

gains.a: The verse gains a condition on its calm, that the king's wealth lasts only while his deeds do.
gains.b: The quatrain gains a king in full peace, whose praise stops where its warning would begin.

note: The couplet says a life lives on not eating flesh and keeps hell closed; the verse adds worldly beauty, victory and birth.
teaches: The couplet gives the reason for not eating flesh as fear of hell, and the verse gives a gain in this life, so the reader sees two arguments for one abstention.

gains.a: A reason for the flesh ban drawn from the Kural's own side, the closing of hell, which the verse lacks as it offers only rewards.
gains.b: A reward in this life, of radiance, beauty and victory, which the couplet lacks as it argues from fear of hell.

note: 2101 shows the princes wailing as the crown falls from the lord; Kural 347 says griefs hold those who hold attachment.
teaches: The princes' grief shows the couplet's point from the other side: the renouncer is free while those who still cling to him suffer.

gains.a: The princes' sorrow is named as the cost of their own attachment, not only of his act.
gains.b: The couplet gains persons whose grief arises from clinging to another renouncer, not to things.

note: The Kural says the loser of a lovers' quarrel is the winner, as union shows; Civakan casts himself as the small one who erred, yields, and wins her.
teaches: The epic gives the couplet's paradox a plot: a woman who swore to see the man defeated gets his surrender, and his surrender is exactly what wins him her.

gains.a: the hero's bow at her feet reads as a known strategy of oodal rather than humiliation
gains.b: the couplet's abstract loser and winner become a named pair whose defeat had been sworn as a vow

note: At 465 the townspeople say the mother who bore Civakan must have done great penance; at 1912 the mother herself, now an ascetic, speaks of her penance as having seemed fruitless until this meeting.
teaches: The crowd's easy inference from a splendid son to a fortunate mother meets the real mother's view from inside the hermitage, where penance felt barren for years.

note: Kudapulaviyanar tells the Pandya that food makes the body (உண்டி முதற்றே உணவின் பிண்டம்), so those who bind water to land give body and life, and bids him build tanks; the goddess uses the same phrase, the body is a lump of food, to give Manimekalai a mantra that cuts off her own hunger.
teaches: The same maxim drives two answers to hunger: the Sangam poet makes it a king's duty to feed a people by irrigation, the epic turns it into an ascetic's private release from hunger, the first step before the bowl that will feed others.

note: Kural 681 names birth in an honourable family among the first qualities of an envoy; verse 564 comes after the two clan recitals and praises the envoy's knowledge of clans and customs.
teaches: Family is not a bare boast but a thing the host tests by having the envoy recite and understand it.

gains.a: The recital of clans gets a reason: the envoy's family is a qualification the host checks before the message.
gains.b: The couplet gets a scene where family is spoken aloud and judged against the host's own.

note: 1967 sends the false ascetic to an animal birth; Tirumanthiram 1659 sends those of false austerity to hell and says austerities hold only through true knowledge.
teaches: Jain and Saiva texts agree that false austerity is punished and differ on the place: a beast's birth in the one, hell in the other.

gains.a: The false ascetic's fate gains a rival account, hell for the Saiva text, that shows the animal birth is a Jain choice.
gains.b: The Tirumanthiram's hell gains a Jain counterpart in which the punishment is a rebirth that can still be left.

note: 1103 shows the bride's shyness at the hand-clasp; 1106 has her scorn herself as shameless when shown the star.
teaches: Her shyness grows from trembling in the body to a spoken reproach, so the poet follows one feeling across the rite.

note: 1471 shows wives falling and beating their faces at a husband's death; Naladiyar 25 shows kin wailing as a corpse is carried to the burning ground.
teaches: Both pass from mourners' grief to what it shows about life, but the epic keeps the grief in the scene and the quatrain turns it into a reason to give up household life.

gains.a: 1471 lacks the quatrain's turn from grief to a judgement that household joy is empty.
gains.b: The quatrain gives wailing in general and lacks the specific grief of a king's wives.

note: Both epics put a king with his beloved in a built pleasure-park of hills, falls, pools and deer.
teaches: The same crafted royal park is, in the Manimekalai, interrupted by news from the prison that turns the king to charity, and in the Cintamani the setting of a desire that costs the king his rule.

note: Verse 36 measures the city against the serpents' world below, and verse 50 against Indra's heaven above.
teaches: The poet bounds the city between the Naga world beneath and Indra's world above, so its praise is a scale with two ends, not one comparison repeated.

note: The god freed Civakan and taught him spells, asking to be remembered; Civakan now heals the snakebite by reciting a spell.
teaches: The spells given in return for the nectar Civakan once gave a dying dog become the means that win him a princess, so the chain of gratitude the patikam began pays out as a cure, here reached through the mantra and not through any call on the god himself.

note: In the first cattle raid Civakan swears that if he does not protect cows, renunciants, women, children and brahmins he may become like a shameless eunuch; here he swears by his fame to bring raiders to a foreign king.
teaches: Set beside the first raid's vow, which rests on the duty to protect the helpless, the second vow rests on fame and loyalty to a host, and the friends' choice of a cattle raid to draw him out repeats the very scene that first made his name.

note: The Kural's man finds one pain inside the sulk, the worry that union may be delayed; Padumai says that if a husband leaves even in the sweet hour of the sulk, the wife's life leaves her.
teaches: The game of sulking assumes the lover stays to be won back; the epic names the case the couplet only worries about, where the partner leaves during the sulk and the delay becomes loss.

gains.a: the Kural's view of the sulk as a sweet risk, which explains why she names the sulk-time as the worst moment to be left
gains.b: the risk carried to its end from the woman's side, where the delay the man fears becomes desertion

note: Both praise the Jain god as light: the Soolamani's light of the world above after splitting the deeds, the Cintamani's holy form that blazes brighter than flame.
teaches: The Soolamani's light is the result of cutting the deeds, while the Cintamani's is a body brighter than flame and marked with signs, so the same image names an act in one and a form in the other.

note: The mother left the newborn to aram in the forest; the grown son now says penance was his mother and the teacher his father.
teaches: The child commended to dharma by a departing mother is answered, in the son's own words, by a parentage of penance and teaching, as if aram had taken him up through the ascetic.

note: 256 parodies 'all is suffering' as a greedy monk's complaints; the Manimekalai teacher gives suffering as the first truth and clinging as its cause.
teaches: The parody works by dropping the cause: the Buddhist epic ties suffering to clinging and its end to non-clinging, which the Jain song omits so the doctrine sounds like grumbling.

note: The fire in the town carries out the trick Yugi sets in verse 109.
teaches: Yugi's disguised talk of bathing is only a lure; the fire that follows shows what the lure was for.

note: 1616 has the king end the quarrel by embrace and plea; Kural 1304 says that not reconciling those who sulk is like cutting a withered creeper at its root.
teaches: The king's embrace shows what the couplet's warning needs: the sulk is healed by the one who gave cause, and the quarrel comes to an end in a wedding scene.

gains.a: The scene gains a rule behind the king's acts: the Kural says a sulk left unreconciled kills love, so his bow and embrace are what love needs.
gains.b: The couplet gains a king with a crown at his wife's feet, a case where reconciling costs a ruler his dignity.

note: Kural 463 says the wise do not undertake a deed that loses capital for the sake of gain; the kings tell Civakan, as a merchant's son, that a true trader would save his capital and flee, leaving the girl.
teaches: The couplet's prudence is turned into a class insult, and the battle that follows shows that the rule cannot say what counts as capital: for the kings it is life and goods, for Civakan it is his name and the bride.

gains.a: the general maxim of not risking the principal, which the kings bend into an argument for cowardice
gains.b: a case where the maxim is quoted by the side that loses, showing that it holds only once one has judged what the capital is

note: 2902 has Nandan turn away from release to worship a brother's feet; Tirumanthiram 284 has devotees who bow in devotion given release in return.
teaches: One text makes devotion the door to release, the other makes devotion a choice that outweighs release.

gains.a: the verse's refusal of release reads as a break with the devotional bargain, which gives the refusal weight it lacks alone
gains.b: the Tirumanthiram claim that devotion earns release meets a devotee who does not ask for the reward

note: 1144 shows Arikethu holding back his own view and speaking courtesies at the angry king's feet; the couplet says to stay neither far from nor near a quarrelsome king, as with a fire.
teaches: A courtier's distance from an angry king can be a matter of what he withholds, not where he stands.

gains.a: the epic shows how a counsellor keeps from the fire by silence and flattery while holding his own admiration of the enemy
gains.b: the couplet's fire is made literal in a king whose eyes spit flame, and its measure of distance is shown to be one of speech

note: The proclamation that the man who shoots the boar shall marry the princess is fulfilled when Civakan brings down machine and boar together.
teaches: The impossible condition set in 2177, tested by a catalogue of failing kings, is what makes Civakan's single shot read as proof of a destined claim rather than mere skill.

note: The Naladiyar's best of men renounce house, youth, wealth and strength because they see these do not last; Civakan renounces in full possession of all of them.
teaches: The quatrain grounds renunciation in seeing that goods pass away, while the epic's king renounces while every good still stands and gives fear of kingship, roused by the dharma, as his motive, so impermanence is not the only road to leaving.

gains.a: Civakan's sudden turn is set against the standard ethics-book reason, showing that his motive is moral fear of rule rather than loss
gains.b: the quatrain's list of passing goods is tested on a case where none of them has yet failed

note: 1382 begins the speech that 1379 announces when Kanaka Chitran steps in and speaks.
teaches: The announcement of a speech in 1379 only becomes a taunt of fear and manhood in the verses after it.

note: 1935 carves and feeds back to meat-eaters their own limbs; Kural 255 ties eating flesh to hell.
teaches: The Kural's single claim about meat and hell becomes a punishment that mirrors the meal, limb for limb.

gains.a: The carved-and-fed vision gains a general rule that makes meat itself, not cruelty only, the ground of the penalty.
gains.b: The couplet gains a concrete form of the hell it names, in which the eater's own body becomes the dish.

note: Both set the regions of the Tamil land together in one country: the four regions mingled here, the tunes and creatures of each region exchanged there.
teaches: Both poems prove a country's wholeness by letting the four regions share each other's things, but the epic only lists them while the Pattupattu ties the mingling to the king's just rule.

gains.a: A political reason for the blend, the king's one umbrella, which the epic's list leaves unsaid.
gains.b: A plain statement that the regions simply lie together, without the court's praise.

note: 1601 has the king say they will sit and wait for the queen; 1602 has her enter the grove with her maidens.
teaches: The waiting on the stone is a brief pause that gives the jester's fright its place before the queen enters.

note: 1408 sows fame in a field ploughed with the plough; 1415 ploughs open the warriors' chests with the same plough.
teaches: The metaphor of a farmer's field opens as a boast and returns as the literal wound, showing the plough as both sign and tool of the hero's rule over the battle.

note: She holds back her life on the strength of the bee words, in which the mate stays on without grief when the other goes.
teaches: The pairing shows the covert message doing its work: the image of the mate who waits without grieving, left in place of a goodbye, becomes the rule by which she chooses to live.

note: The crowd grieves at the binding of Civakan in Rajamapuram and again at the king's threat of fetters here.
teaches: The poet replays Civakan's arrest as comedy: the crowd that once wept for real bonds now weeps for a fetter that proves to be a bride, so the second scene answers the first.

note: The Kural's man asks whether her look is Death, an eye or a doe and answers that it has all three; Civakan asks whether it is her bow, her eyes, her speech or her look and says he cannot tell.
teaches: Both men ask the same 'is it this or that' of a woman who wounds them, but the Kural settles the question in her look, while Civakan gives it up and lays the cause on his own desire, so the epic turns the couplet's question about her into an admission about himself.

gains.a: the convention of the bewildered list of alternatives, which shows the force of its refusal to answer
gains.b: an alternative ending to the convention, in which the cause moves from the woman's look to the man's longing

note: 1906 says no one but the Lord, who harms no life, can be counted as god; Tirumanthiram 1451 says there is one God in all ten directions and bids us take refuge in his feet to dry up the sea of deeds.
teaches: Both hold one God whose feet end the deeds, but they name different ones, and the pair turns on whether the one at whose feet deeds are shed is a Jina who gave up his own, or a God who gives grace.

gains.a: The hymn gains a rival that makes the same demand, to take refuge at one pair of feet, but on the strength of a different god.
gains.b: The verse gains a Jain claim that the Lord who deserves such refuge is the Jina, who has no part in creating or ruling.

note: The Kural promises the sky to those who have left doubt and become clear; the teacher describes two sound-looking proofs of opposite theses that together leave only doubt (சங்கயம்).
teaches: The epic shows a doubt that more argument cannot remove, since each side's reasoning holds, so the clarity the couplet praises cannot come from matching proofs alone.

note: Both verses have a dream read by the wise as a promise of union.
teaches: In each, the dream is read aloud by experts and then fulfilled, but here the reader names the lady's survival while verse 63 names a groom to come.

claims.gist: fame and giving do not guard a man from death
going with the learned's depth lets one reach the limit of the elders' conduct
a woman's adorned beauty can bewilder even those not given to bewilderment
worship belongs only to the one who has destroyed the eight karmas and gives bliss, not to gods who live in desire
those who killed and ate fish and flesh are made to swallow molten metal in hell
one who dies thinking on the mantra leaves a low body and gains a god's body
teachers who show the true path and teach the fivefold conduct to the fit remove sorrow
pleasure is to be enjoyed within the way set out by the text
the killing of living beings brings the killer into animal births with long pain
at the sight of the liberated one the two kinds of deed scatter
pleasures enjoyed now are the fruit of earlier austerity, and more must be sown for the future
a god's radiance fails as his heavenly life runs out
a king's life is the guarding of his people, and the duty costs him his sleep
a king's wealth is safe from kings and thieves but not from Death
a humble word that carries pure meaning is to be valued as an ornament
hell life spans rise by fixed sea-measures down the seven layers
the one who has conquered is not moved by praise
a foe must not be scorned as small but must be known by going to see
the Jina's feet shelter all who come to them, beyond what any pleasure of the senses gives
killing a kid before Chandikai wards off the dream's evil
those who worship the lord of the vow of not killing cut off an evil birth and reach release easily
the sage's discipline holds back all deeds
a king must check what one spy reports through another
a king should take learned men as his eyes and widen his kin
old deeds drive the soul to wander through animal births where it is hurt and killed
no one is agreeable to everyone: what delights one flower closes another
a person is dying from birth, so fear at the end shows knowledge has not been used
living on hanging fruit removes evil deeds, as the Lord taught
a diet of fruit does not destroy old deeds, or the bat would be freed

note: The white hair seen in the mirror is the cause of the king's crowning of his son and departure.
teaches: The poem lets one sign of age carry a whole renunciation, so the choice to leave is the king's own and no teacher's.

note: Kural 1051 says that if the worthy giver withholds, the blame is his and not the asker's; Pazhamozhi 384 shows a never-refusing giver hiding what he has because many ask one thing, and puts the fault on the crowd of askers.
teaches: The Kural places the blame for withholding on the giver; Pazhamozhi names a case where withholding comes from pity for those who would be turned away, so the blame moves to the number of askers.

note: 1435 tells the listener not to gaze on pleasure like a sick old monkey; here a lusting monkey stands in an actual grove.
teaches: The sermon's monkey of appetite becomes a scene a king may watch, so the lesson reaches him as sight, not speech.

note: 1224 shows enemy kings holding to pride though they know it brings ruin; Kural 969 praises those who give up life when honour is at stake.
teaches: The couplet's honour is tested on the wrong side of a war the poem says is already decided, so pride that kills is shown as heroic and also as futile.

gains.a: The epic verse gains a named value, honour as a reason to die, for conduct it only calls rage.
gains.b: The couplet gains a case where those who would die for honour serve an unjust demand, which the couplet's praise does not distinguish.

note: Kattiyangaran took the land by a gift of law that was no true gift (வஞ்சம்) and gathered its wealth; Civakan now picks out all that belonged to him and gives it to Govindan, the uncle who stood with him.
teaches: The usurper's hoard is not destroyed but passes to the kin he had wronged, so the plot closes the fraud of 240 by moving the goods, not by punishing anything beyond the man.

note: In both a sage's saying about who will rule or serve is fixed as a prophecy: here the sons will serve the conqueror, there the hearers affirm the prophecy that one will protect the world under one umbrella.
teaches: Jain epics let a sage's sight settle a future rule and the later scene confirm it, so succession is told as fate foreseen, not as a contest.

note: Kural 10 says those who do not reach the Lord's feet cannot cross the sea of births; 1467 says those who do not praise the Jina with flowers and tongue do not reach the world of release.
teaches: The Kural leaves the Lord unnamed and the means as reaching his feet; the Jain hymn names him by the pindi tree and the triple umbrella and makes the condition a concrete act of worship, so the same exclusion becomes sectarian and ritual.

gains.a: the general frame of the couplet, which shows that the hymn's threat belongs to a shared Tamil form of praise
gains.b: an instance of how a Jain reader could fill the Kural's unnamed Lord with the Jina and its reaching with flowers and song

note: 2057 says right vision is easy for the great and rare for others; 2067 says that standing in right vision with austerity keeps one from hell and animal births.
teaches: 2067 turns the rarity of right vision into a promise: who holds it with austerity escapes the lower births and keeps unfailing wealth.

note: In 260 the councillor says the king will be killed by Death, by the woman and by his own fault; here the queen says he died through the love he fixed on her.
teaches: The cause the councillor named in passing, the woman, is accepted by the woman herself, so the epic's verdict on the king's fall is confirmed by the one it blamed rather than by the narrator.

note: In 281 the discus cuts the king's shield as the snake joins the sun's disc; in 290 the minister is the great snake that swallows the king, sun of the Kuru line.
teaches: The eclipse simile moves from the shield to the man, so a battle image becomes the narrator's verdict that the usurpation is a swallowing of the sun.

note: The portrait the old woman carries in verse 131 is the one she shows the king in verse 133.
teaches: What the portrait is for is clear only when the king sees it and breaks into grief, so the picture works as a message that needs no word.

note: The envoys give an ultimatum with no softening; the couplet says an envoy speaks briefly, removes offence and gets the good done.
teaches: The envoys act as the opposite of the couplet's envoy, brief but offering only two harsh options, and it shows the rule's cost.

gains.a: The verse gains a measure by which the envoys' manner reads as a failure of diplomacy, not strength.
gains.b: The couplet gains an example where the envoy's brevity serves the sender's pride and brings about war instead of a good result.

note: Kural 382 names fearlessness, giving, understanding and drive as a king's nature; in 719 the prince taunts a lion in its own cave.
teaches: The couplet's first quality is shown here as a deed done before a foe with no help, so fearlessness is seen at its cost.

gains.a: The verse lacks a general name for what the prince is doing, which the couplet gives.
gains.b: The couplet lacks a test of fearlessness against a danger, which the verse supplies.

note: Both describe the lute part by part with the same names, the bowl (பத்தர், பத்தல்), the pegs (ஆணி), the stem (மருப்பு) and the strings (நரம்பு), and both credit its music with power over the hostile and the wild.
teaches: The Cintamani takes over the Sangam bard's catalogue of the lute but makes it gold, coral and diamond, and makes knowing the instrument's parts and faults the contest itself, so the bard's working tool becomes the test of a prince.

gains.a: the epic's list of parts is shown to be an inherited form of praise, which explains why the lute is described before it is played
gains.b: the bard's poor lute, praised to win a patron's gift, gains a later setting where judging its wood and strings decides a royal marriage

note: The companions bowed at the feet of Vijayai in her penance grove before setting out; now they tell Civakan whom they met.
teaches: The pair shows the companions' news running in the order the story requires: the mother's ascetic state, seen first by others, reaches her son only as their report, and he must ask to hear it twice.

note: Tirumanthiram 533 says those who grieve the ascetics who teach the mantra are born as dogs; in 945 a dog dying with no merit hears a mantra and is born a god.
teaches: Both texts tie the mantra to rebirth as a dog, but run the scale in opposite directions: Tirumular uses the dog's birth as the punishment for wronging the mantra's teachers, the Jain epic uses the mantra to lift a dog out of that birth even without merit.

gains.a: the sharpness of its choice of a dog, which in the Saiva text is the very emblem of a fallen birth
gains.b: a view in which the mantra's power reaches the lowest birth directly, not only as a sanction protecting its teachers

note: The mate who saw the pair in 2721 now speaks, rebuking the male and refusing his chest.
teaches: The tryst of 2721 is answered here, so the wrong and its rebuke are told in two steps, and the injured mate's voice is heard.

note: Naladiyar 274 uses a daughter of the house, enjoyed by a stranger, as a figure for wealth that others will use; verse 228 calls a girl the jewel beyond all earthly and heavenly jewels.
teaches: The Naladiyar's picture treats a daughter's going to another house as a thing to be expected, while the epic makes her the treasure whose giving is a king's weightiest care.

gains.a: A plain statement that a daughter's passage to a stranger is as sure as hoarded wealth falling to another.
gains.b: A measure of how much the girl was worth to the one who gives her, which the simile treats as a mere example.

note: 290 asks the king to give this warrior toddy before he drinks himself; 298's warrior complains the king gave his men the dregs and drank the clear, and now does not send him first.
teaches: Together they show the order of drinking as the measure of the order of dying: 290 asks for the first cup on the strength of the family's dead, 298 reads a poor cup as the loss of the vanguard.

note: The wedding verses lay out darbha, sticks and ghee for the fire with care; siddhar 372 lists observances, vows, the Vedas, fire rites and water offerings as among the outward forms the Siddhar puts aside.
teaches: A Jain poem makes the fire rite the centre of a happy wedding while the Siddhar counts the same fire rite among forms to be left behind, so what counts as a sacred act depends on whether the aim is a household or release.

gains.a: The rite's careful detail gains a sceptic who judges all such rites as outward.
gains.b: The Siddhar's list gains a case of the rite performed for a wedding, a purpose the Siddhar does not address.

note: Verse 123 calls the lady's breast a raft in the sea of desire; Naladiyar 17 warns that the same woman will one day walk bent on a staff.
teaches: The epic's rapture and the quatrain's warning use the same woman and cannot both be the last word on her.

gains.a: The epic's image of desire as a sea gains a bounded end in the quatrain's picture of age.
gains.b: The quatrain's warning gains a living king who does not heed it and pays with his land.

note: The patikam promises that Civakan wins the maternal uncle's red-eyed daughter; here he sits beside the spear-eyed bride on the wedding couch.
teaches: The patikam's one-line promise is cashed here as a full wedding in which the groom is shaved, bathed and seated, so the reader sees what 'winning her' came to in rite.

note: Both rank learning above birth: in 183 a man of the highest order defers to a learned man of the lowest, and Kural 409 says the unlearned high-born lack the worth of the learned low-born.
teaches: The Kural's maxim was already a king's teaching in the Purananuru, where Nedunchezhiyan keeps the four orders by name and lets learning reverse them, so neither text abolishes birth rank: both use it as the measure that learning overturns.

note: The mate asks who would take bitter neem after mountain honey; Tirumanthiram 207 says the sweet of young women turns to neem within the body.
teaches: The same pair of sweet and bitter serves a wife's refusal and a sage's warning, showing the image works both for pride and for renunciation.

gains.a: The honey-and-neem pair gains a second use, as the ascetic's verdict on pleasure, behind the wife's refusal.
gains.b: A lived case of the image, in a quarrel where bitterness is what the mate will not accept, not the end of pleasure.

note: Just after the hero takes his pleasure with Ilakkanai, sages arrive and he asks them about it.
teaches: The sage's coming in the same breath as the marriage shows the poem placing the hero's pleasures under the teaching that follows them.

note: Verse 251 compares a king in love's grip without learned men to a rutting elephant ridden by a fool; Cintamani 9 tells of a king whose dense desire made him refuse counsel and lose to a plot.
teaches: The Cintamani's story gives the cost that the Soolamani's maxim only warns of, a king who would not hear and lost the throne.

note: Kural 54 says nothing is greater than a woman who has the firmness called karpu; Gunamalai shows such firmness before marriage, against her own parents, for a man she has only chosen.
