teaches: Read together, the couplet's firmness moves from a wife's fidelity back to a maiden's choice, where it shows itself as resisting her parents with death or renunciation rather than as serving a husband.

gains.a: the Kural's naming of karpu as திண்மை, a strength, which lets her threat read as firmness of virtue rather than wilfulness
gains.b: a case of that firmness exercised before any marriage and directed against the girl's own parents, which a couplet about a wife does not foresee

note: Verse 409 says the sign about the garlanded one means that within a month Tivittan will split a lion's mouth; verse 639 has the king ask whether the book of omens may be a deceit.
teaches: The king treats as doubtful the omen-book that the other court has already taken as certain, which is the difference between the two courts' fates.

note: 3101 has worship of the feet cut karma like a weapon; Tirumanthiram 219 says the fire worshipped and risen burns the deeds of ages.
teaches: Both promise that worship removes karma, but one gives the cutting to an enlightened teacher's feet and the other to a worshipped fire.

gains.a: the Jain feet-as-spear gets a rival agent of the same removal, a burning fire that the Jain verse does not use
gains.b: the Tirumanthiram's burning fire gets a rival that cuts by the feet of a liberated one who does not answer prayer

note: At the height of empire and eight thousand queens, the Naladiyar says kings on elephants under umbrellas are carried off like all others; the next kandam is a renunciation.
teaches: The peak of enjoyment is set right before the work's renunciation kandam, so the Naladiyar's warning is the story's own turning point.

gains.a: the list of queens gets the Naladiyar's warning of what such splendour is worth, which the verse never voices
gains.b: the quatrain gets a case of a king's splendour at its height, which gives its warning a particular king to fall on

note: 2938 strips the body of its sandal and flower to fat, blood, pus and soiled skin; Naladiyar 46 lists entrails, fat, blood, bone, sinew and skin and asks which part is the woman.
teaches: Both teach desire away by breaking the body into its parts, and the epic does it to the very women who are the audience.

gains.a: the verse's list of fluids gains the quatrain's question of where the woman is to be found among the parts
gains.b: the quatrain's analysis is placed in a scene where the one who is analysed is listening

note: The city's wealth is compared to a grove of wish-granting trees with honey-dripping garlands and ambrosia in the first ilampakam; here the festival goods held up in incense smoke make the city look as if the golden wish-trees and the wish-creeper had taken it.
teaches: The same wishing-tree figure that praised a city's standing wealth is now used for the wealth brought out for a wedding, so the epic's image of plenty follows the occasion.

note: Purananuru 92 is Avvai's song to Anji calling her words a child's babble he graciously hears; 352 measures the friend's sweetness against a famous bard's new tune for Anji's praise.
teaches: The praise songs for Anji, which Avvai offers modestly as babble, had become in akam a byword for sweetness, showing that puram performances were known to the love poets' audience as celebrated pieces of music.

note: 1720 has brahmins, kings and elders praise those who bore the child, and Kural 70 says a son's worth lies in making others ask what penance his father did.
teaches: The epic voices the praise at the newborn stage, before any deed, while the couplet says the praise belongs to the father only after the son has proved himself.

gains.a: The praise of the parents gains the couplet's reason: it is the son's worth that earns the parents' credit, here advanced to birth.
gains.b: The couplet gains a scene where the praise is spoken aloud in an assembly of every order, and for a child whose worth is only promised.

note: Tirumanthiram 2133 has the subtle body, its old deeds following, take up a new body; 799's arrows warn the slain against evil in the body they will take next.
teaches: Held together, the epic's warning to the dying presupposes the passage Tirumular describes, and Tirumular's mechanism is given a moral use: deeds follow, so the dead are urged to change their conduct across the change of body.

gains.a: the mechanism, deeds carried by the subtle body into a new birth, that makes 'the body you will take' literal
gains.b: an ethical address to the dying that the doctrinal account of transmigration leaves out

note: The king had ordered the prince's goods taken; in 72 the prince, enriched by dice, gives away all that he wins to the kings and his mother.
teaches: The order to strip the prince is answered not by revenge but by the prince's giving, so the seizure leaves him richer in standing than the king who ordered it.

note: Vijayai urged her son to give and said people never give a handful to the poor; the teacher now gives the reason, that a gift in good soil grows like seed and one in barren soil withers.
teaches: The mother's plain call to give is answered by an account of why it matters who receives, so giving is a sowing whose crop depends on the field.

note: 1666 ends by saying the king did a great penance that gives him whatever he wishes; Kural 265 gives wish-fulfilment as the reason penance is practised.
teaches: The wish that penance buys here is a prank to win an embrace, which tests whether the Kural's reason for tapas needs any worthy wish.

gains.a: 1666 gets a stated rule behind its claim, that penance pays in whatever is wanted, so the king's power reads as a fruit of tapas.
gains.b: Kural 265 gets a case where the wish bought is a trivial love-ruse, so its 'whatever is wished' is shown to cover small and worldly wishes.

note: 2791 shows the body as a skin of filth swarming with worms; Siddhar 41 calls it a worm-nest from which excrement and urine flow.
teaches: Both teach disgust at the body, one to warn of birth, the other to leave the body for the feet of Siva.

gains.a: the verse gains a goal beyond disgust, which the Siddhar names as the feet
gains.b: the Siddhar song gains the womb and birth as the origin of the body's filth

note: Kaman's shaft of 1019 has landed by 1021, where the youth himself lets desire swell slowly.
teaches: Love enters by a god's act but is then fed by the lover himself, so the verses show both cause and indulgence in one fall.

note: The pavilion where the king dwells with desire burning in him is what a minister later names as the liquor of desire in which the king drowned and left the path of justice.
teaches: The lavish pavilion that reads as ornament is the poet's first, unjudged sign of the vice the minister will later blame for the king's ruin.

note: The couplet tells courtiers to keep near a king like men warming at a fire; the epic gives the same fire conduct to pupils with their teacher.
teaches: The epic moves the rule from court to schoolroom, and since the teacher is a hidden king, the princes unknowingly keep the courtier's rule toward a real king.

gains.a: the epic verse gains the couplet's reason for the distance: the one served can burn as well as warm
gains.b: the couplet gains an application beyond kingship, to any one whose favour is sought, here a master of an art

note: The patikam says Suramanjari, beaten, resolved to look on no male form and withdrew into the guarded mansion; here she states the vow's condition, his coming defeated to her feet.
teaches: The patikam's 'no male form' is in the verse itself a vow with one exception named in advance, the man who shamed her, so the summary hides that her withdrawal is aimed at Civakan.

claims.gist: A life of lust and drink leads to rebirth as an animal
a cruel king throws aram into confusion and the whole world into suffering
those who gave rightly are reborn as twins in the land of enjoyment
weapons win the same kind of fame that learning wins
the feet of the Tirthankara remove all sins one has done
those who live on a greater man's favour forget how deeds work
a true teacher's words remove the sins they speak of and bring right seeing
the heroic way is not to strike with scorn at one who flinches and not to shame one who has fled
no emperor, however great, has outlasted death
her loss is the fruit of the sin she herself has done
the many ways of effort fall into four: conduct, giving, austerity and worship
the great pleasure of heaven is won by austerity and has an end
a state higher than heaven exists
beauty is paint on a skin bag, and poets elaborate the flesh in order to kindle desire
a match that destiny has brought, shown by likeness of looks and form, should be fulfilled
knowledge gained by hearing the texts dispels delusion and shows the truth
a king's rule that ends killing and miserliness makes his land a golden age like Uttarakuru
the passions, in their several kinds, are destroyed one by one in the field of the mind
a goddess who is angered sends disease and takes lives
the span of life is unknown and passes unrecoverably; hope to live on blinds one to this
the Lord's feet free one from the sea of deeds and the darkness of karma
making foes of the harmless and friends of the ill-minded both bring later pain
a youth who has not learned to tell good from ill can be undone by a trick
offering even the likeness of a living creature to a deity brings its fruit upon the offerer
the term of hell is measured in oceans of years

note: Naladiyar 371 says the friendship of harlots ends when the hand is empty, as the lamp's light ends when the oil runs out; in 2588 Anangamalai, a woman of the stage, is jailed and released and keeps worshipping a painted image of Civakan with no payment.
teaches: The quatrain's rule is a claim about women of her station, and her story tests it, which shows the epic treating constancy as the person's, not the profession's.

gains.a: a hostile frame that makes her constancy a deliberate answer to a standing charge against dancers
gains.b: a counter-case in which a woman of the stage keeps love without income, which shows the rule as a generalisation about types, not a law

note: The friend answers desire by loathing the body's foulness, as the quatrain does with every body.
teaches: The remedy of disgust works in the quatrain as meditation and fails in the story, where one repellent body cannot cool a mind already taken.

gains.a: her appeal to the keeper's sores and deformity is shown as a kind of the meditation, but aimed at one man, so it lacks the quatrain's reach
gains.b: the quatrain's instruction to see the body as a bag turned inside out is tried on a real person and is found weaker than the desire it was meant to quiet

note: In 759 Civakan tells the princess the kings are already food (இரை) for his arrows; in 798 he greets the kings as guests and feeds (ஊட்டினான்) each of them one or two arrows.
teaches: The consolation's figure of kings as food is carried out as a mock feast in which he is host and the arrows are the meal, so his reassurance to her is kept literally.

note: Tirumanthiram 200 counts killing as a mountain-sized sin that is put away by reaching Siva's feet; verse 321 says the killing's result cannot be undone by anything given, and only the dharma's austerity loosens it.
teaches: The Saiva text frees one from the sin by reaching the Lord, while the Jain verse leaves the deed to be worn away by conduct alone.

gains.a: the verse lacks any Lord whose feet remove the sin
gains.b: the quatrain lacks an account of how long one killing travels through births

note: In 683 the dancer wrote a letter in figure, calling her streaked eyes the letter and her smile the friend who carried it; in 2586 she hands over a letter in the proper manner and he reads it.
teaches: The earlier letter of eyes only hinted; the written letter now makes the same appeal in words, which shows the epic turning a figure into a document, so her love must now be answered in the open.

note: Purananuru 236 is Kapilar's lament that Pari told him to stay behind and did not take him in death; Patitruppattu 61 has Kapilar, Pari gone to the land from which none returns (வாராச் சேண்புலம் படர்ந்தோன்), arrive at the Chera's camp drawn by a fame for giving without regret.
teaches: Together they show the bard's two answers to his patron's death, the vow to be with Pari in the next birth and the journey to a new patron whose giving is praised in Pari's terms, so the Chera's praise is partly an elegy carried over.

note: A calf finds its mother among many cows as an old deed finds its doer; here the mother, now a dog, finds the son in a bird's body and kills him.
teaches: The quatrain's mother-finding image is turned over: the deed that finds the doer wears the face of a mother meeting her child.

gains.a: the dog's attack is shown as the finding of a doer by an old deed, not a chance of the hunt
gains.b: the quatrain's calf-and-mother simile gains a case where the finder and the found are in fact mother and son

note: The verse says a vow, worship and gifts conquer the binding deed; the Tirumanthiram says the Lord made the bond that fastens the soul to what went before.
teaches: One text lets the soul loosen its own bond by vow and giving, while the other makes the bond the Lord's work, so the question of who can undo the bond divides them.

gains.a: the vow-and-gift path to conquering the bond is set against a view in which the bond is not the soul's own doing
gains.b: the Saiva verse's bond meets a rival claim that effort alone can undo it

note: 2774 gives hell's tortures by molten copper and the oil-press without a cause; Tirumanthiram 198 binds those who urged 'kill, stab' and sets them in fire-mouthed hell.
teaches: Together they show hell as the fruit of a named sin and as a daily mechanical punishment, which neither shows alone.

gains.a: the verse names no crime for its tortures, and gains the sin of urging killing
gains.b: 198 gives only a fiery pit, and gains the machines and repeated daily torment

note: 2113 has the lord ride the elephant of knowledge with a diamond goad that is awareness; Kural 24 guards the five with the goad of firmness.
teaches: The same goad turns from a means of guarding the senses to a means of driving the army that kills the karmic enemy.

gains.a: The goad is no longer a guard against the senses but a driver of an assault, which the couplet leaves out.
gains.b: The couplet's goad gains the elephant it only implies, and gains a battle for the elephant to carry the rider into.

note: 2918 orders the women brought without saying why; 2923 shows them fading once they read the king's intent.
teaches: The summons hides its purpose, and the women's withering shows that his intent is a farewell.

note: Kural 774 has the warrior laugh as he pulls a spear from his body; in 726 the victor of a harder fight shows neither joy nor wonder.
teaches: The Kural's soldier takes pleasure in the fight and the epic's prince does not, so the same bravery is shown with two moods.

gains.a: The verse lacks the picture of a fighter who delights in the wound, which the couplet gives.
gains.b: The couplet lacks a hero who is plain after victory and calls it the removal of a harm.

note: The Naladiyar sets the fool who sighs and breaks when deeds ripen against the wise who say 'it is old desert' and go free; Vijayai says exactly that her deeds are to blame, yet sobs (விம்மா) as she says it.
teaches: The quatrain makes knowing one's karma the cure for grief, but the queen shows that naming one's own deeds as the cause can be itself a form of grieving.

gains.a: Vijayai's lament gains a measure: her self-blame is the doctrine the wise hold, held without the calm it is said to bring
gains.b: the quatrain's clean division between fool and wise gains a case that falls between them, a mother who knows the rule and still breaks

note: The Kural says one remembers for seven births the friendship of those who wiped away one's sorrow; the Vidyadhara king says his people and the merchant's have held friendship for seven generations, bound by fate.
teaches: Side by side, the seven-fold span of friendship rests on two different grounds: in the couplet on gratitude for a single act of rescue, in the epic on an inherited tie that fate fixes and no deed has to earn.

gains.a: the king's claim gains a measure of what such a bond is normally owed for, showing how much he gives in asking nothing of the merchant
gains.b: the couplet's seven births gain a case where the span runs through generations of a family rather than one person's rebirths

note: Kural 895 says those who draw a mighty king's anger will survive nowhere; Kantukkatan reasons that to contend with the king is the work of the doomed (விளிகுற்றார்) and sends his son bound.
teaches: The merchant applies the couplet's prudence to a king who is a usurper and his son's true father's killer, showing that the rule of not provoking the strong counsels submission even to injustice, a cost the couplet does not weigh.

gains.a: Kantukkatan's choice gains the weight of received wisdom, so it reads as prudence rather than cowardice
gains.b: the couplet gains a case in which obeying it means yielding to an unjust king, which tests its scope

note: 1850 has crows and kites guarded off with a hand stick; Naladiyar 41 has the stick that drives the crows from the torn body.
teaches: The same stick appears for two different speakers, a king guarding himself and a poet mocking the lover, which shows how fixed the picture was.

gains.a: The verse gains a second use of the stick and the crow, as a rebuke of those who call the body lovely.
gains.b: The quatrain gains a king speaking of his own body in the same terms.

note: In 270 the fruit follows honour or scorn though the ascetics hold neither favour nor anger; in Tirumanthiram 36 grace comes in the measure of the praise.
teaches: One text lets the result come from the one who honours without any granting, the other makes the Lord answer; the two differ over whether anyone grants the fruit.

gains.a: The epic verse lacks any figure who gives the fruit, and the Saiva verse shows what the ascetic's indifference excludes: a giver.
gains.b: The Tirumanthiram verse lacks the Jain case in which a reverence has result with no one pleased by it.

note: In 359 Vijayai, failing in spirit, watches the road for news of her son; here her watching ends when Padumukan announces him.
teaches: The long wait set up at the hermitage is closed by omens and then a messenger, so the mother's watch that began at his birth is fulfilled by the son's own coming rather than news of him.

note: Kovalan's yazh song praises the Kaveri for not sulking when the Chola unites with the Ganga and calls that a noble woman's karpu; Gandharvadattai's yazh songs show the cuckoo's mate estranged and won back only when the male coaxes her and bows at her feet.
teaches: Two yazh songs on lovers' estrangement take opposite sides: the Silappathikaram's makes the woman's not sulking her virtue, while the Cintamani's makes the man's humbling the end of a just sulk, which fits a heroine who yields only to the man who outdoes her.

note: In Akananuru 117 the foster mother says the girl did not think of the nochchi or her playmates when she left; in Natrinai 184 the mother cannot bear to see the nochchi and the terrace where the girl played.
teaches: The pair shows the same household shrub on both sides of the elopement: forgotten by the daughter who has gone, and unbearable to the mother who stays, so the left-behind play things measure how unequal the parting is.

note: The hunters who gather at dawn in verse 117 have fired the wood by verse 119.
teaches: The ambush that begins with a surround is not ended by Udayanan's arrows alone; it ends when the hunters fail and Vayantakan comes.

note: The Kural says all pains rest on those who caused pain (நோயெல்லாம் நோய்செய்தார் மேலவாம்); Neelakesi applies the rule to the Buddha's pain-bearing gifts and says he must himself suffer what they caused.
teaches: Applied without limit, the rule that pain returns to its causer condemns even the giver who bears pain for others, and only a theory of what makes a deed evil can stop that.

note: Kural 380 says nothing is stronger than oozh, which arrives before any device; Kannaki blames the strong deed that pressed on her but also names herself the woman of cruel deeds.
teaches: Kannaki grants karma the force the couplet gives oozh yet keeps the burning of Madurai as her own act, so the epic holds fate and the agent's deed together where the couplet speaks only of fate's priority.

note: Verse 1037 shows lotuses opening in the glow of the feet and worshippers blooming at the Jina's feet; Kural 3 promises long life to those who reach the feet of the one on the flower.
teaches: Both join feet and flowers, but the epic gives the bloom as the worshipper's own joy while the couplet gives a lasting earthly life.

gains.a: The verse lacks a stated reward for reaching the feet, which the couplet names as long life.
gains.b: The couplet lacks the verse's picture of the flower opening in the feet's light, which the worshipper's joy is likened to.

note: Kural 1320 has the sulking woman accuse a man who only sits gazing at her of thinking of someone else; here Civakan's unblinking gaze and watering eyes make Ilakkanai say he weeps thinking of others.
teaches: The epic shows that the suspicion in the couplet can grow from the very rapture of the gaze, so the quarrel is a love's misreading and not a sign of a wandering heart.

gains.a: the sulk is placed in the Kural's recognised pattern of a wife who suspects her husband for what he does with his eyes
gains.b: a story in which the suspicion is false and ends in laughter, which the couplet does not tell

note: Kural 775 counts it flight for the fierce to blink when a spear is thrown; Kattiyangaran says that if he blinks when a spear comes, Civakan may laugh.
teaches: The king splits outcome from courage: he grants victory to fate yet stakes his honour on the couplet's unblinking eye, so the pair shows the unblinking gaze as the one part of valour fate cannot take.

gains.a: the boast is read against a fixed measure of valour, which answers Civakan's taunt of fear
gains.b: the couplet's standard is shown held by a man who believes the battle's result is not his to decide

note: 3134 has the penance end in birth as gods; Kural 346 says one who cuts off the pride of I and mine goes to a world above the gods.
teaches: The epic's ascetics end among the gods, but the couplet puts above the gods a world reached only by cutting off the self, so heaven is not the last goal.

gains.a: the rebirth among gods is shown as not the top of the scale, which the verse itself does not say
gains.b: the couplet's world above the gods is given a case of ascetics who stop at heaven short of it

note: Vijayai says no one knows how many days are given and that the dead cannot be recalled; the Kural says good must be done before the hiccup rises and stops the tongue.
teaches: The Kural's urgency is made a mother's plea to a king at the height of pleasure, showing the rule's cost: it must be heard just when it is least welcome.

gains.a: the verse's general lament about the span of life gets a concrete deadline of the final hiccup
gains.b: the Kural's call to hurry is placed in a scene where the one urged is a king surrounded by wives and enjoyment

note: Kural 471 says weigh the work, one's own strength, the foe's and the allies' before acting; in 708 and 709 the prince sends away his elephants, chariots and men and goes with no allies.
teaches: The prince's vow sets aside the allies' strength that the couplet counts, leaving the outcome to his own strength.

gains.a: The verse lacks a standard that names the dismissal of the host as the risk it is.
gains.b: The couplet lacks a hero who deliberately gives up the allies' strength to keep his word.

note: Purananuru 369 sings the battlefield as a harvest where the ghoul-woman holds the corpses and jackals thresh, and the bard asks the king for a gift; in 804 ghouls already fed sing over what was given them.
teaches: The epic hands the bard's role to the ghouls: in the Puram poem the singer asks for a share of the field, while here the scavengers have had their share and their song is thanks, so the field is a patron's gift completed.

gains.a: the kalavazhi frame that explains why ghouls 'sing what was given', as bards sing a patron's bounty
gains.b: the reversal that shows how close the Puram bard stands to the scavengers who share the same harvest of corpses

note: The couplet likens death to sleep and birth to waking; here the death by fast is followed at once by waking as a god.
teaches: The couplet's sleep-and-waking comparison is made literal, and the waking place depends on how the sleeper died.

gains.a: the death in meditation is read as a sleep that ends in a chosen waking
gains.b: the couplet's comparison is shown with a destination fixed by the way of dying

note: Vikraman gives up his kingdom and goes to the forest, as the quatrain's best of men renounce home and wealth on seeing they do not last.
teaches: The epic shows a king doing what the quatrain says, with the order of arranging his heir first and then leaving, which the quatrain does not mention.

gains.a: The epic's king gets the reason for his act, the failing of home and wealth, which the verse does not say.
gains.b: The quatrain's renouncer gets a concrete case, a king who provides for his kingdom before he goes.

note: Kural 355 says knowledge is seeing the real in whatever thing; Soolamani 201 sets discerning true things as the first of three, followed by knowledge and conduct kept to the text.
teaches: The epic makes the couplet's seeing the start of a sequence that does not end until conduct is kept, not the whole of release.

gains.a: the discerning of true things is placed first and so not enough alone, it must be followed by conduct
gains.b: the couplet's seeing is given a place in a larger course ending in disciplined conduct

note: Vijayai urges penance and giving before black hair turns white; the Naladiyar says the wise renounced in childhood, knowing grey hair would come, and the youth-lovers later lean on a staff.
teaches: The pairing shows that the call to act before age is made both to a king in his prime by his mother and as a general rule, so the epic's mother is speaking the Naladiyar's counsel in her own household.

gains.a: the verse's address to the young gets the image of the staff in old age that makes the urgency felt
gains.b: the Naladiyar's general advice is given a speaker who has lost a husband and knows how fast it comes

note: The couplet makes austerity and giving depend on the sky's rain; here the ascetics themselves send the rain.
teaches: The dependence of austerity on rain in the couplet is reversed in the unit, where the austere supply the rain.

gains.a: the sages' power is placed within the dependence of giving on rain, so the rain relieves the very distress that would stop giving
gains.b: the couplet's one-way dependence on the sky meets a case where austerity feeds the sky

note: The couplet allows a falsehood that yields faultless good; the narrator excuses the hero's false name in similar terms.
teaches: The epic gives the couplet's exception a concrete case, a fugitive prince hiding his name from a usurper, and shows a narrator reaching for the exception to keep his hero truthful.

gains.a: the epic verse gains a recognised rule under which its awkward excuse of the hero's lie can be judged
gains.b: the couplet gains a test case where the 'good' is the liar's own safety, which leaves open whether its strict condition is met

note: Vijayai's dream in 223 showed the asoka tree falling and a crowned shoot rising from its foot; 313 shows her as an evening where the sun has set and a young moon has risen.
teaches: The fall Saccandan would not interpret in 225 is now fulfilled, and the poet restates the dream's double meaning, loss and rising heir, in a new figure of sun and crescent moon.

note: 1054 names the wedding day as the day to enjoy good deeds; 1057 uses the passing of good deeds and the coming of evil ones as a figure for night's darkness.
teaches: The same karmic words serve first for a bride's joy and then for the dread of night, so the story's fortune is read through deeds both times.

note: 2764 shows hell-beings rising and falling on blades; 2770 shows that the same beings are tormented daily by others who throw them in a boiling pit.
teaches: The sermon moves from the bare place of hell to those who work in it, so a reader sees that hell has both a ground that hurts and agents who add to the hurt.

note: A king of full worldly success leaves pleasure behind, which tests the couplet's question about going outside.
teaches: The couplet asks what is gained by leaving the household that keeps virtue, and the story answers with a king who leaves out of disgust at its pleasures, not out of failure.

gains.a: the king's turn gets a standard against which his leaving can be judged
gains.b: the couplet's question gets a case of a successful householder who leaves

note: In 899 Suramanjari vows to wait until the generous one comes defeated and worships her anklet feet; in 2012 Civakan arrives bent, panting and begging at her gate.
teaches: Her vow's terms are fulfilled to the letter in comic form, since the proud judge of the powder contest comes stooped and humbled, but in a guise he chose himself, so her victory and his stratagem are the same act.

note: The king gives up kingship at the height of his state and takes austerity, as the couplet urges renouncing while there is time.
teaches: The couplet urges haste in the abstract; the king's act shows what haste costs, a throne handed to a son, and what it is paid for.

gains.a: the king's going forth is shown as renouncing in time, not in old age
gains.b: the couplet gains a prince who leaves a throne, a cost it does not state

note: Kural 1251 has the axe of desire break the door of restraint bolted with shame; Soolamani 981 has restraint vanish because desire runs straight on, and puts it in the poet's voice about the girl.
teaches: The Kural gives restraint a lock that desire can break, while the Jain epic says the restraint was not broken but given to the one she loves.

gains.a: The verse lacks a picture of how restraint fails; the couplet gives the door, the bolt and the axe.
gains.b: The couplet lacks a case where the woman's restraint is not lost to chance but handed to a particular lover, and the poet argues it a worthy gift.

claims.gist: the Jina cast out the enemy deeds and taught the path of the scripture rightly
the four states of birth are to be feared and escaped by tapas
merit has seven doors: compassion, clarity, love of virtue, praise, austerity, knowledge and meditation
the feet of the Lord who stands beyond beginning are the one refuge that ends great suffering
being the father of fine sons is the fruit of penance
one who kills and eats living beings sinks into hell
a minister who kills his king sinks into leprosy and hell
betraying a friend, adultery and violating a maiden lead to hell
deeds already gathered can fall away in a moment
nothing helps the soul but virtue and nothing harms it but vice
fear of an evil rebirth should lead one to leave vice and live by virtue
right vision lit without vows still leads to heaven or to bliss without return
lust, drink and meat ripen into evil deeds and must be renounced
no one is kin across births, since all were strangers before and will be strangers again
renunciation leaves behind those who lived by one's body and ornament
a king who gives all his hours to pleasure no longer rules
crossing old deeds leads to bliss at the top of the world above
the world of the gods is reached through truth faithful to the mantra and great austerity, or through unslackening just rule
flesh of an animal killed today is good for the rite of the dead
the great bear without complaint the wrongs done by the small
fasting joined to meditation washes off evil deeds
the craving of the tongue is to be feared as poison
one who protects all lives as one's own is reborn in a higher state
love directed to the right end helps wear away the eight karmas, yet as attachment it cannot itself end them
givers and the virtuous reach lands of enjoyment through their giving
a man given in sacrifice to the goddess is a good deed for the king
a fault against an ascetic is wiped out by giving one's head at his feet

note: The lute the youth receives from the sage in verse 18 is the instrument that tames the elephant in 19.
teaches: The gift of grace in 18 is shown working at once, so the lute is the means by which Udayanan wins allies.

note: 908 left one exception in her refusal: union with Civakan's gold-bright chest; 2057 asks Kama for exactly that chest (சீவகன் அகலம் சேர்த்தின்).
teaches: The exception hidden inside her vow of self-containment becomes the whole content of her prayer once a disguised song has worked on her, so the refusal was a waiting all along.

note: Sight in 256 becomes union in 257.
teaches: The ball-play scene is not an end in itself: the sight of her carries at once into union, which makes her loss in 258 sharper.

note: Purananuru 56 equates the Pandya with four gods, one for each of his powers; 160 equates Saccandan with Dharma, Varuna, Death, Vaman and Kama.
teaches: The epic keeps the Sangam form of measuring a king god by god but shifts it from war powers to grace, giving and beauty, and puts the god of desire in the list, which the story makes the king's flaw.

gains.a: the epic's god-list is placed in an inherited praise form, so its departures (Dharma, Kama) stand out
gains.b: the Sangam form is shown surviving into Jain narrative with new gods and an ironic edge

note: Naladiyar 101 says an old deed finds its doer like a calf its mother; verse 604 says merit joined this pair.
teaches: The Naladiyar's law of the old deed is shown working for good here, where its examples elsewhere fall on the wicked.

gains.a: The verse lacks the idea that the old deed seeks out its own doer, which gives its merit a mechanism.
gains.b: The quatrain lacks a joyful instance, since its law is usually shown on sinners.

note: Kural 261 defines tapas as bearing the pain that comes and harming no life; Sirupanchamoolam 31 keeps both, adds three more, and says penance so made is sweet, not lowly.
teaches: The couplet defines penance by two ethical acts; the verse keeps them, turns bearing pain into forgetting it, and meets an objection the couplet does not raise, that penance degrades the one who does it.

note: 37 treats Death as the overpowering thing no plea escapes; 39 calls dying easy beside the hard work of character.
teaches: Within one chapter the work views death from two sides, as the terror that drives penance and as the easy thing beside lasting virtue, and the pair shows death's weight depends on what it is measured against.

note: Kural 685 asks the envoy to speak in brief, remove offence and gain the good; verse 566 has the king bid the envoy show faultless virtues in sifted words.
teaches: The host asks for the craft the couplet describes and does not simply receive it, so the envoy's skill is put on trial at the host's court.

gains.a: The king's bidding gets a named standard of speech: brief, free of offence and sifted.
gains.b: The couplet gets a scene where the host himself demands what it asks of the envoy.

note: 206 bars entrusting wealth to untested kin and eminent men; 208 bars handing it carelessly to worthless men; both turn on wealth put into another's hands.
teaches: Read together, the two verses show the danger of entrusting wealth from both sides: the keeper may be untested though respectable, or plainly base, and in each case the owner's own lapse is the fault.

note: Gandharvadattai held back her spells lest a wife's rescue shame him; Civakan says he himself preferred death to being saved by a woman.
teaches: Put together, the wife's restraint and the husband's choice turn out to be one scruple about his honour, held by each without the other's knowing, which is why the rescue had to come from the god and not from her.

note: In Neelakesi 370 the Buddhist Mokkalan likens those who give trees life to men in madness; the Cintamani calls those who deny it madmen or ghouls.
teaches: The same charge of madness is thrown from both sides of the dispute over plant life, so the insult marks a live sectarian quarrel and not a settled view.

note: Gandharvadattai sealed the letter with her earring and handed it to the companions; here it reaches Civakan and the seal is broken.
teaches: The pair closes the errand she began: the earring-seal that made the leaf hers is the thing Civakan must remove to read her, so the seal guards her words until they reach the one reader they were for.

note: 1592 shows the asoka cured of longing by women's feet; 1593 has the jester say the king too blooms when the queen's foot touches his head.
teaches: The grove lesson becomes a jibe at the king, who is made the asoka's counterpart in his need of a woman's foot.

note: In 297 the usurper has the drum beaten in his own name after burning his king and 'takes Fortune'; in 609 the city's drum blesses first the lord who embraces the earth as his bride.
teaches: The same drum that announced a murderer's seizure now opens a wedding proclamation by hailing him as the earth's rightful husband, so the formula of royal blessing shows how quickly usurpation becomes the ordinary order of the city.

note: Verse 36 grieves over the bodies taken in each birth; verse 63 gives the youth's cause for the suffering, harm done to living bodies.
teaches: The earlier verse only laments births; this one names harming living creatures as what the sufferings come from.

note: The ministers say the elephant cannot pass the king's vina; verse 97 shows it coming and bowing at his feet.
teaches: The poem lets the ministers' claim of music's power be tested by what the elephant does in front of the crowd.

note: The Kural says that if one eats flesh hell does not open its mouth; Civakan sets hell for the meat-eater against a god's birth for one who abstains and makes the hunter choose.
teaches: The epic turns the couplet's one-sided warning into a two-way choice with a reward on the other side and has the eater himself pronounce the verdict, so the Kural's rule becomes a conversion by question and answer.

gains.a: the epic's hell gains the couplet's sharper image of a mouth that will not reopen, which makes the threat permanent
gains.b: the couplet gains a positive alternative it does not state, a god's birth bought by the wasting of the body, and a listener who accepts it

note: Madanan falls like the moon swallowed by Rahu plunging into the sea; the Kalinga king falls like the sun dropping into the sea with a planet.
teaches: The two eclipse similes make the enemy's captains the moon and the sun of their side, so their two deaths together read as the setting of both lights of Kattiyangaran's host.

note: 387 names the birth star Uttirattathi; 404 makes the horoscope the cause of the prince's eloquence and beauty.
teaches: The birth scene's star is not ornament: the teacher reads Civakan's qualities as written at that birth, so the foundling's worth was fixed before his parentage was known.

note: Civakan praised Gunamalai so that even her girdle and anklets had done penance; to his wife he calls her the sand of a seep-well beside the Ganges.
teaches: Within a few verses the hero ranks the same woman as worthy of the jewels' penance and as a puddle beside his wife, so the poem lets the reader see his words to each woman fitted to the listener.

note: Kural 906 says the man who fears his wife's shoulders is worthless though he live like the gods; Dharmadattan says the king valued a woman's pleasure above heaven and nectar.
teaches: The Kural weighs the wife-ruled man against the gods' life and finds him worthless, while the epic's king makes the same comparison in reverse, and the cost falls not on his worth but on the whole realm.

gains.a: the counsellor's charge is seen as the Kural's chapter on being led by a woman, applied to a king
gains.b: the couplet's private failing is shown with a public cost, a world that sinks with its king

note: Verse 1029 compares closing lotuses to chaste women whose beloved has left; Akananuru 71 compares bees leaving pool flowers for branch flowers to graceless men.
teaches: The same evening scene casts the flower as a faithful wife and the bee as a leaving man, so each poet gives the figure a different party to blame.

gains.a: The verse lacks the blame that Akananuru puts on the one who leaves, since its simile is only a praise of women's constancy.
gains.b: The Sangam poem lacks the picture of the wife as the shut lotus, which turns the flower into the one who stays loyal.

note: 1738 has the child grow in the guard of women who tend him; Naladiyar 20 says Death takes even the newborn while the mother wails.
teaches: The poem's guarded growth is the thing the quatrain says cannot be guaranteed, so the child's safety is read against death's stealth.

gains.a: The guarded child gains the quatrain's reminder that guard does not keep death off, which the poem does not say.
gains.b: The quatrain gains a child as well cared for as can be, the strongest case for its warning.

note: The Mullaippattu's king cannot sleep for thinking of the elephant with its trunk cut, the men who fell and the wounded horses; Civakan sleeps through the noise of wounds, weeping women and drums as if he heard none of it.
teaches: The two kings face the same night after battle with opposite responses, the one kept awake by the wounded and the other asleep amid their cries, so the epic's sleep is a sign of a war ended where the Sangam king's waking is a sign of one still going on.

gains.a: a reason to read Civakan's undisturbed sleep as the peace of a finished war rather than mere indifference
gains.b: a view of its king's sleeplessness as tied to an unfinished campaign, which the poem alone does not test

note: 1345 names the arrow Naama; 1346 shows it cutting bow, arrows and illusion.
teaches: The poet shows the arrow's effect on the magic itself, so the king's last arrow answers the illusion that had outlasted every earlier shot.

note: In 687 the captive cried out unceasingly to Civakan, the bowman who took her maidenhood; in 2593 the king, now secure, answers 'how could I forget you?'.
teaches: The cry in the usurper's grip is answered only after the usurper's fall and a letter, so the epic shows that the king's help comes late, long after her call.

note: In 67 and here a king puts down the weapon in his hand under pressure of a speech; in 67 it is the victim's own sermon, here a third party's plea.
teaches: The two scenes show that the sword is laid down for different reasons: there the king is moved by what the victim teaches, here by what a friend says of the victim's greatness.

note: Verse 7 praises Saccandan's கோடாத செங்கோல் and unfading victory; verse 9 has the same king, sunk in desire and deaf to counsel, lose the kingdom to a plot.
teaches: The patikam builds the epic's first lesson from its own praise: the unbending sceptre and unfading victory are undone not by a stronger enemy but by the king's private desire.

note: The ministers of 1916 ask the sage to turn aside the tangled births; 1920 lists what he will teach in answer.
teaches: The sage's list of topics shows that the answer to a plea for escape from births is first a map of the births themselves.

note: The verse allows deeds to be shed in order, where the couplet says fate gets there first whatever one devises.
teaches: The Jain verse leaves room for undoing deeds that the Kural's fate overrides, though the dispute is over what one can do to a deed.

gains.a: the shedding of deeds is set against a strong claim of fate that it must answer
gains.b: the couplet gets a doctrine on which fate can be worn down

note: 1426 has a king order the destruction of all men; Tirumanthiram 238 says an unlearned king who says 'kill' is worse than Death, since Death spares the good.
teaches: Set side by side, the king who commands total death is judged by a rule the epic's own narrator does not state.

gains.a: the unit gains a standard by which its royal order is judged as the act of a king who says 'kill'
gains.b: the verse gains a case of a king with the power to turn Death into his tool

note: Both verses show evening birds going to their nests and young while one who is away or lovesick suffers.
teaches: Pairing the two shows that the happy birds are used as the measure of the lover's loneliness in both, only here the sufferer is a youth and there it is a wife.

gains.a: The verse lacks the akam frame of a wife whose husband is on his work, which Natrinai 69 supplies and which gives the birds' return a cause for grief.
gains.b: The Sangam poem lacks the wide epic eye that lists the fields, the fish-carrying birds and a generous man's spear-like feeling in one evening.

note: Verse 314 speaks of the aeon's time running out for Achuvakandan; verse 333 says the words spoken of him match the old words of the aeon.
teaches: The council's reasoning comes back to the same fated end, so the choice of a husband is set under a doom the epic has already spoken.

note: 1956 grades animal births by the number of senses from one to five; Neelakesi 77 splits animals into fixed and moving and counts five kinds of the fixed.
teaches: The sense-ladder of the Soolamani and the fixed and moving divisions of the Neelakesi are two cuts of one Jain classification of life.

note: 2992 has the wives lay aside their ornaments like a vine shedding flowers; Siddhar 19 asks when the speaker will leave silk and gold ornaments and desire the feet.
teaches: The Siddhar's wish to leave ornaments is shown done by women who give them up, but without the god's feet as its aim.

gains.a: the stripping of ornaments gets an aim in a god's feet that the epic's scene never names
gains.b: the Siddhar's wish to leave silk and gold gets a scene where it is carried out, with the cost to those who give up beauty

note: Kural 133 says that conduct is nobility of birth; verse 535 has the first lord make the five royal lineages and teach each its conduct and occupation.
teaches: In the epic, lineage is a thing made, with conduct as one of its parts, so the couplet's identity of conduct and birth is the made thing's own mark.

gains.a: A sense that a lineage's standing rests on its conduct, so that it is not simply handed down.
gains.b: An origin story in which lineages are set up by an act of the first king together with their occupations.

note: Kural 388 calls the king who protects with justice the இறை of his people; verse 267 calls him god-like because he orders a man's lot in both worlds.
teaches: The epic gives a reason for the Kural's word இறை as god: his rule reaches the next world's lot as well as this one's, which the couplet leaves untouched.

gains.a: The ground for calling the king godlike, which is a claim about both worlds.
gains.b: A reading in which இறை means a power over a man's fortune and not only a title of rule.

note: Kural 510 warns against trusting one not examined; Pazhamozhi 52 names unquenchable anger as a sign that a man fails the test and is to be avoided.
teaches: The pairing turns the Kural's general rule on examined trust into a usable test, since a man whose anger never cools shows by it that he is never clear and so not to be trusted.

note: Verse 670 holds that earlier kings paid and pleased their overlord and that this is the way; verse 685 says that paying tribute would make one's own arms and sword useless.
teaches: The same demand draws the king's resigned precedent and the prince's refusal, so one court holds two ideas of what a king is for.

note: 248 claims the king's splendour guards the world even while he sleeps; 261 shows the king sunk in pleasure, his army given up, and helpless against his minister.
teaches: The story refutes the councillor's extravagant praise of royal power: a king who has let go of rule is not protected by his majesty.

note: 2876 gives the old deed as a thread that cannot be torn away and burns the soul; Tirumanthiram 117 says the malas burn like cotton only when the sunstone meets the sun's presence, and not before.
teaches: The Jain verse leaves the deed unbroken and the Saiva verse says what ends it, so the Saiva verse limits the Jain one's permanence.

gains.a: the thread that follows through every body is shown to have, in a Saiva view, an end at the coming of grace
gains.b: the malas that grace burns gain a rival account in which the burden is a clinging deed that no god is said to remove

note: Kural 389 puts the world under the parasol of a king who can bear bitter words; verse 264 says that a parasol grown hot scorches the cool ponds and groves under it.
teaches: The Kural gives the cool shade as a gift of the king's patience, and the epic gives the reverse: when the king is hot the shade itself scorches.

gains.a: The danger the Kural leaves unsaid: shade turned to heat when the one under it loses his patience.
gains.b: A named cause of the parasol's coolness, the king's duty of guarding, in a parallel to the Kural's patience.

note: Both name the Charanas as a class of ascetics, one by their powers of flight and one at the mountain where they wash away karma.
teaches: The class appears with its powers in one epic and its purpose, washing karma away, in the other.

claims.gist: a warrior who dies in battle leaves his fame on earth and takes up the guarding of heaven
birth is passage through foul water and a helpless fall, without provision of deeds for the next road
the first hell has thirteen levels and thirty lakh blazing pits
even a killing of a mere effigy, done once, is not wiped out and returns in each following birth
killing real living beings brings far worse pain in later births
the Jina enthroned under the asoka and worshipped by the gods removes the darkness from all worlds
kings surpass the gods in many respects
hell torment does not pause for the whole span of life in hell
the seven hells are named for darkness, smoke, mire, sand and gravel
the ascetic holds that neither 'I' nor 'mine' nor even benefit is real
the greatness of dharma hides even a being's small karmas and carries it into a human birth
the dharma of the Jina is a raft across the sea of sorrow
justice is the eye of kings, and lust like liquor robs a king of his learned sense
of all the wombs, a human birth is hardest to gain
the Jina's halo clears the darkness of the worlds and dries up the deeds of those who see it
the pleasure of desire is small and the grief of parting vast
one who dies of grief at parting loses the fruit of both this world and the next
the young lord's rising fortune comes from good austerity

note: The youth at 35 describes beings spun by their deeds through births without number; the kid in 199 speaks from one of those births.
teaches: The doctrine told by the youths in 35 is borne out in the king's own case, so that the reader sees it as lived and not as preached.

note: In 306 Vijayai imagines the royal order that should have opened the gold hoards for suppliants at a prince's birth; in 331 a merchant opens his own hoard like a mountain of red gold for the same child.
teaches: The birth-gifts denied the prince in the burning ground are given after all, but by a stranger who believes the child his own.

note: The fire in the town of verse 110 is again a fire here, now a stage prop.
teaches: The same device of fire serves Yugi twice: first to free the fugitives, now to fake a death, so it is his habit and not a one-off.

note: The Vidyadhara king said he would not give his daughter even if kings with sea-like armies fell at his feet and begged; here the kings who fought for her lose their sea-like army, which breaks like a salt hill in flood.
teaches: The father's refusal was spoken before any war, and the battle turns his figure of speech into fact: the same sea of soldiers he would not bow to is now the thing that dissolves.

note: The Naga poet's lamp kept despite its smoke is the same plea for lenient reading.
teaches: The minor epics repeat the formula of asking that a work's worth outweigh its faults, each choosing a different household object.

note: In 695 the minister says he will show a magic and set a lion on the youth; in 696 he calls Arikethu and commissions the magic lion.
teaches: The plan of 695 becomes an order, and the instrument is named.

note: 2909 compares a king to a driver who must know the ground his chariot runs on; Purananuru 185 compares the realm to a cart that sinks if its driver cannot steer.
teaches: Both set a skilled driver against one who does not know the way, and the epic ties the skill to knowing the land.

gains.a: the verse's chariot is shown to belong to an old comparison of kingship with driving
gains.b: the Sangam poem's cart gains the condition that the driver must know the ground, not only steer

note: Naladiyar 1 shows men who ate six-flavoured meals served by a willing wife and then beg gruel here and there; 2624 shows a woman who drank boiled milk from a golden bowl and now holds out a wide bowl for alms.
teaches: The Naladiyar's quatrain draws the rule that wealth cannot be counted on, and the Cintamani turns the same beggar's fall into a sight the preacher points to while urging the hearers to turn to dharma.

gains.a: the sermon verse gets an old, general proof (those who ate richly and then beg) behind its single sight, so the woman reads as a type and not a pity
gains.b: the quatrain gets a woman, her hunger and the posture of begging bent like a creeper, which it lacks as an anonymous list of eaters, and the sermon's turn from the picture to dharma

note: Verse 560 makes kevala the bride whom the renouncer takes and by which he rises above the gods; Tirumanthiram 494 calls those who have left the kevala state the Vijnanars, so the same word marks the state to be left.
teaches: The same word names the goal in one text and the soul's first bound state in the other, so the two cannot be read on the same ladder.

gains.a: The epic's kevala gets a rival ranking in which the same name is the bottom, which the Jain verse does not know.
gains.b: The Tirumanthiram's kevala gains a case where the word is the highest prize, showing that the term's rank turns on the school.

note: The couplet ranks not killing and eating above a thousand sacrifices; the epic's rite of the dead is a sacrifice whose flesh is the dead man.
teaches: The couplet states the rule; the epic's story shows its cost to the rite's own beneficiaries, so that the rule is tested by a case where the dead eat the dead.

gains.a: The rite of 196 gets a stated standard against which a brahmin's flesh offering is shown to be worse than none.
gains.b: The couplet's contrast of ritual and abstention gets a story in which the sacrifice's own beneficiary is the victim.

note: Maduraikanchi lists a must elephant that kills its goad-men, breaks its post and roams, beside horses drilled in circling courses; 1831 and 1839 give the same post-breaking elephant and the same circling drill.
teaches: The Sangam city poem sets the rampaging elephant and the drilled circles side by side as separate noises of the capital, while the epic joins them as two stages of one hero's mastery, riot turned into drill.

gains.a: the epic's set piece is seen to draw on a Sangam catalogue of the capital's elephants and horses
gains.b: the catalogue's separate items gain a story in which one man turns the first into the second

note: The Kural's hero pulls the spear from his own body and laughs; the epic's youth plucks out the spear that fed on his flesh and laughs (பறித்து நக்கான்).
teaches: The epic gives the couplet's laugh a cause the couplet leaves open: the spear had been thrown by a man who kept his spear for elephants, so the wound is an honour and the laugh is the pride of having been judged worth it.

gains.a: the youth's laugh is placed in a known code of valour, so it reads as a canonical act rather than bravado
gains.b: the couplet's bare gesture gets a situation, the foe's choice of target in 2289, that explains why a wound is a matter for joy

note: Kar Narpathu 19: the returning man sees the maraa blossom white like the plough-bearing god's colour and his heart runs ahead. Thinaimalai 96: the moonlight is like the pale colour of the discus-bearer's elder brother and falls like a spear on the parted.
teaches: Balarama's whiteness is a stock likeness in the Kilkanakku mullai poems, but it serves the hurrying man as the colour of the flowers that call him home and the waiting woman as the colour of a moonlight that wounds her, so the same divine colour signs joy or pain by who sees it.

note: 1210 sends away envoys who brought evil words that burned the ears; Kural 685 says an envoy should remove what would offend.
teaches: The envoys fail the Kural's standard of speech and are still protected, so the immunity of an envoy is shown to stand apart from how well he speaks.

gains.a: The epic scene gains a measure by which the envoys' evil words count as a failure of the office, not just of manners.
gains.b: The couplet gains the case of an envoy who offends and yet may not be harmed, which the couplet's ideal of inoffensive speech does not reach.

note: Kural 1263: she lives on, longing for the return of the man who went desiring victory with his resolve as his only companion. Kar Narpathu 7: the friend says he went to give to seekers and crush foes, and the rain will bring him back.
teaches: The couplet's woman treats his heroic aim as the rival that left her behind, while the friend names the same aim, giving and conquest, as a reason to trust he will return in the rains: one motive is a grievance in the Kural and a guarantee in the venba.

note: The mate refuses a chest that has lain with courtesans; Kural 1311 has a woman refuse a husband's chest, calling him a philanderer.
teaches: The Kural's refusal rests on a seen glance, while the monkey's rests on a proved infidelity, so the sulk is shown with a real cause.

gains.a: A named, human form of the refusal that makes the monkey's speech a wife's quarrel rather than animal noise.
gains.b: A case where the fault is real, which tests the couplet's sulk against a cause beyond being looked at.

note: 1259 pitches the camp on Arungalam hill; 1266 sets the two armies against one another.
teaches: The poet readies the field in one verse and the clash in the next, so the camp's choice of ground leads straight into the fight.

note: In 3033 the bees mourn the cast-off hair and garland; Siddhar 329 lists a loincloth, a porch and leaves to eat as all one needs once ornament is gone.
teaches: The Jain epic gives the loss of ornament a lament by those who lived on it, while the Siddhar counts it as pure gain.

gains.a: the bees' lament shows the cost of renunciation that the king's calm stripping leaves out
gains.b: the Siddhar's cheerful poverty is tested against those who lose by it

note: Verse 254 has the king thank the ministers for his rule; Cintamani 206 has a counsellor press the king to hear counsel he does not want.
teaches: The Soolamani's council shows a king who welcomes counsel, while the Cintamani shows the counsellor who must speak when the king would not listen, so the ideal depends on a willing king.

note: Gandharvadattai's vow to bind the unknown youth with a garland is kept when she fastens the gold garland on his chest after the contest.
teaches: The garland in 738 is the answer to an inward vow, so the public result of the contest was settled in her heart before a string was touched.

note: The letter owns the elephant that Pradyotan's side made in verse 39.
teaches: Pradyotan's own letter turns the trap of verse 39 into an offer of kinship, which shows how a captor explains his trick afterwards.

note: The hero calls his release ஊழ்வினை; five verses later the god who freed him explains that Civakan once eased his suffering as a dog and gave him his body.
teaches: Read together, the 'former deed' the hero blames is no hidden deed of a past birth but his own recent kindness to a dying dog returning to him, so the epic's karma is visible to the reader while the hero speaks of it as unknown.

note: Vijayai, hearing the usurper's victory drum, fainted like a doe struck by a spear (எஃகு எறி பிணையின் மாழ்கி); the usurper's queen, hearing of his death, sinks like a doe that has taken a spear (வேலேறு பெற்ற பிணை ... மாழ்கி) and dies.
teaches: The epic gives the usurper's wife the very simile it gave the queen he widowed, so the wrong done at the start comes home in the same figure, except that Vijayai survived to bear the avenger and this woman does not survive.

note: The quatrain warns men not to desire the spear-eyed woman because she too will stoop and walk with a staff; Manimekalai, the woman desired, points her pursuer to an old woman and shows him eyes and face already changed.
teaches: The quatrain's warning against desire is spoken by a man to men about a woman, while the epic puts it in the mouth of the desired woman as her own defence, turning the lesson on aging into a refusal.

note: The king holds that offering a pair of humans at the sword is a fitting rite; the brother holds that harm to the body is no harm to the self and so no loss.
teaches: The same act of killing is a gain to the king's worship and no harm to its victims in their own account, so the doomed two defuse the rite's meaning by their view of the body.

note: Vikraman's resolve to take up ascetic life in verse 22 is carried out in verse 23 when he goes into the forest.
teaches: A resolve voiced in one verse is kept in the next, with the kingdom handed over first.

note: Both make a weapon a feeder: the sword drinks demons' blood to still its hunger, the plough turns blood into a sown field.
teaches: Two boasts turn the same thing, blood, from a loss into food or seed, which shows how the council's talk makes killing a work of cultivation.

note: Verse 427 chooses Marusi as envoy because he is learned and can put kin and affairs into words; Kural 686 names learning, fearlessness and sense of the time as the envoy's marks.
teaches: The ministers' test for an envoy stops at learning and speech, where the Kural adds fearlessness before hostile eyes and a sense of the moment, so the gaps show what the court has not yet asked of Marusi.

gains.a: Two further qualities, fearlessness and sense of time, that the verse's choice does not name.
gains.b: A court that picks an envoy by the stated learning and speech, which shows how a rule is applied in practice.

note: 1508 counts a discus-lord's wealth in jewels, treasures, lands, cities and gatherings of kings; Kural 381 counts a king's parts as army, people, resources, ministers, allies and fort.
teaches: The epic's list is of things owned and has no ministers or fort, while the couplet's list names the organs a state cannot do without.

gains.a: the epic list lacks counsellors and defences, and gains the couplet's organs of a state
gains.b: the couplet lacks the epic's treasures and festive cities, and gains a picture of imperial wealth

note: Kural 346 says the one who cuts 'I' and 'mine' enters a world higher than the gods'; 2988 calls the wives to cross old deeds and reach bliss at the top of the world above.
teaches: The Kural names the pride to be cut and the height, the epic names the deeds to be crossed and the place, so each gives what the other leaves open.

gains.a: the summit above the world gets a condition the verse does not state, the cutting of 'I' and 'mine'
gains.b: the Kural's higher world gets a location at the top of the universe and a means in crossing old deeds

note: The women hold that union with Civakan is the reward of penance (அண்ணலைத் தவத்திற் றந்தார்); the patikam ends with Civakan, as one who has eaten nectar, no longer wanting the pleasure of women.
teaches: The epic plants early the crowd's belief that penance buys the pleasure of this man, and its own close makes the same man's penance the end of all such pleasure, so the word தவம் is turned against the hope it first expressed.

note: Kural 445 says counsellors are the king's eyes and he should take counsel; verse 641 has the king, who has already said he will fight regardless, tell his ministers to counsel.
teaches: The couplet's rule is shown with its limit, as counsel asked after the king has made up his mind.

gains.a: The verse lacks a rule saying why counsellors matter, which the couplet gives.
gains.b: The couplet lacks the case where counsel is asked only to confirm the king's mind, which the verse shows.

note: Naladiyar 3 says kings who rode elephants at the head of armies fall and change when their deeds turn against them; verse 635 has a king boasting that mere men cannot shake him.
teaches: A king's claim of strength is read as the very certainty that, in the Naladiyar, precedes the fall of such rulers.

gains.a: The verse lacks a standard that sets his boast against what happens to powerful kings, which the quatrain supplies.
gains.b: The quatrain lacks a living king speaking the boast it warns against, which the verse supplies.

note: Verse 192 praises Vijayai's red-cornered eyes as fighting carp (களிக் கயல் பொருவ); Naladiyar 44's renunciant refuses men who call eyes பொருகயல் and sees an eye as a scooped-out palm fruit.
teaches: The Naladiyar's renunciant names the epic's own stock of praise as the temptation he walks past, and the epic shows that praise doing its work on a king who does not walk past it.

gains.a: the stock carp-eye simile is shown to be a recognised snare in the ethical literature, not neutral ornament
gains.b: the quatrain's 'petty men' who praise eyes are given a full instance in a celebrated poem, and a consequence in the king's fall

note: Both describe flesh-eating as feeding flesh with flesh (ஊனைப் பெருக்குதல், ஊன் பெருக்கற்கு); the Kural asks how such a person can hold அருள், the Innaa line ranks the act as the first of pains.
teaches: The pair shows one image doing two jobs: in the Kural it proves the loss of compassion, in the Innaa verse it is a pain ranked above even soured honey and kingless armies.

note: The sermon says to fear a bad rebirth and leave vice; the quatrain gives the bad rebirth as the fruit of wronging others' wives.
teaches: The sermon names fear of an evil birth without a case, and the quatrain supplies one, so the fear gets a concrete deed and fruit.

gains.a: the sermon's fear of an evil birth is given a concrete deed behind it
gains.b: the quatrain's penalty is shown as the ground of a whole poem's moral

note: The wedding dresses the bride in a necklace that seems to own her body; the quatrain says nothing goes with a person but their deeds, and the body they guarded and adorned is no use when Death seizes it.
teaches: Set beside the quatrain's warning, the wedding's lavish adornment of a body reads as the thing the Jain moral is aimed at, which the festive verse itself does not say.

gains.a: the adornment gains a counter-voice that questions what the necklace and razor-work are for
gains.b: the quatrain gains a concrete, joyous scene of body-adorning to push against, where it only names the body in general

note: In 304 the kings of the sea-girt earth pay Acuvakanthan tribute for fear of his anger; in 690 the prince says tribute refused has only a trial of force to answer it.
teaches: The prince's refusal reads as a break from the fear that made every other king pay.

note: In 138 elephant-kings bow to the father; in 159 kings with fierce-eyed elephants bow to the daughter.
teaches: The homage the father wins by victory passes to the daughter by beauty alone, so the poem lets beauty hold the sway that the king's sword held.

note: Kaluzhavegan kept the suitor kings in hope without telling them his mind; now the kings of the earth arrive in Rajamapuram, the city the horoscope named.
teaches: The king's hidden purpose turns his daughter's suitors into unknowing escorts to the city where her destined husband lives, so their rivalry serves a plan they were never told.

note: The mother once told the father that their daughter burned with anger at Civakan's verdict on her powder; now she tells him the same man has won her.
teaches: The grievance that made the girl shun all men is reread as the cause of her chastity for one man, so the anger and the love are shown to have had one object.

note: 2911 forbids a king even one false syllable for fear of losing fame; Kural 292 allows falsehood to stand as truth if it yields good free of fault.
teaches: One text bars all falsehood from the king, the other lets a blameless good justify it.

gains.a: the verse's total ban is shown to be stricter than the Kural's exception allows
gains.b: the Kural's exception gains a counter-case in which a king's word is watched by all and cannot be bent

note: Tirumanthiram 1626 says that people who ask for many things get their wealth, but those who do great tapas win the end of birth; verse 547 has Nami ask a god's servant for wealth.
teaches: Nami stands as a case of the first sort, asking for wealth at the feet of a yogi, and the Tirumanthiram supplies a rank by which his wish is lower than release.

gains.a: A standard by which Nami's request looks lesser than a request for release, a judgment the epic does not make.
gains.b: A named person who asks for wealth in the presence of a yogi and gets it, which makes the verse's contrast concrete.

claims.gist: fate decides the outcome of human planning, and plans may end otherwise than intended
life and rule cannot go on if harming living things is given up
one who has taken the vow is no longer a husband's own, and the order is a stranger to his claim
the killing deed that was about to bind the king has been stopped before it joined him
a king's pleasures bring him pain like that of hunted beasts
those who leave the body through hard penance of right conduct gain an imperishable golden body
those who do penance gain joy in this world and the next
killing a beast that preys on others lets the world rest in safety
for a noble man, death is better than living on while a woman's life is in danger
A king who finds lands taken from the gods' places and the learned must restore them twofold
to set oneself against the king is the act of men who have come to their death
a sage's teaching can turn away the tangle of births
one who has had the Jina's teaching no longer craves other people's wealth
women submit to the husband their elders choose, whether or not their hearts consent
the god's grace ends deep sorrow
the lord has perfect omniscience of the three worlds and endless qualities
release comes by leaving cruel deeds behind, and it is this that the lord's feet are praised in order to teach
a gift sown in good ground and watered with virtue brings fame in this world and the pleasures of the gods after it, while true penance is harder
refuge at the first lord's feet and grace ends the darkness of beings
conquest of the four binding karmas is what leads to release
a king's desire can break the restraint of learned counsel and lose the kingdom
slandering those above one is repaid by tearing out the tongue
the teaching comes from the boundless ocean of complete knowledge and nourishes the world like nectar

note: The hero takes five hundred princesses by the mantra-rite; the couplet praises the man who does not look at another's wife.
teaches: The couplet bars only another's wife, and the poem's heroes win unmarried women, so the epic's polygamy sits outside what the couplet forbids.

gains.a: the hero's many marriages are measured against the couplet's one fixed limit
gains.b: the couplet's limit is shown to leave room for many wives who are unmarried

note: 1886 has offered flowers falling in a rain at the king's approach; 1897 has a divine rain of flowers burying the golden ground at the Lord's appearance.
teaches: The same flower rain is first the king's offering and then the heavens' answer, so the worship and its reception share one image.

note: Perunkoppendu refuses the widow's life of plain food, gravel bed and no ghee and chooses the pyre; Vijayai refuses the milk offered her and takes up a widow's diet of greens in the forest.
teaches: The diet the Sangam queen calls the lot of wretched widows and rejects for death is accepted by the epic's queen and renamed divinity (வனத்து உறை தெய்வம்), which shows how the Jain frame revalues the widow's abstinence the heroic poem despised.

gains.a: the verse's greens and refused milk are recognised as the widow's regimen, not only an ascetic's
gains.b: Perunkoppendu's scorn gains its counterpart, a queen who lives on and makes the same regimen a way of holiness

note: In 233 the king's wisdom rebukes him for bathing in the liquor of lust and losing his senses; in 2729 Civakan names desire as toddy drunk on the tongue and turns back like an elephant to the goad.
teaches: The same intoxication that unmade Saccandan and cost him his throne is seen by his son in time to leave it by choice, which sets father and son side by side.

note: Verse 175 draws spring shoots as copies of the women's hands and waists; Naladiyar 48 tells those who praise sandal and garland without knowing the body to look at vultures tearing the carcass.
teaches: A court poet delights in the body's beauty while a moral quatrain holds the same body as carrion, so the same poem tradition holds two views of the body.

gains.a: A counter-voice that sees the beauty it praises as fading.
gains.b: A quatrain's image set against a living scene of pleasure, so its rebuke has a concrete target.

note: After taking refuge, Manimekalai's teacher begins on the three jewels of Buddha, Dharma and Sangha; Soolamani 201 gives three things to hold after the refuge in 200: true seeing, knowledge and conduct.
teaches: Both sermons give threes after refuge, but the Buddhist three are what one goes to for refuge and the Jain three are what the follower must hold.

note: Kural 352 says that for those of stainless sight darkness leaves and joy arises; Soolamani 203 has the light of knowledge from the sage's words split the darkness of evil deeds in the whole assembly.
teaches: The two verses use darkness and light, but the epic has the light come to a crowd from a teacher's words, while the couplet leaves it to one's own clear sight.

gains.a: the darkness is given as the darkness of evil deeds, and the light comes by hearing a teacher
gains.b: the bare word 'darkness', which commentators read as hell, ignorance or births, is shown in one reading as the darkness of deeds

note: Manimekalai traces Kayasandikai's elephant-fire to a named act, crushing an ascetic's fruit, and his curse; the Cintamani says only that sin came upon the ascetic in his penance.
teaches: Set beside the Manimekalai's exact chain of act, curse and term, the Cintamani's unnamed sin shows karma striking even a guileless penitent with no deed in this life to explain it.

note: The journey in 150 carries out the plan Vayantakan puts in 149.
teaches: The reader learns that the long mourning ends with an act, as the king follows the counsel and sets out.

note: Naladiyar 30 says kin come unasked and go silently, leaving the body as a bird leaves its nest-tree; 993 says Gunamalai spurns her kin's talk like those who know their births.
teaches: The epic borrows the renouncer's detachment from kin, which the Naladiyar grounds in kin's passing, to picture a girl whose turning from family is love for one man, so the same outward withdrawal is shown to have opposite causes.

gains.a: the reasoning about kin as passing visitors that the simile's 'those who know their births' assumes but does not state
gains.b: a sign that the quatrain's lesson had become a known figure of speech, usable even of a lover's absorption

note: Naladiyar 34 tells one who has this rare body to take its full fruit, as juice from cane; 2749 gives the odds that make the body rare, the pole in the yoke-hole.
teaches: The quatrain's advice to use the body gets a reason in the epic's image of how improbable it is, and the epic's image gets a use to put it to.

gains.a: the verse's picture of chance gains the plain duty the rarity implies, to use the body's fruit
gains.b: the quatrain's word 'rare' gains a concrete measure, with a drifting pole and an unlikely yoke-hole in place of the bare word

note: Kural 685 asks an envoy to speak so as to bring a smile and remove what would offend; here the envoys carry the king's taunt whole, because the minister of 700 wants the youth angered.
teaches: The envoys' offence is the lord's chosen means, a purpose the rule for envoys does not allow for.

gains.a: The verse lacks the standard that shows the envoys' unsoftened message as a choice of policy.
gains.b: The couplet lacks the case where giving offence is exactly the work the lord sends an envoy to do.

note: 1923 counts the lower hells in all; 1926 narrows to the first and its thirteen levels and thirty lakh pits.
teaches: The sage's numbers are first given as a whole and then broken down hell by hell.

note: Vijayai's blessing at Civakan's birth, that he would utterly destroy his old enemy, is fulfilled when the city's women say he has killed the deluded one with all his sons.
teaches: The blessing spoken alone in the burning ground is fulfilled in public speech: the city, not the mother, now announces the destruction she foretold.

note: The king had proclaimed by drum that whoever cures the girl will have land, wealth and the bride; now Civakan is told to sow fame and reap kinship in this land.
teaches: The public offer of a prize is restated to one man as a bond of kinship, so the marriage that the drum put up for any healer becomes, before the cure, a relationship offered to Civakan in particular.

note: Kural 1187: she lay in his embrace and turned aside, and at once pallor was on her thick enough to scoop up; in 399 pallor is moss on the village well that parts where he touches and spreads where he lets go.
teaches: The couplet's instant hyperbole is given a mechanism by the poem: pallor is a surface like well-moss that closes the moment the hand lifts, so the Kural's 'at that very moment' is not exaggeration but what anyone at a village well has seen.

note: In 1130 she uses 'he lives within me' to refute the town's gossip. In 1249 she uses the same fact against her own heart, to stop it from leaving.
teaches: The argument that once consoled her now traps her.

note: Kural 1085 asks whether the maiden's look is Death, an eye or a doe; Civakan asks whether her eyes are swords, mango slices, lilies, lotus, spears, arrows, carp, eyes, or Death come to kill.
teaches: Set beside the couplet's three-way doubt, the epic's ten guesses show the question turned into a catalogue that closes by choosing Death, where the couplet leaves the look holding all three at once.

gains.a: the verse's list gains a model: it is the couplet's riddle of the look, widened, not a loose string of comparisons
gains.b: the couplet gains a voiced scene, a hero dazed on a merchant's step, in which its question is asked of one particular woman

note: 1172 warns that a great king should not march against lowly foes; 1181 has the king ask what kind of war this is.
teaches: The king answers the warning by asking whether this war is human, divine or both.
