note: In 427 the Vidyadhara ministers choose the learned Marusi to carry the letter; in 608 Podanam's ministers choose a learned man to answer.
teaches: Both courts treat the embassy as the work of learning, so the exchange between them is a matching of one practice on each side.

note: In 1946 the breasts of the sandal-painted women turn even those who think of release back; in 2651 a woman of the court puts pleasure down and goes to austerity.
teaches: The poem keeps both outcomes in front of the reader: the same world of women that can undo a renouncer can also be left by one of its own members.

note: Verse 1017 asks whose daughter the picture shows; 1018 answers that she is no earth-woman and so the Vidyadhara king's daughter.
teaches: The answer is reached by elimination from the picture's beauty, not from any name, so the maiden's identity rests only on how she looks.

note: The Kural calls it flight when a fierce man blinks at a flung spear; the epic's warrior does not blink at all (இமைத்திலன்) as the spear comes, and takes it on his chest.
teaches: Set beside the couplet, the verse shows where its standard leads: the unblinking eye is kept to the end, and the warrior who will not blink is the one the spear kills, so the code costs the life it measures.

gains.a: the stillness of the eye, one detail among many, is shown to be the decisive proof in the code of courage
gains.b: the couplet's test is followed to its consequence, a death embraced like a garland, which the couplet's question stops short of

note: The Kural praises those who keep the path of the one who quenched the five senses; the epic gives Vijayai that sense-restraint (பொறிதவ நெருங்க நோற்று) in the verse that sends an army out at her word.
teaches: The couplet makes quenching the senses the way to a long, settled life, while the epic shows the same restraint in a widow who still commands a war of revenge, so ascetic control of the senses is shown sitting with, not ending, worldly purpose.

gains.a: Vijayai's penance gains the weight of the Kural's opening ideal, so her austerity reads as the highest discipline and not mere widowhood
gains.b: the couplet's ideal gains a case where it is kept by a householder's widow with an unfinished duty, showing it need not mean withdrawal from affairs

note: 2904 calls the handsome body hollow and moves at once to choose an heir; Naladiyar 42 asks the viewer to look at a body whose skin hides its openings as a bag turned inside out.
teaches: The quatrain teaches the contemplation and the verse shows it driving an abdication.

gains.a: the verse's bare word 'hollow' gets a concrete picture of what lies under the handsome surface
gains.b: the Naladiyar's meditation on the body gets a king who acts on it by giving up his throne

note: 2871 says the one who goes to another's wife is like a bright sword over his own neck and falls into heavy suffering; Naladiyar 84 says if caught the leg is cut, the family shamed and hell follows.
teaches: Both put the cost of adultery in a worldly punishment and a future one, with the same image of a blade.

gains.a: The verse's blade image gets the actual penalties it stands for, caught, maimed and shamed
gains.b: The Naladiyar's list of penalties gets one picture that holds them, the sword that hangs over him

note: The king who refuses to take a kid's life to save his own is the same Yasodharan that the muni names as caught in beast births for killing.
teaches: The refusal in verse 139 does not hold in the story's end; the reader sees that a good stand can still be overturned and then paid for.

note: Verse 1016 puts the portrait before the youth; 1019 shows love begin as soon as he looks, with Kaman taking aim.
teaches: The poet makes the painted likeness itself the occasion of love, so no meeting has taken place when the wound is given.

note: In 1340 the king reads the match as having come by destiny; in 1359 the hero's destiny (பொறி) is the chariot that takes him away from the same bride after two months.
teaches: The same fate that the king cites to make the marriage is what carries the husband off, so in this epic destiny grants a union without promising that it will last.

note: Both works end by saying the sage overcomes the two deeds by meditation and reaches liberation.
teaches: Two Jain epics close on the same formula, the two deeds overcome by meditation, and so show it as the fixed ending of a Jain life-story and not a feature of one work.

note: 1921 says four states turn the souls; 1922 names them as hell, beast, man and god.
teaches: The four are named at once, so the turning wheel is shown to carry a soul as easily into hell as into heaven.

note: Tirumanthiram 670 says siddhis come through eightfold yoga and Shakti's grace; verse 548 has Dharanan hand Nami the sky-going lore and a mountain for the asking.
teaches: In the epic, powers are a gift passed through a go-between to a man who asks for wealth, where the Tirumanthiram sets them at the end of discipline and grace.

gains.a: A contrast showing that a power may be had by asking when it is not had by yoga.
gains.b: A case in which the powers called siddhis go to someone who has done no yoga and wanted only wealth.

note: 2901 gives Nandan the heritage of the army; 2902 declines it together with heaven and release.
teaches: Nandan answers a plain offer of a throne by ranking his brother's feet above every prize the work weighs elsewhere.

note: Sivavakkiyar asks whether a planted stone will speak; in 2058 a worshipper hears the shrine speak, and the narrator says the voice was a man's trick.
teaches: The Siddhar's scorn assumes the stone is silent; the epic shows a voice supplied to it by a hidden man, so the credulity he mocks can be steered by whoever stands behind the image.

gains.a: the comic oracle gains a doctrinal edge, since the Siddhar names the error of taking an image for a speaking god
gains.b: the Siddhar's rhetorical question gains a narrative case of what follows when worshippers do believe the image speaks: they can be deceived

note: 1390 raises the brothers' host; 1392 shows the younger brothers and kings joining the press.
teaches: One hero's entry draws in kin after kin, so the battle spreads by loyalty rather than by order.

note: Tirumular puts in fire-mouthed hell those who said 'kill, stab'; the Neelakesi puts there those who ate the flesh as well as those who killed.
teaches: A Saiva and a Jain text each carry the guilt of a killing beyond the hand that strikes, one back to the man who ordered it and the other forward to the man who eats, so between them the whole chain around a death is held to account.

note: Both are the plea of the one left behind against a departure: the couplet says tell your quick return to those still alive; 387 asks him to say he will return, and then shows a road where great men turn back at a lizard's cry.
teaches: The couplet only doubts the traveller's promise; the poem shows why it is empty, since on that road a return depends on omens and beasts, not on the man's word.

note: Tirumanthiram 2026 tells of five lions in a forest whose claws and teeth must be cut before the Lord is reached; verse 723 has a prince seize a lion by the fangs and tear it.
teaches: The same beast is mastered here by force of arm and there by a cutting of the claws, so the lion stands both for an outer foe and for an inner one.

gains.a: The verse lacks any sense of the lion as something within, which Tirumular's five lions give.
gains.b: The Tirumanthiram verse lacks the act itself, a seizing of the fangs and a tearing, which the epic supplies as a deed.

note: 2929 says the beggar stands begging because he never gave; Naladiyar 107 says those who stand begging at great gates are living out their former deeds without saying which.
teaches: The epic names the former deed behind the begging, a life of not giving, where the quatrain leaves the cause as deeds in general.

gains.a: the beggar of the epic gains the Naladiyar's plain statement that begging in public is the working out of earlier deeds, not an accident
gains.b: the quatrain gains a named cause, never giving, for the former deeds that fill the begging bowl

note: The teller says that understanding that events arise from deeds gives true companions and joy; the Siddhar says the body is the enjoyment of deeds and joins those who think of Siva's feet.
teaches: The epic makes understanding the nature of deeds the first step; the Siddhar names grace at the feet as what takes one beyond them.

gains.a: The epic's lesson meets the Saiva claim that a god's feet, not understanding, release one from deeds.
gains.b: The Siddhar's body-as-deeds gets a long case in which deeds ripen through poison and rebirth.

note: 1425 has a king's grief and anger lead him to loose a spell that destroys the world; Kural 305 says anger kills the one who does not guard against it.
teaches: The epic shows anger as a power that reaches the world and not only the angry man, which limits the couplet's 'yourself'.

gains.a: the unit gains a rule that makes the king's anger the cause of what follows and not only an act of war
gains.b: the couplet gains a case where the harm of anger goes outward and the self is not the only victim

note: Both sides consult birds: the hunters' omen-reader reads a bird's cry before the raid, and the herders' announcer warns of an ill-omened bird; each side goes ahead.
teaches: The episode gives an omen to raiders and herders alike and lets both ignore it, so omens here foretell outcomes without ever restraining anyone.

note: In 681 the prince's long-held anger kindles like a fire at the word tribute; in 1147 fire is born in Acuvakandan's eyes at the news of the marriage.
teaches: The two rivals are drawn with the same image of rage as fire, so the coming war reads as two fires meeting.

claims.gist: women's minds lack great knowledge and unmoving firmness
those whose minds are fixed on the vision of the good dharma do not cling to this life
austerity and the burden of rule are harder to bear than lifting a mountain
souls in the nigoda state have one sense and suffer, and only some move on from it
wealth and the whole earth are to be counted as dust by the one who renounces
a king settles a weighty matter after counsel with those who know the science of policy
Giving to ascetics, with learning, ends rebirth and leads to bliss
one's past births are beyond counting, more than the sands of the shore
in the states of birth (கதிகள்) beings pass through, those joined now meet as strangers and do not stay together
kinship within a household lasts two days and should not be grieved
saving a life from the king's own beast cannot be a crime against the king
a king who has beaten many kings need not fear lesser foes
a horoscope cast by rule at birth fixes the man a girl belongs to
a retainer who fails to avenge harm done to his lord forfeits the name of a man
those who live in the heavens of enjoyment cannot give anything up
nothing is seen that departs from what the Lord's word has said
preparing for war is easy for anyone, bearing it is hard
a prince who follows the sage's teaching of dharma gains the four ends and mastery of learning
the world stands only because of a king's gentle grace
a king's glory of one day is gone the next
one reaches heaven by a teaching whose substance is true, so its faults of diction do not lessen it
austerity stops the springs from which deeds flow in
when the enemy kings of karma fall, infinite knowledge is gained and the soul becomes lord of all the worlds
those who have done wrong find the state of austerity hard to reach
hunters are made to suffer as the hunted did, without the release of death
parting and death belong to human birth by its very nature
those who grieve over what is natural sink deeper into the sea of births
the union of the pair follows the course of fate
the world is unstable and its pleasures do not stay

note: Dharmadattan sends the one who kills and eats flesh to hell; Neelakesi 97 shows hell's tormentors burning beings while naming the sins of killing and eating flesh.
teaches: Dharmadattan files regicide in one list with killing and flesh-eating, the very sins Neelakesi's tormentors name as they burn the damned, so a political crime is set inside the minor epic's catalogue of injuries to life.

note: 1867 promises the festival-goers a celestial form; 1882 shows the procession wearing their deeds away.
teaches: The promised heaven of 1867 is fed by the dying of deeds in 1882, so the festival works as a means of release in the ledger of karma, not a mere celebration.

note: The astrologer's reading places the princess's destined husband in Rajamapuram; as Civakan takes the lute the poet calls him கணிபுகழ் காளை, the youth the astrologers praised.
teaches: The epithet at the moment of playing marks the contest as the working out of the horoscope, so the reader hears the song as a prophecy being fulfilled rather than a match in doubt.

note: Kural 47 puts the householder who lives the household life rightly first among all who strive; 2632 has the nun say that penance is hard and that a gift sown with virtue yields fame and then the pleasures of the gods.
teaches: The Jain nun grades the gift of the householder as a fruit of fame and heaven and keeps the harder penance above it, so the Kural's 'first among strivers' is put against a ladder of fruits.

gains.a: the nun's rule that gift watered with virtue gives fame and heaven gets a rival ranking that puts the householder at the head of all effort
gains.b: the couplet, which does not say what is striven for, gets one answer: for the Jain the striving is for fame and heaven by gift, or for more by penance

note: Arisenan names himself and offers the foe the choice to flee; Kural 777 calls the war-anklet an adornment for those who value fame above life.
teaches: The epic shows the cost of the bold stance the couplet praises: the one who proclaims it is among the first to fall in 1294.

gains.a: The boast of 1283 is read against a standard of honour, so the proclamation becomes a claim to fame and not mere bravado.
gains.b: The couplet, which gives no outcome for the bold man, is given a case where the fame-seeker is cut down at once.

note: Verse 838 has the king raise a host like a sea swallowing the world; verse 949 shows the two hosts meeting as the Ganga and the Yamuna.
teaches: The host first likened to a sea is now the river that mingles with another, so the image turns from size to joining.

note: The Kundalakesi's invocation praises its lord as one who kept nothing for himself and laboured only for others' good (பிறர்க்கே உறுதிக்கு உழந்தான்); Neelakesi 222 mocks the monkey-king's self-offering, which saved no one, as no greatness.
teaches: The dispute is not whether the Buddha gave himself away but whether labour for others counts when, as the Jain argues, it profits no one; the Buddhist praise rests on intention, the Jain rebuttal on result.

note: In verse 58 the king draws his sword at the goddess's place; in verse 67 he puts the sword in his hand aside.
teaches: The same sword marks the king's turn: first the instrument of offering, then what he sets down when the youth's mercy reaches him.

note: The quatrain praises those who hold their vows through unbearable trouble; here the trouble of hunger is the vow itself.
teaches: The quatrain sets trouble as the test of a vow, but the fast makes the trouble a part of the vow, so holding firm means keeping a hunger that ends the keeper's life.

gains.a: the hunger of the fast is seen as the very trouble the vow-keeper is told to bear
gains.b: the quatrain's trial is given an extreme case in which holding on ends in death

note: 1849 shows the adorned body undone by one small prick; Naladiyar 41 says a bit of skin torn off needs a stick to drive away crows.
teaches: Both break the body's finery with a trivial injury, but the epic does it for a king examining his own display, the quatrain to answer a lover's praise.

gains.a: The king's reflection gains the quatrain's crows, which the injury will draw.
gains.b: The quatrain gains a body decked with garland, paste and incense that the injury undoes.

note: 1173 has the king's anger die at his kin's words; Naladiyar 68 says the worthy's anger cools of itself like boiled water.
teaches: The king's anger dies at others' words rather than by itself, so the epic shows a cooling the quatrain says only the worthy manage unaided.

gains.a: The epic king's anger cools only after his kin speak, which the quatrain says the worthy do alone.
gains.b: The quatrain's worthy cooling has no scene of a king and his kin, which the epic gives.

note: 1973 puts the Milechchar of the islands among the animals; 1977 adds that even those of human form among them, who live by cruelty, are brought down.
teaches: The classing with animals in 1973 is widened in 1977 to cover people of human form, so the test shifts from form to livelihood.

note: 3108 has the one who harms for food thrown by two deeds into burning flame; Kural 320 says pains rest on those who caused pain.
teaches: The verse names the form the returning pain takes, a hell of fire, which the Kural's general law does not.

gains.a: the verse's hell is shown as one case of a general law that pain returns to its cause
gains.b: the Kural's law gets a specific place and fire where the pain lands

note: 1762 has the king command the drum after council; 1763 has the drum struck.
teaches: The order given in the council is carried out at once in public sound.

note: 1951 and the following verses give conduct as the ground of hell; Tirumanthiram 165 puts those who do not worship the Lord's form in the seventh hell.
teaches: The sage's list of sins contains no failure of worship while Tirumular's contains little else, so the two define the sinner differently.

gains.a: The sage's conduct list gains a contrast in which hell's gate is worship, which none of its sins names.
gains.b: The Tirumanthiram verse gains a list of acts of harm and greed that earn hell without any lack of worship.

note: 374 separates wealth and wisdom as different fates, and 400 goes further by calling learning the only true wealth.
teaches: Read together, they redefine wealth.

note: 167 says Vijayai's eyes are poison and nectar that madden even sages; in 181 Saccandan is caught in the net of her long eyes.
teaches: The descriptive claim that her eyes overturn the self-controlled is cashed in the plot: the first one they capture is the king whose fall drives the epic.

note: In 256 Madanan's sweating, garlanded chest is likened to the Karthikai lamp lit on a hill; in 262 Kattiyangaran's seizure is a blazing lamp of infamy lit on a hilltop.
teaches: The festival lamp that first flatters the usurper's ally turns, six verses later, into the sign that shows the usurper's shame to the whole land, so the image passes from praise to blame.

note: In kaathai 26 she is told to hear each school's doctrine, see it lacks truth, and only then follow the Buddha's way, and she takes an ascetic's form to do so.
teaches: The debate chapter carries out a method laid down beforehand: hearing the schools is a prescribed stage of her training, not an open inquiry.

note: The Kural calls not looking at another's wife the great manhood; the epic's simile grants that the heart goes out to her and places virtue in the wise man's recalling it.
teaches: Set beside the couplet's ideal of never looking, the simile shows a working form of the virtue the Kural allows only as perfection: the desire arises and understanding turns it back.

gains.a: the simile gains a fixed ethical rule, so the turning arrow is measured against the standard the Kural names as manhood
gains.b: the couplet gains a picture of restraint as a movement out and back, a second chance the couplet's flat 'not looking' leaves out

note: Both cities leave goods unguarded: Puhar's open court keeps bundles safe because a spirit punishes the thief, the Cintamani's merchants leave fallen jewels lying as a matter of their own conduct.
teaches: The pair gives two different accounts of why a rich city's goods are safe, one by fear of a guardian spirit's punishment and one by the citizens' surfeit and habit, so honesty is shown as either enforced or assumed.

note: The idyll's bards wander like birds that search for fruiting trees on a hill the rain has left; the Kural likens the wealth of a man with nayan to a fruit tree ripening in the middle of the town.
teaches: The patron-as-fruit-tree image is seen from the tree's side in the Kural and from the birds' side in the idyll, and the idyll adds the condition the Kural's town tree removes: the guide poem exists because, for the wandering bard, the fruiting tree is far off and must be pointed out.

note: 2906 tells the heir to guard the earth with the sceptre unbent and calls the guarding of dharma a king's highest joy; Kural 546 says the unbent sceptre, not the spear, wins victory.
teaches: The Kural says the straight sceptre wins, and the epic gives the heir a motive beyond winning, that it is the best joy a king can have.

gains.a: the verse's unbent sceptre gets a stated effect, victory, that it does not name
gains.b: the Kural's unbent sceptre gets a motive from inside the king's own heart, a joy of keeping dharma

note: 253 names killing and eating flesh among the sins that sink into leprosy and hell; 2776 names the killers and the deniers of the next world as those who go.
teaches: The reader sees the Cintamani widen the list of sinners from conduct (253) to belief, since the one who denies the next world is sent there too.

note: After the earlier battle Padumukan tended the wounded with ghee and cloths and sent them to beds; here Civakan himself charges his uncle with the care of the wounded before he rests.
teaches: The care of the wounded moves from a friend's improvised kindness to a king's first order, so the epic marks Civakan's kingship by who is told to look after the men who bled for him.

note: Prithidevi fears her senior co-wife will let her fall; the Silappathikaram lists a woman who reared her co-wife's child as her own as a type of pathini.
teaches: The epic sets the co-wife's presumed envy beside the Tamil ideal of the co-wife who cares, so the new queen's fear is read as a convention the other works already know and answer.

note: The plot confessed here is the trick of Yugi set out in verse 109.
teaches: The trick is described in its working in verse 109, but only here does its author call it a departure from the treatises and ask pardon.

note: Verse 140 faults a mighty king for want of grace to the lowly; Kural 557 says that a king's lack of tender regard is to his people as lack of rain to the earth.
teaches: The epic names one flaw in a king otherwise perfect, so the Kural's claim that lack of regard undoes all else is tested against a ruler praised for everything else.

gains.a: A measure of the flaw's weight, which the verse names without saying how much it costs.
gains.b: A concrete king whose every other virtue stands, so the couplet's rule faces a hard case.

note: Dharmadattan forestalls the excuse of sending the king to heaven; in 259 Kattiyangaran uses exactly that excuse, dressed as a promise that the earth will brim with gold.
teaches: The counsellor named the usurper's rationalisation before he spoke it, so 259 reads as a man walking into a trap already shown to him.

note: Maduraikkanchi 24-42 sets fat-mouthed demon women dancing the tunangai around a battle-sacrifice whose cook serves flesh-rice to the soldiers; in 803 a pregnant ghoul dresses herself in the field's remains while Civakan watches and laughs.
teaches: The Sangam poem makes the ghouls' feast part of a rite the king performs, while the epic removes the rite and keeps the dance as a spectacle for the hero's delight, so the motif survives as ornament of heroism.

gains.a: the ritual setting from which the battlefield ghoul descends, which makes Civakan's laughter a presiding king's pleasure
gains.b: a later afterlife of its demon women, cut loose from sacrifice and turned into a toilette parody

note: The mourners link the king's death to the flour cock he struck.
teaches: The mourners trace the poison back to the offering at 145, a reading the narrator does not himself make.

note: The king asks whether his two sons will rule or serve; at 109 the two come to Naga Kumara and become his servants.
teaches: The ascetic's foresight is shown to be exact, so the story makes the sons' loss of the kingdom a matter of fate that no choice of the king's undoes.

note: Both epics give the elephant-fire hunger and both measure it by mountains poured into the sea: here the silver mountain filling the sea, there the hills the monkeys threw into the ocean.
teaches: The Jain and the Buddhist epic share the disease and its image, but the Cintamani cures it with a child's meal in a Jain household while the Manimekalai cures it with the bowl of a renunciant, so each makes its own kind of giver the remedy.

note: The king's cry at 147 that his deed calls him into a garland of births is answered here: the garland is now told birth by birth.
teaches: The lament and the account together show that the foreseen chain was real and also how it runs, which the foreboding alone does not.

note: 1416 shows Kanaka Naman coming to the fight on hearing of the plough-bearer; 1417 shows him struck on the shoulder.
teaches: The listener who joins a fight because he heard of a rival's feats is also the one who is struck down, so the fame that draws him is what ruins him.

note: Nandagon argues from Murukan and Vishnu that lineage should not be thought of in marriage; Civakan at once thinks that a man may not take an unequal wife before one of his own rank.
teaches: The hero answers the herdsman's mythic precedent not by denying unequal marriage but by ranking it, so birth still governs the order of wives in a story that lets him marry across it.

note: Verse 323 claims no one, not even the red-eyed Tirumal in anger, can harm Arikandan; verse 2 says the tale is of the red-eyed tall one who tore the lion.
teaches: The boast of an unassailable prince is held against the hero the poet promised at the start, so a reader hears the council's confidence as a setup for its overturning.

note: 1597 has the jester fear a spirit that is not there; Kural 428 says the knowing fear what should be feared while the fool does not fear it.
teaches: The couplet names the fool who feels no fear where it is due, and the scene shows the other fault, a fear aimed at something unreal.

gains.a: The jester's panic gains a name: a failure to judge what is truly to be feared, not simple cowardice.
gains.b: The couplet gains a counterpart it does not state, in which fear is misplaced on an empty object.

note: 1283 has Arisenan boast that none can stand against his sword; 1294 has a younger youth cut him in two as he draws back.
teaches: The poet puts the boast and the death a few verses apart, so a name proclaimed before the fight is shown to guarantee nothing in it.

note: Kural 1083 has a man say he never knew Death and now does, it being a woman's grace and large war-eyes; 2451 says Death has come in a king's daughter's form and her own jewels bid the onlookers flee.
teaches: The couplet turns Death into one man's private discovery, while the epic makes it a public warning given by the jewels, so a figure of suffering becomes a danger announced to a crowd.

gains.a: a source for the figure of the woman as Death, which shows the jewels' warning is a figure for the pain beauty gives and not an idle boast
gains.b: a scene of bride, ornaments and a watching crowd that shows what in her dress the poet reads as a weapon, which the couplet leaves to the word பெண்டகை

note: Yugi's plan in verse 129 answers the king's forgetting of his lost land in verse 124.
teaches: The poet first blames the king's neglect and then shows who will act on it, so the neglect becomes the cause of the plot that follows.

note: 2843 promises that virtue makes gods in heaven; 3056 says the heaven-dwellers of the enjoyment lands renounce nothing and see nothing but what the Lord's word has said.
teaches: Heaven is the reward of virtue in one verse, and in the other it is a place where renunciation, and so release, is not done.

note: 1256 closes that no one finishes an aim except by hard ripening after kings flee; Kural 473 says many who rose on enthusiasm broke midway.
teaches: The epic offers no cause for the kings' failure, while the couplet blames ignorance of one's own strength.

gains.a: The generalising closing lines get a stated cause of ruin, rising without knowing one's strength.
gains.b: The couplet's warning gets a scene of kings who marched and fled, which makes the broken rise concrete.

claims.gist: the upper gods are free of sickness, anger and enmity
to be a king under whose guard dharma departs is the worst fate a man can call down on himself
the world's sorrow was ended by the grace of the lord of dharma
the ram, with rice set before its face, is the right offering by the books of merit
what seems pleasant in hell becomes a burning
sin from former deeds can overtake even one who does penance with a guileless mind
trees are living beings, as their flowering at a woman's look and touch shows
a tree has no life
a king may offer many killed creatures and a buffalo to the war goddess
brahmin conduct and kings' lives need counsel to flourish
even Indra's rule is borne by masters of the treatise
hearing and copying this story brings children, wealth and heaven
one's remaining span is short and the time to act is now
a king must rely on counsel, and failed counsel destroys him
a king flourishes only through learned poets and counsellors
honour (shame at disgrace) is dearer than life to the warrior
the Jina's lordship is such that Indra himself comes and bows at his feet
the fall from silk to rags is the working of one's own deeds, so wealth gives nothing to hold
a king who has conquered himself is hard for others to conquer
the land of a self-mastering king is rich, as if gold rained on it
the line of great persons is foretold, and a particular man's birth as a Kesava is fixed beforehand
the supreme lord ends the births of ascetics
teaching takes hold only in those of merciful mind who love dharma, not in the deluded and cruel
a harm aimed at a blameless man returns on its sender
the soul has taken and left more human bodies than the sea has sand
suffering begins in the womb and cannot be avoided even by a faultless birth
gods arise without a womb and do not touch the earth

note: 1215 asks whether lives or honour weigh more with the enemy kings; 1224 answers that they keep pride though they feel ruin near.
teaches: The ultimatum's question is answered by the kings' choice, which shows honour overriding fear of death in those the poet says were told to bow.

note: Sridharan arrives in anger and meets the prince in 83, and in 85 he is rebuked and withdraws in fear.
teaches: The threat built in 83 is ended not by a battle but by a minister's speech, so the epic makes counsel the thing that turns the king back.

note: Ainkurunuru 159's friend demands that the lord give back her friend's beauty and go, insisting she is not begging; Kuruntokai 349's heroine refuses her friend's proposal to take back their beauty, saying that asking for it back is like demanding the return of what was given to those who begged, and worse than losing life.
teaches: On a defensible reading the two make incompatible claims about the demand 'give back her beauty', a just reclaiming of what was taken or a shameful asking-back of a gift, which shows the formula belonged to the friend's voice and that the heroine could reject it as beneath her.

note: The youth's fall into the forest in 267 brings the sage's rescue in 268.
teaches: The brother's cruelty ends not in the youth's death but in an encounter that sets his future, which turns the fall into the start of his rise.

note: 498 gives the merchant's reason for the voyage: men born into a weakening lineage must hold it up. Kural 1026 defines good manliness as making oneself able to rule the house one was born into.
teaches: The Kural's manliness of the house is the motive that sends a merchant onto the sea, and the verse adds a division the couplet lacks: restoring the line is the men's part, guarding against shame the women's.

gains.a: the merchant's resolve gains a named ideal, so the voyage reads as family duty and not greed
gains.b: the couplet gains a concrete undertaking and a risk: ruling one's house can mean staking one's life on a voyage

note: Both lay out the city streets full of offering and goods.
teaches: The streets are filled first with sound and incense, then with goods, building one festival picture.

note: 2074 uses three pleasant senses, jewel-light, sandal coolness and flower scent, for the bliss of release, which it calls சிவகதி; Tirumanthiram 325 uses a drink, the nectar of Siva's bliss in samadhi, for the same kind of state.
teaches: Both reach for sensory pictures of a state they say is beyond the senses, but the Jain verse's சிவகதி names a state of release while Tirumular's Siva is the god whose bliss it is.

gains.a: The comparison to light, cool and scent gets a drink image that shows the bliss as unbroken from sitting to lying, which 2074 does not say.
gains.b: The drink of bliss gets a calmer set of images that carry no hint of the intoxication Tirumular is guarding against in this chapter.

note: The epic likens the hero's arrows to the straight minds of the refined; the couplet holds that the straight arrow is cruel and that form proves nothing about worth.
teaches: Read against the couplet, the simile shows the epic choosing the arrow's straightness as a sign of virtue at the very moment the arrow starts a war of slaughter, which the Kural warns is the arrow's real nature.

gains.a: a check on its own praise: the straight arrow it calls a refined mind is, by the couplet, a killer's shape
gains.b: a case of exactly the misreading it warns against, where an admired shape stands in for goodness in a famous poem

note: The Naladiyar says that when a banyan is eaten hollow its aerial roots hold it up, as a son covers a weakened father; Nandagon's banyan seed is the hope that a son of the fallen king lives.
teaches: Set beside the quatrain, the herdsman's seed image takes on the son's work of propping a fallen house, which the epic will make a war for a kingdom rather than a household's shame.

gains.a: the obscure seed image is given its point: a hidden son is the root that will hold the line up
gains.b: the household maxim is seen stretched to a dynasty, where the father is dead and the son does not yet know whom he props

note: Kural 557 says a king's lack of grace is for those who live what the lack of rain is for the earth; 2376 has the king's wealth go as grace to the blind, the sick and the wives abandoned.
teaches: The couplet states the cost of a king's lack of grace in the language of rain, while the epic names those who would be left dry, showing who counts as the people the sceptre owes.

gains.a: The proclamation gains the couplet's picture of grace as rain: help that reaches those who cannot ask.
gains.b: The couplet gains named sufferers, the blind, the sick and the abandoned wife, who are the dry land of its simile.

note: Dhumaketu's boast in 1318 is repeated clause by clause and turned back by the younger king in 1320.
teaches: The answer uses the boaster's own clauses to cut him down, so the boast is shown to be what ruins him.

note: The kid eaten for the sake of heaven is the father who would not kill a kid even to save himself.
teaches: The father who would not purchase his safety with a kid's life is bought into 'heaven' by his son as that kid, so the rite of 196 turns his own refusal into its victim.

note: Naladiyar 3 says kings who rode elephants under the umbrella fall when their deeds turn and enemies take their wives; here the usurper mounts the elephant to proclaim himself and takes Fortune.
teaches: The quatrain names only the fallen king, but the epic shows the other half of the turn: the enemy who rises on the same elephant, a figure the poem's logic marks for the next fall.

gains.a: The epic scene gains a general frame in which the usurper's elephant-back triumph is itself unstable.
gains.b: The quatrain gains a named winner and a cause the poem leaves out: the fallen king's own neglect of rule.

note: 3117 pictures omniscience as a maiden embraced by the king at the top of the worlds, the self still distinct; Tirumanthiram 134 says those who feel the teacher's word become the reality, like ghee mixed in milk.
teaches: Both end in bliss, but the Cintamani keeps lover and beloved two, while the Tirumanthiram dissolves the self into what it meets.

gains.a: the verse's embrace is shown as release that keeps a separate self, which the milk-and-ghee image of union would remove
gains.b: the Tirumanthiram's merging gets a rival picture where the freed one stays apart and enjoys

note: Tirumanthiram 634 says those who do austerity become lords of Amaravati and live in bliss by the Lord's grace; verse 354 says a king who leaves his rule for austerity becomes lord of the gods, with no god named as the giver.
teaches: The same heavenly kingship is credited to the ascetic's own austerity by the Jain sage and to the Lord's grace by Tirumular, so the two disagree about who gives the reward.

gains.a: A giver of the reward, which the sage's prophecy leaves out, against which the claim of earned rule can be measured.
gains.b: A path to the same heaven that needs no grace, which tests the claim that grace gives it.

note: Bhadragiriyar longs for the day he will stop killing and eating lives and hold them as his own life; in verse 60 the two at the killing ground wish the king to spread mercy to every life.
teaches: The Siddhar states mercy as a vow about his own food and conduct; the epic has it spoken as a blessing by the victims to the one holding the sword.

gains.a: the blessing is shown to carry an ethic a Siddhar names as the aim of his tapas, so mercy is the road and not a courtesy
gains.b: the Siddhar's wish to see lives as his own gains a scene where the victim does so for the man about to kill him

note: In 139 Yasodharan refuses to kill a living thing even to save his own life; here he and his mother are said to have killed a cock of flour with a sword.
teaches: Set side by side, they show a stated rule and the later act that breaks it, with 250 giving the cost that carries through every birth.

note: Kural 90 says a guest wilts when the host's face changes on seeing him; verse 963 has the host drink in the guest's beauty and seat him on his own elephant.
teaches: The welcome here is warmer than a kept face, since the host shares his own mount, a test the couplet does not set.

gains.a: The verse lacks the couplet's test that a host's welcome is read from the face.
gains.b: The couplet lacks the case of a host who answers by sharing his own seat of rank.

note: Kural 616 says effort brings prosperity and its absence brings want; Natrinai 252 states the same as the man's resolve (no rare wealth for those who stay) and then shows the planned work blocked by the woman's beauty.
teaches: The pair shows the maxim of effort accepted in full by the lover and yet not acted on, so the Natrinai marks the limit of the Kural's rule: it decides nothing while something dearer than prosperity stands in the way.

note: 1247 praises the god of the asoka as the one who ended karma that cannot be ended; 2745 asks the ascetic's grace to end the darkness of the karma Civakan himself did.
teaches: The hymn's praise of a Lord who ended karma becomes Civakan's own request to have his karma ended, so doctrine turns into a personal petition.

note: 2847 lists the four infinites of the liberated, and 3082 lifts the banner of the fourfold infinite.
teaches: The list of what release gives is shown as something one person takes, with the world swallowed, and not only a catalogue.

note: In Kural 1316 the woman turns the man's 'I thought of you' into proof that he had forgotten her; in 1070 Gunamalai turns his praise of a powder into proof that he forgot her and keeps another in his heart (மறந்தீர், மனத்துள் உறைகின்றாள்).
teaches: The couplet's sulking logic, that any word of the lover proves his neglect, becomes in the epic a weapon aimed at a named rival's beauty, so feigned jealousy is how the epic's wife claims the hero among his many loves.

gains.a: the epic verse gains a recognised move of the ஊடல் convention that shows its accusation is play, not real suspicion
gains.b: the couplet gains a rival woman and a remembered contest as the occasion of the twisted word, which it leaves abstract

note: 686 calls the tribute-seeker a fool who would take the jewel from a venomous cobra's hood; 1225 gives the cobra's venom to the foe's laugh.
teaches: The cobra moves from the hero's image of the danger the foe courts to the foe's own laughing venom, so the image of the poisonous snake cuts both ways.

note: The Kural says the fruit of tending a guest has no fixed measure but is as great as the guest's worth; Suramanjari feeds a guest she takes for a poor old brahmin.
teaches: The couplet assumes the host's offering and its fruit are reckoned by the guest's true worth; the epic shows a host who cannot see that worth, so the fruit she reaps, the end of her vow, is far beyond what she thought she was giving.

gains.a: the feast gains a frame in which its unforeseen consequence is the guest's hidden worth returning on the host
gains.b: the couplet's measure by the guest's worth is tested where that worth is concealed, showing that the return is fixed by what the guest is, not by what the host believes

note: In 402 the lord says that because of a girl he will take the life and the discus of Ashvagriva; in 638 the king names that very discus as the power by which he could cut down the shoulders of the gods.
teaches: The weapon the king trusts is the thing the earlier verse says will be taken from him with his life.

note: Kural 547 says the ruler guards the world and justice guards him if he does not falter; 248 says the king's splendour guards the world even as he sleeps.
teaches: The Cintamani's king, who sleeps in pleasure and loses everything, illustrates the Kural's condition by its breach: majesty without unfaltering justice guards nothing.

gains.a: the verse's claim is placed against a rule that names the condition it leaves out
gains.b: the couplet's 'if he does not falter' is shown at work in a king who faltered through pleasure, not cruelty

note: In 676 her eyes and brows moved as she danced and the watchers were overcome; in 2594 the same eyes and brows play while the king himself watches, his garland opening.
teaches: The dance that once undid a crowd of strangers now undoes the one man it was aimed at, which shows how the same art, once open to all, has been turned to a single patron.

note: The Vidyadhara astrologer read in the planets that her destined husband lives in Rajamapuram; here an omen-reader in Rajamapuram fixes the contest's hour from the moon's conjunction.
teaches: The open contest is framed by two readings of the stars, one naming the city and one naming the hour, so what looks like a public trial of skill is staged as the working out of a decree already read.

note: Kural 388 calls the ruler who does justice and protects இறை; Dharmadattan calls the king a great deity because his favour makes and his anger burns.
teaches: The Kural makes the king's divinity a reward for just rule, while Dharmadattan makes it a matter of the king's power, which lets him use it to protect even a king who has abandoned rule.

gains.a: the councillor's claim is seen to drop the condition the Kural sets, which explains why the story can refute it
gains.b: the couplet's condition is shown to be what separates a just king's sanctity from mere fear of his power

note: The lamb in the slaughter ground nibbles the garland unaware; the kid in 197 knows its fate and its son.
teaches: The Naladiyar's lamb stands for the heedless; the epic sets beside it a lamb that knows, so the reader sees what the heedless have lost.

gains.a: The kid's awareness of 197 gets an older picture of the slaughter-ground lamb that is unaware.
gains.b: The lamb of the quatrain gets a counter-case in which the victim recollects who it was.

note: The dresser draws the creeper of desire in sandal paste on the bride's breasts; the Naladiyar asks whether those who praise sandal and garlands have not seen vultures tear the body when the axle of its cart breaks.
teaches: The painted creeper is told as a high art at its best, so the Naladiyar's corpse image is shown to answer not coarse adornment but the finest.

gains.a: the other side of the sandal-paste art, the body that lies under it, which the tender scene never looks at
gains.b: a worked scene of sandal and garland laid on with great skill, which shows what its warning is aimed at and why it needs saying

note: The companions, taking a passing song as a sign that Civakan lived, put off revenge and scattered to search for him; here they find him and their grief ends.
teaches: The search the companions began in place of revenge ends in this verse, so the grief that had nearly turned into killing the king is finally discharged by a bow at the hero's feet.

note: The Pattupattu's mullai is wild woodland of avarai and kaanthal on a hunters' road ending in a meal of roast game; verse 30 gives the mullai as cropland of sesame, avarai and tuvarai pods.
teaches: The same named tract is a place of hunters' hospitality in the older poem and a place of pod crops in the epic, so the epic poet has turned the mullai from forest road to farmland.

gains.a: The verse gets the older mullai as foil and so shows that its pods mark a farmed mullai that the Sangam poem does not describe.
gains.b: The Pattupattu passage gets a later poet who reads its woodland by its yield, which shows that the tract was open to being counted as farmland.

note: The sage foretold that Civakan would be seized, carried off by a yaksha, and seen again after some days; in 2095 he comes home and his mother's grief ends.
teaches: The prophecy promised only that he would be seen again, and the return shows its cost: the mother was comforted by the word yet still wept herself thin until he stood before her.

note: Kural 351 says the joyless birth comes from a confusion that takes the unreal for real; Soolamani 198 says deeds grow from a seed of lacking true knowledge and ripen into pain through a chain of births.
teaches: The sage supplies a growth path (seed, deeds, ripening, rebirth) for the couplet's bare claim, while the couplet says what kind of knowledge fails.

gains.a: the missing true knowledge is made specific as seeing the unreal as real, a wrong seeing and not just an empty gap
gains.b: the confusion gains the steps by which it ends in birth: a seed that grows into deeds that ripen as pain

note: Verse 108 foretold a man of good speech coming with a letter; in 605 the envoy has come and is paid for his words.
teaches: The astrologer's forecast is kept to the letter, the envoy's reward being the fruit of the arrival it named.

note: The proverb says one's suffering is one's own old deed and the foe only the sent servant; the friends see the usurper's deed ripen and the heir become its agent of Death.
teaches: Read together, the two show the sent-servant idea from both ends: the proverb tells the sufferer not to rage at the agent, while the epic shows men rejoicing to become the agent of another's ripened deed.

gains.a: the friends' cry gains a stated account of how a ripened deed uses a human hand, which explains why they can call Civakan Death without calling him the cause
gains.b: the proverb's consoling rule gains a scene from the agent's side, where the instrument of the deed is glad and armed, which the proverb never considers

note: The cocks take the vow and the nectar of dharma, and in 257 the arrow that kills them still sends them into human birth.
teaches: The vow in 255 is what makes 257 a rebirth and not a fall, and the arrow shows how far the vow's protection reaches.

note: Kural 84 says the fair goddess dwells in the home of one who tends good guests with a glad face; Subhadran, who has kept a great guest-feeding for years (1451, 1453), receives a guest he calls திருமகள் கணவன்.
teaches: The Kural's promise that fortune lives in the hospitable house is made literal: the guest the merchant takes in is the lord of fortune himself and becomes the son of the house.

gains.a: a reason, in the ethics of hospitality, why the long feeding is rewarded by the arrival of Tirumagal's husband
gains.b: a story in which the goddess's dwelling in the host's house arrives as a person, a guest who joins the family

note: Patitruppattu 11 likens the Chera, who reached the sea and felled the enemy's guarded kadamba at the root (முழுமுதல் துமிய), to Murugan who cut down Sur at the root (சூருடை முழுமுதல் தடிந்த); Thirumurugatruppadai 45-60 tells the god's deed itself: he entered the cold sea and cut Sur at the root (சூர்முதல் தடிந்த), the mango at its trunk.
teaches: Thirumurugatruppadai shows that cutting the root in the sea was already the god's signature deed, so the Chera poet's repeated phrase is a claim that the king's sea raid re-enacted Murugan's myth, with the enemy's guardian tree standing in for Sur's tree.

note: In 695 the minister plans to enrage the prince into running into a lion; in 1136 the same minister hides the lion's death and has the cunning lion himself tell it.
teaches: The minister who used the king's pride against the prince now shelters the king from news that wounds it.

note: The Kural's man says the woman who causes his love-sickness is its only cure; Civakan writes that the little parrot she sent has cured his swelling sickness.
teaches: Set beside the couplet's rule that only the beloved herself can heal, the letter shows the cure passing to her token: a sent message relieves the sickness before any meeting, so the remedy can be borne by a proxy.

gains.a: the convention that love's cure is the beloved, against which the parrot's cure reads as a claim about messengers
gains.b: a case of courtship by letter, where the remedy the couplet confines to the woman's presence is carried by a go-between

note: Here a pleasant word beats a gladly given gift. In 225, relieving hunger is a power above the ascetic's.
teaches: A hungry person's view of 92 might differ, which suggests the ranking in 92 assumes someone who isn't in need.

claims.gist: a king sunk in pleasure ruins himself by ignoring wise counsel
the god worshipped is the one who destroyed the ghati karmas
a ruler with every virtue is still at fault if he lacks grace toward the lowest living beings
a dream read by the learned foretells a coming marriage
the Arhat is omniscient but cannot be fully known even by one who names him so
a brave king need not heed a petty word of omen
the mantra heard at the hour of death brings birth among the gods
a small enemy left alone until he has spread can come to conquer
a misfortune that befalls one is the fruit of sin committed
lament befits women, not a man whose enemy lives
a king's duty is to relieve a city's distress and to go back to his own land
right knowledge, faith and conduct together bring heaven, rule on earth and release
it is a king's justice to weigh scheming over fighting and see what can be gained
pride is born of the fire of anger and feeds on the heart's food
flesh dried in the sun and open to crows is unfit for the rite
souls differ in worth like metals according to the deeds that bind them
a woman's joy in love comes at its own ripe time, as the bee comes to the opening bud
the Jina, the victor, who is free of stain, is worthy of praise and worship
harmful deeds return as just such harm
the childless are like trees
the human body is won only by those firmly holding good karma, out of 8.4 million kinds of birth
those who come to bow at the feet of the great must have done hard penance in the past

note: 1985 says only those who hold firmly to good karma come to the human body, out of eighty-four lakh births; Naladiyar 34 says to take the great fruit of the rare body.
teaches: The epic gives the count and cause of the rare body that the quatrain only calls rare, so the urgency has a reason.

gains.a: The count of births gains a use: the rare body is to be pressed for fruit like cane.
gains.b: The 'rare body' gains a measure and a cause: eighty-four lakh births and firm good karma.

note: The quatrain weighs great fear against small pleasure and counsels against another's wife; the keeper, who has just said the king will kill him, then calls the queen's love his best reward.
teaches: The quatrain's reckoning of fear against pleasure is tested on a man who does the sum and then goes ahead.

gains.a: the keeper's boast is set against the king's sword he named in 112, so his reward reads as a risk he has chosen to ignore
gains.b: the quatrain's prudence gets a speaker who has done the sum and gone past it, which the plain rule does not allow for

note: Kural 270 says the destitute are many because few do penance; the rich merchant says he and his daughter have done none.
teaches: The couplet ties lack to the absence of penance; the epic puts the same reasoning in a rich man's mouth, so the want that penance would have prevented is a want of good fortune in a child, not of wealth.

gains.a: the merchant's cry gains a doctrine behind it, that misfortune is the fruit of austerity not done, which makes his helplessness a moral account rather than a complaint
gains.b: the couplet gains a case where the one who lacks is wealthy, showing that its இலர் need not mean the poor

note: The nectar given to the dying dog in verse 14 and the god who comes down to carry Civakan out of prison in verse 15 are, in the story, one being.
teaches: The patikam sets a small mercy and a great rescue one verse apart without naming their link, so the reader learns the epic's working of deeds by noticing that the rescuer is the dog.

note: At 409 the astrologer's sign says Tivittan will split a lion's mouth within a month; at 497 the envoy meets the two princes and weighs them by the rules of his lore.
teaches: The foretold hero now meets the person who must find him, so the astrologer's sign is put to a test of eyes before the envoy speaks.

note: Verse 37 makes the city a woman's body and verse 46 fills its ponds with swans that hear her anklets and fear their mates are gone.
teaches: The poet moves from city as woman to a woman's sound as the cause of the birds' fear, so the beauty praised is also felt as loss, which verse 37 does not show.

note: Tirumanthiram 207 says that union with young women is sweet cane juice in the hand and turns bitter neem in the body; 2598 sets the same pleasure as a sweet harvest of love enjoyed in peace.
teaches: Set against the Saiva warning, the epic's closing image of the king resting in love reads as a stage in a life the epic itself will end in renunciation, not a conclusion.

gains.a: a counterweight inside the poem's praise of enjoyment, to set against the epic's later turn to the Jina's path
gains.b: a worked scene of the pleasure it warns against, drawn at its sweetest, which shows why the warning is needed

note: Asokan takes the vow with fifty-two kings; Maridattan renounces with kings and a merchant.
teaches: The tale that began with a king's renunciation among kings ends with a former sacrificer doing the same, so the vow is shown to reach even the cruel.

note: The Jain five vows and flesh, honey and toddy against the Buddhist ten evil deeds of body, tongue and mind.
teaches: The two lists overlap on killing, theft and lust and differ on the rest, so the reader sees which wrongs the two faiths treat as common ground and which they do not.

note: 1843 has Payapati say that his umbrellas and bowing kings are a gift of his good-deed deity; 1997 says the givers of food become kings with armies and umbrellas.
teaches: The earlier remark that kingship is earned acquires a stated source: a gift of food to the hungry becomes the umbrella.

note: Vijayai's three dreams, which leave her trembling at dawn, are told in 223: the ashoka tree falls and a sprout rises from its root.
teaches: The dream that frightens her is a dream of fall and succession, and when the king reads it (225) he speaks only of the heir and keeps silent on the fall, so her fear at 219 rightly answers the half that is withheld.

note: 2034 says the painless pleasure is the fruit of what was given to austere kings; Kural 42 makes the householder the support of those who have let go.
teaches: A householder's gift to renouncers, a duty in the Kural, is shown in the epic as the cause of a later birth in a land of ease.

gains.a: The pleasure gains a stated cause in an act of giving that any householder can do now, not only in a distant rank of merit.
gains.b: The couplet gains a reward beyond the support of the renouncer: the giver's next birth, which the couplet leaves unsaid.

note: In 239 Dattai, angry in 238, comes with flowers to worship the king and the second marriage is completed.
teaches: Dattai's anger at the news is not allowed to stand; the next dawn shows her worshipping the king anyway, so the epic treats a first wife's resentment as a passing mood rather than a break.

note: Kural 734 defines a land as one free of crushing hunger, unceasing disease and destructive foes; Patitruppattu 13 ends that the land the king guards has flowered, rid of disease and hunger (நோயொடு பசி இகந்து), after showing the enemy lands he ruined.
teaches: The Kural states the absences that make a land; the Chera poem shows who secures them and at whose cost, since the same king's anger is the destructive foe of his neighbours, so the definition is met at home by being broken next door.

note: The companions seized the king's herd as a ruse to bring Civakan out; the princess greets them as the thieves to be punished.
teaches: Read against the staged raid, her mock sentence shows the household already knows the theft was a summons, so the crime against the king becomes a joke at his table.

note: Both picture the bought embrace through a body: the Kural's woman of wealth embraces a stranger's corpse (பிணந்தழீஇ); the epic's net-woman embraces the flesh of wealth (தசை தழீஇ) and throws the body away.
teaches: Set beside the epic's hunter who keeps the meat of wealth and drops the carcass, the couplet's corpse reads naturally as the client handled by the woman, so the disgust in Kural 913 belongs to the trade itself rather than only to the man.

gains.a: the epic's hunting conceit is seen reworking the Kural's own corpse image and verb of embrace
gains.b: the couplet's disputed embracer gains a later poet's figure in which the woman is plainly the one who embraces and the man is the discarded body

note: 1460 lists Civakan's bodily marks without saying who sees them; in 1465 the father, having examined them, decides he is his daughter's husband and takes him in his chariot.
teaches: The catalogue that reads as the poet's praise is revealed as a merchant's inspection, so the marks of a great man work as a test of a bridegroom alongside the astrologer's sign.

note: The fivefold conduct the first teachers spread in verse 54 is here set out as the five vows and three abstentions.
teaches: The earlier verse only names the fivefold conduct, and this one says what the five are.

note: Civakan says that if plunging in water won release the bear would gain it; Tirumular says the holy waters are within the heart, and those who do not bathe there so their deeds perish wander the land.
teaches: Both deny that outer bathing destroys deeds, but Tirumular keeps the bath and moves it inward, while the Jain hero drops it and replaces it with knowledge, vision and conduct, so the two show different ways out of the same criticism.

gains.a: an inward alternative its own mockery does not offer, which shows its answer is substitution rather than interiorization
gains.b: a blunt test, the bear in the pool, for the outward bathing its verse dismisses

note: 2635 has the women fling off garlands and ornaments and sow thorns on Kama's road; Siddhar 19 asks when the singer shall leave silk clothes, gold ornaments, pretence and evil deeds and desire the Lord's feet.
teaches: Both strip off ornament, but one is done as a rite with no god in it and the other is a longing aimed at a god's feet.

gains.a: the epic stripping gets the Siddhar's aim, the Lord's feet, which the verse leaves blank, and shows that its rite aims only at closing Kama's road
gains.b: the Siddhar's longing gets a finished ritual, a fixed hall and day, where the song only asks 'when shall I'

note: Purananuru 233 is a bard's cry at the dawn news of Evvi's wounds, wishing it false; Akananuru 115 recalls the battle where Evvi fell and, on our reading, the bards breaking off and laying down the curved necks of their harps in worship.
teaches: The puram poem gives the bards' words at Evvi's fall and the akam poem their gesture, so together they show that his death was mourned with a known bardic rite that a love poet could cite as an image for seed pods on a road.

note: 3116 has the pyre burn the Lord's jewel-bright body with gods circling and rejoicing; Naladiyar 24 has the drums beat three times and the corpse be covered and the fire taken up.
teaches: The same flame ends an ordinary corpse in grief and a Lord's body in festival, so the pyre's meaning depends on who is burning.

gains.a: the festival pyre is shown in contrast with the common corpse's plain burning, which the gods' honours dress up
gains.b: the quatrain's grieved burning gets a body whose burning is celebrated because nothing of the person is lost

note: In 772 the kings foretell that Civakan will lie pierced by arrows, his beauty and youth wasted; in 816 those same kings vanish like lightning in rain and the Vidyadharas praise his victory.
teaches: The kings' prophecy of his death is answered by their own flight, so the scorn they pour on his youth becomes the measure of their defeat.

note: 1022 has the youth fear her glance as an arrow that will kill him; 1117 takes her eyes as the arrows and his austerity as their reward.
teaches: The same arrow that the fear of the picture-scene dreads is accepted as the prize of the wedding night.

note: Naladiyar says even kings who rode elephants under the white umbrella have been carried off and no one is left over; the verse says kings who kill to last also die and then sink in rebirth.
teaches: The quatrain ends at death; the verse adds that for a king who killed to last, the end is only a sinking into more births.

gains.a: The verse gets the common picture of kings carried off as a witness that the body's span cannot be bought by killing.
gains.b: The quatrain gets a destination after death and the cause that sends a king there.

note: 1680 has the king and his wives clinging to a float in the pond; Akananuru 266 has the husband bathing with young women on a float, whose gossip the wife throws back at him.
teaches: The same float-play is a king's marital pleasure in the epic and a husband's scandal in the akam poem, so what makes it fair or shameful is who the partners are.

gains.a: The pond scene gains a measure of the play as a thing that, with other women, would be a wrong, which the epic never states.
gains.b: The wife's reproach gains a version of the same play with no reproach in it, showing that her anger is aimed at the partners and not the bath.

note: 2985 calls the fruit of good deeds poison and says only crossing the flood of deeds gives bliss; Tirumanthiram 258 makes penance and virtue the boat that carries one across the sea of deeds.
teaches: Both see deeds as a sea to cross, but one holds virtue's fruit to be poison and the other makes virtue the boat, so the two disagree on whether good deeds help or only bind.

gains.a: the epic's claim that merit too binds meets a text that sets virtue and austerity as the crossing itself
gains.b: the Tirumanthiram's boat of virtue meets the Jain view that its fruit is a poison to be crossed

note: 2885 has the prince reason that there is no kin and cut the bond of love; Siddhar 55 wishes to put kin away, like a lotus leaf on water, with the mind far off.
teaches: The Siddhar states a wish for detachment and the prince acts on an argument, so together they show the wish and its grounds.

gains.a: the prince's cut gains the Siddhar's image of being among kin without being wetted by them
gains.b: the Siddhar's wish to put kin away gains the argument that kin were strangers across births, which the song never gives

note: 3120 has the women see the dirt on their adorned bodies and think of ending woman-birth; Naladiyar 46 breaks the woman into entrails, fat, blood and bone and asks which part she is.
teaches: The quatrain gives the analysis of the body's parts and the verse shows women applying a like seeing to themselves.

gains.a: the verse's women get the reasoned list of parts that grounds their disgust, so their turn is more than a mood
gains.b: the Naladiyar's list, offered to men about women, gets a case where women use it on their own bodies

note: The falling crown of 1377 is followed at once by the army's flight in 1378.
teaches: The crown's fall is shown as the cause of the rout, not merely its sign.

note: At 1580 the woman tells Civakan that a Vidyadhara carried her off and his wife made him drop her in the forest; at 1592 her husband says she sent him for water and was gone when he came back.
teaches: The husband's plain account exposes the woman's story as a lie told to the hero, so the reader learns that her helpless plight was itself part of the seduction.

note: 1847 concludes that nothing is better than austerity; Kural 46 asks what is gained by going the outside way if household life is lived in virtue.
teaches: The pair turns on whether household virtue is enough: the king answers from the certainty of death, the couplet from the sufficiency of aram.

gains.a: The king's resolve gains the opposing case that a householder who keeps aram may need no leaving.
gains.b: The couplet gains a ruler for whom death makes household virtue seem insufficient.

note: 2923 has the women wither like garlands on a burning vine when they read the king's intent; Naladiyar 392 has women without their companions hear the rain's thunder as a funeral drum.
teaches: The Naladiyar's grief comes after the absence, while the epic's grief comes before it, from the husband's choice.

gains.a: the verse's withering is shown as the same grief of parting that the Naladiyar describes, felt in advance
gains.b: the Naladiyar's sorrow of parting gains a case in which the man leaves by choice and is not away by chance

note: Tirumanthiram 1464 says kings of the just sceptre and countless great ascetics have fallen; verse 273 says austerity and rule are heavy burdens, harder than lifting a diamond hill.
teaches: The epic stresses how heavy the two burdens are, and Tirumular says that even those who bore both have fallen, so the weight is not the end of the road.

gains.a: A measure of the fall: the ones who fell had borne the hardest burdens.
gains.b: A sense of what the fallen kings and ascetics had carried before they fell.

note: 2957 recalls the rescue of Gunamalai from the elephant, which 1068 shows Civakan teasing her about in the early love.
teaches: The wives hold his old rescue against him, so a joke between lovers turns into a debt called in at the parting.

note: The Kural's man says she will not look at him directly but smiles as if narrowing one eye; the epic says Padumai bound Civakan with a look that looked as if it did not look.
teaches: The averted look that the Kural treats as a sign the man must decode becomes in the epic an act with an effect: the same not-quite-glance does not hint at love, it ties the hero fast, so the convention moves from evidence to force.

gains.a: the convention behind its paradoxical look, which shows the line is a known sign and not a fresh conceit
gains.b: a scene in which the half-look is followed by its consequence, the man bound, which the couplet leaves unstated

note: 784 says friendship isn't for laughter (நகுதல்). 860 makes நகல் the very source of good ways, which Parimelazhagar glosses as friendship.
teaches: The same root gets very different valuations in the chapter on what friendship is for and the chapter on hostility.

note: The quatrain says an old deed seeks out its doer as a calf finds its mother; here the old deed 'stands and burns' the queen in hell.
teaches: The calf's search takes the deed to its doer, and the epic shows what the deed then does once it has arrived.

gains.a: The epic shows the deed after it has found the doer, still burning her.
gains.b: The quatrain gains a case where the deed, once arrived, does not leave until spent.

note: Purananuru 194 sets the dirge drum in one house beside the wedding drum in another and concludes that the maker of the world is unkind; in 2356 one band of women swims in a sea of sorrow and another in a sea of joy on the same morning, while the hero washes his face.
teaches: The epic puts the Puram poet's split world of grief and joy inside one palace and makes one man's victory its cause, so what the Sangam poet blames on the world's maker is shown here as the plain consequence of a deed.

gains.a: a reflective frame that names what is unsettling in its quiet line about two seas of feeling side by side
gains.b: a concrete case in which the division of grief and joy is made by a human act, not by an unkind creator

note: The Naladiyar's wife sets her ever-renewed shyness against women who join many chests for wealth; the Valayapathi says those women serve their payers like பத்தினிப் பெண்டிர்.
teaches: Together they put the difference between wife and courtesan not in the service given, which the fragment says can look the same, but in what the Naladiyar's wife names: a shyness that never wears off and a bond that wealth did not buy.

note: Kattiyankaran bows and promises to bear the yoke so that no blame falls on the land; in 241 he asks his council how to kill the king, laying the impulse on a hostile deity.
teaches: The minister who vowed blameless guardianship later disowns his own intent by blaming a god, so the story pairs the king's excuse by destiny (213) with the usurper's excuse by possession.

note: Kural 24: one who guards the five senses with the goad of firmness is a seed for the finest ground; 962 builds the whole farm, with zeal as the plough, the body as the field, vows as seed, conduct as water and the five senses as the fence.
teaches: The couplet's one image of the guarded self as seed is spelled out as a season of tillage, and its unnamed 'finest ground' gets two harvests, heaven first and release after.

gains.a: a classical root for its allegory, in which the guarding of the five senses already leads to the best place
gains.b: an answer to what வரன் yields, given as a sequence of heaven and release, and a place for vows and conduct beside the guarding of the senses

note: The Kural's lover says his bond with the girl is that of body and life; Civakan tells his sulking wife they are one life in two bodies.
teaches: Spoken with another woman's portrait still in his arms, the claim of a single life becomes an appeasing formula, so the Cintamani shows the Kural's declaration of union put to use in a marriage that is about to take a second wife.

gains.a: Civakan's line gains the weight of the classic declaration it reworks, which makes its hollowness here visible
gains.b: the couplet, spoken in first love, gains a later setting that tests whether the claim survives a rival

claims.gist: the six classes of bodied beings are to be protected with compassion
the senses are to be held in the mind
the fruit of a vow kept in one birth is enjoyed as rank and a wife in a later birth
the sight of the Lord's festival and procession wears away the deeds of those who watch
a king's rule is to be laid aside and the realm passed on when he turns to renunciation
cheating others for gain and lacking compassion lead to animal birth
old deeds drive the soul into suffering
the follower of the Jina's dharma honours the worthy, avoids the mean, gives up anger and pride, and is kind to all
the karma that still remains is removed by giving up rule and standing in penance
what force cannot win might at most be had in gifts brought by women
reviling ascetics, hoarding food and selling the body lead to rebirth as an animal
beauty and high birth are no safeguard against desire's ruin
to leave the doings of desire is the best course
austerity cuts off the fierce deeds of past births and so wins final release
these people are human by birth alone and otherwise animals, for want of shame and conduct
austerity and yoga conquer both deeds and bring perfection, and lesser austerity brings heavenly joy
a king's one-sixth share is his dharma, to be taken only with grace and without oppression
a king should subdue foes by making them bow, not by killing in wrath
a gift to a worthy recipient grows into great wealth; a gift to the unworthy yields little and vanishes
a fish taken for the kin's rite is a fitting thing for the king to use
a forest life that keeps its wives is no renunciation and breaks no deeds
the ascetic's life frees a man from anger and cares
the ground of the rite must be prepared and its measure learned by reciting the Veda

note: Vijayai says deed's force scatters us like clouds and there is no lasting fellowship; the Naladiyar says kin arrive unasked and leave wordless, leaving the body as a bird leaves its nest.
teaches: The Naladiyar says parting happens at death; Vijayai says it is the working of deeds even in life, which is why she can ask her son to loosen his own attachments now.

gains.a: the verse's cloud image of scattering gets the further picture of the bird leaving the body
gains.b: the Naladiyar's kin-leaving is given a cause in deeds, which it itself leaves unstated

note: The Naladiyar calls those who prattle of astrology the greatest fools; the epic has a king act on an astrologer's word, which proves true.
teaches: Two Jain-tradition texts judge the astrologer oppositely: the quatrain dismisses his lore beside the duty death makes urgent, while the epic makes his reading the hinge of its plot. The tension holds only if the quatrain is read as denying astrology's truth, not just its worth.

gains.a: the epic's trust in the astrologer is set against a strand of its own tradition that scorns that lore
gains.b: the quatrain's scorn is shown to stand in a renouncer's frame that a court narrative does not share

note: The Kural says a king who does not think matters through with his circle and then lashes out in anger sees his fortune shrink; in 37 Pradyota rages after the ministers have spoken.
teaches: The king here has taken counsel and yet his anger still rules the outcome, so the Kural's warning is about whether counsel is heard, not just whether it is asked.

gains.a: a king who does hear his circle and still gives way to rage, which the Kural's rule does not cover
gains.b: a scene in which the king's anger leads at once to a plot rather than to a loss of fortune, as the couplet only warns

note: Verse 463 puts a fire of desire within the women that sends up lines like smoke; Naladiyar 89 says desire burns the mind itself and is more to be feared than arrow, fire or sun.
teaches: The epic shows the fire of desire as marks on the body, and the Naladiyar says what the fire burns, the mind, so each supplies what the other lacks.

gains.a: A statement that this fire burns the mind and is worse than outer fires.
gains.b: A body in which the fire shows as smoke-lines of fine hair.

note: Both list the body as a thing of filth with nine openings that dazzles the deluded; Naladiyar's fool is the lover, Civakan uses the inventory to refuse a woman.
teaches: The epic shows the Naladiyar's anatomy of the body being used by a man at the very moment of seduction, as a defence rather than a sermon, and by a hero who will still take wives, so the disgust is a tool of restraint, not a rule for life.

gains.a: Civakan's catalogue is placed in a known tradition of meditating on the body's foulness to cure desire, which marks it as a deliberate discipline and not a passing mood
gains.b: the quatrain's general mockery of the fool gets a speaker, a woman before him and a test, which it lacks, and the test is passed by one who is no ascetic

note: Those who saw the princess, the narrator says, would never look upon the world of release; at the epic's end Civakan, having tasted the pleasure of women whose beauty makes the heavens bow, wants it no more and goes to release.
teaches: The hyperbole that beauty shuts out release is a claim the epic's own ending answers, since its hero is the one who saw all such beauty and still reached release, so the line marks the stake of the story rather than its verdict.

note: Pattinathar asks what breasts, union with women and gathered wealth can do against the coming struggle, and says the god put an eyeless needle in his hand; Civakan stops wanting women's pleasure because he has tasted a greater sweetness.
teaches: Both rich men turn from women and wealth, but the Siddhar's ground is their uselessness before death and a sign from Siva, while the epic's is a higher bliss already tasted, so the same turn can be told as a loss seen through or as a lesser pleasure outgrown.

gains.a: the epic's sweet simile is set against a bitter Saiva account of the same turn, showing that the Cintamani makes renunciation a gain of pleasure, not a flight from it
gains.b: the Siddhar's turn, which rests on death and a god's token, is shown to be one motive among others, since a Jain hero leaves the same goods with no god sending a sign

note: Both speak of a help weighed against earth and heaven: the couplet says they cannot repay it; the king says the help itself gave him earth and heaven, and finds no requital.
teaches: The pair shows a king accepting the couplet's verdict that such a debt is unpayable and answering it with a daughter, so the unpayable gift becomes a bond of marriage instead of a repayment.

gains.a: The king's 'I see no requital' is placed within the Kural's doctrine of gratitude, which explains why he does not offer wealth.
gains.b: The couplet's abstract measure of earth and heaven gets a case where the debtor still acts, choosing kinship over payment.

note: Verse 52 gives Payapati a gentle face for those who come near; Kural 386 says a king easy to see and gentle in speech is praised above others.
teaches: The epic's king is gentle only to those who draw near and hot to foes, so the Kural's single ideal is shown split in two by the king's own enemies.

gains.a: The verse gains a standard that says why being easy to approach counts as praise in a king, which the city-description leaves unstated.
gains.b: The couplet gains a king who keeps his gentleness for friends and is hot to foes, a limit on a rule the couplet states without exception.

note: 2904 orders the youth who will guard the world brought; 2912 shows the king dressing a youth and making him crown prince.
teaches: The call for a successor is answered by the king's own hands adorning him.
