note: 251 says no rival word can rise under a king's command, as no tree grows under a tree; 253 says keeping would-be leaders on equal footing is living with a snake.
teaches: 251 states the fact of single authority and 253 the danger of breaking it, so together they explain why a king keeps the ambitious beneath him.

note: In Purananuru 248 the white water lily that was a girl's garment becomes the alli a widow eats; in 355 the stamens of ripe water lilies and wild rice dry in the hermitage courtyard as Vijayai's food.
teaches: The water lily carries the widow's fall from adornment to bare food in both poems, but in the epic the lily-food sits beside a nursing calf that sends her thoughts to her son, so the widow's diet is joined to a mother's longing the Sangam widow does not have.

gains.a: the passing detail of drying lily stamens is identified as the widow's food, so the hermitage scene is read as widowhood
gains.b: the Sangam widow's lily gains a later life in which the same food marks a mother waiting for her son

note: The patikam tells how the king of the middle country (மத்திம தேய மன்னன்) came out to receive Civakan on seeing his bow; in 1214 the god foretells that meeting (மத்திம தேயம் ஆளும் ... கண்ணுறு குணம்) before the journey begins.
teaches: The meeting the summary reports as the king's response to the hero's bow is, in the god's speech, a fortune already laid out on the road, so the poem frames a political welcome as the fruit of a divine guide's foreknowledge.

note: The ministers settle on taking an elephant by showing one; Udayana walks into the grove and sees the false elephant.
teaches: The ministers' choice of lure in 38 is fitted to a king who is hunting for his elephant, which verse 47 shows working.

note: 1208 likens the straight red road to the minds of chaste women; 1212 likens a road splitting into many forks to the hearts of women on the path of marriage.
teaches: If மணநெறி மகளிர் are married women, the same speech makes women's minds the figure of both the one straight road and the forking one, showing the simile serves the road and carries no settled view of women.

note: Both place the work before an assembly of the discerning: the Soolamani says the discerning in the king's assembly accepted it, while the Cintamani says it was set out to be told to the assembly of the discerning.
teaches: The Soolamani states the assembly's acceptance as already given, where the Cintamani only offers the story for it, so one poet claims approval and the other asks for it.

note: Kural 228 asks whether hard-eyed hoarders who keep and lose do not know the joy of giving; the verse ranks those without wealth above those who have it and only guard it.
teaches: The couplet says the hoarder misses a joy; the verse goes further and ranks him below the man who has nothing, so wealth kept unused is shown to be worse than poverty, not merely less than giving.

note: Both show a queen's resentment at a king's divided heart, but Dattai's anger ends in worship and the Pandya queen's sulk ends in the king's blindness.
teaches: The Silappathikaram makes a queen's sulk the opening that lets the goldsmith's lie in, while here the first queen's anger is quickly absorbed; the same domestic feeling has opposite consequences.

note: 1627 crowns the groves as kings and hangs jewels on every branch; 1643 says the women conquer the flower-grove with their waists, glances and limbs.
teaches: The grove made a king in 1627 is taken by the women, so the same grove is first a court and then a thing conquered.

note: 1517 shows the hero holding a mountain in one hand; 273 says even a man who could carry a diamond hill finds austerity and rule heavier.
teaches: The hero's lift is the lighter of the burdens that 273 weighs, and rule, not strength, is what he must still carry.

note: 2072 has the hero reach release by his own vision, knowledge, mastered mind and long meditation; Tirumanthiram 126 has the freed ones climb the thirty-six tattvas as a ladder to release, enter the light of bliss and see Sivam.
teaches: Both texts describe release as a climb by stages, but 2072 ends in a world of release won by the self's own effort while Tirumular's ladder ends in seeing Sivam.

gains.a: The hero's path gets a counter-picture in which the top of the ladder is a seen god, which the verse, with no god in it, does not have.
gains.b: The ladder gets a way of release in which the climber is complete without the vision of a lord, which the couplet does not allow.

note: In Purananuru 71 the Pandya swears that if he does not see the backs (புறம்) of the kings who have joined against him, may he be parted from his wife; Civakan swears that unless he sees the kings' backs (புறக்கொடை) and embraces the lady, may his name perish.
teaches: The vow keeps the Sangam form, allied kings and the sight of their backs, but moves the woman from the forfeit to the prize: the Pandya risks his wife, Civakan stakes his name to win a bride.

gains.a: its genre: the வஞ்சினம் of a king facing allied enemies, with the shape of a named forfeit
gains.b: a variant in which the beloved is what the vow wins rather than what it puts at stake, showing the form can serve courtship as well as kingship

note: Puhar's open court leaves traders' bundles unguarded because a thief is made to carry his load and whirl; Hemangadam's pools hold gold that lies untaken because no one wants it.
teaches: Two epics praise a city by its untaken wealth but give opposite grounds, fear of a punishing power in the Silappathikaram and simple satiety in the Cintamani, so the marvel is not one convention but two theories of order.

note: The spies' bare report in 169 is followed in 170 by the minister's own telling of Udayanan's deed.
teaches: The king's judgment in 169 rests on spies alone, and the minister's account in 170 is what turns it into joy.

note: The Kampili king dies by arrows in the chest that women's breasts had ploughed; later the warrior whose chest is flushed from pressing women's breasts scatters burning arrows.
teaches: The chapter uses the lover's chest twice, once as the place where death enters and once as the source of the killer's fire, so the same mark of love signals both the victim and the victor.

note: 797 says dropping a fool's friendship is gain. 805 says when an old friend hurts you, consider it folly and go on.
teaches: The same பேதைமை is a reason for leaving in one chapter and an excuse for staying in the next, and the only difference is how old the bond is.

note: Verse 845 puts Arkakirti on his own elephant; verse 963 has the Podanam king raise him onto the king's own young elephant.
teaches: Arkakirti's own elephant is replaced by the host-king's, marking the passage from commander to honoured guest.

note: Kural 329 says those whose work is killing are base in the eyes of the discerning; 1205 calls the forest bowmen who kill travellers embodiments of sin (பாவ மூர்த்தியர்).
teaches: The couplet judges a deed, killing, while the epic fixes the same judgment on a forest people as a class, so the pair shows how the ethics of not-killing could harden into a picture of hunters as sin incarnate.

gains.a: the couplet's ground for the label: the hunters are condemned for the work of killing, not for being foresters
gains.b: evidence of how the principle was applied to whole groups living by the bow, which the couplet's general wording does not show

note: In 103 the friend is glad that the keeper's form will end the queen's passion; in 111 the same friend carries the queen's desire to that body.
teaches: The sight meant to cure the queen's desire turns into the errand that fulfils it, so loathing proves no barrier once the friend takes the queen's side.

note: 2002 offers the vow of not killing to kings as one that leaves no conquest out of reach; Kural 325 ranks not-killing highest among those who renounced.
teaches: The epic recasts non-killing as a king's way to win, where the couplet ranks it only among renouncers.

gains.a: The sage's claim for kings gains a ranking from the Kural, which sets non-killing above every other renunciation.
gains.b: The couplet gains a ruler as its audience: a king who keeps the vow and still seeks conquest, which it never considers.

note: 1412 cries that the young prince has fallen and the army heaves; 1414 brings the elder brother and the plough and the army roars again.
teaches: The army's despair and its roar are made by one man's presence, so the verses show whom its courage hangs on.

note: Both use the wood-apple swallowed by the elephant, whole in shell and emptied within: the Cintamani for a king whom Fortune has left, Tirumular for Siva swallowing soul, states and world.
teaches: The same figure of a shell kept whole while its substance is taken means ruin for a king and consummation for a soul, so Tirumular turns a stock image of loss into one of absorption in Siva.

gains.a: the epic's compressed simile is confirmed in its sense of an outwardly intact but emptied reign
gains.b: the Saiva verse is shown inverting an image whose ordinary use in narrative was loss of fortune

note: Verse 107 has Podanam's astrologer read a dream that a Vidyadhara king will come and give a daughter; here the Vidyadhara king's own astrologer reads the same match from the ridge and adds what the king gains by it.
teaches: Two astrologers on two sides of the sky foretell the same match, and only the ridge's gives the giver's reason, two rows of the ridge.

note: Kural 1268 has the man, held by the king's war, wish that the king win so that he may join his wife and hold the evening feast for guests; Natrinai 374's man, returning from his work, asks travellers about the wife who longs to feast guests yet weeps.
teaches: The couplet gives the feast for guests as the man's own goal after duty, while the Natrinai poem puts the same wish in the wife and shows it unfulfilled in her tears, so the household's guest-feast was the shared picture of reunion that each partner ascribed to the other.

note: Both put the parted woman at night with no companion but herself.
teaches: The couplet's woman mocks the night for having only her as companion, and the epic's woman, as alone, makes her own reflection the companion and consoles it, so the loneliness turns inward on the self.

gains.a: the epic verse gains the Kural's frame of the night that has no companion, which shows her talking to her image is the extreme of that solitude
gains.b: the couplet gains a scene where the absence of any companion is acted out, not stated

note: 3132 has Nandan and his friends piling up penance by effort; 3134 ends their lives on the mountain with rebirth as gods.
teaches: The penance begun in one verse comes to its fruit two verses later, so the story shows the deed ripening into a heavenly birth and not into release.

note: Nandagon turned back from suicide hoping, like a banyan seed, that the royal line survived; the patikam at 26 has Civakan spread his just sceptre over the land.
teaches: The cowherd's private hope is the plan of the whole epic, and he states it to the very heir he thinks may be lost.

note: She knelt in Kama's shrine and begged the god for Civakan's chest; he now bows to her feet as to a goddess and begs her grace.
teaches: Worship runs both ways in one shrine: the girl's prayer to Kama for the man is turned into the man's prayer to the girl, so the deity she addressed is replaced by the lovers themselves.

note: Rudradattan counts the konrai-wearing god's taking the mountain-daughter as his half as a stain and a great blame; Tirumanthiram 16 names the same god by that half-woman form as the one the gods delight in.
teaches: The same mark of Siva, his body shared with Uma, is a counsellor's example of lust's disgrace in a Jain epic and a title of praise in Tirumular's invocation, so the image itself is where the schools part.

gains.a: the counsellor's slight is seen to strike at a form the Saiva poets hold central
gains.b: the invocation's epithet is shown to be one a rival tradition read as a scandal

note: Padumai, after one look at Civakan, lost restraint, bloom and bangles; the women of the city now say they lose their bloom and bangles after seeing him.
teaches: What Padumai suffered alone is now the whole city's lot, so his beauty is shown to unsettle a crowd as well as one girl.

note: The Neelakesi praises those who leave home for forest and hill and strive with knowledge to wear away their deeds; Civakan says leaving the house of women for the forest does not wear away old sin carried within.
teaches: Read together, the two Jain epics place the cause of release not in the forest but in the knowledge the Neelakesi names (ஞானமொடு), which the Cintamani's ascetics lack until Civakan supplies it in 1436.

note: The conch and its sound answer the weighing and the sealed pit that Chandakarman offered as proof.
teaches: The reply meets each of his tests by name, so the reader sees that his proof depends on the soul being a thing that could be weighed or seen leaving.

note: The Yasodhara's opening praises the omniscient lord whose feet teach release by leaving karma; the Naga hymn praises him as all-knowing and as the one who burned every old deed.
teaches: The Jain epics' praise of the lord is the same act twice, here as a promise of teaching and there as a list of what the lord has already done to his own karma.

claims.gist: assent to the teaching while still killing is not understanding it
the dream is a sign that the lost wife lives and will be won back
the rare austerity born of giving is found only in a few
the self cannot be destroyed, and harm done to the body is not harm to what is one's own
those who do not know suffer the faults of their own deeds, yet can put off evil deeds by keeping small good vows
a gift paid for by killing animals yields no fruit that can be reckoned
omniscience is a bliss at the height of the three worlds, pictured as the embrace of a maiden
each vow brings its own worldly fruit: lordship for not killing, trusted speech for truth, great standing for not stealing
killing without pity swells karma, and the suffering it brings in later births ends only through good dharma
one who cages and parts others is in turn caged and parted
present enjoyment is the fruit of earlier austerity
the gods are of four kinds
no one stays free of attachment once he has gained such riches
when the king's sceptre bends, rain fails, chastity breaks and the world is ruined
the ancient teaching is a sweet word that cuts the enemy-deeds that cling
fear is of no use against what must come
no outward sign, not even reverence or tears, should be trusted, for those who trusted have perished
love's burning comes as the fruit of a former deed
the interval before death is shorter than a blink
births recur, and a woman may wish her future births to repeat a present joy
the Jina destroyed his deeds, spread unending knowledge and taught a good path
those who dispute the Lord's greatness are bound by a quarrel of deeds that can be undone
robbing and oppressing the weak for their wealth is repaid with beating in hell
the Arhat of the three umbrellas is to be worshipped at his feet
one king's shelter over the whole earth outdoes the lands of effortless enjoyment
the king, learning and the sun are the three eyes of the world
austerity overcomes the binding deeds and brings final perfection

note: Verse 50 says the golden city seems an Indra's heaven come down to earth; verse 469 has a Vidyadhara, who knows the sky, judge that this is heaven.
teaches: The poet's praise of the city as heaven is confirmed by a sky-dweller who can compare, so the boast is turned into an outsider's verdict.

note: 2797 says the body is a grove burned by the fire of disease; Siddhar 63 says this life has no standing, like a bubble on water.
teaches: Jain teacher and Siddhar agree that the body does not stand, but one asks escape from disease and the other from rebirth by grace.

gains.a: the verse gains a prayer for release, which the Siddhar adds
gains.b: the Siddhar song gains a concrete picture of how the body ends, in disease

note: The prince at 496 asks why the Vidyadhara bows to them; 500 gives the answer, that those who bow at their feet have done hard penance.
teaches: The bow is first met with surprise and then given a reason, so the envoy's courtesy is shown to rest on a belief about merit and not on mere flattery.

note: Amirthamathi once defended her fortune as the fruit of an earlier deed; the same law now explains her disease.
teaches: The queen's own argument for her desire turns on her: she cited former deeds as the source of what one has, and her sickness is that source's other side.

note: Kural 10 says only those at the Lord's feet cross the sea of births; the hymn says those who bow to the lord on the lion throne become gods and then reach release.
teaches: The hymn makes the crossing of births a graded gain, gods first and release after, where the couplet states it only as a crossing for those who reach the feet.

gains.a: the hymn's promise of release is read as the Kural's crossing of births with a stage of divine rank before it
gains.b: the couplet's one-step crossing is given a sequence of worlds the worshipper passes through

note: 1759 has the father hold his sweat-brow daughter after ball-play; Akananuru 17 recalls a girl too tired for a ball game who lay in her mother's arms.
teaches: The tired child resting in a parent's arms is the last scene before she leaves for a husband, by public choice in the epic and by flight in the akam poem.

gains.a: The epic's scene of the father holding his daughter gains the foreboding of loss that the akam poem builds from the same picture.
gains.b: The foster mother's memory gains a case where the father arranges the girl's marriage openly, which the elopement she mourns has bypassed.

note: The Kural asks what one who keeps household life in dharma could gain by going the outer way; in the Cintamani the whole household, brother, friends and wives, goes that way and reaches a higher state.
teaches: The Kural's question assumes a householder could gain nothing more by leaving, but the epic answers it by having a just king's whole household leave together and arrive at the state that is ever new.

gains.a: the epic's mass renunciation is read as an answer to a Tamil defence of household life, not only as story
gains.b: the couplet's rhetorical question is shown to be contestable from inside Tamil literature, by a narrative that claims a gain beyond the householder's

note: Both turn on a small child's hand in the food: Kural 64 says gruel stirred by children's small hands is sweeter than nectar; 188 lists the child's touching, biting, stirring and scattering of ghee rice.
teaches: The Kural makes the image a measure of sweetness, while the Pandya king makes its absence a verdict that a rich man's feasting life is profitless, so one scene serves as delight in one book and as the test of a wasted life in the other.

note: 1862 has the minister name the austere sage's feet as the only refuge; 2003 is the sage's first reply, that austerity is hard to say even for sages.
teaches: The refuge sought in 1862 answers only by admitting that the thing sought is hard to put into words, so the king must be taught in steps.

note: The kings in the battle cried that Civakan's chariot was the peacock and he was Murugan; the women now call him Murugan's younger brother.
teaches: The same god-likeness that struck the kings with terror strikes the women with desire, showing the epic fits one figure to two audiences.

note: 1556 shows the king settled under the moon-white umbrella; Naladiyar 3 says kings who rode under umbrellas have fallen when their deeds turned.
teaches: The poem sets Tivittan at the top of his glory, and the quatrain supplies the warning that such a place is held by deeds and can be lost.

gains.a: The opening praise gains a measure that the umbrella is no guarantee, so the lord's net of women reads as a risk.
gains.b: The quatrain gains a king shown at his height with no fall yet in sight, which is the moment it speaks to.

note: The Kural says penance is striven for here because what is desired is obtained as desired; the onlookers say only women who did rare penance before could be born to sleep on Civakan's chest.
teaches: The onlookers take the couplet's promise at its word and fill 'whatever is desired' with a husband's embrace, showing how the motive the Kural offers for penance could be heard as making penance the price of pleasure in the next birth.

gains.a: a doctrinal rule behind its onlookers' wonder, that what is gained now is the fruit of penance done before
gains.b: a concrete example of what ordinary people wanted penance to bring, which tests how wide the couplet's 'whatever is desired' is meant to be

note: 1869's people hear the drum as the sign of a long life and a blessing; Naladiyar 23's wedding drums turn to funeral drums the same day.
teaches: The same drum is a promise of long life in the epic's crowd and a warning of death in the quatrain, and the pair shows how a listener's state decides what it announces.

gains.a: The citizens' blessing gains a shadow of death that they do not see but the king, who has just asked whether anything beats Death, does.
gains.b: The quatrain gains a case in which the drum's joy is not reversed into mourning but turned to a king's resolve to leave.

note: The Kural's woman demands to be told whether her man will go; Civakan leaves while Kemasari sleeps, so that she cannot ask.
teaches: The secret night departure is the hero's way of avoiding exactly the plea the couplet voices, and the couplet names what Kemasari is denied: the chance to speak before the going.

gains.a: Kemasari's silent loss is given the words she never gets to say
gains.b: the couplet's plea is shown its counter-move, a leaving timed so the plea cannot be made

note: The queen's longing named in 242 is given its object in 243.
teaches: The vague longing of 242 is shown to be a wish for flight in the sky, which sets the plot of the next verses in motion.

note: 90 asks whether deer herds can stand where a fierce tiger rages; Kural 599 says even a huge, sharp-tusked elephant fears when a tiger attacks.
teaches: In both the tiger is the spirit that neither numbers nor size can resist, but Avvai sets it on a herd to praise a king while the Kural sets it on an elephant to teach ookkam, so one image served both royal praise and a general maxim on energy.

note: Marusi's pairs, fire in command and cool in giving, name two of the four things Kural 390 calls the light of kings: giving and a straight sceptre.
teaches: The envoy's pairs put two marks of the Kural's ideal king into the temperature of one man, so command and giving are shown as tempers, not as separate duties.

gains.a: The verse lacks the standard that makes its pairs more than ornament: the four marks the couplet calls the light of kings.
gains.b: The couplet lacks a picture of how command and giving sit together in one king, which the fire and cool pairs give.

note: In 899 Suramanjari, hearing Civakan call her powder unfit, vows penance until he comes defeated to worship her anklets; in 1069 Civakan asks Gunamalai whether that harsh word is arrow or nectar to him.
teaches: The hero knows his verdict both won him Gunamalai and earned him a rival's vow against him, so his teasing question names the double fruit of one judgement.

note: The couplet says to cut a thorn tree while young; the verse says no enemy, however soft and small, should be called small, using the snake that kills an elephant.
teaches: The couplet's remedy is to strike early, while the epic's is to guard always, so the same fear of a small foe yields attack in one and vigilance in the other.

gains.a: the verse's warning gains the couplet's point that a small foe grows, which explains why softness is no safety
gains.b: the couplet gains an alternative to striking first, the defence of a man who cannot yet fight his enemy openly

note: In 707 the prince swears to split the lion's mouth; in 1135 the spy tells that the younger bull has split it and the sky-dwellers shake.
teaches: The vow's keeping is told from the enemy's side, where it is felt as terror rather than triumph.

note: Naladiyar 34 tells one to take the great fruit of a rare body while it lasts; verse 774 says the body yields no fruit if it cannot help the afflicted.
teaches: The body's fruit is named as aid to others in trouble, where the quatrain leaves what the fruit is to the word virtue.

gains.a: The verse lacks the impermanence of the body, the cane refuse that makes using it now urgent.
gains.b: The quatrain lacks a concrete form of virtue, the relief of the helpless, that the verse gives it.

note: The maid argues that moisture makes the bad good and drying makes the good bad; the Kural bids one examine qualities and faults, see which prevail, and take that.
teaches: The maid's argument exposes what the couplet assumes, that qualities hold still to be weighed; if condition changes them, weighing by inspection cannot settle a dispute, which is why the epic turns to the bees.

gains.a: the maid's retort is seen to strike at the method of judgement itself, not just at Civakan's verdict
gains.b: the couplet's method gets a limit: it needs qualities that are stable or a test that does not depend on the examiner's eye

note: The father has every carved figure made female so no male form is seen; later Civakan is told to hide by the golden image of Kama in the god of love's temple.
teaches: A ban thorough enough to change the sex of statues still leaves the love god's own image standing, and that is the gap through which the excluded man is brought in.

note: 2628 has the matrons go in palanquins to their renunciation; Tirumanthiram 153 has the lord of the town mount for the last time a palanquin of the burning ground.
teaches: One kind of vehicle is shown going two ways: a rich woman's palanquin carries her to a life given up while still alive, and the lord's palanquin carries him to the burning ground whether he chooses or not.

gains.a: the epic palanquin gets the Tirumanthiram's irony that the ride of honour ends in the burning ground, so the matrons' ride reads as taking that last ride first and by choice
gains.b: the Tirumanthiram's palanquin gets a counter-case in which the ride is boarded willingly before death, which its picture of the lord's last journey leaves out

note: Veeranathan's rain of virtue in verse 5 is set beside the Kural's rain that comes where the king rules justly.
teaches: The epic gives the rain to the tirthankara's teaching, where the Kural makes it the reward of the ruler's sceptre.

gains.a: The epic's rain of virtue gets the Kural's older idea that rain follows the justice of the ruler.
gains.b: The couplet's rain of justice gets a second source: the lord's dharma, not the king, brings the fall.

note: Mullaippattu's king lies sleepless in his tent thinking of elephants wounded by spears and of men who fell repaying their food; Nedunalvadai's king rises and goes out at midnight to see his wounded.
teaches: The two camp kings show one care in two forms, remembered in bed in Mullaippattu and acted out by walking the lines in Nedunalvadai, so the night-time thought for the wounded is a fixed mark of the good war king in these idylls, the more vivid of them putting it into motion.

note: 1305 sets Kamukan, learned in the arts, with his bow; Naladiyar 386 likens a modest woman's beauty to a sharp sword in a clear-minded hero's hand.
teaches: The epic shows the learned hero whose skill the quatrain only uses as a simile, so a warrior's mind and weapon are tied.

gains.a: The learned bowman is placed in a stock of images where skill governs the weapon, which the verse alone does not state.
gains.b: The comparison gets a concrete clear-minded hero who actually wields the weapon in the next verse.

note: 3082 tells the cutting of the four destroying karmas and the knowing of the three worlds; 3092 sings it as the Lord's own deed.
teaches: The event of 3082 becomes the praise of 3092, so the narrator's story is shown as the hymn's ground.

note: The Kural binds the one at the king's side to speak what is good even to a king who destroys counsel; in the Cintamani the counsel comes from Wisdom as minister, after the realm is already given away.
teaches: With the minister's office handed to the usurper, the duty the Kural lays on the counsellor falls to the king's own wisdom, and it speaks only when advice can no longer save the realm.

gains.a: the figure of Wisdom as minister is placed within the Kural's account of the counsellor's duty
gains.b: the couplet's duty is shown with its limit: counsel that comes too late can only plan an escape

note: Kural 1269 says one day is like seven to those waiting for the absent one's return; Civakan tells Gunamalai the day he was parted from her was like an aeon.
teaches: The epic moves the measure of absence from the waiting woman to the returned man and inflates it from seven days to an aeon, said only once the parting is over and as a gift of words.

gains.a: Civakan's hyperbole is placed in the Kural's tradition of time stretched by longing
gains.b: the couplet's longing, which commentators argue about assigning to the man, is here plainly spoken by a man to the wife he left

note: Kural 1087 likens the cloth over her firm breasts to the face-cloth over a rutting elephant's eyes; in 1483 her breasts are bound by a bodice as cruel things must be bound.
teaches: Both treat the covering of the breasts as a restraint put on something dangerous; the epic adds that the binding fails, since the bound breasts still wreck her waist and him, while the Kural's cloth only warns.

gains.a: a reading of the bodice as a restraint on a dangerous force, which explains why the verse calls the breasts கொடியன
gains.b: a sequel to the image, in which the covering does not hold and the danger it marked comes to pass

note: Two claims about the sharpest edge (எஃகு). In 759 wealth is the sharpest steel for cutting an enemy's pride. In 773 the edge of valour is helping that enemy when he falls.
teaches: Cutting and sparing are both called sharpness.

note: The omen-reader foretells that the king's army will break leaving umbrella and பிச்சம்; in 437 the army breaks, throwing down elephants, peacock-plumed standards, பிச்சம் and banners.
teaches: The first half of the prophecy comes true to the detail of the dropped standards, which gives the reader warrant to trust its second half before Civakan has even set out.

note: Siddhar 696 says the poet wandered over every forest and hill until his legs ached without seeing the Lord who moved within his body; 1603 shows crowds climbing a hill to shed their sins.
teaches: Within the Saiva tradition itself the climb that the epic describes approvingly is mocked as wasted walking, so the pairing shows the Siddhars turning against a practice that Jains and Saivas otherwise held in common.

gains.a: a critic's view that shows what the epic's narrator takes for granted in describing the pilgrims
gains.b: a picture of the very pilgrimage the Siddhar rejects, with its anklets, lac and crowds

note: 1591 has the jester ask why the asoka bears red shoots at its foot; 1592 has the king show that they are women's lac-stained footprints.
teaches: The jester's puzzlement is the setting for the king to show how the grove's flowering is linked to women's feet, which 1593 then turns on the king himself.

note: Kural 550 likens a king's killing of the cruel to pulling weeds from young corn; verse 772 praises a prince's killing of a beast that preyed on the herds, as a gift of safe sleep to the world.
teaches: The epic carries the weeding rule from criminals to a beast, and gives the reason in the world's sleep, though a Jain poet still has to justify a killing.

gains.a: The verse lacks a rule that makes the killing of the cruel a king's care for the many, and so answers why a Jain work may praise it.
gains.b: The couplet lacks a case where the killed is a beast and the killer a prince, which tests how far the weeding image stretches.

note: Verse 462 has men blame the Creator for making women, whose beauty they take as the cause of desire; Tirumanthiram 204 turns the same beauty into an etti fruit that looks good and poisons, and tells the heart to hold back.
teaches: The men's wonder at the Creator's sin shows desire as a thing done to them, and Tirumular sets it as a choice of the heart, which marks where the epic stops short of the Saiva remedy.

gains.a: A remedy for the cry of the men, who only blame the Creator.
gains.b: A scene of men who feel the beauty the verse warns against, and who blame another for it.

note: Both make the Earth a woman on the battlefield: the Kalavazhi's Earth is wrapped red as in a fine cloth by the king's slaughter, the Cintamani's beats her breast and pines.
teaches: The same personified Earth that the praise-poem dresses in the victor's blood becomes in the epic a mourner, so the pair shows the one figure serving both the glory and the grief of a war.

gains.a: a sense of how pointed its grieving Earth is, set against the battle-praise convention that adorns her
gains.b: a counter-voice that turns its red-robed Earth from ornament to wound

note: In 1090 Sunandai and her husband call going under the king's protection the right course; in 1093 she falls into a sea of unending grief as he is led away bound.
teaches: The foster mother who counselled submission as virtue cannot bear its result, so the chapter sets the household's prudent counsel against its cost to the one who gave it.

note: In 3037 the god Sutanjanan praises Civakan's feet, whom in 945 he met as the dying dog taught the five mantras.
teaches: The god's praise repays a debt the dog could not repay: what Civakan gave a dying animal returns as a god's worship.

note: Kural 1103 has the lover ask whether the lotus-eyed god's world is sweeter than sleep in the beloved's arms; 836 says even Indra, lord of the gods, could not have had this wedding.
teaches: Both set a human union above a god's world, but the Kural's lover measures it by private sweetness while the epic narrator measures it by public splendour, so the same boast ranks feeling in one and rank and wealth in the other.

gains.a: the narrator's hyperbole joins a known topos of love outranking heaven
gains.b: the couplet's private boast gains a version voiced in public about a wedding rather than an embrace

note: The epic gives the usurper the larger host, and the couplet says that many steadfast men make no army without leaders.
teaches: The counts set Kattiyangaran's bigger force against Civakan's smaller one, so the coming defeat of the larger host turns the couplet's rule about leadership over numbers into a plot.

gains.a: a rule that explains why the counted advantage of the usurper will not decide the battle
gains.b: a story where the two armies are counted unit by unit and the larger one is the one fated to lose

note: Boothappandiyan swears that if he does not see his enemies' backs he may be parted from his wife; Civakan swears that if he does not live with Gunamalai he may be one who turned his weapon on the beaten.
teaches: The vanjinam form stakes one domain against the other in both directions: the king pledges his marriage to secure a victory, and the epic hero pledges his warrior honour to secure a marriage, choosing as penalty an attack on fleeing men, the very thing the king's vow hopes to see.

gains.a: the Sangam vanjinam kaanji as the source of its self-curse, which the epic turns from a battle vow into a love pledge in a letter
gains.b: evidence that the vow's frame outlived the battlefield and that a later poet could read its stake, the beloved, as reversible with the warrior's code

claims.gist: pleasure, wealth and youth are as fleeting as cloud, lightning and the rainbow
the king fell because of his love for his queen
birth and death come from the fruit of one's own deeds
gain and loss are the nature of all things
grief and pity arise from lack of subtle understanding
a king's power protects the world even while he sleeps
the soul exists and is known by its own nature
the soul does not arise from any other thing
holding the five in mind without forgetting frees one from dark karma and brings unbroken joy
the body is consumed by disease and Death, so one must give and do good while it lasts
a noble who begs from the base earns blame
the earth has left every king who held her and stays with none
to live alone is the greatest misery, even amid unfailing heavenly pleasures, and a lover's embrace equals the gods' state
a counsellor must say what is for the king's good even at the risk of his anger
the born gain fruit by their own effort only, the dead are not reborn and there are no two deeds
delusion is the king of the enemies; the three desires (vedam) are its bow, and dislike and the contemplation of impurity are what defeat it
a woman wins a husband like this through penance done before
one must establish the truth of a death before punishing for it
a single strong one can rout a great host, as one lion scatters a herd of elephants
the queen who acts on her hurt will fall into burning hell
the grace of a holy teacher can clear the darkness of one's own evil deeds as a flame clears darkness

note: In 1349-1350 the arrow goes through shield and chest and the warrior falls; Kural 774 has a warrior laugh as he pulls a spear from his own body.
teaches: The couplet shows the wound as a thing a brave man shrugs off, and the epic shows the same pierced body falling, so wound-laughter and wound-falling mark two ends of one warrior ideal.

gains.a: The verse gains a standard by which the fall is read: a warrior is judged by how he takes the wound.
gains.b: The couplet gains a body that does fall, the other end of the laughing warrior.

note: Kural 216 likens wealth in a man of goodwill to a fruit tree ripening in the town's midst; 828 likens the crowd at the hero's house to birds on a tree heavy with fruit.
teaches: The couplet's tree is a figure for wealth that others may share, and the epic shows who actually comes to such a tree: a crowd that gives as well as takes, as 829 and 831 go on to say.

gains.a: the simile gains the couplet's moral sense that the house's wealth is held for others
gains.b: the couplet's fruit tree gains a scene showing the throng that gathers and the exchange of gifts both ways

note: Here the lovers' delight is called the eating of the good of their deeds; in 408 the teacher leaves to do penance that wears away old deeds.
teaches: Within one Jain epic, pleasure counted as the good fruit of deeds is still deeds, the very store that the renouncer's penance sets out to wear away.

note: 2060 says heaven's wealth ends; Tirumanthiram 184 says time cuts down both the heaven-bound and the deed-bound.
teaches: Both deny that heaven is lasting, but the epic counts the ending in fixed spans of seas and tells of a state beyond, while Tirumular makes time's cutting a general law with no way out in that line.

gains.a: The ending of heaven gets a law of time that reaches everyone, in place of a bare statement of limit.
gains.b: The cutting down by time gets a scale, from a palya to thirty-three seas in 2061 to 2063, and a way above it by austerity.

note: 497 restates Kural 759 (make wealth; no steel is sharper against foes) and joins to it the claims of 760 and 751 as a merchant's motto, a few verses before the sea swallows the wealth.
teaches: Put in the mouth of a man about to lose everything at sea, the Kural's praise of wealth as the sharpest steel is shown to say nothing about wealth's own exposure to loss.

gains.a: the merchant's motto gains its source and is seen as a borrowed rule of statecraft applied to trade
gains.b: the couplet gains a test case in which the wealth it praises is destroyed by forces no amount of it can subdue

note: Kural 894 says the weak doing harm to the strong is beckoning Death; Pazhamozhi 47 says the strong tormenting the weak find the victims' tears fall on them as Death.
teaches: The pair makes Death the outcome on both sides of an unequal fight: the weak who strike the strong invite it by their act, the strong who strike the weak receive it from their victims' tears.

note: The world asks 'what penance must he have done' and the king repays the one who reared him with a queen's title; the couplet makes that very kind of question the repayment a son owes his father.
teaches: The couplet's repayment is a sentence the world speaks; the epic adds a repayment made in rank and land and paid to the nurse, so the debt to one who raised a child need not stay in words and is not only the father's.

gains.a: the couplet's frame that the world's astonished 'what penance did he do' is itself the son's gift, which the verse leaves as bare talk
gains.b: a case where the debt is paid in rank, land and the title of queen, and to a rearing mother, which the couplet's wish for a father's good name never reaches

note: The narrator says Civakan relieved the elephants hemmed in by fire; Civakan's own account says rain fell while he stood grieving.
teaches: The narrator credits the hero with the rescue, while the hero credits a holy rain that came as he stood helpless, so his compassion is shown to act without any deed and he does not claim it.

note: In 82 Asokan reasons that greater merit now may win Indra's world; in 284 the ascetic says Asokan reached a divine world by earlier penance.
teaches: Asokan's reasoning about merit is shown to bring about the heaven he had thought of, only now told by another.

note: 3020 praises the Jina as the master whose spoken word frees those who repeat it from suffering; Tirumanthiram 105 has the Lord stand beyond the two kinds of deed.
teaches: Jain release comes by hearing and keeping the word of one who went before, while the Saiva text puts the Lord beyond deeds so that deeds cannot reach him, and the two disagree on whether a liberated one also helps.

gains.a: the praise of a teacher whose word wears away deeds is shown as a path with no god above it who removes them
gains.b: the Tirumanthiram's Lord beyond both deeds meets a rival in which the one beyond deeds is a teacher who shows a way and does not grant grace

note: Kural 37 bids the reader look at palanquin-bearer and rider instead of being told what virtue is; 303 offers the queen alone among skulls as sight for those who know sin only by report.
teaches: Both turn visible fortune into evidence for unseen merit, but the epic applies it to one life reversed from palace to burning ground, and the proof falls on a sufferer the poet does not blame.

gains.a: The epic's 'as if to show' gains the general argument from sight that Kural 37 states.
gains.b: The couplet gains a case where rider and bearer are the same person in one life, which exposes the cost of reading misfortune as proof.

note: 2844 says release lies in the scripture of the Lord under the three umbrellas and the pindi tree; 3051 shows that same Lord preaching to kings who leave their retinues outside the golden wall.
teaches: The sermon only names the Lord as the source of the doctrine; the assembly shows what following him costs a king, who leaves his army at the gate.

note: 1931 has the sufferers receive the fruit of former deeds; Naladiyar 33 says the fool sighs hotly when the fruit arrives, and the wise who treat it as old debt pass beyond confusion.
teaches: 1931 shows the fruit received with no way to reinterpret it, which is the state Naladiyar 33 says the wise avoid.

gains.a: The hell scene gains the stance it lacks: the sufferers receive their deeds' fruit without the calm that frees.
gains.b: The quatrain gains a concrete picture of the fool it describes, shown in the pit rather than only named.

note: Kural 879 says cut a thorn tree while young before it wounds the hand; Pazhamozhi 308 removes a thorn with a thorn.
teaches: Both read the enemy as a thorn, but the Kural deals with it by timing, cutting early, and the proverb by means, setting one thorn against another.

note: Both build a field guarded by a fence against stray beasts: Cintamani 379's crop is life from infancy to old age, its beasts diseases and its fence the vows (சீல வேலி); Pattinattar's field is the heart, its cattle the five senses, its fence calm (சாந்த வேலி), and its fruit Siva's form.
teaches: The shared Tamil figure of the fenced crop carries opposite ends: the Jain teacher fences a life to be kept from harm by vowed discipline, while the Saiva poet fences a devotion that ripens into the god, so the doctrine lies in what each names as fence and fruit.

gains.a: the teacher's brief farm image is seen as a choice: he fences life itself and names no fruit beyond it
gains.b: Pattinattar's devotional field is set against a Jain version where no grace ripens, showing his fruit of the five letters as the Saiva addition

note: Kural 360 names three roots of pain, desire, anger and confusion; 3080 names four passions, Anger, Pride, Deceit and Greed, as warriors who must be slain.
teaches: The Jain list of four widens the Kural's three, showing that one counts the roots of pain differently depending on the school.

gains.a: the four passions, as warriors, get a rule that when their very names perish pain perishes
gains.b: the Kural's three roots get a fourth and a fighting form: pride and deceit, and a weapon against them

note: The epic lists unmet wishes, parting, lost youth and old age as suffering; the quatrain lists home, youth, beauty, repute, wealth and strength as things that do not last and the best therefore renounce at once.
teaches: The epic names the pain of loss where the quatrain names its passing, and the quatrain supplies the action, renouncing without delay, that the epic verse leaves unsaid.

gains.a: The epic verse gains the Naladiyar's practical conclusion, to renounce at once, which it does not draw itself
gains.b: The quatrain gains the Jain account of why passing things hurt: wishes unmet and the loved parted from, not mere decay

note: The quatrain has mother seeking mother through the world; here father, mother, son and daughter change places among themselves across births.
teaches: One shows kin passing the world on, the other shows kin turning into each other, so grief for kin has no fixed object.

gains.a: The epic's twins and king have actually been one another's father, mother and children.
gains.b: The quatrain's general chain of mothers gets a family that names its members.

note: The king's order to play outside the city becomes, in verse 73, his command to build the prince a city of his own and name it.
teaches: The expulsion is turned into an honour by the end of the chapter, so the sentence of exile never takes effect as a punishment.

note: Kural 756 counts what falls to the king, customs and what he takes from crushed foes as his wealth; verse 665 lists treasure and royal marks demanded of a king who has not been crushed.
teaches: The epic shows the third kind of the couplet's royal wealth being claimed before any war, by an overlord's letter and not by victory.

gains.a: The verse lacks a rule that foe-wealth is a king's by right, which would make the demand lawful as the speaker claims.
gains.b: The couplet lacks a case where such wealth is demanded by letter before any fight, and where the foe is asked to give up his own umbrella.

note: 1815 says women who reached this king's chest had done austerity; Naladiyar 31 says present comfort comes from earlier austerity and is lost without more.
teaches: The herald's line puts a marriage on the same ledger of past austerity that the quatrain keeps, and the quatrain adds that it runs out.

gains.a: The praise gains a warning that earlier austerity wears down, which the herald omits.
gains.b: The quatrain gains a new case, a bride's good fortune, where its past austerity pays out in a marriage rather than a house.

note: The queen leaves the king for the keeper, as the verse says men leave the ripe jackfruit for the thorny date.
teaches: The poem uses the Tirumanthiram's choice of poor fruit over rich fruit for a woman, and for a far more extreme pair.

gains.a: her turning from the king is named as a choice of the worse fruit, which the epic's narration leaves to the reader
gains.b: the image of the jackfruit and the date, spoken of men, is shown to hold for a woman and for the sharpest contrast of rank and body

note: The maid cites the praise of the whole city, the merchant included, against Civakan's verdict; the Kural says understanding is seeing the true substance whoever's mouth one hears a thing from.
teaches: The pairing shows the couplet's rule tested where it is hardest, against unanimous acclaim, and shows that the epic does not let the lone judge rest on his authority either but makes him prove the truth by a test both sides accept.

gains.a: Civakan's refusal to follow the city is given a principle, so it reads as discernment rather than vanity
gains.b: the couplet's abstract rule gains a case where the many and the respected are wrong and the truth needs a witness, not a second opinion

note: 1330 gives back 1329's words almost unchanged.
teaches: Giving the same words to both fighters leaves the taunt itself as the thing the poet shows, with neither side ahead.

note: Verse 1 says release is taught by leaving cruel deeds behind; Tirumanthiram 117 says the malas burn only when the sun-like Lord appears, as the sunstone burns cotton.
teaches: Whether release is something the one freed does by shedding deeds or something the Lord does by his presence is the exact point where the Jain and Saiva ways part.

gains.a: the Jain opening gains a rival account of what burns away karma, which it states without answering
gains.b: the Tirumanthiram image gains a contrast, a teaching in which the omniscient lord is only the one who shows the way and does not burn anything

note: The south breeze is sent as envoy to prepare the groves for spring; in the Silappathikaram's song the same breeze is the messenger who announces spring to the land.
teaches: The breeze as spring's herald serves different ends: the Cintamani uses it to dress the groves as a host's welcome, the Silappathikaram to bring the news to a Tamil land.

note: The Vidyadhara king calls living alone the greatest misery even amid heavenly pleasure; the patikam ends the epic with Civakan, his brother, friends and wives renouncing the senses and going to release.
teaches: The king's praise of married joy over solitary pleasure is one character's view, and the epic's own close, where the household and its pleasures are renounced for a higher state, rejects it as a final value.

note: The couplet asks how one who eats another's flesh to fatten his own can hold to compassion; here the flesh is possibly her victim's.
teaches: The epic turns the couplet's general 'another creature' into a creature that may be her own victim's next body, which sharpens its question.

gains.a: the unit gains a rule that eating flesh is a failure of compassion in itself
gains.b: the couplet gains a case where the flesh may belong to someone she wronged

note: The Kural's lover says the flood of desire carries off the raft of shame and manliness; the epic's princess has a sea of desire that overruns the fence of shame round her nirai.
teaches: Shame is a raft for the Kural's man and a fence round a prison for the epic's woman, so the same flood threatens a man's means of crossing but a woman's enclosure.

gains.a: the princess's sea of desire is placed in the Kural's account of what desire sweeps away, naming shame as the first loss
gains.b: the couplet, spoken by a man, gains the woman's version, where shame guards nirai rather than carrying her

note: The Kural says the two kinds of dark deed do not cling to those devoted to the Lord's true praise; the epic says the Tirthan's feet remove all the sins done, and has Civakan worship there after killing in battle.
teaches: The couplet's claim covers both good and bad deeds and asks only praise, while the epic narrows it to sins and stages it as a rite after a specific act of killing, showing how a general promise was put to work as expiation.

gains.a: the epic's rite gains a measure of how much less it claims than the couplet, which frees from good deeds too
gains.b: the couplet's abstract Lord gains a named object, the Jina's feet, and a concrete occasion, the sin of war

note: The failed kings laugh, asking whether the boar will break and fall of itself; in 2204 Civakan's shot brings down the machine and the boar together.
teaches: The mockers' jibe is answered in a few verses: what they said could not happen without effort happens at one shot, so their laughter becomes the 'fire' 2201 says they lit against themselves.

note: The idyll's king answers both those who seek justice and those who seek their needs, with a clear sight that discerns between them; the couplet says a ruler not easy of access who does not examine and do justice perishes by himself.
teaches: The couplet names access and examined judgment as two duties whose lack ruins a king, while the idyll shows them as one daily audience in which judgment and gifts are granted together and discernment joins them, so justice and giving were seen as a single court function.

note: 339 says death is like sleep and birth is like waking from it, as an image of impermanence. 1216 wishes waking away altogether, for the sake of staying with her lover.
teaches: If the two were read together, her wish would come close to a wish not to be reborn, though nothing in the verse says this.

note: With Kemasari he rose while she slept and slipped out through the door unseen (1504-1505); with Vimalai he tells her he is going and promises a quick return.
teaches: Against the silent night escape from Kemasari, the open farewell to Vimalai looks kinder, yet it ends the same way in a departure, so the change lies in how he leaves, not in whether he stays.

note: Civakan renounces kingship at its height after hearing the dharma; in the Manimekalai the minister tells the king who wants to leave his throne that the Buddha's dharma, which protects others' lives, is not that.
teaches: The two epics weigh the same act differently: the Cintamani's patikam praises a just king's leaving the throne once he hears the dharma, while the Manimekalai has a minister argue that a king who abandons the people he guards departs from the Buddha's dharma.

note: 1113 mixes union, delight and sulking in one daze; Kural 1109 lists sulking, making up and union as love's fruits in order.
teaches: The epic blends what the couplet puts in a sequence, so the sulk is a flavour inside union and not a stage before it.

gains.a: The epic verse gets the Kural's claim that the sulk is itself a reward of love, which explains why it sits in a list of pleasures.
gains.b: The couplet gets a scene where the three do not follow each other but occur together, without any making up needed.

note: Udayanan turns from pleasure after reflecting on past penance; Civakan turns from kingship after hearing the dharma.
teaches: The two epics give a king's renunciation different starting points, one from his own reflection and one from a sermon, and this shows how the Jain epics motivate it.

note: 1380 calls flight from one man loathsome; Kural 775 says even a blink at a hurled spear is flight.
teaches: The two texts set the line of disgrace at different places: the epic at running away, the Kural already at the flinch.

gains.a: The taunt gains a stricter test: by Kural 775 the Vidyadharas' shame began before they turned.
gains.b: The couplet gains a speaker who shames living men in front of their army, not a rule stated apart.

note: Civakan proves the powder by what the bees do with it; the Kural says one's own deeds are the touchstone of greatness and smallness.
teaches: Both put the proof in what a thing does rather than in what is said of it, but the epic adds that a touchstone convinces only when both parties accepted it beforehand, as the maid did in 890 and 891.

gains.a: the bee test is shown to rest on a recognised rule of judging by effects, not on a trick
gains.b: the couplet's touchstone, stated of persons, gains a scene showing it must be agreed in advance to settle a quarrel

note: Kural 969 says the honourable give up life when honour is at stake, like the yak that will not live without its hair; 978 has Civakan reckon death better than life when a stranger woman's life is in danger.
teaches: The epic moves the Kural's honour-death from guarding one's own standing to rescuing another, so that honour is measured by whose danger a man will not stand by and watch.

gains.a: a rule that names the choice Civakan makes in a single line as a settled standard of honour, not a hero's impulse
gains.b: a case where the life given up for honour is risked to save someone else, which the couplet's self-regarding image of the yak leaves out

note: Sridattan told his crew in the storm that their suffering was the ripening of old deeds; Dharan now says the wreck was his own staged deceit.
teaches: The epic lets the merchant read the wreck as karma and then shows a planned human cause behind it, so the karmic explanation stands beside an agent's plan rather than replacing it.

note: In 454 Civakan returns from the cattle raid like the full moon the Tall One freed from the planet's mouth; in 665 the defeated kings dim like the full moon seized by the serpent.
teaches: The eclipse image is split between them: the rivals are the moon swallowed and Civakan the moon released, so the poet marks him as the winner before he has touched the vina.

note: 2111 shuts the five sense-gates of a fortress and posts guards; Naladiyar 59 names the five gates (body, mouth, eyes, nose, ears) and promises release to one who can guard and steer the craving that comes through them.
teaches: Guarding the senses is shown as one wall among several defences and not a lone act, so restraint looks like the start of a campaign and not its end.

gains.a: The gates, which the fortress leaves as an unnamed row, are named as the five organs through which craving enters.
gains.b: The rule that guarding the gates leads to release gains walls, armed guards and a mind kept within, so sense-restraint is pictured as part of a larger war.

claims.gist: a woman's destined husband is fixed and can be read from the planets at her birth
men born into a declining family must bear the burden of restoring it
a large body hides a small spirit that battle exposes
good deeds are a way of escape from Death, as some birds escape the fowler
killing the king to rule in his place is not pure conduct
merit enters by doors that the texts count in different numbers
a king who has settled the succession should leave the throne for forest austerity
deeds accumulated in the past are made to end by austerity and yoga
the ascetic who has lost his throne turns to a teacher's feet for release
dreams carry a fruit that can be read by the rules of a treatise
wealth buys an army, the army wins land, and land yields more wealth, so that wealth gathered commands everything
whoever lays hands on a king is destroyed with his kin
the hell-beings suffer as they made living beings suffer
women are great in compassion
vows lead to the heavens and lands of enjoyment
a fortunate place is the fruit of penance once performed
bodies of hell and heaven alike perish whether hated or loved
the many vows are gathered into five heads
bearing such a son is the fruit of a mother's past penance
it is right to nourish others' lives like one's own, and destroying one's own life is not grace
to demand tribute from a strong man is like taking a jewel from a cobra's hood

note: The narrator says past destiny sprouted and the king followed his heart; the minister of 233 tells the king he left the path of justice and bathed in the liquor of lust.
teaches: The epic gives the king's fall two causes in two voices, destiny in the narrator's and the king's own wrong path in the minister's, and does not let either cancel the other.

note: Both console a waiting woman by saying the flowers have been fooled by a false rain; in the epic the thunder is an elephant's trumpet and the song is overheard by warriors.
teaches: The akam friend's denial that the season has come is lifted whole into the epic and read by men as an omen that their lord lives, so a love convention becomes a sign in a war story.

gains.a: the epic verse gains its key: the Kuruntokai poem shows that the song is the friend's claim that he has not yet broken his word, which is why it comforts
gains.b: the Kuruntokai poem's consolation is shown working outside the love situation, as a formula strangers could overhear and apply to their own loss

note: Verse 248 says counsel, not strength of arm, is the quality of a king; Kural 546 says it is not the spear but the unbent sceptre that gives victory.
teaches: Each puts a different power above the weapon, counsel in the epic and justice in the couplet, so the pair shows that the Tamil tradition names more than one winner of a war.

gains.a: A moral check: counsel that is clever but crooked would still fail the sceptre's test.
gains.b: A practical account of how victory is planned, where the couplet gives only its moral condition.

note: Tirumular's single five-hooded serpent lives in the anthill of enjoyment and, its hoods drawn into one, makes the body its fit home; the epic's snake of desire lives in the anthill of the body ruled by the five senses and bites again.
teaches: Both poets house a serpent of the five senses in the body's anthill, but Tirumular's can be stilled by discipline into one hood while the epic's strikes the moment a spell has cured the real snake, showing that a remedy for poison is no remedy for the senses.

gains.a: a yogic reading of its anthill and five senses, which makes the love-bite a statement about the body and not only an ornament
gains.b: a narrative case where the serpent of the senses is shown striking in a living person, against which its taming is measured

note: The letter looks back at the seizure of the garlanded king in verse 57.
teaches: The capture shown in battle is later acknowledged as a fault to be pardoned, which is not said in the fight itself.

note: In Kural 1164 the woman parted from her lover says there is a sea of love but no safe raft to cross it; here Gunamalai, parted from Civakan and near death, crosses the sea of grief on the raft of the ascetic's words.
teaches: The Kural's parted woman has no raft because no one sends word; the epic gives its parted woman a raft from outside love altogether, an ascetic's prophecy, so the same plight is solved by religious authority rather than by the lover.

gains.a: the convention behind its image: the sea and raft are the parted woman's set terms, and Gunamalai's grief is cast as a lover's
gains.b: a case where the raft the couplet denies is supplied, and by whom, which shows what the woman of the couplet lacks

note: Naladiyar praises those who renounce in childhood for foreseeing grey hair; Asokan renounces only after he sees it.
teaches: The king meets the Naladiyar's test late but still before the staff, so renunciation after the first white hair counts as wise, not foolish.

gains.a: The epic gets a measure for the king's timing: the quatrain says the wise act before grey hair, and he acts only at the first strand.
gains.b: The quatrain's warning of the staff gets a person who is shown acting at the first strand, which the verse alone never describes.

note: 509 opens as Kural 621 opens and turns the couplet's laughter into a steel that cuts trouble, spoken by a captain to his crew in a storm that drowns them all but him.
teaches: The couplet's laugh in trouble becomes a leader's duty to others, and the scene shows its limit: composure saves the one who keeps it but cannot save the ship.

gains.a: Sitattan's exhortation gains a known maxim behind it, which explains why he speaks in aphorisms at the height of the storm
gains.b: the couplet's private resolve gains a public setting, where the person who laughs is responsible for others who perish

note: The poet's opening hymn praises the god who conquered the sum of his deeds; the princess's hymn here names what he conquered, desire and Death.
teaches: The invocation praises the god's victory in general terms, while the princess's hymn names the enemies; one is left to see that the poem's single praise is told twice, in two voices.

note: 1378 shows an army breaking at the sight of its king's fallen crown; the Kural says an army needs leaders.
teaches: A fallen crown scatters an army that Kural 770 would call leaderless, showing the leader's role as a matter of sight as much as of command.

gains.a: The rout gains a general rule: the army broke because it had no head to keep it together.
gains.b: The couplet gains a scene in which the leader's loss is not death but a crown struck off, and the effect is instant.

note: The couplet says the two deeds born of darkness do not cling to those who praise the Lord; the epic says that those who have understood both deeds and the Lord's scripture neither exult nor scorn, because every being eats its fruit.
teaches: The epic sets the escape in understanding, in a world where even Indra eats his deeds, while the couplet sets it in devotion, so the two give different accounts of how the deeds stop clinging.

gains.a: The epic verse gains the couplet's promise that the deeds can fail to cling, which it does not state
gains.b: The couplet gains an account of the mechanism, understanding the two kinds of deeds, and the equal reach of karma over Indra and a monkey, that devotion alone does not give

note: Kural 6 says that those who stand on the path of the one who quenched the five senses live long; Cintamani 375 sets those who reach the path that wears away hard deeds in a sea of bliss and those burnt by the five-mouthed snake of the senses in a sea of pain.
teaches: Where the couplet promises long life on the path of one who quenched the senses, the Jain teacher makes the reward the wearing away of karma and the penalty a sea of suffering, turning a blessing of the householder into a choice between release and pain.

gains.a: the epic's senses-snake and its path are tied to the Kural's opening praise of the one who quenched the five
gains.b: the couplet's 'long life' is shown read by a Jain teacher as the destruction of karma, a reading its words allow but do not state

note: Both use the moon's spot: the Naladiyar to say the noble cannot bear one stain as the moon does, the Neelakesi to say a work, like the moon, may carry a fault and still be loved.
teaches: The same image yields opposite counsel: for a person's character a single stain is unbearable, but for a poet before an assembly an acknowledged fault is excusable.

note: Both verses list the tricks of ball play, hiding the ball in a garland and making it dance like a snake.
teaches: Two Jain epics share one catalogue of ball tricks, so the hidden-in-garland and snake-dance play is a conventional set of skills, not either poet's invention.

note: Pattinathar calls vows, Vedas, Agamas, fire rites, offerings, mantras and pujas all pretence; Civakan mocks standing in the five fires and eating grass, but goes on to urge austerity in the Jina's form (1435).
teaches: Both reject the Vedic ascetic's fire and diet, but the Siddhar rejects observance as such, while the Jain hero rejects one school's austerities only to set up his own, so the pairing separates a critique of ritual from a rivalry of disciplines.

gains.a: a contrast that shows its polemic is not anti-ritual in general, since it keeps tapas
gains.b: a reasoned reductio, the beast that already lives the practice, where the Siddhar only lists and dismisses

note: Kural 719 says those who speak well in a good assembly should not speak in a mean one, even by slip; Pazhamozhi 15 calls fine speech among the unlearned the worst thing for a man and a lapse of conduct.
teaches: Pazhamozhi moves the Kural's rule of assembly into the field of ozhukkam, so speaking to the wrong audience is a fault of character that lowers the speaker, not only a tactical error.

note: The Kundalakesi fragment calls the body a deed-made thing where swarms of worms small and grown feed and live; Neelakesi says the many lives within the bodhisattva's body die when he gives it to the beast.
teaches: The Buddhist verse uses the body's teeming worms to teach disgust for it, while the Jain debater uses the same teeming body to charge the Buddhist hero's gift with mass killing, so one image serves renunciation on one side and non-harm on the other.

note: Kural 903 says stooping before one's wife brings a man shame among the good; Gandharvadattai, able to free Civakan, holds back because being saved by his wife would shame his strength and learning.
teaches: The couplet's shame is a man's fear of his wife's power, but here the wife herself fears it on his behalf and keeps her power idle, so the rule's cost falls on the woman who could act.

gains.a: a source in Tamil ethics for the code that stops her hand
gains.b: a scene showing the rule enforced from the woman's side, at the price of leaving the husband in danger

note: 1149 has Acuvakandan rage and boast, then say he will gather his people before deciding; the couplet faults a king who does not think with his circle and then lashes out.
teaches: Consulting after the rage has set may offer none of the couplet's protection, because the order of anger and counsel is reversed.

gains.a: the epic's king says he will consult yet has already boasted and resolved, so counsel is shown arriving after the anger
gains.b: the couplet gets a case where consulting follows the outburst, which it does not consider

note: 1856 tests whether any statecraft can escape Death; Naladiyar 6 says none here has leapt clear and bids the wealthy give.
teaches: The king tries the four expedients the quatrain never names, and by their failure the quatrain's rule is shown by a ruler's own attempt.

gains.a: The question gains the rule that no one leapt clear, so the ministers' failure is not their own.
gains.b: The quatrain gains a ruler who actually tries every device of power to escape.

note: 1099 has the father give the bride with water; 1102 has the groom lead her round the fire holding her fingers.
teaches: The gift only becomes a marriage when the groom takes her hand and walks the fire, so the two verses give the two halves of the one act.

note: The companions told Vijayai they would bring Civakan to her feet within a month; he now leaves Kanakamalai's city with them.
teaches: The departure answers the mother's charge: what moves Civakan to leave a new wife is the promise his friends made to his mother, not any call of his own.

note: For Parimelazhagar, the schools conflict on everything in 242 and yet converge on அருள். On 353, he says that their conflict leaves doubt only experience can settle.
teaches: Together they give his view of religious pluralism: agreement in ethics, and no resolution by argument in metaphysics.

note: Both verses close on the princes reaching an age that sets a fire in the women's hearts; 79 puts the cause in their youth, and 84 adds the women's sickness for wealthy lords.
teaches: The repeated line first locates the fire in the princes' youth, then ties it to wealth and rank, so the same phrase shifts what the women are said to burn for.

note: Verse 50 gave the youths' knowledge of the soul as other than the body; verse 238 gives it to the man who denied it.
teaches: The same doctrine, first held by ascetics going to their death, is now put as the answer to a man's disproof, so the reader learns it was framed to meet doubt as well as to console.

note: Pavadattan swears that after seeing him his wife never looked at another man; at 1581 she has begged Civakan to take her or let her die.
teaches: The husband's certainty about his wife's chastity is false in the reader's sight, and Civakan's silent laugh, not exposure, is how the epic lets the household survive the truth.

note: The hero kills Vayuvegan to avenge a father's murder; the couplet makes not killing the whole of virtuous action.
teaches: A Jain-framed epic lets its hero kill a usurper without comment, so the couplet's absolute not-killing meets a case where the story itself counts killing as justice.

gains.a: the hero's killing is seen against a rule the poem's own faith holds
gains.b: the couplet is shown meeting a hard case of vengeance for murder

note: Both set war as a sea with ships: in the epic the two armies meet as two seas with elephants as ships, in the Kalavazhi the blood drags elephants and drums like boats meeting on the sea after the slaughter.
teaches: The epic uses the sea at the moment of the clash, the Kalavazhi uses it for the blood that remains after, so together they show the sea image passing from the armies' living mass to the flood of their dead.

gains.a: the aftermath its own image points to: the seas that meet become a sea of blood
gains.b: the moment before its blood-sea, when the boats it shows were the living elephants of two hosts

note: In 269 Saccandan consoles Vijayai that birth and death come from one's own deeds and that grief shows want of understanding; at the birth she blames her own deeds for the child's wretched birth and grieves.
teaches: The doctrine the king offered to end her grief becomes, once he is gone, the ground of her self-accusation, so the same teaching consoles the dying and burdens the survivor.

note: 2868 says killing a life brings great suffering; Kural 321 says not killing is virtuous action and killing brings all other evil.
teaches: One tells the rule and the other the fruit, so together the rule has a reason.

gains.a: The verse's warning of suffering gets a plain statement of the rule behind it, that not killing is the chief virtue
gains.b: The Kural's rule gets a scene, a king giving it to a prince who has just scattered the swans, to show who must hear it

note: Naladiyar 48 asks those who praise sandal and garlands whether they have not seen vultures tear the body once it breaks; 2244 sets the sandal-smeared chest that women embraced in the blood, embraced now by the sword.
teaches: The Naladiyar uses the ruined body to turn a man from desire, but the epic shows the same ruin of the beloved body in battle and draws no lesson from it, keeping beauty and slaughter in one image without preaching.

gains.a: the epic's image gains a name for what it shows, the body's adornment undone, which it leaves unspoken
gains.b: the quatrain's argument meets a case where the body is broken by war rather than age, and the poet still sees it as beautiful

note: Suramanjari vowed that no one but Civakan would break her restraint; now Civakan says her beauty has carried off his.
teaches: The vow that guarded her நிறை against all men is answered by the loss of his, so the restraint the story set out to test breaks first on the man's side.

note: The house-priest foretold in 446 that the youth would come blazing in anger against the discus-lord; verse 681 shows the first blaze, lit by the word tribute.
teaches: The prophecy of anger is given its trigger, a single word of demand, so the fire that is foretold is also provoked.

note: The epic defines sila as giving up what the great condemn, and the couplet says neither shaving nor long hair is needed if one gives up what the world condemns.
teaches: The two agree that sila is the giving up of what is condemned, but the epic's ascetics keep the plucked hair as discipline (2820) where the couplet makes the mark unnecessary.

gains.a: The epic verse gains the couplet's insistence that the test of renunciation is what one gives up, not an outward mark, which tests its own list of marks
gains.b: The couplet gains a Jain case where the mark, plucked hair, is itself an austerity borne with patience, so its dismissal of marks is not complete

note: The Kural's woman asks why her eyes weep, since they showed him to her and so gave the unending sickness; the epic says Padumai lay sick with the love her own eyes had given her.
teaches: The couplet's blame of the eyes is spoken long after, by a woman left alone; the epic places the same diagnosis on the very first night, so the eyes are blamed before the love has any history.

gains.a: the convention that the eyes are the cause and so the culprit, which gives தன் கண் தரு its edge
gains.b: an instance of the eyes' guilt at the start of love, where the couplet knows it only in separation

note: Kural 233 says nothing in the world stands undying except towering fame; 2107 takes the same unstable world and fame that stands, and uses the fame-seeker's wealth as a figure of what vanishes fast.
teaches: The pair shows the price side of the Kural's maxim: the fame that alone stands is bought with wealth that goes as fast as a desert crossed in a day, so lasting renown and fleeting riches are one transaction.

gains.a: the simile's ground, why a fame-seeker's wealth should be the very type of the fleeting, which the epic leaves unstated
gains.b: a concrete measure of how quickly the giver's wealth leaves him, which the couplet's praise of fame never shows

note: Verse 53 says that in this king's days nothing but Kama's arrows mingled in the land and no killing force troubled it; verse 466 has the women report to Kama their victory over an army of lovers.
teaches: The earlier verse treats Kama's war as the only gentle one, and here it has victims and a victor, which shows the gentle war is still a war.

note: The king's question in verse 229, which youth is fit for his daughter, is met in verse 238 by sending for the ministers learned in policy.
teaches: The king does not choose the groom himself but turns his open question into a council of treatise-learned ministers, so the epic makes a marriage a matter for counsel.

note: 1910 praises the Lord as one who has struck down fierce deeds and lit the lamp of knowledge; 2 hails him as light of the world who split fierce deeds.
teaches: The king's praise repeats the poet's opening praise, so the king's worship matches the epic's own account of the god.

note: Kural 259 ranks refusing to take and eat one creature's life above a thousand oblations; verse 58 shows the rite at its far end, a man led to the goddess's place with the king's sword drawn.
teaches: The couplet weighs a ritual's merit against one life in general; the epic puts the weighing at the altar, where the offering is a man and the weigher is the king holding the sword.

gains.a: the sacrifice is seen to be what a Tamil couplet already ranks below a single creature's life
gains.b: the couplet's thousand sacrifices gain a concrete victim and a king's hand

note: 2913 decrees that the boy become the great lord; 2914 crowns him and seats him among elephants.
teaches: The decree is kept in a crowning that shows the whole court's weight behind the boy.

note: The prince is named Pirathapan at birth; after he is found on the serpent's head the king gives him a second name, Naga Kumaran, which becomes the poem's title.
teaches: The infant's first name is replaced by one taken from the miracle, so the name the book carries marks what the serpent did, not what the king first chose.
