note: 1975 says that a people is human only in the bare fact of birth and otherwise animal for want of shame and conduct; Kural 1071 says the base look just like human beings.
teaches: The Kural tests humanness by conduct in each person, while the Soolamani ties the same test to a whole island people's birth.

gains.a: The island people's humanity gains a conduct test: the Kural makes the difference lie in what a person does, not in a land.
gains.b: The Kural's resemblance gains a case where the look-alike is a named people, not a type of person.

claims.gist: reproach does not mend a deed already ripened
the disc has six mountain ranges, seven lands and fourteen rivers
those of right understanding are not reborn as animals or women, nor in the seven hells nor among the lowest gods
some who avoid hell are still born as animals in the lands of enjoyment
a man of low birth and a sore-ridden body is not a fit object of a queen's desire
a woman should confine her heart's restraint and let her desire go
the bodies of hell-beings are larger in each lower layer
the great wealth of the high state falls to those who earlier practised austerity and cannot be won by later effort
to abandon a wife in endless sorrow is conduct unfit for a worthy man
a man with a sword in hand who flees from one man has a loathsome manliness
winning this king's embrace is the fruit of austerity done earlier
a woman wins such a husband by penance done before
Even an animal that hears the dharma can come to know the birth it has passed through
manliness lies in giving oneself to end the suffering of living beings, and living on while they suffer is empty
a vow taken even in an animal's body leads to a human birth
sin born of desire for women cannot be removed while one keeps lying with women
a gift of the middle sort is rewarded by whatever one desires in the land of enjoyment
killing the weak to preserve one's own life turns the killer from the way to heaven
a human life ends in death on earth whatever is done to keep it
the books of protection are studied because kings must guard the world
fortune does not embrace those who fail in their conduct
a bride given privately to one suitor brings the anger of the rival kings, so the choice is made public
the body is a jointed contrivance whose senses all fail together when one joint gives way
a grudge a woman has taken up does not let go of her
joy comes only to those who have first suffered

note: 2555 has the city say that anyone who sees how Civakan was born in the burning ground, grew up a merchant's son and was worshipped by kings must ask why live heedless instead of doing penance; 3016 has the Jina tell the king that renunciation is the excellent thing.
teaches: The people's question about heedlessness at the crowning is answered by the lord's own word here, so the end of the book fulfils what its hero's rise had begun to pose.

note: Kural 84 says a glad face towards good guests draws the goddess of wealth; verse 471 shows the host women doing every service to the guest for the Vidyadhara.
teaches: The Kural's rule is given a court in which welcome is a trained skill and not a feeling, and the Kural shows what the women's service is for.

gains.a: A rule that the welcome depends on the host's face, which the women who set aside their looks only half meet.
gains.b: A setting in which the guest-duty is done by those whose art is desire.

note: Both feed flesh-eaters molten metal; the Cintamani calls them to come, 1934 shows them the 'flesh' first.
teaches: The shared molten-metal meal marks flesh-eating as a fixed offence of the Jain hell, with 1934 adding the mocking offer of food.

note: At 473 the foster father, more to Civakan than a mother, receives him home; at 1915 the birth mother herself declares Sunandai his mother and Kandukkatan his father.
teaches: The foster bond the story showed in action is ratified by the one person entitled to dispute it, turning the merchant's care into a parenthood the queen confers.

note: Verse 528 reads the Vidyadharas' high wealth as the fruit of earlier austerity; Naladiyar 265 reads the wealth of the unjust as the fruit of old deeds.
teaches: The same rule that makes the Vidyadhara's wealth a sign of past austerity makes a rich man's wealth no sign of present merit, so the epic's reasoning holds only for those of known past.

gains.a: A warning that wealth is a poor sign of present worth, which the king does not consider.
gains.b: A group, the Vidyadharas, for whom wealth is taken as proof of earned austerity, which the quatrain gives to no one.

note: The hunter's cry and his wife's imprisonment in 93 are met in 95 by her release.
teaches: The prince's help answers the plea at once, so 93 and 95 show the hero's mercy as action rather than promise.

note: The hymn says the soul is not from anything other than itself; the Neelakesi's sage asks whether a child is the body, made of the parents' blood, or the soul, which came to a human birth by its own former deed.
teaches: The Neelakesi spells out what the Cintamani's brief formula denies: the soul is not produced by the parents or the elements but brings itself into each birth by its own deeds.

note: The city women take Civakan for Kama who has put down his arrows and come in person; here Kama himself forgets his bow and arrows before the adorned bride and hides.
teaches: The poem gives the hero the god's looks, then lets the bride overcome the god, which sets her beauty above the hero's.

note: While the youth in 1020 burns for the maiden's picture, 1035 shows her elsewhere, praised by women, going to worship at dusk.
teaches: The reader sees the youth's fire for a girl who is far away and busy with prayer, so his longing has no answer from her yet.

note: After the last battle Civakan bows to the Jina and flings out gold before putting on his royal ornaments (2357); in 2641 he takes flowers and touches his crowned head to the nuns' feet.
teaches: The crown is lowered twice, first before the Jina in victory and last before the women who have given up, so the epic marks the end of his kingship by whom he bows to.

note: In 1339 Padumai's royal father gives her because Civakan bears marks fit to rule the earth (பொறியினன்); in 1465 the merchant Subhadran gives his consent on the same kind of reading of the body.
teaches: Two fathers of different rank, a king and a merchant, both choose the stranger by reading his body rather than asking his birth, which shows that in the epic the hero's hidden royalty is legible on his skin to anyone trained to look.

note: In 306 the counsellor argues that the girl is fit for Asvagriva, whose mind is set and whom the Vidyadharas fear; in 1146 the girl has gone down to earth as wed to another.
teaches: The rejected suit explains why a marriage far away becomes a cause of war against the whole discus-lord's host.

note: In 2628 the matrons go in palanquins to renounce and the king is left; in 2998 he boards a palanquin himself and the gods carry it.
teaches: The palanquin of renunciation first carried the mothers by men, and now carries the son by gods, so the epic shows the same vehicle changing in meaning from parting to ascent.

note: In 627 the astrologer warns that pride falls like frost on the lotus of wealth; in 634 the king, smiling, boasts that his shoulders have beaten the Vidyadhara kings and so he need fear no foe.
teaches: The warning is answered by the very boast it described, so the king's reply is what the astrologer's image forecasts.

note: The Kural's huge tusked elephant fears the tiger's attack; Civakan comes at the elephant like a lion (1833), but it ends not in fear but in one mind with him.
teaches: Against the Kural's picture of the strong beast cowed by a fiercer one, the epic's elephant is won into agreement, so mastery here is shown as concord after force, not fear alone.

gains.a: the epic's claim that rider and beast share one mind gains force against the common image of the elephant ruled by terror
gains.b: the couplet's image of fear as the end of the contest gains a counter-case in which the stronger spirit ends in rapport

note: The king asks what the cry of the flour cock means and fears the sin.
teaches: His question turns the marvel at 146 into doctrine: the cry is read as the sign of a sin that binds to births.

note: 2018 has vision destroy karma's darkness by itself; Tirumanthiram 116 has Nandi remove the malas as fire rises from bamboo, out of grace.
teaches: Release by one's own seeing, without any god, meets release by a lord's grace, and the same fire-and-darkness language serves both.

gains.a: The lamp of vision gains a rival cause, grace, for the same burning away of the dark.
gains.b: The grace-fire gains the Jain demand that the soul's own seeing bear the work, so the cause is not left wholly with the lord.

note: The couplet calls even the body excess for those who would cut off births; Nagadattan lets go of the body by fasting.
teaches: The couplet calls the body surplus for one bent on ending births, and the story shows that a householder who lets the body go by fasting is rewarded with a god's birth, so the Jain fast does not by itself end births.

gains.a: the fast is read as the couplet's 'body is excess' acted to the end
gains.b: the couplet's claim gets an actual practice, and a limit: the first reward is a heaven, not the end of births

note: Purananuru 287 says warriors who do not run, if they die, enjoy the weddings of flawless women in the higher world; in 2265 the slain challenger is showered with flowers by celestial women and reaches heaven.
teaches: The Purananuru's reward is promised to one's own unflinching men to steady them; the epic grants it on the field to an enemy killed by the hero's companion, so the heaven of the brave is shown to belong to the fallen of either side.

gains.a: the apsaras' welcome is read as the old Puram reward for the unflinching dead, not a passing ornament
gains.b: the poem's promise, a speech to warriors before battle, is seen fulfilled as an event, and extended to the man who loses a fair duel

note: 1262 has a brother laugh at the humans; 1270 shows the warriors as too great for the world.
teaches: The laughing Vidyadharas misjudge their foe, since the poet next shows those warriors as towering figures.

note: The sign written at Vimalai's birth, that the unsold cargo will sell when her husband climbs onto the shop, is the sale of 1973, made while Civakan sat lovesick at the shop front (1966).
teaches: The sale the merchant boasted of turns out to be a sign he had waited for since his daughter's birth, so Civakan's idle lovesick sitting is retold as the fulfilment of a prophecy he did not know.

note: Kural 617 says the goddess of misfortune lives in sloth and the lotus goddess in the labour of the unslothful; in verse 621 the goddess of fortune takes offence and looks for another place, because the king has not come to her.
teaches: In the Kural fortune leaves a man for sloth; here she leaves a king for his pleasure, so the fault is attention given elsewhere.

gains.a: The verse lacks a rule saying what kind of man keeps fortune, which the couplet gives.
gains.b: The couplet lacks a picture of fortune as a slighted lover, which the verse gives.

note: 101 argues at length that Athiyaman's gift never fails however long it is delayed; the akam poem 162 calls Athikan, of the same house, one who never let a suppliant's hope fail (நசைபிழைப்பு அறியா).
teaches: What 101 has to argue as a bard's private reassurance had become, in an akam poet's line, a fixed epithet of the Athiyaman house, so the praise poem shows the experience behind the epithet.

note: Kural 1075 says fear is the conduct of the base; Pazhamozhi 97 says the base do not care about the great blame that falls on them.
teaches: The pair separates two fears: the base may be held in line by fear of punishment, as the Kural says, but blame, which works on others through shame, has no hold on them at all.

note: Nandagon's drum promises the maiden to whoever brings back the herd; in 479 the herd chief, now naming himself Govindan, offers her with seven golden images to Civakan.
teaches: The public prize proclaimed to all the city's warriors is paid to the one outsider who answered it, which makes Govindai's marriage a contract kept rather than a match made.

note: 3027 has the king take off jewels and garlands because the world is a drop of milk; Kural 345 says that for those cutting off births even the body is excess.
teaches: The epic stages the stripping as a royal act step by step, while the Kural makes the body itself the last thing to be let go.

gains.a: the king's removal of ornaments is shown to be the first step of a series that reaches the body
gains.b: the Kural's rule that even the body is excess gets a worked case of a king who has things to lose

note: Marusi says the world would not be without the king's gentle grace; Kural 544 says the world clings to the feet of the king who embraces his people with the sceptre.
teaches: The envoy states the Kural's idea of the world's dependence on the king's grace as a bare condition for existence, and in the mouth of a rival's envoy.

gains.a: The verse lacks a mark of how the grace works, which the couplet gives as the king first embracing his people.
gains.b: The couplet lacks the strong form of the dependence, that without the king's grace there is no world, which the verse speaks.

note: Siddhar 1790 scolds the stony mind for wanting to rule the whole earth under one umbrella; 69 closes the king's praise on exactly that single umbrella and his pleasure under it.
teaches: The Siddhar treats the one-umbrella rule as a desire to be given up, while the poem treats it as the king's finished wealth, so the same picture means a trap in one and a reward in the other.

gains.a: The verse gains a rival reading of the one umbrella as the object of craving, against which its praise sounds partial.
gains.b: The Siddhar verse gains a king who has the whole earth under one umbrella, so its warning has a figure who is already there.

note: 681 lights Tivittan with anger on hearing the word tribute; 1206 to 1207 show the same anger spreading through his body at the envoys' second round of words.
teaches: The poet lets the first anger be inward at the demand and the second visible at the insult, so the hero grows from controlled to burning as the embassies go on.

note: 3093 repeats 3082's swallowing of the three worlds, there as the narrator's victory, here as praise in the worshippers' mouths.
teaches: The same image is first an event and then a creed, and the hymn shows how a story becomes what a community says.

note: Kural 49 says that what is called virtue is household life; the verse ends that in the Kali age household life alone is true.
teaches: Both favour the household, but the Kural grounds it in what virtue is and the Jain verse in the corruption of the age, so one preference has a timeless and an historical ground.

note: In 2607 Vijayai begs the wives never to part from the king; in 2991 he entrusts them to her as he goes.
teaches: The mother who wished the wives to stay with her son is the one who now receives them as he leaves, so the wish is kept in a changed form.

note: 628 prevents pain by not desiring pleasure. 669 accepts pain for the sake of the pleasure that results. One asks you to stop wanting joy and the other to work for it.
teaches: They may differ in scope, since 628 speaks of how one meets pain and 669 of which tasks to take up, but neither verse says so.

note: 708 records a king who came and fell in the sea of the vina; 798 has Civakan remind the kings that she beat them at the vina before he serves them arrows.
teaches: Civakan's taunt makes the musical defeat the first round of the battle, so the kings now lose twice to the same bride, once to her skill and once to his.

note: The Siddhar blames a deceiving demon in woman's form; the king blames desire itself and has just spared the woman.
teaches: The Siddhar locates the theft of understanding in the woman, while the king locates it in desire, and so he can leave her alive.

gains.a: The king lacks the Siddhar's picture of desire as a demon that robs understanding.
gains.b: The Siddhar's blame of the woman lacks the king's separation of the woman from her desire.

note: 2098 has gods carry the king's crown and cast it into the milk sea; Cintamani 3035 has gods lift the tray with Civakan's hair and let it fall into the milk sea.
teaches: Both Jain epics end a royal career with the same act, gods taking the shed sign of rank to the milk sea, so the image reads as a convention for a king's completed renunciation.

note: Kural 701 makes one who knows a mind before it speaks an ornament to the world; Kattiyankaran, once the minister, reads from the dancer's signs that she loves Civakan and turns the knowledge into grudge and seizure.
teaches: The pair shows that reading an unspoken mind is praised in the Kural for a use the couplet assumes, and in a jealous ruler the same skill feeds only his grudge and his violence.

gains.a: a name for the faculty the usurper uses, which the epic shows only in action, and a measure of how far he has fallen from the good counsellor's use of it
gains.b: a case where the sign-reader serves himself rather than the one he reads, which the couplet's praise does not consider

note: Civakan lays his endowment at the feet of the one who walked on the red lotus; the Kural's opening couplets name the one who walked on the flower and promise long life to those who reach his feet.
teaches: The epic names the lotus and puts a temple and a gift at the feet, filling in the figure the couplet leaves open, so it shows one tradition's reading of the lotus-walker as the Jina's temple god.

gains.a: the couplet's idea that to reach the lotus-walker's feet is the aim of the faithful and not only a courtesy
gains.b: a worshipper's act of endowing the feet with lamp, towns and chariots, and a reader who takes the lotus-walker as the Jina, which the couplet does not say

note: Kural 761 calls a complete army the chief of a king's wealth; verse 874 shows the host as a spreading display round a bridal vimana.
teaches: The pair shows that the host here is wealth on show, not strength at work as the couplet rates it.

gains.a: The verse lacks any test of whether the host is the king's strength; the couplet gives one.
gains.b: The couplet lacks the sight of an army spent on a wedding escort; the verse gives it.

note: Verse 140 names the one fault of the Vidyadhara king as want of grace toward the lowly; verse 262 has a minister say that great lords who bear the lapses of the lowly are followed by the whole earth.
teaches: The council offers the remedy for the king's single fault, so the earlier flaw reads as a fault the poem expects the counsellors to mend.

note: 1757 has the parents call the tired daughter from behind the curtain; 1758 shows her letting the ball go and reaching her father's feet.
teaches: The call becomes obedience: the daughter breaks off her play at once, which is how a swayamvara's choice is later left to the father's council.

note: Kural 431 says the wealth of those without arrogance, anger and smallness has a dignified quality; verse 627 makes arrogance a frost that destroys the lotus of wealth.
teaches: The couplet says what spoils the dignity of wealth; the verse shows how, with arrogance falling on wealth like frost on a lotus.

gains.a: The verse lacks the positive side, that wealth without arrogance keeps its dignity, which the couplet gives.
gains.b: The couplet lacks an image of the ruin pride causes, which the verse supplies.

note: The brother's thought is that women's minds lack firmness; the Kural names firmness, called karpu, as the greatest thing in a woman.
teaches: Both books turn on a woman's firmness, but the epic locates it in renunciation and the Kural in chastity, so firmness is not the same virtue in the two.

gains.a: a firmness of mind that is not wifely, here set on leaving life, which the Kural's word does not reach
gains.b: a rival test of the same word, a woman who stands firm in leaving the world and not in keeping her husband

claims.gist: wealth is the one weapon that subdues one's enemies
wealth brings pleasure and virtue and all else with it
a man who touches the king's queen will be put to death by the king
people should live the household dharma daily, obedient to their parents
one must do penance and give before youth passes into age
a courtesan's son lacks the standing of good birth
the sacred grass is laid with its tips to the north and east for the rite
worship of the Jina's feet cuts through accumulated karma
some low births pass quickly into lower states and are beyond ordinary knowing
births, deeds, anger and desire are bound in a chain, and the Lord's dharma is great against it
the Jina destroyed fierce deeds and lit the lamp of true knowledge
pride in wealth makes a ruler forget the way of virtue
sages who have crossed the four Vedas sow virtue and gain earthly joy through the sacrifice
good birth in a good land is very rare among endless wombs
sin done by harming the bodies of living beings in earlier lives brings sufferings through birth after birth
a wish of long life for a king who kills creatures can bear no good fruit
a king who sinks in pleasure forgets his lost land and virtue
when the destined time comes, no one can prevent what is destined
killing animals for meat is punished in hell by being carved and fed one's own flesh
a rite carried out with flesh-eaters does not lift the dead to heaven
the king's favour and anger make and destroy at once, as the gods' do not
rejoicing at the Lord's festival earns a heavenly body
a merchant's life is taking others' goods in exchange for his own
the liberated ones, freed from karma and possessed of eight qualities, are the refuge that ends sorrow
a youth firm in austerity is not shaken by women's glances
the Vidyadharas' wealth cannot be enjoyed by men, whose bodies are frothy hollows

note: Perunkoppendu argues against the elders that the widow's life of plain food and gravel beds is not for her and the pyre is a lotus pool; Saccandan's women make the same choice in a simile and a vow of the other world, without the argument.
teaches: Set beside the Sangam queen's reasoned refusal, the epic's wives choose death as a group and by figure alone, while the one queen who must live, Vijayai, is spared the choice by her unborn son.

gains.a: The epic verse gains the explicit alternative its women reject, the austere widow's life Purananuru 246 describes.
gains.b: The Purananuru poem gains a counter-case in the same scene: a queen (Vijayai) whom motherhood bars from the pyre.

note: 1663 has the king order a god to become an elephant; 1664 shows the god taking the shape and nearing the women.
teaches: The king's order is carried out at once, so the fear in the grove is the king's own design and not an accident.

note: Ainkurunuru 219: the friend asks why the girl's forehead pales since the hill man went away. Kural 1188: the woman complains that people say she has grown pale, and no one says that he left her.
teaches: The friend's question names the man's leaving together with the pallor, which is exactly the acknowledgement the Kural's woman says the world withholds, so the pair shows the friend as the one voice that ties the girl's pallor to the man who caused it.

note: 2927 makes food to the hungry a well in heaven and guarding life a title to earth and sky; Kural 222 says that even if there were no higher world, giving alone is good.
teaches: The epic gives the reward of heaven for giving, while the Kural says giving is right even with no reward, so the two differ on whether the gift needs a world to come.

gains.a: the heaven-reward of the verse is shown to be an extra, since the Kural holds giving good without it
gains.b: the Kural's no-heaven giving is given a school's account, Jain karma, in which giving does bring fruit

note: The Kural says nothing is stronger than fate, which arrives first even when one plans against it; the verse bows to a lord who has conquered fate.
teaches: The Kural makes fate the strongest force and the Jain verse puts one who has beaten it in front of the worshipper, so release means the end of the thing the Kural says cannot be passed.

gains.a: the lord's conquest of fate is weighed against a Tamil saying that nothing is stronger than it
gains.b: the couplet's claim that fate cannot be beaten is shown to have a Jain exception, and the exception is the god

note: 2831 says merit is measured by the gift as iron takes water in proportion to its heating, a gift for the next birth; Purananuru 134 says Ay is no trader who buys virtue with gifts for the next life.
teaches: The verse sets a gift's reward in an exact ledger, and the Sangam poem names that ledger as what its patron does not do.

gains.a: the doctrine of measured merit, shown from outside, looks like the trade it is accused of in the Sangam poem
gains.b: the poem's refusal of a 'trader's' giving gains a worked-out doctrine of gift-for-fruit that makes the refusal pointed

note: 1987 draws childhood, youth and old age as a wilderness ending in another state; Naladiyar 11 says the wise renounced in childhood, knowing grey hair would come.
teaches: The epic shows what lies past old age, another birth, and so the quatrain's renunciation at the start is not a mere fear of aging.

gains.a: The wilderness of life gains an answer: renounce early, before the other state.
gains.b: Old age gains a sequel in another birth, which the quatrain's staff and grey hair do not name.

note: 1286 taunts a rival with a bride won by another; Cintamani 769 taunts rivals with their wives' sulking looks lost after the battle.
teaches: Both epics make a pre-battle taunt turn on the rival's wife or bride, so the insult reaches his private stake and not his strength.

note: The patikam promised that Civakan would enter the city's sky-high streets and fall into the sea of nectar of a maiden born by a boon; 1951 brings him into the street and shows her at her ball.
teaches: The patikam's figure of him falling into her sea of nectar is set up with a reversal: in the street it is the other women who shoot their eyes at him, while the destined maiden is first seen paying him no attention at all.

note: 187 says the two were joined by the பான்மை for joining; 215 says the king followed the way of her mind because a former பான்மை (முனம் ஆகிய பான்மை) sprouted, ignoring all warning.
teaches: If பான்மை in 187 is read as destiny, the marriage and the king's ruinous absorption have one source in the epic's account, apportioned former deeds, while 187 also names the ministers' reasoning: fate and judgment are both given as causes.

note: Thirikadugam lists a husbandless woman's adornment among things unfit; Nandattan argues from the same norm that a wife still adorned has a living husband.
teaches: The ethical list states the rule as unfitness, while the epic turns that rule into a piece of inference, showing the norm was strong enough to serve as proof of a fact.

gains.a: the Cintamani's argument gains a stated norm outside the story, so Nandattan's reasoning rests on a known rule and not on a guess
gains.b: the bare rule gains a scene in which someone actually relies on it to learn whether a man is dead

note: Kural 901 says desire for a wife costs a man what action needs; Yugi concludes the same of the king's union, and cures it by a stratagem, not by the king's restraint.
teaches: The couplet speaks to the man who must resist his own desire, while the epic gives the cure to a minister who engineers an absence.

gains.a: The epic scene gains a general rule that makes the king's fault a known failing of men intent on pleasure, not only his own.
gains.b: The couplet gains a case in which the fault is not mended by the husband's restraint but by an outside plan, which the couplet never considers.

note: The people see the hero's birth in the burning ground, rearing as a merchant's son and the kings' worship and ask why one should not do tapas; the quatrain has the best renounce home, youth, beauty, repute, wealth and strength because none lasts.
teaches: The Naladiyar argues renunciation from the failing of goods in general, and the epic argues it from one life in which a single man has held every state, so the argument rests on a case the hearers have seen.

gains.a: the quatrain's list of what fails (home, youth, wealth, strength) as the reason that makes tapas the sensible answer to his rise
gains.b: a named life that has lived through desolation, rearing and kingship, which the quatrain's list of goods never shows in one person

note: Both brides' fathers wait on an astrologer's word about the destined husband: Gandharvadattai's says he lives in Rajamapuram, Kemasari's that she will know him by her own shame.
teaches: Set side by side, the two horoscopes show the epic varying one device: the Vidyadhara princess's husband is found by place and contest, the merchant's daughter's by a sign in her own body that no contest can stage.

note: 1001 has Madhavasenai fix the bride's form in her heart and begin to paint; 1010 has her tell the queen the form was beyond any painting and that her hand was steadied by the queen's grace.
teaches: The painter's pride in the likeness turns into modesty when it is presented, so the portrait serves as praise of the bride and of the queen.

note: Gunamalai's red-beaked parrot, her only refuge, was made her go-between in love; here the household parrot, with its mock death, becomes the go-between that ends a lovers' quarrel.
teaches: The parrot appears again as the love-story's helper, but at Gunamalai's side it carries a plea across a distance while at Ilakkanai's it mends a quarrel within the bed-chamber.

note: Verse 40 gives the women's eyes rain-dark paint and the wishing tree, and verse 44 shows bees fooled by the same eyes into taking them for flowers.
teaches: The women's eyes are praised once by their effect on lords and once by their effect on bees, so the poet treats the same beauty as ruling men and nature alike.

note: 513 has the sea swallow the merchant's guarded wealth and the loved ones with him; 580 shows the ship and the companions intact.
teaches: The loss that the wreck scene narrates as final is revealed as illusion, so the earlier verse's grief was real while its facts were false.

note: 1614 has the queen, once the king has bowed, smile and turn her anger into a game on the jester; Naladiyar 384 praises the wife who knows when to sulk and relents sweetly.
teaches: The queen relents by moving her anger on to the jester in garlands, which the quatrain's wife does not do.

gains.a: The queen's smile gains a standard: a wife is praised who sulks at the right time and gives way sweetly, and she does so at once.
gains.b: The quatrain gains a wife who is also a queen, whose sulk is ended in a public game that costs a third person.

note: 1066 says nothing shames the tongue more than begging, even water for a cow. 780 says this death is worth begging for, with the same root (இர-).
teaches: Only something beyond the Kural's worst disgrace could justify the word.

note: The couplet bids one forget anger at anyone at all; the teacher asks Civakan to hold his anger against one man for one year only.
teaches: Against the couplet's unlimited forgetting of anger, the epic's ascetic sets a term to restraint, so a teacher who renounced anger for himself still leaves a prince's just anger intact for its time.

gains.a: the request is seen to be partial: it is a delay with an end, not the forgetting the ethics books ask
gains.b: the couplet's 'at anyone at all' is tested by the case of a usurper who killed one's father, where even an ascetic does not ask for it

note: Verse 230 brings in Mananigai, named in verse 228, to meet Dattai's defeat.
teaches: The newcomer introduced by name and rank as a chaste princess in verse 228 first acts only in verse 230, when she steps in to answer the defeated Dattai.

note: 1068 sends the sun up to see the fire-circling; 1070 reports the rites complete.
teaches: The poet makes the sun a witness, so the unseen wedding is told through daybreak and not in itself.

note: Kural 417 says men of deep heard learning do not speak folly even when mistaken; Thirikadugam says friendship with such men clears the tangle of words.
teaches: The couplet says kelvi keeps its owner's own speech clear; the verse adds that it clears others' confusion, so the virtue passes to the friend.

note: Both bid people take provisions for the journey because Death is coming.
teaches: The quatrain's bundle carried on the shoulder stays a figure; the epic sets it against the food anyone packs for a visit to kin, and says it to a man actually on the road, so the figure is pinned to an everyday act and to the hearer's own journey.

gains.a: the epic gains the quatrain's warning that Death takes even the unborn, which makes the provision urgent
gains.b: the quatrain gains the comparison with the ordinary traveller's food that shows why neglecting it is folly

note: The spies' report in 169 is confirmed in 170 by a second voice, the minister's.
teaches: The king rejoices only once a second voice agrees, which suggests the second confirmation is a habit of a court and not only a rule.

gains.a: The shift from spy to minister shows how a second source is found at a court, which the verse alone does not name.
gains.b: The rule of confirming a spy's finding gets an instance in which the second source is a friendly minister, not another spy.

note: Gunamalai fears she has no way to live, like little people who have done no tapas; Civakan says her very ornaments did penance to be on her.
teaches: Apart and unknown to each other, both lovers reach for the language of penance: she counts herself among those without its merit, while he grants its merit even to her jewels, so the same idea marks her despair and his worship.

note: In 1432 Civakan mocks the ascetics who leave soft beds only to lie with women in leaf huts; in 1437 they put away their households and go to the Jina.
teaches: The jibe was not only abuse but a charge the converts accept, so the poem counts their earlier forest life as no renunciation and their conversion as the first true leaving of home.

note: The couplet praises the host who tends the departing guest and watches for the guest to come; Subhadran feeds a thousand and eight guests a day for twelve years watching for one guest who will be his son-in-law.
teaches: The epic takes the couplet's watching for the coming guest literally and turns it to a private end, so hospitality becomes a search, rewarded with a husband in this life rather than with welcome among the gods.

gains.a: the father's twelve-year feast is given the standing of a recognised householder's virtue rather than a mere device of the plot
gains.b: the couplet's 'watching for the guest to come' is shown to admit a host whose care has a hidden aim of his own, a case the couplet does not weigh

note: 395: the chief shows his wife to the bard and tells her to care for him as for himself; Kural 81: the whole of keeping house and guarding goods is for tending guests.
teaches: The couplet says the household exists for the guest; the poem shows the moment that claim is enacted, when the master hands the guest over to the mistress of the house, so the guest is taken into the household rather than merely fed by it.

note: Verse 26 in the opening summary has Civakan winning the nectar-like beauty of his maternal uncle's daughter; 2460 brings that daughter, from Govindan's mountain, to the sacrificial hall to be given.
teaches: The poem's opening promise of this marriage is kept here with Vedic rite and a king's gift-water, so the reader sees the match as one planned from the start with the uncle's daughter given by her father's house.

note: At 1577 Civakan reflects to himself that the body is a flesh-filled hut (ஊன்பயில் குரம்பை) of bone, sinew, blood and skin with nine gates; at 1584 he tells the woman it is a worm-filled hut (புழுப்பயில் குரம்பை).
teaches: The hut image moves from the hero's private thought when the woman first appears to his spoken answer to her, so the reader sees that his rebuff was prepared in silent meditation before she spoke.

note: The sage foretold that the son would bear austerity and reach release; here the father renounces and the son is crowned.
teaches: The prophecy of the son's austerity is not yet kept; the father takes the sage's way first, so the work leaves the son's renunciation for later.

note: The queen who offered the low man her whole love is the woman who plots with the old mother to poison the king.
teaches: The poisoning and hell here are the fruit of the passion the earlier verse shows only beginning.

note: In 1948 the city's women ask whether he is Murugan or the five-arrowed Kama; in 1961 Vimalai decides he is the son of the five-flower-arrowed god come down to earth.
teaches: The question the crowd of women asked and left open is answered by the one woman who will marry him, and for her the answer costs her modesty and restraint.

note: The letter softens the wrong of the seizure with words of pardon; the couplet asks the envoy to remove what offends.
teaches: A letter that must confess a seizure can keep to the couplet's rule of avoiding offence only by naming the fault and asking for pardon in the same breath.

gains.a: the letter's gentle admission of fault is seen as the envoy's craft of removing offence
gains.b: the couplet is tried against a message that carries a fault of the sender, where removing offence is hard

note: The errand to the Panchala king in 179 is carried out in 180, where the kings are driven off and the Panchala army comes on.
teaches: The errand is meant as stratagem and ends in open battle, which shows the plan did not remove the war.

note: 1112 makes two bodies one heart by ripening; Kural 1122 says the bond is as body is to life.
teaches: The epic gives the oneness of lovers a history of slow ripening, while the couplet states only the result as a bond of body and life.

gains.a: The epic verse gets a measure of how total the oneness is, as between body and life, which its bud-and-fruit figure does not give.
gains.b: The couplet gets a story in which the bond grows from bud to fruit instead of being given.

note: The Kural says the two deeds do not cling to those who praise the Lord's true fame; verse 4 promises a poem that shows the fruit of deeds, good and bad, as they actually ripen.
teaches: A story shows karma bearing fruit in merit and fear, which limits the couplet's picture of deeds that simply do not cling to the devout.

gains.a: the Yasodhara plan gains a Tamil ethical text which holds that devotion keeps deeds from clinging
gains.b: the Kural couplet gains a case where deeds do bear fruit in birth after birth for those not freed, which the couplet's statement leaves unshown

note: The Kural says those who reach the Lord's feet swim the great sea of births; the verse says the lord has ended birth, old age and death.
teaches: The couplet makes ending birth the reward of reaching the feet, and this verse names the three things the lord himself has ended, so the poem tells what is meant by crossing the sea.

gains.a: the epic's hymn is shown to say what the crossing of the sea of births consists of
gains.b: the couplet's promise is shown to be read as freedom from birth, old age and death

note: Women's perfumes weaken even ascetics here; the Thiruppugazh poet confesses his own ruin from craving women.
teaches: The scenic verse already carries the temptation that the poet of the Thiruppugazh later tells in the first person.

gains.a: A named cost of the pleasure it lightly sketches, which the verse itself does not state.
gains.b: An earlier poetic case in which the same allure reaches ascetics, not only a self-confessed sinner.

note: Verse 11 says the perfumes and flowers of the land are so heavy that even ascetics in good austerity are weakened; verse 350 shows a youth who stands high in austerity while women's glances strike him.
teaches: The poem first lets the land's pleasures unseat ascetics, then offers a youth who stays firm, so the earlier fall is shown as common and not necessary.

note: Kural 65 also names the joy of hearing children's words; in 825 the king revives when his son tells him he went along.
teaches: The king's lifting at his son's words gives the couplet's pleasure of the ear a sudden effect on life itself.

gains.a: The verse lacks a general statement that a child's speech alone can be a parent's joy.
gains.b: The couplet lacks a case where those words carry news of a danger passed, so joy follows relief.

claims.gist: men on earth, even the clever, do not know what is fitting
the sage's teaching gives the highest state
one who has crossed the sea of karma is worthy of praise, and his praisers become world-rulers
pleasure that blots out awareness is a king's blindness
sleep, appetite and heedlessness are enemies of the ascetic to be destroyed
a man caught by a woman's eyes is in the grip of a deadly danger
a king's duty is to carry out his rule as the learned have taught
the counsellor's task is to seek the king's good, keep blame from him and break proud foes
compassion is to feel another's suffering as one's own and to keep a moist heart even where relief fails
wealth ends at the burning ground with a funeral and a widow's tears
youth and wealth, the gains of deeds, are fleeting, so grieving their loss is pointless
Vidyadharas and men of the earth do not join in marriage
ill-treatment and honour alike are the fruit of old deeds and must be met with equal mind
a sound and perfect body is hard to gain
zeal, vows, right conduct and guarded senses, worked on the body, yield heaven and then the release of the Jinas
a former deed drives the soul into its next birth

note: Innaa Narpathu 33 counts as painful the matter of business a drunkard speaks of; the line says a drinker free of lapses is false.
teaches: The Innaa line names the pain of dealing with a drinker's affairs and the Muthumozhikkanchi line gives its cause, the lapse that is certain in him, so one reports the effect and the other the reason no business with him is safe.

note: Kural 379 asks why those who take good fortune as good should grieve when it turns; Civakan, freed after imprisonment, neither grieves nor rejoices and ascribes both to former deeds.
teaches: The epic answers the couplet's question with a stricter ideal: not only bearing ill as one bears good, but declining joy at good fortune too, since rescue is as much karma's working as captivity.

gains.a: the hero's indifference gets a recognised ethical frame, the Kural's reasoning that what fate gives cannot be graded into welcome and unwelcome
gains.b: the couplet's rhetorical question gets a test case in which the good turn comes through another's hand, a god's, and is still referred to one's own deeds

note: Kural 376 says what is not one's own will not stay however guarded and what is one's own will not leave though thrown away; 848 says what is to come comes and what is to go goes, as the sea and river receive unasked.
teaches: The Kural states the rule of fate about possessions, and the letter applies it to a dispossessed heir in the same breath as an offer of arms, showing fate being cited to back an effort rather than to forbid one.

gains.a: the letter's proverbial lines gain the weight of a known maxim on fate and property
gains.b: the couplet gains a case where 'what is yours will come' is a political promise to a man whose throne is held by another

note: The epic praises the city's women for drawing back even minds bent on release; the Siddhar reproaches his heart for sinking into lust for women after keeping the company of ascetics.
teaches: The same lapse, a seeker of release pulled back by women, is the epic's yardstick of beauty and the Siddhar's confession of madness, so what one poet spends as a compliment is the very failure the other's renunciation is built to fight.

gains.a: the epic's hyperbole gains the view of the seeker it uses as a measure, for whom being drawn back is ruin and not a tribute to anyone's beauty
gains.b: the Siddhar's self-reproach gains the voice of the world he turns from, where the same pull is celebrated as a city's glory, so his struggle is against a culture's praise as well as his own heart

note: The Kural says the three humours counted by the learned, beginning with wind, cause disease when they exceed or fall short; one healer blames out-of-balance wind, bile and phlegm for the girl's state.
teaches: The humoral theory the Kural states as the general cause of disease is here invoked for a snakebite and fails, so the epic marks a limit the couplet does not: a correct doctrine of illness misleads when the cause is a poison from outside.

gains.a: the healer's line is identified as learned medicine, so his failure is the failure of sound theory misapplied, not of quackery
gains.b: the couplet's account of disease gains a case outside its reach, a harm that does not arise from the body's own balance

note: Dharmadattan argues that Fortune deserts the man who seizes his maker; Madanan answers that he can speak only with the sword, not the mouth.
teaches: The counsel fails not by being refuted but by being refused, so the plot proceeds with its warning on record, which the story will make good.

note: 1937 tears out the tongue of those who slander their betters; Kural 183 says death is better than living by backbiting and falsehood.
teaches: The couplet's preference for dying over slander assumes death ends the matter; the epic says it does not and takes the tongue after death.

gains.a: The torn tongue gains an ethical comparison that sets the slanderer's life against death before any hell is shown.
gains.b: The couplet gains an afterlife in which the death it prefers is not an escape.

note: In 605 the drum proclaims alms to ascetics and hard penance while still in the body; in 2389 the drum cries to wear pearls and sandal and dress in fine cloth.
teaches: The one royal drum serves both a call to wear away the body in penance and a call to adorn it, so the epic's ideals of renunciation and of festival sit side by side without being reconciled.

note: Kural 10 has those who reach the Lord's feet cross the sea of births; Soolamani 1 has those who bowed at the feet lose their deeds, after a god who conquered deeds himself.
teaches: The Kural says the feet carry one over births, and the Soolamani names a ground for it: a god who has himself overcome the deeds that bind.

gains.a: the departure of the devotees' deeds is set in the crossing-of-births frame that Tamil praise of the Lord's feet already uses, which the verse does not state
gains.b: the Lord's feet get a reason for their power, a victory over deeds, which the couplet leaves unsaid

note: Both queens wake from dreams of the king's fall: the Pandya queen sees umbrella and sceptre drop; Vijayai's dream (told in 223) shows the tree that is the king falling and a sprout rising.
teaches: The Silappathikaram's queen dreams only the end of a reign, while the Cintamani's queen dreams an end that carries an heir, so the same omen-form serves tragedy in one epic and a story of restoration in the other.

note: Innaa Narpathu 4 counts doing harm to the very strong as painful; Pazhamozhi 302 counsels keeping silent before the strong.
teaches: The counted verse names the pain of provoking the strong, the proverb verse the policy that avoids it and turns force on the weak instead, so the two give cause and remedy.

note: Her eight thousand outdoes Ariyai's three thousand, the score that had silenced Dattai's side.
teaches: Ariyai's three thousand is shown as the peak only until Mananigai's count, so the contest's score is a ladder and each verse's number is meaningful only against the one before.

note: The Kural says that for the flesh-eater hell does not open its mouth; here the flesh-eater is told 'you ate' and hot copper is forced into her mouth.
teaches: The couplet's closed mouth of hell becomes a scene in which hell feeds the eater, and the penalty is shown to match the eating.

gains.a: The epic gives the couplet's warning a named sufferer and a tormentor's reproach.
gains.b: The couplet gets a mechanism: the penalty copies the meal rather than being a general threat.

note: After the cattle-raid the women wished that the young elephant of a man wed the earth too; at the anointing they now wish that he be wheel-lord and live in Fortune.
teaches: The earlier, offhand wish for him to wed the earth returns as a formal blessing in a rite, so the epic marks how far his standing has risen since the cattle-raid.

note: Naladiyar 23 has wedding drums turn into funeral drums in the same hall the same day; the friend sees parting within union, age within youth and sickness within health.
teaches: The quatrain shows one reversal as an event; the verse turns it into a rule that every good state already holds its opposite, and uses that rule to forbid even a blink of grief.

gains.a: a concrete scene of union turned into loss that grounds its abstract list
gains.b: a generalization of its single reversal into four, with parting from kin named among them

note: In Purananuru 253 a wife whose husband fell asks how she can go among her kin raising an empty hand without bangles; in 351 Vijayai breaks her own bangles in a hermitage among ascetic women.
teaches: The widow's bare hand, which the Sangam wife dreads as a sign shown before her kin, becomes in the Jain epic an act the widow performs herself as part of an ascetic initiation among strangers.

gains.a: the breaking of bangles is shown to be the old widow's sign, so the initiation reads as widowhood as much as renunciation
gains.b: the Sangam poem's shame of the empty hand gains a later setting where the same sign is turned into a chosen discipline

note: 1790 has kings of five great lines wait with elephants and hosts for the choosing; Naladiyar 21 says kings who rode elephants under moon-like umbrellas have been carried off and called dead.
teaches: The kings' show of force at the choosing is the same show that the quatrain says does not save a king.

gains.a: The roll of kings gains a measure by which their armies and elephants seem brief.
gains.b: The quatrain gains the sight of kings gathered in full strength and ready to be seen, at the moment the strength is displayed.

note: 1810 praises a king for the line that bred him; Naladiyar 195 says a lineage is made by austerity, learning and effort, not by name.
teaches: The herald's whole mode of praise is descent, and the quatrain offers another test for the same kings, what each has done.

gains.a: The suitor's praise gains a test the herald does not apply, effort and learning in the man himself.
gains.b: The quatrain gains a hall of kings praised for birth, which shows how common the claim it denies was.

note: In 316 the deity foretells that one man will come at once and carry the child off; in 320 Kandukkatan appears out of the dark with a sword.
teaches: The foundling's rescue is framed as foretold before it happens, so the merchant's chance night visit reads as the working of the prince's destiny.

note: In Akananuru 289 a wife waiting for her husband prays at each chirp of the lizard; here Vijayai reads the lizard's call, a dream and a throbbing eye as signs of her son.
teaches: The lizard omen of the akam wife waiting for her lover is given to a widowed mother in an ascetic's robe, showing that the epic carries the akam signs of reunion over to a son.

gains.a: Vijayai's omens gain their conventional sense from the akam waiting, which makes her longing read as near-erotic in intensity
gains.b: the akam image gains a non-erotic use, showing the omen signals any longed-for return, not only a lover's

note: 2849 has the hearer bid the people bow to the lord's feet to be clear of sins of earlier births; 2846 gave the sermon's release as three together burning the tree of deeds.
teaches: The sermon sets release as a burning of deeds, and the hearer answers with worship as the first step, so the doctrine becomes a practice.

note: They leave Jayanti, the refuge reached in verse 120, for Kausambi.
teaches: The safe city reached at the end of the flight is only a stage; the return to the king's own capital is what completes it.

note: The Kural's lover asks whether the lotus-eyed god's world is sweeter than sleep in the beloved's arms; the Cintamani's narrator says those who saw the princess would not look upon the world of release.
teaches: Both weigh a woman's beauty against a world beyond this one, but the Jain epic raises the Kural's god's heaven to release from births and gives the preference to dazzled onlookers rather than a lover, which makes it a danger to be overcome rather than a joy to be asked about.

gains.a: the epic's hyperbole is shown to be a set figure of the lover's voice inherited from the Kural's third book, not a doctrine of the narrator
gains.b: the couplet's open question gets an answer from a tradition for which the other world is release, where preferring beauty is a peril to the soul, which the couplet does not consider

note: Kural 80 says a body without love is bone wrapped in skin, implying love makes it more.
teaches: The Naladiyar treats every body as filth wrapped in skin and allows no such exception.

note: The women treat the powder contest as a wager (வெல்வது சூது); the Kural says not to want gambling even when one can win, since the winnings are the hook the fish swallows.
teaches: The epic shows a wager whose real stake is not wealth but pride, and whose cost falls in a vow of seclusion on the loser, so the Kural's warning about winnings is widened to what a wager does to the one who loses face.

gains.a: the women's game is shown to belong to a kind of act the ethical tradition already condemns, which the narrator's mild கண்ணற்றார் only hints at
gains.b: the couplet, which counts gambling's harm in money, gets a case where the harm is a loss of honour that reshapes a life

note: Verse 116 has the ministers post Turumakanthan as guard in the garden for the day the astrologer named; Marusi recalls a bright man with a tight girdle who met him there and bade him come up.
teaches: The ministers' preparation is confirmed from the envoy's own side, which shows the plan worked.

note: The prince mounts and rides a vicious horse through the streets; Tirumular tells the reader to hold the reins of the running horse firmly.
teaches: The ride of a hero is shown in the epic as skill before a crowd, and in the Tirumanthiram as the discipline of the mind that needs no show, so the two use one image for different ends.

gains.a: The prince's horse-taming gains a reading as the discipline of a restless will.
gains.b: The Tirumanthiram's running horse gains a visible rider and a crowd, a show that the verse tells its hearers to do without.

note: In 388 the merchant takes up the infant 'as the great ascetic had foretold' (அருந்தவன் முந்து கூற); here, years later, the father tells what that foretelling was.
teaches: The foundling's adoption, told earlier as a bare fulfilment, turns out to rest on a promise given to a mother in despair, and the same prophecy also held the hero's capture and rescue.

note: Dhumaketu's boast of lifting hills and drinking the sea is the kind of word the Naladiyar says the excellent never speak.
teaches: The epic gives the Naladiyar's rule a case in which the boast comes just before a fall.

gains.a: 1318 gains a standard by which its hero's boast marks him as the lesser man
gains.b: Naladiyar 346 gains a warrior's boast whose price is paid in the next verses

note: The naga weapon of 1451 is cut down by the Garuda weapon of 1452.
teaches: The duel runs by counters, each weapon answered by its natural enemy, not by greater force.

note: Kural 680 has a small ruler bow to the great out of fear; verse 960 has the princes fold hands before the king at a meeting arranged for a wedding.
teaches: The bow of a wedding visit is shown as courtesy between equals, where the couplet sees bowing as a way of buying safety.

gains.a: The verse lacks any reading of the bow as a policy, and the couplet supplies the cold case of a bow from weakness.
gains.b: The couplet lacks a bow made freely by allies who gain nothing by it, which the verse supplies.

note: Kural 901 says men set on their wives miss the fine fruit and men of action do not want that desire; the epic shows a king whose rule is given up for it.
teaches: The Kural's flat warning becomes in the epic a seductive scene, so the reader is drawn into the very desire the couplet tells the man of action to refuse.

gains.a: The epic verse gets the moral frame its narrator withholds: the king's desire is the kind that a ruler is told to refuse.
gains.b: The couplet's unnamed 'fine fruit' is given concrete stakes: for a king the loss is his kingdom and his life.

note: Love explained by a former deed: Civakan's father ran after his queen because an earlier disposition sprouted; Civakan takes the garland saying it comes by ūzhvinai.
teaches: Set beside the father's fatal infatuation, which the narrator blames on former deed, the son's acceptance under the same explanation shows the epic marking each of his loves as karma at work, but here with a pause of scruple the father never had.

note: Naladiyar 101 says an old deed seeks out its doer as a calf finds its mother; the youth traces the pair's sufferings over many births to harm done to living bodies.
teaches: The quatrain gives the deed's aim but not its kind; the epic names the kind, injury to living beings, and spreads its return over many births.

gains.a: the youth's account is given a Tamil image of how a deed finds its doer
gains.b: the old deed gains a named kind, harm to living bodies, and a span of many births

note: Kural 261 defines austerity as bearing the pain that comes and causing none to living beings; 3072 has Civakan live four months in the cold open field and guard sweet life.
teaches: The couplet joins the endurance and the harmlessness in one definition, and the verse shows them in one season, if the 'guarded life' is the lives of creatures.

gains.a: the verse's four months in the open are measured against a rule that endured pain counts only with harmlessness
gains.b: the Kural's two-part definition is given an ascetic who lives it out in one cold season

note: Both tell of an animal dying while a mantra is spoken to it so that it is reborn a god.
teaches: In the Cintamani the dog must consent and think on the words, while here the elephant is simply spoken to and the change is at once.

note: In the patikam Civakan cures her by saying only 'let not your heart melt'; here he tells the household that she will not die and they must not weep.
teaches: The patikam's bare word of comfort turns out to be the promise of a man who, unlike every healer before him, first diagnoses and then cures, so the comfort is earned by the lore of the next three verses rather than given as a hero's charm.

note: In 943 Civakan promised the dying dog a god's body shining like the sun's disc if it thought on the mantra; in 1172 the god, now in that body, says the man gave it to him.
teaches: The promise made through a mantra is remembered by the one who received it as a personal gift of the man, so the epic lets doctrine (the mantra's power) and gratitude (the debt to the giver) both stand as the cause of the rescue.

note: Both foster mothers ask யாங்கு வல்லுநள்கொல் தானே of a girl who refused milk held up in a fine vessel at home: Akananuru 105 follows the question with the raiders' road of Ezhini's bowmen, Kuruntokai 356 with the scalding muddy water she must gulp.
teaches: The shared formula of the refused milk and 'how will she manage' is a stock frame of the foster mother's lament, and the two poems show its slot filled differently: the long poem measures the girl's leaving by the road's dangers, the short one by what she must now drink, so the same frame can carry either fear or tenderness.

note: The victory in 172 is repaid in 173 with the king's sister as bride.
teaches: The marriage reads as the price of the war: the bride is paid for the battle won.

note: Verse 406 names the younger of two sons as the purana's hero; verse 78 describes the younger prince as bearing the conch and discus marks on his palm.
teaches: The marks of verse 78 and the purana's foretelling in this chapter are two proofs that the younger prince is the hero, one of the body and one of the story.

note: Kural 107 says people remember through seven births the friendship of those who wiped away their sorrow; Civakan, facing death, counts on the friend whose death-sorrow he eased in another body.
teaches: The epic makes the couplet's seven births literal: a dog that became a god still keeps the debt, and the debtor runs to the man who wiped his tears.

gains.a: a moral frame that makes Civakan's appeal to the god a claim of gratitude rather than a call on magic
gains.b: a case where the remembered friendship crosses an actual rebirth from beast to god, which the couplet only asserts as a span of time

note: 1745 has the father sink in a sea of joy at the naming and the gathering of kin; Kural 69 says a mother is gladder to hear her son called worthy than at his birth.
teaches: The epic's joy comes at the naming and the kin's praise, while the Kural puts the greater joy later, in the son's worth, so the verse's delight is the first joy, not the last.

gains.a: The father's delight gains a measure, that it is the joy of the birth and the Kural counts a greater one still to come.
gains.b: The couplet gains a scene of a father's joy at the naming, a joy of the birth that it sets as the lower mark.

claims.gist: a ruler should gather wealth only by just and righteous means
enemies are to be found out by setting enemy against enemy and broken by sowing confusion among them
the firmest clinging to the world can be broken by a single word
fierce lust for women's beauty brings evil deeds that torment one in hell
in hell only the Omniscient Jina is a refuge
a maiden denied the man she has chosen should die or renounce rather than marry another
all embodied existence, even a god's, is suffering
gods suffer subjection to other gods
wealth raises those who have fallen low and brings victory and standing
the body is a worm-infested hut that only appears golden
hell-beings suffer without dying
a worthy bride, wealth and kin come only to one of rare austerity
climbing the holy hill removes the evil deeds one has piled up
deeds that wear down living beings cast the doer into hell
one who understands how souls are born into the states of existence, leave the body and rise in release does not grieve at misfortune
attachment, even as small as a split sesame seed, is a fault
the five mantras, heard at death, free even one with no merit from past karma and sow good karma
the whole world is as nothing beside renunciation
those who rejoice at the festival of the Lord are reborn to wear a king's crown
the Lord has cut away the karma that makes enmity, and his feet outshine the gods
the king's custom permits settling by single fight
a life that has turned as fortune turns should lead one to take up penance and not live heedless
no one can ward off the ripening of deeds
the merit of earlier penance ripens together in a good marriage
the son to be born will rule the world as lord of the Vidyadharas
a ripening good deed of the past together with the dawning of one's own understanding brings one to refuge in the Arhat
hell punishes with violence that has no end
victory belongs to those who win it in battle, not to those who rage
austerity is practised in dread of the disease of rebirth

note: In Kural 1146 the woman says gossip spread like the serpent seizing the moon after one sight of him; in 2461 the shy bride's hidden face is the moon in the serpent's grasp.
teaches: The same moon-and-serpent figure stands for exposure in the Kural and for modest hiding in the epic, so the figure is a flexible one for a face that is partly seen.

gains.a: The bride's shyness gains a ready sign of what is hidden, a shame that the Kural's woman does not have because her secret is out.
gains.b: The Kural's couplet gains a contrast in which the same image means a lawful, guarded display, not a scandal.

note: The Nedunalvadai's king walks the camp at midnight, a few men with him, looking each wounded man kindly in the face; Civakan tells his uncle to have the wounded tended and lies down to rest with women stroking his feet.
teaches: Set beside the Sangam king who goes out in the cold to see the wounds himself, the epic's victor delegates the duty and sleeps, which shows how far the later court poem has moved the king's care from presence to command.

gains.a: an older measure of royal care for the wounded against which Civakan's delegation and rest stand out as a choice
gains.b: a contrast in which its king's personal midnight round reads as a distinct ideal, not the only way a poet could honour a king

note: The sage says kings who kill to keep the body last only a few days and then sink in rebirth; the couplet forbids taking a life even to save one's own.
teaches: The couplet gives a bare ban; the sage supplies the reason that the life one kills to save is brief and the killing makes the next birth worse.

gains.a: The verse finds in the couplet the absolute rule its argument from the body's brevity is trying to reach.
gains.b: The couplet gets a reason against killing to save oneself that it does not itself give.

note: Verse 9 tells how the king, sunk in desire and deaf to counsel, fell to a plot while the queen fled to the burning ground; verse 25 has the son kill the enemy.
teaches: The usurpation that verse 9 blames on the father's own desire and deafness to counsel is settled only by the son's killing, so the father's fault and the son's revenge frame the whole plot.

note: Both make the adulterer embrace a figure of red-hot copper in hell.
teaches: Two Jain epics share the same matched punishment, but only 1932 begins from the secret night-visit and the wardens' mocking words.

note: Kuruntokai 73 (Paranar) tells of the Kosar who cut down Nannan's fragrant mango and drove him from his land; Kuruntokai 292 (Paranar) tells of Nannan killing a girl who ate a green fruit the stream carried down, refusing eighty-one elephants and her weight in gold.
teaches: Read together, Paranar's two poems hold both halves of one tale, the cruelty over a fruit and the tree's later felling, and each friend uses a different half: one as a model of hard scheming, the other as the type of cruelty to curse a watchful mother with.

note: Kural 632 names a minister excellent in resolve, guarding the people, learning and labour; Elathi 17 names guarding the people, resolve and strength in learning, then adds secret counsel, keeping off sloth and good company.
teaches: The two share three of their qualities in near-identical words (குடி, வன்கண், கற்றல்/நூல்வன்மை), and Elathi's additions show a minister judged also by the company he keeps and by his secrecy.

note: 1880 sets the king under his umbrella with fly-whisks at the head of his army; Naladiyar 3 says those who rode in such state fall when deeds turn.
teaches: The quatrain's fall of the umbrella-borne is forced by deeds, while the epic king's glittering display is the height from which he will walk away by choice.

gains.a: The parade gains the quatrain's warning that its splendour is borrowed from deeds that can turn.
gains.b: The quatrain gains a king whose descent is not a loss to enemies but a renunciation he has already chosen.

note: 1706 shows pleasure on the bed as the cause of the longed-for son, while Naladiyar 54 says the wise see pleasure's pain and keep away from household life.
teaches: The poem lets the pleasure that Naladiyar condemns bear fruit in an auspicious child, so the householder's pleasure is not shown as barren.

gains.a: The union gains a measure by which its fruit, a son, is the gain that a renunciant verse never counts.
gains.b: The quatrain gains a case where the pleasure ends in a birth greeted by all, which tests how far its warning holds.

note: Tirumanthiram 204 tells the heart to turn away from smiling women as the etti fruit is poison under a good look; Soolamani 980 shows a man's looks seize a girl's eyes and holds the pull as natural.
teaches: The epic tells love as a force that wins the heart, and Tirumular gives the warning that such pull is the poison.

gains.a: The verse lacks any warning that the seizing of the eyes may harm.
gains.b: The poem lacks a case that shows the pull working, from the woman's side.

note: The couplet likens the bond of body and life to a bird flying off and leaving its nest alone; the epic has the abandoned wife as a body searching for its departed life and as a bird searching the nest for its mate.
teaches: In the couplet the forsaken body is an empty shell that feels nothing, which is its lesson on impermanence; the epic gives the left-behind body and nest a longing of their own, turning the image of death's indifference into one of grief.

gains.a: the double simile is seen to rework the Kural's figure of body, life, bird and nest, so its pathos rests on a known image of death
gains.b: the couplet's bare picture of the life leaving gains a view from the side of what is left, which the couplet passes over

note: The sage's saying that the groom will rule the earth with the wheel is met by the wheel and nine treasures.
teaches: The sage's prophecy is fulfilled step by step, so the reader sees how the promised wheel comes to him through Indra's grace.

note: The fall of the spear-bearer in 1350 is followed by the fall of the golden banner and the rout in 1351.
teaches: The army breaks at the moment its banner-holder falls, so the poet makes the champion's body the whole army's footing.

note: The king in 78 leaves for forest austerity after crowning his sons, the move Kural 46 asks the householder to question.
teaches: The epic shows leaving for the outside way as a late step after the duty of rule is done, which narrows how far the Kural's rhetorical question reaches.

gains.a: The king's departure gains a test: it is not flight from household duty but follows its completion.
gains.b: The couplet gains a case of a ruler who goes outside the household way and loses nothing it names as virtue.

note: 2010 asks equal calm toward abuse, praise and neglect; Kural 151 asks the bearing of scorn only.
teaches: Level calm includes praise, so the couplet's forbearance covers only half of what the sage asks of the clear-minded.

gains.a: Equanimity gains the image of the earth that bears the digger, a reason to take scorn without answer.
gains.b: Forbearance gains the other side, praise, which also stirs the heart and needs the same steadiness.

note: Udayanan divides towns among those who served him; the couplet names apportioning as one of a king's tasks.
teaches: The poem shows apportioning as reward to friends who risked themselves for the king, which the couplet names without saying to whom the share goes.

gains.a: the grants of towns are seen as the king's last duty of rule and not as favour alone
gains.b: the couplet's word for apportioning gets a scene where the shares go to those who served in the captivity

note: The king who put aside his sword in verse 67 now asks the twins to forgive his earlier wrongs.
teaches: The softening at the altar is only a first step; the king completes it by asking pardon and taking his own refuge.

note: 1191 calls requited love the stoneless fruit, the ideal of enjoyment with nothing in the way. 1306 says love without quarrels is fruit gone bad or not yet ripe.
teaches: So the obstacle that 1191 wishes away, 1306 says is what makes the fruit ripe.

note: The patikam in 10 says a deity stood at the mother's shoulder as companion and ended her distress; 314 shows how: the deity comes in the shape of the hunchbacked maid who never left her.
teaches: The summary's 'divine companion' turns out to work through disguise, choosing the most familiar servant's form, so the help comes as continuity of the queen's household rather than as a marvel.

note: 1104 has both families pour gold and gems on the priests; 1105 names the learned chief priest who gets the greatest rain of wealth.
teaches: The gift is shared out by the priest's learning, so the wealth follows the Veda and not the families.

note: In 319 Vijayai cries that she has done no good deeds (நல் வினை செய்து இலாதேன்); 343 has the dawn drive off her night like evil deeds' suffering fleeing when old good deeds come forward.
teaches: The narrator quietly contradicts the mother's self-blame: the karma she said she lacked is the image he chooses for her deliverance, so her despair is shown to be mistaken about her own merit.

note: The minister's trick answers the prince's offer of a method against those who refuse tribute: it will enrage him and make him run to the lion.
teaches: The prince's challenge is turned into the trap that the minister builds in reply.

note: 1233 sets cloud against cloud and sea against sea as two hosts meet; Purananuru 17 sees the Chera king's host as an army like the sea.
teaches: The sea-army that praise sets at rest as a king's glory here meets another sea, and the figure turns from praise into clash.

gains.a: A source for the sea-army figure, here shown as one sea among two.
gains.b: A second sea set against the king's, so the image of an unopposed host meets its match.

note: Gandharvadattai is bathed in scented water brought in gem pots on elephants' heads; the king's daughter is bathed with water in a jewelled pot on a white musth elephant.
teaches: The bath on an elephant's pot is the royal bride's rite in two marriages, which marks Lakkanai's wedding as one in the line of the contest bride's.

note: Both use the tiger that will not eat prey that has fallen on its left side and goes hungry instead.
teaches: The Naladiyar uses the tiger's refusal as a model of one's own honour, while the Chola poet uses it to choose whom to befriend, so the image was a shared emblem of high-mindedness that each book bent to its own question.

note: Naladiyar tells the listener to do what good he can at once, because Death comes; the king acts at once on the news of the elephant.
teaches: Naladiyar's warning comes with no figure to act on it; the king gives up a throne, a wife-court and his lands within a verse of the warning, so the rule is shown at its full price.

gains.a: the king's turn gets a general rule behind it, that what seems to stand does not, and that good must be done before Death
gains.b: the quatrain gets someone who pays a kingdom's worth for it at once, instead of only urging it

note: Both brides have their husbands fixed by astrologers: Gandharvadattai's horoscope names the city where her destined groom lives (வந்தடை பான்மை), Vimalai's names the sign he will give.
teaches: Read together, the two horoscopes show the epic making each of Civakan's marriages a destiny read in advance, and fitting the sign to the father's world: a king's question about a place, a merchant's about goods that sell.

note: 274 says he ruled the whole land alone like a lion; 276 has him cast off that land, women and army.
teaches: What the king of Kalinga gives up in 276 is given its size by the merchant's earlier account of how entirely he held it.

note: 1467 lists strength, wealth and beauty that do not last; Kural 332 likens wealth's coming and going to a crowd gathering and breaking up at a dance hall.
teaches: The verse names what is lost, the couplet gives the image of its loss, and together they show loss as an ending without warning.

gains.a: 1467 gives a list of lost things but no image of how they go.
gains.b: The couplet gives wealth alone and gains strength and beauty with a king's body as the proof.

note: Naladiyar 33 sets the fool who sighs when the fruit of past deeds arrives against the wise who accept it; 2762 says the evildoer sows deeds in the soul and eats their harvest.
teaches: The quatrain names the response to the fruit, the epic names how the fruit is formed, so karma is shown as both cause and the way to meet it.

gains.a: the verse's farming image of sowing and eating gains the quatrain's wise way of facing the harvest, which the hell scenes never show
gains.b: the quatrain's 'fruit of past deeds' gains the hell-sermon's scale, which shows how severe that fruit can be

note: In 1137 the soldiers who hem in Civakan scatter like deer that have seen a killing tiger; here Kattiyangaran himself cries out like a deer that has seen a tiger.
teaches: The same simile moves up from the king's soldiers to the king: the fear Civakan once struck in the men sent against him now reaches the man who sent them, and his own words in 2197 call Civakan the tiger.

note: 1839 says wealth and heavenly pleasure are the fruit of deeds and bids remembering; Tirumanthiram 267 says joy and sorrow were fixed by earlier acts and that fools who see joy yet do not give know no virtue.
teaches: The poem asks only for remembering the fruit and keeping to the way; the couplet names what that way includes, giving, and what its absence shows.

gains.a: The poet's advice to keep to the way gains one concrete act, giving, as the proof that the fruit has been understood.
gains.b: The quatrain gains a story of fruit at its fullest, a royal wedding and gods' pleasure, set against which its warning to the unmoved has its force.

note: 2560 has Civakan circle the shrine and say he has been born and will not be born again; 3017 has a worshipper at the end say he was born in a fearful course and feared his deeds, and that those who circle the feet do not suffer.
teaches: The coronation-day boast of no more births is brought to its ground at the end, where the fear of deeds, not the pride of a king, is what sends the worshipper to the feet.

note: The four chaste women of 241 are Dattai, Padumai, Mananigai and Virisikai; Virisikai's marriage in 240 completes the number.
teaches: The count of four in 241 only makes sense once 240 adds Virisikai to the three queens, so the closing contentment is the sum of the marriages.

note: In both the man asks bees to judge whether any flower matches the woman, and both name her teeth and hair.
teaches: The epic keeps the Kuruntokai's appeal to the bee as the expert in flowers but asks about her teeth against the mullai, and its bees already live in her hair, so the witness the Sangam poem sends out to the flowers has been drawn inside the woman's own beauty.

gains.a: the epic verse gains a known model, which shows its address to the bees as a learned borrowing of the oldest Tamil praise poem
gains.b: the Sangam poem gains a later reading that moves its test from her hair's fragrance to her teeth and puts the bee in her hair

note: The minister's praise rests on law-treatise, omen-books and learning; Kural 636 says that natural wit joined to treatises cannot be matched by any scheme.
teaches: The poem's model minister is made by treatises alone, where the couplet gives native wit the first place, so the court poet and the Kural weigh a counsellor differently.

gains.a: The minister's praise gets a measure that asks what books alone can do without native wit.
