gains.b: The couplet's pairing of wit and learning meets a counsellor described only by learning, so it is tested against a case where one half is missing.

note: Marusi adds, beyond his message, his own eye-witness judgement that no other king he has seen equals the host; Kural 688 asks of an envoy purity, support, resolve and truthfulness in delivering the message.
teaches: The envoy's truthfulness here covers a judgement of the other king that the message does not carry, which is more than the couplet's duty of faithful relay.

gains.a: The verse lacks a standard to test the praise against: the couplet's truthfulness makes the eulogy a testimony that can be trusted or doubted.
gains.b: The couplet lacks the case of an envoy who adds his own appraisal of the other king, which stretches truthfulness from relaying words to judging men.

note: Kural 327 forbids taking another's life even to save one's own; Madanan's men, fearing the king, kill a stranger and pass him off as Civakan to save themselves.
teaches: The story shows the exact deed the couplet forbids and shows its source in the tyrant's terror, so the rule against killing is seen giving way first where the sceptre is bent.

gains.a: the Kural's measure for judging an act the narration only reports
gains.b: a case of the forbidden trade of life for life driven by fear of a king, which ties the chapter on not killing to the chapter on oppressive rule

note: 2907 sets the elephant fed balls of ripe paddy against the elephant that grazes the field and perishes; Purananuru 184 uses the same two elephants for a king who takes his due against one who grabs.
teaches: Both poets reach for the fed and the loose elephant, and the epic puts the old Sangam figure in the mouth of a king handing on power.

gains.a: the verse's image is shown to be an older figure of the taxing king, not the poet's own
gains.b: the Sangam poem's counsel to a king gets a speaker who is himself a king instructing his successor

note: Both say deeds do not cling to those devoted to the Lord.
teaches: The Kural's unnamed Lord, to whose devotees the two deeds do not cling, is given a Jain identity in the epic, the Great One under the asoka and triple umbrella, so the couplet's claim is read as one about the Jina.

gains.a: the epic's hard verse gains a clear parallel for its claim that karma will not cling, which supports the reading of line 4
gains.b: the couplet gains an early reader who names its Lord, showing one tradition's reading of the Kural's opening chapter

note: On the sea the merchants are told not to weep over the suffering ripened deeds have brought but to think on the flower-feet of the lord; here the lotus feet of the Lord under the asoka are praised and wished upon the head.
teaches: The sea-scene told the crew to take refuge in the feet of the Lord, and this sermon names whose feet they are and why they save.

note: Verse 181 praises him who conquered the harsh dust of karma; Kural 5 says the two deeds do not cling to those devoted to the Lord's true praise.
teaches: The epic names the conqueror of karma whose praise the Kural says keeps deed from clinging, so it names the one the couplet leaves as 'the Lord'.

gains.a: A Lord defined by his conquest of karma, so what the praise protects against is plain.
gains.b: A reader's reason why praise should loosen the deeds' hold.

note: At 2308 Civakan is likened to the white moon seized by a serpent; at 2324 he is the young sun that splits the serpent's mouth after many days.
teaches: The eclipse image moves from moon in the serpent's grip in the thick of the fight to sun breaking free after the king's death, so the hero's figure grows brighter as the usurpation ends.

claims.gist: loving worship of the lord's feet is repaid by the rank of Indra in heaven
a master's fall can be the fruit of his dependants' own deeds
when one resolves to leave home for penance, the wise urge only the way of renunciation
a dying creature that hears the sacred mantra is reborn as a god
one who has escaped the prison of birth would not return to it
no matter of policy is beyond what an envoy can say
those with desire in their mind have no refuge in places or in themselves
what befalls a man is the ripening of his deeds
in this strife-filled birth the strong seize the wealth the weak have won
self-restraint and penance in good time lead to a world free of affliction
a strong deed of the past snares a creature more surely than Death itself
Right knowledge and trust come first, and right conduct follows from them
Restraint of the six senses, ten virtues and twelve contemplations belong to the path
pride destroys the wealth that understanding has built
the fruit of good and evil deeds reaches the one who did them, and no other receives it
in trouble one should laugh without fear, since that laughter cuts the trouble
no one has been saved by weeping
a woman's body is stained and her birth lowly, to be ended by renunciation
a body cut in two shows no life, so no soul is to be found
the first lord's word, borne with the wheel of dharma, makes clear what is to come
a king may demand a girl or the life of the man who loves her
the wise guard the lapses of lesser people rather than exposing them
Reality is known by six substances, five space-occupying extents (astikaya) and seven truths
adultery and slander and taking another's spat-out leavings are wrongs unworthy of a man
dharma has a real nature (tattva) that a teacher can set out for lay hearers
pity that feels another's pain as one's own, with restraint, upholds the chief vow of not killing
a gift is rightly given to one restrained in the three (mind, speech and body) after worship of his feet

note: Jayandhara falls in love with a painted woman who is real elsewhere; the Manimekalai prince sees the living girl as a painted image.
teaches: The two works run the same trope in opposite directions, so a reader sees that the poets use the picture to say a desire is shaped by a seen form before the person is known.

note: The storm the god raises in 1157 to hide the rescue is the rain, darkness and wind Madanan cites in 1164 as the reason he had Civakan cut down.
teaches: The one storm serves two ends: it hides the god's rescue and gives the killers the alibi that lets the usurper believe his rival dead.

note: 1183 sorts war into human, divine and mixed; 1185 lets the lecture go and settles on men against men.
teaches: The long taxonomy of war is dropped for a single practical choice, so the lecture serves the decision.

note: The mother tells him to kill a kid to protect himself; his answer is that no life may be taken to guard his own.
teaches: The mother and the son give opposite answers to one fear, and the poem lets the son's answer stand.

note: Kural 776 counts as wasted the days without a noble wound; 782 has the companions offer their chests to the tusk so the scar may lie beautiful.
teaches: Where the couplet keeps a sober ledger of wounded days, the epic turns the wound into ornament, so the same ethic moves from a reckoning of duty to an aesthetic of the body.

gains.a: the reason a scarred chest should count as beauty: a wound is the record of a day not wasted
gains.b: the place of the noble wound on the body, the chest that faces the foe, which the couplet does not name

note: Kural 967 holds it better to be called ruined than to live following those who scorn one; Civakan says he does not want to live if he is set free by his wife's spells.
teaches: The epic turns the couplet's preference for ruin over dishonour onto rescue by a wife, so honour can refuse even a loving help, and the story then lets a male friend's help pass as honourable.

gains.a: a name, maanam, for the choice Civakan makes in chains
gains.b: an instance where the dishonourable life is not servitude to enemies but survival by a woman's power, which shows how gendered the couplet's honour could be made

note: Kural 1251 says desire's axe breaks the door of restraint barred with shame; 2477 shows the bride's shame giving way within a sanctioned marriage.
teaches: The Kural treats the fall of shame as a defeat, while the epic shows it fall inside a rite-bound marriage, so shame is given up here without the loss the Kural fears.

gains.a: The bride's drained state gains a rule against which shame's giving way is not a fault.
gains.b: The Kural's couplet gains a case in which the bar of shame lifts lawfully.

note: The Kural says help to a foe in misfortune is the cutting edge of valour; Nabulan, seeing the Magadha king flinch, holds his blow, reassures him and goes elsewhere.
teaches: The couplet calls kindness to a stricken foe valour's sharpest point, and the epic shows what drives it in the moment: shame in the stronger man (நாணி), so that sparing is felt as a duty to one's own honour rather than as pity.

gains.a: Nabulan's laughing restraint is given a name as the height of valour, so it is not read as weakness in the middle of a battle
gains.b: the couplet's abstract ஊராண்மை acquires a motive and a gesture, the laugh and the word 'do not fear', that it does not describe

note: 2988 has the wives cross old deeds by leaving the household and gives no god; Tirumanthiram 219 has the worshipped fire rise and burn the diseases of deeds.
teaches: One text frees from old deeds by the renouncer's own crossing, the other by a fire that burns them when worshipped, which is the split between Jain effort and Saiva rite.

gains.a: the call to cross old deeds on one's own meets a text where a worshipped fire does the burning
gains.b: the Tirumanthiram's fire that burns deeds meets a rival route with no fire and no god

note: In both works a former birth's vow explains what happens in this one: a broken vow there, a kept vow here.
teaches: The same cause by a vow of a past birth explains a loss in one work and a gain in the other, so the epics do not tie past deeds to suffering alone.

note: Kural 1094 has the man see that when he looks she looks at the ground, and when he does not she smiles; in 982 the lad looks boldly while her modesty holds her back and she melts.
teaches: The Kural gives the lover's inference from the lowered eye, and the epic shows the same shyness from within, as a pull she cannot hide.

gains.a: The verse lacks the timing of looking and looking away that tells the watcher she is moved.
gains.b: The couplet lacks the girl's inner melting and the power of her modesty over her, which the epic shows.

note: Vikraman leaves his kingdom to a nephew he has just found, while the Cintamani's Lokamapalan sets his young son on the throne and takes the ascetics' guise.
teaches: Both epics tell of a king handing over rule and turning ascetic, but here the heir is a sister's son and the turn follows childlessness, where the Cintamani's follows the setting up of his own son.

note: Amritamati in a guarded palace chamber is moved by a song from the stable: the confinement fails and her own steadfastness is the real guard.
teaches: The Kural says that only a woman's own steadfastness guards her, and the epic shows the guard fails through the ear, not the door, so steadfastness is a matter of the mind.

gains.a: Her wavering gets read against a test the Kural states: guarding is by the self, and her self is the one that gives way.
gains.b: The couplet's claim gets a case where walls hold and the guard within breaks at a voice.

note: In 1290 the poison leaves Padumai's body as darkness breaks before the sun; two verses later she is bitten again by the snake of desire.
teaches: The poet makes the cure the cause of a new sickness: the instant the real venom is drawn out, the girl's first look at her healer lets in a second venom, so the rescue and the love are one event told twice.

note: Quarrel (201-202), making up (203) and union (204) run in the order the couplet gives.
teaches: The couplet lists the three as a gain of love, and the run of verses shows them as one evening in a king's house.

gains.a: the verse gains a naming of its sequence as love's reward, not merely a king's pleasure
gains.b: the couplet gains a plot in which the quarrel is caused by a second wife and made up by flattery

note: 436 tells how the hunters destroyed the king's swordsmen; in 691 men of that army, speaking to Kattiyankaran, recall that they broke twice before Civakan won the herd back.
teaches: The rout told by the narrator as a battle scene returns as the soldiers' own confession to their king, which is why praise of Civakan reaches the usurper as an indictment of his rule.

note: 1851 says those who did evil take its seed and sow it and die wanting pleasure; 1939 shows the harvest as impalement and splitting, named the fruit of deeds.
teaches: The king's earlier fear of sowing evil gets its full price here, where the sage's list shows what the sown seed becomes.

note: The seven kings named in verse 164 now make their demand and march on the land.
teaches: The list of names becomes a real threat only when they refuse tribute, which is what makes the stratagem necessary.

note: Routed kings cried that Civakan was Murugan on his peacock; the city's women now ask whether he is Murugan or Kama.
teaches: The likeness to Murugan that the defeated kings shouted in terror returns as a question of desire in the women's mouths, so one image carries both his name in war and his effect in the street.

note: Kural 81 says all household life exists for caring for guests and doing வேளாண்மை; Thirikadugam defines the வேளாளன் as one who does not eat while a guest waits.
teaches: Both books use the vel- word for help to guests; the verse makes it a definition of a person, showing that in this group the name is earned by hospitality, not given by birth or land.

note: Cintamani 1344 has the astrologer fix the day; verse 866 has learned men judge the hour before the girl boards.
teaches: The pair shows the wedding hour as a learned decision in both Jain epics, with the Soolamani making it the king's cue to act.

note: The couplet asks a wife to guard the good name of the house; Gandharvadattai guards her husband's name among her people by sending a false message.
teaches: Together they show the wife's duty of guarding the good name pulling against truthfulness: Gandharvadattai keeps the couplet's charge by deceiving her own father's envoy, and names the couplet's duty as her reason.

gains.a: her deception gains the standing of a wife's recognised duty, the guarding of the house's name, rather than mere cunning
gains.b: the couplet's சொற்காத்து gains a hard case in which keeping the name requires a wife to tell something other than what happened

note: 3133 says fasting and meditation wash off evil deeds; Naladiyar 51 says austerity drives off sin as a lamp drives off dark, but only while the good deeds last.
teaches: The story shows the ascetics' fast washing deeds away, and the quatrain adds that the lamp burns only while its oil of good deeds holds.

gains.a: the verse's washing of deeds acquires a limit, that austerity works only while the store of good deeds lasts, which is not said in the verse
gains.b: the quatrain's lamp and oil acquire a case in which a company of ascetics is seen to carry the austerity through to their deaths

note: Cintamani verse 44 shows ploughmen and buffalo rushing into the fields; Soolamani verse 31 shows the sugarcane and paddy standing with no one in the field.
teaches: Two Jain epics describing the land differ in whom they let in: the Cintamani fills its fields with the labour that makes the crop, and the Soolamani leaves the crop standing alone.

note: Verse 927 shows a keeper who knows the elephant's ways re-roping it and handing it to its riders; Tirumanthiram 2023 sets five rutting elephants in the body that will not come to the post of the Agamas' teaching.
teaches: The same craft of the keeper is both a working skill here and the picture of a discipline that fails without a teaching there.

gains.a: The verse shows a keeper's craft but not why such taming might matter beyond the ride.
gains.b: The verse names the inner elephants but has no scene of a keeper who actually succeeds with one.

note: 2965 shows the wives stripping bangles and weeping at the king's going, while Tirumanthiram 157 has the wives and kin who wailed turn back at the town's edge.
teaches: The epic shows grieving women at a living man's leaving, where the Tirumanthiram shows the same women turning back at a dead man's bier.

gains.a: the wives' grief gains a Saiva reading in which wives, kin and children turn back at the edge of town
gains.b: the Tirumanthiram's turning back gains a living scene where the same grief ends in a king's choosing to go

note: 2846 says knowledge, faith and conduct together are a fire that burns the tree of deeds; Tirumanthiram 117 says the malas burn only in the sun's presence, as the sunstone burns cotton only in the sun.
teaches: Both burn the impurity by fire, but one fire is the seeker's own three virtues and the other needs the Lord's sun.

gains.a: the verse's fire of karma is shown to burn on its own, which the sunstone image says it cannot
gains.b: the Tirumanthiram's sunstone gets a rival that claims the stone burns without a sun

note: Naladiyar 17 warns against the woman's spear-like eyes, since she too will age and lean on a staff; at 486 the blue-eyed women pour out their hearts to the princes.
teaches: The epic shows love's pull in full while the quatrain names its price, so the two together show what a reader is warned off and why.

gains.a: A test of the women's rush of feeling against the thought that youth and beauty do not last, which the scene does not raise.
gains.b: A scene in which the beauty it warns against is shown in full, in the women's own act of giving up their hearts.

note: In 332 the beasts fail to tell him that parting is cruel; in 333 the birds fail to tell him that they themselves live paired.
teaches: Read in order, the decade moves from the argument the beasts should have made by precept (parting is cruel) to the one the birds should have made by their own example (we live with our mates), so the wife tries both ways of restraining a man and puts each in a creature's mouth.

note: 926 says that drinkers are eating poison. 1201 says love is sweeter than liquor because it delights even in memory, taking liquor's delight as the benchmark.
teaches: The book of love borrows, without judging, the pleasure that this chapter condemns.

note: The brahmin's promise of the lost queen meets the king's hope in verse 152.
teaches: The promise is aimed at a hope the king already holds, so the deceit works because it answers his grief.

note: 1053 proposes to beg the moon to bring tomorrow near; 1056 shows the moon shrinking and sinking.
teaches: The moon she meant to petition simply sets, so the night she wished short is shown passing without her asking.

note: The king at 139 refused to end one life to save another; his son, not knowing, beats the dog who is his grandmother.
teaches: The father's vow against taking life does not pass to the son, so harm continues through ignorance, not malice.

note: At the birth the deity foretold that the boy would crush the king who stood against him; here the friends, learning his birth, hail him as the life that will be Death to the usurper.
teaches: A prophecy spoken only to a hidden mother passes, through her grief, into the mouths of armed men, which is how the epic moves a foretold fate from secret knowledge to a plan of war.

note: Soolamani 200 recommends refuge in the Lord's feet as the cure for suffering; Civaka Cintamani 380 shows Civakan going to the Wise One as a raft because an old deed drove him.
teaches: The sermon says why to take refuge and the story shows why someone does, adding that the going is itself moved by an old deed.

note: In 2124 the women claim they learned their gait from the she-elephant and plead for a slow walk; in 2125 others call the same beast no she-elephant for its rough gait.
teaches: The two verses turn one convention, woman's gait as a she-elephant's, against itself: the beast that is the model of womanly walking is scolded for failing womanhood when its speed takes the hero from their sight.

note: The wedding instruments sound and the carp-eyed women go to the bath; the Naladiyar quatrain says the drums that sounded as wedding drums may sound that day in that place as funeral drums for the bridegroom.
teaches: The epic gives the drums only their joyful sound, and the quatrain reminds the reader that a hero's wedding festival is not yet a safe ground for pride, which matters in a poem that ends with its hero leaving the throne.

gains.a: The festival's drums and blessings, which the verse sounds only for joy, gain the warning that the same drums can turn funereal, which the verse never says.
gains.b: The quatrain's general rule gains a long, fully dressed wedding of a hero who will later fear kingship, so the lesson meets a concrete story.

note: Verse 44 makes feeding hungry kin the reason to seek wealth; verse 45 shows the kin scorning and avoiding a man once he is ruined.
teaches: The kin's claim on a man's wealth is not matched by any claim of his on them: their loyalty lasts only as long as the wealth they are owed.

note: Purananuru 73 has the fool who ignored a king's strength as a blind man stumbling on a sleeping tiger; verse 686 has the demander as a fool reaching for the jewel in a cobra's hood.
teaches: Both pictures make provoking the strong a blind mistake, and the epic moves the blame from stumbling to coveting.

gains.a: The verse lacks the Sangam king's gentler half, that he would give even his life to men who come with courtesy, which makes the cobra's rage a reply to manner.
gains.b: The poem lacks an image in which the fault is covetousness and not mere ignorance, which the jewel in the hood supplies.

note: The companion is sure the crowned suitors will drown in the flood of the princess's music; the patikam has already told the story as the Vidyadhara king's daughter losing at the vina.
teaches: The companion's certainty is half right, since the kings do lose, but the one it never imagines losing is the princess herself, so the reader hears her boast through the outcome the poem announced at the start.

note: In 770 a speaker says the lion was beyond even the gods and only Tivittan could destroy it; in 1155 the kings say no god or man can match Acuvakandan.
teaches: Each side's champion is raised above the gods in speech, and the story means to test the two claims against one another.

note: The youth said that harm to living bodies brought them birth after birth of pain; here the muni names the first harm and the beasts.
teaches: The muni's account gives the cause the youth's earlier remark leaves unnamed: a single killing carried through many beast births.

note: In 2998 the king mounts a palanquin that the gods carry; Tirumanthiram 153 has the lord of the land mount the burning ground's palanquin for the last time.
teaches: The same royal vehicle is a bier in one and a god-borne chair to release in the other, so the reader sees how renunciation and death can wear the same procession.

gains.a: the king's palanquin gets the contrast of the bier in which a king is carried to the burning ground
gains.b: the Tirumanthiram's royal bier gets a counter-case where the royal palanquin leads to release

claims.gist: nothing is better for any people than the shelter of a king who stands in aram and guards them like his own life
a fire that rises turning right when ghee is poured foretells fortune for the land
gods have powers of shrinking, growing, arriving at once and taking many forms
a life from infancy to old age must be fenced with the discipline of the vows against the beasts that bring sickness
a life offered to the goddess pleases her and averts evil
bodies in hell grow in size to five hundred bows and are full of burning pain
a thing absent from the cut pieces may still be real, as fire is in wood that shows it only when rubbed
wealth leaves a man when his merit is used up, as courtesans leave the poor
the ascetic wipes away the dust of the two kinds of deed (good and bad) that cling to the soul
those without restraint fall into a hell of blades
a man's present fortune is the fruit of penance he has done
eating the flesh of an animal ends craving
love of a woman's beauty makes a man take on even a ghastly form
the Jina conquered the five senses and knows without flaw
those who do not sing the Jina's feet do not reach heaven
craving and want of fine discernment lead one to gather evil karma
the tirthankara won over the senses and hard karma
he ended the pull of desire in Kama and rules the city of release
men whom fate favours cannot be faced even by the strong Vidyadharas
the priest learned in the limbs, the four Vedas and the kalpa deserves the gift of wealth
the Jina, stainless and master of the senses, is the first of merit
human pleasure is only a drop of honey tasted while death and birth threaten on every side
a king should guard the whole world and those who serve him

note: In 43 the man calls leaving a companion for wealth folly (மடமை) and pities those who do it; in 53 the heroine says her man left because his heart could not refuse the needy, a virtue she still reads as love of wealth over her.
teaches: Read together they show the paalai debate from both sides: the same departure is folly to one man and an unrefusable duty of giving to another, and the woman left behind refuses to call either grace.

note: The patikam announces that the Vidyadhara king's daughter was defeated at the vina by Civakan; here the assembled kings, faultless masters of music, fail before her.
teaches: Against the patikam the failure of the kings, praised as masters, shows that the victory announced there belongs to no ordinary skill, and raises the merchant's son above a crowd of crowned musicians before he appears.

note: In 1915 Vijayai tells her son that his mother is Sunandai, always, and his father Kandukkatan; in 2646 Sunandai is called 'no mother' for leaving.
teaches: The mother whom the epic made the true one by love is accused of not being a mother when her vow takes her away from her son.

note: Verse 2 promises the lion Tivittan tore open; verse 409 is the first time the story itself foretells it, a month away.
teaches: The opening's promise is tied to a named date inside the story, so the lion's killing is something the plot is steered toward, not only the poet's announcement.

note: In 225 the king reads the dream's crown as her son and leaves the falling tree unexplained; here she says that reading was the raft that kept her alive.
teaches: The half-told dream reading the epic first showed as the king's tact becomes, years later, the single hope a widow lived by, so the omitted part of the omen proves the part she could not afford to hear.

note: The brother recalls births among animals driven by old deeds; the Siddhar asks when he will say enough to births as stone, tree, fish, bird and grass.
teaches: The recalled animal births become the very cry of 'enough' that the pair will act on, so the epic gives the Siddhar's wish a remembered cause.

gains.a: the first-person plea to end the lower births, which in the epic is only recounted as past
gains.b: a stated cause of those lower births, old deeds that drive the soul among beasts, with the siblings' own kin as the killers

note: 1552 gives the prince's elation at fortune with no hint of its cause; Naladiyar 93 says wealth gathers when its time comes and leaves when the deeds that sent it run out.
teaches: The Naladiyar supplies a karmic account the epic withholds in these verses: his elation is for a fortune whose source and end are deeds, though the verse says no such thing.

gains.a: The prince's elation gains a limit that the poet does not state: the fortune is held by karma and not by his own act.
gains.b: The quatrain gains a case where wealth, wife and rule arrive together, so its claim is tested against a complete success.

note: 1165 makes pride the child of anger's fire; Tirumanthiram 266 says the swollen-headed die without support, fallen into withering anger.
teaches: Pride that grows from anger in the epic is shown by Tirumular to end in a death without any support.

gains.a: The warrior's anger-born pride has no account of its end, which Tirumular gives as dying unsupported.
gains.b: Tirumular's proud man has no face or voice, which the epic gives in a swordsman boasting of his anger.

note: The Kural forbids trusting anyone unexamined but bids trust after examination; Vijayai bids the friends trust no one at all with the secret except Civakan.
teaches: The Kural's two-step rule of trust assumes time to examine people, and the epic shows a mother hiding an heir from a usurper dropping the second step altogether, so that danger turns examined trust into blanket silence.

gains.a: Vijayai's charge gains a rule against which its absoluteness can be measured, showing how far beyond ordinary prudence her fear has pushed her
gains.b: the couplet gains a case where its own first clause, தேறற்க யாரையும், is held without the second, marking the limit of the time to examine it presumes

note: Civakan whispered the five mantras into the dying dog's ear, seed that frees one of former karma, and the dog became a yaksha; the friend whose story he now has danced and whose golden image he sets up is, if the friend is that god, the debt repaid for that mercy.
teaches: A kindness to a dying animal is paid back in a rescue and then in the first public memorial the epic records, so the charity of 945 outlasts the dog's death in the city's own ritual.

note: Naladiyar says even kings on elephants under the moon-bright umbrella are carried off and spoken of as dead; Jayavarma lays down his kingdom while living.
teaches: A king's leaving rule by his own act, before it is taken from him, is the story's answer to the impermanence the Naladiyar says no king escapes.

gains.a: the abdication is seen as a chosen answer to the loss of rule that the Naladiyar says death forces on every king
gains.b: the Naladiyar's lament over fallen kings is given a king who acts on the lesson while still ruling

note: Kural 882 bids one fear the bond with enemies who are like kin more than enemies like swords; the usurper delights in the kinsman-like gifts of the king who means to kill him.
teaches: The couplet's warning is spoken to the potential victim, and the epic shows that victim praising the gift that should have frightened him, while placing the kin-like enemy on the side the story favours.

gains.a: the scene gains a name for the usurper's error: he guarded against the sword but not against the friend
gains.b: the couplet gains a plot in which its danger is visible to everyone but the one it warns, and in which the false friend is not the villain

note: Suramanjari vowed in 899 to keep apart until Civakan came defeated (தோற்று) and worshipped her anklet feet; in 2088 he lays his head on her anklets and her sulk ends.
teaches: Her vow is kept not by a defeat he admits but by a lover's bow inside a quarrel he says he did not cause, so the pride that began in a contest is satisfied by the rites of love.

note: Both start from crowned kings brought to nothing and rebuke those who see it unchanged: Pattinathar's கண்டு பின்னும், the Valayapathi's கண்டால் மயங்காதே. Pattinathar's way out is reaching the feet of the Lord of the golden hall; the Valayapathi's is standing in the highest path and striving.
teaches: From the same sight the two draw opposed remedies, refuge at a god's feet for the Saiva poet and one's own steady effort for the fragment, which names no god; the tension holds on the reading that the fragment's ஊக்கம் is sufficient by itself.

note: Kural 265 says tapas is striven for because whatever is wanted comes as it is wanted; the city's women say the princess must have done penance (நோற்றனள்) to enjoy Civakan's beauty.
teaches: The women apply the couplet's promise to a marriage, so the pair shows penance taken in common talk as the merit behind erotic good fortune, the very use the Kural's next verse warns against.

gains.a: the doctrinal basis of the women's idiom, which the epic uses only in passing
gains.b: evidence of how the couplet's motive of getting what one wants was heard in popular speech, where the wanted thing is a beautiful husband

note: 1992 treats giving as graded with a lowest grade; Tirumanthiram 505 says gifts to those without conduct and vows are like milking a barren cow.
teaches: The lowest grade of giving may still be a gift, and the Tirumanthiram says that at some point there is no crop.

gains.a: The grading gains a limit below which a gift is wasted, which 1992 does not name.
gains.b: The barren-cow image gains a scale: the poem shows that giving is not simply worth or not worth, but graded.

note: The Sirupanarruppadai paints the kinai bard's hunger in his kitchen, his wife boiling unsalted greens behind a shut door, until a patron's gifts end it; the Cintamani puts the porunar's distress down in half a line, through the carts of paddy and cane.
teaches: The epic keeps the Sangam bard's want only to cancel it at once, and moves its relief from one named patron's gift to the anonymous traffic of a rich land.

gains.a: the stock phrase about the kinai bards is seen to carry a whole earlier genre of hunger and rescue
gains.b: the guide poem's patron-centred relief is set against a later picture where plenty, not a giver, ends the bard's want

note: Kattiyankaran plotted to send the king to rule heaven and keep the earth himself; Govindan now resolves to take his life by the same kind of guile.
teaches: The guile that won Kattiyankaran the throne becomes the means of his own destruction, as Govindan names the symmetry outright, so the plot's justice is shown as treachery turned back on its maker.

note: Sirupanchamoolam 16 says that before the worthless anger is good and nobility bad, as good meat is wasted in a biting dog's mouth; Pazhamozhi 109 says good done to the graceless base puts the doer in danger.
teaches: Holding them together shows the two halves of one counsel: Sirupanchamoolam says kindness to the base is wasted, Pazhamozhi that it is also dangerous, the tiger's face being closer than the dog's mouth.

note: 3081 fires the arrow of pure meditation like a roaring fire to destroy the foes; Tirumanthiram 219 has deeds burnt by the fire that is worshipped and fed with ghee.
teaches: One text burns deeds by an inner meditation like fire, the other by an outer fire kindled in worship, so the two disagree on where the fire is.

gains.a: the meditation that burns is seen as an inner fire beside the Saiva fire kindled in ritual
gains.b: the ritual fire that burns deeds is set beside a Jain fire that burns them with no offering

note: The patikam gives the episode one line, the victorious elephant that terrified Gunamalai, beaten on the same day Civakan gave nectar to the dying dog; 974-985 tell it as a scene in which the bearers flee, the companion offers to die, and Civakan chooses death over life before he knows who the girl is.
teaches: The patikam's pairing of the dog and the elephant on one day is borne out by the scene's terms: both deeds are mercy to a life in danger, not courtship, and the love follows only afterwards.

note: The couplet wants a spy in a guise that raises no suspicion; Yugi's mad guise draws every eye but carries speech meant for one hearer, the king.
teaches: A disguise can be conspicuous to everyone and still be a secret to all but one, which the couplet's rule of unsuspected appearance does not allow.

gains.a: The epic verse gains the Kural's test of a disguise as one that does not draw suspicion, so Yugi's loud madness stands out as a deliberate exception.
gains.b: The couplet gains a case where the disguise is meant to be seen, because the message is in the madman's talk and not in being unseen.

note: 1040 has the bride praying to the Jina to lose the disease of birth; 1107 ends her wedding with some going to the forest and others returning to enjoy.
teaches: The wedding that the maiden began by praying to be freed of birth closes on the same two answers, release or return.

note: The Naladiyar quatrain says that as darkness rushes back when the lamp's oil runs out, evil settles in when good deeds are spent; Kattiyangaran says that as a lamp dwindles when ghee and wick are gone, wealth perishes when the two kinds of deed wear away.
teaches: Both make karma the lamp's fuel, but the quatrain teaches renewing merit by austerity while the epic's usurper uses the image to explain the loss of a throne, so the lamp shows its political use: a fall can be read as fuel run out instead of a wrong repaid.

gains.a: the speech is seen to draw on a renunciant teaching image, sharpened by counting both good and bad deeds as fuel
gains.b: the quatrain's image is applied to kingship and wealth in a story, where it can be heard as self-excuse

note: Kural 871 says no one should want enmity even in jest; verse 647 says that making foes of the harmless and trusting the ill-hearted both burn later.
teaches: Arimanju's caution answers the counsellors' haste with the Kural's own rule against courting enmity, so the epic stages two readings of Kural 879 and 871 as rival counsel.

gains.a: The verse lacks the couplet's reason that enmity has no good in it, and gives only its later pain.
gains.b: The couplet lacks the second warning, against counting the ill-hearted as friends, which the verse pairs with it.

note: After losing the powder contest Suramanjari vows that none but Civakan shall break her reserve and shuts herself away (902, 908); after winning it, Gunamalai vows death or penance if she is denied him.
teaches: The quarrel Civakan judged ends with both rivals bound by vows only marriage to him can release, the loser by seclusion and the winner by threat of death, so his verdict sets up two of his marriages at once.

note: In 109 those in the hall say Tivittan will guard the whole world under one umbrella; in 722 the gods tremble before the lion he is about to overcome.
teaches: What the hall only affirmed of Tivittan's coming rule is tested here by a foe even the gods fear.

note: In Purananuru 284 a warrior straightens his twisted sword with an elephant's tusk as lever (மிறையாக ... திருத்தா) and laughs at the fleeing back; Salanidhi straightens his elephant-bent sword in a lever (மிறைக்கொளீஇ திருத்துவான்) and the kings flee.
teaches: The pair shows the epic taking over a Sangam war vignette in its own words, the sword-straightening and the enemy's flight, but turning the Sangam hero's laugh into the foe's fear and making the man a spear-pierced warrior who dies in the next verse.

gains.a: Salanidhi's obscure gesture is clarified by the older poem's clearer picture of a sword set against a lever
gains.b: the Purananuru vignette is shown to have lived on as a set piece of heroic poetry long after the Sangam

note: 2906 calls guarding dharma the king's highest joy; 2922 turns to the women and asks them to hear the lasting good.
teaches: The same speaker ranks the joy of ruling highest for the heir and then offers a different good to those he leaves.

note: 1556 says the king who has set the world under his umbrella is caught in a net of deer-eyed women; 1624 shows the net at work, with arrows from the women's brows.
teaches: The poem's opening image of the netted king becomes a scene in which the quarrel's cause returns at once.

note: The epic says even Indra-like lords of the gods lost their forms; the quatrain says kings on elephants under moon-like umbrellas have been carried off and no one is left over.
teaches: The quatrain's visible proof that kings die is stretched by the epic to the gods, so no rank in any world offers refuge from loss.

gains.a: a human instance to rest the claim on, kings borne off whom a reader has seen, where it offers gods only by doctrine
gains.b: a reach beyond the visible, to ranks above the world of men, so heaven too is no way out

note: 1136 shows a minister hiding the lion's death for days; the couplet says the world rests under a king who can bear a bitter word.
teaches: The cost of a king who cannot bear bitter words falls first on his ministers, who delay the news and arrange who tells it.

gains.a: the epic gives a concrete delay and a go-between, where its king has only been called proud
gains.b: the couplet gets a named cost of an intolerant king, the stage-managed late report, which it states only as the world's shelter lost

note: Kalittokai 11 gives the three tender creatures of the burning waste: the tusker who lets his mate drink first, the dove that fans its mate with its wings, the stag that gives its shadow to the shadeless doe; 1187-1188 give the elephant shielding its calf, the cock bird sheltering the hen with its wings, and the stag shading the doe with its body.
teaches: The Cintamani keeps the palai triad but changes its use: in the Kalittokai the creatures' care is the heroine's ground for hoping the man will return, while here it only measures the heat for a lone traveller with no beloved at home, so the akam sign of love becomes a road-guide's warning.

gains.a: the god's description is shown to be a set piece of Tamil palai convention, which explains why these three animals and no others appear
gains.b: the Kalittokai's images are seen to outlive their love setting, showing that the triad had become a stock mark of the desert itself

note: 1435 says the missile cannot be turned back; 1439 shows its deity frightened and returned to its own shape.
teaches: The warning rests on a rule about hate-loosed weapons that the scene then breaks, so a claim of certainty is answered by the hero's greater strength.

note: The prince masters a rutting elephant; Tirumular's body holds five rutting elephants that will not come to the post of the Agamas' teaching.
teaches: The epic's taming is an outward feat of the body, and the Tirumanthiram carries the same image inward to the senses, so the story's word மதம் is read both as rut and as the pride the senses breed.

gains.a: The epic's elephant gains a second sense: its mastery is also a figure for the senses held in check.
gains.b: The Tirumanthiram's inner elephants gain a narrative picture, a man who actually stops a rampaging beast.

note: The king holds that worship of the goddess is rightly done by killing, beginning with humans; the Kural says refraining from killing and eating one creature is better than a thousand sacrifices.
teaches: The two rank sacrifice and non-killing in opposite orders, and if the Kural is read as applying to blood offering as well as to oblations, the king's rite is the very thing the couplet ranks lowest.

gains.a: the king's claim is set against a Tamil rule that puts non-killing above every rite
gains.b: the couplet's comparison of sacrifices with non-killing gets a case where the sacrifice is of humans

note: Puram 26 praises a Pandya who cooked a battlefield sacrifice with crowned heads for the hearth, blood for water and bangled arms for ladles; in 2235 the slain warriors themselves are the ghoul-woman's feast, their wedding garlands replaced by entrails.
teaches: The Sangam battlefield-feast is the victor's rite and his glory, while the Cintamani tells it from the side of the slain, as bridegrooms whose wedding garlands become entrails.

gains.a: the epic's ghoul-feast is placed in the old genre of the battlefield sacrifice it inherits
gains.b: the Puram's feast, sung only from the victor's side, is shown from the dead men's side, where it costs a marriage

note: 388 says a king who rules justly and protects is held to be a god among people: the title is earned. On Parimelazhagar's reading of 698, the divinity belongs to any king, young or kin, and the courtier mustn't ask.
teaches: Other readings of ஒளி remove the conflict.

note: 1357 shames men who run to save life; 1380 calls a swordsman who runs from one man loathsome.
teaches: The rally and the taunt are one argument in two voices: flight is judged first as lost honour, then as disgusting manhood.

note: Both ask whether a woman is a goddess, a rare bird or a human, but in verse 1017 the question is asked about a painted likeness and answered by reasoning.
teaches: The question that Kural 1081 puts as a lover's reeling is here a calm puzzle about a portrait, so the same three-way wonder can come from sight alone.

gains.a: The verse lacks the lover's own giddy heart, which the couplet puts first and which the woman's reasoned question leaves out.
gains.b: The couplet lacks any sense that the wonder can be a deliberate question put to another person about a likeness.

note: At 1585 Civakan says the kavya poets have dressed up the flesh to kindle desire; at 1482, lying in Kemasari's house, he himself laments that her hair, brows, eyes and breasts kill him.
teaches: The hero who now condemns the poets' painting of the body was a few scenes before its most eloquent practitioner, so the epic sets its own love poetry under judgement and leaves the reader to weigh whether desire for a wife differs from desire for another's.

note: 1798 shows kings' desire swelling as she enters; Naladiyar 17 tells the man not to desire a spear-eyed girl, who will stoop on a staff.
teaches: The poem lets the reader see her with the kings' eyes, and the quatrain supplies what those eyes will not see.

gains.a: The kings' longing gains a limit set by age, which the verse does not state.
gains.b: The quatrain gains a young woman actually seen, so its warning is tested against an entrance that wins every eye.

note: The Caranas at Aranapatham wash away their own karma (தம்வினை கழுவுகின்றார்) by renouncing rule; Tirumanthiram 2422 says the soul is cleaned of its dirt as cloth by a washer, and everything that comes to it is the bond of grace.
teaches: Both use the image of washing a stain from the self, but in the Jain epic the ascetic is the washer and the dirt is his karma, while in Tirumular the washer is grace and even the soul's bonds are its soap; the shared image exposes the rival accounts of who does the cleansing.

gains.a: the Cintamani's brief phrase about karma-washing is shown to carry a doctrine of self-effort that a Saiva reader would contest
gains.b: Tirumular's claim that all is grace's bond is sharpened against a named alternative, ascetics who clean themselves without a god

claims.gist: the one who killed pays with his own life
no god, demon or man can stand against the discus-lord's might
the Jina's law is a rare gem to one who has escaped the sea of birth
one who keeps his attachments cannot cross the sea of births
the pleasures and the lifespan one enjoys are measured out by the penance of a former life
the possessor of the discus and the other royal jewels is a god among kings of men
deeds ripen into painful, release-less births, and the dharma the sage taught gives its own fruit
even a creature with no merit can, by the mantra heard at death, be reborn a god
one who does not learn from seeing a rival's strength is without good sense
a woman's nature is to join whoever merit brings and to leave again
it is right to pass beyond them
a king is the guard of living creatures and may not take one life to guard his own
one must not harm a life to protect one's own
a warrior who dies in battle has paid the debt he owes for the rice his lord fed him
fifteen days before a god falls his eyes blink and his garland fades, and he sees his pleasure as wasted
wealth, victory over enemies, friends, wives and children can be gained, but a brother born of the same parents cannot be made
those who abandon the root of good deeds for fleeting pleasure perish
women's beauty is where desire is seen to take birth, and so the Creator's making of them is blamed
the bliss of the state of release can be shown by comparisons with light, coolness and fragrance

note: The pierced Sarthulakan fights on and kills the thrower, as in the Kural's warrior who sends his spear off and smiles at the one in his own body.
teaches: The poem makes the Kural's warrior who smiles at a spear in his body into a man who turns the wound into a weapon.

gains.a: 1316 gains a norm that treats a wound received in the fight as a mark of the warrior, not a loss
gains.b: Kural 774 gains an actual wounded fighter who turns the thrown trident on its thrower, not only a smile

note: Gunamalai reproaches him for being able to eat without his lord; at Kanakamalai's table he eats beside him.
teaches: Held together, the two meals show that for the women of the epic eating is a measure of grief: the brother's meal without Civakan reads as betrayal, his meal with him as reunion.

note: Here the narrator makes the couple one life in two bodies; in 1510 Kemasari, deserted, throws back at Civakan his own saying that love makes two lives one.
teaches: The oneness the narrator grants Vimalai is the formula Kemasari already turned against Civakan after he left her, so the reader knows before the dawn music that this union too ends in his going.

note: The patikam tells that the god Civakan once helped untied the flower-cord with which soldiers had bound his arms.
teaches: The bond that holds the lion here is as weak as a spider's thread and is in fact loosed by a god, so the image of 1116 is fulfilled literally: it is never the king's force that holds him.

note: 453 hails the women's eyes as the killing sign of love; Naladiyar 44 refuses the sword-and-lily praise and sees only a scooped-out palm fruit.
teaches: The two cannot both stand: one accepts the eye as a weapon, the other denies the image on the ground that the eye is only flesh, and which holds depends on whether the speaker is praising or renouncing.

gains.a: Its praise of the eyes is shown to rest on a metaphor a renunciant would call blindness.
gains.b: The target of its refusal is given a full, dazzling form in a poem written to enjoy it.

note: The patikam's 24 says only that Civakan took counsel with his mother (தாயொடு எண்ணி) before entering the city; 1918 to 1931 give that counsel as a full lesson in kingcraft.
teaches: The summary's two words turn out to hold the epic's most compact statement of royal policy, placed in the mouth of a widowed ascetic queen.

note: 1694 has the Vidyadhara drop from the sky and bow; 1697 has the king make him tell the message in his own words.
teaches: The envoy's arrival is the start of an exchange which waits on the king's leave, shown in the order of events rather than said.

note: 1339 asks whether one may stand aside while another fights; 1341 takes the single fight as the king's custom.
teaches: The duel is argued as a question of courage first and accepted as royal custom second, so the rule is made by the debate and not given in advance.

note: Kural 674 says what is left over of a deed or a feud scorches like a fire's remnant; verse 643 draws the same fire but warns of a foe still small.
teaches: The epic's counsellors aim the couplet's fire at an enemy not yet seen to strike, which turns a rule about unfinished business into a case for striking first.

gains.a: The verse lacks the rule that an unfinished enmity is a remnant that will burn, which the couplet states as a general law.
gains.b: The couplet lacks a counsellor's use of it against a foe who has done nothing yet, which the verse supplies.

note: Verse 2 says the slips of speech of one praising the faultless are no slips; verse 17 says a fault stays a fault even in those who have reached truth and in a god.
teaches: The fragments hold two standards side by side: the poet excuses faults by the worth of what is praised, while the moral verse refuses to let any height excuse a fault, so the apology rests on devotion, not on a rule about faults.

note: The attendants call the princess's eyes not carp but blue lilies sheltering in the moon and line them with kohl; the Naladiyar's renunciant scorns those who call eyes water-lilies, carp or spears and sees the eye as a scooped-out palm fruit.
teaches: The comparisons the Jain quatrain names as the talk of the blind are exactly the ones a Jain epic's attendants weigh and choose between, so the pair shows the same tradition keeping the lover's rhetoric in its epic and rejecting it in its ascetic verse.

gains.a: the epic's ornate conceit is set against a reading in which it is the very speech that endangers the renunciant, which the epic leaves unsaid until its last book
gains.b: the quatrain's anonymous praisers of eyes get a concrete scene, women adorning a bride for a crowd, showing the rhetoric it resists at work in public

note: 1018 sees shame as the condition of virtue, with virtue itself ashamed to approach the shameless. 1075 is a kind of counter-case: the base still have conduct, with fear and desire in place of shame.
teaches: Their conduct looks alike and differs in its source.

note: 1627 fears she will die in the fire of parting; 1631 argues she cannot have, since he lives.
teaches: Together they show the hero answering his own fear with an argument rather than news, using the lovers' shared life as evidence, so that separation grief turns into reasoning.

note: The seizing bird that threatens the queen in verse 13 is shown in verse 14 to set her down unharmed.
teaches: The bird's danger in 13 is answered in 14, so the abduction is told as a passage to the hermitage and not as an injury.

note: 1675 opens the women's spray-war against the king; 1678 has the queens cry that they have beaten him and the pool run dry.
teaches: The water-play is told as a war from first volley to cry of victory, so the king's surrender is the planned end of the game.

note: The friends suspect Gandharvadattai because her body does not waste; she has already sent his brother to him by her spell.
teaches: Read against 1747, the calm the friends take for deceit is knowledge: a wife who knows by her arts where her husband is has no cause to pale, and the convention they judge her by misleads them.

note: Kural 559 says that when the king bends justice the sky will not rain; 255 extends the effects to the planets, the hours, harvest, hunger, women's chastity and dharma.
teaches: The Cintamani turns the Kural's warning to an unjust king into an argument against a minister seizing power, treating usurpation itself as the bending of the sceptre.

gains.a: the councillor's list is anchored in the Kural's best-known statement of the bent sceptre
gains.b: the couplet's single effect, failed rain, is shown as the first of a cascade that reaches into household morals

note: 2033 gives the pair unbroken pleasure for their whole span; Naladiyar 16 says the joy of youth is fleeting like the lamb eating the garland before the slaughter.
teaches: The epic can promise pleasure that lasts a full span only by moving it out of this world, which is exactly what the Naladiyar's warning denies is possible here.

gains.a: The long pleasure gains a warning that without a world apart it would end as the lamb's does, which the verse's calm account does not say.
gains.b: The quatrain gains a counter-picture: a place where youth's joy is not a trap, though it too ends in the next verses with the pair's rise.

note: 2886 compares the body to a doll that falls apart joint by joint when its pins are loosed; Siddhar 42 asks when the puppet taken up to match the two karmas will be thrown down.
teaches: The epic shows the doll's falling as a mechanism and the Siddhar wants to throw it down, so one explains how the body fails and the other why it is to be cast off.

gains.a: the doll's failing joints gain the Siddhar's reason for the body, a payment for two deeds, to be thrown down
gains.b: the Siddhar's puppet gains an account of how it comes apart, each pin loosing the rest

note: Kural 1109 names sulking, making up and union as love's rewards; verses 1071, 1072 and 1074 enact the three in order, sulk, appeasement at her feet, embrace.
teaches: The epic plays out the couplet's triad in full and then cuts it off with the king's runners, so love's three rewards are set as the calm the hero's karma-laden story breaks.

gains.a: the three verses gain a frame that makes them one completed movement rather than a string of descriptions
gains.b: the couplet gains a narrative cost: its rewards are shown as fragile, interrupted by a power outside the lovers

note: 496 has the merchant hold that effort alone can bring a flood of wealth in a day; Siddhar 641 tells the heart that the wealth it has came by the order of deeds done in earlier lives and was not got today.
teaches: The two disagree about where wealth comes from, today's effort or earlier lives, and the epic lets its merchant hold the first view only until the storm turns him to the second.

gains.a: the merchant's creed gains its direct opposite, which shows how much it denies
gains.b: the Siddhar's claim gains an opponent who believes the reverse and is then brought round by events

note: The Kural's man sees two looks in her eyes, one that gives the sickness and one that cures it; the epic says her eyes are poison and nectar at once.
teaches: The couplet's private double look of lover's sickness and cure becomes, in an epic, a public force that maddens sages and later unseats a king.

gains.a: the epic's poison-and-nectar image is placed in an older Tamil account of the look as both wound and remedy
gains.b: the couplet's two looks are given consequences beyond the lover, reaching ascetics and the state

note: Sathanikan gives up the throne while living, where the quatrain says kings under the umbrella on elephants are carried off as dead.
teaches: The epic's king keeps his rank by choosing to leave it before death, which the quatrain does not allow for.

gains.a: The king's leaving gets a sharper meaning, since the quatrain says death is how all kings finally lose the umbrella.
gains.b: The quatrain's claim that none escape gets a qualification: one can leave the throne by renouncing before it is taken.

note: Both liken giving to rain; Kural 211 makes the rain a duty that asks no return, while 142 notes that rain also wastes itself on salt land and calls Pekan's giving கொடைமடம், folly.
teaches: The Kural keeps only the dutiful side of the rain image, but the Purananuru poet saw its waste as well, so the rain figure for generosity carried an admitted cost of indiscrimination that the maxim leaves out.

note: The Pandya Kudumi warns cows, brahmins, women, the sick and the sonless to take shelter before he shoots; Vipulan will not strike beasts, the wounded, the young or the old.
teaches: Both armies spare the weak, but on different grounds: the Purananuru's warning is the way of right (அறத்துஆறு) protecting those who cannot fight, while the epic grounds each refusal in the striker's own glory, so the same restraint can rest on dharma or on pride.

gains.a: Vipulan's code is seen as the epic's version of an old battle rule, and its distinctive turn, honour rather than protection, stands out
gains.b: the Pandya's proclamation gains a contrast that shows how particular its reason is: it names the protected by their vulnerability and their rites, not by what striking them would cost the warrior

note: Naladiyar 13 shows those whose speech fails, who lean on a staff and lose their teeth, yet stay in the house with their eyes on desire; 2626 shows a youth in a garland and spear who comes to lean on a staff and drool.
teaches: The sermon shows the young man whose decline the Naladiyar describes only from its end, and so makes the same warning about desire outliving the body's strength.

gains.a: the epic's youth gets the Naladiyar's charge that the old man who lingers in the house is blind to the road to safety, which the sermon only implies
gains.b: the quatrain gets the garland-and-spear picture of the youth before, which it lacks, so its old man is someone who was once the Kama of women's eyes

note: Evening as what eats the lives of the separated: the couplet's woman says it is not evening but the hour that devours; Kanakamalai sees it as a demon gaping to swallow her.
teaches: The epic makes the couplet's figure of devouring evening into a visible monster, the moon its tooth and the red sky its mouth, showing how a Kural conceit was expanded into scenery.

gains.a: her terror of evening is placed in the Kural's convention of the devouring hour
gains.b: the couplet's bare 'eats life' is given a body and features drawn from the evening sky

note: Kural 202 says evil is to be feared more than fire because evil yields evil; in 799 burning arrows kill the mean-minded kings and warn them off evil even in their next body.
teaches: The epic makes the fire itself the preacher: the burning arrow that kills is only the lesser fire, and its warning points to the evil that will follow the dead into the next birth.

gains.a: the ground of the arrows' warning, that evil breeds evil and so outlasts the body the fire destroys
gains.b: a picture of evil outlasting death, which gives the couplet's comparison with fire a span beyond one life

note: The friend reads the owl's paired call as a sign that he has not left her; Civakan, unrecognized, sends word that her beloved will be seen within ten months.
teaches: The omen is confirmed out of the absent man's own mouth, and given a term, so the chapter closes the friend's consolation with the hero's pledge.

note: 2845 defines release's path as knowledge, faith and conduct together; Kural 356 says those who learned here and saw the real thing reach the path of not coming back.
teaches: The Kural pairs learning and seeing, and the Jain verse adds the third (holding it in conduct), so the two give different recipes for the same release.

gains.a: the verse's triad is shown as a larger version of the Kural's learning and seeing
gains.b: the Kural's two-part path is given a third part that the verse insists cannot be left out

note: Kural 110 says there is no escape for one who kills a benefit; 253 names a minister who kills the king who raised him among those who sink into hell and leprosy.
teaches: The epic gives the Kural's abstract unforgivable sin a concrete political form, the minister's regicide, and spells out where 'no escape' leads.

gains.a: the regicide is ranked as ingratitude, the sin the Kural puts beyond remedy
gains.b: the couplet's general rule receives its gravest case and an explicit punishment

note: 2096 has the ministers put down the heavy burden they bore through the disease of birth; Kural 345 says that for those set on cutting off births even the body is excess.
teaches: The burden of the body in the epic is lifted by a king's grace, whereas the couplet lays it on the renouncer's own will.

gains.a: The ministers' burden gets a stated reason, that the body itself is surplus when one wants to end births.
gains.b: The couplet gains a scene of a king's court letting go together, where the renouncer is no lone figure.

note: The epic says fear can neither stop the coming harm nor do anything but add pain and fresh deeds; the quatrain says the fool sighs when the fruit arrives while the wise take it as old desert.
teaches: Fear is shown as a new cause of karma before the fruit comes, which extends the quatrain's advice on taking fruit that has arrived.

gains.a: the quatrain's picture of fruit taken calmly as old desert, which the brother states only as the uselessness of fear
gains.b: a case of the advice under the nearest threat, two captives of a sacrifice, where calm is hardest to keep

note: The Kural says nothing is stronger than fate, which gets ahead of every contrivance; the king says that when the destined time comes no one can stop it, and so refuses every royal suitor.
teaches: Read with the couplet, the king's appeal to fate is not a surrender but a policy: he uses fate's strength as the reason to refuse every suitor and leave the choice to a contest, where the Kural sees fate only as defeating a plan.

gains.a: the king's line gains the Kural's general law, which explains why even begging kings cannot move him
gains.b: the couplet gains a case where acknowledging fate guides a decision instead of frustrating one

note: Purananuru 19 (lines 8 to 9) likens arrows lodged in a wounded elephant to a flock of sparrows settled on a hill (குன்றத்து இறுத்த குரீஇஇனம் போல); Kalavazhi Narpathu 8 says elephants hidden by arrows look like countless hills with flocks of sparrows (எண்ணருங் குன்றிற் குரீஇயினம்).
teaches: The near-identical image shows a stock battle simile passing from a Pandya victory poem to a Chola one, and the frames show it carries no fixed feeling: in Purananuru 19 it leads into mothers weeping for sons and Death fleeing in shame, while in Poigaiyar it is pure spectacle of the victor's field.

note: 1381 has the Vidyadhara kings turn back from fated men; 1552 says no rival is left.
teaches: The Vidyadharas' flight from the battle is what leaves the prince without an enemy at the wedding; his joy is the victory's late fruit.

note: In 698 the roar of the made lion fills the Himalaya and Sindhu land; in 706 the envoys, who do not say so, describe it as a lion of the gem hill.
teaches: The envoys repeat the false lion as a fact, so the reader sees the trick work on the very messengers.

note: Kural 348 says that those who have wholly renounced have reached the head and all others are caught in the net; Cintamani 376 names the net as Death's and austerity (நோற்று) as the way out of it.
teaches: The couplet divides men into renouncers and the netted, while the epic shows the netted as knowing their state, so renunciation is not only clear seeing but a doing that knowledge alone does not bring.

gains.a: the epic's net is tied to the Kural's chapter on renunciation, making நோற்று the renouncer's act
gains.b: the couplet's bare 'net' is given an owner, Death, and a cause for staying in it, the pull of pleasure

note: 2060 says heaven's pleasure comes by austerity yet ends, and that something is higher; Kural 346 says one who cuts off 'I' and 'mine' enters a world above the gods'.
teaches: The couplet's 'higher than the gods' is given a reason in the epic: the gods' world has a measured end, so only what lies above it can be a goal.

gains.a: The vague higher state is given a means, the cutting of ownership and the self, which the verse leaves unnamed.
gains.b: The couplet gains a ground for ranking the gods' world below renunciation: its joys are counted in years and end.

note: The mantra the god gave in the hunt is now used.
teaches: The god's rescue is not only a past kindness: it left a means to call him, so the gift becomes the tool for the present trouble.

note: Soolamani 1 praises the one who conquered the sum of deeds, whose worshippers are freed; the verse praises the lord of non-killing whose worshippers cut off the evil birth.
teaches: Two Jain epics open with the same promise of release through the conqueror but name his victory differently, over deeds in one and in vow of non-killing in the other.

note: 1706 shows the moon entering the queen's mouth in union, and 1712 gives the birth of the radiant son the vision announced.
teaches: The moon's entry in the bed finds its fulfilment in the birth, so a reader sees the poem treat the dream as a true prediction.

note: The patikam says the younger brother, desolate as a star that has lost the moon, came to join Civakan at a woman's bidding; here Civakan sees that Nandattan has come with the peacock-like woman's word.
teaches: The patikam's 'by a woman's command' is shown to mean Gandharvadattai's spell and bargain, so the summary's single phrase hides a whole scene of grief, vision and magical travel.

claims.gist: flesh-eating is punished in hell by being made to swallow molten metal
four deeply rooted karmas are burned to ash before the soul reaches its end
when the four destroying karmas fall, the soul knows all three worlds and the non-world (aloka) and holds the four infinites
a king whose rule shelters all alike stands to the world as a father, and the world rejoices in that care
going away for deeds and wealth is a man's duty, and staying at home with dignity a woman's
desire destroys thought, fame, honour and manhood and brings blame
at death wealth and wives are left and only dharma remains to carry one to heaven
one-sensed beings are killed by those too dull to perceive that they live
eating the flesh of a slaughtered creature feeds only the body and brings its own fruit
worship can move the goddess to remove the city's distress
death and birth are no more than putting off a cloth or leaving a house for another
the learned guard even a just king from later blame and from cruel deeds
a man of high birth should not marry a woman of unequal birth before he has married one of his own rank
one who has escaped the pit of birth and pain would not choose to go back to it
a king must bear both tapas and the burden of rule, each held to its proper work, or great sorrow follows
giving harmful things to those who do evil is no gift and brings a bad fruit
one who holds right vision and bears austerity escapes hell and animal births
such a one gains a great wealth that does not leave
victory in battle comes by fate
wealth is no ground for trust, since cruel deeds can bring one fed from gold to beg, so one should turn the mind to good dharma

note: In 640 some suitors vowed to plunge into battle only if a man other than the vina's victor took her; in 791 the kings who desired her fight after Civakan has won at the vina.
teaches: The kings' war breaks the very terms they set at the contest, so their fight is shown as desire that will not accept its own rule, not as a defence of the bride.

note: 3133 says fasting and meditation wash off evil deeds; 3145 closes on the Lord's feet as the way across the sea of deeds.
teaches: The first verse gives the ascetic's own washing of deeds, the last the worshipper's crossing by the Lord's feet, so the work ends by joining effort and devotion.

note: Soolamani 1 praises a god who won the sum of deeds himself and lets those who bow be freed; Tirumanthiram 1649 says by Siva's grace deeds do not cling.
teaches: Release from deeds is credited to a conqueror's own victory in the Jain verse and to the giving of grace in the Saiva one, so the two differ over who removes the deeds.

gains.a: the god is seen as a conqueror who had deeds to overcome, not a giver, set against a Saiva grace that works without such a victory
gains.b: grace is seen against a god who earned the freedom by his own conquest, which makes the Saiva grace read as a gift and not a result

note: 1460 shows the discus halting at the youth's side; 1463 explains it by saying a harm aimed at a blameless man returns on its sender.
teaches: The strange halting of the discus is given a moral frame only a few verses later, so the poet explains the marvel by a rule of rebound.

note: Tirumular says the holy waters are within the heart and that those who wander the land without bathing in them do not destroy their deeds; Civakan takes the water of a jewelled conch at the Tirthan's feet as part of putting away his sin.
teaches: Read as part of the sin-clearing rite, the conch water is the outward tirtham Tirumular says cannot destroy deeds, so the pair sets an epic's confidence in rite against a Saiva yogi's insistence on the inward bath.

gains.a: the epic's ceremony gains a sharp critic, who would ask whether the water touched the heart
gains.b: Tirumular's verse gains a case from another faith of the outward practice he dismisses, done sincerely by a hero after war

note: The Kural counts dividing others among a minister's skills; Padumukan exposes the minister-turned-king's plan to divide the kings so they perish fighting each other.
teaches: The craft of division that the Kural lists without moral comment as a minister's skill is shown here in the hands of a minister who betrayed his king, and the epic names its result as a world made cruel.

gains.a: Padumukan's charge gains a recognised name: Kattiyankaran is practising the minister's art of division, not mere spite
gains.b: the couplet's neutral skill gains a case where it is turned against the realm, which the couplet does not consider

note: The king and his mother enter the animal state at death, and the youth at 34 tells of wandering among animals and being killed by kin.
teaches: The animal birth at 153 is the state whose pains are told later in the youth's account, so the ripening is followed across births.

note: In 273 the king puts down the weapon but scorns the dust-grimed man; in 283 he bows so that his crown-flowers touch the ascetic's feet.
teaches: The king's change is made in two steps, so the first (weapon) does not yet carry the second (reverence).

note: Dharmadattan warned that if Kattiyangaran seized the king who made him, Fortune would turn from him; here his rule, called a Kali-reign, perishes and the war is declared over.
teaches: The usurper's fall fulfils the councillor's warning given before the crime, so the story names his own deed as cause even though, dying, he gave everything to karma at 2314 to 2316.

note: The patikam says that Civakan renounces while kings bring tribute and his sceptre runs just; this verse ends the ilampakam on the people's peace and turns to what befell the king of kings.
teaches: The peace of 2377 is the height from which the patikam says he turns away, so the praise of his rule is the setup for the renunciation, not the end of the tale.

note: Kural 550 likens the king's removal of the cruel to weeding a crop; 824 gives a lion ruining the king's forest, removed by his sons.
teaches: A king's clearing of harm to his land can be done by a beast-slaying prince, which widens the weeding image beyond wrongdoers.

gains.a: The verse lacks any rule that makes the removal of the menace the king's own charge, which the couplet supplies.
gains.b: The couplet lacks a menace that is a beast and not a criminal, and a son who acts for the king.

note: In 215 a destiny formed before (முனம் ஆகிய பான்மை) sprouts in Saccandan and drives him after the queen to his ruin; in 380 the old deed (ஊழ் வினை) drives his son to refuge in the Arhat.
teaches: The epic uses one mechanism, a ripened past deed pushing a man, to drown the father in pleasure and lift the son to the Jina, and only the son's case adds his own understanding as a second cause.

note: In 201 Saccandan hands his kingdom to Kattiyankaran out of trust; here the son's brother warns that those who trusted have died.
teaches: The brother's rule against trusting anyone is drawn from the family's own ruin, so the epic makes prudence an inheritance learned from the father's fatal trust.

note: Verse 308 gives the reflection behind the turn verse 304 announces.
teaches: The earlier verse only says the vow is taken; the later one shows the king's disgust with pleasure and his seeking out the teacher as how it comes about.

note: Both epics let the washed-off paste and saffron of bathing women thicken a pool, here in the Vidyadhara palace and there in the city's ponds.
teaches: Both Jain epics fix wealth in the cosmetic that the bath washes into the pool, so the image is the genre's mark of luxury.

note: Verse 941 shows women along the route losing their composure at the sight of the young men; Kural 1254 says the restraint she boasted of passes beyond concealment into the open.
teaches: The public street is the occasion where the Kural's private breaking of restraint becomes visible to all.

gains.a: The verse lacks the woman's own account of the restraint she once claimed.
gains.b: The couplet lacks the crowded occasion that draws desire out in public.

note: 1843 reads the kingship and the bowing kings as the gift of the good-deed deity; Naladiyar 3 says kings on elephants under umbrellas fall when deeds turn.
teaches: Read together, the umbrellas that 1843 credits to past merit are the same ones Naladiyar says a turn of deeds can remove.

gains.a: The grant of kingship gains an explicit reversal: what a good deed gave, a turn of deeds can take back.
gains.b: The quatrain gains an account of why the king rose, through the good-deed god, which it assumes without saying.

note: Kattiyankaran sneers at the merchant's son: is he then king of this city? In 316 the deity tells the queen this child will crush the king who stands against him.
teaches: The usurper's mocking question unknowingly names the rightful king, so the story makes the villain voice the prophecy he means to deny.

note: Hurt done in the forenoon returns in the afternoon of itself, as the king's offering returns on him through the poison.
teaches: The couplet says the hurt returns of itself; 153 shows it returning through a third person's crime, so the doer suffers without being punished by the doer's own victim.

gains.a: The poison is seen as the late fruit of an earlier act of harm.
gains.b: The couplet gets a case where the returning hurt comes through another's crime, not the victim's hand.

note: The couplet's lover says he would recall her if he forgot, but he knows no forgetting; Gandharvadattai says she need not recall her husband, since he never leaves her heart.
teaches: The conceit that one who never forgets has nothing to remember becomes, in the abandoned wife's letter, a reproach: the same words that pledge constancy remind the new bridegroom that she has not moved and he has.

gains.a: her line gains its source in the Kural's play on remembering and forgetting, so the sulk is a known figure of love
gains.b: the couplet's lover's boast is turned around into a wife's, said to a husband who is with another woman, where it carries blame as well as love

note: The astrologer foretells that Kemasari's husband is the man at whose sight she will feel sudden shame; in 1472 at first sight her restraint and shame give way and she melts.
teaches: The prophecy names shame as the sign, but its fulfilment is shame overwhelmed by desire, so the virtue that should guard a maiden is made the very place where the destined bond shows itself.

note: Both epics walk through rich wet fields; the Silappathikaram's Jain nun warns that a careless step may hurt crab and snail, while the Cintamani's narrator delights as the ploughing herds scatter the fish.
teaches: The ahimsa scruple that a Jain nun in one epic applies to every footstep in the fields is absent from the Jain poet's own celebration of ploughing, so the epics keep that scruple for the ascetic and not for the land's prosperity.

note: Purananuru 186 says the world lives by its king, so it is the king's duty to know he is its life; 246 puts kings above the gods.
teaches: The Purananuru turns the king's exalted place into a duty laid on the king, while Dharmadattan turns it into a ban laid on the subject who would harm him.

gains.a: the councillor's exaltation of kingship is seen as one use of a shared idea, aimed at the subject
gains.b: the poem's claim is shown to cut the other way when a minister, not a king, is the one being warned

note: In 978 Civakan, seeing the girl in danger, judges death better than a life that lets her perish and charges the elephant; in 1049 she calls service at his feet the wage for that toil.
teaches: Her refusal of the cousin is set up as repayment of a specific risk, so the epic makes her love the answer to his choosing death over a shamed life.

note: Kural 1091: her eyes have two looks, one that gives the sickness and one that is its cure. Civakan, shot by her brows, asks what medicine there is for the wound and looks back at her.
