teaches: The couplet's two looks are both hers; the epic gives the second look to him, so the exchange of glances, not one woman's eyes, carries both the wound and the hope of a cure.

gains.a: Civakan's question gains an answer the verse does not state: the cure lies in the look itself
gains.b: the couplet's single-eyed paradox is staged as a mutual exchange in which both lovers fall sick at one glance

note: The Kural's woman (or her friend) refuses a promise of speedy return: tell it to those who will still be alive. Civakan makes exactly that promise, quicker than an arrow, and Vimalai answers only with tears.
teaches: The epic stages the very speech the couplet refuses to accept, and the bride's silent tears in 1994 are the wordless form of the couplet's retort.

gains.a: Civakan's light promise is shown to be the stock comfort the Kural's speaker has already judged worthless.
gains.b: The couplet's retort gains a concrete farewell scene with the promise spelled out and a listener who cannot answer it.

note: The false death that frees Yugi to act (69) leaves his own lands to be taken once they think him hidden or dead.
teaches: Guile that saves the plan has a price paid by the realm, which verse 69 alone does not count.

note: The powder is first held out here; the patikam says Suramanjari's powder was beaten and she withdrew vowing to look on no man.
teaches: A trifle of pleasure called the powder that bears desire becomes the cause of a vow against all men, so the section's marriage turns on a toiletry rather than a battle.

note: The sage says the king's father and mother went into animal births because of their deeds; the Siddhar asks when he will say enough to the births he has had as stone, tree, fish, bird and grass.
teaches: The Siddhar mourns the animal births without naming a cause; the epic traces the animal birth to a particular killing and makes it the fruit of a deed.

gains.a: The verse gets from the Siddhar the weariness of the rebirth it only reports as a fact.
gains.b: The Siddhar's lament gets a case in which an animal birth is the named fruit of a killing and not simply a stage to be escaped.

note: The Kural likens death to sleep and birth to waking; Civakan uses the waking from heavy sleep for the soul's appearing in the states of birth, adds release as a third motion, and draws from it a refusal to grieve at his own arrest.
teaches: The Kural's calm figure of sleep and waking only describes the cycle, while the Cintamani makes it an argument for conduct, so understanding birth as waking becomes the ground for refusing grief, and the cycle gains an exit the couplet never names.

gains.a: the hero's consolation is seen to rest on a figure the ethical tradition already held, which makes his calm learned rather than merely brave
gains.b: the couplet's image is shown as the first step of a larger scheme in which knowing the cycle aims at leaving it

note: In the Kural the woman's automatic blessing at her lover's sneeze is withdrawn the next moment in jealousy; in the epic the blessing at the infant's sneeze comes from a mother who cannot show herself, and sticks as his name.
teaches: The everyday sneeze-blessing, which the Kural shows can be taken back, here becomes the one bond between the hidden mother and her child that cannot be undone.

gains.a: the epic scene gains the domestic usage behind it: a blessing said by those who love the sneezer, which makes the hidden voice a mother's
gains.b: the couplet's small rite gains weight: the same word can name and protect a life, not only open a lovers' quarrel

note: The Kural likens the cloth over a woman's breasts to the face-cloth on a rutting elephant; Vinapati jests that the gods hid her breasts altogether because her eyes already killed.
teaches: The two take opposite sides of one premise, that a woman's breasts are a danger to be covered, and the pedi's jest pushes it to the end by having the gods remove what the cloth only veils, with the eyes left as the whole of the threat.

gains.a: the obscure jest becomes legible as a play on a known figure of the veiled danger
gains.b: the couplet's covering gains its limit case, a body in which the covered danger is absent and the eyes do all the harm

note: On Mudaliar's reading, 132 says learning lasts as long as its owner lives; 398 says learning gained in one birth protects through seven.
teaches: Shanmuganar's reading, that it lasts through fame, is closer to the Kural's.

note: In 200 Kapilar offers Pari's daughters to Vichikko as a suppliant and brahmin; in 201 he offers them to Irungovel as their father's friend, naming himself அந்தணன், புலவன்.
teaches: Read together, Kapilar's two offers show him grounding the same gift in different claims, his standing as suppliant and brahmin in 200 and his friendship with their father in 201, so the reader sees how a bard, not a kinsman, asserted the right to give a dead patron's daughters.

note: In 2366 a god crowns Civakan with gold and sea-water; Tirumanthiram 1601 says that those who rule the three worlds wear crowns, but the bliss of the kings of the Lord's feet has no measure.
teaches: The Cintamani lets the crowning be the height of splendour, while the Saiva verse ranks the same crowned kings below those who serve at the feet, so what counts as the highest state is exactly what the two texts divide on.

gains.a: The coronation gains a rival measure of rank, in which crowns do not count, against which its splendour can be weighed.
gains.b: The Tirumanthiram verse gains a full scene of a crowned king receiving the highest earthly honour, so its contrast has a concrete case.

note: In 203 Neelakesi told Kundalakesi that a power passing between moments is either a sixth thing beyond the five aggregates or total destruction; here she tells the Buddha the lac is a further thing, and the aggregates have none.
teaches: The same dilemma defeats the disciple's power and the teacher's lac, which shows Neelakesi's case is one argument: every Buddhist carrier of karma is either a soul under another name or nothing.

note: In 377 the poet laments that the nectar that ends birth is rarely won and yet men pamper the senses; in 2749 the teacher shows the rarity itself, a human birth as unlikely as a drifting pole finding a yoke-hole in the sea.
teaches: The earlier complaint is given its measure here, so a reader sees that wasting the human birth is wasting a one-in-a-sea chance.

note: Kural 1329 has the man wish the sulk would go on and the night lengthen so he might keep pleading; Civakan, pleading through the bees, calls her anger the fruit of his own past sin.
teaches: Where the couplet relishes the plea as part of love's game, the epic lets the husband feel the quarrel as an undeserved punishment, so the same scene reads as pleasure or as pain by the speaker's mood.

gains.a: his plea is shown to be, in the Kural's terms, a stage of love's play that he has not yet found pleasing
gains.b: the cost of the pleading, which the couplet leaves out, the fear that one's love is being punished for a past wrong

note: Naladiyar 68 says the anger of the low keeps spreading and never dies; Pazhamozhi 111 shows it spreading onto those who come to part the fighters.
teaches: Pazhamozhi gives the Naladiyar's spreading anger its concrete path, from the quarrel to the peacemakers themselves, so that intervention becomes one of the ways it spreads.

note: The Kural's woman says the herdsman's flute is the burning evening's messenger and a killing weapon; Padumai finds the bull's bell, the moon, the anril and the evening burning like smokeless fire.
teaches: The evening's pastoral sounds that burn the parted wife of the Kural are given to a girl who has not yet been joined or parted, showing that the epic transfers the whole thurai of evening grief to the first night after first sight.

gains.a: the source convention of its list, which shows the bull's bell and the evening as the settled tokens of separation
gains.b: a case where the separation grief is felt before any union, widening the occasion the couplet presupposes

note: 1864 gives the order to sound the drum for the festival; 1868 shows the drum sounded and the whole city rising in joy.
teaches: The order and its carrying out show a king's single word turning a whole city to festival, so his authority is shown at its greatest before the sarukkam's later turning away.

note: 2824 names lying, killing, theft and lust as what ascetics guard against; 2868 to 2873 teach these to a prince as duties of a layman.
teaches: The four sins the ascetic keeps from are given to a layman with their fruits, so the rule is seen to reach a king's son.

note: The Kural's lover says the beloved is life when present and death when she leaves; Civakan offers to live serving her or leave his body, then is himself the one who leaves.
teaches: The couplet assumes the woman is the one who departs and the man the one who dies of it; the epic reverses the roles, so the parting the man dreads is the parting he chooses.

gains.a: Civakan's live-or-die hyperbole is shown to be a formula of the lover's art, not a vow
gains.b: the couplet's life-and-death image is seen from the side of the one who goes rather than the one left

claims.gist: karma does not cling to those who hold to the feet of the Jina
love for dear ones is let go entirely by the one who renounces
anger and the passions linked to it are killed one after another in the battle against karma
killing animals as offerings to deities is part of the cruelty animals suffer
liberation is an entry into a city from which there is no return
union with the beloved is the reward of austerity done before
when ruin draws near, a wrong course appears right counsel
serving the beloved elder brother's feet is a worthier life than kingdom, heaven or release
the birth of a great being dries up the clinging residue of harmful deeds for many
life, with its stages from infancy to old age, ends in passage to another state
a lover's love is insatiable and is drawn in at once, like a drop on hot gold
the scriptural way is hard for those who live by enjoyment and easy for single-minded ascetics
wealth, power, beauty, learning and birth are the fruit of what one stood and did before
a deed done in a former birth brings suffering in this life
desire and hatred toward sense objects pile up deeds that bring the same nature again after death
a union so fitting must have been earned by austerity in a former life
those who give nothing and lack virtue should let go of their empty wealth
a householder must greet a visiting ascetic with joined hands and a bow
the Jain dharma holds back karma, gives heaven and then release
youth and beauty do not last, for age drives out understanding and leaves the body a ruin
the Lord knows the three worlds without being stained by them, sowing qualities in himself
the book of omens may be false
faultless conduct in the Jina's way, avoiding the four states of rebirth, is hardest to attain
the lives of true lovers are so joined that one cannot die without the other
going forward against the enemy's spears is what honour is
a king's anger is a fire that burns all near it unless quenched with gifts

note: Verse 308 vouches for Sachchutan's truth and learning; verse 309 says the speaker saw a fault and will not stay silent.
teaches: The second minister grants his colleague's praise and then withholds assent in the same breath, so agreement on facts does not carry agreement on the verdict.

note: 2824 has the ascetic wither the five senses and so subdue them by effort; Tirumanthiram 140 says the senses come under control of themselves once the Lord is met.
teaches: One text holds that the senses are conquered by the ascetic's own labour, the other that they are conquered by meeting the Lord, so the two disagree on who does the work.

gains.a: the verse's effortful mortification is shown to be one of two ways to the same end, and the one that leaves out a god
gains.b: the Tirumanthiram verse's claim that no effort is needed meets its rival, a school that does not wait for grace

note: Civakan asks her to command whether he lives to serve her or goes; six verses on he goes without a word to her.
teaches: The hero's offer to let her decide his going is contradicted by a departure she is not even awake to know of.

note: In Akananuru 18 the friend tells the lover that if her friend suffers harm for a single day she will not live after; in 976 Gunamalai's companion, facing the elephant, resolves that it should kill her together with her mistress.
teaches: The akam friend's stock claim that her life hangs on the heroine's is put to the test in the epic by a real beast, and the companion keeps it, so the convention is shown as a loyalty that can be acted on.

gains.a: the akam convention behind the companion's resolve, which makes her offer a known role rather than a passing panic
gains.b: an enacted instance of the friend's pledge, which the poem only states as a warning to the lover

note: 1766 has the drum summon the world's kings to a marriage open to all; Naladiyar 86 praises a wife married with drums beaten for many to know.
teaches: A marriage announced to all is a mark of honour in the Naladiyar, and the swayamvara pushes the same openness to where the bride is chosen before the world.

gains.a: The proclamation gains a measure: public marriage is thought to guard the bond from later claims.
gains.b: The quatrain gains a case where the drum summons rival suitors as well as witnesses.

note: Kural 542 has the people looking to the sceptre as the world looks to the sky; verse 598 runs it the other way, with the king glad or hurt as the world is.
teaches: The pair shows rule as a two-way dependence, where the couplet states only the people's need of the king.

gains.a: The verse lacks a picture of the people's side of the bond, which the sky and sceptre image supplies.
gains.b: The couplet lacks the king's felt share in his people's fortune, which the verse adds.

note: 1809 gives the harp-playing boon-winner of the northern mountain; 543 has Dharanan come at Nami's song, which is how the boon was won.
teaches: What the herald says in two lines is the story told at length at 538-547, so the hall's praise draws on the book's own earlier telling.

note: 2000 says the gifts of one who knows the true principles lead him among the best gods; Tirumanthiram 1867 says charity to tireless ascetics sinks deep karma and becomes the golden world.
teaches: One text places the fruit of giving in a higher birth, and the other in the removal of karma, which are different ends.

gains.a: The Jain verse gains a different reward, since removal of karma is not what it names, only a birth among gods.
gains.b: The Saiva verse gains a condition: here the giver's knowledge of the principles is part of the reward, not only the receiver's austerity.

note: The king had asked Civakan for his clan when the alarm of the raid broke in; now the companions answer the question for him.
teaches: The interrupted question is finished by others: Civakan's birth, which he was about to tell, is declared by his friends, so the hero's lineage reaches the king as testimony rather than his own claim.

note: The prince is accused through a lie told against him and keeps his bearing; the Naladiyar says the pure of heart are not shaken by cruel slander, like a lamp's flame.
teaches: The Naladiyar's steadiness under slander is shown in the epic as a prince who answers the false charge with a procession and with giving, not with protest.

gains.a: The verse gains a character who passes the Naladiyar's test of staying unshaken by false speech.
gains.b: The Naladiyar quatrain gains a story in which the slander is followed by exile and a city, so the cost and the outcome of steadiness are shown.

note: The patikam summarizes this episode as the hero giving nectar (அமிர்தம்) to a dog that came to harm at the bathing festival; 947 shows that the nectar is the five padas, swallowed in the heart (பதவமிர்தம் நெஞ்சின் அயின்று).
teaches: The patikam's 'nectar' turns out to be a teaching rather than a drink, so the summary's word is the poem's own metaphor for the mantra and not a miracle of healing.

note: 3107 says that guarding all lives as one's own brings a high birth; Kural 327 says not to kill even if one's own life is the price.
teaches: The verse makes non-injury pay in a later birth, and the Kural cuts the rule loose from payment even at the price of one's life.

gains.a: the verse's reward for protection is tested by the case where protection costs the protector his life
gains.b: the Kural's absolute rule gets the Jain account of what the careful guarder wins in later births

note: The garden one cannot leave without losing one's life anticipates the king's words that he cannot bear to part from Vijayai, for which he gives his rule to Kattiyangaran.
teaches: The garden's power to hold its owner is the same inability to part that later makes the king hand his kingdom to a minister.

note: In 1296 the onlookers say that he alone restored her remaining life and that the king will give the girl to the spearman; here the king, on his minister's counsel, decides exactly that.
teaches: The marriage is first the crowd's verdict on the cure and only then the king's decision, so royal policy here ratifies a public judgment that the healer has earned the bride.

note: Tirumular says an unlearned king blind to dharma says 'kill'; the king here, without clarity in dharma, takes the people's advice and goes to the goddess's shrine.
teaches: The epic shows how the unlearned king's killing begins: he is led by piety and the people's fear rather than by anger, so the rule applies to a devout king too.

gains.a: the king's choice is read as the failure of learning that Tirumular names, not as cruelty
gains.b: the rule gets a king who kills out of religious duty and not out of tyranny

note: The Naladiyar says friends who share joys but not sorrows do nothing for each other; Dharan inflicts sorrow on his king's friend to give him joy.
teaches: The quatrain's test assumes sorrow comes from outside and asks who will share it, while the epic's friend authors the sorrow himself and stands apart from it, a case the rule of sharing does not cover.

gains.a: Dharan's apology is measured against a standard of friendship that his deceit plainly fails
gains.b: the quatrain's rule meets a friend who causes, rather than shares, the grief, which shows its limit

note: 1814 puts a moon-line king under a tall umbrella with cloud-like elephants; Purananuru 3 puts the Pandya under a white umbrella like the full moon.
teaches: The poem makes the moon-line king's umbrella the sign of his kind, as the Sangam poem does for the Pandya, so the herald's king reads as the Pandya of that tradition.

gains.a: The verse gains a Sangam picture that fills in the umbrella and moon that it names only in passing.
gains.b: The Sangam poem gains a late epic that keeps its image but brings it to a marriage hall, not a battlefield.

note: 1139 shows a king's blow breaking a diamond pillar; the couplet says the ruin of one who prizes anger is sure as a hand that strikes the ground.
teaches: The blow succeeds first, so the couplet's ruin is shown as not yet in sight and the story has to come back to it.

gains.a: the epic's king strikes stone and the stone breaks, which shows how anger can seem to succeed before any cost appears
gains.b: the couplet's ground that never misses gets a case where the blow visibly lands and the ruin it promises is still withheld

note: The king is an அணங்கு to women (157); the princess is an அணங்கு even to the goddess on the lotus (162).
teaches: The poem sets an afflicting beauty against a greater one before they meet, so the king who wounds others by his looks is the one wounded by hers.

note: Kural 321 calls not killing the first of dharma and says killing brings every other kind of deed; verse 321 shows one killing without a real life still following across births.
teaches: The couplet's rule is tested at its smallest case, the effigy, which shows how far the epic extends the rule beyond the couplet.

gains.a: the verse lacks a general statement that killing leads on to all other wrongs
gains.b: the couplet lacks the story of a symbolic killing whose pain still lasted through births

note: Kural 638 makes it the minister's duty to tell a king what is good for him; Yugi, given a king who will not hear, chooses a trick.
teaches: The couplet assumes the king can be told, while the poem shows a minister who judges telling useless and acts in secret.

gains.a: The epic scene gains the name of a duty that Yugi both keeps in aim and breaks in method.
gains.b: The couplet gains a case where the minister's duty to speak is overtaken by deceit for the king's own good.

note: The epic says those who eat the wounds of other creatures and honey with worms destroy their inner knowledge and are beasts; the couplet says that if men saw flesh as another creature's wound they would not eat it.
teaches: Both call flesh another creature's wound, but the epic adds the charge that eating it destroys the eater's discernment, so the loss is the eater's own.

gains.a: The epic verse gains the couplet's single image of flesh as a wound, which makes the grammar of its பிறவற்றின் புண் clear
gains.b: The couplet gains an account of what the eater loses, inner discernment and the name of beast, rather than only what the eaten suffers

note: In 2149 the Videha king tells his counsellors that as the usurper meant to kill him by deceit, they will take his life by deceit, and bids them keep it secret; 2176 has the narrator announce that very plan, with love as its sword.
teaches: The secret the king swore his counsellors to keep is opened to the audience but not to the victim, so the listener watches the gifts of 2174 and 2175 knowing what the usurper cannot, and the narrator names the plan deceit without blaming it.

note: 454 shows the women shaping the face's work with glance and smile; Siddhar 10 prays to forget women who show hand, eyes and face.
teaches: The siddhar's prayer names the same tools the epic's women use, as the lure to be forgotten, where the epic presents them as skill.

gains.a: The women's play of face is seen as what the renunciant fears, not only what the poet admires.
gains.b: Its infatuating gestures get a full picture of them performed, which the prayer names but does not show.

note: 204 praises Ori as a giver who pours like the rain cloud without limit; Akananuru 209 names Kari of Mullur, who killed Ori of the strong bow and gave Kolli to the Cheras.
teaches: The puram poem preserves Ori as a living patron while the akam friend cites his killing as a famous deed of another chief, so one man's fame survives in the anthologies as both a patron's praise and a rival's trophy.

note: The bangled women stand desiring the bride's eyes, breasts, hips and hair; the Naladiyar tells the reader not to desire a woman for her spear-like eyes, for she too will stoop and walk with a staff for eyes.
teaches: The gaze that the epic lingers on is the one the Naladiyar answers with the staff of old age, giving the scene's longing a time it will pass through.

gains.a: a limit of time on the beauty so intently looked at, which the scene itself does not offer
gains.b: a particular pair of eyes, hips and hair worth the longing the quatrain says to resist, so its warning has something to weigh against

note: The teacher binds Civakan to a year without anger toward Kattiyankaran, yet before leaving writes into his mind the policy of destroying enemies.
teaches: The ascetic's restraint on his pupil is a postponement of revenge rather than its renunciation: anger is suspended while the means of war are taught.

note: 2934 follows the embryo through the channel and into muddy water where it falls weeping without provision for the road; Tirumanthiram 451 has the Lord stay within the womb and form the embryo.
teaches: One text lets the body come into the world helpless and left to its deeds, the other has a Lord who forms it, so the same birth is read without and with a maker.

gains.a: the epic's helpless birth meets a verse that says a Lord forms the embryo within the womb
gains.b: the Tirumanthiram's Lord within the womb is set against a Jain account of birth with no one forming it

note: Ainkurunuru 69 has the wife say she has seen the husband's woman crying, eyes reddened, when the cool flood with its flowers swept her sand-play away at the crowded ford; Paripadal 7.25-26 lists among the town's cries the young women weeping that the flood broke the dolls they drew in the sand.
teaches: In the hymn the weeping over sand dolls is one anonymous cry among many on flood day, while the akam wife picks out one such girl to mock as her husband's new woman, so the pair shows the akam poet taking a stock festival scene and turning it into a mark of the rival's childishness.

note: Both poets answer the flaw in their verse with the lamp and its smoke, and ask hearers who grasp the matter to accept the work.
teaches: The Jain epics share an apology formula in which the poem's worth lies in its meaning, and each poet hangs a different request on it.

note: 690 sends the envoys back with a defiant word; 1210 again lets them go unharmed, now by naming the custom that protects envoys.
teaches: The hero's first dismissal is only defiance; the second gives the reason, that the envoy is not the one at fault, so he is shown as a lawful and not merely angry fighter.

note: 1782 has the builders finish the hall and the musicians play; 1783 has the herald call the kings in at the auspicious hour.
teaches: The hall is finished before the hour is announced, so the festival's order moves from building to music to the kings' entry.

note: Naladiyar 198 holds up the lion's strength as the measure of a man who would die poor rather than shame himself; in 724 the lion is the foe whose strength the gods marvel to see overcome.
teaches: The lion is first the model of honour and then the thing a stronger man destroys, so strength is not a single measure.

gains.a: The verse lacks the use of the lion as a standard of honour, which the quatrain supplies.
gains.b: The quatrain lacks a case where the lion's own strength is beaten, which the verse shows.

note: 1844 calls those who destroy the root of good deeds base; 1851 shows them leaving the root that feeds them sweetly.
teaches: The root of good deeds is a recurring image whose repetition shows the king returning to the same fear from two sides.

note: Both speak of householders who provide for renouncers.
teaches: The couplet chides those who give to renouncers in place of doing austerity themselves; the epic's householder does both, counting the gift to renouncers and his own fasts as two of four equal duties.

gains.a: the epic gains the Kural's worry that giving to ascetics can stand in for austerity, which its fourfold scheme answers
gains.b: the couplet gains a worked-out lay discipline in which its implied rivalry of giving and tapas is resolved

note: The Naladiyar warns that grey hair will come and youth will not return; Suramanjari scoffs that those who think a dead tree revives by rain are mad.
teaches: The Naladiyar's truth that age is irreversible becomes, in the epic, the very certainty a schemer relies on: because everyone knows the old cannot become young, no one looks for the young man inside the old one.

gains.a: Suramanjari's scoff is shown to rest on a sober didactic commonplace, so her being deceived is not folly but the misuse of a sound belief
gains.b: the quatrain's warning acquires a social use it never considers: the general certainty about age is a cover that disguise can exploit

note: In 97 the queen is alone in thought while the king is by; in 117 she leaves the sleeping king for the keeper.
teaches: The inward desire of the first night becomes the act of the night the king watches, so the poem takes her from thought to deed.

note: 785 says the companions were born on the very day Civakan was born; 1793 says that day was also the day the king perished, through their own deeds.
teaches: The birthday the battle verse gave as a warrior's pedigree is retold to the king's widow as a day of death, and the companions take the guilt of it on themselves.

note: Kural 377 says even the rich enjoy only as the apportioner has apportioned; the king says his pleasures and life-days are measured by past penance and so refuses counsel.
teaches: The couplet's limit on enjoyment becomes, in a king's mouth, a licence to stop listening, which shows that a doctrine of allotted fruit can be turned against the duty to act on advice.

gains.a: the king's refusal is seen to borrow a recognised ethical teaching rather than being bare infatuation
gains.b: the couplet is shown to be open to a fatalist misuse it does not itself guard against

note: Elathi 35 promises kingship to one who feeds the renouncers, the powerless, the unknown, the dead or bereaved (இறந்தார்), the destitute and the young; Acharakkovai 100 frees from ஆசாரம் the stranger, the destitute, the old, the young and one who has lost a life.
teaches: The two books name nearly the same weak persons, but the Elathi makes them claims on the giver's food while the Acharakkovai lifts the rules of conduct from them, so the vulnerable are owed help in one code and excused in the other.

note: Both admit that outcomes don't track merit. 375 says so within the chapter on fate, and 169 only asks for thought, though Parimelazhagar explains it through past deeds.
teaches: The tension in chapter 38 is here in an earlier and quieter form.

note: Verse 129 ends the poet's praise of the ridge by asking what more need be told once its groves are wishing-tree gardens with golden lotuses; verse 282 ends on a question of the same kind.
teaches: The same closing question over wishing-tree groves is first the poet's boast and then the counsellor's pitch to the king, so the ridge's beauty is now used to move a decision.

note: Kural 1081's man cannot tell whether the woman is a goddess, a peahen or a woman; here the women cannot tell whether the man is Murugan or Kama.
teaches: The epic gives the first-sight bewilderment of the Kural's lover to a crowd of women looking at a man, and narrows the choice to two gods, so the doubt is no longer whether the beloved is mortal but which divine lover he is.

gains.a: the epic verse gains a recognised convention, the lover's dazed question at first sight, which marks the women's cry as love struck at a glance rather than plain praise
gains.b: the couplet gains a case with a plural female speaker, showing its doubt is a form of first sight that the tradition could turn round, not something tied to the man's voice

claims.gist: giving up the body and doing dharma would have stopped the birth that follows; those who do not do it die countless times
deeds of cruelty done before bear unbearable suffering as their fruit
the fruit of deed cannot be overcome
failing to honour the goddess in her season brings misfortune on the people
the classes of living beings are destroyed by the heedless
knowledge, protection of life, mercy and virtue are the weapons and armour with which the self conquers its enemies
a woman, however desire burns her, does not make the first advance
a divine word has fixed that the hero will win and reign
tapas done with regard for conduct and shame earns lordship of heaven
those ruined by negligence should be remembered when one is strong and glad
the primal Lord gave the rare scripture
there are four states of birth: hell, animal, human and divine
a king who answers one animal's act by plundering the merchants who owned it is not guarding his people
a plot done by force departs from the way of the treatise and needs the king's pardon
all things are contained in the scripture of the lord of great penance, as all rivers in the sea
an ascetic of great penance sees hidden things with unhindered knowledge
even the gods ask for release from birth, not for more heaven
beings are born in the dangerous course through evil deeds and fear their fruit
those who circle the Jina's feet do not suffer
a lord sustains his warriors so that they will serve him on the day of battle
the one worthy of praise is he who has conquered the karma that torments
ascetics make their deeds (vinai) vanish
men of deceitful mind are not truly strong, and calling them so is cowardice
a noble man's manhood is not diminished by submitting at his parents' plea

note: The spectators of 682 waste away like a butter doll in the sun of desire; in Thiruppugazh 142 the poet, melting like wax in fire for women, asks whether he must stay bound to that shame.
teaches: The same melting is in the epic the measure of a dancer's art and in the hymn a bondage to be prayed away, so the image shows how one bodily figure serves praise and penitence.

gains.a: a devotional reading of the melting as delusion, which the epic, praising the dance, leaves unsaid
gains.b: a narrative where the melting is collective and caused by a staged performance, not only by a woman's body

note: Pattinattar confesses to killing and eating many lives and trusts the Lord to bear the fault; the youth holds that harm to living bodies brings suffering through births.
teaches: Whether the guilt of killing can be borne by another turns on whether a god stands in the account: the verse sets a chain of sin and suffering with no pardoner in it, while the poet's plea counts on one.

gains.a: the youth's law of deeds is set against a pardon a Saiva poet counts on
gains.b: the poet's trust in the Lord is seen as a step outside a doctrine where the harm simply follows the doer

note: Civakan says he will not be born again, having found the unborn one; Tirumular says that after he renounced and saw the light the lord of the gods set him here so that he would not die and be born again.
teaches: Both end births by reaching a lord who is not born, but the Saiva verse makes the lord the one who sets the seeker free while the epic verse puts the claim in the worshipper's mouth and does not say the Jina acts.

gains.a: the Saiva verse's mechanism, a lord who sets the seeker beyond birth, which Civakan's cry of certainty lacks
gains.b: a parallel from a worshipper of the unborn Jina who rests his claim on reaching the feet, which shows how the end-of-birth language is shared and the cause differs

note: Naladiyar 115 says the words of the poor glance off while the rich are heard; Marusi says that anyone who speaks wanting something is slighted, even when he speaks for the stronger lord.
teaches: The Naladiyar finds the cause of being ignored in the speaker's poverty, while Marusi finds it in the act of asking, so a rich lord's messenger can be slighted too.

gains.a: 518 gains the rule it assumes, that how a man is heard follows his standing, which shows Marusi's complaint to be about rank
gains.b: 115 gains a case where the unheard speaker comes from the richer side, so need rather than poverty may be what silences him

note: Kural 1224's parted wife meets evening as enemies at a killing ground; verse 1033 gives a lit, scented evening that burns only those who carry desire.
teaches: The epic locates the pain in the viewer's state ('for those who have it'), while the couplet makes evening itself the attacker.

gains.a: The verse lacks the couplet's starkness, in which evening is a force with an army, not a charming hour.
gains.b: The couplet lacks the verse's detail of lamps, smoke and birds, which show evening pleasant in itself before it hurts.

note: Kemasari cited his doctrine that lovers' lives become one to reproach him for leaving her; he now uses the same doctrine to reassure himself about Gandharvadattai.
teaches: Held together, the verses show one premise serving opposite ends: for the wife he has just left it proves his desertion wrong, for the absent first wife it proves she is safe, so the doctrine binds him only where it comforts.

note: Verse 179 praises Vijayai's soles as if made without bone or sinew (என்பொடு நரம்பு இன்றி); Naladiyar 46 lists bone (என்பு) and sinew (நரம்பு) among the parts of the body and asks which of them is the garlanded woman.
teaches: Two Jain works use the same two words to opposite ends: the epic's praise must imagine the beloved's body without bone and sinew, while the quatrain dissolves her into them, so the courtly portrait depends on the very forgetting the ascetic verse is written to undo.

gains.a: the hyperbole of the boneless foot is seen to deny exactly what the renouncer insists on, showing what the praise leaves out
gains.b: the quatrain's list is shown answering a real literary convention of praise, not an abstract desire

note: 1746 closes with the girl whose name is that of lightning growing up; 1750 shows the young women's ball-play at the swayamvara chapter's start.
teaches: The girl born here grows into the maiden of the later chapters, so the birth is the root of the swayamvara story.

note: Verse 13 has Suramanjari, shamed over the scented powder, refuse to look on any male form and shut herself away; verse 25 has her lower her banner.
teaches: Read together, the two verses frame Suramanjari's vow against men as a challenge the plot exists to undo, so her yielding is told as a conquest like the boar and the enemy in the same verse.

note: Gandharvadattai's horoscope placed her destined husband in Rajamapuram; Kanakamalai's names him by his bow.
teaches: The first bride's horoscope and this one frame the series: from the first marriage the stars, not the hero's pursuit, name his wives, and here Civakan's teaching of arms itself becomes the sign.

note: The keeper first refuses from fear of the king, and the friend's persuasion turns him to count the queen's love a prize.
teaches: His boast of reward is bought by overcoming the very fear he voiced, which shows how little weighing of cost enters the match.

note: 81 says youth and kinship are fleeting and the mind should leave them; 275 adds wealth and pleasure and ends with the pleasure-rich heaven as the aim.
teaches: The same impermanence argument that leads one king to give up the kingdom is shown aiming at heaven rather than release, in both.

note: At their first meeting in the hall Manimekalai told the prince in words that the human body is a vessel of birth, age, disease and death; here she shows him an old woman's body feature by feature.
teaches: Manimekalai moves from stating the doctrine of the suffering body to making the prince look at one, which shows that she treats his desire as a failure of seeing that a statement did not cure.

note: Kural 445 says a king walks with his counsellors as his eyes and must choose them with care; 1921 has Vijayai give the same rule, and at 1924 she says there are no learned counsellors here.
teaches: The couplet assumes a court to choose counsellors from; the exiled prince has none, so the rule becomes a measure of what he lacks and throws the choice back on his own resolve.

gains.a: Vijayai's lament gains force from the rule it cannot meet, showing why she asks what he himself has resolved
gains.b: the couplet gains its limiting case, a ruler without a court, where the eyes it requires must first be found

note: Kalladanar asks whether the Pandya's spear did not stop short when he saw the widows of his enemies beating their breasts and cutting their hair; Civakan's anger stops at the usurper's death and he offers the widows a living in the city or gold to leave with.
teaches: Where the Sangam poem praises the conqueror only for holding back his spear at the sight of the widows, the epic makes restraint into provision, the victor feeding or endowing the women his war has widowed.

gains.a: an older warrior ethic of sparing the enemy's women, which shows Civakan's speech as the fulfilment of a known ideal
gains.b: an example of how far the restraint it praises could be carried, from not killing to giving the widows a livelihood

note: The Jain sage says the son's own austerity will cut his deeds and end birth; Tirumular says austerity and virtue are a boat across the sea of deeds only because the Lord makes them fruitful.
teaches: The same word, tapas, ends karma by the doer's effort in the sage's mouth and by the Lord's grace in Tirumular's, so the release the two promise rests on opposite sources.

gains.a: a rival account in which release is not won by the ascetic's effort alone but by the Lord's help
gains.b: a case of austerity credited with ending karma with no god at all in the account

note: Kural 1183 says the lover has taken a woman's modesty and given her sickness and pallor; at 487 many women grow pale and sigh for men who have only passed by.
teaches: The Kural's single lover is replaced by two princes and a crowd, so pallor from love is shown as a common mark of beauty's reach as well as a private ache.

gains.a: A name for the paleness of the women's shoulders and a cause for it, the lover's taking of their modesty.
gains.b: A scene in which the same paleness comes at first sight of strangers, with no parting that the couplet takes as its cause.

note: 2083 compares the departing goddess of wealth to courtesans who leave the penniless; Naladiyar 371 says harlots' friendship ends when the hand is empty, as a lamp's light ends when the oil is gone.
teaches: The epic turns the Naladiyar's warning about courtesans into a figure for wealth itself, so a man is asked to see in his fortune the same cold arithmetic.

gains.a: The goddess's leaving gets a plain reason, that the love was only for what the hand held, which 2083 leaves implied.
gains.b: The warning about courtesans gets a larger target: the same trade-friendship is shown to run through wealth and fortune, not only through women.

note: Both use the water bubble for what forms and bursts.
teaches: The impermanence figure that in the quatrain moves the wise to end their wandering is used by the epic's mother to keep a bride steady in the household until her husband returns.

gains.a: the mother's simile gains the quatrain's renunciant force, which shows how strong a medicine she is giving for a lover's absence
gains.b: the quatrain gains a domestic use of its argument, as comfort rather than a call to leave the world

note: Naladiyar 101 says an old deed seeks out the one who did it as a calf finds its mother among many cows; verse 274 says a deed done in a former birth rises into fruit and shows that it was real.
teaches: The epic uses karma's sureness as the model for counsel, so a plan's result is as certain as a deed's fruit, a use of karma that the quatrain does not make.

gains.a: A comparison for the way a royal plan works, which turns karma into a model of policy.
gains.b: A second sign of how settled the doctrine is in Tamil verse, said in passing by a counsellor.

note: Udayana orders the land searched for his vanished divine elephant; the hunters, seeing the decoy, think it is our lord's elephant and run to him.
teaches: The search for the lost elephant is what makes the decoy believable, since his own people hurry to bring him the news.

note: The goat born to the outcaste hamlet in 183 becomes the womb in which the king is reborn as her son.
teaches: Reading 183 and 187 together shows that the doe of the births is the mother and the new kid her own husband's former son, a link neither verse states.

note: The king's vow to die in 140 is turned aside by counsel in 146.
teaches: A king's wish to die with his queen is checked by minister's counsel, which is the work of a minister in the epic's picture of rule.

note: Civakan's own account of being led bound names his reason, to please his father, and adds what he saw of his kin.
teaches: The narrator showed him yielding to his parents' plea; his own retelling turns that yielding into filial choice and adds a sight the earlier scene did not report, kin armed and ready to die.

note: Verse 1036 gives a woman setting lamps, incense, flowers and music before the Jina; Tirumanthiram 1005 sets golden lamps and incense in every direction and promises release.
teaches: A Jain maiden's temple rite and a Saiva verse use the same lamp-and-incense offering, though only the Tirumanthiram names its fruit.

gains.a: The verse lacks any statement of what the offering brings, which the Saiva verse gives as release.
gains.b: The Tirumanthiram lacks a person doing the rite, with her doors, garlands and strings, which the epic shows in motion.

note: Verse 304 said that kings of the sea-girt earth, fearing Asvagriva's anger, had paid tribute and sent word; verse 680 brings the same demand to Podanam.
teaches: The earlier claim that every king pays Asvagriva becomes a case at Podanam, where it is the prince who first meets it with anger.

note: Paripadal 5.9 names the split hill only by its crane name (குருகொடு பெயர் பெற்ற மால் வரை); Thiruppugazh 38 names it க்ரவுஞ்சம் and has it split together with the drying of the sea.
teaches: The Sangam poet renders the Sanskrit name Krauncha by its Tamil meaning, a hill named with the crane, while Arunagirinathar uses the Sanskrit name outright, so the pair shows the same deed passing from a translated to a borrowed name across a thousand years.

note: Kural 361 names craving as the seed that produces unceasing birth; the Soolamani's sage names lacking true knowledge as the seed of the deeds that bind.
teaches: Two Tamil teachers name different seeds of rebirth, so the root of bondage is a question of doctrine and is not common ground.

gains.a: its seed is set beside a rival one, so lack of knowledge is shown as one choice among Tamil answers
gains.b: the couplet's craving gets an older cause to answer, whether craving grows out of not knowing

note: In 355 the mother in the hermitage sees a forest cow suckling its calf and thinks of her son; in 362 the son drinks the milk of a foster mother and grows.
teaches: The nursing that Vijayai can only watch in a beast is happening to her own son at another woman's breast, so the two halves of the story are tied by the milk she cannot give.

note: The she-elephant that falls bleeding in 114 becomes a god at the king's mantra, and the elephant of 354 becomes a god through its own samadhi.
teaches: An elephant's rebirth as a god is first something the king does for it in a crisis, and in 354 something its own discipline wins for it, so the king learns to treat release as a person's own work.

note: Manasavegan, who had seized the pair in verse 266, is the one whose mind is afraid at the wedding.
teaches: The rival who once held the hero captive now fears him, so the wedding shows the rivalry turning in the hero's favour.

note: The couplet pictures the life as a lodger in the body; the verse argues it by the conch's sound.
teaches: The couplet takes the soul's separateness for granted and the verse offers a reason for it, so the reader sees what the couplet's picture assumed.

gains.a: A figure, the lodger in a body, for the thing that the cut and weighed body fails to show.
gains.b: A reason for the lodger's separateness, which the couplet only assumes.

note: The Kural tells those who serve hot-tempered kings to be like those warming at a fire, neither too far nor too near; Kantukkatan judges the king's anger a fire that burns all who come near and sends gold to quench it.
teaches: The Kural's fire teaches distance, while the merchant adds a remedy, gold poured like rain, so the pair shows a courtier's caution and a merchant's purchase as two answers to the same burning king.

gains.a: Kantukkatan's payment is seen as a known prudence toward royal anger, not mere fear
gains.b: the couplet's image is shown to allow a means of putting the fire out, which its advice of keeping distance leaves aside

note: 10 says the Chola, seeing a proven wrong, weighs it fairly and punishes fittingly (ஒப்ப நாடி அத்தக ஒறுத்தி); Kural 561 defines a king as one who inquires fittingly and punishes in proportion (தக்காங்கு நாடி ... ஒத்தாங்கு ஒறுப்பது).
teaches: The two share the very words for inquiry and proportion, so the Kural's definition of the just king reads like a rule drawn out of praise such as this, and 10 adds what 561 leaves out: the sentence is softened for the one who comes and stands at the king's feet.

note: 496 holds that a resolute man's effort can bring a flood of wealth in a day and that nothing fails to yield to it; Kural 620 holds that tireless effort sees even fate's back.
teaches: The epic puts the Kural's boldest claim for effort in the mouth of a man whose voyage ends in shipwreck, so the claim is made to depend on the life-span and deeds he later invokes.

gains.a: the merchant's boast gains the weight of a rule from the Kural's chapter on exertion
gains.b: the couplet gains a story in which tireless effort does meet fate head on and loses the wealth while the man survives

note: 739 says a land that makes you labour for riches is no land. 619 says bodily labour pays its wage even where the divine does not help.
teaches: The ideal of the place and the ethic of the person pull in opposite directions.

note: 1637 has the women paint the king and themselves sulking at him; Kural 1329 has the man wish the woman would go on sulking so that he may go on pleading.
teaches: The women fix the sulk in paint, where no pleading can follow, so the picture keeps the lovers' quarrel without its making-up.

gains.a: The portrait gains the reading that a sulk is something the lover wants, which explains why the women paint it for him.
gains.b: The couplet gains a sulk that is drawn, not spoken, which separates the delight of being sulked at from the pleading that follows.

note: The closing sermon says nothing helps the soul but virtue and nothing harms it but vice; the couplet says no gain surpasses virtue and no ruin surpasses forgetting it.
teaches: The couplet's ruin is forgetting virtue, while the sermon's is positive vice (maram), so the story hardens the Kural's lapse into a deed that harms the soul.

gains.a: the sermon's rule is seen as a hard form of a rule the Tamil tradition already held
gains.b: the couplet's ruin of forgetting is made sharper by a vice that actively harms

note: In 1456 Subhadran consoles the grieving mother that the man of merit will meet her daughter's eyes tomorrow (கண்ணுறு நாளை); in 1471 their gazes meet as Civakan enters the city.
teaches: The meeting of the eyes is the fulfilment of a precise prediction, so the first-sight love of the next verses is framed as a fate announced in advance rather than a chance encounter.

note: 2031 has the youth's lotus-like eyes and the girl's blue-lily eyes meet and press; Kural 1082 has the girl's answering look strike like an army.
teaches: The same meeting of eyes is a fated, gentle union in the enjoyment land but a conquest in the Kural's world of passion.

gains.a: The meeting look gains the sense of an attack that ends the other's resistance, which the epic's soft image of lilies leaves out.
gains.b: The couplet gains a setting where the look leads to fulfilment with no cost and no shame, unlike the pain the Kural's lover goes on to feel.

note: Both are the man's first sight of the woman and his doubt whether she is a goddess.
teaches: The couplet leaves the heart reeling in doubt, while the epic expands the doubt into a list of named goddesses and settles it in the next verse, so the Kural's moment becomes the first stage of a scene that ends in union.

gains.a: the epic verse gains the Kural's frame for reading its list of goddesses as the lover's conventional doubt (ஐயம்) and not as worship
gains.b: the couplet gains a sequel the Kural never gives: the doubt is resolved by signs of humanity and acted on

note: The couch scene rubs off the sandal and tears at the garlands; Naladiyar 48 mocks those who praise sandal paste and garlands without knowing the body they decorate.
teaches: Both pass through sandal, garland and body, one to delight in them and one to say the body is the cart that vultures will tear at.

gains.a: The sandal rubbed off the women's breasts gains the quatrain's view of what lies under it, the body that decays.
gains.b: The quatrain's sandal and garlands gain a scene in which they are being worn and spoiled in the way that it mocks.

note: Kural 4 says those who reach the feet of the one without liking or aversion have no suffering; verse 541 sings of the Lord as one who put away every desire and yet gives his servants unfailing bliss.
teaches: The hymn lets the desireless Lord be a giver, which the couplet avoids by saying only that no suffering reaches those at his feet.

gains.a: A statement of what the desireless one does for his servants, which the verse puts as a gift.
gains.b: A hymn in which the desireless one is nevertheless the one who gives, a tension the couplet does not face.

claims.gist: a king shares the joy and the pain of the people he rules
the lord taught the way of the nine categories, the five ranks and the two deeds from which becoming is made
Killing living beings brings sorrow, animal birth and hell as its fruit
the fast, worship of the arhats and gifts to ascetics bring the rank of Indra, then kingship
the soul can conquer the binding deeds by vow and reach the final state (பஞ்சம கதி)
the body is perishable and consumed by disease
to strike at those already defeated in battle is a disgrace fit to be sworn by
the gods cling to the objects of lust as though to a raft across the sea of lust and cannot let go
a king who has heard the teaching resolves to strive for the final world
flesh eaten from others is paid back by eating one's own flesh
the one who has conquered karma is the object of the world's worship
austerity should be practised in stages matched to one's strength
going to the forest does not wear away old sin that one carries within
a chaste wife will not touch a chest that has lain with courtesans
men who live by a king's command are left only with austerity or death when the king torments others
women who sell love trap lustful men with their eyes, take their wealth and cast the men off, and worth lies in not being caught
death comes on its day and takes life whole
the god has overcome desire and Death
sila is a body of 18,000 guarding rules and a hundred crore virtues
those who tear creatures from their kin and cage them will themselves be parted from their kin

note: The friend asks the queen to confine her restraint; the couplet says desire breaks that bolted door.
teaches: The couplet's door of restraint is shown here as one a friend urges the queen to keep shut and which the queen has already broken.

gains.a: the plea to imprison restraint is shown as too late, since the couplet says desire already breaks the door it names
gains.b: the couplet, spoken in a woman's voice, gets a case where another woman tells a queen to hold the door and cannot

note: Kural 381 counts the army among the six limbs of a king; verse 898 shows an army encamped with allied kings rimming the forest around the royal banner.
teaches: The camp shows the army as a ring of allies as well as a limb, which the couplet's list of six does not show.

gains.a: The verse lacks a rule that makes the host a part of kingship, which the couplet gives.
gains.b: The couplet lacks any picture of an army in the field with its allies pitched around the king.

note: Kural 380 holds nothing is stronger than fate, which forestalls any scheme; Kattiyangaran says the wise do not think of killing or being killed because deeds decide.
teaches: The epic gives the couplet's fatalism to a schemer whose own plot made the war, so the reader sees how the doctrine that fate outruns all devices can also serve to excuse the devices one has already used.

gains.a: the speech is seen to quote a sanctioned teaching, so its self-serving use is the point and not an error of doctrine
gains.b: the couplet gains a test case where fate is invoked by the guilty party at the moment of reckoning

note: The queen's dream of a bull and a young sun is told as an omen with no meaning given; the sage's reading in 44 turns it into a son who is king, ascetic and freed.
teaches: The dream is not left as an omen: the sage's reading supplies its meaning, and the prince's whole later life is fixed in it before his birth.

note: Kural 920 puts double-minded women, liquor and dice together as the company of the man Fortune has left; verse 615 makes desire itself the liquor.
teaches: The verse folds two of the Kural's three vices into one, so the women's eyes are the cup.

gains.a: The verse lacks a verdict on the man who loses day and night, which the couplet supplies.
gains.b: The couplet lacks an account of how women and drink become one vice, which the verse gives.

note: Ilango's patikam says dharma becomes death to those who err in kingship and that past deeds ripen; 260 lists Death, the woman, the king's own fault, his wealth and his grace as what will kill the king.
teaches: The Silappathikaram's king dies for an unjust verdict, while the Cintamani's is killed for lust and misplaced trust, so 'erring in kingship' is shown to include neglect, not only injustice.

note: The Silappathikaram sets Kannaki's wedding under a pearl canopy on diamond pillars; verse 852 hangs gems and pearls on a hall.
teaches: The pair shows the same jewelled hall at two scales: a city wedding and a palace one dressed like the gods' own.

gains.a: The Soolamani hall lacks any rite; the Silappathikaram unit gives the fire and the blessing.
gains.b: The Silappathikaram canopy is only a canopy; the Soolamani hall grows into a wishing-tree.

note: 1179 says a king's justice is to prefer scheming to fighting and see what can be got; Kural 546 says victory comes not from the spear but from the unbent sceptre.
teaches: The counsellor rests victory on scheming and the Kural on the king's justice, so the two name different grounds for winning.

gains.a: The counsellor's rule asks only what can be gained, which the Kural answers with the question of whether the king's sceptre is just.
gains.b: The Kural's sceptre has no scheming rival, which the epic supplies in a council voice that puts craft first.

note: 2129 has Tirumal lift a straight sceptre with the gods guarding him; Kural 547 says the king guards the world and justice guards him if he does not falter.
teaches: The guard of a king comes in the epic from the gods and in the couplet from his own justice, so the pairing asks what really protects a ruler.

gains.a: The gods' protection, which the epic gives as a plain fact, is made to depend on the rule of a straight sceptre.
gains.b: The couplet's guard of justice gains a mythic setting in which the gods are the guards.

note: In Akananuru 5 the man says he gave up the journey because of his wife's silent, tearful sign; in Kalittokai 17 the friend says her own words, like medicine, made him give it up.
teaches: The same outcome is credited to whoever speaks the poem, the husband to the wife's mute grief and the friend to her own argument, so the given-up journey is a shared ending each voice claims.

note: The patikam's 9 says Saccandan would not hear counsel (சொல்லாறு கேளான்) and was beaten by a plot (சூழ்ச்சியில் தோற்ற); at 1925 his son asks what need a lion has of strategy (சூழ்ச்சி).
teaches: The son's first reply to his mother repeats his father's fatal contempt for counsel, so the lesson of the patikam must be learned again within the family.

note: The women of another city asked whether Civakan was the Vel of the kadamba or the son of the five arrows; Videham's crowd hails him as both, the spear-bearer who slew the mountain and Kama.
teaches: What was a puzzled question of desire in one city becomes a public litany of titles in the next, so the likeness to Murugan and Kama hardens from a woman's doubt into the name a whole city gives him.

note: Both set a wife's or beloved's shoulders against heaven. 906 says that fearing those shoulders leaves no worth even in a godlike life, and 1103 asks whether the lotus-eyed god's world is sweeter than sleep on them.
teaches: Fear and love differ, but the books value the same intimacy in opposite ways.

note: The Naladiyar's eel-like doubleness belongs to women who sell intimacy; Vijayai, the faithful queen, puts the hearts of girdled women in general among things that do not go straight.
teaches: The quatrain confines double dealing to a class of women and blames the men who embrace them, whereas the epic's chaste widow extends the suspicion to all women when a secret is at stake, so the pair shows the charge widening from a trade to a sex.

gains.a: the queen's maxim gains a narrower ethical source, which shows how much she generalises the doubleness the moral books assigned to courtesans
gains.b: the quatrain gains a woman speaker who uses its suspicion as practical counsel, testing whether its warning was about trade or about women

note: 1642 has the women say a garland bent their slender waists; Kural 1115 has the man say a woman who wore anicham flowers with their stems has a waist too weak for good drums to sound.
teaches: What the couplet gives as a lover's praise of a woman's delicacy the poem gives to the women as their own complaint, so the delicacy becomes something they offer to be noticed.

gains.a: The women's complaints gain a source in the convention of praising a woman's frailty, so they speak in the lover's idiom.
gains.b: The couplet gains women who claim the praised frailty themselves, so the frailty is shown as performance as well as praise.

note: The couplet holds that one's own understanding prevails however many subtle books one learns; the epic says the deed blinds those who have swum through learning.
teaches: The epic gives the limit of learning that the couplet states a cause and a scene, the deed covering one's eyes at the moment of desire, so the 'own understanding' that overrides books becomes the karma that defeats even the learned.

gains.a: the epic's claim that learning gives no protection is set against a known ethical rule about learning's limit, sharpening its point that knowing is not seeing
gains.b: the couplet's unstated reason why learning fails is supplied as karma at work in desire, one answer to the question its nuance leaves open

note: Kural 280 says neither shaving nor long hair is needed if one gives up what the world condemns; 2637 has the matrons pluck out their own dark hair and enter renunciation pondering the settled meaning of the Lord's book.
teaches: The Jain rite of plucking the hair is joined to inward thought in the verse, which is the answer to the Kural's doubt whether the shorn head means anything without giving up.

gains.a: the plucking is given a test, whether it comes with giving up what is condemned, which the epic verse supplies only as pondering the scripture
gains.b: the couplet gets a rite that is neither shaving nor matting, hair plucked by one's own hand, which it does not consider

note: The Kural prefers a spear that missed an elephant to an arrow that hit a hare; the epic's thrower would not cast except at a young elephant, and spends that spear on one warrior.
teaches: The couplet ranks targets; the epic shows the ranking used as a courtesy between enemies, a man of the elephant-only code paying a foot soldier the honour of the elephant's spear.

gains.a: the thrower's habit is recognised as the standard the couplet names, so his choice reads as tribute to the youth
gains.b: the couplet's private scale of glory becomes something one warrior can confer on another

note: The Kural says one whose mind ponders and knows what is with certainty need not think again of birth; Civakan says knowledge, right vision and right conduct must all three be full before both kinds of deed pass.
teaches: Where the couplet lets true knowing alone end rebirth, the Jain formula makes knowing only one of three and insists on vision and conduct of non-harm as well, so the pair shows the Kural's chapter on true knowledge as a narrower account of release.

gains.a: a single-cause claim against which its insistence on all three, each made full, stands out
gains.b: a fuller account of what knowing must be joined with before birth ends, which the couplet leaves unsaid

note: 1870 piles up festoons, banners, drums and conches that drown the sea; Kural 34 calls virtue the mind's spotlessness and the rest a noise (ஆகுலம்).
teaches: The epic lingers on the din of worship while the couplet measures a rite by the mind within, so the pair asks whether the festival is aram or only clamour.

gains.a: The festival's din gains a standard the poet does not apply in this passage: the mind of the worshipper.
gains.b: The couplet gains a full, glittering example of outward worship against which its charge of mere noise can be tried.

note: The attendants read the king's sign and withdraw unasked; Kural 701 praises one who reads what is meant before it is said.
teaches: The reading of a sign here serves privacy and not counsel, so the Kural's praise of sign-readers is shown at work in a small court habit.

gains.a: A name for the skill of the attendants who leave, which the verse mentions in a clause.
gains.b: A scene where reading a sign is discretion and not advice, a use the couplet does not mention.

note: Kurinjippattu opens with the friend disclosing to the mother the marriage the girl chose past her father's guard; in 1052 the nurse who sounded Gunamalai tells the mother, who tells the father.
teaches: The epic runs the akam disclosure through the whole household chain and adds the nurse's verdict that the match ripens from past penance, so a convention of love poetry becomes a step in a karmic marriage plot.

gains.a: the logic of அறத்தொடு நிற்றல், by which the nurse's report reads as a recognised duty to disclose rather than gossip
gains.b: a narrated sequel in which disclosure reaches the father and produces the wedding, which the idyll's speech to the mother can only argue for

note: Verse 934 shows a king riding an elephant under a high umbrella; Naladiyar 21 says kings who rode elephants under umbrellas like the moon over a hill have been carried off.
teaches: The same pomp that the Soolamani shows as the king's splendour is the thing the Naladiyar sets against death, so the display is also a reminder of its end.

gains.a: The verse lacks any hint that the splendour of the ride is brief.
gains.b: The quatrain lacks the scene whose brightness gives its warning weight.

note: The king reads the outcome of the errand from the envoy's face before he speaks, as Kural 706 says the face shows what the heart holds strongest.
teaches: The epic extends the couplet from a feeling to a piece of news, so a returning envoy's face can carry the result of a mission before his words do.

gains.a: The verse lacks the reason a king can read success unspoken, which the couplet gives: the face shows what is strongest in the heart.
gains.b: The couplet lacks a case where what the face shows is the end of a mission, not a mood, and this verse supplies it.

note: Soolamani 155 has her modesty make a flower-vine droop in shame; here modesty is the curtain she draws round the prince she carries in her heart.
teaches: Modesty shifts from an ornament of her beauty into the screen that hides her love.

note: 1792 has the women's eyes already settle on the prince; 1793 has the king then call the maiden to come in.
teaches: The assembly's gaze is decided before the maiden is called, so her choice enters a room that has already leaned.

note: 2873 tells the prince to abandon wealth got with lies, deceit and dice; Kural 283 says gain got by stealth seems to grow and then perishes.
teaches: The Kural says the ill-gotten gain will not last and the verse adds that the greed behind it is itself what to drop.

gains.a: The verse's abandoning of greed gets a reason from this life, the loss of the gain
gains.b: The Kural's lost gain gets the cause it leaves out, the lie and the dice that win it

note: In 66 the friend calls the konrai foolish for taking the untimely rain for the season; in 382 the friend says the rain itself is untimely, since if it were the season the man would have come.
teaches: The friend's comfort moves from blaming the tree to denying the season: in 66 nature is fooled by false rain, in 382 the man's promise is made the test of what the rain is, so his word outranks the calendar of flowers.

note: Both close on a king with tribute-paying kings around him, but Civakan turns away from it in dharma and Udayanan stays in it.
teaches: The same picture of a king whom others serve ends in renunciation in the Cintamani and in enjoyment here, so the minor epic's close is not the great epic's close.

note: In both epics a prince wins a battle for a king and the king rewards him with a bride (Gunavati there, Padumai here).
teaches: The reward-bride after a won battle is a pattern the Jain kavyas share, which marks the match as a convention and not one king's habit.

note: Naladiyar 11 says the wise, knowing grey hair will come, renounced in childhood; 191 says grey hair has not come to the poet because of his good wife, children, servants, king and the worthy men of his town. On the reading that both speak of how to meet old age, one counsels leaving the household and the other credits it.
teaches: The Naladiyar's answer to ageing is renunciation, while Pisirandhaiyar's is a good household and good company, so the pair shows two Tamil remedies for the same fear, one by leaving the world early and one by living well in it.

note: The bride's ornaments protest that the 'king of kings' turned cruel-sceptred will not look into or hear their clamour (ஆய்ந்து கேட்டு மருளான்); the couplet says the ruler who does not examine daily and do justice loses his land.
teaches: The poet borrows the courtroom picture of the deaf king who spurns a plaint to make a lovers' jest, which shows how familiar the Kural's failed-hearing image was as a figure.

gains.a: the jest gets its edge from a standard of judging that the verse never states and the couplet supplies
gains.b: the couplet is shown being used by a poet to joke about, not to condemn, the king who will not hear, which its own grave tone cannot show

note: The Kural says those who set their desire on the home do not reach the fine fruit; the Cintamani's whole frame begins with a king whose desire for his queen grew thick and cost him his throne.
teaches: Held against the Kural's warning about desire fixed on the wife, the patikam locates the whole fault in the husband's excess while calling the queen's chastity unfailing (வீடாத கற்பு), and gives the couplet's lost 'fine fruit' a political price, the kingdom itself.

gains.a: the king's fall, told without any doctrine named, gains the Kural's category of being led by desire for the wife as its ethical name
gains.b: the couplet's unnamed 'fine fruit' is given a concrete price: a throne and, in the story, a life

note: The king's order to Candakarman to bring a pair of humans for the goddess is carried out here as the two are seized.
teaches: The poem sets an officer's seeing the pair's gentleness against the order he serves, and the order wins, which shows duty to the king ruling over mercy.

note: 1804 sets this king's glory 'after Bharata'; 397 says the First Lord's grace made a king of the earth Bharata.
teaches: The herald's yardstick, Bharata, is the ruler the earlier verse shows as the First Lord's gift, so the king's glory is measured against a grace-given one.

note: Kural 901 says men who fix their desire on the wife miss life's fine fruit; the narrator says the king followed his heart to the queen because a past destiny sprouted.
teaches: The couplet treats being led by desire for one's wife as a fault to be avoided, while the epic adds a ripening past deed as its cause, which raises the question the couplet does not face: whether such a man could have chosen otherwise.

gains.a: the king's surrender to desire is named as a recognised fault of rulers, not only a love story
gains.b: the couplet's simple prohibition is set against a story where karma also pushes the man

note: Kural 780 says a death that fills with tears the eyes of those who sustained one is worth begging for; Ariccandan's speech promises rewards to men who die helping the leader who raised and kept them (தற்புறந் தந்து வைத்த தலைமகற்கு).
teaches: Together they show the couplet's patron-bond being used as a battlefield appeal, and that it can be spent on a bad master: the leader these men are asked to die for is the usurper, and the speech wins only their deaths.

gains.a: Ariccandan's speech is seen to rest on the moral claim of the sustained man's debt, not merely on bribes of heaven
gains.b: the couplet's ideal is shown with its blind spot: it weighs the bond to the sustainer and not whether the sustainer deserves the death

note: The Kural's warrior laughs as he pulls a spear from his own body; 1255 has a king laugh at his army's rout.
teaches: The laugh of a warrior pulling a spear from his body is a private triumph, while a king's laugh at a lost army is a boast over others' loss.

gains.a: A measure of what the king's laugh costs against the warrior who laughs at his own wound.
gains.b: A contrasting laugh, from a leader and not the wounded fighter, which tests how far the Kural's praise reaches.

note: Spring's feast-dance in the groves rests on the loosened bangles of forsaken women; the Silappathikaram's closing venbas make spring the command that sulking lovers unite.
teaches: The same spring brings reunion for sulkers in one telling and shows the cost to women left apart in the other, so the season's joy is not shared by all.

note: The king, after seeing the portrait in verse 133, asks the sage whose answer verse 134 gives.
teaches: The king's grief turns not to action but to a sage's assurance, so the answer to Yugi's lure is a prophecy that makes him wait.

note: 2014 calls knowledge from the texts a lamp; 2018 calls seeing the true thing a lamp of vision that ends the dark.
teaches: One lamp is lit twice, once by hearing and once by seeing, so the sage joins the two as stages of one light.

note: Disguised ministers sell jewels in an enemy camp, as the Kural describes a spy who takes an unsuspected form.
teaches: The epic's spies are the king and his own minister, and gems are the means, which the Kural's spy has no word for.

gains.a: The verse gains a rule, a spy's form must raise no suspicion, which shows why the jewel trade is chosen as the disguise.
gains.b: The couplet gains a case in which king and minister both act as the spy, which its plain listing of the spy's duties does not offer.

note: Kural 1251 makes restraint a door bolted by shame, broken by desire's axe; Suramanjari drives off the bee of shame and waves the garland of chastity.
teaches: In the couplet restraint stands only while shame bars it; the epic has a woman put shame away in order to keep her chastity, so the two virtues the couplet binds together are parted and ranked.

gains.a: the epic image gains a known structure to depart from, so that her casting off shame reads as a choice for chastity rather than a fall
gains.b: the couplet gains a counter-case in which shame is given up without restraint failing, which shows its door-and-bolt bond is not the only order of the two

claims.gist: a ruler should be fierce in command yet cool in giving, great in nature yet modest with friends
there is no soul, no rebirth, and no good or bad deed
those who deny soul and rebirth and live by harm go to the nigoda state
kevala, the soul's full knowledge, is gained by the renouncer and puts him above the gods
a body that does not help others in their trouble yields no fruit
the ascetic's life is built on knowledge, right vision and conduct
killing in battle, even a just one, leaves a sin that worship, festival and giving can put away
each is strongest on its own ground, the crocodile in water and the forest people in the forest
even a child formed whole may be lost
the Arhat is without blemish and is the source of the scripture
those who learn and hear this work rise in the world and are guarded by Tiru
bathing in the sacred waters of Kumari takes away old age
men who are bold in love but tremble in battle have no manliness
when good deeds are spent the evil deeds that oppress a person take their place
desire is a sin and birth a disease from which one must be healed by giving it up
the wealth of the wedding is so great that it may be taken for a dream and so is to be left for the forest penance
kings of the high line guard the world without a word of reproach
to wound an old Brahmin, even by harsh words, is sin
when love is excessive, learning gives no help
the sight of a passing thing turns a king from rule to renunciation
trusting women's smiles leads to endless rebirth in states of sorrow
deeds of an earlier birth and of this one ripen on the doer
karma does not perish with the body
killing beings sends the doer to hell
there is no next world or soul, and penance and giving are a waste
the sin that clings to lives, known to most only by hearsay, can be seen in a reversal of fortune
the human body perishes without leaving a trace
men who fight men should do so without trickery
eating grass and standing amid the five fires cuts off cruel deeds
bodily mortification and diet do not conquer deeds, or the dove would be freed
the mind is to be held firm by the army of virtues and disciplines
the companions' own strength suffices and no outside allies are needed
those who quibble endlessly over virtues and refuse to accept them are base and not truly human

note: In 454 Civakan turned back the hunters' raid on the king's herd; here his friends plan a raid on a king's herd to make him ride out.
teaches: The cattle raid that first made Civakan a public hero becomes a signal his friends can send him, so the epic treats his response to niraikol as a known trait that others can plan on.

note: The Kural promises distinction to one who takes what hurts as pleasure; the friend says that bearing sorrow as joy is harder than weeping or dying.
teaches: The couplet's discipline for a man in adversity becomes, in a deserted bride's chamber, the hardest thing in the world, set above death itself in difficulty, so the epic measures the cost the couplet only rewards.

gains.a: a recognized rule of endurance, which shows its consolation to be ethical counsel and not just comfort
gains.b: a test case in grief over a loved one, where the rule is admitted to be harder than dying

note: Tirumanthiram 258 names austerity and virtue as a boat across the sea of deeds that the Lord makes fruitful; verse 355 says austerity ends all evil and reaches Sivagati, with the god unnamed.
teaches: Both name austerity as what ends deeds, but one adds a god who makes it bear fruit and the other leaves effort alone to do it, so the dispute is over what austerity needs.

gains.a: A second agent, the Lord, against which to weigh the sage's claim that effort alone ends evil.
gains.b: A case where austerity is said to bring release with no god named, which tests how far it depends on grace.

note: In 1240 the young Civakan goes round the temple of the god who cut the ghati karmas and passes on; in 2743 he circles the Charana lord's shrine as an old king and stays to be taught.
teaches: The circling that was a stop on a road is here the last one, and what it leads to is a teaching and not a journey.
