note: The guards wave countless whisks and the festival's wealth is beyond count; the poem's summary says that while kings brought tribute and fortune stayed, Civakan heard the dharma, feared kingship like a snake struck by thunder, and renounced.
teaches: Read with the closing renunciation, the countless whisks mark the height of the splendour he will later flee, so the poem's praise of kingship is held against its end.

note: Kural 270 says the have-nots are many because few do penance; 997 has Gunamalai ask whether, like the small folk who did no penance, she has any door to escape her longing.
teaches: The couplet's explanation of want by the lack of past tapas is taken up by a lover as an account of why the man she wants is out of reach, showing the doctrine at work in ordinary speech about desire.

gains.a: the doctrinal sense of her simile: that what one lacks is owed to penance not done, which turns her cry into a judgment on her own merit
gains.b: a reading of the couplet's unspecified 'those who lack' as covering the lover's lack, which the couplet leaves open

note: The sage makes feeling another's pain as one's own the base of the chief vow; the Siddhar wishes to think of the lives he would kill and eat as his own life.
teaches: The Siddhar offers this as a wish on the way to completing his tapas, while the verse makes it the support without which the vow of not killing cannot stand.

gains.a: The verse gets a voice from a different tradition that reaches the same rule and ties it to a seeker's tapas.
gains.b: The Siddhar's wish gets a Jain statement that names the pity that must come first and the restraint beside it.

note: The mourners say he took no part in dharma and has no good death; the king had refused to kill even to save his own life.
teaches: The mourners judge by what they saw, but 139 shows the refusal that belongs to the king's dharma, so their verdict is incomplete.

note: The poison she meant for the king is poured back into her mouth in hell.
teaches: The punishment copies the crime, so the reader sees the hell as the working out of her own deed.

note: The Kural makes it the duty of a minister at the king's side to tell him what is good for him; in 36 the ministers tell Pradyota of Udayana's merits.
teaches: The ministers do speak, as the Kural asks, but to a king in anger the truth ends in a plot, so the duty to speak does not guarantee it is heard.

gains.a: a case in which ministers do speak in the king's presence and yet are turned aside
gains.b: a test of the duty to speak when the king, angry, has no wish to be told good of his enemy

note: 240 calls Aay Andiran never stinting singers of horses, elephants and chariots; Akananuru 152 names 'Aay's forest' after the Aay who gives elephants to all who come, skilled or not (வல்லினும் வல்லார் ஆயினும்).
teaches: The akam poet uses Aay's open-handedness to name a place, while the puram poem records what followed his death, his poets scattering to other lands, so the patron's giving outlived him as a landmark in love poetry even as the household it fed dissolved.

note: In 213 King Saccandan dismisses warning by saying pleasures and days of life are measured out in advance; in 510 Sitattan uses the same doctrine of a measured life-span to steady his crew, and alone survives.
teaches: The doctrine of the measured life-span is voiced twice before a disaster, once as an excuse for heedlessness that ends in a king's death and once as courage that ends in rescue, so its worth in the epic depends on what the speaker does with it.

note: The invocation's demons who lost their god's refuge are, in the story, the demons who complain to Neelakesi that the sage stopped their offerings.
teaches: The phrase 'removing refuge in the god' turns out to mean ending blood offerings, so the demons' grievance is the loss of sacrifice, the poem's first act against killing.

note: The Kural weighs help given at the moment of need as greater than the world; Civakan's gift comes at a dying dog's last moment and is repaid by a god at his own.
teaches: The Kural measures timely help by its worth to the one helped, while the Cintamani shows it returned across species and births, so the couplet's weight becomes a debt that the receiver carries into a new life.

gains.a: the dog episode gains the Kural's measure of why so small a gift counts
gains.b: the couplet's timely help is shown being repaid in kind at the giver's own hour of need

note: Kural 1083: the man never knew Death and now knows it in a woman's warring eyes. Civakan: those who named her called her woman; had they called her Death, men would flee the city.
teaches: The pair shows two steps of one discovery: the couplet's man learns that Death has a woman's form, and the epic adds that the name 'woman' hides it, so no one is warned in time.

gains.a: the epic's joke about naming is grounded in the couplet's discovery that Death and a woman are one
gains.b: the couplet's private discovery is made public: if it were known, a whole city would empty

note: The couplet promises that those who reach the feet of the one without liking or aversion have no suffering anywhere; Vijayai worships at the Jina's feet and in the next verse weeps for her son.
teaches: Placed beside the couplet, the scene shows worship at the passionless one's feet asked to remove a fault while the grief of attachment to a child runs on, so the promised freedom from suffering is a goal still far off, not a present state.

gains.a: the epic's silent worship gains a standard, the couplet's 'no suffering at any time', against which her tears in 1785 read as the distance still to go
gains.b: the couplet gains a case of a worshipper at the right feet whose suffering persists, which tests whether 'reaching' the feet means worship or attainment

note: Kural 549 says guarding and caring for the people is the king's work and no stain; verse 599 shows that work as sleeplessness.
teaches: What the Kural calls work, the verse shows as a worry that costs a king his sleep.

gains.a: The verse lacks a rule saying the guarding is his own task rather than a burden laid on him.
gains.b: The couplet lacks the felt cost of that work, which the verse gives.

note: At the burning ground in 309 she asked the newborn whether this was how kings are born; here she remembers that same birth as the son appearing as her companion.
teaches: The birth among corpses, first lamented as a disgrace to a king's son, is remembered as rescue, and the loss she now fears is told as the loss of that companion of the cremation ground.

note: Both apologies use the moon's spot for the poet's flaw: the Neelakesi's poet will own a fault since even the moon is not spotless; the Cintamani's asks the learned to wash the spot away with their wit.
teaches: The two Jain poets put the same flaw in different hands: the Neelakesi's poet takes it on himself, while the Cintamani's poet makes cleaning it the learned reader's task.

note: 381 makes six assets (army, people, wealth, ministers, friends, fortress) the mark of a lion among kings. Parimelazhagar's 'others' in 661 are exactly army, fort and friendship, which he says don't count as firmness.
teaches: The list of assets is empty without the mind that uses them.

note: Both give hell as the fruit of the deed; the verse adds animal rebirth to it.
teaches: The epic widens the couplet's hell into an order of fruits that includes animal birth, which the couplet does not name.

gains.a: the sermon's hell is borne out by an old rule that links it to killing for food
gains.b: the couplet's hell gets a longer road of sorrow and animal birth before it

note: The quatrain says kings under the umbrella fall when their deeds turn; the epic shows the fall as the same soul living on as a timid bird in his son's house.
teaches: The couplet's fall of kings is made concrete: the king does not end, he is reborn lower, and at his own son's door.

gains.a: the frightened bird gains a general rule that explains why the great fall
gains.b: the quatrain's fall gains an afterlife it only hints at, the same soul continuing in the palace

note: 2870 says theft is punished by kings and drops the thief into a fallen birth; Kural 290 says the thief loses his footing and the one who does not steal does not lose the world of the gods.
teaches: The verse spells the two punishments the Kural gives in one line, in this world and in the next.

gains.a: The verse's king-tortured thief gets the Kural's measure that the loss is of the very footing of life
gains.b: The Kural's lost footing gets a picture, the elephant's tusk and then the fallen birth

note: The astrologer waits on the king's sign and then speaks to show his learning, with a sight of all three times; Naladiyar 52 calls those who prattle of the stars the most foolish of the foolish, set against the thought of death.
teaches: The story rests its plot on an astrologer who is admitted, heard and believed by the whole court, while the quatrain calls his craft folly, so the two give opposite verdicts on the same trade.

gains.a: The poem's own motive line, that he speaks to display his learning, gets an outside judgment on whether that learning is worth the court's trust.
gains.b: The quatrain's charge of folly meets an astrologer who is welcomed by a king, which shows the claim being tested against a trusted practitioner.

note: 1071 beats the drums for the worship day; 1075 lays out the stages of the day's procession.
teaches: The festival's religious worship and its marriage procession share one day and one set of stages.

note: The astrologer foretells a messenger with a letter in the Pushpakarandam garden; the ministers propose to set the stone platform in order and post a guard in the garden on his day.
teaches: The court does not wait on the prophecy but prepares the place it names, so counsel here means arranging the ground for a sign the king has only just heard.

note: Gunamalai stood before the charging elephant looking about with doe eyes and trembling like lightning; Civakan paints exactly her look and her trembling.
teaches: The lover's image of the beloved is the instant of her mortal fear, so what he desires and keeps is the moment he saved her, and the rescue becomes the ground of the love.

note: The couplet says tavam is striven for because it gets whatever one wants as one wants it; the kings vow that if they lose her they will fight, or else do great penance.
teaches: The kings take penance on the couplet's own motive, as a way to the thing desired, and so show the weakness the couplet's next verse attacks: penance offered as the consolation of a failed suitor stays bound to the desire it should end.

gains.a: the kings' fallback is seen as a reading of tavam the Kural itself supplies
gains.b: the couplet's promise of getting what one wants gains a speaker for whom the wanted thing is a woman lost at a contest

note: Both poems show a young prince making a rutting elephant submit before the king.
teaches: Both minor epics test a hero's worth before a king by his mastery of an elephant, but here the man is a captive and the rider's skill earns him his captor's trust.

note: The sage had foretold that the prince would curb the rut of a great elephant; verse 57 shows him doing so on the city's own mad elephant.
teaches: The sage's prophecy is not left as a promise: the city's real elephant is the first thing that proves it, so a reader sees the prince's prowess as the working of what was foretold.

note: Verse 880 has wild elephants mistake clouds for a rival elephant; verse 951 says clouds and young elephants cannot be told apart.
teaches: The mistake of cloud for elephant is the beasts' in one verse and the poet's own wit in the other.

note: The sage says austerity will cut away the prince's heated deeds so that he reaches release; the quatrain says austerity drives sin out as a lamp drives darkness, and that evil settles in again when the good deeds that feed it run out.
teaches: The sage's promise of a final release by tapas is answered by a warning that austerity burns sin only while its good is kept up, so the prophecy needs the prince's own lasting effort.

gains.a: a limit on the prophecy: release by tapas has to be kept up and is not given once
gains.b: a story in which a lamp-like tapas is foretold of one person, with the end of deeds as its goal

note: The astrologer says the bite, given the hour, is hard to cure even for the Lord; within ten verses the venom leaves her at Civakan's gaze.
teaches: The epic sets a reading of the stars that declares death against a cure that follows at once, so the hour the astrologer trusted is shown not to bind, and the outcome turns on the healer's learning rather than on the time of the bite.

note: Kural 380 says nothing is stronger than fate, and that it arrives first even when one devises another course; verse 668 has the king put fate's power to use as the ground of giving way.
teaches: The couplet's law of fate is turned by the king into a reason to submit, which the hero rejects in the same chapter.

gains.a: The verse lacks any statement that no counter-plan can outrun fate, which would turn the king's despair from a mood into a rule.
gains.b: The couplet lacks a person who reaches for its truth to excuse giving way, which shows the rule serving as an alibi.

note: Verse 179 opens the shrine's gem doors at the king's coming; verse 185 shuts them after his praise.
teaches: The worship is bounded by an opening and a closing of the doors, so the whole of the praise lies between them.

note: The patikam foretold that the younger brother, like a star that lost the moon, would come at a woman's bidding; here the image returns and Gandharvadattai appears.
teaches: The pairing identifies the patikam's unnamed woman as Gandharvadattai, whose song follows, and shows the brother's search starting exactly as the patikam framed it.

note: Kural 567 says harsh words and punishment past all bounds file down a king's conquering strength; in 1079 the king, raging over a sulking elephant, orders the hero seized and his strength rooted out.
teaches: The epic shows where such excess comes from: a usurper's envy of a subject's fame finds a trivial cause, and the order that follows is the first stroke of the file that will bring his own fall.

gains.a: the king's order gains a rule by which the reader can judge it as the self-wearing excess of a bad ruler, not just anger
gains.b: the couplet gains a source for excessive punishment in wounded pride, and a story in which the file's work can be traced

note: The patikam tells that a god came down the sky's path like lightning from a cloud and carried the strong one away from the king's prison; here Sudanjanan feels the omen, learns the danger and descends in storm.
teaches: The patikam's single line is filled out with the god's heaven, his omen and his far-seeing knowledge, so the rescue is shown as the answer of a bond, not a stroke of luck.

note: Kural 685 asks an envoy to speak briefly, to leave out what offends and to say it so that it wins a smile; Marusi's words in 518 to 523 offend the king and end by calling men of the earth unable to know what is fitting.
teaches: A couplet of what an envoy should do is seen broken in a scene where the envoy's anger grows from the court's silence rather than from ill will.

gains.a: 523 gains a standard against which the envoy's pride reads as a failure of his office, not just a mood
gains.b: 685 gains a case where the pressure on the envoy comes from a silent king, so softening speech means bearing silence as well as choosing words

note: The Manimekalai's teacher sets out the forward chain from contact to craving, clinging, becoming and a birth whose fruit is aging, death and grief; the friend's tree runs from the seed of ignorance through deeds and desire to the fruit of death.
teaches: The two epics share the shape of a causal chain from ignorance to death, but the Cintamani makes it a single growing tree with love and elation among its branches and uses it to dry a lover's tears, where the Manimekalai gives it as a doctrine of release with named links.

note: In 446 the priest names the foe's destroyer as the lion-slaying man; 772 shows the deed that gives him that name.
teaches: The lion-slaying title that the priest later uses against the rival king is shown being earned here as a protective act.

note: Both open with frogs in every hollow (அவல்தோறு, அவல்தொறும்) and the formula கார்தொடங் கின்றே/கின்றால் காலை; in Akananuru 364 the woman concludes that he in the king's camp does not think of us, in Ainkurunuru 453 that his chariot has set out toward us.
teaches: The same signs of the first rains, in nearly the same words, lead one wife to despair and another to expect the chariot, so the season's onset in mullai poetry is not itself a message: its meaning is decided by what the woman believes of the man.

note: The women speak a desire and beg with their eyes, while Kural 1100 says that when two pairs of eyes agree, mouth-words are of no use.
teaches: The Kural's silent agreement of two pairs of eyes needs the other side's glance; the women here ask in words and eyes for what he has not yet answered.

gains.a: A standard that shows the women's begging as one-sided and so not yet the eye-agreement the Kural names.
gains.b: A counter-case where eyes and words both ask, showing the couplet's agreement needs two parties.

claims.gist: a kingdom cannot stand without able counsellors
a king who dies fighting, bearing the Jina's feet and the mantra-sandal, goes as guest to the gods
a death in lustful delusion brings rebirth in an animal body
a mother's great austerity shows in the glory of her son
the greatest vow among women is a chaste wife's unbroken steadfastness
Lakshmi does not stay with those whose minds are not clear
a king who strikes in anger without examining the matter is carried off by his own pride
old deeds loosen when the vow taught by the muni is taken
in hell neither any companion nor dharma stands by the sufferer
birth, growth, waning and death are the nature of all things, as the moon shows
understanding the nature of birth leads to fear of attachment to pleasure
cows, renunciants, women, children and brahmins have a claim on a warrior's protection, and failing them is unmanly shame
a king's son's chief duty is to relieve the danger of living beings without counting his own life
knowledge, faith and conduct together burn away karma, and that is release
release gives the fourfold infinite
the pleasures of women in this world end at death, when the beloved herself closes the lover's eyes, so the world is not good
a warrior who flees brings shame so that even women shrink from him
a day of joy is the day on which earlier good deeds are enjoyed as their fruit
one who dies in evil should shun evil in the body of the next birth
children win worth only through the grace of kings
even gods, when they fall, are scorned like anyone; this is human nature
the way a king must rule is an ancient norm that learned poets hand down
pleasure without thought of the end is cut off by Death
gifts of one who knows the true principles lead among the best gods
the right sight that gives rise to dharma can come from knowing one's own earlier births, not from the ascetics' teaching alone
giving up attachment and hatred wholly makes the ascetic, whose kindness shields the mind from darkness
the learned bow while the wealth of the base holds its head high
in an unstable world it is generous fame that stands, and the wealth of one who seeks it does not stay
the anger of holy men does not last
a deed done without grace returns on the doer as ripened deeds
the body begins as a drop that grows in foul flesh
one who thinks of great dharma escapes the hut of flesh and gains lasting pleasure
conduct held first by those who have cut off passion is good austerity and brings rule of heaven
the body, though handsome, is hollow and cannot be relied on
the gods are ten Bhavana, eight Vyantara, five Jyotishka and sixteen kalpa

note: The king fears the blame of sending a captive before an elephant but admits the capture was by a lie.
teaches: The king dreads the stain of one act and ignores the one before it, which the couplet's test of fame would catch.

gains.a: the king's fear of blame is shown to cover only the last act, not the deceit that made it needed
gains.b: the couplet's warning against acts that win neither renown nor good is shown failing to bind a king who counts only visible blame

note: Siddhar 910 calls the mountain of Ekambar the one that removes the hard deeds of those who bow (பணிவாரருவினை தீர்க்கும்); in 1603 women climb a hill so that their accumulated evil deeds may leave them (நிரைத்த தீவினை நீங்க).
teaches: A Jain epic and a Saiva poet share the belief that a sacred hill wears away karma, which shows a common practice of pilgrimage beneath the doctrinal quarrel over how deeds are destroyed.

gains.a: evidence that the pilgrims' purpose is a widely held Tamil belief and not a doctrine peculiar to the epic's hill
gains.b: a parallel from another faith that shows the hill's power over karma as shared ground rather than a Saiva claim alone

note: Naladiyar 4 tells the hearer to do good at once because Death comes in anger; verse 317 grades austerity to each one's strength.
teaches: Urgency in the quatrain is made practicable by the epic's graded vows, which say how those not yet able to renounce fully are to begin.

gains.a: the verse lacks the sense that time is short and delay is costly
gains.b: the quatrain lacks any ladder of vows for those who cannot yet give up everything

note: The Naladiyar says an old deed seeks out its doer like a calf its mother; this verse says deeds already gathered can be shed in a moment.
teaches: The Tamil ethics book makes old deeds unavoidable, while the Jain epic's poet leaves a way to drop them at once, so karma is binding in one book and removable in the other.

gains.a: the Jain poem's claim is set against the stricter view that old deeds always find their doer
gains.b: the calf-and-mother image is shown to have an exit in the Jain account of karma

note: Kattiyangaran swears to write 'thief' on Civakan's chest; in 1165 he praises Civakan as without equal in grace, strength, learning and generosity and rewards the man who claims to have killed him.
teaches: The usurper's own praise in 1165 shows that his charge of theft was never a judgment, so the bent sceptre here is a king punishing a man he knows to be the best of his subjects.

note: The mother asks a kid for Chandikai; the Tirumanthiram describes Chandika as holding the four directions, without an offering.
teaches: The Tirumanthiram gives Chandika a cosmic form and no offering, while the epic shows how a mother worships her.

gains.a: The epic shows the offering practice and not her cosmic form.
gains.b: The Tirumanthiram's Chandika gets the folk offering that the epic makes the king refuse.

note: Civakan fears his absent wife will die in the fire of separation; Kemasari, whom he has just left, held back her own life in 1530.
teaches: The man who imagines a wife dying of separation has just left another wife who, contrary to his fear, chose to live for his sake, so the pairing shows the deserter's imagination of grief running behind what the deserted woman actually did.

note: 1427 has the spell call Death; 1428 shows the spirits and the goddess coming and the spell loosed on the army.
teaches: Death's summons is joined by a feast of spirits, which shows the destruction as a gathering that feeds many.

note: In 303 the woman who once went into sky-touching palaces like a heavenly maiden is left alone in a forest of white skulls and is said to be shown so that hearers may see sin; 2625 offers another woman in a half-covered rag as the same lesson.
teaches: What the epic first set before the eye as Vijayai's own fall is later handed on as a spoken example, so the story and the sermon the story ends in draw on one fund of images.

note: In 908 she resolved that only union with Civakan could break her nirai; here her women hear the song and praise the youth wrought into her mind.
teaches: The single exception she allowed in her seclusion is the one man already inside it, so the guard she set against all men admits the very one it was kept for, unrecognised.

note: 1791 has the prince outshine the other kings; 1792 has the young women's eyes leave the kings for him.
teaches: The brightness the poet claims for the prince is proved by where the onlookers look, not by the poet's word alone.

note: In 1139 Acuvakandan shatters a diamond pillar with a blow; in 1151 the arriving kings see it lying burned and tremble.
teaches: The broken pillar is left standing as the proof of rage that the summoned kings read before he speaks.

note: 1122 has him gaze unblinking so as not to lose her; Kural 1129 has her not blink lest he be hidden.
teaches: The refusal to blink is common to both lovers, but the epic's reason is that she seems to recede each time he blinks, and the Kural's is that he lives in her eye.

gains.a: The epic verse gets proof that not blinking is a common sign of love, said by the woman in the Kural and by the man here.
gains.b: The couplet gets the groom's reverse case, where the fear is that she herself becomes a stranger at each blink.

note: 1386 has the hero push through slanting spears for honour; Kural 774 has the soldier laugh as he pulls a spear from his own body.
teaches: Both link honour to the warrior's joy in danger, but the epic gives the motive as honour itself and the couplet as the pleasure of the wound.

gains.a: gains the wound-joy of the couplet, which its hero does not show: he is only seen advancing
gains.b: gains a stated motive, honour, which the couplet leaves unnamed

note: The couplet calls the tears of those who cannot bear their suffering a weapon that wears away wealth; here a widow's tears and words take the king's life.
teaches: The couplet's slow wearing-away of a bad king's wealth by the people's tears becomes, in the epic, the instant death of the king at one wronged woman's tears and words.

note: In both a searching woman asks brahmins on the waste road (அந்தணீர், அந்தணிர்) and they answer that they saw the girl (கண்டனம், கண்டனெம்); Kalittokai adds the sandal, pearl and lute argument and says the way never leaves aram.
teaches: The scene that Ainkurunuru leaves as a bare eyewitness report of the lover's tenderness was later expanded by Kalittokai into an argument that a daughter belongs to the man she follows, so the brahmins' reply grew from testimony into doctrine.

note: In 1092 the king's men bind Civakan's shoulders with their belts (கச்சின் வீக்கலின்); the patikam (16) tells how the god removed the flower-belt (பூங் கச்சு) that bound his shoulders.
teaches: The belt that binds the hero here is the very thing the patikam has the grateful god remove, so the eclipse simile's promise of a passing darkness is already answered at the epic's opening.

note: Naladiyar 3 has kings who rode under the umbrella fall when their deeds give out; 797 shows the kings' white umbrellas overturned by Civakan's arrows.
teaches: The quatrain names only spent deeds as the cause of a king's fall, while the epic shows the immediate cause, an archer and the kings' own desire, and in 799 sorts the fallen by their minds, so karma and the battle are both given as cause.

gains.a: a frame in which the overturned umbrellas are a lesson in impermanence and not only a victory
gains.b: a scene that names the human cause beside the karmic one, which the quatrain's 'other deeds' leaves blank

note: Austerity and yoga bring the brothers perfection and the rest heaven, as Tirumular says austerity and virtue together are a boat over the sea of deeds.
teaches: The story shows austerity giving two different ends for two sets of people, which the single boat in Tirumular's line does not.

gains.a: the story's two ends are seen as a way to read the one boat of the verse
gains.b: the verse's boat gains a case where the same austerity reaches two shores

note: Both use the rain bubble (மாரி மொக்குளின், படுமழை மொக்குளின்): the Naladiyar for the body that keeps forming and bursting, the epic for the moment the released teacher's form ends.
teaches: Holding the two together shows the bubble used for opposite ends: in the quatrain its bursting is why the wise resolve to end their wandering, and in the epic the bursting is that resolve completed, the last end of a body that will not form again.

gains.a: the epic's simile gains the sense of repeated birth the quatrain gives the bubble, so Accanandi's vanishing reads as the end of the round, not just a death
gains.b: the quatrain's resolve to end the wandering gains a narrated case of someone who did it, and what its end looks like

note: Kural 3 gives the Lord as the one who walked on the flower, at whose feet one arrives; Soolamani 214 gives the girl's hymn to the primal Lord who gave the scripture, who stood on the flower, at whose holy feet she bows.
teaches: The hymn uses a flower-footed epithet close to the couplet's and gives it to the Jain Lord with titles that name him, which the couplet does not.

gains.a: a familiar Tamil epithet for the flower-footed Lord is borrowed as a form of worship, so the girl's praise sits in a shared idiom
gains.b: the couplet's disputed 'one who walked on the flower' appears in a later Jain work applied to the Arhat, one data point on how the epithet was read

note: 2940 shows the body's colour, breasts and eyes fading with age as the women watch; Siddhar 23 asks when the speaker will see the bones within as white bones and see himself lowered like a cast-off corpse.
teaches: The epic shows the body's fading from the lover's side, the Siddhar from the renouncer's, so one is a loss and the other is a practice.

gains.a: the verse's fading colour gains the Siddhar's practice of looking through the flesh to the bones
gains.b: the Siddhar's look at the bones gains a view of the same body as it loses its beauty to a lover

note: Verse 180 says the shrine and its god end births; Kural 10 says only those who reach the Lord's feet swim the sea of births.
teaches: The epic locates the ending of births in the shrine and its god, where the Kural puts it in the devotee's reaching.

gains.a: A statement of what the god gives, not only what the devotee reaches.
gains.b: A place in which the reaching happens, the shrine.

note: 2962 asks whether a husband may give up the wife he took, while Naladiyar 56 says a husband cannot easily put away a wife even if she lacks good qualities.
teaches: The wife's plea is that the bond cannot be cast off, which the Naladiyar says too but only to praise those who avoid marriage.

gains.a: the wife's plea that a husband is bound gains the support of a rule from the moral literature that she does not cite
gains.b: the Naladiyar's argument that marriage binds hard gains a case where the bond is felt by those left, not by the husband

note: Both are reports of having seen the enemy's ruined land (கண்டனென் in Purananuru 23, கண்டுவந் திசினே in Patitruppattu 15), and both mark the ruin by white velai flowers growing over it (வேளை வெண்பூ; வெண்பூ வேளை).
teaches: The shared white velai shows it was a stock sign of a razed settlement in both Pandya and Chera praise, and Patitruppattu 15 extends the form: where Purananuru 23 ends on the waste, the Chera poet adds a second sight, the king's own guarded land, so the ruin becomes one half of a judgment on rule.

note: Vijayai says that no return can match those who ended her distress and gives them every delight; the Kural says that help given when none was given before cannot be paid back even by earth and sky.
teaches: The Kural states that such help is beyond repayment, and the epic shows what a queen does about it: she gives all she has and still says the debt remains.

gains.a: the verse's claim that there is no requital is shown as an ideal measure, with the Kural giving the rule that explains why gratitude must outrun the gift
gains.b: the Kural's rule for gifts in need is tested against a person with a whole kingdom's power to repay, who still declares it not enough

note: 1939 gives hell as the ripening of the sufferers' own deeds with no one allotting it; Tirumanthiram 2544 says the Lord set hell and heaven for souls by grace.
teaches: The same pain is explained once by deeds ripening and once by a lord's grace, which marks where the Jain and Saiva accounts of hell part.

gains.a: The sage's verdict gains a rival answer to who stands behind the ripening, which its last line leaves unnamed.
gains.b: The Tirumanthiram verse gains a picture of what hell contains and a cause in the sufferer's own deed, neither of which it gives.

note: The Purananuru poem says warriors who stand under arrows care nothing for fields because, dying, they wed flawless women in the high world; Ariccandan offers the same heavenly women (கடியரமகளிர்) and adds the poets' praise and the hero-stone.
teaches: The pairing shows the Sangam promise of heavenly brides surviving into the Jain epic as a commander's rallying formula, now stacked with fame and stone into a three-world reward, while the following verse turns its hearers into food for the hero's arrows.

gains.a: the speech is placed in a long tradition of the warrior's reward, which explains why the beaten men return to the fight
gains.b: the poem's confident claim is set in a story where those who believe it fight for the losing, unjust side

note: 2121 has the sky filled with the gods' regalia, flowers, sandal and powder; Cintamani 3090 has the gods rain flowers, coloured sandal and incense that fill the quarters.
teaches: The same festival of gods is set at the end of the war in the Soolamani and at the teaching in the Cintamani, so it honours victory in one and instruction in the other.

note: 1576 has the jester's mouth water at the fruit and him call the king to eat; 1618-1620 turn that greed into songs on the fruits of the grove.
teaches: The jester's appetite from the arrival in the grove is now his act for the couple, so his greed is what pays for his pardon.

note: 2847 names what the freed soul has (endless knowledge, seeing, power and joy); Kural 362 says to want, want not to be born.
teaches: The Kural describes release as an absence of birth and desire, and the Cintamani's sage describes it as a fullness, so one calls release emptying and the other filling.

gains.a: the verse's release is set beside the Kural's, which describes it only as not being born again
gains.b: the Kural's release by not wanting gets an account of what the one released then has

note: In 223 Vijayai dreamed of a tree falling and a shoot growing with a crown for eight pearl garlands; in 2607 she tells the eight queens they came as that eight-garland crown in her dream and begs them never to part.
teaches: The dream of the shoot and the crown is shown fulfilled in the eight wives, and the reader sees that the dream's fruit is the Cintamani's marriage-chain, now held together by the mother who dreamed it.

note: The verse takes up the couplet's hands joined in worship and weeping tears that hide a weapon, adds hair and jewel caskets, and ends with those who trusted being dead.
teaches: The couplet names where a weapon hides; the epic turns it into a bodyguard's order and adds the outcome, showing the rule read as a practical protocol against poisoning.

gains.a: the brother's warning gains a known authority, so it reads as received wisdom rather than a young man's fear
gains.b: the couplet gains a situation and a consequence, a prince among strangers and the death of those who trusted

note: 291 defines truthfulness as speech without harm; 200 demands use.
teaches: Harmless idle talk passes the one test and fails the other, so the two chapters set different standards for speech.

note: Kural 49 calls the householder's life itself what is named virtue; in Cintamani 382 the teacher, once Civakan has taken the Jain refuge, teaches him the householder's dharma alongside the errors of false paths.
teaches: The Jain teacher does not set renunciation against the household here but gives the new convert the householder's dharma as his first instruction, so the epic holds the Kural's household virtue as a stage inside the path to release rather than its rival.

gains.a: the content of the teacher's instruction, left unstated, is placed against the Kural's account of what household virtue is
gains.b: the couplet's praise of household life is seen kept, but subordinated, by a tradition whose hero will renounce at the end

note: The Kural likens the wise man's wealth to water filling the village tank; the Cintamani likens the river's flood to the hand of a generous man carrying wealth to those who have nothing.
teaches: The tradition's image ran both ways, wealth explained by water and water by giving, and the epic adds movement and direction toward the needy, where the Kural's tank waits to be drawn from.

gains.a: a moral precedent that makes the river's simile a statement about how wealth should behave
gains.b: an active counterpart to its still tank: wealth that goes out town by town to the needy instead of waiting to be drawn

note: 3036 says the mantra heard at the hour of death brings birth among the gods; 945 shows Civakan whispering it to a dying dog.
teaches: The general rule of 3036 and the dog's rebirth in 945 together show the mantra's promise kept, since the dog returns as Sutanjanan who here praises the one who gave it.

note: 1462 shows the king falling from the elephant like a cloud struck by fire; 1464 turns the same fall into a moral on impermanence.
teaches: The poet first shows the fall and then lets onlookers draw the lesson, so the doctrine comes from the scene and not before it.

note: The kural's evil that follows the doer like a shadow that never leaves is shown in the snake who becomes a crocodile and follows the fish into the river.
teaches: The pursuit shows that the shadow of deed can pass through the animal births, which the couplet's one life does not show.

gains.a: the mother's following through snake and crocodile is seen as deed's shadow, not mere hatred
gains.b: the couplet's shadow gains a path across several births and species

note: Nabulan will not strike an unarmed youth or even his elephant; two verses later the narrator states the code of not striking beasts, the wounded or the young.
teaches: The scene acts out first and the rule is stated after, so the code of 2261 reads as a summary of how this whole company fights, not as one man's quirk.

note: The astrologer names Rajamapuram as the place of the princess's destined husband; the patikam (11) already tells that the Vidyadhara king's daughter was defeated at the vina.
teaches: The prophecy that sends the princess to earth is the start of the contest the patikam announced, so her defeat at the vina is the means by which her horoscope comes true.

note: The couplet says pains rest on those who caused pains; here the crocodile's pain comes but at the hands of men who themselves do harm.
teaches: The epic shows deed's return working through the very cruelty of new doers, so the rule is true but puts another debt on those who carry it out.

gains.a: the crocodile's torn body gains the rule that explains why it suffers
gains.b: the couplet's rule gains the complication that the one who punishes is himself adding to his own account

note: In 318 Vijayai suckles the newborn, puts her husband's ring on him and leaves him; here the grown son falls at her feet.
teaches: The parting at birth and the reunion are linked by the son's self-naming as her servant, so the child she gave up returns as a worshipper of the renouncer she has become.

claims.gist: the earth has no real tie to any king and clings only to him who clings
a warrior slain in battle goes to heaven
the ascetic's state is beyond the understanding of the people who bow
liberation is won by a campaign against the army of karma
one who harms living beings for his food is cast down by karma into a burning hell
kin who bind one to the world are enemies rather than kin
merit joins with enjoyment as its fruit, and cruel deeds have a fearful fruit
a wife who kills her husband for a base lover is the greatest sinner among women
wealth bewilders a man so that he does not look for release
a sacrifice made with an image of a living creature can please the goddess and ward off the dream's evil
delight in a sinner brings bodily ruin as its fruit
it is wise and good to give the girl to the suitor whom all fear
in suffering a being has no protector in the sea, forest or hills
a king must know the land he governs as a charioteer knows the ground
passion for women leads to punishment and death in a sea of sorrow
the one who cut the throng of karma is worthy of the gods' praise
those who sleep in women's arms come to suffering and death
even the heavenly bodies won by austerity are lost in their countless number
the standing of the learned grows through the grace of kings who guard the law of command and treatise
envoys must not be harmed, and their offence is to be borne, by ancient custom

note: The Kural condemns those who clung to dice (கவறு) and the gaming hall (கழகம); the epic makes the woman's body a board, dice and gaming hall for love.
teaches: Borrowing the Kural's own words for ruinous gambling, the epic frames love as a game one should give up for penance when it cannot be won, so the condemned dice become a figure for the pleasure renunciation replaces.

gains.a: the conceit's choice of dice gains the Kural's moral weight against gaming, which prepares its turn to restraint
gains.b: the Kural's dice and hall are shown entering a love conceit, a use the couplet does not foresee

note: The sulk of 2678 is answered by the consoling words and embrace of 2679.
teaches: The quarrel turns on one conceit: her sulk makes the moon a paled rival, and his answer keeps the moon and makes it pale before her face.

note: The father leaves because youth and kin do not last; the son, once king, lives for wealth and pleasure.
teaches: The father's lesson on impermanence does not pass to the son, so the story shows wisdom as personal and not inherited.

note: Pattinathar asks what forest life, eating wind, rags and the bowl avail without inner love, and says the Lord's true lovers reach release even living at home beside their women; Civakan says sin born of desire for women cannot be removed by union with women.
teaches: The two agree that going to the forest is nothing in itself, but they part on the household: the Saiva poet lets love free one beside one's wife, while the Jain hero makes leaving the wife a condition, so the shared attack on outward renunciation hides opposite views of the married life.

gains.a: a rival conclusion from the same premise, which shows that its demand to leave women is a doctrine of its own and not implied by its critique
gains.b: the strongest objection to its claim, that sin born of desire cannot be cleansed while desire continues

note: Kural 481 says the crow beats the owl by day and that kings need the right time; 1927 tells of one crow that went among the owls in their own place and killed a thousand crore.
teaches: The couplet's even match, decided by the hour, becomes in the epic one against countless decided by time, place and cunning together, so judgment is shown to multiply strength and not merely to time it.

gains.a: the mother's fable gains the authority of a known royal maxim, so it reads as counsel from the books of kings rather than a nursery tale
gains.b: the couplet's image gains a story in which the crow's advantage is pressed home by stratagem in the enemy's own ground, beyond what daylight alone gives

note: Pisirandhaiyar and many others sit fasting with the Chola; Buddhisenan would follow Civakan in death, but only after vengeance and without knowing he is dead.
teaches: Against the Purananuru's companions who die beside a living king by his own choice, the epic's vow to follow a lord in death rests on an unverified death and a killing first, and the next verse checks it.

gains.a: Buddhisenan's vow gains its model, the companion who dies with his lord, which shows what kind of loyalty he is claiming
gains.b: the Purananuru poem's sitting-with gains a contrast in which the same loyalty is armed, hasty and turned outward

note: 1862 names the austere sage's feet as the only refuge from Death; Tirumanthiram 2 praises Siva who kicked Death and became king of the south.
teaches: The two refuges differ in kind: a teacher's feet to be reached by one's own austerity, against a god who defeated Death himself.

gains.a: The sage's feet gain a rival refuge in a god who has already defeated Death.
gains.b: The invocation gains a Jain-framed answer that makes the sage, not Siva, the shelter.

note: 176 draws spring as a copy of women; 451 has the women confuse the peacock with their gait.
teaches: One image runs both ways: spring is drawn from women's bodies in 176, and in 451 women outdo nature, so the poet changes which side is the model.

note: 1547 announces the coronation at dawn; 1550 carries it out.
teaches: The announcement and the crowning make a promise and its keeping, so the festival is a prelude to the crowning, not merely its decoration.

note: 1473 opens the laments with praise of the king's rule; 1481 closes with a question about his abandoned land and servants.
teaches: The women's laments move from praise of the king to a complaint that he left his duty, so grief ends in a charge against him.

note: The Ajivika holds the elemental atoms to be without beginning; Sivavakkiyar says the elements and senses, and even the soul, are not beginningless, and only the truth mingled with them is.
teaches: The question of what is beginningless divides the two: for the Ajivika matter itself is eternal, for the Siddhar matter and soul are both made, and only the one truth is without beginning.

note: 1573 has the jester win debate by beating reciters; Tirumanthiram 51 says the wise gave up disputation and recited the Veda to gain release.
teaches: The jester practises debate for a gift and the verse in the Tirumanthiram says the wise leave debate for recitation, so the farce is set against that view.

gains.a: The jester's boast gains a standard against which debating for a gift looks like a caricature of the learned.
gains.b: The Tirumanthiram's rejection of disputation gains a figure for whom argument has become a way to get food.

note: 2883 has the father tell the youth who wants to renounce to rule and pass on the kingdom first; Kural 342 says to renounce while there is time.
teaches: The Kural leaves open what counts as time, and the father fixes it as the time after the duties of a king are done.

gains.a: the father's delay gains the Kural's urgency, which makes his 'first rule' a hard answer and not a mild one
gains.b: the Kural's 'while there is time' gains a worked limit, the discharge of a kingdom's duties, that its bare phrase does not give

note: The turtle in the heated pot plays on unaware of its end, as the king and city sit in wealth without seeing release.
teaches: Both place the danger in comfort that blinds, but the Naladiyar names death as the one waiting, while the epic leaves the danger as the loss of the road to release.

gains.a: the king's ease is shown as a dangerous state like the turtle's warm water, not a harmless background
gains.b: the turtle's image is given a named case, a whole city and king, and a consequence in a scene that follows

note: Both define tavam.
teaches: The Kural defines austerity as enduring pain and harming none, with no rite named, while the epic's lay teacher defines it as fasting on fixed moon days: the pair shows the same word as an ethic and as a calendar.

gains.a: the epic's fasts gain the Kural's ethical core, the bearing of hardship, which gives them their point
gains.b: the couplet gains a concrete practice by which a householder can take up its definition

note: Tirumanthiram 114 has Nandi cut away the tarnish and open the eye of grace so that a light shows that nothing can darken; 2745 asks a Jain ascetic's grace to clear the darkness of karma.
teaches: Both ask a teacher's grace to clear a stain, but Nandi gives it as a lord who acts on the soul, while the Jain sage is only asked and is a teacher, not a god.

gains.a: the verse's plea, which does not say how the darkness goes, is given the Saiva picture of a god who cuts the tarnish, against which the sage's role looks much smaller
gains.b: the verse's image of Nandi's gift is set against a request made of a man who is no god, so grace is shown there as something that a teacher can only point toward

note: 3064 has Civakan cut the eight karmas by the strength of his own mind; Tirumanthiram 120 has deeds made into seeds that have touched fire and will not sprout, by the one who parts milk from water, the Lord or guru.
teaches: The seeds will not sprout in both, but one makes the ascetic himself the burner and the other leaves the burner a god or teacher.

gains.a: the verse's self-won end of karma is set against a Saiva reading in which the burning is done for the soul
gains.b: the Tirumanthiram's burnt seeds meet a Jain account in which no one else burns them

note: Both use ஒறுத்தல், punish. 314 says to punish wrongdoers by shaming them with kindness; 550 says that the king punishing the worst of them with death is simply weeding a crop.
teaches: The word keeps its form while the ethics of person and state divide.

note: 1424 brings the messengers' report; 1425 has the king resolve to loose the spell.
teaches: The report is the whole cause of the spell, so the epic ties the world's destruction to one man's grief.

note: A simile for the maids' eyes mentions Civakan's resolve to cut Kattiyangaran down; much later a voice from the sky proclaims that Civakan will swallow Kattiyangaran's life.
teaches: The revenge is never dropped even in a scene of scents and maids: the poet plants it as an aside here, so the heavenly proclamation reads as the public fulfilment of a purpose already settled in private.

note: Neelakesi 859 gives the materialist's own words, that the world is only the elements and belief in a soul only makes fruitless quarrels; verse 72 gives the denial in one summary and calls it ignorance.
teaches: The same opponent appears as a speaker in one poem and as a target in the other, so the epic's verdict can be set beside the debating poem's long hearing.

note: 2009 defines compassion as melting for another's life and counts a moist heart where rescue fails; Kural 315 calls understanding useless without guarding another's pain as one's own.
teaches: The pairing shows compassion as both the test of understanding and a state that stays even when help fails.

gains.a: Compassion gains a test, since understanding is judged worthless without it.
gains.b: The couplet gains an allowance for failure: the moist heart still counts where the pain cannot be removed.

note: Anangamalai pleads that she not be left outside the shade of Civakan's white umbrella, which she calls the shade of dharma; Purananuru 35 tells Killivalavan that his tall umbrella is not for shade but to shelter suffering subjects who may come to him for justice.
teaches: The Sangam poem tells a king to keep his umbrella for the sufferer, and the epic shows a sufferer actually using it, which puts the claim to the test of whether a king's sheltering reaches a woman's private petition.

gains.a: an older standard of the umbrella as the king's duty to the suffering, which her petition invokes but the epic does not itself state
gains.b: a petitioner who stands in the position it only imagines, which shows what it asks of a king in practice

note: The couplet calls virtue the companion that does not perish when one perishes; Visakai calls great virtue the true companion (விழுத் துணை) in place of youth, body, wealth and sons.
teaches: Visakai uses the couplet's idea of virtue as companion to replace the wife-companion the brahmin demanded, so a teaching about virtue outlasting death becomes an answer to the claim that a man needs marriage for heaven.

note: Kural 918 says the embrace of deceiving women is an அணங்கு to those without discerning sense; in 1183 the god warns of ghoul-women who come as pining lovers and, embracing, wring out a man's life.
teaches: The epic turns the couplet's metaphor into a literal creature of its geography: the deceiving lover really is a life-drinking demon, and what saves the hero is the god's forewarning, standing in for the 'discerning sense' the couplet demands.

gains.a: the ghoul episode is seen to carry the Kural's ethics of the courtesan rather than being a mere marvel of the road
gains.b: the couplet's அணங்கு, which might be read as hyperbole, gets a narrative that spells out what the word threatens: the embrace that kills

note: 2109 posts five great captains of the vow-army against incoming karma; Kural 343 says the domain of the five must be crushed and all desire let go.
teaches: The epic's five are vows that hold karma back, not the five senses of the couplet, so the same number is taken from two different disciplines.

gains.a: The five vows gain the older frame of crushing the five senses, which shows what they guard against.
gains.b: The couplet gains a Jain version in which the defence is a set of vows and an army, not a single act of crushing.

note: 1743 calls the teachers 'rich in unfailing learning' (பொய்யாக் கல்விச் செல்வர்); Kural 400 says learning is the one wealth that does not perish.
teaches: The epic uses the language of wealth for learning, which Kural 400 claims for it alone, but gives it to men who serve a king whose other wealth is shown at length.

gains.a: The teachers gain the Kural's ground for the title 'rich', that their wealth is the one that does not fail.
gains.b: The couplet gains a court where learning and the other wealth stand together, a test of whether learning is the only wealth.

note: The king's disenchantment with the court and the queen leads him to leave the throne; the Siddhar lists town, kin, women, glory and wealth as things that do not last.
teaches: The Siddhar states what does not last; the king shows the grief and betrayal through which a man comes to accept it.

gains.a: The king's resolve gets a doctrine of impermanence that makes it more than hurt pride.
gains.b: The Siddhar's list gets a worked case in which the loss of a wife and rank is lived, not recited.

note: 3044 has King Senikan call for a feast to the Jina's feet with kings gathered; Purananuru 134 has a patron who does not give to buy merit for the next birth.
teaches: The king's feast here is made an act of worship whose fruit the next lines of the work will tell, and so the poem's patron who gives without bargaining is set against it.

gains.a: the king's feast to the Jina gets a foil in a patron who refuses to give for reward
gains.b: the poem's refusal of trade-giving meets a king whose gift is plainly an act of worship

note: The patikam opens with Saccandan, king of the unbending sceptre; Civakan's first order from the throne is to clear his realm of afflictions and have the drum announce it.
teaches: The son's first act as king is the sceptre's work that his father's reign set at the start, so the epic sets his crowning as the repair of the wrong the story began with.

note: Kattiyankaran tells cowardly kings to leave their crowns and go to the hermits' forest; the patikam says Civakan renounced at the height of his rule.
teaches: In the villain's mouth giving up the crown for the forest is the punishment of a beaten king, while the epic's own ending makes it the free act of a victorious one, so the book stages the courtly contempt for renunciation it will overturn.

note: The earlier king calls a king the shield of all living beings; this king's order falls on merchants and an animal.
teaches: One king's rule that a ruler guards every life is set against his successor's order that brings pain on innocent persons and a beast.

note: Both have the man, on seeing the girl, take her for an அணங்கு (Kural: அணங்குகொல்; Ainkurunuru: ஆர் அணங்கினளே).
teaches: Valluvar's man hesitates between goddess, peahen and woman, while the Sangam man has settled the question and pins it on her youth (இளையள் ஆயினும்), so the couplet's doubt is a refinement of an older certainty that a hill girl can be a striking power.

note: Kural 1085 asks whether the young woman's look is Death, an eye or a doe; verse 458 says the women's long dark eyes are skilled at killing.
teaches: The eye as Death is a shared trope of the lover's tradition, which the epic makes the plea of many men at once.

gains.a: The Kural's own line that the look is Death, which sets this plea in a known convention.
gains.b: A crowd of men instead of one man, the Kural's one lover made general.

note: Puram 62 ends with the gods of the unfading flowers receiving many guests from a field where two kings died; 291 says the dead king became a guest of the gods, adding the Jina's feet and the mantra-sandal.
teaches: The Jain epic keeps the Sangam honour of the fallen king as heaven's guest but makes devotion to the Jina part of his passage, so the warrior's heaven is re-founded on religion.

gains.a: the epic's phrase is shown to be the old battlefield honour, which explains why a negligent king's end can still be glorious
gains.b: the Puram formula, which grounds heaven in fighting alone, is shown being given a religious condition by a later school

note: Kural 1327 says the one who yields in a lovers' quarrel wins; Civakan yields first, but the quarrel ends when the parrot threatens to hang itself.
teaches: Yielding does not by itself end the sulk in the epic; it takes the comic shock from a third party to break it, which limits the couplet's rule that the loser wins.

gains.a: Civakan's earlier abasement is shown to be only half of what wins her, as the Kural's rule would suggest
gains.b: a case where a rule about the two lovers alone needs an outside agent, here the pet

note: 3121 sends the women who gave up desire to heaven as Indras; Kural 346 says one who cuts off 'I' and 'mine' enters a world higher than the gods'.
teaches: The verse ends in the gods' world and the Kural says release lies above it, so the same renunciation is given two different ends.

gains.a: the verse's heaven is shown as a stop below where the Kural puts the one who has left 'I' and 'mine'
gains.b: the Kural's world above the gods gets a case of renouncers who stop at the gods' world

note: The dog appears as a god in 948; the patikam's next verse tells how a god came down the sky like lightning and carried Civakan out of the king's prison.
teaches: Read together, the hero's kindness at the festival is the cause of his rescue later: the creature he saved by a mantra returns as the god who saves him, so the plot itself runs on karma's return.

note: 1366 shows the hero mounted and frightening all; 1381 shows the enemy kings turning back in fear.
teaches: The terror one rider causes at the start is what finally sends the whole Vidyadhara line home.

note: The life she says in 1509 is leaving her body is held back in 1530.
teaches: The two verses frame the lament between a life about to go and a life restrained, and show that what turns it is not his return but her fear of harm to him.

note: Kural 110 says there is no escape for one who kills a good done to him; Dharmadattan warns that Fortune will leave the man who seizes the king who made him, and that loyalty secures his line.
teaches: The Kural's 'no escape' for ingratitude is turned into a political forecast, the loss of fortune and lineage, and offered to a would-be usurper as prudence rather than only as virtue.

gains.a: the counsel is grounded in the Kural's ranking of ingratitude as the sin without remedy
gains.b: the couplet's abstract doom is given a concrete form, a usurper whose line will be uprooted

note: 2875 sets caged birds crying for their kin and warns the captors that they will be parted from theirs; Naladiyar 122 says those who cage partridges and quails will go as slaves to strangers in irons.
teaches: Together they show the same crime repaid in two forms, loss of kin and loss of freedom, which neither names alone.

gains.a: the verse's warning of parting from kin gains a second, bodily form of repayment, irons and service under strangers
gains.b: the quatrain's repayment for caging gains the grief of the caged, the birds' separation from their flock, that its sentence mirrors

note: The Kural's bewildered first sight is here mutual and immediate.
teaches: The epic carries the Kural's bewilderment through to union within a single verse, with no doubt, no gossip and no delay, so the bewilderment is a path to union and not a state of suffering.

gains.a: The verse shows both lovers bewildered, and it leaves out the mourning and doubt that the Kural's chapter dwells on.
gains.b: The couplet's lone man, unsure whether she is goddess, peahen or woman, gets a case in which the sight is answered and the doubt never has time to arise.

claims.gist: killing sinks the doer in hell's long pain
for a king, to renounce is the excellent thing
Death gathers and takes the life of all who have no refuge
sila is to give up what the great condemn, including honey with worms and flesh
those who destroy inner discernment through such food are beasts
right faith and good vows lead to merit and a place among the gods
such mastery in teaching arms belongs only to one born a king or a twice-born
wives and sons are the fruit of earlier good deeds and are lost when evil deeds ripen
a king who harms no life and spreads mercy to all will guard the world and live long
the holy dharma ends the confinement of birth
a husband who took a wife's love ought not to forsake her
those who win release from rebirth are the best in the world and come by austerity
no enemy is small enough to be ignored; deceit must be guarded against
to withdraw from a fight once begun brings blame
a house without children is empty, like a grove without flowers
brave men also feel fear, but they cast it off at once
suffering that is the ripening of one's deeds is not to be wept over
meditating on the feet of the Arhat beneath the asoka tree dispels fear
greed for wealth through lies, deceit and gambling must be abandoned
restraint and desire cannot dwell together: where one is whole, not a trace of the other remains
hell mocks desire with water that turns to pus
a daughter is a jewel beyond every treasure of earth and heaven
a being descends from heaven and takes birth on earth as the purana foretold
a king who pays written tribute lives like a tenant, and that is no royal life
A king owes the helpless, the sick and the abandoned a share of the treasury

note: The couplet makes the parted woman's pallor spread the moment the man goes; the friends treat its absence as proof of deceit.
teaches: The epic turns the Kural's sign of parting into a test applied by men to a wife, and shows the test failing, since a wife who knows her husband is safe does not pale.

gains.a: the epic verse gains the rule behind the friends' suspicion, that pallor follows the lover's going at once
gains.b: the couplet gains a case where its sign is read from outside as evidence and its absence is misjudged

note: Kural 972 says birth is alike for all and distinction comes from work; verse 531 says Vidyadharas are men, distinguished only by their lore.
teaches: The couplet is turned from a general saying into the reason a marriage across a supposed divide may go ahead.

gains.a: A principle that makes sameness of birth the ground, so that the Vidyadharas' lore becomes a difference of work and not of kind.
gains.b: A use of the principle to open a marriage across a boundary of rank, a case the couplet does not take up.

note: The patikam lists Civakan's winning of his maternal uncle's daughter beside the spreading of his just sceptre; 2133 shows the first look between them in the uncle's palace.
teaches: What the patikam pairs as a dynastic gain alongside the sceptre begins here as a private exchange of looks before any council has met, so the marriage is grounded in love before it serves the war.

note: The Kural's wife takes offence even at his adoring gaze, asking whom he is thinking of; Gandharvadattai's sulk blazes at a portrait of another woman painted by her husband.
teaches: The Kural's comedy of jealousy depends on the husband's innocence, and the epic removes it: here the suspected other woman is real and painted by his own hand, so the sulk is no longer love's game but a just grievance.

gains.a: Gandharvadattai's flare is placed in a known type, the wife of the pulavi nunukkam who reads every look as a rival
gains.b: the couplet's baseless suspicion is set against a case where suspicion is right, showing how much its charm rests on there being no rival

note: The city given by Vanaraja's sacrifice-gift of his daughter in 99 is repaid in 100 by the prince winning back a city for Vanaraja.
teaches: The marriage in 99 is returned by a kingdom in 100, so the gift of a wife is shown as an obligation the husband repays in arms.

note: Tirumular lists removing poison among the powers that yoga brings; Civakan removes the venom by a spell he learned, after seven thousand Brahmins with mantras have failed.
teaches: Where the Tirumanthiram makes curing poison a sign of the yogi's attainment, the Cintamani gives it to a young layman as a learned art and lets the ritual mantra-masters fail, so the same power is moved from spiritual rank to skill and from priest to hero.

gains.a: Civakan's cure gains its weight as a power the Saiva tradition reserves for adepts, which makes its ease in a householder's hands notable
gains.b: the siddhi list gains a contrasting account in which poison-cure needs no yoga, only taught knowledge, which sharpens what Tirumular claims for his discipline

note: 2466 reports the fire rising right as an omen of fortune; Tirumanthiram 551 says the way of sacrifice has no way through while the eight-limbed yoga path leads to samadhi.
teaches: The epic reads the fire as a sign of worldly fortune, while Tirumular reads the same fire path as a dead end for release, so the same rite is a good for the household and no good for release.

gains.a: The omen of fortune gains a view that the fire gives no release.
gains.b: Tirumular's dismissal gains a scene in which the fire's use is worldly luck and not a claim to release.

note: Nandattan found Gunamalai wasting and reproaching him; Gandharvadattai's letter now reports her worse, unable to tell sun from moon.
teaches: Set beside the brother's account, the letter shows Gunamalai's grief growing in the interval and makes the co-wife, not the brother, the one who carries it to Civakan.

note: Kural 390 names giving, kindness, a straight sceptre and care of the people as the four that make a king a light; the proclamation of 2375 turns them into acts: remission of dues and the end of hunger, disease and enmity.
teaches: The couplet's four virtues become a single proclamation with named relief, which shows what giving and care of the people cost a treasury and who is to benefit.

gains.a: The proclamation gains a standard by which its remission and the ending of hunger are measured as the work of a king.
gains.b: The couplet gains concrete acts, a remitted tax, for virtues it only names.

note: 1576 has the jester at the fallen fruit with his mouth watering; 1569 has him holding a belly full of modakas.
teaches: The same belly-led jester returns, now drooling instead of groaning, so greed is drawn as his trait and not one joke.

note: The wife's hell is reckoned at ten and seven oceans, the father's heaven at ten.
teaches: Counting both fates in oceans of years shows one standard measuring the reward and the punishment, with the wife's term the longer.

note: The couplet calls the bond with the girl that of body and life; the epic draws an inference from it during separation.
teaches: The epic turns the couplet's simile into a test a separated lover can run, that one life cannot end while the other goes on, and so shows the image used as reassurance rather than praise.

gains.a: the epic verse gains the couplet's settled formula, so the hero's inference rests on a known saying about lovers
gains.b: the couplet gains a situation of separation and a consequence drawn from its image, which it never states

note: 278 has the ascetic hold neither 'I' nor 'mine' nor even benefit; Kural 346 says cutting off 'I' and 'mine' reaches a world above the gods.
teaches: The epic adds a third term, benefit, to the Kural's pair, so letting go includes even what one might claim as one's own good.

gains.a: 278 gains the Kural's statement that this giving up has a result beyond the gods' world.
gains.b: Kural 346 gains a figure who has done it, a king turned ascetic.

note: Soolamani 109 has the court confirm that Tivittan will guard the whole world under one umbrella; here Prajapati, holding the bride, says that his earlier austerity is the reason and that the wheel is certain.
teaches: The prophecy gets a cause in Tivittan's earlier austerity, which the court's earlier confirmation lacked.

note: Buddhisenan would die after killing the king; Nandattan resolves to die alone if he cannot find his lord.
teaches: The same either-find-him-or-die resolve is a public war vow in the companions' mouths and a private one in the brother's, and it is the private one, aimed at no enemy, that brings him to the woman who can reunite them.

note: The king asks which kind of war to fight; the couplet says weigh the work, one's own strength, the foe's and the allies' before acting.
teaches: The Kural states the weighing as a rule; the epic shows a council doing it by splitting war into human, divine and mixed kinds.

gains.a: The council's question gains a stated rule behind its caution: the choice of war is a weighing and not a taste.
gains.b: The couplet gains a concrete case where the foe's strength includes divine arts, which its list of four strengths does not foresee.

note: 2883 tells the youth to rule first and give the kingdom to a son before renouncing; Naladiyar 11 says the wise renounced in childhood, knowing grey hair will come.
teaches: One praises renouncing at the earliest, the other puts duty before the vow, so they mark two views of when the right time begins.

gains.a: the father's order of duties gains the opposing view that foresight, not age, marks the wise and that waiting is the fool's course
gains.b: the quatrain's praise of early renunciation gains a king's reason for delay, the kingdom that must be handed on

note: Pattinattar lists the body as a feast thrown to the pyre's fire (ஈமக் கனல்) and a leaf scorched in the fire of desire (காமக் கனல்); Civakan's body, called a pyre (ஈமம்), burns in desire's fever (காமக் கடுநோய்க் கனல்).
teaches: The same pairing of pyre and desire's fire is a reason to renounce the body in Pattinattar and a lover's complaint in the epic, so the image does not carry its lesson with it: the hero who will one day renounce here uses it only to say how much he burns.

gains.a: the epic's hyperbole is shown to borrow the renouncer's figure, which the Cintamani will later take back seriously when Civakan renounces
gains.b: Pattinattar's figure is seen to be older than his use of it: in love poetry the pyre-body burns without teaching contempt for the body

note: Akananuru 86 recalls a wedding of rice, sand, lamps, water poured with petals and paddy by four mothers, and the kin giving the bride; the epic father gives his daughter before the fire with a dowry he announces.
teaches: Set beside the Sangam wedding, which names no fire and no dowry, the epic's gift before the flame with women, gold and villages shows the giving of a bride recast as a fire rite with property declared.

gains.a: the epic verse gains a measure of what is new in it, the fire and the declared dowry, against an older Tamil wedding
gains.b: the Sangam poem gains a later counterpart that shows by contrast what its rite lacks: a sacred fire and a stated transfer of wealth

note: Verse 289 names the pleasures of lovers as ripe fruits they taste; Tirumanthiram 201 names a man's wife as the ripe jackfruit he will not eat while he toils for the wild date.
teaches: Both speak of sexual joy as fruit, but the poem lets lovers eat it freely in the grove while the Tirumanthiram asks whose fruit it is, so the image carries opposite moral weights.

gains.a: The fruit image gets a question the verse leaves unasked, whose fruit it is and whether it is one's own to eat.
gains.b: The jackfruit image meets a scene of lovers who eat the ripe fruit freely, so the verse is seen against the pleasure it warns about.

note: Kural 680 says those with a small domain, afraid of unrest within, bow to the great and take what they are offered; verse 670 has the king bowing on the strength of earlier kings who pleased their overlord.
teaches: The king's submission follows the couplet's prudence step by step, so the prince's later refusal is a refusal of that prudence and not of mere cowardice.

gains.a: The verse lacks a stated policy that a small domain bows to the great, which gives the king's reasoning its general standing.
gains.b: The couplet lacks the felt cost of such bowing, which the epic shows in the king's swallowed insult in 666 and his hiding the deal from the princes in 672.

note: 1420 shows an army scattering before a mountain-lifter; Kural 765 sets the standard of an army that stands together even when Death comes at it.
teaches: The scene gives the Kural's test a failure that the couplet only describes as a standard, and shows the Kural's army needs a leader to hold.

gains.a: the unit gains a measure by which the scattering is a failure of the army and not only the fault of one man
gains.b: the couplet gains a scene where the standard is not met, showing what its unbroken army is set against

note: Verse 875 starts the guide's naming of the lands below; 889 ends the tour at the grove where the host alights.
teaches: The tour is a framed journey that ends with the host's landing at Podanam, so the descriptions serve the arrival.

note: Tirumanthiram has old deeds following the subtle body into a new body; the muni gives the bodies one by one for the king's father, with a vow taken in the cock's body turning the chain upward.
teaches: The epic shows that the following deed can be altered by a vow made in a beast's body, which the Saiva line says nothing of.

gains.a: The epic names each body and the vow that changed the course.
gains.b: The Saiva verse's general passing of the old deed gains a concrete life, a beast birth by beast birth.

note: The Kural says to think before resolving, since rethinking after resolving is a fault; Buddhisenan says that once the raid is made, turning back brings blame, so weigh it first.
teaches: Buddhisenan supplies the reason the Kural leaves unstated: in war, the deed once begun shuts off retreat through blame, which is why the thinking must come before the resolve.

gains.a: Buddhisenan's caution gains the standing of a general maxim of deliberate action, not mere timidity
gains.b: the couplet's bare 'lapse' gains a concrete cost, the blame of retreat before a king's army

note: 741 allows that a ruler may fear and protect himself behind walls. 775 counts even a blink before a spear as flight.
teaches: The chapter on the state and the chapter on the warrior hold different standards for fear, and both are the Kural's.

note: Manimekalai 6 lists young mothers just delivered and helpless infants among those Death heaps for the burning ground to eat; in the Cintamani a mother gives birth in the burning ground and its deities bow.
teaches: The Buddhist epic makes the burning ground the end that spares no new mother or infant, while the Jain epic makes the same ground the birthplace of a king, so the place teaches impermanence in one and providence in the other.

note: Tirumanthiram 244 calls the king's share one sixth of the produce and ties it to keeping dharma without lapse; 54 shows the king taking his sixth only as grace.
teaches: The verse puts the one-sixth rule into practice as restraint on both tax and killing, while the Tirumanthiram makes it a step on the road to release and wealth.

gains.a: The verse gains the Tirumanthiram's claim that dharma kept without lapse is the road to release as well as wealth, which its own praise of the king leaves unsaid.
gains.b: The Tirumanthiram gains a king who actually takes only the sixth and refuses wrathful killing, so its rule has a figure who keeps it.

note: 1997 promises the giver of food a later kingship; Kural 222 says that even if there were no higher world, giving alone is good.
teaches: The epic's giving is promised its fruit, and the Kural says it is worth doing without one, so the reward is a bonus to a duty and not its ground.

gains.a: The promise of kingship gains a test: would the giving stand if there were no later birth.
gains.b: The Kural's 'even if no higher world' gains a case of the world's usual motive, the later kingship.

note: Civakan says desire churns him (கடைகின்றது காமமே); Padumai says her heart is the ocean churned for nectar.
teaches: The poet gives the two lovers, lying apart on the same night, one verb: he says it plainly of himself, and she expands it into the whole churning of the ocean, so the image binds their separate laments into a matched pair.

note: Madanan swore to the king that he had split Civakan's chest and rolled him over; Kattiyangaran now sees Civakan alive and names Madanan's failure as his ruin.
teaches: Together the two verses show the usurper undone by his own system of lies: he rewarded a false report of a killing, and the man he believed dead returns to the very contest set as his trap.

note: In Akananuru 110 a stranger asks the bathing girls if he may eat with them and stay in their noisy fishing hamlet, and they turn him away; in Kuruntokai 345 the friend herself asks the man whether staying with his chariot at their small town by the great water would be a fault.
teaches: The night's stay in the fishing hamlet is the neythal courtship's measure of trust: asked for by the stranger at the start and refused, it is offered by the friend once the love is known, so who proposes the stay marks how far the affair has gone.

note: Verse 106 gives the dream of the elephant that garlands the young lord; 107 gives its fruit, a Vidyadhara king's gift of his daughter.
teaches: The astrologer first tells the dream and only then its fruit, so the reader sees a sign turned into a forecast of a marriage and an alliance.

note: Buddhisenan's plan in 1140 is to burn the city and free Civakan by force; Civakan here sets both that and his wife's magic aside and waits on his friend.
teaches: The prisoner overrules all the rescues offered him, so his deliverance comes only from the bond he made himself, which is the episode's point about merit.

note: The ministers, army and friend the king adds to the dowry in 176 are the same things the Kural counts among a state's six parts.
teaches: A king who has lost a state can rebuild its parts by marriage, which the Kural's list of parts does not say.

gains.a: The bride's gift reads as the means by which the exiled Udayanan regains the army and ministers of a ruler.
