gains.b: The list of six parts gets a case in which allies and ministers are acquired by a marriage gift and not by long building.

note: In Tirumanthiram 1775 worship of the Lord's feet brings grace by which the worshipper's own five senses are conquered; in 1468 the Jina conquered his own senses, and the worshipper's singing earns heaven, not sense-conquest.
teaches: Both tie the five senses to praise of holy feet, but the conquest is done by different hands: Saiva grace subdues the devotee's senses for him, while in the Jain hymn the conquest belongs to the Jina alone and remains the worshipper's own task.

gains.a: a contrast that shows the hymn gives the worshipper no grace that does the work of restraint
gains.b: a Jain counterpart in which the feet are praised for a conquest already achieved by their owner, not for one they bestow

note: The Naladiyar says a harlot's love ends when the hand is empty, like a lamp without oil; the Cintamani's dancer calls the saying that chastity breaks for gold a lie and vows herself to one man.
teaches: The dancer answers the very proverb the Naladiyar states, in her own voice, so the pair shows the epic giving the woman of the stage a reply that the didactic tradition never lets her make.

gains.a: the dancer's 'those who said it lied' gains a named target: a saying of this kind stood in the ethical books
gains.b: the quatrain's general rule gains a counter-claim from inside the class it judges, which tests whether the rule is observation or stereotype

note: 1037 compares the lotus and the worshippers of the Jina's feet to the maiden's red feet; 1119 has the groom call worship of those feet enough.
teaches: The poet moves the worship of feet from the Jina to the bride through the groom's mouth and so shows love borrowing a devotional form.

note: Kuruntokai 206 tells the wise to keep from love because the woman is too sweet, her words like ambrosia; Naladiyar 41 tells men to turn from desire because the admired body is a frail bag the crows would tear.
teaches: The same counsel, keep away from love, rests on opposite judgments of the beloved: the Sangam lover flees because she is ambrosia and the pain is love's own, the Jain moralist because she is carrion under skin, so the later ethic keeps the advice and reverses its reason.

note: Chandramathi urged her son to cut down a kid to the goddess; the crocodile that was she is now cut and torn by killers.
teaches: The cutting that she asked of the king is returned on her own body, so the offering she urged is the cost she herself pays.

note: Both epics open by going for refuge to the feet of the tirthankara: the Cintamani's red feet, this poem's feet of Nemi under the pindi.
teaches: Two Jain epics begin with the same act of going to the feet but name different lords, so the invocation is a convention and the chosen tirthankara tells which tradition the poem draws on.

note: The Kural's man says love is sweeter than toddy because merely thinking of it brings unfailing joy; in Ainkurunuru 325 the man says the scorching waste does not harm him because he has her nature as companion.
teaches: The couplet states that remembered love never fails to give joy, and the Ainkurunuru puts that claim to a hard test, the peopleless summer waste, where the memory works as a travelling companion (துணை), so the maxim gains a situation in which its truth is a matter of survival.

note: Dhumaketu is likened to the Death of the age's end; Tirumular says the Lord's thinkers are beyond Death's messengers.
teaches: The war poem sets Death above all fighters, while Tirumular sets one who thinks of the Lord above Death.

gains.a: 1317 gains a view in which the Death its hero resembles can be turned back
gains.b: Tirumanthiram 176 gains the epic's warrior who becomes Death's own image on the field

claims.gist: one should give to others before one eats oneself
Fortune turns from one who overthrows the lord who raised him
loyalty to one's maker secures one's lineage on earth
a man freed from danger by his wife loses the credit of his own strength and learning
the Arhat takes no joy in praise, yet the world rejoices in him
theft is punished by kings here and by a fall to a bad birth hereafter
giving to ascetics who practise penance is a way toward the ending of births
everyone, not only the renouncer, should strive at hard penance while in the body to reach release
those who have crossed the sword may be answered with deceit
those who live by killing travellers are sin embodied
when the king abandons his duty to guard, the cool places of the land are scorched along with him
one who bears the great burden of dharma is to be honoured, and not attacked
the birth chart shapes a person's eloquence and beauty
a falsehood told without harm, by one who loves honour, is not a lie
a king who shrinks from battle should give up his crown and leave for the forest of ascetics
a woman's love, which is won by embrace, cannot be taken by the sword
those who fight for land fight anyone, elder or not
the pleasures of the gods' world are a sea in which they sink, and they are without a rival
meditation is a tool that is thrown away once the karma is burned
liberation is a city from which none returns
a king's mind, sight, strength, rule and sceptre depend on his ministers
wife and kin are to be feared like a heap of fire by one who seeks release
old age takes away the body's beauty and so the use of Kama's arrows
shutting the five sense-gates and guarding the mind is the first defence in the fight against karma
a wife may follow and serve her husband in the world beyond
young men who trust courtesans lose their wealth
the lamp of right vision destroys the darkness of karma
right vision should be held as one's own wealth
one who follows scripture, gives up evil and holds to the Lord's path is nectar to souls in all four states of being
killing a life brings deeds that ripen into great suffering, so it must be shunned
what befalls a man and his child follows the penance they did or did not do
worship of the lord of the three worlds makes one the chief of the gods

note: Kalittokai 143's woman asks why the king who guards the world's lives as his own does not guard hers; Purananuru 186 says the world lives by its king and the king must know he is its life.
teaches: The deserted woman takes the puram doctrine that the king is the people's life and finds its edge: a king can guard every life from war and want but not from a lover's leaving, so the akam poem marks a limit of royal protection that the puram counsel does not state.

note: The Kural says it is not the spear but the ruler's unbent sceptre that gives victory; the epic says victory goes to the virtuous mind, and a betel leaf thrown by such a man becomes a spear.
teaches: The couplet ties victory to the justice of a king's rule, while the epic moves it into each fighter's heart and applies it to a war over a woman, where no sceptre is in question.

gains.a: the epic's moral of battle gains a political form, the rule that a just state wins, which its private quarrel over a bride lacks
gains.b: the couplet gains a test case where the side with fewer arms wins and the cause is put in character rather than in government

note: Vasavadatta arrives at Kausambi as the sages in verse 192 foretold.
teaches: The sages' reading is shown to be true when the lady the king thought dead walks into the grove.

note: Kattiyangaran promised to guard the earth so it would brim with gold once the king had gone to heaven; at the end the Earth goddess, bathed in his allies' blood, is taken by Civakan.
teaches: The usurper's claim to be the earth's guardian is reversed by the closing marriage of earth and rightful heir, which shows the ilampakam's title answering his first speech of seizure.

note: The raft (புணை) on the deep sea: in 380 the Wise One to whom the youth goes for refuge, here the hero's garland on the sea of night.
teaches: The Jain epic uses one image for refuge from the sea of births and for a girl's hold on her lover's token, so the reader sees desire offering a false copy of the refuge the teacher gives.

note: 3122 sets the lovers as wishing-trees wrapped in creepers; 3141 puts the gods in a sea of the senses, so one pleasure is drawn at two levels.
teaches: The poet writes human and heavenly love with the same figures, so the heaven reached by penance is a purer form of the bed that penance left.

note: Kural 685 describes the envoy who speaks briefly, removes what would offend, and brings a smile; in 1011 Madhavasenai carries the bride's greeting to the groom's mother as a go-between.
teaches: The same tact of an envoy is shown in a domestic errand between two households, where the greeting claims kinship before the wedding.

gains.a: The verse lacks a stated measure of what makes a message-bearer good, which the couplet gives.
gains.b: The couplet lacks a case of such tact used between a bride's house and a groom's, not between kings.

note: Kural 879 tells the king to cut a thorn tree young lest the hand that cuts it be hurt; verse 644 adds a nail for the sprout and that axe and hatchet fail once it has grown.
teaches: The verse makes the couplet's thorn tree an argument for haste, though Arimanju's reply in 646 to 648 shows the story doubts that the tree is a thorn at all.

gains.a: The verse lacks the couplet's warning that the grown tree harms the hand that cuts it, a cost to the cutter and not only to the tree.
gains.b: The couplet lacks the image of tools failing, which makes the delay one of means as well as of danger.

note: The danava pierces Sarthulakan in 1315, and in 1316 the pierced man cuts him down with the trident.
teaches: The wound does not decide the duel; the wounded man's counter-stroke decides it, so the pair shows the fight reversed in one verse.

note: Kural 1102 says the cure for a disease is usually other than its cause but this woman is herself the cure for the sickness she brings; Soolamani 991 says love's sickness has no cure and that looking coolly at loved ones only doubles the wound.
teaches: The Kural finds the remedy in union with the beloved, and the epic denies any remedy before the union.

gains.a: The verse lacks the possibility of a cure in the beloved, which the couplet names.
gains.b: The couplet lacks the stage before union, where the girl sees no cure and fear doubles the pain.

note: A hill chief tells a visitor he cannot keep his body alive without liquor and meat; in the Manimekalai Saathuvan concedes and gives the Naga chief a reduced dharma, while Civakan presses on and wins full renunciation.
teaches: Faced with the same objection from a forest people, the Buddhist epic tailors a lesser rule to what the hearer can bear while the Jain epic refuses any compromise and makes the hunter choose heaven over his body, which shows how differently the two works weigh abstention against a hearer's livelihood.

note: Verse 268 says all living beings worship the one who has gained his own self; verse 556 has kings bow at the feet of a man who left a throne and let creepers climb him.
teaches: The beings who worship the self-conquered man in the story are kings and serpents together, as the couplet does not say.

gains.a: The scene gets a stated reason why even kings bow, which is his gaining of himself.
gains.b: The couplet gets a picture in which the worshippers are those whose rank he gave up.

note: The Kural says birth is alike for all beings and distinction comes from the work they do; Civakan holds that birth decides which wife a man may take first.
teaches: The pair shows the Kural's levelling of birth stopping at the threshold of marriage in the epic, where rank of birth remains a rule of conduct even for a hero honoured for his deeds.

gains.a: the hero's private rule is seen against a classic denial that birth confers worth, which makes its reliance on birth visible
gains.b: the couplet's claim is tested on a case it does not name, the ordering of marriages, where birth kept a force the couplet does not grant it

note: 2908 says that of rice and water, both life, the king is the world's good life; Purananuru 186 says neither rice nor water is life, the wide world lives by its king.
teaches: The poem makes the king life by denying that rice and water are, while the epic keeps them as lives and adds the king beside them.

gains.a: the verse's ranking of the king above rice and water is shown as a traditional claim
gains.b: the Sangam poem's flat denial that rice or water is life gets a gentler form in which they remain lives and the king is a further one

note: Kural 235 speaks of a death that is really existence, a growth through ruin; verse 776 says the flesh body goes while the form of fame stands.
teaches: The verse supplies the two-body picture that explains the couplet's death that is existence, as the fame body that survives.

gains.a: The verse lacks the couplet's claim that only the skilled manage this exchange, which makes the fame body an achievement.
gains.b: The couplet lacks a plain statement of what survives the death, the form of fame, that the verse gives.

note: The hero's garland as her raft: first in her own lament, then in the narrator's account of failed remedies.
teaches: The raft she claims in despair in 1663 is confirmed by the narrator in 1674 after every cooling remedy fails, so the image moves from a lover's hope to the story's fact.

note: Vijayai says the body is a fire of disease with life as ghee, and urges giving and good before Death leaves; Tirumular says give out the rice before the pot burns near, since the days slip away.
teaches: Both turn the household fire and the measure of rice into a warning that gifts must go out now; the epic frames it as the end of a king's pleasure, the Saiva verse as ordinary housekeeping.

gains.a: the verse's body-as-fire gets a plain rice-pot image for what is given up first
gains.b: the Tirumanthiram's counsel to give is placed under a Death who drinks the household, with the Jain epic's warning of disease and awareness as fuel

note: Both use the reaped millet stubble of the hill farmer: in Kuruntokai 133 the stubble cropped by parrots puts out leaves again in the rain, as the girl lives on after his first taking of her beauty; in Ainkurunuru 286 the stubble bears pods for his ever-yielding land while her own glow is taken.
teaches: The same stubble is a figure of the girl's own survival in Kuruntokai 133 but of the man's endless plenty in Ainkurunuru 286, set against her fading, so the image of renewal cuts both ways: what revives on his hills need not revive in her.

note: Verse 385 names the first lord as the light who bore the wheel of dharma (அறக்கதிர் ஆழி); Kural 8 calls the god அறவாழி அந்தணன், where ஆழி can be taken as sea or as wheel.
teaches: A Jain epic uses the words aram and aazhi for a god where the Kural's phrase leaves open sea or wheel, so the same wording is read two ways across the corpus.

gains.a: A much older Tamil praise-phrase for a god, which shows its wording is not a coinage but a shared devotional idiom.
gains.b: A second reading of ஆழி, the wheel an epic plainly bears, which the couplet's own words do not decide.

note: In 1973 Sagaradattan suddenly sells six crores of goods while Civakan sits at his step; in 1977 the merchant tells that it was written at Vimalai's birth that goods would sell when her destined husband sat at his shop.
teaches: The unexplained sale is the fulfilment of a birth-sign told only afterwards, so the narrator lets the reader see the sign come true before learning that it was one.

note: In both a hen swan is misled by a reflection in the water.
teaches: In the Kalittokai the hen swan runs to the moon's reflection thinking it her mate and is shamed when he appears, an image of a wife who welcomes a straying husband; in the epic the hen takes her own reflection for a rival and sulks, so the same mistake that there yields shame here yields jealousy of herself.

gains.a: the epic scene gains the akam convention in which a swan deceived by a reflection stands for a wife's misjudgment of her husband
gains.b: the Kalittokai's image gains a version in which the false image is the bird's own, which turns misplaced longing into baseless jealousy

note: Verse 130 names a golden city, Ratanupura-Chakravalam, on the southern ridge; verse 285 names a golden city of Ratna-pallavam in the same realm.
teaches: The counsellor's golden city may be the poet's or a second one, so the king hears of the Vidyadhara country in terms that differ slightly from the poet's own.

note: The Kural calls good children the ornament of a house's excellence; the verse makes bearing children of an old family the act by which the wife is mistress of the house.
teaches: Children move from ornament to office: what the Kural treats as the crown of a good home, Thirikadugam treats as a debt the wife owes in order to hold her title.

note: The onlookers of 637 say the bride's girdle and breasts are Death upon Death and that the anklet bells cry to the suitors to run and save their lives; here Death has come in the king's daughter's form and her girdle, anklet and bells cry to the onlookers to go and guard their hearts.
teaches: The cry that was gossip at Gandharvadattai's contest becomes the ornaments' own speech at Lakkanai's wedding, so the adornment itself is made the warning.

note: Saccandan, ringed in his palace, was a roaring lion hemmed in at a cave mouth and died fighting; his son, seized by the same usurper, goes as a lion bound with a spider's thread.
teaches: The lion image marks the difference between father and son: the father was caught by force and fought to death, the son could break his bond at will and keeps it, so the son survives the trap the father did not.

note: Puram 246's queen rejects the widow's austerities and chooses the pyre; Nandattan names penance and the fire as two equal courses for a widow.
teaches: Where the Sangam queen ranks the fire above the hard widow's life, the Jain epic's speaker leaves the two as alternatives, so the pair shows the choice the queen made was one of two recognised paths.

gains.a: Nandattan's passing phrase gains the weight of a real choice argued for in the Sangam queen's own voice
gains.b: the queen's refusal gains a later witness that the austere path she scorned stayed a full alternative to the fire

note: The sage says the suffering of births ends only by good dharma; Tirumular names austerity and virtue the boat across the sea of deeds, which the Lord makes fruitful.
teaches: The Jain verse makes dharma sufficient to end the fruit of deeds; Tirumular makes the Lord's act the thing that gives austerity and virtue their effect.

gains.a: The verse gets a rival account in which dharma needs a god's act to bear fruit.
gains.b: Tirumular gets a Jain case where dharma alone is said to end a deed's fruit, which tests his added condition.

note: Both invoke Vishnu's realm as the highest measure. 610 offers it to the sleepless ruler, and 605 has just listed sleep as a boat to ruin. 1103 asks whether that realm is even as sweet as sleep on a beloved's arms.
teaches: The Porul and Kamam books rank sleep and sovereignty oppositely.

note: 1920 promises the way of conquering deeds as a thing the sage will teach; Tirumanthiram 219 says the fire worshipped burns up the many ills of deeds.
teaches: The Jain sage treats conquering deeds as a teaching to be given, while Tirumular treats it as a rite whose fire burns them.

gains.a: The sage's 'way of conquering deeds' gains a rival method, burning by rite, against which the Jain way can be read.
gains.b: The fire rite gains a Jain counterpart in which deeds are conquered by teaching and austerity, not by offering.

note: 1919 counts taking the daughters of hill and forest chiefs as the settled custom of kings whose rule stands; Purananuru 336 shows a king hot for a girl whose father will not give her, and the war that waits on it.
teaches: The epic's 'custom' is the king's side of a transaction that the Purananuru shows from the chief's side as a demand refused and a battle coming, so the policy's cost becomes visible.

gains.a: the mother's maxim gains the cost it leaves unsaid: a chief's daughter is not always given, and the alliance may first be a war
gains.b: the Purananuru's refusal gains the ruler's reasoning, marriage as policy for a firm throne, which the poem's anger does not state

note: The patikam says that while kings paid tribute and his sceptre ran, Civakan heard the dharma and was afraid of kingship like a snake; in 2627 Sunandai says she will renounce too and Civakan melts.
teaches: The turn the patikam gave in one line is shown here as it happens, in the answer of a mother and the dissolving of a king, not as a decision of his own.

note: Kural 560 says that if the guardian does not guard, the cows' yield fails and the learned forget their books; Civakan's oath calls such a guardian's fate down on himself if he fails her.
teaches: The bent sceptre that the Kural treats as a public disaster becomes, in a lover's oath, the worst private penalty a man can name, which shows how deep the guardian's duty sat as a measure of shame.

gains.a: the oath gains its weight: without the couplet's picture of a land ruined by an unguarding king, the curse Civakan names would read as a stock phrase
gains.b: the couplet gains a use as an oath-penalty, showing that failing to guard was held a dishonour fit to stake a promise on, not only a policy failure

note: Vijayai asked that her son be told all the evil she suffered after her lord died and be brought to her; here hearing his victory her tear-filled eyes grow cool.
teaches: Her grief, laid on the son as a charge, is answered by the victory, so the battle closes the mother's wrong and not only the father's loss of the throne.

note: In 259 Kattiyankaran proposed that the king go to rule heaven as lord of the gods; in 291 the king does go to the gods, as their guest.
teaches: The usurper's euphemism for murder comes literally true, but the narrator gives the king the heaven of a warrior and a Jain devotee, not the throne the usurper mockingly offered.

note: At 440 Nandagon had it proclaimed that the maiden would be given to whoever brought back the herd; at 479 he offers her to Civakan, adding seven golden statues.
teaches: The proclamation is kept to the letter, yet the hero's decline at 483-484 shows the prize could be honoured only by being passed to another.

note: Nandagon promised Civakan to fill the underworld with ghee of red cows, sweet milk and thick curd; here the keeper of the herds brings four hundred thousand pots of curd, milk and ghee to Civakan's wedding.
teaches: The herd chief's boast at his own daughter's giving is paid at Civakan's wedding instead, so the bond made by the recovered cattle carries from one marriage of the hero's circle to the next.

note: Kural 445 tells a ruler to take counsel from ministers as his eyes; verse 237 says that kings' lives and even Indra's lordship do not flower without counsel.
teaches: The epic widens the Kural's rule from a ruler's prudence to a claim about all rule and even the gods' rule.

gains.a: A statement of the rule as a duty of a ruler, where the verse shows only that counsel is needed.
gains.b: An example from the Brahmanical and divine world that the couplet's own kings never reach.

note: Verse 427 names Marusi because he can say what is fit; in 517 the same envoy answers the king's silence with anger and a rebuke.
teaches: The ministers chose a speaker for fitting words, and the scene tests that skill when he is met by silence and shows how quickly it turns to pride.

note: The astrologer in 204 warned that if the king put his power in one man the land's fortune would leave; in 263 that man's army surrounds the palace.
teaches: The siege fulfils a warning the king dismissed, so the fall is shown as foreseen and refused, not as blind chance.

note: Tirumanthiram 346 reads Siva's burning of Kama as the yoga that destroys desire's work; the Cintamani says Civakan is as if the burnt Kama had risen again on earth.
teaches: Set beside the Saiva reading, the Jain poet's simile shows the burning of Kama handled as a story whose victim returns, so the myth becomes a measure of a hero's beauty instead of a victory over desire.

gains.a: the doctrinal weight of the myth the simile borrows, which the simile does not state
gains.b: evidence that the Kama-burning circulated as a stock image outside Saiva devotion, with its yogic sense dropped

note: In 1360 Civakan slips from Padumai's sleeping arms in the dark like a good life leaving the body; here the friend teaches that parting and death both belong by nature to human birth.
teaches: The narrator's simile of departure as death is taken up as doctrine: the parting that was likened to the soul's leaving is now said to be of the same kind as death, and as little to be grieved.

note: 1760 shows the father seeing his daughter's ripening body; 1762 follows with a council that sets the swayamvara.
teaches: Her ripeness is the unspoken cause of the proclamation: the poem lets the father's look become public policy.

note: Kural 550 likens a king's putting killers to death to weeding a crop; here the king sentences the youth who stopped the royal elephant from killing a girl.
teaches: The couplet's justice assumes that the king punishes the killer; the epic shows a king whose own beast is the killer punishing the rescuer, so the weeding image fails when the king himself decides what the weed is.

gains.a: a rule by which Kantukkatan's question 'if this is a fault, what is virtue?' becomes a charge of inverted justice
gains.b: a case in which the one who owns the deadly force is the judge, which the couplet's farming image cannot address

claims.gist: birth as a woman is not an honoured birth
the eunuch and the blind are not counted among humans
a good deed is a child nursed by compassion that lifts the soul upward
learning, beauty and generosity do not save one from death
austerity taken up by strength and practised leads to the two heavens
those who do not praise the Jina's virtues are not praised in return
a king's wealth leaves him when he neglects it for pleasure
freed ascetics relieve the world's distress with a rain of virtue
a learned man of knowledge is the proper one to send as envoy
the body does not last, so killing to prolong life is futile and leads to endless rebirth
giving away wealth to those who ask holds back the sea of craving
a king guards the earth by a straight sceptre, and the gods protect him
daughters, like the conch's pearls, profit others and not those who bore them
restraint cannot hold when desire rises unopposed
no one but the Jina may be reckoned the Lord
the Lord harms no living being and is easy for his worshippers
the body is a hut full of filth
the dharma destroys desire for sense-pleasure and the cruelty of killing
tapas protects from poison and the tusker, and when it is spent no flight saves
dharma itself is the refuge of the fearless who are strong in tapas
those who follow the counsel of the learned meet only good
those who sink in pleasure with women incur sin and blame
one who has shed the two kinds of deed shines with a light no eye can take in
a king's anger may end only when the youth's life and the maid are laid at his feet
the eight karmas can be cut away by an ascetic's firm will
truthful speech raises one to heaven, falsehood to hell
a king who ruled the whole earth should not meet defeat
a bond of friendship kept for seven generations is fixed by fate and cannot be broken
those who share one dharma are not divided as king and merchant

note: In 2616 Vijayai tells Civakan in a few lines that we are born not knowing our days and that the past cannot be recalled; in 2748 the sage lists the rare body, its end, the pain of leaving and the release as the subjects of a full teaching.
teaches: What the mother says as a warning is turned into the heads of a doctrine, so the reader sees which of her points the sermon will take up.

note: The prophecy ends with the raiders broken by one man in a chariot; in 449 the hunters, stunned by the roar of the generous one's chariot, lose heart and give up the fight.
teaches: The poet names Civakan only through the hunters' own omen, so the hero's victory is foretold by his enemies before it is told by the narrator.

note: 1827 shows kings who lose the bride calming themselves by seeing the loss as karma; Naladiyar 33 contrasts the fool who sighs hotly at the fruit of deeds with the wise who call it old desert.
teaches: The same step from sighing to calm is shown as a group's act on a public loss, where the quatrain gives only the principle.

gains.a: The kings' calm gains a named opposite, the fool who sighs and breaks, which the scene alone does not give.
gains.b: The quatrain gains a case of powerful men who choose the wise answer after having sweated and sighed, as 1826 shows.

note: Thinaimozhi Aimpathu 24: the friend rests her comfort on the man who swore an oath (வஞ்சினம்) and held to it, with the rain as his token. Kural 1154: if he who said 'fear not' leaves, is there any fault in those who trusted his assuring word?
teaches: The friend builds her comfort on his oath, while the couplet asks who is to blame if such an oath fails, so together they show that the whole mullai argument of waiting rests on trusting a man's word, and the Kural names the risk the friend leaves unsaid.

note: The husband tells his wife the moon pales before her face and thereby ends her sulk; Kural 1118 tells the moon it would be loved if it shone like her face.
teaches: The face-and-moon compliment is shown at work in a quarrel as a way to end a sulk, not only as praise.

gains.a: The conceit of the moon outshone by her face has a well-known formulation in a Kural couplet.
gains.b: A scene in which the same compliment is used to win a wife back from a sulk, which the couplet's address to the moon does not show.

note: The ministers propose to place Turumakanthan as guard in the garden; he goes to the garden after bowing to the king.
teaches: The proposal becomes action in two verses, and the guard sets out only after the king's approval, which shows how a counsel becomes an order.

note: 2904 has Civakan act on the body's hollowness by handing on the realm; Siddhar 642 warns the heart that Yama takes the body from a golden throne and the gold stays behind.
teaches: The Siddhar only warns that the throne cannot be carried away, while the epic king acts on the warning and descends from it.

gains.a: the verse's choice of an heir is shown as an answer to the death the Siddhar says takes the throne's owner
gains.b: the Siddhar's warning to the heart meets a ruler who actually leaves the gold throne before Yama comes

note: Naladiyar 27 praises the firm who see the body as a bubble and resolve to end their wandering; verse 356 says the body's nature of leaving, with austerity and knowledge, brings the mind to the divine seat.
teaches: The quatrain stops at the resolve born of seeing the body pass, and the epic names where that resolve is said to lead.

gains.a: A reason that the body's passing matters: it is the ground of the resolve that leads to the divine seat.
gains.b: A destination for the firm resolve, which the quatrain leaves at the ending of birth.

note: Both give the Jain doctrine that a thing persists in kind while its form arises and perishes: the Manimekalai's Jain with gram cooked into a dish and the sprouting neem, Neelakesi with a gold pot remade as a crown, applied to the soul passing from man to god.
teaches: On arising, persistence and destruction the Buddhist epic's report of the Jains matches a Jain debater's own illustration, so here the polemical account is one the school would accept, and the Neelakesi shows it was aimed at the soul's rebirth.

note: After the victory by arms, the king in 185 tends the wounded and rewards them, which is the work of a ruler's rule and not of the spear.
teaches: The epic shows victory first by the sword and then by care, so the Kural's claim is borne out only in the part after the battle.

gains.a: The healing and gifts after the battle are given a name as the sceptre's work, which the verse does not claim.
gains.b: The couplet's contrast of spear and sceptre gets a case in which both are used one after the other.

note: Here the bees prove Suramanjari's powder the lesser; in her own ilampakam a woman says the guarded chastity Suramanjari kept is because the lord dimmed the powder he tested by producing a witness.
teaches: The later verse reads the bee test as the cause of Suramanjari's guarded maidenhood, so a judgement of scents becomes in the story's memory the origin of a chaste seclusion.

note: Yugi and Vayanthakan wait for the right hour and rope, as the couplet says nothing is hard for one who knows time and means.
teaches: The rescue is built on the couplet's rule, but at the cost of others, which the couplet does not weigh.

gains.a: the choice of hour and means is shown as the rule that makes a prison break possible
gains.b: the couplet's claim is tested by a case in which the same skill harms the innocent

note: 1561 has the queen resolve to see the parijata and the Kama creeper wed; 1621 sets the tree as bridegroom and starts the rites.
teaches: The queen's wish is carried out only after a quarrel and its mending, so the wedding is the end of an unplanned scene.

note: Naladiyar 25 says the man who sees kin wailing at a corpse and yet marries and expects joy is answered by the funeral drum; 2758 shows men in the heart of pleasure cut off by Death while the living beat their faces.
teaches: The quatrain shows the lesson refused, the epic shows the death that teaches it, and together the reader sees that pleasure and mourning are the same scene seen at different times.

gains.a: the verse's death in pleasure gains the quatrain's voice of the one who watches and still does not learn
gains.b: the quatrain gains the verse's scene of pleasure at its height, with the jewelled women and their anklets, so the cost of ignoring the drum is made concrete

note: Kural 65 says touching one's children is joy to the body; the king here holds both sons in both arms as soon as he sees them.
teaches: The king's embrace shows a father's bodily joy in his sons coming before any royal question.

gains.a: The verse gives the embrace but not why it is joy, which the couplet names as the pleasure of touch.
gains.b: The couplet lacks a scene of a king, who must rule, undone by the sight of his sons safe.

note: 1842 says more seed must be sown for the austerity that bore present pleasure; 1851 shows those who instead cut the root and die.
teaches: The warning of 1851 is the unsown field that 1842 fears, so the king's wish to sow is shown as the way out of that ruin.

note: The Purananuru's warrior, with no chariot and no forest fort, watched the enemy's herd go, counted it and turned it with his bow (சிலையின் மாற்றியோனே); Civakan turns the herd by the bow's twang alone (சிலையின் னொலியால் தொறு மீட்டு).
teaches: The epic keeps the Sangam feat of turning a herd with the bow but removes even the drawn arrow and gives the deed to a city's darling, so a poor warrior's unsung skill becomes a prince's proof of worth before the town.

gains.a: the Cintamani's bow-sound recovery is shown to rest on an existing heroic type, the lone bowman who turns a herd, rather than on the poet's invention
gains.b: the Puram poem's quiet single-handed recovery is seen to be the seed of a scene that later poetry could magnify into public triumph and crowd adoration

note: 1687 has the wedding announced with the drum and the whole world knowing; 2388 shows how it is done, with the proclaimers dressed in white and sandal and carried on a battle elephant.
teaches: The wedding drum is a royal herald's act with its own costume and mount, which the earlier wedding announcement only names.

note: Kural 1082 says her returned look is like a striking goddess (தாக்கணங்கு) bringing an army; in 1473 Kemasari's look becomes an afflicting goddess (நோக்கணங்கு) and Civakan wonders whether she is a தாக்கணங்கு or a mortal.
teaches: The Kural settles that the woman is human and keeps the goddess as a figure for her look; the epic stops at the doubt and stacks அணங்கு on lute, look and woman, so the hero's own art is made one of the goddesses that strike him.

gains.a: the term and its sense of a look that strikes back, which the verse expands in its triple pun
gains.b: a narrative moment in which the man's doubt is left unresolved and he sinks under it

note: Naladiyar 53 has the best renounce home, youth and wealth at once to save themselves; 275 renounces for the pleasure-rich heaven.
teaches: The epic shows that the same reflection on impermanence may end in heaven rather than in release.

gains.a: 275 gains Naladiyar's view that the point of renunciation is saving oneself.
gains.b: Naladiyar 53 gains an instance in which the reflection leads to a heaven of pleasure, not release.

note: The onlookers guess whether he is a Vidyadhara hero or a prince of the gods; Padumai asks her maidens whether he is Kama or a young god, and says she does not know.
teaches: The question of the stranger's identity, a public puzzle in 1296, becomes in the girl's mouth a symptom of love: her not knowing who he is is now part of her sickness, since she cannot even name the thief.

note: Vijayai went from a sky-touching palace to the burning ground alone after the usurper killed her husband; now the usurper's women go from flower-cushions to the bare hot ground after his death.
teaches: The epic gives the usurper's household the very fall it gave the queen he wronged, and 303's reading of that fall as sin made visible is left for the reader to carry over.

note: 1488 has the beaten Vidyadharas bow in fear; 1489 has the victor answer with mercy and a drum for the dead king's kin.
teaches: The fear of the defeated is answered with grace, which turns a conquest into a settlement.

note: Naladiyar 46 lists entrails, fat, blood, bone, sinews, skin, flesh and grease and asks which part is the garlanded woman; 1583 gives nearly the same list (குடர்கள், வழும்பு, நரம்பு, தோல்) but starts from the adorned hair and adds the three humours.
teaches: The Naladiyar's renunciant catalogue is put in the mouth of a hero who is not renouncing, as a weapon against another man's wife, so the meditation on the foul body becomes a householder's defence against adultery rather than a step out of the world.

gains.a: a recognised ascetic form, the list of tissues, that tells the reader Civakan's reply is a teaching and not merely a rebuff
gains.b: a dramatic occasion: a particular woman pressing a particular man, against whom the list is used and proves effective

note: 450 sets the women's eyes above the deer's; Kural 1085 finds the deer, the eye and Death all in one look.
teaches: The epic uses the same deer-and-eye comparison as the couplet but lets the deer lose, where the couplet lets the look hold the deer's frightened shyness as one of its three natures.

gains.a: The women's eyes get the couplet's three-natured look, so the poem's deer is more than a measure of beauty: it is something the look can frighten.
gains.b: The deer-eye comparison shown at work in a procession where a king sends the women out for a purpose, rather than a lover's chance meeting.

note: The Kural says the many lack because few do penance; the city women say they lose Civakan because they did no penance.
teaches: The couplet's account of why most people lack is turned into a mourner's self-blame, so lack of penance explains not poverty but the loss of a beloved, and the women accuse themselves while blaming the king and the father in the same verse.

gains.a: the lament's first cry is seen to rest on the ethical rule that what one keeps is earned by austerity
gains.b: the couplet's severe claim is shown working as consolation and self-reproach in grief, a use its general form does not show

note: 2014 makes hearing the meaning of the texts a lamp that clears delusion; Kural 423 makes wisdom seeing the true thing in whatever is heard.
teaches: The sage trusts the text as source, where the couplet makes the hearer's seeing the test of any source.

gains.a: Knowledge from hearing gains a check, seeing what is true in the words and not trusting the speaker.
gains.b: The couplet gains an end for its seeing: the clearing of the darkness that binds one to deeds.

note: The Charana appears as a teacher who reads the travellers' minds in the Silappathikaram and as a flier in Udayana.
teaches: One epic shows the Charana's mind-reading and the other his flight, so the powers attributed to him go beyond either.

note: In 2467 drums, conches and kings roar as the bridegroom takes the water; Naladiyar 23 says the same wedding drums can sound as funeral drums that very day.
teaches: The roar of the wedding drums sets Naladiyar's warning on how soon joy turns, and the epic's later turn to renunciation is its own answer.

gains.a: The wedding's loud joy gains the reminder that it may not last.
gains.b: The quatrain gains a full wedding in which the drums actually sound.

note: 2842 ranks gifts by the receiver, with a debased birth for a gift to the unrestrained; Kural 221 says only giving to those who have nothing is giving.
teaches: The Kural names the needy as the only true recipient, but the Cintamani's sage names the restrained, so who deserves a gift is answered in opposite ways.

gains.a: the verse's grading of recipients by restraint is set against the Kural's grading by need
gains.b: the Kural's 'the destitute' is shown as one possible answer, where the sage answers 'the restrained'

note: At the birth in the burning ground the child shone like the sun from the sea, gem lamps drove off the dark and the place's deities bowed; the people now call up that same birthplace beside his rise as a merchant's son and kings' lord.
teaches: The burning-ground birth that was a picture of desolation becomes the first term of a turn of fortune that the epic offers as a reason to take up tapas.

note: After killing Saccandan the usurper had his own name drummed from an elephant and, the poet said, the dark-hearted man won the goddess of fortune; now he and his sons lie dead and no one can say which of his women wore the queen's fillet.
teaches: The fortune the usurper seized in 297 is shown at its end as an empty title, and the ilampakam named for that goddess opens by taking her back.

note: Naladiyar 45 scorns men who praise teeth as jasmine buds, having seen fallen teeth in the burning ground; in Kalittokai 22 the woman asks the man who praised her teeth like jasmine buds whether he praised them falling out.
teaches: Both deflate the same compliment with the same decay, but to opposite ends: the ascetic uses the fallen teeth to free a man from desire, the wife uses them to bind him to her for life, so the image of the body's ruin cut both for and against staying with a woman.

note: 3039 has the freed ascetic reach it by wholly dropping attachment and hatred; Tirumanthiram 497 has the siddhas free of the bonds by becoming Siva and destroying the five malas.
teaches: The Jain epic makes release the result of the ascetic's own dropping of passions; the Saiva text has it come by becoming Siva.

gains.a: the verse's self-made release is set against a release by becoming the Lord
gains.b: the Tirumanthiram's grace-based freedom meets a school that gives no role to a god

note: The sons learn arts, weapons and horse-riding at five; Kural 61 prizes children who come to know what should be known.
teaches: The couplet names knowing as the child's worth, while the epic's lesson is the skills of a warrior's house, so what is 'known' differs.

gains.a: A measure that asks whether the princes' skill in arms and arts is the knowing a father should prize.
gains.b: A concrete household where the child's gain is skill at arms, which tests whether the couplet means moral knowing only.

note: 2846 says knowledge, faith and conduct together are a fire that burns the tree of deeds; 3082 shows the fire's end: the four destroying kings fall and the three worlds are known.
teaches: A teaching that the three burn deeds is fulfilled in the hero's own omniscience, so the doctrine is shown as an event in a life.

note: Naladiyar 44 refuses the petty men who call eyes water-lilies, carp and spears; 1585 blames the poets of kavya by name for painting brows, eyes and nose on a bag of skin.
teaches: Where the Naladiyar's opponents are anonymous fools, the epic names its own craft as the source of the illusion, so the critique of the simile becomes a self-critique of the epic genre.

gains.a: a precedent that makes Civakan's attack on poets part of an older ascetic argument rather than a passing jibe
gains.b: an identification of who the praisers of eyes are: the poets of the great poems, not only foolish lovers

note: 333 says wealth is by nature unstaying; 753 calls it the unfailing lamp that drives out darkness wherever one intends.
teaches: The chapter on impermanence and the chapter on acquiring wealth describe the same thing in opposite terms.

note: Verse 1037 sets the lotus drinking the feet's glow beside the worshippers; 1038 repeats the figure with bees singing.
teaches: The second verse adds the bees' sound to the lotus image, so the worshippers' bloom is also heard as a hymn.

note: The Kural's hero pulls the spear from his own body and laughs; Ulokapalan plucks the arrow from his forehead and the gushing blood is likened to the dawn sun's first ray.
teaches: Together they show the wound pulled from the body as a fixed sign of the hero, and that the epic turns the Kural's psychological shock, a laugh, into visual glory, so the same act is valued as composure in the one and as splendour in the other.

gains.a: the forehead-arrow is recognised as a stock heroic act, not a chance detail, which explains why the verse lingers on it before the kill
gains.b: the couplet's bare gesture gains a full scene with its consequence: the man who pulls the arrow is the one who kills in the next verse

note: The Kural defines a land as where unfailing yield, the worthy (தக்கார்) and the undiminished wealthy gather; the Cintamani's closing verse on Hemangadam makes it a place for those who do penance and those who make wealth, after ten verses of harvest.
teaches: The epic fills the couplet's three-part definition with a whole country, and reads its worthy ones as those who do penance, so the Kural's land is given room for renunciants beside the wealthy.

gains.a: the hyperbole of heaven fallen to earth is anchored in a received Tamil definition of what makes a land
gains.b: the couplet's unspecified தக்கார் receives a concrete reading as ascetics living alongside the rich

note: 1541 darkens the streets with incense and gold; 1544 makes the sun give up and set.
teaches: The festival's smoke is first a lamp for the elephant's eyes, then the cause of the sun's flight: the poet builds one hyperbole across two verses.

note: In 917 the king seats Maruci on a gold-fronted elephant before him; in 933 the king himself mounts the dressed elephant.
teaches: The elephant first honours the guest's envoy and only afterwards carries the king, so the ride is a courtesy given in order of rank.

claims.gist: desire joined to hatred can lead a wife to kill her husband
each age holds twenty-four lords, twelve wheel-kings, nine Kesavas and nine rivals
men do not grieve at parting, and women who waste away over them are foolish
a warrior's strength is for refusing tribute, and paying it makes arm and sword useless
a killing, even of a lifeless likeness, brings suffering in every following birth
killing, even of a made likeness, brings a sin that binds to a chain of births
present suffering is the fruit of sin done in an earlier life
one who fears may withdraw, and only one who does not fear even Death should stay in battle
the vow of not killing, kept by kings, leaves no conquest beyond them
a wife who flowered for her husband will not flower for another after his death
a king who prizes a woman's pleasure above all brings down the realm and its fortune with him
one's own deed, produced in a former birth, ripens into one's present state
lack of true knowledge is the seed from which harmful deeds grow
the births that deeds produce form a chain of suffering whose length cannot be reckoned
a king, however virtuous, can understand subtle matters only through the treatises of the learned and has no counsel of his own to decide by
the Jina's wheel of rule is a wheel without killing
people honour those with wealth and abandon the poor as kinless
weapons do not fell those who do good, and those who do evil cannot strike home
victory belongs to the virtuous and never to those whose minds harbour evil
a wife whose husband dies puts off her ornaments and either keeps a vow of penance or enters the fire
a future hero's victory over his rival is foretold
a good done in distress is owed a lasting public memorial

note: The Kural warns that honouring one's own spy openly lets out the secret; Govindan honours Civakan's companions exactly as his own men so that the enemy's spies cannot pick them out.
teaches: The couplet's insight that visible honour leaks a secret works in reverse too: honour spread evenly conceals, so a king can hide his guests by treating them like everyone else.

gains.a: the epic verse gains a statecraft rule that explains why the even-handed gifts are a security measure and not plain hospitality
gains.b: the couplet gains the inverse case, where the same logic of visible favour is used to defeat an enemy's spies rather than to protect one's own

note: 785 makes acquaintance unnecessary, while a whole chapter on old friendship opens at 801.
teaches: Parimelazhagar's gloss on 801 eases this by saying that பழைமை is not elapsed time but a certain kind of friendship.

note: The god foretold that the king of the middle country would give him his daughter; Civakan reports that he has.
teaches: The god's itinerary is fulfilled step by step, and the pairing shows that the marriage, which Civakan reports as a fee for teaching archery, was already fixed as his fortune before he set out.

note: Verse 875 has the host go across the sky past seas and hills; verse 948 gives the order to leave the air and walk the ground.
teaches: The sky journey ends in an order of descent, so the aerial tour serves the protocol of a meeting on earth.

note: The patikam told in one line that a snake took the king's daughter's face for the moon and bit her; verse 1271 tells the bite in scene.
teaches: The patikam's line already made the bite a praise of her face; the full scene keeps that conceit but sets it at the instant she reaches for a flower she raised, so the compliment and the danger arrive in the same gesture.

note: Verse 418 gives the saying that the childless are like trees and the queen's joy at a daughter; Kural 61 holds children valuable only when they come to know what should be known.
teaches: The Kural makes the worth of a child depend on understanding, where the epic king's praise rests only on having a child at all and on her marriage prospect.

gains.a: A measure of children's worth beyond the bare fact of having them, which the verse does not state.
gains.b: A scene where a child is prized for the marriage she will make, which tests the couplet's call for children who know what should be known.

note: Civakan says the body will drop at once like a ripe fruit from its stalk; the Naladiyar warns that a harsh wind can drop the green fruit while the ripe stays on the tree.
teaches: The epic's ripe fruit makes death a ripening that comes in order, but the quatrain's fallen green fruit warns that it need not wait for age, and the two urgings to act now rest on different pictures of when the body falls.

gains.a: a caution that its own image of ripeness understates the danger to the young
gains.b: a renouncer's use of the falling fruit that turns the urge to do good into a call to austerity

note: The sage names the temple doors opening at the son's foot and a pond among the signs; verse 51 shows the doors swing open at the child's foot-touch and the boy fall into the pond.
teaches: The sign comes true as an ordinary accident of an outing, so the story shows the prophecy fulfilling itself without anyone seeking it.

note: The monk conquers both deeds by his own austerity, where the couplet says the two deeds do not cling to those who praise the Lord.
teaches: The couplet places freedom from both deeds in devotion to a Lord; the story gives the same freedom through a man's own austerity and no god, so the same result has two causes.

gains.a: the hero's liberation is set against a rule that places it in devotion
gains.b: the couplet's route is shown to have a Jain rival that reaches the same end by effort alone

note: Naladiyar 17 says youth falls like fruit, so do not desire a woman for her eyes; Kalittokai 15 says wealth can be made any day but youth cannot be brought back, so do not leave her.
teaches: From the same fact that youth passes, the moralist counsels turning from desire and the love poet counsels holding fast to it, so the two books read the brevity of youth as a reason for opposite lives.

note: Cintamani 1344 has jewelled women standing guard round the bride before her wedding; verse 868 posts two thousand armed maidens round the princess.
teaches: Both epics guard the bride with women, but this one makes the guard an armed troop of the magic-learned.

note: 1571 limits the king's gifts to Vedic brahmins; 1572 has the jester answer that debate-skill will win them.
teaches: The rule meant to bar the jester is met by a claim that skill in debate can stand in for Vedic learning.

note: In 1294 Civakan strokes her whole body as a cure, thinking her life will stay if she is seen, spoken to and touched; here the narrator cites that touch, with the maxim that a woman belongs to the one who touched her, as the ground of the marriage.
teaches: Read together, the physician's touch made to save a life becomes after the fact a claim on the woman, showing how the epic fuses healing and betrothal into one act of fate.

note: In 1116 Civakan is led off bound like a lion caught in a spider's thread; the spy's report explains the thread: his parents' embrace and tears.
teaches: The spider's thread of 1116 is glossed by the scene of 1138: a weak bond holds the lion because he will not break his parents' hold, and he feels the shame of it toward his friends.

note: In 1147 Gandharvadattai's recited spells bring armed powers to free Civakan; here her spell shows Civakan far away and then sends his brother to him.
teaches: Her vinjai, first a weapon of rescue, becomes a means of sight and passage over distance, so the Vidyadhara wife is the household's power to reach Civakan wherever he goes.

note: Verse 81 says the women swoon with fear that the dark-gemmed prince, who came in a dream, will take their lives; verse 476 has the women faint on the terraces as the princes pass.
teaches: The dream-fear of the women becomes a public swoon, so the epic shows the prince's coming as the fulfilment of the fear.

note: The couplet says a ruler who does not examine and do justice perishes by himself (தானே கெடும்); the Pandya, who did not examine, pronounces his own death.
teaches: The epic makes the couplet's 'perishes by himself' literal: no enemy or court condemns the king, he passes the sentence on himself the moment his error is shown, and he was easily approached, so only the failure to examine undoes him.

note: The Kural's friend clears distress at once; the god's help waits to be called.
teaches: The god's reproach shows a friend's help can be bound by the call, which limits the Kural's picture of friendship that acts in the moment of trouble.

gains.a: The god's ask-and-answer scene shows that friendship with a god runs on being remembered, and that the king neglected it until now.
gains.b: The couplet's friend who acts unasked gets a counterexample: help that needs a call, and stays silent through prison and war.

note: The couplet defines a king as one who weighs a case before punishing; Devadattan asks the same of companions planning to punish a king.
teaches: The pair shows the rule of inquiry before penalty binding not only the ruler but those who would avenge themselves on him, and its first question is not guilt but whether the wrong has happened at all.

gains.a: Devadattan's caution gains the couplet's standing as the definition of just punishment, not mere prudence
gains.b: the couplet gains a case where the punishers are subjects and the punished a king, outside the royal court it assumes

note: The couplet says the pleasure of love is a sea but its pain, when it strikes, is greater; 491 gives the bridegroom the sea of pleasure that cannot be contained, and no pain.
teaches: The epic uses the couplet's measure of pleasure as a sea but leaves out the greater sea of pain that the woman in the Kural speaks from, because the wedding has no separation in it.

gains.a: the uncontained sea of 491 is seen to be half of a measure, the half that a married union can claim
gains.b: the couplet's first clause is given a scene where it stands alone, which shows its second clause belongs to separation

note: The king gathers allies after the spy's report; the couplet says a king who does not gather through spies and judge has no victory ready.
teaches: The epic shows a spy's report prompting a council, which is what the couplet calls the ground of victory.

gains.a: The scene gains a reason why the spy's word is repeated before the whole council: the report is the first step in the war.
gains.b: The couplet gains the next step it leaves out, what the ruler does with the report once he has it: he convenes allies.

note: Kural 57 holds that guarding women by confinement is no use and their own steadfastness is the best guard; verse 861 sets armed women round the princess.
teaches: The pair shows the guard of arms as outward show beside the inward guard the couplet values.

gains.a: The verse lacks a measure of what really guards the girl; the couplet gives one.
gains.b: The couplet lacks a concrete household that does guard its women by force; the verse supplies one.

note: The quatrain praises those who see the body as a bubble and resolve to end wandering; the unit shows a sermon only heard.
teaches: Hearing a sermon on suffering is not yet the resolve the quatrain praises, so the unit stops short of its conclusion.

gains.a: the sermon's claim that life is a bondage of suffering gets an image, the body as a bubble that forms and bursts
gains.b: the quatrain's resolve gets a scene of its audience hearing the teaching, though not yet acting

note: The time-keepers tell the king the hours that have passed; Kural 482 says acting in season is the rope that binds fortune.
teaches: The epic shows the machinery of a court that keeps its king aware of the hour, which is what the couplet's rule needs before it can be followed.

gains.a: A reason why a king's day is measured and reported, which the verse treats as ceremony.
gains.b: A working instance of how a king could know the season, which the couplet states only as advice.

note: Akananuru 84 sets a rainbow on the mountain under rain clouds as the season of return; verse 754 uses Indra's broken bow among dark clouds only as a likeness for blossom.
teaches: The same bow-on-the-hill image works as a season marker in the Sangam poem and as a bare comparison here.

gains.a: The verse lacks any use for the image beyond decoration; the poem shows it can mark a season and a waiting.
gains.b: The poem lacks the Indra's-bow naming that ties the rainbow to a god's weapon, which the verse supplies.

note: The hunters restate the couplet's crocodile, strong in deep water, and apply it to themselves in their forest.
teaches: The couplet's rule of ground is here voiced by the losing side, so the pair shows the rule cannot by itself predict a fight and must be weighed against the enemy's strength.

gains.a: the hunters' boast gains a known maxim of statecraft, so their defeat reads as a misapplied rule and not mere bluster
gains.b: the couplet gains a case where the strong-on-its-ground party still loses, a limit the bare maxim does not state

note: Verse 781 shows the dry forest in the heat; verse 795 shows the same wooded country green and dancing with peacocks.
teaches: The two verses show that the harsh forest of the first part gives way to a country of plenty as the party travels on.

note: Yugi's briefing of the ascetic and the portrait carry out the plan he forms in verse 129.
teaches: The plan to part the king from the queen is not carried by Yugi's own presence but by a woman and a picture, so the stratagem works through trust in others.

note: 2075 has the king resolve, after hearing the teacher, to strive for the final world; verse 355 has the counsellor repeat the sage's word that the hero will not be dazzled by kings' wealth and will reach the state of release by austerity.
teaches: The sage's early prediction that the king will refuse kings' wealth is kept in 2075, where the king himself declares the resolve.

note: Kural 603 says the family of the slothful fool perishes before him; Thirikadugam counts falling into sloth while one's dependants go hungry as painful to all.
teaches: The couplet gives the end of sloth, the family's death; the verse gives its moment, idling while those bound to one hunger, so the harm is seen as it begins.

note: The verse promises release for gifts to ascetics; the couplet says giving is good even if there is no higher world.
teaches: The verse pays giving in release, while the couplet holds that giving is good without any reward, so the two differ on why one gives.

gains.a: the promise of release for giving is tested by a rule that gives without any reward
gains.b: the couplet's giving for its own sake meets a doctrine that fixes a reward

note: Kural 1171's woman blames her eyes for showing her the man; verse 1020's youth melts as his eyes take in only a picture.
teaches: Love through the eyes does not need the person present, so the eyes' guilt in the couplet is wider than a meeting.

gains.a: The verse lacks the couplet's turn on the eyes themselves as the cause of sorrow, which names an instrument for the fire.
gains.b: The couplet lacks any case where the eyes meet only a painted form and still bring the sickness.

note: The Vidyadhara kings pay tribute and send word out of fear of Asvagriva's anger; Kural 680 says those of small domains, afraid, bow to the great and take what is offered.
teaches: The kings' tribute is the couplet's counsel carried out, but the minister then asks for the girl to be given, which shows how bowing to a great king can end in a marriage and not only in a payment.

gains.a: The tribute out of fear gets a name in policy: the small bowing to the great for what they can get.
gains.b: The couplet's bowing is shown running on from tribute into the giving of a daughter, a cost it does not name.

note: Kural 265 says penance (செய்தவம்) is undertaken because what one wants is got as one wants it; the city women say Civakan's mother must have done penance (செய்தவம் உடையள்) and ask on which mountain to do it so that they too may attain.
teaches: The couplet's frank promise that penance gets what one wants is taken literally by lovesick townswomen, who plan austerity on a mountain to win a man, showing how the Kural's motive can be bent toward the very desire the next couplet condemns.

gains.a: the women's talk is shown to repeat a recognised ethical doctrine of the fruits of penance, not merely a crowd's fancy
gains.b: the couplet's unqualified wording is shown to license a use, penance for erotic gain, that its own chapter would reject

note: The epic makes merit's fruit a throne and pleasure in this life, where the couplet calls virtue the companion that stays when you die.
teaches: Merit gathered earlier is repaid here as sovereignty, so the couplet's 'companion' is shown paying out in the same life it began.

gains.a: the verse's merit gets a test against the Kural's claim that virtue's worth is what survives death, which the verse alone does not state
gains.b: the couplet gets a case in which virtue's reward comes while the doer lives, a limit it does not state

note: In 257 Madanan told the council he settles things only by the sword, never by the mouth; in 2245 he falls at the mouth of a sword (வாளின்வாய்) in the war that the usurpation he urged has brought on.
teaches: The man who refused talk for the sword dies by the sword's 'mouth', so the epic answers his boast with its own wording and makes his death the fruit of his counsel.

note: The king had judged that women are not fit to be killed and spared the queen.
teaches: His mercy at 124 is read here as the cause of his death, so the poem asks whether sparing the guilty was a fault or a virtue.

note: Naladiyar 51 says that, as darkness rushes in when a lamp's oil runs out, evil takes its stand when good deeds are spent; 1057 sets the passing of good deeds beside the thickening of darkness at night.
teaches: The Naladiyar teaches the lamp-and-darkness figure as a rule; the epic turns it into a description of night, which shows how common the figure was.

gains.a: The verse gives the darkness-and-deeds figure without a rule, which the quatrain's lamp and oil supply.
gains.b: The quatrain lacks a scene in which the darkness is a real night around a sleeping city.

note: Kural 827 says the humble words of an enemy are like a bending bow; Kattiyankaran's letter bows, offers his life and calls Govindan lord.
teaches: The letter shows the bowed bow of the couplet in a full text, and Govindan's laughter (2148) shows the reader the couplet applied: the humbler the words, the plainer the threat.

gains.a: the epic letter gains a rule by which its humility is read as menace before the story confirms it
gains.b: the couplet gains a concrete instance with its parts in view: the professed loyalty, the false excuse, the invitation to come close

note: 3145 ends on the Lord's feet as the way over the sea of deeds; Kural 10 says those who reach the Lord's feet cross the sea of births.
teaches: Both place the Lord's feet beyond a sea, but the Cintamani names the water as deeds and the Kural as births, so the epic fixes on karma as the thing to be crossed.

gains.a: the sea is placed in a fuller tradition of birth as the sea to be crossed, so karma and rebirth are read together
gains.b: the couplet's sea of births is given a cause by the epic, since the water is made of deeds

note: Both compare a woman and her lover's view of her with the moon and its mark.
teaches: The Kural uses the moon's mark as the flaw her face does not have, while Civakan uses it as the figure of a bond that cannot be parted, so one image carries opposite values according to whether the lover is praising her face or swearing to their union.

gains.a: the epic verse gains the contrast that shows its moon-and-mark pledge reverses the usual praise, making the mark the point and not the blemish
gains.b: the couplet gains a counter-use that shows its image of the spot as a flaw is a choice, not the only reading of the moon

note: The Kural's woman says there is a sea of love but no safe raft to cross it; Kanakamalai finds her raft in the garland Civakan made.
teaches: The pair shows that the raft the couplet denies can be supplied by a token of the beloved, but only as a raft through the night, not a way out of the sea.

gains.a: the epic's raft is read against a known claim that love has none, which makes the garland's comfort pointed
gains.b: the couplet's abstract missing raft is given a concrete candidate, a love gift, and the epic's later failures of cooling test whether it holds

note: 3039 has the ascetics shed the milk of kindness on every life; Kural 30 names the virtuous, clothed in cool kindness to every being, as the true brahmins.
teaches: Both define the ascetic by his kindness to all lives, not by any robe or rite.

gains.a: the verse's milk of kindness gets a name for the sage whom it makes
gains.b: the Kural's kindness to every living thing gets the practice of an order that has put away hatred

claims.gist: a learned king who earns, guards and gives wealth becomes the protector of others
nothing is hard to those of spotless inner virtue
men of this earth, of a small life, cannot win the greatness of the Vidyadharas by waiting for a boon
a warrior slain fighting fairly is welcomed by the celestial women and goes to heaven
the Lord holds the whole world within his unbounded knowledge and guards it as the king of dharma
a king's standing rests on kin, lineage, learning, the discus and the finishing of what he plans
it is the duty of men to rescue those in danger
one who comes asking for something is slighted, whoever he is
a king secures his rule by marrying the daughters of hill chiefs and of powerful rulers
one's loss comes from one's own sin
what destiny brings cannot be undone and what it takes cannot be kept
what is due to one comes without being sought
days measured out to the living are devouring them, and small pleasures hide this
gems and gold do not follow the dead
the wealth of the earth is for those who do penance
karma waylays the soul like a robber and takes its eight qualities
those who do not praise the Jina do not reach release
letting go of attachment is the mark of the best
a life may end in the womb before birth
a restrained giver who feels the hurt of all lives gains knowledge and conduct and reaches lands of joy
A king's reign is to be marked by remission of dues and the ending of hunger, disease and enmity
the three jewels (அரதனத் திரயம்) give greatness and bring the release that cuts off birth
remedy sought after ruin has begun is useless, as it is to plant seed after the crop is lost
learning is true wealth and a support in grief, all other things being false
the body of flesh passes but the form of fame remains after death
the adorned body is a foul thing and no cause for pride
the Lord cut the four destroying karmas together and knows the three times
a king who hands his rule to another out of desire for his queen brings about his own ruin
a king without clarity about right dharma takes a harmful rite to be good
a king's life remains his only if he bows to the overlord's feet

note: The Kural's lover asks whether the lotus-eyed god's world is sweeter than sleep on a beloved's arms; the Vidyadhara king says even the endless pleasures of the Jain land of enjoyment are misery alone, and sleep in a lover's lap is the gods' own state.
teaches: The couplet leaves its comparison with heaven as a question, and the epic answers it outright, turning a lover's boast into a father's argument for giving his daughter in marriage.

gains.a: the king's maxim gains the akam voice behind it, the man who first set the embrace against heaven
gains.b: the couplet's open question gains an answer, and a use outside the lovers' scene, as a reason to marry a daughter

note: Vayuvegan kills a king and seizes his land; the hero kills him, as the king's weeding of the cruel in the couplet.
teaches: The couplet puts the punishment of the cruel in a king's hand; here a wandering prince does it, so the story shows the same duty fallen to whoever happens to be there.

gains.a: the hero's killing is read as the weeding-out of a cruel man
gains.b: the couplet's weeding is shown done by a prince with no throne

note: Tirumular says the subtle body eats the fruit in heaven and hell and then takes another body with the old deeds following; 2762 says the evildoer eats the harvest of deeds sown in the soul.
teaches: Both let the deeds ripen as an experience of hell, but the Saiva verse carries the sufferer on into a new birth by a subtle body, which the Jain verse does not say here.

gains.a: the verse's farming image of deeds gains the Saiva account of what survives to carry the deeds, the subtle body
gains.b: the Tirumanthiram verse gains a vivid account of what 'eating the fruit' means, in the hell scenes that follow

note: Vijayai's blessing that her son will destroy his old enemy (நுன் பழம் பகை) is fulfilled when Kattiyangaran's rule ends in the Manmagal ilampakam.
teaches: The epic's whole plot of revenge and restoration is set down at the cradle as a mother's word, two thousand verses before it comes true.

note: Kural 447 prizes counsellors who rebuke the ruler; 58 shows a court where no one proposes anything except at the king's hint.
teaches: The couplet praises the courtier who dares to rebuke, and the verse depicts a court where none speak unless prompted, which shows what the king gives up by having no one to correct him.

gains.a: The verse gains a measure that reveals its silent court as lacking the correction a ruler needs.
gains.b: The couplet gains a concrete court of obedient, fearless speakers, showing what its rebuking counsellors would stand against.

note: After the victory, 2327 had him enter the old city worshipped by its people; now, wedded, he rides into the street among kings with whisks and drums.
teaches: The victor's private return becomes a king's state procession, with the same city now seeing him as a husband and sovereign.

note: In 1609 Madhavan slips away from the angry queen; in 1613 her people trace him into the grove and bring him back by his cloth.
teaches: The jester's flight is undone by the queen's command, which shows who in the household has power over the king's companion.

note: The king says such excellence belongs only to a king or a twice-born; the couplet says the learned low-born outrank the unlearned high-born.
teaches: Read together they show the epic using learning as a sign that betrays hidden royal birth, the reverse of the Kural's use of learning to override birth rank; the conflict holds on reading the king's line as a general rule rather than a compliment.

gains.a: The king's remark is exposed as a claim about birth that the Kural explicitly denies, not just praise of a teacher.
gains.b: The couplet meets a narrative where its opponent's view is spoken by a sympathetic king and even happens to be right about the man in question.

note: The patikam says only that Civakan delighted in her for two months and then cut through the mountains and swiftly took the road; this run gives the night of that leaving from the side of the wife left behind.
teaches: The patikam's swift departure is told from the hero's road, and only here does the epic count its cost, a wife who blames birds, lamps and her own eyes and falls to the floor.

note: Tirumular says there is no dharma that leaves out the Veda, and the wise gave up disputation and recited it to gain release; Neelakesi argues by inference that the Veda is made and, being joined to killing, drives its followers to evil births.
teaches: The two verses disagree both on the Veda and on method: Tirumular sets recitation above argument as the way to release, while Neelakesi makes argument the test that the Veda fails.

note: Vikraman's grief at having no child (verse 21) meets the Kural's praise of children who know what should be known, and the epic gives him a sister's son in place of his own.
teaches: The epic shows that the heir the Kural praises can come by a sister's son, not only by birth, and that the want of a child can lead to renunciation.

gains.a: The verse's grief at being childless gets a standard by which an heir is valued, which the epic's king only feels as loss.
gains.b: The couplet's praise of knowing children gets a case where the lack of one's own child is answered by taking a nephew as heir.

note: Kural 9 praises the one of eight qualities; 3092 praises the one who has cut four deeds together and knows the three times.
teaches: One text counts a Lord by eight qualities and the other by four deeds cut, so the reader sees two different measures of the same worshipped figure.

gains.a: a Lord counted by four destroyed karmas is seen beside a Lord counted by eight qualities
gains.b: the Kural's eight qualities, left unnamed, can be compared with a Jain account of what is cut and known

note: 1766 has the drum fix the day and call the kings; 1768 shows kings and others arriving round the city.
teaches: The proclamation is answered by the arrival, and the crowd outruns the invited kings.

note: At 123 the king in human form held a sword and let it fall; the bird, with only a beak, strikes the lover's eyes.
teaches: The restraint of the man and the blow of the bird together show that the epic does not make the king's patience a trait of his soul but of that one body.

note: In Akananuru 38 the friend imagines the hill man finding the swing, the pool and the reaped field empty, and regrets that she forgot to tell him 'the high hill crowned with that white waterfall is our village'. Ainthinai Aimpathu 12 is that telling: the guarding is over, and this village by the clean waterfall is our place.
teaches: The longer poem shows the cost of not telling him where the house is when the field closes, and the quatrain makes the telling itself, so the pair shows pointing out the village by its waterfall as the friend's expected move at harvest, the step that turns field meetings toward the house.

note: 1611 has the queen turn to leave and the king bow with his crown at her feet; Kural 1302 says sulking is like salt in right measure and a little more ruins it.
teaches: The king's bow comes before the sulk can become too much, so the scene shows the couplet's measure kept.

gains.a: The quarrel gains a gauge: the Kural's salt means the queen's anger is a proper amount of love's seasoning, which the king answers at once.
gains.b: The couplet gains a ruler for whom the cost of ending the sulk is a bowed crown, making the measure a matter of rank.

note: Tirumanthiram 1006 says that worship brings Indra's wealth, then the siddhis, then release; verse 272 says the world of the gods is reached by the true word and great austerity or by unslackening rule.
teaches: The same prize, Indra's world, is reached by worship in one and by one's own austerity or rule in the other, so the paths differ over whether a god's favour is needed; the conflict holds if Tirumular's worship counts as asking his grace.

gains.a: A path that asks for no god: the epic's way depends on the doer's truth, austerity and rule.
gains.b: A way to see worship as one route among several to Indra's wealth, which the epic's king-or-ascetic choice does not need.

note: Akananuru 59: on the road for wealth an elephant bends a yaa tree so its young mate can eat, yet the man forgets her; Kuruntokai 255: on that road the elephant strips the yaa tree to feed its whole hungry herd, and the men went to fulfil their duty.
teaches: The same road-sign is turned two ways by the friend: feeding one mate in Akananuru 59 shames the man who forgets his wife, while feeding the whole herd in Kuruntokai 255 matches the man's duty to his household, so the friend can use the elephant to reproach the journey or to justify it.

note: Verse 49 holds the soul to be other than the body that joins it; verse 72 reports those who say the dead are not reborn.
teaches: The denial in 72 is the denial of the premise 49 had stated, so the dismissal there rests on a claim made earlier in the book.
