note: The Kural's woman says desire's axe breaks the door of nirai bolted with shame; the princess says the youth has opened the door of her hard nirai and entered her heart's guarded chamber.
teaches: The Cintamani keeps the Kural's door of nirai but changes the breaker from desire to the man and the outcome from lament to a vow of marriage, so the breach of self-containment can be the start of a lawful bond.

gains.a: the princess's image is read with the Kural's exact logic of door and bolt, so her 'hard nirai' is a guarded virtue, not a figure of speech
gains.b: the couplet's breach, spoken by a woman already in love, gains a first-sight case in an unmarried girl, where it leads to the garland instead of grief

note: 1464 shows a king who rode elephants under the umbrella brought low; Naladiyar 3 says kings on elephants fall when their deeds turn against them.
teaches: The quatrain gives the cause as the king's own deeds and the verse gives the scene, so the pair joins the rule to a particular fall.

gains.a: 1464 states only that glory ends and does not name why; the quatrain supplies deeds that turn against a king as a reason.
gains.b: The quatrain states the rule in general; here a named king in a battle is the case it applies to.

note: Kural 10: only those who reach the Lord's feet swim the great sea of births. Vijayai asks that the Jina's dharma and her newborn son be her raft across a sea of sorrow.
teaches: The epic keeps the Kural's sea and crossing but moves the sea from rebirth to present grief and doubles the raft, placing a mother's hope in a child beside the lord's dharma.

gains.a: Vijayai's plea gains the doctrinal sea and swimmer the couplet fixes.
gains.b: The couplet gains a human raft alongside the divine one, which it does not allow for.

note: 1902 has the crowned king bow until the gem-crown touches the earth; Kural 9 says a head that does not bow at the feet of the eight-quality one is a useless organ.
teaches: The couplet's useless head becomes the crowned one of a king who sets power on the ground, which shows what the bow costs a ruler.

gains.a: The king's bow gains a stated reason, that a head which will not bow is as dead as a sense that does not sense.
gains.b: The couplet gains a ruler whose head carries a crown, so the bow costs a pride the couplet's speaker does not mention.

note: The Kural bids one cling to the one free of clinging in order to let clinging go; the Cintamani's hymn says love wears the karmas away and yet, being love, cannot end them.
teaches: The couplet makes attachment to the unattached the way out of attachment, while the Jain hymn admits that very attachment and counts it still a bond, so the two disagree on whether devotion can itself be the final cause of freedom, on the reading of காதல் as love of the Jina.

gains.a: a sharp foil showing that its paradox denies what the couplet affirms, devotion as the last step to freedom
gains.b: an objection the couplet does not face, that clinging to the unattached remains a clinging

note: 2845 gives knowledge, faith and conduct as the three that make release; 3074 turns knowledge into the chariot, mercy into armour and virtue into the sword.
teaches: The ilampakam's plain teaching of the three jewels is here made into an army, so the reader sees what the three do and not only that they are three.

note: In 67 women plunge into the country pools and their girdle strings break and scatter; in 2662 the defeated women in the king's pool give up their girdles and earrings to him.
teaches: The scattering of gold that the landscape verse shows as nature's wealth is shown here as a gift laid at the king's feet, which changes whose ornament it is.

note: 1436 names knowledge, right faith and conduct whose fulness ends both kinds of deed; 1437 has the hearers rise and take the path of release.
teaches: The doctrine of the three jewels is tested at once by its hearers, and the epic settles the debate by conversion rather than by any further argument from the ascetics.

note: The dresser takes off the bride's tusk studs and plain ear-rings and sets wedding ear-ornaments (கடிப்பு); the herdswomen take off the herd girl's gold ear-studs and gem pendants and set the same auspicious கடிப்பு with a small simple adornment.
teaches: The same step in the rite is done in the same words for a king's daughter and a herd girl, showing the rite fixed while the stuff of the ornaments shows the wealth of the house.

note: 1538 has attendants tie the bride's fine cloth and gem girdle for the wedding; 1753 has her daughter tie the same silk and gem girdle for ball-play.
teaches: The girl's self-dressing repeats her mother's bridal dressing and shows the game as a step toward marriage.

note: Shamed by the verdict, Suramanjari withdraws under a vow; the Kural says those like the yak that will not live once its hair is lost give up life when honour is lost.
teaches: The epic offers a third path to the couplet's choice between life and honour: a withdrawal from the world that keeps the wound open and names the act that will restore her honour.

gains.a: Suramanjari's seclusion is seen as a measure of honour like the yak's, not mere sulking
gains.b: the couplet's stark alternative of death gains a case where honour lost is answered by a vow with terms, which the couplet does not imagine

note: Naladiyar 331 shows people revelling in the world's net while Death waits to seize them, like a turtle sporting in the pot over the fire; Cintamani 376 makes Death the one who laid the net and the revellers people who know it is there.
teaches: Set beside the quatrain, the epic's step is to take away the excuse of ignorance: the turtle does not know its state, but the teacher's 'we' know Death's net and still turn to pleasure, so folly becomes a failure of will.

gains.a: the teacher's irony (பெரியமே) is sharpened by the quatrain's ignorant turtle, against which knowing captives look worse
gains.b: the quatrain's net and killer gain an agent who sets the snare deliberately and an exit it does not name, austerity

note: Both turn on the same word. In 594 wealth seeks out அசைவிலா energy. In 371 அசைவின்மை is itself produced by a fate of gain.
teaches: The causal arrow reverses, so the question becomes whether steadfastness is one's own at all.

note: 1783 has the herald call the kings in and the drums sound; 1784 has the first king, of Ayodhya, enter.
teaches: The call is answered at once by named kings entering one after another, so the roll-call of kings is the proclamation's result.

note: Tirumular says those who grieve the ascetics who taught the mantra are born as dogs (சுணங்கன்); the Cintamani's dog (சுணங்கன்) is raised to a god's birth by the mantra heard from Civakan.
teaches: Read together, the teacher's mantra decides birth in both directions: offending its teachers sinks a man to a dog, and receiving it lifts a dog to a god, so the same word names the bottom of the scale in both books.

gains.a: the Saiva warning that the dog's birth is itself the fruit of offending the bearers of the mantra, which deepens the narrator's 'no good in it'
gains.b: a story in which the same creature climbs back up the scale by the same means that, in the couplet, cast men down

note: Kural 57 says the guard of confinement is useless and the best guard is the one women's own நிறை keeps; 1597 says women do not hold their restraint within (உண்ணிறை யுடைய வல்ல) and yield to pressing.
teaches: The Kural trusts the guard inside a woman, the epic's hero denies most women have it, and the story of this chapter is offered as his proof, so the two texts disagree on whether a woman's restraint can be relied on at all.

gains.a: a precise contrary, the Kural's நிறை, that shows the hero's view as a position taken against a known teaching
gains.b: a narrative challenge to its trust, in which a wife thought steadfast is not

note: Soolamani 199 has deeds breed deeds until a refuge is reached; Tirumanthiram 120 has a teacher make the seeds of births like seeds touched by fire, which will not sprout.
teaches: Both see rebirth as a growing seed; the Jain verse tells how the chain runs, the Saiva verse how it is cut at the root by a teacher.

gains.a: it gains a picture of how the chain can be stopped at the seed, which the sage only says is by reaching a refuge
gains.b: it gains the chain that the scorched seed stands against, deeds producing deeds through their fruit

note: In 703 Acuvakanthan calls the prince a child; in 707 the prince says the king is a child if the lion is not killed.
teaches: The same insult is thrown back, with the prince staking his word where the king staked nothing.

note: 1713 lets the drums sound for the birth, and Naladiyar 23 says drums that sound for a wedding can sound the same day for the bridegroom's funeral.
teaches: The rejoicing of the birth is set beside the quatrain's warning that the same drum serves joy and death, so the festival is read against impermanence.

gains.a: The drumming for the royal birth gains a darker echo, that what is loud with joy is a loan, which the poem does not say here.
gains.b: The quatrain gains a scene of joy at its height, a king's son born to a palace city, in which its warning has the most to undo.

note: 1629 says the lord hides by a stratagem; 1630 shows the stratagem, an art that makes darkness a curtain, with Madhavan beside him.
teaches: The hiding is done by a magic art and with a companion, so the king does not slip away but joins the women's game unseen.

note: Ninety-six armed men are put inside the machine in 40; in 49 they break out as it becomes a fighting host.
teaches: The machine of 40 is shown to be a hiding place for troops, and 49 is the moment it is turned into one.

note: 1992 grades a gift by the receiver's fault-lessness, the giver and the gift; Tirumanthiram 508 sends giver and receiver to hell if the receiver does not bow in worship of the Lord.
teaches: The two ask what makes a receiver worthy and give different answers, so one cannot tell from either how to judge a fit receiver.

gains.a: The Jain scheme lacks a test of worship: it names no receiver whom a gift would harm the giver by reaching.
gains.b: The Saiva verse lacks a grading of gifts and a role for the giver's own qualities, which it reduces to the receiver's bowing.

note: 2082 makes wealth a woman who leaves the men she has joined and always wants someone new; Kural 332 says great wealth comes like a crowd gathering at a dance hall and goes like the crowd breaking up.
teaches: The couplet's crowd goes without any reason in itself; in 2082 the going has a will, the goddess who tires of her man and wants another.

gains.a: The goddess's leaving gets an image of a crowd that comes and goes for its own reasons and owes the owner nothing.
gains.b: The crowd gets a person with a wish behind its going, so wealth's departure reads as desertion and not only as an end.

note: 2958 recalls Padumai restored after the snake bite that 1285 shows him curing with his spells.
teaches: The cure that made him a hero is cited as the proof that his love gave life, so leaving takes it back.

claims.gist: the merit of former deeds is what joins this pair
one who delights in rule and does not take up dharma has no good death and an uncertain next birth
teachers who speak what is not good are mothers who give birth to many deeds
a king who keeps his people from blame is followed by other kings
a king must not speak even one false syllable, for fear of losing fame
a woman's birth is a wavering, unsettled lot, made sweet only by union with such a man
a king is wiser to put aside grief for a dead wife than to go on weeping
kings who give up the violence of rule and renounce without desire wash away their own karma by austerity
a ruler must first overcome six classes of foe
fortune leaves a king sunk in pleasure without warning
penance wears away the deeds of the past
desire is a poison that one has been eating, and tapas is its cure
an ascetic must wither the five senses and keep from lying, killing, theft and lust
the Jina's wheel of dharma guards life and clears the world's darkness of hunger, hatred and disease
the rite of eating flesh sends the dead king and his mother to a good world
the valour that conquers the world is a lesser thing than the king's renunciation
a king who gives himself to women and has no learned counsellors is out of control like a rutting elephant under an ignorant rider
those who abandon their wives for other men's wives fall into hell
youth and kinship are fleeting and the mind should not rest on them
the fitting course is to let go of the bonds of the mind
gain of wealth depends on fortune, not on travel and toil
tapas should be practised in preference to toil for wealth
disgust for pleasure clears a mind muddied by love
the senses fail and the lover dies in the beloved's arms
the ascetic is unmoved by praise and by scorn
the ascetic's heart is stored with the meanings of the Anga scriptures
the fire raised for the rite stands as the god before whom the bride is given
the ascetic guards every living being with compassion
the nectar of release is what the all-knowing one teaches
a foe is to be tested and known before action is planned against him
one who fattens his body by eating meat dwells in hell, and one who lets the body waste by abstaining becomes a god
to give up meat and become a god is the right course
the Lord of renunciation destroyed Desire and Death, and worship of his feet is for the end of births
a wife's part is to guard her husband from the blame that has befallen him and spread his fame
craving of the senses drowns beings and karma makes them wander
the Lord has gone beyond birth and rejected the unstable world
the lord has ended birth, old age and death
he taught the six substances
parents who give a girl only for the groom's side's sake leave her grieving
singing the Jina's qualities stops karma from settling

note: 2939 says we begin dying from the day we are born and knowledge is useless when one shakes at the end; 2616 has Vijayai say we are born not knowing our days and cover our eyes only when the cow is milked.
teaches: The mother's warning in the first sermon returns in the king's own words to his wives, so the doctrine is passed down rather than invented.

note: Both are the woman telling her friend that the rainy season he promised has come without him; the colophon files 183 under paalai and 194 under mullai.
teaches: The pair shows the colophon thinai following different cues for one situation: 183 is labelled by the road he crossed and 194 by the fields at home, though both speak from the waiting house in the rains.

note: After the first great battle Civakan made a gold image of the Jina, gave wealth and put away the sin of the battlefield with lament; after the final battle he bows to the Jina and flings out gold before putting on his royal ornaments.
teaches: Read with 820, the morning worship and gift of 2357 are not ornament but the same rite of expiation after killing, now made the first act of the new king's day.

note: The gods watch the goddesses dance and still take their fill of fortune without being content; the opening of the ilampakam says the hero has lost his wish for women whose beauty makes the heavens bow.
teaches: The sermon's heavenly pleasures supply the reason for the hero's turn from women in the opening: even the gods' unlimited enjoyment does not satisfy.

note: ஏதிலர், the 'stranger', has been her word for him in the town's mouth, in 1129 and 1130. In 1300 the same word is used for a stranger, and now the one who isn't one's own is one's own heart.
teaches: By the end, the outsider is inside.

note: Mastering a king's must elephant brings Civakan the usurper's threat to brand him a thief with the elephant's tusk in 1121, and a lawful king's assembly's acclaim here.
teaches: The same feat earns punishment under Kattiyangaran and honour under Tadamittan, so the epic makes the court's response to Civakan's prowess a measure of the ruler, not of the deed.

note: The ministers' counsel to a grieving king meets Kural 638 on a minister's duty to speak to a king who will not listen.
teaches: The Kural rule covers a king who destroys good counsel, but the epic shows a king who accepts counsel and is still deceived because the advisers' facts are false.

gains.a: the ministers' speech gains a named duty, so that their advice reads as a minister's task and not only comfort
gains.b: the couplet gains a case in which good counsel is taken and yet rests on a false premise, a test the couplet does not make

note: Kattiyankaran wept and joined his hands over Saccandan's body; his letter now protests that the blame of that death is false.
teaches: The usurper's tears at the pyre and his wounded innocence in the letter are one performance in two forms, which is why the reader, and Govindan, can see through the letter at once.

note: The hounds loosed in 265 to seize flesh are shown in 279 not coming near the ascetic.
teaches: The weapon that the king relied on is turned back by the very one it was loosed on, so the story shows his force failing before his remorse begins.

note: The merchant could not say why five hundred women sing daily at the temple; Dharanisundari gives the cause.
teaches: The merchant's wonder is only a wonder until the women speak, showing the poem makes a marvel into a wrong that the hero is to put right.

note: The couplet says the bond between the lover and the girl is that between body and life; the epic has the husband leave his sleeping wife as a good life leaves the body.
teaches: The couplet's simile is a promise that the two cannot part; the epic takes the same simile literally, so the husband's going is a death for the wife, which is the cost the couplet's image leaves unstated.

gains.a: the departure simile is read as the turning of a known love image, the lovers as body and life, into a picture of loss
gains.b: the couplet's image is shown to cut both ways: if he is her life, his leaving makes her a lifeless body

note: Both name the Jain god by his qualities: the Cintamani's ஓவாது நின்ற குணத்து and தேவாதி தேவன், the Charana's litany with குணவதன், குணப்பெருங் கோமான், தேவன், and also சங்கரன் ஈசன் சயம்பு.
teaches: The Silappathikaram's Charana absorbs Saiva and Vedic titles into the Arhat's praise, while the Cintamani's invocation keeps to self-won bliss and qualities, so two Jain epics show two strategies, inclusive litany and bare definition.

note: Gunamalai's parrot answers her plea and flies as her envoy to Civakan; Padumai's myna, swan, peacock and lamp neither stopped him nor will tell where he went.
teaches: Set beside the parrot that carried Gunamalai's love, Padumai's mute household creatures show the same convention emptied: the love-messenger exists only when the lover is still within reach.

note: Vijayai tells diners to think of austerity, not riches, as they eat milk-rice from gold bowls; the Naladiyar says the fool who hoards his wealth and dies is laughed at by the wealth itself.
teaches: The epic says wealth is not a thing to rely on at the table; the Naladiyar says what wealth does to the hoarder, and together they show that gifts and penance are what the dying keep.

gains.a: the verse's call to austerity gets a figure of wealth laughing at its owner
gains.b: the Naladiyar's hoarder is set at a banquet table in a king's palace, where the temptation is not stinginess but ease

note: Pradyotan pleads the tie of uncle and nephew; the couplet tells a man not to presume on kin degree with a king.
teaches: Here the stronger party pleads kinship and not the lesser, which shows the couplet's warning running the other way once the king has wronged his kinsman.

gains.a: the plea of kin is seen as a way to cover a wrong and not as a sign of equal standing
gains.b: the couplet is tested where the one pressing kin degree is the king himself

note: Kural 780 calls a death that fills the eyes of one's patron with tears worth begging for; 2240's warriors have paid their debt of the red rice, and the only ones who cry over them are jackals.
teaches: The epic keeps the Kural's logic of a death owed to the lord but removes the weeping patron who gave that death its worth, leaving the debt paid with no one to mourn it.

gains.a: the Kural gives the epic's 'debt of red rice' its moral frame, a death owed in return for being sustained
gains.b: the couplet's patron's tears are shown to be absent on the actual field, where the howling of jackals takes their place

note: 79 shows youth as a fire kindled in women; Tirumanthiram 180 has a man recall being sweet as cane juice to women and now bitter as the kanjiram fruit.
teaches: The epic shows only the rising stage of desire's arc, and Tirumular supplies the other end, so together they place the princes' present blaze on a curve that ends in the speaker's bitterness.

gains.a: The epic's fire of youth gets the end of its arc, which the verse does not show.
gains.b: Tirumanthiram 180 gets the beginning of its curve, the stage and the women's fire from which its speaker later falls.

note: A war of men without trickery is proposed; the Pandya Kudumi proclaims dharma to the weak before battle.
teaches: Both limit war, one by limiting means, the other by sparing those who cannot fight.

gains.a: The proposal gains a second sort of limit, protection of non-combatants, which it does not name.
gains.b: The poem gains a limit on means, no trickery between combatants, beside its limit on who may be harmed.

note: Naladiyar says a wife married on a fixed day, with the drum beaten that many may know, is the wife a man should keep to; the epic shows that drum beaten from an elephant and the day set by an astrologer.
teaches: The Naladiyar's drum and fixed day are the public face of a marriage, which the epic acts out as a city-wide command.

gains.a: the epic's drum is given its moral weight, since a bond announced to all is the bond that shuts the husband off from another's wife
gains.b: the Naladiyar's drum and fixed day, only named in the quatrain, get a full royal scene: the herald, the elephant, the seven days of orders

note: Naladiyar 3 says that even kings who rode in state under the umbrella fall when their deeds turn against them; 2371 seats the victor on the lion throne in the full pomp of such a king, after the usurper's fall.
teaches: The throne scene stands on the ground the quatrain describes: the pomp the winner now enjoys is what the usurper lost, so the crowning is shown as one turn of a wheel, not a rest.

gains.a: The enthronement gains a warning that the seat is held only while deeds support it.
gains.b: The quatrain gains a case in which the fallen king's rival, not death, is the agent of the fall.

note: The god gives Civakan three mantras because Civakan once whispered the five padas into the dying dog's ear (செல்கதி மந்திரம் செவியிற் செப்பிய).
teaches: The mantra that carried a dying dog to a god's birth comes back to the hero as mantras of power for his road, so the epic lets an act of compassion bear its fruit in this same life through the very being it saved.

note: Kural 363 says there is no fine wealth like not wanting, here or hereafter; Pazhamozhi 273 uses the same word வேண்டாமை to say that a king's servant who asks nothing even in hardship is given all he wants.
teaches: Together they show the renouncer's highest wealth being turned into a courtier's method: the Kural's not-wanting is its own reward, while Pazhamozhi makes it the means by which a king's servant is given everything, so the same virtue serves release and preferment.

note: The Kural says the cows' yield fails when the guardian does not guard; the epic shows the king's herd driven off while the king sits fanned on his throne, and 437-438 his army breaks.
teaches: The pairing turns the Kural's cows into the actual herd of the realm: the raid becomes the first public proof that the usurper cannot guard, and clears the place for Civakan, who will.

gains.a: the cattle raid gains a political sense beyond adventure: it measures Kattiyankaran as guardian
gains.b: the couplet's abstract link between guarding and the yield of cows gains a concrete scene of what failure to guard looks like

note: Kural 360 says pain perishes when even the names of desire, anger and confusion perish; verse 330 names dharma, giving up anger, knowledge and the vow as what to do.
teaches: The couplet names what must perish and the epic's last verse names the practices that make it perish.

gains.a: the verse lacks the three faults of desire, anger and confusion that the couplet names
gains.b: the couplet lacks the practices of dharma, knowledge and keeping a vow

note: Kural 618 says lacking fortune is no one's disgrace; Pazhamozhi 236 says that men who reach a generous king and still get nothing are not to be called dull or small, since gain comes by one's lot.
teaches: The couplet's general absolution becomes a defence of a particular figure, the empty-handed petitioner at court, and the pair shows the Kural's line on blame used to protect a man from the court's contempt rather than to urge him to work.

note: 1839 states for everyone the thought that 1827 reports of the rejected kings: the fruit of deeds is what comes.
teaches: The kings' private resignation is the lesson the poet then gives to all readers, so the swayamvara scene is built to carry it.

note: In the Pattupattu the fishers sing the kurinji tune, the hill people wear neythal chaplets and the tracts are said to gather under one umbrella; in verse 33 each kind of woman wears the flowers of her own tract.
teaches: Both poems sort a land by its peoples and flowers, but the Sangam poem mixes the tracts to show one king's rule, while the epic keeps each tract's women with her own flower and ends in a catalogue.

gains.a: The verse gets from the Pattupattu the reason such sorting of peoples matters, the unity of a realm under one ruler, which the epic verse leaves unstated.
gains.b: The Pattupattu passage gets the women of each tract, whom it does not describe, as the carriers of the tract's flowers.

note: The king reads the crown, garlands and shoot but will not speak of the falling tree; at 267 he tells the queen that all she dreamed that night has come to fruit.
teaches: The withheld half of the dream was the king's own death, so his kindly silence at the reading becomes, at the fall of the city, an admission that he knew.

note: The Naladiyar's lamb nibbles the garland in the slaughter ground; here pairs of animals are brought together at the shrine as victims.
teaches: The quatrain uses the victim's unawareness as an image for the thoughtless, and the epic shows the gathered victims themselves, so the image can be read back onto the sacrifice.

gains.a: the gathered animals are seen as victims who do not know their end, which the verse does not say
gains.b: the lamb's image is tied to an actual rite and its scale: pairs of five kinds, then humans

note: Both verses use the lion bound in a spider's thread for Udayanan's capture.
teaches: The image first comes in Vayantakan's report of the capture and returns in the captor's own letter, so the same fall is told once by the losers and once by the winner.

note: In 2840 the pair are bound by the garland of desire in the pleasure that their gifts earned; in 2610 Saccandan, swallowed by pleasure, would not come out and fell.
teaches: Pleasure that is the fruit of merit is still a bond, and the story of the old king shows what happens when one stays bound.

note: 1921 turns the soul like a cart wheel through four states; Naladiyar 2 turns wealth like a cart wheel, never level with anyone.
teaches: The same cart wheel is used for what turns beneath a person in Naladiyar and for the person who is turned in the Soolamani.

gains.a: The wheel of 1921 gains a lesser double: the turning of wealth within one life as a small copy of the soul's turning through births.
gains.b: The quatrain gains a larger turning behind its wheel: wealth turns like a wheel because the one who holds it is turned by deeds from birth to birth.

note: Yugi uses the king's own rutting elephant to break the king's hold, as the couplet binds a rutting elephant with another.
teaches: The Kural's image of one task serving another is shown as a plan that also costs lives.

gains.a: the stratagem is named as a type: a means turned on its owner, with a price the couplet does not state
gains.b: the couplet's image of an elephant bound by an elephant is acted out with a real elephant and a real rescue

note: Naladiyar 41 says that if skin the size of a fly's wing is torn from the body a stick is needed to drive off crows; 1584 opens the body and sets crows at the eyes.
teaches: Both poets end the lover's gaze with crows at the body, but the epic uses the image on the living woman standing before the hero, turning a general memento into a refusal spoken to her face.

gains.a: a traditional image whose force a Tamil reader already knows, which lets the hero's rebuff be brief
gains.b: evidence that the crow at the torn skin was a stock figure that a narrative poet could place in a scene

note: 1669 sends the king to the pool to see the women bathe; 1674 has the bathing turn into a water-fight with him.
teaches: The watcher he meant to be becomes a target, so the pleasure goes from looking to joining.

note: 1628 calls the wealth of sweet-smiling sons sweet to all; Kural 63 says people call children their wealth because their wealth comes through their own deeds.
teaches: The poem's child is a tree that has no deeds, so its sweetness comes wholly from rearing, which tests whether the couplet's reason is the only one.

gains.a: The wedding gains a reason for the parents' joy that lies in the child's own deeds, which the plant cannot supply, so only the rearing is left to explain it.
gains.b: The couplet gains a case in which the child is a plant and cannot earn anything, so the joy it names is shown to rest at least partly on the care given.

note: Kural 378 says drily that the destitute would renounce if only fate let what they must suffer pass them by; 347 has a queen stripped of everything reach the ascetics' grove because a former-birth deed made her suffer.
teaches: The epic takes up the case the couplet treats as hypothetical: the destitute queen does renounce, and the following verses show the couplet's point surviving the renunciation, since her fated grief for her son goes on inside the hermitage.

gains.a: the verse gains a test of whether entering tapas ends the suffering the narrator ascribes to ஊழ்வினை, which the Kural answers in the negative
gains.b: the couplet's ironic 'if' gains a concrete instance in which renunciation is chosen from loss, not from strength

note: The astrologer reads a night's dream as true knowledge of what will come; the Siddhar song says all he saw has turned into a dream, like moonlight on a forest.
teaches: One poem trusts a dream to show what is real in the future, and the other uses the dream as the name for the whole of what is seen, so the same word divides prophecy from unreality.

gains.a: The prophetic dream gets a view that holds waking sight itself to be dream-like, which unsettles the court's easy trust in the sign.
gains.b: The Siddhar's figure of dream as unreality meets a dream treated as sure foreknowledge, which shows what the figure is set against.

note: The Kural's lover says his bond with the girl is that of body and life; the narrator says Civakan and Vimalai became one life in two bodies because they never parted.
teaches: The epic makes the couplet's body-and-life bond conditional on never parting, and then has the husband part at the next dawn, which tests the image the couplet offers as a pledge.

gains.a: The narrator's formula gains the force of a pledge, so his departure in 1994 reads as a breach of it.
gains.b: The couplet, a lover's pledge with no sequel, is given a sequel that shows what such a pledge is worth when the lover is a wanderer.

note: Wisdom's remedy for the king's lost sense is to build a rare machine; at 272 the king tells the queen the vehicle is ready and she must go first.
teaches: The machine ordered as penance for the lust that cost the kingdom becomes the means of saving the heir, so the fault's remedy is escape rather than reform.

note: The Kural ranks the slackness of great joy below anger as a cause of ruin; in 47 the king goes on though omens and Vayantakan warn him.
teaches: The Kural's slackness is not ignorance: Udayana is told and warned, and in the verse it is his gladness at sight of the elephant that wins.

gains.a: a case where the heedless one has both omens and a friend's warning, so slackness is a choice made in delight, not a lapse of knowledge
gains.b: a story in which joy's slackness is shown over a few verses, before the trap closes on a king and a friend who knew better

note: The king mourning a body that was never found is set against the town that wails, buries and forgets in Tirumanthiram 145.
teaches: One poem shows grief for a real death that is quickly ended, the other grief for a false death that the king cannot end, so lament is shown to follow belief and not fact.

gains.a: the king's lament gains the ordinary course of mourning the song describes, against which his unfinished grief over a lie stands out
gains.b: the song gains a case of mourning for someone not dead, showing that a staged death can draw the same grief as a real one

note: The women of the verse are worn and pale from love itself; Naladiyar 17 tells a man not to crave a woman's spear-like eyes, since age will bend her.
teaches: The Naladiyar waits for age to wear a woman's beauty, but the epic shows love's own use wearing it at the bed, long before old age.

gains.a: The wan lips and thin shoulders read as the body's early decline, not just tiredness after love.
gains.b: A young case of the wearing it foretells, where no staff or grey hair is needed to show the same loss.

claims.gist: strength, wealth and beauty do not last; do not exult
humans of cruel livelihood and shrunken mind are base though in human form
a man gains himself by the penance he piles up with his own effort
At death the soul passes on and is born again as another
meditation burns both good and bad deeds and brings perfected, supreme bliss
when one's twofold deeds are spent, wealth perishes and no care can keep it
one who comes to the feet of the unborn one is not born again
matted hair, ritual bathing, sleeping on the ground and wasting the body win the highest state
bathing and bodily hardship do not yield release, or the bear would gain it
good conduct (சீலம்) is the fare that carries one across the river of sorrow
the deeds of a former birth alone work out what each person gains, and effort in the later birth does not bring what they have not earned
the learned love those whom fortune slights, and the sons should not trust her
the fruit of good deeds is itself poison; undivided bliss comes only by crossing the flood of deeds
one who cannot tell the fit from the unfit is not a true human being
the worth of a gift depends on the receiver, the giver and the gift
a householder's austerity is fasting on the new and full moon days and the eighth day while keeping conduct
worship is offering flowers, incense, sandal, powder and lamps to the feet of the Lord under the triple umbrella
fear of the wheel of births leads to renunciation and a compassionate conduct that ends in a state free of forgetting

note: Kural 9 says a head that does not bow at the feet of the one of eight qualities (எண்குணத்தான்) is useless; 961 vows to bow the head to no one but the one who removes the eight karmas (எண்வினை) and gives bliss, and sets aside the gods of desire.
teaches: The epic turns the couplet's positive command into an exclusion and fills its unexplained 'eight' with a count of karmas destroyed, so the Kural's open epithet is given a Jain content it does not itself state.

gains.a: a canonical model, the bowing head of the Kural's first chapter, for its refusal
gains.b: one reading of its undefined eight, together with the inference that the bow must be withheld from other gods

note: Kural 255 says that if one eats flesh hell does not open its mouth; 2770 shows the killers of beasts and fish thrown daily into a seething pit.
teaches: The couplet says that hell waits, and the epic shows what its mouth holds, so the reader sees the rule enforced by the pain of the killer, not by a judge's word.

gains.a: the verse's hell for killers gains the couplet's plain rule that eating flesh is itself the reason
gains.b: the couplet's 'hell' gains the epic's concrete view of the pit that waits for killers

note: After the ornaments cry that Death has come, the chowries, sandal fans and white parasol hide the girl for fear of what the graceless would do to the rolling world.
teaches: The screening is the household's answer to the danger the ornaments announce, so the verse before it is read as a threat to be guarded against and not praise only.

note: The Kural names not killing as the chief virtue; the king names the lack of mercy joined to seeking wealth and pleasure as his fault.
teaches: The king adds the motive of wealth and pleasure to the couplet's plain count of killing, so greed becomes part of the fault.

gains.a: The king's lament names the greed that drives the killing.
gains.b: The couplet gains a cause for the killing it forbids.

note: Kannaki's 'he who relieved the distress of the bird' repeats the Purananuru's praise formula for the Chola's ancestor (புள்ளுறு புன்கண் தீர்த்த).
teaches: The epic takes a genealogical compliment that a Sangam poet paid a Chola king and turns it into a legal precedent that a Chola woman holds against a Pandya, showing the ancestor-legend working as a standard of justice across kingdoms.

note: The goddess's slaughter-place recurs, once for the two youths and now for a flour cock struck by the king.
teaches: The same altar shows the poem's shift: from killing living victims to a substitute that still cries out, so the question is not only the victim but the act.

note: The Perumpanarruppadai's girls on sky-touching terraces move like peacocks rejoicing on a great hill's slope; the Cintamani's women on the mansion rows look like peacocks spreading their wings in the mist on a high hill.
teaches: The epic inherits the Sangam figure of terrace women as hill peacocks but makes the hill's mist out of the houses' own perfume smoke, turning a natural setting into manufactured luxury.

gains.a: the simile is traced to an older description of a port city's rich women
gains.b: the older image is shown surviving into the epics with its landscape replaced by the household

note: The hidden voice's blessing சீவ on the child's sneeze becomes, in 361, the name சீவகன் given him by his foster parents.
teaches: The hero's name is his lost mother's unseen blessing, given unknowingly a second time by the people who raise him.

note: Civaka Cintamani 215 makes a king heedless of a warning because an earlier-formed destiny rose in him; verse 358 has a counsellor name fate as the power over plans and still press counsel.
teaches: One epic makes fate the reason a king ignores counsel and the other makes it the reason counsel must be given with humility, so fate is shown as excusing the king in one and humbling the adviser in the other.

note: In Kalittokai 103 a herdsman wrenching a charging bull by the ear is likened to Mayon tearing the horse's jaw, and the herd girls will embrace only one who falls between the killer bull's horns; in 984 Civakan facing the elephant is likened to the gem-coloured lord facing the elephant sent to kill him, and Gunamalai's love follows.
teaches: Both poems make the man who masters a charging beast a Krishna figure whom a girl then loves, but the herders' bull-catch is a set contest whose price the community names, while the epic's rescue is unplanned and the girl chooses for herself.

gains.a: the older pattern of beast-taming as a bride-winning feat under a Krishna simile, which explains why the elephant fight leads straight into Gunamalai's love
gains.b: a later merchant-city version of the pattern in which the danger falls on the girl and the feat is a rescue, not a sport

note: 1783 has conches and a great drum sound the hour of the kings' entry; Naladiyar 23 says the drums of a wedding hall can be the funeral drums of that very day.
teaches: The same drums that open a wedding hold the thought that joy and loss come under one roof.

gains.a: The festival scene gains the quatrain's warning that its drums do not guarantee the happy end it announces.
gains.b: The quatrain gains a hall with real drums and a gathering, set before the bride has chosen.

note: On the commentators' reading, 37 treats the difference between rider and bearer as virtue made visible.
teaches: In 972, birth is the same for all beings, and distinction comes from what one does, which still leaves open whether the palanquin bearer's lot is deserved.

note: In the Kural the bangles slip from the wasting wrist and so announce the parting; Padumai pulls her bracelets off herself, blaming them for having come between her and his embrace.
teaches: The epic turns the couplet's involuntary sign into a deliberate act: the bangle no longer reports the grief but is punished as one of its causes.

gains.a: the convention of the bangle as the body's witness to separation, which makes her gesture legible
gains.b: a scene where the woman acts on the sign herself, so the bangle becomes a culprit rather than a gossip

note: Kural 338 says body and life part like a bird leaving its nest; 2754 says the life may be lost even before it leaves the womb, as a bubble bursts.
teaches: The Kural's picture begins at the nest-leaving; the epic starts earlier, with the embryo itself already at risk, so the loss is not only a late one.

gains.a: the verse's tale of the embryo gains the bird-and-nest image of parting that gives the loss its shape
gains.b: the couplet's parting of body and life gains an earlier start, in the womb, so the risk is shown to begin at conception

note: 56 says the king guards himself and the earth; 67 has the queens draw his mind from the work of ruling.
teaches: The king whose guarding of the world is praised is shown giving up the work of ruling to the queens' hold on his mind, so the poem sets one claim against the other.

note: The Kural orders the healer to find the disease, its cause and the means that subdue it, then act; Civakan names the causes and kinds of bite and the snake's type before he recites the cure.
teaches: The epic stages the couplet's order as a contest: a crowd of healers who act first and diagnose in contradiction all fail, and the one who examines cause and kind before acting succeeds, so the rule is shown by the cost of breaking it.

gains.a: Civakan's string of classifications gains a reason for being in the story: it is the diagnostic step the ethics book requires and the rival healers skipped
gains.b: the couplet's three steps gain a scene of failure beside success, which shows what is lost when treatment comes before finding the cause

note: The birth closes the pregnancy that began with the longing for the sky.
teaches: The longing, met by the flight, is followed by an easy birth and gifts, so the god's help is shown to have ended the trouble as well as quieting it.

note: 1850 turns on the body's filth to set aside kingly pride; Thiruppugazh 146 describes the same filth as a house of diseases and asks Murugan for grace.
teaches: The Jain king ends his disgust in a plan to leave and seek sages, while the Thiruppugazh ends the same disgust in a plea for a god's feet.

gains.a: The verse gains a different exit from the body's foulness, a god's grace in place of the sage's feet.
gains.b: The poem gains a king who draws the opposite practical conclusion from the same catalogue.

note: Naladiyar 160 says the base follow the rich as their one hope; verse 166 says people leave the rich once their sweetness turns.
teaches: Naladiyar shows the crowd that clings to wealth and the cuckoo shows it is not loyal, since it goes the moment the taste turns.

gains.a: A reason why the followers come: wealth is their only hope, which the cuckoo's simile does not state.
gains.b: A limit: the clinging lasts only while the sweetness lasts, which the quatrain does not say.

note: Thirikadugam 23 calls giving, faultless conduct and a mind free of possessions a rope that binds good deeds; Pazhamozhi 371 calls penance and aram practised falsely a rope that binds oneself.
teaches: The same rope image holds merit fast in Thirikadugam and holds the person fast in Pazhamozhi, so whether giving and penance are a rope that secures good or one that ties up the doer turns on sincerity.

note: Kural 1180: the town reads the secret of those whose eyes are beaten drums. Vimalai: her pallor beats out her desire like a drum (பறையாய் அறையும் பசப்பு).
teaches: The drum that proclaims a hidden love sits in the eyes in the couplet and in the skin's pallor in the epic, so the pairing shows the body as a whole betraying what restraint tries to keep.

gains.a: Vimalai's drum image is placed in an old line of thought about love that cannot be hidden
gains.b: the couplet's eyes gain a partner: the skin too announces the secret, and at first sight, not only after long love

note: Kural 29 speaks of the anger of those who stand on the hill of virtue, held even for a moment; 2107 counts the anger of the holy among things that do not stay.
teaches: Read together, the couplet's crux over whether such anger lasts only a moment or is unbearable for a moment is settled one way in the epic, which takes its brevity as proverbial enough to serve as a simile of speed.

gains.a: a source and authority for the figure of the holy man's short-lived anger, which the epic uses without explaining
gains.b: an early reader's construal of its disputed second line, showing the brevity reading in use as common speech

note: Marusi describes those under the king's umbrella as learned men bound by love who give their lives; Kural 389 says the world dwells under the umbrella of the king who bears bitter words.
teaches: The umbrella's shelter is filled by learned retainers who die for the king, and the couplet shows what keeps them there: a king who can bear their bitter words.

gains.a: The verse lacks the quality that holds the retainers, which the couplet supplies as a king's patience with bitter words.
gains.b: The couplet lacks a picture of who stands under the umbrella and what they give back, which the verse supplies.

note: The king says no one can turn back the ripening of deeds, then agrees to the rite meant to ward off the dream's evil.
teaches: The king's own words deny the rite he accepts, which shows his consent as weakness, not belief.

note: 513 shows the wealth Sitattan guarded and gathered (ஓம்பிப் படைத்த பொருள்) swallowed by the sea while he stands unhurried; Naladiyar 93 holds that wealth, however tightly held, leaves when the deeds that sent it run out.
teaches: Read with the quatrain, the wreck becomes the ending of a merit that had held the wealth, and the merchant's calm becomes the right response to a loss that no grip could prevent.

gains.a: the loss of the cargo gains a cause the verse does not give, the exhaustion of the merit that brought it
gains.b: the quatrain's abstract leaving of wealth gains a sudden, visible event and a man who loses it without clutching

note: Both name two kinds of deed; the Kural says they do not cling to those devoted to the Lord's praise, the verse names the two as what makes becoming, as something the lord taught.
teaches: The Kural states that the two deeds fall away from the devoted, and the Jain verse says it is the lord's own teaching of them that frees.

gains.a: the 'two deeds' are put in the Tamil devotional frame where deeds both good and bad are what binds, a reach the verse's own wording does not state
gains.b: the lord's praise gets a content: in the epic it is the lord's naming of the two deeds that the devotee takes up

note: Kural 226 says that ending the ruinous hunger of the destitute is where one should store wealth; the usurper's soldiers recall that Civakan fed them in a thousand pots when they were faint, and the telling makes the king fear him.
teaches: The pair shows the couplet's store paying out in loyalty: feeding hungry men lays up for Civakan the hearts of the usurper's own army, which is exactly why the giving is felt as a threat.

gains.a: the ethical frame in which the feeding is a virtue and not merely a political move
gains.b: a case where the return on feeding the hungry is political allegiance, and where that return endangers the giver

note: Verse 187 hails the god as walking above the lotus, as Kural 3 speaks of the one who walked upon the flower.
teaches: The same lotus-walker of the opening couplet appears here as an epic's praised Arhat, so the image carries a Jain form where the Kural leaves the Lord unnamed.

gains.a: The lotus-walker is given an addressee, a congregation that loves him though he feels no pleasure, which the verse's own words alone do not show for any named god.
gains.b: A worship scene in which the image sits within a story of devotees, where the couplet states it as a bare mark.

note: Kural 17 states that the sea itself depends on the cloud returning what it took; verses 32 to 38 narrate that loop, from clouds grazing the sea to the flood reaching the sea again.
teaches: Read together, the couplet's abstract dependence becomes a full itinerary, and the epic's long description gains its shape: it is a circuit of giving back, not a string of pictures.

gains.a: a reason for its sea-to-sea ordering: the run enacts a return the couplet says the world depends on
gains.b: the intermediate stages the couplet skips: mountain, falls, sluices and fields through which the returned water passes

note: The ministers name his elephant-taming and his veena as his glory; in 48 he plays the veena at the decoy.
teaches: The skill that makes a man formidable is also his weak point, since his veena is what carries him to the trap.

note: In Kural 1311 the woman refuses his chest because all women feast on him with their eyes; Suramanjari refuses a chest many embrace like the Ganges.
teaches: The Kural's sulking pretext is that other women merely look at him, but in a polygamous epic where the hero has already married several wives the same refusal names a fact.

gains.a: Suramanjari's complaint is placed in the oodal convention, so it reads as play that leads to reunion
gains.b: the couplet's mock charge is seen with a literal referent, which shows how close the convention runs to real grievance

note: The poet says a desiring mind outruns counsel; the verse says even learned men and yogis cannot turn a mind once bewildered.
teaches: The queen's fall is made one case of a general weakness that knowledge and attainment do not guard against.

gains.a: the queen's loss of restraint is set beside the learned and the yogis, which makes her case a human one and not only a woman's
gains.b: the verse's claim that attainment gives no protection gets a case where even a queen with every comfort is undone by one night's song

note: Civakan once bade the forest hunter give up meat, honey and toddy; now a wayfarer bids him give up lust, drink and meat.
teaches: The teacher becomes the taught, and the triad changes as it is aimed at him: honey drops out and lust comes in, the vice of a man who has just left a bride.

note: The couplet makes one day pass like seven for those waiting for a return; the epic's girl, told 'tomorrow', asks her parrot whether tomorrow is near or far.
teaches: The pair shows that a promised day of return does not shorten the wait but makes it measurable, and the epic turns the couplet's arithmetic into a question the waiting woman cannot answer.

gains.a: Gunamalai's question gains the couplet's rule that the fixed day itself is what lengthens time for the one who waits
gains.b: the couplet's general waiting is given a scene, a comforter's 'tomorrow' and a parrot asked to say when it comes

note: Verse 304 says that kings of the earth, fearing the rival's anger, paid tribute and sent word; verses 663 to 665 show the same demand arriving at Podanam.
teaches: The tribute that 304 named as the rival's usual power is shown here in the act, and its list shows how much he asks of the one he treats as a vassal.

note: Her resolve to bind him with her garland is fulfilled when he takes it.
teaches: Together they show the binding she plans in private take effect only through his hesitant consent, so the exchange of garlands becomes a mutual tie rather than her gift alone.

note: The Kural says envy ruins fortune and leads one to a bad place; the verse shows only a new wife's fear of envy and the retreat to the temple.
teaches: The Kural describes envy's results, and the verse shows how its mere expectation sends a wife to the god instead of to the rival.

gains.a: the fear in the verse gets a name and a moral cost from the Kural's chapter on envy, which the verse leaves unsaid
gains.b: the Kural's abstract envy is given a household: a co-wife whose envy is presumed and never shown

note: Purananuru 20 says the Chera's guard is not shaken by omen birds coming or going; in the usurper's palace owls cry by day, blood rains and earth and sky shake.
teaches: Read together the two make portents a measure of rule: the praised king's realm is not shaken whatever the birds do, while the usurper's palace is shaken by every sign, though the epic does not itself say his usurpation is the cause.

gains.a: the epic's portents gain a puram standard by which a secure realm is one omens cannot move, which marks the usurper's as already lost
gains.b: the poem's claim gains its counter-case, a palace where the omens do strike, which shows what the praise of immunity is set against

note: 1712 shows Tivittan's son born in saffron-bright radiance; 1732 shows the Vidyadhara boy born with a face to shame the moon.
teaches: The two births are drawn with one image, the lit young body, which lets the later chapters set the two boys side by side as equals.

note: In 445 the keeper reports the priest's word that a Vidyadhara lord would come seeking a bride for the king's son; 1015 is the girl's portrait brought to that son.
teaches: A foretold match is finished not by the prophecy itself but by a go-between's practical acts, here a painter carrying a likeness to the groom.

note: In 951 the dog, given the five padas at its ear as it died, is reborn a god; in 3036, in the last ilampakam, those lying at the point of death to whom the ascetic's words are set at the ear appear at once as unaging gods.
teaches: The single rescue of a dog becomes, at the end of the epic, a general working of the teacher's word, so the early episode is shown to be the model case of a rule the work states only at its close.

note: Naladiyar 130 tells the heart that attachment to home and children is idle since nothing but good done goes with it; 2728 names the family itself as the fruit of that good and says it will be lost.
teaches: The quatrain makes the family a hindrance beside merit, while the verse makes the family a result of merit, so the reader sees that giving up the fruit and keeping the merit are different acts.

gains.a: the verse's tree of good deed, which only reports loss, gains the quatrain's directive that the heart should stop clinging and put its hope in good done
gains.b: the quatrain's contrast of home against good deed gains a case in which the home is itself the earlier good deed's yield, so renouncing it is spending, not rejecting, merit

note: Kural 1234: with the partner gone, the shoulders lose their old beauty (தொல்கவின்) and the bangles slip; Ainkurunuru 455: the shoulders, their bangles loosened, have lost their old beauty (தொன்னலம்) just as the rains begin that stop the kings' war.
teaches: The couplet states the wasting of the shoulders as the general mark of separation; the Ainkurunuru poem times it to the rains that end the campaign, so the slipping bangle becomes evidence that he is overdue, not only that he is away.

claims.gist: a match of unmingled families made by elders leaves the girl unable to refuse
only the lord free of desire, anger and greed is worth worshipping, not those who are ruled by them
adultery with a neighbour's wife is repaid in hell by a matching embrace of fire
royal ornaments are burdens to the one who would renounce
the liberated state has no parting, disease, old age, death or birth
great wealth in this world and heavenly enjoyment are the fruit of deeds, and people should remember this and keep to the right way
kings by their way are without fault
birth in a good family is hard to gain after escaping the low callings of killing
an envoy should be learned and able to speak both of kin and of the business
the ascetic's duty is to tell dharma to the king, whose own duty is the sceptre
a king who has been slighted may drive the offender's kin from their land
praise of the omniscient one removes the wavering of the mind
a creature that dies in samadhi is reborn as a god
the king's rule and the enjoyments of the earth do not last
by knowledge one reaches the path on which hard karma is worn away, and stands in bliss
those given over to the five senses stand in a sea of suffering
clinging to pleasure destroys the very thing pleasure is sought for
killing and taking others' property lead to hell
a king who shapes the lot of both worlds for his subjects is as great as a god, and no other deity is greater
the wife who plots her husband's death is repaid in disease and hell
a hard deed brings its fruit in a new birth
one's deeds blind a person to the truth about the body, and neither wisdom nor learning protects against it
the pair of the enjoyment land end their life and rise to heaven

note: Verse 135 shows Yugi appearing to part the queen from the king, as planned in verse 129.
teaches: The plan formed in smiling thought is now set in motion after the king has taken a second bride, so Yugi's scheme and the king's new love run side by side.

note: The companion dares Civakan to win a girl who would refuse even Kama; in 908 Suramanjari had already excepted Civakan alone from her vow of self-containment.
teaches: The dare the companions think impossible was settled in advance by the girl herself, so the reader sees the conquest as a meeting she has already allowed and the hero's oath as courage spent on an open door.

note: The Siddhar says weeping and worship are useless because good and evil come as the lotus-born god wrote; the king says birth and death come from the fruit of one's own deeds.
teaches: The two give the same counsel against grief for opposite reasons: the Siddhar's outcome is written by a creator, the Cintamani's by the sufferer's own deeds, with no god in the account.

gains.a: the king's karma is seen as godless by contrast with a fate assigned by Brahma
gains.b: the Siddhar's fatalism is shown to have a rival ground in self-made deed that leaves worship equally useless

note: Both make the woman's shoulders the record of union and parting.
teaches: In the couplet the shoulders betray the parting to onlookers, while the epic woman questions her shoulders as witnesses of where he went, so the body that tells the secret becomes a confidant.

gains.a: the epic verse gains the convention that the shoulders bear the sign of union and parting, which explains why she turns to them
gains.b: the couplet gains a reason the shoulders should know: he painted them, and they are asked rather than read

note: Kemasari's birth reckoning names her husband by a sign; Kanakamalai's names him as a master of the bow.
teaches: Held together they show the Cintamani's pattern of licensing each marriage by a birth horoscope, so the hero's many brides are presented as fate fulfilled rather than conquest.

note: 1635 has the women sing the king's fame; 1659 begins a pounding song whose next verses list his deeds.
teaches: The fame the women only named earlier is now given its content, war and love together, in the song.

note: The hunters claim the forest as their deep water where even the strong will fall; in 453 Civakan alone destroys six thousand of them there.
teaches: The maxim of one's own ground is turned against the very people who invoked it, so the story shows it fails when the opponent is misjudged.

note: Verse 304 says the kings paid tribute in fear of his anger; verse 305 says that since the girl was born he has stopped taking it.
teaches: The same overlord appears first as one who is paid in fear and then as one who waives his due, so the girl's birth is given as a political turning and the courting rests on that change.

note: The narrator says the king did not inquire because it was the hour of karma's fruit (தேரான் ஆகி); Kannaki calls him the king who did not inquire (தேரா மன்னா).
teaches: The same failure to inquire is excused by karma in the narrator's voice and charged as guilt in Kannaki's, and she herself also names karma, so the epic holds both causes together rather than choosing one.

note: Bhavachutan says that he saw a fault and will speak though the other has praised; Kural 638 says the one at the king's side must speak what is good even if the king is ignorant.
teaches: The couplet binds a minister to speak against a king's folly, and the scene shows the harder case where he speaks against a fellow minister's persuasive counsel.

gains.a: The minister's refusal to join the praise gets a stated rule, so his dissent reads as a duty and not as rivalry.
gains.b: The rule meets a case in which the one to be corrected is a colleague already trusted by the king, not the king himself.

note: The Purananuru poet asks whether the Pandya's spear did not stop short of ruin when it saw women made widows beat their breasts and shear their hair; the Cintamani names the widows' lost adornment as what the hero's spear will bring.
teaches: In the Sangam poem the sight of widows is what checks the spear, while in the epic the widows are counted in advance as the spear's work, so the pair shows grief for the enemy's women moving from a limit on war to its foreseen price.

gains.a: an older measure of a just warrior, who stops at the widows' grief, against which its raging spear is judged
gains.b: a later story where the same grief is foreseen and does not stop the fighting, which sharpens how rare its king's restraint was

note: Kural 902 says shame follows the man whose desire for his woman makes him careless of other things; 67 has two wives bind a king so that he lets the work of ruling go.
teaches: The couplet speaks for any man and the verse shows the cost to a king, whose neglected work is the world's guarding, so the stakes are larger than shame.

gains.a: The verse gains a verdict on a king set aside by love, which the narrator does not give.
gains.b: The couplet gains a ruler whose lapse touches a whole realm, which widens its cost beyond personal shame.

note: The brahmins' blessing on the dead king is answered by the eaten animal's recognition of its own son and city.
teaches: The pair shows the rite's claim failing in its own scene: the one blessed is the one eaten, and he knows it in 197.

note: The astrologer's verdict that the maiden's life lies on the earth is what the king turned into his parting saying that daughters, like a conch's pearls, profit those on the earth.
teaches: The king's consoling maxim at the parting rests on the astrologer's prophecy told only now, so his resignation is obedience to a foretold fate as well as a father's wisdom.

note: Verse 359 puts the question of the yazh-voiced girl's fate to the council, and verse 382 has the astrologer turn to the girl's matter.
teaches: The council's question is carried from counsel to omen-reading across the chapter, so a royal question is settled by two kinds of experts in turn.

note: Kural 796 calls ruin a rod that measures one's people; Nanmanikkadigai says the use of kin is known by being ruined, after the washing of gems, riding of horses and burning of gold.
teaches: Together they show ruin as an assay: the couplet names its single benefit, and the verse sets it in the craftsman's sequence of tests, where the tester pays the cost.

note: Parimelazhagar uses Indra to illustrate both verses: 25 for the failure that shows the ascetic's power, and 144 for greatness lost through another's wife.
teaches: This is one story serving two chapters in the commentary, though neither verse tells it.

note: The patikam (14) tells how Civakan overcame the victorious elephant that frightened Gunamalai; in 1076 that same elephant, ashamed, refuses its food.
teaches: The victory the patikam lists as a rescue becomes, through the beast's shame and the mahout's report, the usurper's pretext for seizing the hero, so a deed of protection ripens into danger.

note: 1866 makes the Lord the foe of deluding deeds and rewards the festival's onlooker with the world of merit; Kural 5 says both kinds of deed do not cling to those who praise the Lord.
teaches: The epic ends in merit's world, a reward the couplet's two-fold deeds would also refuse to cling to, so the pair shows two ways of reading what freedom from deeds amounts to.

gains.a: The promise of a world of merit gains the couplet's reminder that good deeds too are bonds to be shed.
gains.b: The couplet gains a public act, the royal festival, through which a community pays the Lord's praise.

note: Both poems bring in the dark-handed smith (கருங்கைக் கொல்லன்): in 170 the anvil that takes his hammer is the chief facing his foes; in 180 the poor chief asks his town's smith to forge a spear to feed the bards.
teaches: The smith's forge stands in both poems for the link between fighting and giving: 170 makes the chief the anvil that wears out his enemies, and 180 shows the spear made there as the source of the bards' meal.

note: 1355 warns that fleeing warriors will be shunned by women; Purananuru 278 shows a mother who swears to cut off the breast that fed a son she thinks has fled.
teaches: The shame of flight is placed in the women's mouths in both, but the epic's speaker uses it to threaten, while the Sangam mother tests the rumour before she acts.

gains.a: The verse gains a case where the shame of flight is acted on by a woman with a sword, not left as a threat.
gains.b: The poem gains a speaker who turns the same dread of women's contempt into a rebuke before battle, not after it.

note: The couplet's man says he never knew Death and knows it now in a woman's eyes; the onlookers tell the suitors that her girdle and breasts are Death and bid them flee, 'we have told you'.
teaches: Read with the couplet, the onlookers' warning puts the suitors in the state the Kural's man has left behind, knowing Death only by report, and shows that being told does not save anyone, since the crowd stays.

gains.a: the warning gains its irony from the couplet's contrast between Death heard of and Death met
gains.b: the couplet's private discovery gains a public scene in which the same knowledge is offered as advice and goes unheeded

note: 1175 has the minister Arimanju ask the angry king what he now thinks; Kural 445 says a king must take counsel as the counsellors are his eyes.
teaches: The minister's question is the counsel the Kural asks of a king, asked after the king has already raged.

gains.a: The minister's question is put to a king already set on war, which tests whether counsel can still act as the king's eyes.
gains.b: The Kural's counsellor as the king's eyes has no scene, and the epic gives a minister putting the first question.

note: Both use வரைவு for the courtesans: the epic says they sell beauty வரைவின்றி, the Kural calls such women வரைவிலா and their arms a mire for base men.
teaches: The same word that the Kural uses to condemn the courtesan becomes in the Jain epic an item in a city's praise, so the reader sees that a heaven-like city could include the trade the ethical book calls a hell.

gains.a: the epic's praise is shown to carry a word the ethical tradition had already loaded with blame
gains.b: the couplet's condemnation is set against a poem that celebrates the same openness as wealth and beauty

note: In Kuruntokai 333 the friend asks what harm there would be in revealing their secret; in the epic the girl discloses it to her friend, who carries it to the foster mother, then the mother, then the father.
teaches: The Sangam friend only proposes disclosure; the epic plays out the whole chain of telling through friend, foster mother and mother to the father, which ends in marriage the same day.

gains.a: the epic scene gains its name and purpose: it is the akam move of disclosing so that kin will arrange the marriage, not a confession
gains.b: the Sangam poem's single question gains the full sequence it sets going, showing who carries the secret and to whom

note: 1696 has the king give away all but his crown on seeing the letter; 1698 begins the message, which is a suitor's request for a bride.
teaches: The king pays for news before he knows what it asks, so the reward is for coming and not for what is said.

note: The elephant shaking off its foot-fetter may picture the king shedding the delusion the women offer.
teaches: If the elephant is read as the king's image, the same verse turns a rampage into a picture of release, which neither verse says plainly.

note: Kural 327 forbids taking another's life even to save one's own; 281 forbids the king to take his own life even to atone.
teaches: The couplet's rule against killing is shown to cover the doer's own life, which the couplet does not say.

gains.a: 281 gains a forceful general rule against taking life, with no exception for need.
gains.b: Kural 327 gains the opposite case, where the life endangered is one's own, to be spared in atonement.

note: The one sent to break another woman's firmness is overcome by desire herself.
teaches: The plan to ruin Madanamanjikai's steadfastness reverses: the agent of the attack is the one who loses control, which turns the test of one woman into the downfall of another.

note: At Gandharvadattai's contest his song shamed Kama (அனங்கன் நாண, 729); here his song makes him seem none other than the god of spring himself.
teaches: The music that won one bride openly, before kings, is now used covertly to win another, and the comparison moves from surpassing the god of love to being taken for him, as the singer's aim shifts from victory to seduction.

note: Kural 691 tells those who serve kings to keep to them as men warming at a fire, neither near nor far; 250 says the king's fire burns those who touch it along with their kin and can be nectar or poison.
teaches: The Kural's fire is a rule of prudent distance for courtiers, while Dharmadattan extends it to the minister who would seize the fire, and to his whole family.

gains.a: the councillor's threat is grounded in a known maxim of service
gains.b: the couplet's image is carried from caution in service to the fate of a servant who turns on his king

note: 1559 shows a king with the homage of three realms taking pleasure like Kama; Naladiyar 60 says the higher ones see the pain in pleasure and do not cling.
teaches: The poem offers pleasure at its largest scale, and the quatrain asks whether one who has all of it is looking at its pain.

gains.a: The scene gains a standard by which a lord in his harem is judged without the poet having to judge him.
gains.b: The quatrain gains an extreme case of the pleasure it warns about, with gods and kings standing guard over it.

note: The Kural's picture is of binding a rutting elephant by means of an elephant; verse 40 builds an elephant of wood and hide, filled with ninety-six men, to take a king.
teaches: The ministers use the Kural's own method in a worse form, a false elephant with men inside and a king as the catch.

gains.a: a rule for the ruse: using one thing of its own kind to take another, here a false elephant to catch a king who tames real ones
gains.b: a case where the stand-in is a built shell with armed men inside and the quarry is a ruler, not a beast

note: Kural 1115 jokes that her waist will snap if she wears anicham with its stems; the spectators of 679 say the dancer avoids flowers lest her small waist break, and lament that sandal and pearls were hung on her.
teaches: The couplet's lover's joke is turned into a crowd's mock indignation at those who dressed the girl, so the hyperbole of the slender waist becomes a charge against the adorner.

gains.a: a known literary formula of the waist too slight for flowers, against which the crowd's outburst reads as conventional praise rather than real concern
gains.b: a public, theatrical setting in which the private lover's exaggeration is shouted by many and aimed at a culprit

note: Verse 402 says Tivittan will take the life and discus of Ashvagriva; 619 shows Acuvakanthan at his ease, unaware of heat or cool.
teaches: The telling that the rival's life will end is set against a scene of his ease, so the reader looks on his pleasure knowing its end.

note: The king says that without such counsellors there is no kingship; the couplet makes counsellors the king's eyes.
teaches: The couplet asks the king to choose counsellors after counsel, but the verse shows a king recognising the worth of a minister who had worked against him.

gains.a: the king's praise of Yugi gets a rule that counsellors are his eyes, which makes the praise a statement of need
gains.b: the couplet gets a case where the counsellor praised belongs to the other side and has beaten the praiser

note: Naladiyar 47 has the fool call a body of nine seeping openings 'broad-shouldered one, bangle-wearer' because skin dazzles his eyes; Soolamani 987 has Prajapati marvel that the Maker gathered all beauty into one girl.
teaches: The same dazzled look at a woman is a fool's error in the Naladiyar and a bride's honour in the epic, so the epic's praise stands on a view of the body the Jain text refuses.

gains.a: The verse lacks the view of the body as flesh that the epic's praise leaves out.
gains.b: The quatrain lacks a case where the praise of a woman's beauty is made by a worldly king and so shows what it attacks.

note: Verse 252 says failed counsel turns on the king like an angry snake whose charmer's art has failed; Kural 448 says a king with none to rebuke him perishes even without a foe.
teaches: The epic shows a king with counsellors destroyed by counsel gone wrong, where the couplet shows a king destroyed by having no counsellor who dares to rebuke him.

gains.a: A king who had counsellors and still fell: counsel itself can fail.
gains.b: A picture of how the king ruins himself: the instrument turns on the user.

note: The twins are born to Yasomathi after the cocks' death; the youth in chapter 4 says his sight of dharma came from knowing his own births.
teaches: Read together, they let the reader see that the cocks of this chapter are the youth who is telling the story, an inference the poem does not state outright.

note: 1764's herald prays for the king's life, virtue and cool rain and harvest; Kural 545 says rain and harvest gather where the ruler wields his sceptre justly.
teaches: The herald's prayer asks for the rain and crops that the Kural says come as a fruit of just rule, so the blessing doubles as a claim on the king.

gains.a: The herald's list of blessings gains a rule: rain and crops are the sign that the king's sceptre is just.
gains.b: The couplet gains a ceremony in which this wish is spoken aloud as the king's reign is made public.

note: Both say the woman who causes the lover's sickness is its only cure.
teaches: The Kural states the paradox as a lover's hope, but the epic puts it after the union and makes the remedy bodily, the sandal on her breasts, so the cure is something already taken.

gains.a: the epic verse gains the couplet's paradox of cause and cure, which shows its compliment is a set argument of love and not a stray conceit
gains.b: the couplet gains a time and a body: the cure it promises is shown applied, after the meeting rather than before it

note: Tirumanthiram 140 says the five senses come under one's control of themselves once one has met the Lord; verse 624 says a king who has conquered himself is hard for others to conquer.
teaches: The epic gives self-conquest as a ruler's own work with a public reward; the Saiva stanza makes it follow from meeting the Lord.

gains.a: The verse lacks any account of how self-conquest comes about, since it names only its fruit.
gains.b: The stanza lacks a worldly payoff for the mastery it describes, which the verse gives in an unconquerable realm.

note: In 2622 Vijayai says that all who are born are greedy, never give a handful, and should give their wealth away; in 2829 the sage promises to tell what gifts to the worthy yield.
teaches: The mother's plea to give and the sage's account of what giving earns are two halves of one argument, one urging, one promising.

claims.gist: secret dealings in love do not befit him
the goddess is rightly worshipped by killing living pairs, with humans the greatest offering
the soul is by nature other than the body
through evil deeds the soul is bound and wanders through the four states of birth
the soul is known by those who hold right faith, knowledge and conduct
the objects of knowledge fall into groups of five, six and nine
household love and desire bring many sufferings with their ties
in danger, trust no one with a secret
a secret must not be spoken to fools or to women
the body is a hut of bone, sinew, blood, flesh, skin and hair with nine openings, built so as to delude
such a prize is won by the greatness of austerity that has ripened from the past, not by desire and skill at arms
the body is foul within and beauty is only an outer cover
those who take refuge with the victors win victory
a mother's own past deeds account for the wretched birth of her child
even the life the heavens know is as unreal as magic
a warrior welcomes the enemy's attack because it gives the fight he wants
meditation is of four kinds, two leading to ill and two to heaven and release
a fast unto death taken in the sage's presence is the proper close of a householder's life
a mother's misfortune comes from her own lack of good deeds
effort by a resolute man can bring great wealth in a single day
there is nothing that does not yield to effort
a gentle gait is the beauty of womanhood, and a woman who walks roughly will lose her husband
praise of the god keeps off the fearsome enemy of deeds
the Jina knows the whole world and his way has no equal

note: Kural 32 says there is no ruin greater than forgetting virtue; verse 86 says the cause: pride of wealth turns the prince to forget it.
teaches: The Kural names forgetting as the worst loss but not its cause, and the epic gives it as the pride of wealth.

gains.a: The verse's forgetting of dharma gets named as the ruin greater than any other.
gains.b: The couplet's forgetting gets a cause, the swelling pride of wealth in a young king.

note: 2861 has the swan chicks hide in the lotus and the prince find them; 2867 has the king speak of the pains of parting from kin.
teaches: The play with the chicks is read back as an act of parting kin, so a pleasure-scene becomes a moral one.
