note: The king wins the love-god's war in play, with garlands and streams; Naladiyar 17 says youth drops like fruit and the woman desired for her spear-like eyes will walk with a staff.
teaches: The epic's delight at its brightest is the thing the quatrain tells the hearer not to desire, so the water-sport is set to be read against the old age it will bring.

gains.a: The verse's triumph over the love-god gains a time limit: the women who yield are those who will one day lean on staffs.
gains.b: The quatrain's warning gains a concrete scene of the pleasure it warns against, with garlands, powder and a king at play.

note: 2964 and 1104 both show women beating and weeping at the going of Civakan, once into prison and now into renunciation.
teaches: The same hero's leaving is wept over twice, first as a captive and then as one who goes freely.

note: Kural 544 says the world holds to the feet of the great king who embraces his people; verse 266 says no one has anything better than the shade of such a king's feet.
teaches: The Kural makes the king's embrace of his people the condition of the world's clinging to his feet, and the epic gives the reason: they cling because men are wounding one another.

gains.a: A cause for the clinging, which is men's mutual harm, where the couplet gives only the condition.
gains.b: A negative picture of what the world is like without the king's feet, which the couplet only implies.

note: In 704 the envoys carry Acuvakandan's word that the little one cannot kill the lion if he knows his strength; in 1141 he says men's strength is only fear's exaggeration.
teaches: The king's contempt for the prince is stated twice, once before the lion's death and once after, and the death in between has not moved it.

note: The sage promised the silver mountain's realms under his feet; here the Vidyadhara lords are brought under them.
teaches: The promise of the sage's earlier words is kept in the same terms, which marks the conquest as foretold, not chance.

note: 1600 has the jester shown his own acts in his shadow, which does what he does; Kural 208 compares the ruin that follows evil deeds to a shadow that stays at the foot.
teaches: The shadow that is a comic false spirit here is the same thing the Kural uses as a sign that a person's deeds follow them, so the pairing shows the image in two uses.

gains.a: The scene gains a moral dimension: the shadow that copies the jester is the image the Kural uses for a deed's consequence, and the king's order to see his acts in it points that way.
gains.b: The couplet gains a case in which the shadow is an object of comic fear, which shows how readily people fear what is only their own doing.

note: The prince stocks the city's feast for guests as each desires; Kural 81 says a household exists to tend guests.
teaches: The wedding feast is a state's display and a political courtesy, which shows a limit of the couplet's household hospitality that needs no such display.

gains.a: The verse lacks the moral reason that makes feasting a guest the very point of keeping wealth, which the couplet gives.
gains.b: The couplet lacks a case of hospitality scaled to a royal alliance, where the feast also announces rank and ties.

note: The spells the god gives in verse 16 are followed by the cure of a snakebite in verse 18, given only as a word of comfort.
teaches: The patikam never says how Civakan cures the princess, but read after verse 16 the cure is the god's gift at work, so his first marriage is won by the rescue, not by his own arms.

note: The grandson king orders the crocodile killed, while his father at 139 would not take one life even to save his own.
teaches: The son does the very thing the father's last words forbade, which shows how a vow dies when its meaning is not handed down.

note: Verse 7 defines the four kinds of எச்சில்; verse 8 says what they bar and what keeping them yields.
teaches: The pair shows the book's method: a definition followed by its prohibitions and a reward in learning, so purity rules are presented as a discipline of the scholar.

note: Siddhar 16 hopes to avoid being called a sinner and falling into the barren hell, by knowing the breath-thread; 2766 shows what that fall would be, the stake and the fire.
teaches: The Siddhar's wish to avoid hell gains a picture of what he flees, and the epic's picture of hell gets a way out the Siddhar names, knowledge of the breath rather than the Jain sermon's virtue.

gains.a: the verse's torture gains a different way to avoid it, by a yogic knowing, in place of conduct
gains.b: the Siddhar's hope gains a precise picture of the hell, so the escape is not a vague wish

note: Kural 445 calls counsellors the king's eyes, to be taken after counsel; verse 330 asks that the worthy suitor be examined and then Pavachchuthan's word settles it.
teaches: The epic shows counsel working as the Kural wants, by examining before choosing, but one man's word still carries the room.

gains.a: A standard that says who should do the examining and why his word is valued.
gains.b: A scene in which the eyes of the king are tested by a real choice and the room simply agrees.

note: Verse 205 has the king's daughter resolve on a vow and think how to finish it with greatness; verse 212 has her complete the vow of Chakravalam and then wish a great special worship.
teaches: The resolve at the sermon's end is kept here, and it grows into a second act, the worship, beyond the vow.

note: 444 calls greater people as support the chief of all strengths; 497 says no support is needed but fearlessness, if the thinking and place are right.
teaches: Five chapters later, the book seems to qualify its own superlative.

note: 402 foretells that the Kesava will take the discus and the life of Asvagriva; 1216 sets a divine word that this youth will win and reign.
teaches: The prophecy of the lord's word is echoed as a divine pledge at the moment of the first war-answer, so the battle is told as the keeping of an old promise.

note: In both the girl looks and bows her head; the Kural takes it as water poured into the bond, while here the bowed head with checked tears leaves the hero in pain.
teaches: The Kural fixes the bowed head as a sign of consent, but the Akananuru shows the same gesture as unreadable to the man at the moment it happens, so the maxim is a reading made after the fact.

note: 1108 has him climb the tall mansion with the maid; 1130 has him climb the cloud-high mansion again after the grove.
teaches: The two climbs enclose the grove as an interlude, so the chapter starts and ends on the mansion where the wedding night is held.

note: After the last battle he is called a Kama even to the wise as he sits like a lion in his silk; at the wedding bath he again becomes Kama to the women of fragrant hair.
teaches: The poet gives the hero the Kama figure in victory and again in his wedding dress, so the epic ties his beauty first to conquest and then to marriage.

note: The father decides to give Padumai to Civakan just after the two have united in secret in the grove.
teaches: The father's reasons, royal marks and a saved life, lead him to the marriage the secret union already requires, so the kalavu of the grove turns into wedlock without the lovers having to ask or confess.

note: 1099 has the hill-king give the bride with water before the fire as god; Naladiyar 56 says marriage is called கடி because it binds the husband even to a faulty wife.
teaches: The giving of the bride before the fire is the act that creates the hardship of binding which Naladiyar names, so the rite explains why the husband cannot put her away.

gains.a: The gift before the fire gains a consequence, the lasting duty it puts on the groom.
gains.b: The quatrain gains the actual rite of water and fire that makes the binding.

note: Naladiyar 60 says the higher ones look to the pain within each pleasure and do not cling; in 909 Gunamalai, after the game that cost her a friend, sees that play meant for joy became the cause of sorrow.
teaches: The quatrain's discipline of seeing pain inside pleasure appears in the epic first as a girl's tears over a garden game, an early lesson in a story that ends in renunciation.

gains.a: the ascetic frame in which Gunamalai's private grief reads as the first form of the insight that leads to thuravu
gains.b: a lived case where the pain in pleasure is not bodily or moral but a broken friendship, arising from a contest of beauty

note: After the king says no life may be taken, his mother offers a flour cock in the same breath.
teaches: Placing the loophole next to the refusal shows the poem is testing whether a made likeness of life counts as a life.

note: Boothappandiyan's vow wishes on himself, if he fails, separation from his wife, a weak sceptre and the loss of friends; Kattiyangaran's vow wishes on himself fear of his wife and the shame of slighting a guest.
teaches: Both are conditional self-curses whose penalties are drawn from household and court rather than the field, so the pair shows the vanjinam form keeping its structure into the epic while the epic gives it to the losing usurper, who dies at once.

gains.a: the speech is identified as a vanjinam of a known form, with its self-curse clauses
gains.b: the Sangam vow is seen in a story where it is not fulfilled, so the vow's force is shown as a matter of the speaker's cause

note: A king on his throne turns from rule at the sight of a vanishing cloud, as the quatrain's best of people see home, youth and wealth fail and renounce.
teaches: The quatrain gives renunciation as a conclusion of reasoning; the story shows the same turn as a sudden sight on a throne after the heir is crowned.

gains.a: the king's turn is shown as the reasoned choice of the best the quatrain names
gains.b: the quatrain's argument gets a figure who acts on it at the height of his splendour

note: Pleading with Gunamalai, Civakan asked whether a swan that delighted in the flowering Ganges would go near the white sand of a seep-well; here Padumai is a hen-swan left by a dry stony pool after her mate has quit the Ganges lotus bed.
teaches: The hero's own image of a constancy that never leaves the Ganges is turned against him: the swan does leave, and the one stranded at the poor water is the wife he swore by it to another.

note: The flour cock cries and falls under the sword, answering the king's fear that a likeness is like killing.
teaches: The king's disgust at a likeness of life in 144 is borne out by the cry at 146, which shows his instinct was sound against his mother's argument.

note: 1280 has victors decline to strike the blinker or shame the fled; Kural 775 calls a blink at a spear flight.
teaches: The epic shows the winners declining to treat a blink as flight, a gentler ending than the couplet's flat verdict.

gains.a: The epic's chivalry is measured against the couplet's strict rule that a blink is already defeat.
gains.b: The couplet's reflex of valour is shown with a winner's answer, mercy to the one who flinches, which it alone never gives.

note: Tirumanthiram 444 gives the eight qualities (குணம் எண்குணம்) to matted-haired Siva who keeps the world; 1469 has them seized from souls by the robber deeds.
teaches: On my reading of 1469, the two texts disagree about whose the eight qualities are: for Tirumular they are the attributes of a God who protects, for the Jain hymn they are the soul's own and are lost to karma, with no protector named who restores them.

gains.a: a Saiva rival that sharpens the hymn's claim that the qualities belong to the soul
gains.b: a Jain counter-reading in which the eight qualities are not a divine possession but a human one under siege

note: Gunamalai draws a circle in the sand asking that the union come about without fail; the parrot then lands and she hears the message of his pledge.
teaches: The divination is answered not by the circle closing but by the messenger's arrival, so the story replaces the omen with news and lets the girl's private rite be fulfilled by the man's written word.

note: In Purananuru 101 Avvai tells her heart that whether Athiyaman's gift is delayed or not it is sure, since he greets her on the hundredth visit as on the first; the Innaa line counts a poet held back by the giver as painful.
teaches: The poem shows the pain the Innaa line names and how it is borne: a patron's constant welcome makes the delay of the poet's send-off endurable.

note: In 1327 Civakan settles that Padumai is no goddess by three marks (her garland fades, her eyes blink, her feet touch the ground); in 1473 he asks whether Kemasari is a goddess or a daughter and does not settle it.
teaches: The hero who coolly tested a woman's humanity by signs in one ilampakam is in the next too struck to test, which shows the epic varying the same first-sight doubt from a clear-headed proof to helpless wonder.

note: The king spares the woman and the man, but for reasons of sex and rank, not because life is dear.
teaches: The couplet bars killing even to save one's own life without exception; the king's reasons here are narrower, and only at 139 does he come to the couplet's rule.

gains.a: The story shows how an unprincipled restraint falls short of the rule it is made to meet.
gains.b: The couplet's absolute rule is tested against a husband's provoked rage, which it does not itself mention.

note: In 723 the prince seizes the lion by its fangs and tears it to strips; in 1143 Arikethu, who was set to play the lion at 697, marvels at that tearing.
teaches: The one man in the rival court who has played the lion's part is the first to admire the youth who killed the real one.

note: Kural 126 praises drawing in the five senses like a tortoise; the verse lists holding the five senses as one item of a numbered discipline.
teaches: The couplet states restraint as a single act with a reward over seven births, and the verse sets it as one part of a long catalogue, so restraint becomes one limb of a trained life.

gains.a: the catalogue gets a single plain image and a reward for restraint, which a bare list of numbers does not give
gains.b: the couplet gets the full scheme in which restraint is one of many practices, not a stand-alone virtue

note: 2875 warns that those who cage birds will be parted from their kin; in 2880 the prince who heard the dharma sets the captured cygnet free in the pool.
teaches: The warning and the release show a sermon changing a deed within a few verses, which a rule on its own does not.

note: The 'dead companions' Dharan promises to return meet the merchant alive and laugh that what they suffered at sea was a play (நாடகம்).
teaches: The impossible promise to raise the dead is kept only because the deaths were staged, which turns the earlier lament for lost friends into an audience's grief.

note: The king reads Vijayai's dream of the shoot and crown as her son's rising fortune; at the ghee-anointing the women now bless him to be lord of the wheel and to abide with Fortune.
teaches: The fortune that the king foretold from the dream is voiced as a blessing in the rite, so the reader sees the prophecy being fulfilled step by step.

note: The Cintamani calls the Jina the lord of faultless kevala; Tirumular calls kevala the soul's sleep of utter stupor under anava, from which karma drives it out.
teaches: The same word for the soul's state 'alone' is the summit of release for the Jain poet and the lowest darkness of the bound soul for the Saiva, so the two traditions disagree on whether the soul left to itself is free or blind.

gains.a: a sense of how pointed its epithet is: kevala names perfection only in a doctrine where the soul alone, freed of karma, is omniscient
gains.b: a rival use of its technical term, showing that its claim that the solitary soul is in darkness answers a school that called that solitude release

note: Naladiyar 21 says kings under umbrellas were carried off and called dead; in 78 the king leaves the throne alive and by his own act.
teaches: The same fall of royal pomp appears as chosen renunciation rather than death, showing impermanence can be met before it arrives.

gains.a: The king's retreat gains the Naladiyar's reason for giving up rank, impermanence, which the verse leaves unspoken.
gains.b: The quatrain gains a king who acts on its warning instead of only being its example.

note: In 325 the merchant leaves his own dead son at the burning ground and goes off with the royal child; 1124 recalls that Sunandai had borne many children who died before the ascetic came.
teaches: The exchange at the burning ground was the last of a run of dead births, so the merchant's taking of the child answers a grief long prepared for, not a chance find.

note: In Kural 1214 the woman finds pleasure in dreams because they bring the man who gives no grace when she is awake (நல்காரை); the women of 466 ask Civakan to grace them (அருளி) by coming in a dream tomorrow.
teaches: The Kural's dream comforts a woman for a lover who once was hers and now withholds himself, but the Cintamani's crowd asks the dream for a man they have only seen pass, so the convention turns from consolation for loss into the only union a stranger can hope for.

gains.a: the crowd's prayer is shown to draw on the akam convention that the dream does what the absent man will not
gains.b: the couplet's dream-remedy is shown stretching beyond separation to love that never had a meeting, which the couplet's situation does not cover

claims.gist: the ascetic's marks of matted hair, garb and skull bowl do not bring release but sow further birth
a warrior owes his lord loyalty until death
one who is without fault should not be met with harsh anger
a boast that is not made good shames the one who made it
conch and discus lines on the palm show a man who will wield the discus
gain and loss befall everyone, even the god who bears the bird banner
those who eat flesh fatten a body that will only feed vultures
Fortune is a woman common to all, unlike a wife of good family who belongs to one man
birth in a human land does not make one fit for the three classes of people
those who weigh place and time and plan without folly can achieve anything, even the weak against the many
winning the queen's heart is the fruit of earlier merit, greater than the fruit of renowned austerity
ages turn so that a land rises and falls in them
strength that leaps without judgment is caught, as the roaring lion falls into the hunters' net
the highest meditation, the pure white meditation (sukla dhyana), destroys the last of the binding karmas
true giving is giving gladly to renouncers who have conquered the senses
right conduct is abstaining from honey, toddy and meat, because hosts of living beings dwell in them
the Vidyadhara king descends from Kacchan and shares an old kinship with the Podanam line
Tivittan will guard the whole world under a single umbrella
a king who sends a captive taken by deceit before a raging elephant earns great blame
the lasting blame left by the usurper's crime ended with his death and his line's
gifts are due only to brahmins learned in the Veda
a wife wants nothing other than what her husband wants, and his joy is her joy
death comes when one's allotted life-span is spent, and not before
the fruit of good deeds in former lives keeps the good alive even when they sink in the sea
worship of the feet of the lord under three umbrellas is repaid by rule of heaven and then of earth
the Jina is the giver of the first Veda and knower of the way of justice
attachment binds beings in the harmful sea of births

note: 1050 shows birds without mates as fire to the separated; 1061 shows paired birds sheltering mates and young as they sleep.
teaches: The birds that stand for separation in the friends' talk stand for union in the poet's closing picture, which gives the night a second reading.

note: The patikam compares Civakan's younger brother, desolate, to a star that has lost the moon (மதியம் கெடுத்த வய மீன்); 1215 gives the same image (வெண்மதி யிழந்த மீன்போல்) to all his friends.
teaches: The stars-without-the-moon figure belongs to the hero's whole circle rather than to one kinsman, so Civakan is the moon to every follower and his absence dims them all alike, brother and friends.

note: Kural 392 says numbers and letters, learning, are the eyes of living beings; verse 268 names three eyes, the king, learning and the sun.
teaches: The Kural calls learning the only eye of life, and the epic puts learning beside the king and the sun, so what learning sees is made one of three lights the world needs.

gains.a: A rival that sees where learning cannot, the king, the sun's equal in lifting the world's darkness.
gains.b: A list that puts learning's eyes among the world's lights and not only life's.

note: Civakan's hymn praises the Jina for teaching that a deed's fruit reaches its doer and no other; the Manimekalai names fierce vow-keepers who hold that a deed reaches its doer even without intention, and tells of a seat built to answer them.
teaches: Seen from the Buddhist epic, the doctrine the Cintamani's hymn takes for granted has a disputed edge, whether a deed done without intention still binds, which the Jain hymn never raises.

note: In 359 she watches the road for news of her son; in 1785 she still sits thinking of his lot when the news walks in.
teaches: The waiting begun in 359 is answered not by her messenger but by strangers who stumble on her, so the news she longed for comes unsought and unrecognised.

note: Verse 9 has Saccandan, steeped in desire, not hear counsel (சொல்லாறு கேளான்) and lose his throne; verse 27 has his son hear the dharma (அறம் கேட்டு) and give his throne up.
teaches: The patikam opens on a king ruined because he would not listen and closes on his son freed because he did, so hearing becomes the hinge between losing a kingdom and leaving one.

note: The Kural calls those free of craving the freed (அற்றவர்); the epic has Accanandi cut desire's root and then perform austerities before he leaves the body.
teaches: Set beside the couplet, the verse separates what the Kural joins: being free of craving comes first, but release from the body comes only after austerity at the Jina's feet.

gains.a: the epic's sequence gains the Kural's claim that ending craving is the decisive freedom, which explains why it stands first
gains.b: the couplet's freedom gains a narrative that spells out what still remains after craving goes: penance and the body's end

note: The killing of the beaten king in 182 is followed in 183 by the order to stop the war.
teaches: The order to stop comes only after the enemy king is dead, so the killing ends the war and not the king's mercy.

note: 952 has fire burn away iron's nature and turn it to gold, with Civakan as the fire; 960 repeats the forge, adds mercury piercing the iron, and uses it to answer the doubt that a dog could become a god.
teaches: The image moves from praising the friend as the cause of the change to defending the change itself as lawful, so the narrator relies on one figure first for gratitude and then for doctrine.

note: In both epics a god gives a hero a spell to call on, and a later need brings him.
teaches: Both Jain epics let a god leave a gift of spells that later serves the hero, so the helping god is a recurring structure of the genre.

note: Both open with யாயாகியளே and both have the friend tell how the wife hides her husband's cruelty (கொடுமை) out of shame; in 9 she wilts like an unworn flower, in 10 she comes as leader of the festival yet ashamed.
teaches: Placed together the two poets show the wife's concealment as a set karpu situation with two costs: it wastes her body in private and shames her in public, and in each case it is the friend, not the wife, who breaks the silence.

note: The patikam says that his younger brother, friends and richly adorned wives all renounce the things of sense; 2640 shows the new nuns studying the Anga books and shining as tilaka of the order.
teaches: What the patikam announced as a bare fact is shown here as a life of learning and equanimity.

note: Kural 265 says tavam is striven for because what is wanted comes as wanted; in 829 the crowd sees the hero's wedding wealth as the fruit of his tavam and wishes it would come to them.
teaches: The onlookers accept the couplet's premise that tavam yields what one wants, yet only wish for its fruit instead of doing it, which is the very shortcut the couplet rules out.

gains.a: the crowd's wish is shown to rest on the doctrine that good fortune is the wages of penance
gains.b: the couplet gains its counter-case: people who believe its promise and still do not strive

note: The sage foretold that when the graceless king seized Civakan to kill him a yaksha would carry him off; in 1158 a god lifts Civakan and rises away in the storm while the city mourns.
teaches: The rescue the friends are plotting by fire and disguise was already promised to the parents, so the plan of the companions is made needless by a fate a Jain ascetic had foreseen.

note: 1730 gives the dream of a gem as the sign that the child is coming; Tirumanthiram 453 says the Lord, at the moment of the joining, fixes the span and the earthly life of the child.
teaches: The epic reads the conception from omens and the mother's body, while the Tirumanthiram says the life was fixed by the Lord at the joining, so a sign is read against a cause.

gains.a: The gem-dream gains a view in which the child's fate is already fixed, before the sign comes.
gains.b: The verse of Tirumular gains a conception told as a royal dream, a case where signs are read as promises.

note: Both have the bangles slip as the sign of the man's leaving, and both use the verb துற for his going.
teaches: Where the Kural's bangles announce that he has left, the epic's refrain makes the bangles leave as he left, so the body imitates the desertion it reports.

gains.a: The epic princess's song is placed in the Kural's grammar of separation, showing the convention it is varying.
gains.b: The couplet's single image is unfolded into a three-stanza refrain that links his former tenderness to the bangles' going.

note: Manimekalai shows the prince an old woman's body and says flowers, sandal, cloth and jewels hide its flesh; the Neelakesi's sage tells the adorned woman herself that her bath, scents, jewels and garlands only cover filth with skin.
teaches: The Buddhist and Jain epics use one argument with the roles reversed: in the Manimekalai a woman ascetic cures a man's lust, in the Neelakesi a male ascetic rebuffs a woman's, and here the body he unmasks is itself a borrowed disguise.

note: 528 tells a king not to look at all alike but by rank; 541 says to show no favour to anyone.
teaches: Household management and the court of justice have different requirements, though they are only two chapters apart.

note: 1904 says the Lord cut off the dark garlands of fierce deeds; Kural 5 says the two deeds born of darkness do not cling to those devoted to the Lord's true praise.
teaches: The Lord is shown in 1904 as the one who has already done what the couplet promises his devotees, so the cause of their freedom is his own freeing.

gains.a: The hymn gains a stated result for the praiser, that the two kinds of deeds will not cling to him.
gains.b: The couplet gains a named doer who has cut his own deeds, which it leaves unsaid.

note: In 334 Vijayai heard her son's future greatness foretold; in 1796 his first deeds are recited to her by one who does not know she is his mother.
teaches: The prophecy she took on faith returns to her as report of deeds done, and the irony that the reciter does not know his listener lets the mother hear her son's fame as a stranger would.

note: Kural 676 says to act only after weighing the finish, the hindrance and the yield; verse 829 has the king consult his kin and then press on with the wedding.
teaches: A king's deliberation can be a formality over a choice already made by the deed of the suitor.

gains.a: The verse lacks any test of the plan's hindrances, since the lion's death has already decided the match.
gains.b: The couplet lacks a case where counsel follows a settled choice instead of shaping it.

note: Verse 108 foretells that a man good at speaking will come down with a letter into the garden Pushpakarandam; here the letter is read in the king's hall.
teaches: The astrologer's forecast of a letter is now met by its words, which turn out to be the offer of a bride that the dream was read to promise.

note: The prince wins a princess by defeating her at the vina; in the Cintamani the girl goes out to break her opponents with the yaazh.
teaches: Both epics make the vina contest the means by which a king's son wins his bride, so the motif is a standard marriage test rather than one poet's invention.

note: 1743 has Tivittan give his five-year-old son to teachers 'rich in unfailing learning'; Kural 67 says a father's good to his son is to put him first in the assembly.
teaches: The Kural names the goal of a father's care, the seat in the assembly; the epic shows the first step toward it, early schooling in the hands of learned men.

gains.a: The prince's schooling gains a stated purpose, that the father's good lies in the son's standing among the learned, not his wealth.
gains.b: The couplet gains a concrete first step, a royal father handing a child of five to teachers, which the couplet does not name.

note: 1982 refuses the name 'people' to those without discernment; 1984 adds the eunuch, the blind and woman's birth to those not counted as fully human.
teaches: The speaker's two tests of being human are discernment and the kind of birth, and the second does not follow from the first.

note: The Kural calls it the world's 'greatness' that one here yesterday is gone today; 356 gives that greatness a place, the burning ground that has seen everyone's back.
teaches: The Kural's bitter abstraction becomes a physical place in the Purananuru, and the ground that outlives all men is the 'greatness' the couplet names without showing.

note: Gandharvadattai's promise to bring him to his lord's feet is kept when the chapter opens with him lying at Civakan's feet.
teaches: Read after 1747, the opening tableau of the brother at the feet is the exact fulfilment of a Vidyadhara's spoken promise, so the reunion the narrator showed first was her doing.

note: 447 has the priest foretell the slab; 441 has the keeper offer it as a seat made for the man.
teaches: The offer in 441 is the fulfilment of the foretelling in 447, so the keeper is shown acting from a prophecy and not on his own.

note: 1204 puts the ultimatum; 1205 shows the prince's heart catching fire at it.
teaches: The envoy's two options provoke an anger the verse shows as fire, so the ultimatum cannot be accepted.

note: Kattiyankaran tells the suitors that only Kama could win the princess; ten verses later the poet calls Civakan, adorning the dancer, அனங்கன் அன்னான், one like Kama.
teaches: The usurper's boast that no Kama is present is refuted by the man he wants dead, so his taunt unknowingly names his rival.

note: 1380 condemns a fleeing swordsman; Purananuru 278 gives a mother's vow to cut her breast when told her son fled.
teaches: The Sangam poem shows what the epic's taunt costs the one who runs: the family's shame, not only his own.

gains.a: The taunt gains a household that would mourn and punish the runaway.
gains.b: The Sangam poem gains a Jain-epic scene where the same charge of fleeing is thrown at kings in the middle of a battle.

note: The women dress, steam and garland themselves after the play; Naladiyar 16 likens the joy of youth to a lamb nibbling at the garland held out before the slaughter.
teaches: The same garland that is the sign of pleasure in the Cintamani is the bait of the sacrifice in the quatrain, and the reader sees both uses of one object.

gains.a: The garland-wearing at the end of the sport gains a darker reading, in which the adornment is what precedes the loss.
gains.b: The quatrain's lamb and garland gain a courtly setting where the garland is a gift of love and not a rite.

note: The verse thickens a pool with the washed paste and saffron of women's bodies; Naladiyar 48 mocks those who praise sandal paste and garlands without knowing what the body is.
teaches: The epic's picture of the bath as pure delight is set against a Jain verse on the same bodies as flesh for vultures.

gains.a: A Jain corrective the poet never voices, so the bath scene stands as one the tradition itself would look past.
gains.b: A scene of the very perfumed bodies the quatrain mocks, shown as the epic's own delight.

note: 2326 had the victor bathed as for anointing with the blood of crowned kings, joined to the Earth goddess; now, riding Culamani, he treads on the crowns of kings.
teaches: The anointing promised in the battle's aftermath is fulfilled in the procession, where the defeated and allied kings' crowns are laid beneath the hero as a public sign of his rule.

note: Kannaki's dream of trouble in Madurai, told to Kovalan before he leaves, and the astrologer's dream of an elephant garlanding the young lord are both dreams that foretell what is to come.
teaches: In the Silappathikaram the dream is a warning that cannot turn the course of fate, while here it is a promise that the court at once turns into a plan, so one image serves ruin in one epic and fortune in the other.

note: The deity foretells that one will come right now to take the child and bids the queen hide; in 322 Kantukkatan reaches the child lying in the burning ground.
teaches: The prophecy and the command to hide make the mother's absence in 322 an arranged handing-over, not a desertion, which the finding scene alone would not show.

note: The women's show of desire comes as the vow of verse 304 begins.
teaches: A vow is tested at once by the thing it gives up, so the renunciation is shown to cost the king something.

note: Both are a man describing the girl's averted gaze: when he looks she looks down.
teaches: The couplet catches the girl's averted look in the present as a sign of love, and the epic hero recalls the same look from the past while parted from her, so the gesture that once told him she loved him is what memory hands back in separation.

gains.a: the epic verse gains the couplet's reading of the downcast look as a sign of love, not coldness, which is why Civakan treasures it
gains.b: the couplet gains a later moment, in which the shy look survives as a memory and returns unbidden to a husband far away

note: Kural 333 tells the possessor of wealth to do at once what stays because wealth does not; 2983 adds that Fortune stays with the one who is not attached and never clings to the one who is.
teaches: The Kural treats wealth's going as a fact to act on, while the epic makes clinging the cause of its going, so a reader sees what each assumes about why wealth leaves.

gains.a: the verse's claim about Fortune and attachment gets the plainer rule that wealth by nature does not stay
gains.b: the Kural's rule gets a reason for the going: wealth is lost through the very clinging that tries to keep it

note: Soolamani 107 has the astrologer read a dream as a Vidyadhara king coming to praise the lord and give a daughter; here he arrives at Podanam and says he has come gladly to give her.
teaches: The reading of the dream is kept in the king's own gladness, so the prophecy is borne out as willing consent and not only as outcome.

note: In 393 the teacher asks as his fee that Civakan bear no anger against the usurper for a year, and he agrees; in 1090, recalling his teacher's word, he lets his arms be bound with his anger quenched.
teaches: The vow made in private as a teacher's fee is what actually disarms the hero before the king's men, so the plot's turn depends on a kept promise rather than on the parents' prudence or the hero's weakness.

note: 1962 names the flesh-seller, the one who crushes and the hunter as the animal's killers; Neelakesi 104 names battle, the chase for food and the nets.
teaches: Both Jain tellings draw on one stock list of the animal's torments, so the list is a teaching form and not a poet's own picture.

note: 1297 shows Gunasenan roaming like a rutting elephant and tiger; 1304 opens on his falling.
teaches: The praise of Gunasenan's strength is cancelled by his own fall, which turns the new champion's boast into the next test.

a sin of neglecting one's elders comes back as suffering
the nectar of dharma from the teacher frees from the fever of rebirth
the span of a life is fixed at conception and ends when its time comes
penance ends in rebirth as a god
an astrologer can bring a coming event to pass at its fixed hour even when fate does not decree it
a man who fears his wife and turns from his guest is base
the clear-minded stay level to abuse, praise and neglect and are free of three delusions
once an effect has come about, hunting for its cause is not a task; the god of love gives his grace to whom he will
it is a warrior's duty to fight any enemy, god or man, without fear
One who gives himself to lust and neglects duty without fear of sin brings ruin on himself
worshippers of the Jina's feet lose themselves in joy and are glad
a king is credited with the virtues shown in his ministers' work
life lived in pleasure is a fawn grazing before the tiger springs
a great king should not march against lowly foes unless it is a war with demons
no one can know what will be
a warrior who falls or wins in battle gains either the earth or the world of the gods
it is better not to live than to live freed by one's wife's power
dharma yields wealth and enjoyment and must not be forgotten even in distress
a king should rule and hand on his kingdom to a son before renouncing
leaving all outer and inner attachment to enjoyment, with compassion for life, is the way of the ascetic
the land passed through three ages of effortless enjoyment before the patriarchs came
the teaching lords who have driven out the destroying karmas end the sorrows of souls by their word
however well a man's love binds a woman, her heart can still follow another
